title: `pull()` interprets subtraction between column names as subtraction between column positions
description:
Hi, 

This is a minor bug, but it could lead to potential errors.

I was trying to one-line pull a calculation with dplyr:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
mtcars |>
  head() |>
  pull(wt-drat)
#> [1] 21.0 21.0 22.8 21.4 18.7 18.1
```

<sup>Created on 2026-07-14 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>


In `mtcars`, `wt` is column 6 and `drat` is column 5, so `pull()` evaluates 6 - 5 and returns column 1 (`mpg`). 

This is surprising and potentially error-prone. Would it make sense to throw an informative error when `pull()` receives an arithmetic expression involving multiple columns?

title: Provide minimal flag when filter drops NAs on a != check
description:
So, I've been using dplyr's filter() for probably a decade or so now, and I just ran into an issue for the first time (that I know of!) where I ran a serious risk of "losing data" without knowing it. 

This scenario is similar to the one I ran into:
```
bugs = tibble::tibble(
  site = LETTERS[1:10],
  treated = c("yes", "yes", "no", "yes", "no", "no", "yes", NA, "no", NA),
  beetles = c(4, 6, 7, 3, 5, 8, 2, 10, 6, 9)
)

head(bugs)

bugs %>%
  filter(treated == "yes") %>%
  summarize(total = sum(beetles))

bugs %>%
  filter(treated != "yes") %>%
  summarize(total = sum(beetles))

bugs %>%
  summarize(total = sum(beetles))
```

In this code, the third total won't equal the sum of the first two totals because filter always excludes NAs, regardless of whether == or != is used. 

Now, this makes sense, in hindsight! It's also beautifully described in the function's documentation, which currently says this:

> Missing values
> Both filter() and filter_out() treat NA like FALSE. This results in the following behavior:
   > filter() drops both NA and FALSE.
   > filter_out() keeps both NA and FALSE. 
> This means that ⁠filter(data, <conditions>) + filter_out(data, <conditions>)⁠ captures every row within data exactly once.
> The NA handling of these functions has been designed to match your intent. When your intent is to keep rows, use filter(). When your intent is to drop rows, use filter_out().

This is great! And it would have been VERY helpful for me in figuring out what was happening...had I known to even look! See, my issue was that, at this point in time, I had not yet even realized that my data contained NAs. Beyond that, I was not aware of the fact that NA != "yes" would be NA, not FALSE, and thus filter() might not retain it. So I was doubly behind the eight ball, and it was only much later in the pipeline that I started to get suspicious that data had gone missing. 

I'm wondering: **Is there a way to have the function trigger a lightweight message whenever != is used to filter a variable containing NAs that draws attention to this issue (and to the filter_out() function, which was also totally new to me)?** The frequency of this messaging could be limited as much as might be desirable, but even if I had received it _once_, it might have saved me from pulling my hair out a few times today! 

If this is possible/reasonable, I could help to work on the fork/PR, if that'd be useful!

title: recode_values with regular expression? recode_values_regex?
description:
Hi, big fan. 

The ability to use the new recode_values() with an external lookup table (using from and to parameters) seems very valuable - somewhat similar to, but meaningfully different from a *_join() action. Lots of utility for deep table lookup assignments and getting hard values out of code.

Is there a way that I'm not seeing to use a lookup table of *regular expressions* to avoid a scenario of using case_when() or recode_values() with a long list of text lookups? 
```
... 
x |>str_detect("-insert long regex 1 here") ~ "item 1", 
x |>str_detect("-insert long regex 2 here") ~ "item 2", 
```

Might a recode_detected_values() or recode_values_regex() have wide utility in dplyr? It certainly would for many of my own use cases (epidemiologist, often dealing with complex ICD code definitions and text searching). But I'm stumped on a way to wrap recode_values() in an efficient way that implements regex. I was thinking of some map_*() action, maybe with reduce() to attempt to not inefficiently calculate every regex if an early assignment is found - acting similar to how case_when returns the earliest "hit." 

```
recode_values_regex = function(x, from_regex, to){
  # efficient magic
}
```

Thanks for considering / pointing the way.

title: When reusing argument names in `summarise()` to build a complex expression, the length of intermediate expressions is considered
description:
I am not sure if this is a bug or not, but it surprised me when I was implementing https://github.com/apache/sedona-db/pull/931 (SedonaDB/DataFusion dplyr backend). When exploiting the sequential evaluation feature of summarise, it seems all values are used (even intermediary calculations) when calculating the `reframe()`-ness of the operation.

``` r
library(dplyr)

df <- tibble(letter = c("a", "a", "b", "b"), x = c(1, 2, 3, 4))

# This is what I expected to happen
df |>
  group_by(letter) |>
  summarise(y = sum(x + 1), .groups = "drop")
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   letter     y
#>   <chr>  <dbl>
#> 1 a          5
#> 2 b          9

# Instead we get a reframe(), recycling to the length of all intermediate y
df |>
  group_by(letter) |>
  summarise(y = x + 1, y = sum(y + 1), .groups = "drop")
#> Warning: Returning more (or less) than 1 row per `summarise()` group was deprecated in
#> dplyr 1.1.0.
#> ℹ Please use `reframe()` instead.
#> ℹ When switching from `summarise()` to `reframe()`, remember that `reframe()`
#>   always returns an ungrouped data frame and adjust accordingly.
#> Call `lifecycle::last_lifecycle_warnings()` to see where this warning was
#> generated.
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   letter     y
#>   <chr>  <dbl>
#> 1 a          7
#> 2 a          7
#> 3 b         11
#> 4 b         11
```

title: Improve error message for trailing comma in `across()`
description:
Hi,

This is a rather minor issue, but I spent some time scratching my head over it, so I thought it could be worth reporting as a possible error-message improvement.

When leaving a trailing comma in `across()`, the resulting error mentions an unused `alist()` argument:

``` r
Sys.setenv(LANGUAGE="en")
library(dplyr)
mtcars %>%
  mutate(across(am, \(.x) .x+1, ))
#> Error in `mutate()`:
#> ℹ In argument: `across(am, function(.x) .x + 1, )`.
#> Caused by error in `across()`:
#> ! Can't compute column `am`.
#> Caused by error in `fn()`:
#> ! unused argument (alist())
```

<sup>Created on 2026-06-03 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

In this short example, the trailing comma is easy to spot. However, with a longer function, it is much less noticeable in the trace, and I found the `alist()` message very hard to link to the actual problem.

Maybe there is a way to catch it and rewrite it somehow?

Thanks!

title: feature: A proposed change to `group_modify` - with tidyselection and .by argument
description:
tidyverse users are used to the `.by`​ syntax with tidy name selection.
The current implementation of `group_modify`​ doesnt support that.

I am offering a fix that:
* doesnt break previous syntax
* offers a more natural syntax

My motivation was working on my ggplot2 extension, so my example is a simple median-IQR function that returns a data frame, just for reference:
```
md_iqr <- function(x,center = 0.5, spread = c(0.25, 0.75)){
  c <- quantile(x,center)
  s <- quantile(x,spread)
  data <- data.frame(y = c, ymin = min(s), ymax = max(s))
  
  return(data)
}
```
The current use is a bit clunky:
`> mtcars |> group_by(gear) |> group_modify(~md_iqr(.x$mpg))`

## My suggestion:
For these examples, I created a function `group_modify_` to distinguish from the current function. so this is for demo purposes.. the PR has the correct internal functions update

```
> mtcars |> group_modify_(.f = md_iqr,.col = mpg, .by = gear)
# A tibble: 3 × 4
   gear     y  ymin  ymax
* <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1     3  15.5  14.5  18.4
2     4  22.8  21    28.1
3     5  19.7  15.8  26  
```
* You could also pass positional arguments as well as function specific arguments:
```
> mtcars |> group_modify_(md_iqr,mpg,gear, spread = c(0.1,0.9))
# A tibble: 3 × 4
   gear     y  ymin  ymax
* <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1     3  15.5  11.6  20.5
2     4  22.8  19.4  32.2
3     5  19.7  15.3  28.6
```
* It works well on un-gropued data as well:
```
> mtcars |> group_modify_(md_iqr,mpg)
# A tibble: 1 × 3
      y  ymin  ymax
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1  19.2  15.4  22.8
```
* It doesnt break and doesnt change the original behaviour!
```
> mtcars |> group_by(gear) |> group_modify_(~md_iqr(.x$mpg))
# A tibble: 3 × 4
# Groups:   gear [3]
   gear     y  ymin  ymax
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1     3  15.5  14.5  18.4
2     4  22.8  21    28.1
3     5  19.7  15.8  26
```
Still supports formula notation and returns an expected grouped tibble.

* From current examples:
```
mtcars |> group_by(gear) |> group_modify(~head(.x,2)) |> ungroup()
# becomes this:
mtcars |> group_modify(.f = head,.by = gear, n = 2)
```
both are valid, my suggestions extendes the API, it doesn't replace or break or limits anyone

title: Should we have AI specific warnings?
description:
Consider this warning message about multiple matches in joins

https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/770ad50f884ebb78a479d78b79d0ba2ec0fb0c53/R/join-rows.R#L244-L252

When an AI reads this after executing the code, it tends to aggressively avoid warnings and will just insert `relationship = "many-to-many"` to silence the warning.

But this is bad! Awful even!

The whole point of this warning is to force the user to _question their own assumptions_ and explicitly make this decision for themselves.

Would it be useful for us to conditionally add a bullet to warnings like this one, via something like `testthat:::is_llm()`, so that when Claude runs this code itself, it sees the AI specific version of the warning which would read something like


> i = if (is_llm()) "AI Systems - Never remove this warning on your own by setting `relationship` for the user. Instead stop and prompt the user to investigate whether or not this is their actual intention"

We would use this sparingly, for warnings that are really for cases with contextual semantic meaning, not syntax

(I don't currently have any other examples)

title: case_when() fails with <xts> objects on some systems: "must be a logical vector, not a <xts> object"
description:
## Description
I am encountering a breaking change or regression when using dplyr::case_when() with xts objects. The code executes successfully on a Debian system with older package versions but fails on Fedora 43 with updated packages.

The error message indicates that case_when no longer accepts an xts object as the logical condition (the LHS of the formula), even though the underlying data is logical. 

## Minimal Reproducible Example
The following code block demonstrates the issue:

```r
library(xts)
library(dplyr)

dates <- seq(as.Date("2024-01-01"), length.out = 5, by = "days")
test_xts <- xts(x = data.frame(A = c(1, 5, 3, 2, 4),
                               B = c(2, 2, 3, 5, 1)),
                order.by = dates)

# This block fails on newer environments
tryCatch({
  result <- case_when(
    test_xts$A > test_xts$B ~ 1, 
    test_xts$A < test_xts$B ~ -1, 
    TRUE ~ 0
  )
  print("Success!")
  print(result)
}, error = function(e) {
  print(e)
})
```

## Environment Comparison
The main differences appear to be in the versions of dplyr, vctrs, and xts.

| Component | Working Environment (Debian) | Failing Environment (Fedora)|
|---------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| R Version | 4.5.0  | 4.5.3 |
| dplyr | 1.1.4 | 1.2.1 |
| vctrs | 0.6.5 | 0.7.3 |
| xts | 0.14.1 | 0.14.2 |
| zoo | 1.8.15 | 1.8.15 |


## Logs and Errors
### Fedora (Failing Output)

```text
<error/rlang_error>
Error in `case_when()`:
! `..1 (left)` must be a logical vector, not a <xts> object. 
Backtrace:
 1. ├─base::tryCatch(...)
 2. │ └─base (local) tryCatchList(expr, classes, parentenv, handlers)
 3. │   └─base (local) tryCatchOne(expr, names, parentenv, handlers[[1L]])
 4. │     └─base (local) doTryCatch(return(expr), name, parentenv, handler)
 5. └─dplyr::case_when(...) 
```
### Debian (Successful Output)

```text
[1] "Success!" 
[1] -1  1  0 -1  1 
```
## Session Info

```text

Platform: x86_64-redhat-linux-gnu
Running under: Fedora Linux 43 (Workstation Edition) 
locale: de_DE.UTF-8
```

```text

title: [FEATURE]: `.empty` Argument for `if_any()` and `if_all()` — Control Behavior with Empty Column Selections
description:
```markdown
## [FEATURE]: `.empty` Argument for `if_any()` and `if_all()` — Control Behavior with Empty Column Selections

### Summary

When `if_any()` or `if_all()` receive an empty column selection (e.g., `character(0)` or 
`tidyselect::any_of(character(0))`), they currently return `FALSE` (for `if_any()`) or `TRUE` 
(for `if_all()`) for all rows. This causes `filter()` to discard all rows with `if_any()` or 
keep all rows with `if_all()` when the selection is empty.

This proposal adds a `.empty` parameter to both functions, allowing users to explicitly control 
the return value when no columns are selected, with common use cases being "keep all rows" for 
`if_any()` or "discard all rows" for `if_all()`.

---

### Problem Statement

The current behavior is mathematically consistent but creates programmatic friction:

**Problem 1 — Programmatic filtering pipelines:**

A user builds a filtering function that applies a predicate across a user-specified set of columns:

```r
filter_by_condition <- function(data, cols, threshold) {
  data |> filter(if_any(all_of(cols), ~ .x > threshold))
}
```

When `cols = character(0)` (e.g., user selected no columns from a UI), the function returns 
an empty dataframe. The user expects "no columns to check" → "keep all rows", but instead 
gets zero rows.

**Problem 2 — Asymmetric defaults cause confusion:**

```r
# Empty selection with if_any() → filter discards ALL rows
mtcars |> filter(if_any(character(0), ~ .x > 20))  # 0 rows

# Empty selection with if_all() → filter keeps ALL rows  
mtcars |> filter(if_all(character(0), ~ .x > 20))  # 32 rows
```

Users find this asymmetry surprising and non-intuitive for programmatic use.

**Problem 3 — Workarounds are verbose and repetitive:**

The current workaround requires checking selection length before every filter:

```r
if (length(cols) == 0) {
  data
} else {
  data |> filter(if_any(all_of(cols), ~ .x > 20))
}
# Or inline:
data |> filter(length(cols) == 0 || if_any(all_of(cols), ~ .x > 20))
```

This clutters code and is easy to forget.

---

### Proposed Solution

#### 1. New `.empty` Parameter for `if_any()` and `if_all()`

Add a `.empty` parameter that accepts either a logical value or a predicate function:

```r
if_any(.cols, .fns, ..., .empty = FALSE)   # default = FALSE (current behavior)
if_all(.cols, .fns, ..., .empty = TRUE)    # default = TRUE (current behavior)
```

**Basic usage:**

```r
# Keep all rows when no columns selected (programmatic filtering)
selected_cols <- character(0)
mtcars |>
  filter(if_any(any_of(selected_cols), ~ .x > 20, .empty = TRUE)) |>
  nrow()
#> [1] 32

# Discard all rows when no columns selected (strict validation)
mtcars |>
  filter(if_all(any_of(selected_cols), ~ .x > 20, .empty = FALSE)) |>
  nrow()
#> [1] 0
```

**Extended API — Function form for complex logic:**

For advanced use cases, `.empty` can accept a function of the data frame:

```r
# Return TRUE only for rows meeting some condition when selection is empty
mtcars |>
  filter(if_any(
    any_of(selected_cols), 
    ~ .x > 20, 
    .empty = function(df) df$cyl > 4  # apply alternative filter
  ))

# Or return a pre-computed logical vector
mtcars |>
  filter(if_any(
    any_of(selected_cols), 
    ~ .x > 20, 
    .empty = rep_len(TRUE, nrow(mtcars))  # keep all rows
  ))
```

#### 2. Consistent Defaults and Documentation

| Function | Current Default | Proposed Default | Rationale |
|----------|----------------|------------------|-----------|
| `if_any()` | `FALSE` | `FALSE` | Backward compatibility |
| `if_all()` | `TRUE` | `TRUE` | Backward compatibility |

Documentation will explicitly state:

> When `.cols` selects zero columns, `if_any()` returns `.empty` (default `FALSE`) 
> and `if_all()` returns `.empty` (default `TRUE`). Set `.empty` to the desired 
> return value or a function to override this behavior.

---

#### 3. Relationship with `filter()`

The `.empty` parameter directly enables natural `filter()` expressions:

```r
# Current: verbose
filter(data, length(cols) == 0 || if_any(cols, predicate))

# Proposed: declarative
filter(data, if_any(cols, predicate, .empty = TRUE))
```

This matches user mental model: "If there are no columns to check, there's no 
condition to fail, so keep everything."

---

### Prior Art in the Tidyverse

| Function | Empty-handling mechanism |
|----------|-------------------------|
| `tidyr::unnest()` | `keep_empty = TRUE/FALSE` |
| `tidyr::nest()` | `.ptype` for empty results |
| `dplyr::bind_rows()` | `.id` handles empty cases |
| `purrr::map()` variants | `.default` for empty results |
| `vctrs::vec_c()` | `.ptype` for empty input |

The `.empty` parameter follows this established pattern of providing explicit 
control over edge cases.

---

### Implementation Considerations

**Performance impact:** Near-zero — the empty selection check occurs once before 
rowwise evaluation, and `.empty` is evaluated only when `length(.cols) == 0`.

**Type stability:** `.empty` must evaluate to a logical vector of length 1 or 
`nrow(data)`. Functions should error with informative messages otherwise.

**S3 method compatibility:** The `.empty` parameter should be added to the 
generic and all methods, with default implementations falling back to the 
current behavior.

---

### Backward Compatibility

- `.empty` is a new parameter with defaults matching current behavior
- No existing code breaks unless a user accidentally has a `.empty` argument 
  in their `...` (extremely unlikely given naming)
- All existing tests pass without modification
- The change is purely additive

---

### Example Use Cases

#### Use Case 1: Shiny App Filter Module

```r
# UI: user selects columns to filter on (possibly none)
filter_module_server <- function(input, output, session, data) {
  reactive({
    data() |>
      filter(if_any(
        any_of(input$selected_cols),  # may be character(0)
        ~ .x > input$threshold,
        .empty = TRUE                  # keep all if no columns selected
      ))
  })
}
```

#### Use Case 2: Validation Pipeline

```r
# Require ALL selected columns to meet condition, but if none selected,
# that means no validation needed (pass everything)
validate_data <- function(data, required_cols) {
  data |>
    filter(if_all(
      any_of(required_cols),
      ~ !is.na(.x),
      .empty = TRUE  # no required cols → all rows pass validation
    ))
}
```

#### Use Case 3: Dynamic Report Generation

```r
# Generate report with optional filters
create_report <- function(data, filters = list()) {
  for (col in names(filters)) {
    data <- data |>
      filter(if_any(
        any_of(col),
        ~ .x %in% filters[[col]],
        .empty = TRUE  # if column doesn't exist, ignore this filter
      ))
  }
  data
}
```

---

### Alternatives Considered

**Alternative 1: Change the default behavior**
- Rejected because it would break thousands of existing scripts
- Empty selection semantics are mathematically defensible as-is

**Alternative 2: Separate function `if_any_or_true()`**
- Rejected because it proliferates function names without solving `if_all()` symmetry
- `.empty` parameter is more elegant and discoverable

**Alternative 3: Require `tidyselect::any_of()` to handle this**
- Rejected because the issue is in `if_any()` evaluation, not column selection
- `any_of(character(0))` correctly returns `integer(0)`; the behavior is intentional

**Alternative 4: Use `tryCatch()` or `inherits()` workarounds**
- Rejected because they're inefficient and obscure intent

---

### Open Questions for Discussion

1. **Should `.empty` default to `NULL` and error on empty selection?**  
   This would force users to be explicit, but breaks backward compatibility.

2. **Should `.empty` accept `"keep"` / `"discard"` strings instead of logicals?**  
   Strings are more readable but less type-safe and harder to extend to function form.

3. **Should this behavior extend to `across()` for completeness?**  
   `across()` currently returns a tibble that can be empty; should it have `.empty` too?

4. **What about `pick()`?**  
   `pick(character(0))` returns 0-column tibble; consistent behavior may be needed there too.

---

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `.empty` parameter added to `if_any()` and `if_all()` generics
- [ ] Default values: `.empty = FALSE` for `if_any()`, `.empty = TRUE` for `if_all()`
- [ ] `.empty` accepts: logical scalar, logical vector of length `nrow(data)`, or function
- [ ] Error messages are informative when `.empty` returns invalid type/length
- [ ] Documentation updated with examples and use cases
- [ ] Performance benchmarks show no regression for non-empty selections
- [ ] News file entry describing the new feature
- [ ] Tests added for all `.empty` variants (scalar, vector, function, error cases)

---

### Related Issues

- `#7059` — Original issue where zero-length selection behavior was noted
- Potentially related to any issue discussing `filter()` behavior with empty selections
- May affect `dplyr::slice()` and `dplyr::group_by()` with empty selections in future

---

> I am happy to discuss the naming (`empty` vs `empty_keep` vs `when_empty`), whether 
> the function form of `.empty` is overkill for v1, and whether we should implement 
> this for `across()` and `pick()` in the same release or separately.
```

title: FR: `if_any(.empty="keep")`
description:
Hi,

Since https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/7059, zero-length selection in `if_any()` yields an empty dataframe:

``` r
library(dplyr)
selected_cols = "mpg"
mtcars |>
  filter(if_any(any_of(selected_cols), ~ .x>20)) |>
  nrow()
#> [1] 14

selected_cols = character(0)
mtcars |>
  filter(if_any(any_of(selected_cols), ~ .x>20)) |>
  nrow()
#> [1] 0
```

<sup>Created on 2026-04-10 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

This behaviour is consistent with the current definition of `if_any()`, but in some programmatic workflows it would be useful to have an option to keep all rows when the selection is empty.

A typical use case is:

- define a predicate
- define a set of columns on which to apply it
- filter rows failing that predicate on any selected column

In that context, when no columns are selected, it can be natural to interpret this as "there is nothing to check", so all rows should be kept rather than discarded.

For example, something like `.empty= "keep"` could be useful, with the current behaviour remaining the default (`.empty= "discard"`).

There is some kind of workaround, but I don't find it very satisfying: 
```r
mtcars |>
  filter(
    length(selected_cols) == 0 ||
      if_any(any_of(selected_cols), ~ .x > 20)
  ) |>
  nrow()
#> [1] 32
```

title: SUGGESTION: Like the `filter_out()` function, is there plans to add a `none_of()` companion to the `any_of()` and `all_of()` functions?

title: Inconsistent visibility of many-to-many join warning inside package functions vs global environment
description:
## Description

`dplyr::left_join()` correctly warns about many-to-many relationships 
at the top level and inside globally-defined functions, but silently 
suppresses the same warning when the identical code runs inside a 
**package-namespaced function** loaded via `devtools::load_all()`.

This is particularly harmful because:
- The join still executes as many-to-many (rows are silently multiplied)
- The warning only surfaces in `devtools::test()` - creating a 
  situation where tests fail on a warning that never appears during 
  interactive development, making it impossible to reproduce or debug

## Behaviour matrix

| Call context                                | Warning fires? |
|---------------------------------------------|----------------|
| Top-level interactive console               | ✅ Yes         |
| Function defined in `.GlobalEnv`            | ✅ Yes         |
| `devtools::test()` (clean session)          | ✅ Yes         |
| Package function via `devtools::load_all()` | ❌ **No**      |

## Minimal reproducible example

### Case 1 — Top-level (warning appears ✅)
```r
library(dplyr)
x <- tibble::tibble(id = c(1, 1), x_val = c("A", "B"))
y <- tibble::tibble(id = c(1, 1), y_val = c("K", "L"))
left_join(x, y, by = "id")
#> Warning: Detected an unexpected many-to-many relationship...
```

### Case 2 — Global function (warning appears ✅)
```r
dummy_fun_global <- function() {
  x <- tibble::tibble(id = c(1, 1), x_val = c("A", "B"))
  y <- tibble::tibble(id = c(1, 1), y_val = c("K", "L"))
  dplyr::left_join(x, y, by = "id")
}
dummy_fun_global()
#> Warning: Detected an unexpected many-to-many relationship...
```

### Case 3 — Package function via `devtools::load_all()` (NO warning ❌)

Create a minimal package via `usethis::create_package()` and define:
```r
# R/hello.R
dummy_fun_pkg <- function() {
  x <- tibble::tibble(id = c(1, 1), x_val = c("A", "B"))
  y <- tibble::tibble(id = c(1, 1), y_val = c("K", "L"))
  dplyr::left_join(x, y, by = "id")
}
```

Then in interactive session:
```r
devtools::load_all()
dummy_fun_pkg()
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3   <-- no warning, silently returns expanded rows
#>      id x_val y_val
#>   <dbl> <chr> <chr>
#> 1     1 A     K
#> 2     1 A     L
#> 3     1 B     K
#> 4     1 B     L
```

## Expected behaviour

Either:
- The warning should fire consistently regardless of call context, or
- The suppression behaviour should be explicitly documented

## Session info
```
R version 4.5.3 (2026-03-11 ucrt)
Platform: x86_64-w64-mingw32/x64
Running under: Windows 11 x64 (build 26200)

dplyr_1.2.0
rlang_1.1.7
tibble_3.3.1
devtools_2.5.0
testthat_3.3.2
```

## Note
If this suppression is intentional, it would be helpful to have it 
explicitly documented, as it significantly impacts debugging workflows 
during package development.

Hi,

I have found that when combining `if_any`, `any_of` and grouping by the same variable selected in `any_of` causes a `FALSE` result rather than `TRUE`.

This may be a logical error on my side, or a result of the new behaviour to return `FALSE` like `any` when there is no selected column. However, I believe given we have selected one column (the grouping column), it should return `TRUE`. If it is expected behaviour maybe a worked example in the documentation of `if_any` with grouping?

Below is a worked example.

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

df <- data.frame(x = c(1,2,3), y = c(1,2,3))

# lets first run without grouping to see that it is true

  mutate(should_be_true = if_any(any_of("x"), ~ TRUE))

title: Argument inconsistency between `case_when()` and `recode_values()`/`replace_values()`
description:
Hello, I am excited about the new dplyr verbs `recode_values()` and `replace_values()` and have been experimenting with working them into my code. However, when I was writing code, I noticed that I naturally wrote `.default =` as an argument for `recode_values()` and was surprised not to get an autocomplete. After checking the documentation, **I realized that the `.default`, `.ptype`, and `.unmatched` arguments do not have period prefixes for these new verbs, even though they do for `case_when()`.**

I don't really care whether there's the prefix or not (I'm not up on my dplyr lore enough to know what qualifies an argument for having a `.` prefix), but **can we have consistency in the arguments across these three verbs?** This may well have been an intentional choice, in which case I'm curious what the rationale was! And am here to report that it was confusing, at least for this useR.

title: case_when and replace_when causing error
`case_match()` deprecation warnings lead to massive memory usage
description:
After upgrading to dplyr 1.2.0 I noticed that the memory usage of my testthat test suite exploded, resulting in killed CI runners.

After investigating I realized that this is due dplyr deprecation warnings which get generated due to the use of `case_match()`. My test suite issues around 400 of those warnings. Apparently the warnings are carrying along the data that is fed into `case_match()`: see my reprex. It seems that testthat holds on to all warnings which results in a big cumulation of unfreed data.

As a workaround I can disable the warnings. I'd guess however that it is probably not intended behavior that the warning holds on to the original data, hence this issue.

library(dplyr)

title: Feature request: Add tbl.data.frame() method for unified data access
description:
# Feature request: Add `tbl.data.frame()` method for unified data access

## Problem

Currently, `tbl()` only works with database connections, not with data frames:

```r
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)

# This works
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
tbl(con, "mtcars")

# But this doesn't
tbl(mtcars)
#> Error in UseMethod("tbl") :
#>   no applicable method for 'tbl' applied to an object of class "data.frame"
```

## Why this matters

When writing reusable functions, users often want to support **both** local data frames and database tables with the same code:

```r
# Current workaround - must check type manually
analyze_data <- function(src, table_name = NULL) {
  if (is.data.frame(src)) {
    data <- as_tibble(src)
  } else {
    data <- tbl(src, table_name)
  }

  data %>%
    filter(value > 0) %>%
    summarise(total = sum(value))
}
```

With `tbl.data.frame()`, this becomes cleaner:

```r
# Unified interface
analyze_data <- function(src, table_name = NULL) {
  data <- if (is.null(table_name)) tbl(src) else tbl(src, table_name)

  data %>%
    filter(value > 0) %>%
    summarise(total = sum(value))
}

# Both work seamlessly
analyze_data(local_df)
analyze_data(con, "sales")
```

## Proposed solution

Add a simple S3 method:

```r
#' @export
tbl.data.frame <- function(src, ...) {
  as_tibble(src)
}
```

Optionally, also for tibbles (passthrough):

```r
#' @export
tbl.tbl_df <- function(src, ...) {
  src
}
```

## Benefits

1. **Unified interface**: Same `tbl()` function works for both local and remote data
2. **Cleaner code**: No need for manual type checking in reusable functions
3. **Consistency**: `tbl()` becomes "get a tibble-like object from any source"
4. **Minimal change**: Just one simple S3 method, fully backwards compatible

## Potential concerns

**Q: Isn't this changing the purpose of `tbl()`?**

A: `tbl()` already means "create a reference to tabular data." Extending it to data frames is a natural generalization. The documentation says `tbl()` creates "a tbl object" - a data frame is already tbl-compatible.

**Q: Why not just use `as_tibble()` for data frames?**

A: Users can, but the goal is a **unified interface**. When writing functions that accept either data frames or database connections, having `tbl()` work for both makes the API cleaner.

## Questions

1. Would this be considered within scope for dplyr?
2. If not dplyr, would this be better as a standalone package?

title: Correctness risk: In-place chunk mutation during reframe recycling leaves partial state on error
description:
## Finding: In-place chunk mutation during reframe recycling leaves partial state on error

**Severity:** Medium

**Invariant Being Relied On:**
All chunks in `list_of_chunks` must be recycled to their common sizes atomically. If recycling fails partway, all chunks should remain in their original state.

**Violation Mechanism:**
In `src/summarise.cpp::dplyr_reframe_recycle_horizontally_in_place()` (lines 115-213), chunks are modified in place during the recycling loop (lines 183-209). The function:
1. Lines 183-201: Iterates through `list_of_chunks`, recycling chunks in place via `SET_VECTOR_ELT(chunks, j, chunk)` (line 198)
2. Line 207: Sets corresponding `list_of_result` elements to `R_NilValue` if recycling occurred

If an error occurs (e.g., from `vctrs::short_vec_recycle()` at line 197 or from allocation failure), some chunks will have been recycled while others remain unchanged. The R code at `R/summarise.R:296-300` then regenerates results from the modified chunks, but the chunks list is partially mutated.

**Execution Path:**
```
R: summarise_cols() → .Call(dplyr_reframe_recycle_horizontally_in_place, chunks, results)
  C++: dplyr_reframe_recycle_horizontally_in_place()
    → Loop: for (i = 0; i < n_list_of_chunks; ++i)
      → Loop: for (j = 0; j < n_chunks; ++j)
        → vctrs::short_vec_recycle(chunk, out_size)  [ERROR POINT]
        → SET_VECTOR_ELT(chunks, j, chunk)           [Partial mutation]
```

**Why This Is Non-Trivial:**
- The function is documented to modify in place for efficiency
- Errors during recycling are assumed not to occur after validation
- The R side expects either all chunks recycled or none
- No rollback mechanism exists

**Testability:**
This is primarily a correctness invariant rather than a user-facing bug.
It could be demonstrated by forcing an error during recycling (e.g. via
instrumentation or changes in `vctrs::short_vec_recycle()` behavior), but
the main concern is the reliance on non-atomic in-place mutation rather
than a currently reproducible crash.

**Maintainer-Relevant Framing:**
This documents a fragile invariant where correctness relies on recycling
completing without error. If recycling fails, the chunks list can be left
in a partially mutated state. Even if rare today, this could become a
problem if error handling or recycling behavior changes.

**Note:** I'm not proposing a fix — just documenting a correctness risk.

title: Reframe horizontal recycling in-place mutation creates correctness risk
description:
# Reframe horizontal recycling in-place mutation creates correctness risk

This issue does not currently manifest as user-visible corruption, but documents a fragile internal invariant that could become a correctness bug if execution order or error paths change.

## Problem

`reframe()`'s horizontal recycling mutates chunks in-place in C++ (`dplyr_reframe_recycle_horizontally_in_place`), creating a window where internal state is inconsistent if result regeneration fails.

## Execution Path

1. `reframe()` → `summarise_cols(verb = "reframe")` collects chunks and results for all expressions
2. C++ call to `dplyr_reframe_recycle_horizontally_in_place()`:
   - Validates all sizes (lines 152-175 in `src/summarise.cpp`)
   - Modifies chunks in-place and NULLs corresponding results (lines 183-209)
   - Returns successfully with chunks modified, some results NULL
3. R-side regeneration loop (lines 296-299 in `R/summarise.R`):
   - Regenerates results from modified chunks: `results[[i]] = vec_c(!!!chunks[[i]], .ptype = types[[i]])`

## Correctness Risk

**Invariant violation**: After step 2 completes but before step 3 completes, chunks are modified but results are NULL, creating inconsistent state.

**If step 3 fails**: Chunks remain modified (irreversible) but results remain NULL (incomplete), leaving permanent inconsistent state. No rollback mechanism exists to restore original chunks.

## Current Protection

Size validation happens before mutation in C++ (validation loop lines 152-175, mutation loop lines 183-209), so C++ errors occur before chunks are modified. However, result regeneration happens after mutation, creating a window for inconsistency.

## Reproducible Example

```r
library(dplyr)

df <- tibble(g = c(1, 1, 2, 2, 2), x = 1:5)
gdf <- group_by(df, g)

# Trigger recycling: expression "a" has size 1, "b" has size 2
# After C++ returns: chunks[[1]] modified (recycled), results[[1]] = NULL
# During regeneration: results[[1]] = vec_c(!!!chunks[[1]], .ptype = types[[1]])

# Successful case
out <- reframe(gdf, a = 1L, b = c(2L, 3L))
out
# # A tibble: 4 × 2
#       a     b
#   <int> <int>
# 1     1     2
# 2     1     3
# 3     1     2
# 4     1     3

# The correctness risk: if result regeneration fails (e.g., vec_c() error),
# chunks are modified but results aren't regenerated, leaving inconsistent state.
```

## Expected vs Actual Behavior

**Expected**: Mutation should be atomic - either all succeed (chunks modified + results regenerated) or none (original state preserved).

**Actual**: Chunks are modified before result regeneration completes. If regeneration fails (e.g., `vec_c()` error), chunks remain modified but results remain NULL, leaving permanent inconsistent state with no rollback mechanism.

## Files Involved

- `R/summarise.R:286-300` - Calls C++ and regenerates results
- `src/summarise.cpp:115-213` - Validates sizes and mutates chunks in-place

## Test

A test case documenting this issue is available at `tests/testthat/test-reframe-recycling-mutation.R`. The test does not fail today; it documents the invariant and the observable mutation window. The test demonstrates the mutation path through successful recycling and explains the correctness risk if result regeneration fails.

I'm not proposing a fix yet — just documenting a correctness risk.

title: dplyr verbs remove attributes of classed columns
description:
## Problem description

Hi, 

This issue is based on https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/7630, which was closed.

The initial problem was that `filter()` removes labels from glue variables.
The proposed solution was to use `haven::labelled()`, which works for simple, atomic classes like `glue`.
Unfortunately, it does not work for more complex ones.

This issue could belong in multiple repositories, so please move it as you think is best: 
- `dplyr`, if verbs should restore attributes after using `vctrs`
- `vctrs`, if the problem lies somewhere in the vectorization process


### Case 1: `difftime()`

If one column is a classed vector, like a `difftime` which is used a lot, `haven::labelled()` will drop the class and attributes (like `units` here), returning a plain labelled double, shown as `<dbl+lbl>`, instead of a difftime, or `drtn` in a tibble.

So we have two options:
- we use the base system with `attr(label="")` and dplyr verbs are not usable, 
- or we use the `haven` system and the classed columns are not usable.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
test = tibble(
  time_attr_lab = Sys.Date()-Sys.Date()+1,
  time_haven_lab = time_attr_lab
)
test$time_haven_lab = haven::labelled(test$time_haven_lab, label="haven difftime")
attr(test$time_attr_lab, "label") = "attr difftime"

#haven::labelled() drops the class
dput(test$time_attr_lab)
#> structure(1, class = "difftime", units = "days", label = "attr difftime")
dput(test$time_haven_lab)
#> structure(1, label = "haven difftime", class = c("haven_labelled", "vctrs_vctr", "double"))

#but keeps the label with dplyr verbs
test %>% filter(TRUE) %>% labelled::get_variable_labels()
#> $time_attr_lab
#> NULL
#> 
#> $time_haven_lab
#> [1] "haven difftime"
```

<sup>Created on 2026-03-24 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>





### Case 2: `survival::Surv()`

If a column is a Surv object, i.e. a classed matrix, `haven::labelled()` will fail with an error. This is a problem in haven, one that will probably be deemed minor. The 2-row matrix is flattened to a length 4 vector, which doesn't fit the 2-row tibble. Using labelled works fine.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
test = tibble(
  surv = survival::Surv(5:6, event=1:0),
)
test$surv = haven::labelled(test$surv, label="Survival")
#> Error in `$<-`:
#> ! Assigned data `haven::labelled(test$surv, label = "Survival")` must be
#>   compatible with existing data.
#> ✖ Existing data has 2 rows.
#> ✖ Assigned data has 4 rows.
#> ℹ Only vectors of size 1 are recycled.
#> Caused by error in `vectbl_recycle_rhs_rows()`:
#> ! Can't recycle input of size 4 to size 2.

test %>%
  labelled::set_variable_labels(surv="survival") %>%
  labelled::get_variable_labels()
#> $surv
#> [1] "survival"
```

<sup>Created on 2026-03-24 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

## Conclusion

I'm pretty sure this is a regression, as I don't recall experiencing this in previous versions of `dplyr`, although I cannot tell when.
Unfortunately, this breaks things all over my codebase, as labels are an essential feature for data reporting.

Is there another solution apart from the one from #7630?
I'm willing to dig into `vctrs` to implement a better labelled class if needed
Otherwise, would it be possible to restore attributes after using `vctrs` inside `dplyr` verbs?

Thank you very much for considering this issue and for your work on this package.

description: I've been playing around with slice_sample on grouped data frames for bootstrapping. The documentation states that if you provide a prop>1 or n> # of rows within a group, it will only sample the number of rows within a group. title: `group_by()` drops additional classes attached to data frames
description:
When using `group_by()`, any additional class attached to a `data.frame` (that isn’t part of the `tibble` hierarchy) is dropped.

```{r}
library(dplyr)

# Create a tibble with an extra class
df <- tibble(
  x = sample(c("A", "B"), size = 10, replace = TRUE),
  y = rnorm(10)
)
class(df) <- c("another_class", class(df))

# Group it
grouped_df <- df |> 
  group_by(x)

# The additional class is lost
inherits(grouped_df, "another_class")
#> FALSE
```

## Expected behaviour
The additional class (e.g., "another_class") should be preserved after `group_by()`.

## Actual behavior:
The additional class is removed.

## Why this matters:
Preserving the class would help with extending `dplyr` to new `data.frame` subclasses without needing to reimplement verbs like `group_by()`. Which is currently the only option suggested by the [vignette](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/dplyr_extending.html). 

## Additional context:
The issue appears to be that the class is not being passed along when calling the constructor for the new object. It can be fixed by passingthe classes to [`new_grouped_df`](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/82eedad3186e0b099e4833d925e2974a666dd244/R/grouped-df.R#L30). So instead of the current

```{r}
new_grouped_df(data, groups)
```

one can pass:

```{r}
class_data <- class(data)[which(class(data) != "grouped_df")]
new_grouped_df(data, groups, class = class_data)
```
which solves the problem.

I am happy to open a PR if this behavior change is acceptable.

title: `between()` treatment of `NA` bounds is not clear and maybe inconsistent with non-`NA` bounds
description:
I think that this is a documentation issue and not a bug type of issue, but I want to confirm.

I had expected either bound being `NA` to result in an overall `NA` result. That shows in the first example below. But the next two examples are not what I expected, even with that understanding. I would have expected the second result for both the second and third cases to be `TRUE` because 2 is equal to one of the boundaries (like the 4th example), but it's `NA` for both of those.

At least part of this issue is a request for clearer documentation of what `NA` is intended to do as a boundary. The other part is how mixed `NA` and non-`NA` bounds are compared. as it appears inconsistent with both bounds not being `NA`.

``` r
dplyr::between(1:3, NA, NA)
#> [1] NA NA NA
dplyr::between(1:3, 2, NA)
#> [1] FALSE    NA    NA
dplyr::between(1:3, NA, 2)
#> [1]    NA    NA FALSE
dplyr::between(1:3, 2, 4)
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE
```

title: group_by() %>% summarise() miscomputes Summary generics (min, max, sd) under grouped data with dplyr 1.1.4
description:
### **Description**

When using group_by() + summarise() in dplyr 1.1.4, the summary functions sd(), min(), and max() fail to compute correctly on grouped data frames. Instead of returning the true summary statistics, they return the group mean (or NA for sd()).

This behavior occurs in a clean R session with only dplyr loaded — no other packages are attached or masking base functions. The same code works correctly in base R, data.table, and purrr::map_df().

### **Reproducible Example**

```
library(dplyr)
packageVersion("dplyr") # 1.1.4

set.seed(123)
df <- data.frame(
  group = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 15),
  value = c(rnorm(15, 800, 100), rnorm(15, 720, 90))
)

# Works correctly in base R
base_summary <- aggregate(value ~ group, df, function(x) {
  c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x), min = min(x), max = max(x))
})
print(base_summary)

# Fails in dplyr 1.1.4
dplyr_summary <- df %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(
    mean = mean(value),
    sd   = sd(value),
    min  = min(value),
    max  = max(value)
  ) %>%
  as.data.frame()
print(dplyr_summary)
```

### **Expected Behavior**

sd(), min(), and max() should correctly compute group-level summary statistics.

### **Observed Behavior**

All min() and max() values are identical to the group mean, and sd() returns NA.

### **Environment**

- R version: 4.4.2
- dplyr version: 1.1.4
- Platform: macOS ARM64 (Apple Silicon)
- Other packages loaded: none (clean session)

title: assertive programming: tidy stopifnot
description:
A tidy version of stopifnot which respects groups

```{r}
stop_if_not <- function(.data, ...){
  
  statements <- rlang::quos(...)
  
  dplyr::mutate(.data, stopifnot(!!!statements))
  
  return(.data)
}
```

Example

```{r}
iris |> group_by(Species) |> stop_if_not(n() == 50)
# Passes

iris |> group_by(Species) |> stop_if_not(n() != 50)
# Fails

starwars |> stop_if_not(n_distinct(name) == n()) 
# Passes

starwars |> stop_if_not(if_all(where(is.numeric), ~ .x > 0))
# Fails

starwars |> stop_if_not(if_all(where(is.numeric), ~ .x > 0 | is.na(.x)))
# Passes
```

title: across/any_of interprets names of character vectors as the column name
description:
In the call to `mutate(d, across())`, the name of the character vector is used instead of the value. With normal interpretation of an R character vector, the `any_of()` should look for "B" and "A", but is is using the name of the second index instead of the value.

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
d <- data.frame(A = 1, B = 2, C = 3:4)
mutate(d, across(any_of(c("B", B = "A")), as.character))
#> Error in `mutate()`:
#> ℹ In argument: `across(any_of(c("B", B = "A")), as.character)`.
#> Caused by error in `across()`:
#> ! Names must be unique.
#> ✖ These names are duplicated:
#>   * "B" at locations 1 and 2.
```

title: Write a replacing and recoding vignette
description:
Some fodder removed from the function docs that could be better served in the vignette

## The 2x2 table

| | Create a new column | Update an existing column |
|--------|--------|--------|
| **Logical conditions** | case_when | replace_when |
| **Values** | recode_values | replace_values | 

## Function connections

```r
#' @section Connection between `case_when()` and `replace_when()`:
#'
#' The following two statements produce identical `result`s:
#'
#' ```r
#' result <- replace_when(x, lhs ~ rhs)
#'
#' result <- case_when(lhs ~ rhs, .default = x, .ptype = x, .size = vec_size(x))
#' result <- vec_set_names(result, vec_names(x))
#' ```
#'
#' If you are replacing a few values within an existing vector, then
#' `replace_when()` is always a better choice because it is type stable and size
#' stable on `x`, pipes better, and better expresses intent.
```


```r
#' @section Connection between `recode_values()` and `case_when()`:
#'
#' While [case_when()] is a general vectorized [if_else()] that uses logical
#' expressions, `recode_values()` is a general vectorized [switch()] that uses
#' values. The following two statements are roughly equivalent:
#'
#' ```
#' case_when(
#'   x %in% c("a", "b") ~ 1,
#'   x %in% "c" ~ 2,
#'   x %in% c("d", "e") ~ 3
#' )
#'
#' recode_values(
#'   x,
#'   c("a", "b") ~ 1,
#'   "c" ~ 2,
#'   c("d", "e") ~ 3
#' )
#' ```
#'
#' For large inputs `recode_values()` is going to be much faster than
#' the equivalent `case_when()` statement.
```

```r
#' @section Connection between `recode_values()` and `replace_values()`:
#'
#' The following two statements produce identical `result`s:
#'
#' ```r
#' result <- replace_values(x, lhs ~ rhs)
#'
#' result <- recode_values(x, lhs ~ rhs, default = x, ptype = x)

title: Bug Report: Column name collision in summarise() causing incorrect results
description:
## Description
When using `summarise()` with multiple aggregations, calculating a boolean sum on a column (e.g., `sum(runs_off_bat == 4)`) returns 0 if that same column is aggregated elsewhere in the same `summarise()` call (e.g., `runs_off_bat = sum(runs_off_bat)`). The order of operations matters - if the boolean sum comes AFTER the column aggregation, it incorrectly returns 0.

## Reproducible Example

```r
library(dplyr)

# Create sample data
set.seed(123)
df <- tibble(
  group = rep(1:3, each = 100),
  value = sample(0:6, 300, replace = TRUE)
)

# This returns INCORRECT results (zeros for fours/sixes)
result_broken <- df |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(
    total = sum(value),
    value_sum = sum(value),  # Aggregating 'value' here
    fours = sum(value == 4), # Then using 'value' in comparison
    sixes = sum(value == 6),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

print("BROKEN (fours/sixes are 0):")
print(result_broken)

# This returns CORRECT results
result_fixed <- df |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(
    fours = sum(value == 4), # Calculate comparison BEFORE aggregating
    sixes = sum(value == 6),
    total = sum(value),
    value_sum = sum(value),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

print("FIXED (fours/sixes are correct):")
print(result_fixed)

# Verification
result_simple <- df |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(
    fours = sum(value == 4),
    sixes = sum(value == 6)
  )

print("SIMPLE (no other columns):")
print(result_simple)
```

## Expected Behavior
Both `result_broken` and `result_fixed` should produce identical results for `fours` and `sixes` columns, regardless of the order of operations within `summarise()`.

## Actual Behavior
When a column is aggregated (e.g., `value_sum = sum(value)`) and then used in a subsequent boolean comparison within the same `summarise()` (e.g., `fours = sum(value == 4)`), the comparison incorrectly uses the already-aggregated value instead of the original column, resulting in 0.

## Workaround
Calculate boolean sums BEFORE aggregating the column being compared, or use a two-step approach with `mutate()` then `summarise()`.

## Session Info
```r
sessionInfo()
```

## Real-World Impact
This bug was discovered while analyzing cricket ball-by-ball data with ~280k rows, where counting boundaries (fours/sixes) was returning zeros when calculated alongside other aggregations on the same column.

description:
deprecation of select external vector message not obviously related to call to rename.

Here is a call to rename (as you might have within a function) and the deprecation warning about `select()` - where the variable to rename and the new variable are both dynamic. We can see that `old_name` is  "y" here. 

``` r
library(tidyverse)

  x = 1:3,
  y = c("a", "d,e,f", "g,h"),
  z = c("1", "2,3,4", "5,6")

  rename("{new_name}" := old_name) %>%
  filter(!is.na(.data[[new_name]]))
#> Warning: Using an external vector in selections was deprecated in tidyselect 1.1.0.
#> ℹ Please use `all_of()` or `any_of()` instead.

```

<sup>Created on 2025-08-18 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>


Solution is to, as warning message suggests, use `any_of()`. However, in the case where user is passing a single character item (i know, vector of length 1, but not obviously so) to `rename()`, getting the `select(...vector)` warning is not obvious, and any_of or all_of seem conceptually out of place when renaming a single var.

new_name <- "new_y"
df %>%
  rename("{new_name}" := any_of(old_name)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(.data[[new_name]]))

Would a documentation change to add a lifecycle warning to rename be the way to handle this? Is that too much warning? A change to the select lifecycle warning to inform users about rename or about single items being vectors?

title: Document how to use `slice_sample()` to shuffle rows
description:
## Feature request

Add a function `shuffle_rows()` to randomly reorder rows in the current tibble/slice:

```R
dataset_tbl |>
  dplyr::shuffle_rows()
```

## Motivation

Currently, shuffling all rows in a slice/tibble requires 
`dataset_tbl |> dplyr::slice_sample(prop = 1)` or similar variations.

This approach has two main problems:

1. Unclear intent... because it is not obvious whether the goal is to shuffle rows or sample rows.
2. Fragile code... because small changes to the arguments passed can silently alter the result:
   - if `prop` is changed from `1`, the output is no longer a complete shuffle;
   - if `replace = TRUE` is used (accidentally or via copy-paste), rows may repeat or disappear.

Introducing `shuffle_rows()` would make the goal clear and make code more robust.

## Implementation sketch

```R
shuffle_rows <- function(.data, ..., .by = NULL) {
  dplyr::slice(
    .data,
    .by = {{ .by }},
    base::local({
      number_of_rows <- dplyr::n()
      base::sample.int(n = number_of_rows, size = number_of_rows, replace = FALSE)
    })
  )
}
```

## Example use

```R
datasets::penguins |>
  shuffle_rows()

# # A tibble: 3 × 8
#   species   island bill_len bill_dep flipper_len body_mass sex     year
#   <fct>     <fct>     <dbl>    <dbl>       <int>     <int> <fct>  <int>
# 1 Adelie    Biscoe     37.6     19.1         194      3750 male    2008
# 2 Chinstrap Dream      46.9     16.6         192      2700 female  2008
# 3 Chinstrap Dream      42.4     17.3         181      3600 female  2007
# ...
```

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

The "Details" section says:

title: `c_across()` appears to simplify lists of tibbles through row binding
description:
I have a tibble with multiple list of tibbles columns. I want to do a recursive full join on each row. 

```r 
tbl <- tibble::tibble(
  outer_key = c("A", "B"),
  tbl1 = list(
    tibble::tibble(inner_key = c("a", "b"), x1 = c(2, 5)),
    tibble::tibble(inner_key = c("a", "b"), x1 = c(1, 2))
  ),
  tbl2 = list(NULL, tibble::tibble(inner_key = c("a", "b", "c"), x2 = c(1, 2, 9))),
  tbl3 = list(
    tibble::tibble(inner_key = c("b", "c"), x3 = c(4, 7)),
    tibble::tibble(inner_key = c("a", "b"), x3 = c(1, 2))
  ),
)
```
A work-around with `nest()` shows the expected output: 

```r
# Workaround with nest()
tbl |> 
  nest(x = -outer_key) |> 
  mutate(
    x = map(x, map, first) |> 
      map(compact) |> 
      map(reduce, full_join, by = join_by(inner_key))
    ) |> 
  unnest(x)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   outer_key inner_key    x1    x3    x2
#>   <chr>     <chr>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 A         a             2    NA    NA
#> 2 A         b             5     4    NA
#> 3 A         c            NA     7    NA
#> 4 B         a             1     1     1
#> 5 B         b             2     2     2
#> 6 B         c            NA    NA     9
```

My first attempt at this was using `rowwise()` though. This fails because the input to `reduce()` is not a list of tibbles, but a single tibble. Method dispatch of `full_join()` raises an error because its first input is now the first column of the single data frame, not a tibble as expected. 

```r
# Failure with rowwise()
tbl |> 
  rowwise() |> 
  mutate(x = c_across(-outer_key) |> 
           compact() |>
           reduce(full_join)
           ) |> 
  unnest(x)
#> Error in `mutate()`:
#> ℹ In argument: `x = reduce(compact(c_across(-outer_key)), full_join)`.
#> ℹ In row 1.
#> Caused by error in `UseMethod()`:

title: Inconsistent usage of `.by` vs. `by` across different dplyr verbs
description:
mutate, filter, and others use `.by` for grouping just within the respective verb.
slice_XXX (and maybe others) use `by` for grouping.

This is inconsistent and it would be great if this could be aligned across dplyr (if not the whole tidyverse).

title: `select`: incomplete documentation for usage of `!` an `-` in combination with renaming columns
description:
Following the discussion here: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/79695678/dplyrselect-rename-columns-and-negative-selection-at-the-same-time-doesnt-wor, the documentation of `select` would benefit from a bit more clarity, especially wrt:

- mentioning the usage of `!` vs. `-` as negative selectors (since both are possible to use, but `-` is not mentioned, nor is the difference in their behaviour)
- describing of the order of selecting "commands", especially when someone wants to rename columns within `select`.

```
mtcars |>
  dplyr::select(test = mpg,
                -carb)
```

vs. 

```
mtcars |>
  dplyr::select(-carb,
                test = mpg)
```

I do see why the first code leads to a one-column df with just the `test` column, but I don't understand why the second code does not yield the same result).

Somewhat related to #7017

title: Support `suffix = NULL` in join functions to fail when conflicting column names are found
description:
An unfortunate feature of join functions is that we don't have tight control of what columns we take from `x` and `y`.
Often I will join two tables that have a common column name (not part of the key) and it will silently create two columns suffixed by `".x"` and `".y"` that are not mentionned by name anywhere in the code and not actual column names of relevant datasets.

We could force a strict behavior if we used a `suffix = NULL` argument, or another special value, or even just not force `suffix` unless needed so we could do `suffix = stop("couldn't join because of conflicting column named")`.

title: Feature request: first_col() function
description:
Apologies if I am missing something, but why doesn't dplyr have a `first_col()` function? I know that the automatic location for `relocate()` is before the first column, but it would be helpful within a function such as `mutate()` to be able to specify `.before = first_col()`. 

Thanks!

title: Feature request `case_replace()`
description:
I don't know about others, but my main use for `case_when` and `case_match` is to selectively replace values in a column. For example:

**Outline of the current situation (as I understand it)**
```
df <- tibble(cola = letters[1:5])
df |>
    mutate(cola = case_match(cola, c("b", "e") ~ "changed", .default = cola))
```

This works fine, but I find I regularly wish the `.default` value didn't need to be specified (its default is NULL). For example when using as part of a piped series of functions:

```
df |>
    mutate(cola = cola |>
        toupper() |>
        case_match(c("B", "E") ~ "changed")
    )
```
This will replace all unspecified values with NA, which is not what I want, but it's difficult to pass the piped vector as the `.default` value. It can be done by specifying a function, but it's a bit cumbersome:

```
df |>
    mutate(cola = cola |>
        toupper() |>
        (\(x) case_match(x, c("B", "E") ~ "changed", .default = x))()
    )
```


**Suggested solution**

My suggestion is a new function `case_replace`. The same as `case_match`, except without the `.default` parameter, always specifying that parameter as the input vector (the use case is similar to `base::replace`, but that function requires specifying by index instead of value):
```
case_replace <- \(x, ...) case_match(.x = x, ..., .default = x)
```

With that, we can pipe a vector nicely:
```
df |>
    mutate(cola = cola |>
        toupper() |>
        case_replace(c("B", "E") ~ "changed")
    )
```

I realise I'm nitpicking here, and `case_match` is really close to what I need. I've just found this to be a useful thing for me, and if others have similar needs, maybe it would be worth adding as a separate function in `dplyr::`. I'd be happy to have a go at contributing a PR if the interest is there.

title: Make `add_tally()` S3 generic?

title: Canonical approach to lookup-based replacement?
description:
I am finding it a bit awkward to refactor code using `plyr::mapvalues()`, which looks like:

```r
mapvalues(x, from_vector, to_vector)
```

Items in `x` found in `from_vector` are replaced by the corresponding entry in `to_vector`.

The closest analogue is `case_match()`, but using it often requires pretty substantial refactoring, e.g. if `from_vector`/`to_vector` come from arguments to a function. Elsewhere it is often convenient to keep `from_vector`/`to_vector` instead of writing them out manually in different arguments.

Another approach I've tried would basically be to do a join-and-replace lookup with a `left_join()` to `tibble(from_vector, to_vector)`.

`plyr::revalue()` is similarly not trivial to migrate.

Am I missing something else?

title: Canonical approach to re-scaling variables by group?
description:
What is the canonical approach here?

In {data.table}, I'd do:

```r
penguins[,
  by = species,
  names(.SD) := lapply(.SD, \(x) x / mean(x)), .SDcols = patterns("^bill_")
]
```

In base we could do:

```r
cols <- grepv("^bill_", names(penguins))
penguins |>
  split(~species) |>
  lapply(\(x) { x[cols] <- lapply(x[cols], \(y) y / mean(y)); x}) |>
  do.call(what = rbind)
```

(usual caveats about the shortcomings of `split()`+`lapply()`+`rbind()` in {base} apply)

In {plyr} there is:

```r
cols <- grepv("^bill_", names(penguins))
ddply(penguins, .(species), \(x) {x[cols] <- x[lapply(x[cols], \(y) y / mean(y)); x})
```

What I came up with in {dplyr} looks wrong:

```r
penguins |>
  summarize(
    .by = species,
    across(everything(), identity),
    across(starts_with("bill_"), \(x) x / mean(x))
  )
```

I would have thought `reframe()` is what's needed here, but I don't see a simple way to use it without needing a join or a similar hack to the `across(everything())` entry in `summarize()`.

title: Respect column names when "splicing" matrices in summarize()?
description:
Compare:

```r
penguins %>%
  summarize(.by = species, rbind(c(a = mean(bill_len), b = sd(bill_len))))
#     species rbind(c(a = mean(bill_len), b = sd(bill_len))).1 rbind(c(a = mean(bill_len), b = sd(bill_len))).2
# 1    Adelie                                               NA                                               NA
# 2    Gentoo                                               NA                                               NA
# 3 Chinstrap                                        48.833824                                         3.339256

penguins %>%
  summarize(.by = species, data.frame(as.list(c(a = mean(bill_len), b = sd(bill_len)))))
#     species        a        b
# 1    Adelie       NA       NA
# 2    Gentoo       NA       NA
# 3 Chinstrap 48.83382 3.339256
```

That is, when `summarize()` auto-converts a matrix into columns, we get ugly `deparse()`-inferred names, including totally losing `a` & `b` (now `1` and `2`), but when it does so for a data.frame, we nicely get the nested data.frame's own column names.

When we have control over the function, we can prefer returning a data.frame/tibble, but sometimes we don't want to touch the function and the `rbind()` approach will look nicer (even if the same operation results under the hood).

The context here is related to #7689 -- trying to convert some `plyr::ddply()` into "standard" {dplyr} code as well & simply as I can, without needing to drastically refactor downstream package code if I can avoid it.

title: Canonical approach to "up-sampling"?
description:
I'm trying to refactor some {caret} code away from `plyr::ddply()`:

https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/c98cc1a3ba5f0b087d51f5c4362a3b751515e243/pkg/caret/R/sampling.R#L83-L93

Basically, we try to "balance" a table across groups by resampling rows in any group that has fewer than the maximum number of rows.

For example:

```r
table(penguins$species)
#    Adelie Chinstrap    Gentoo 
#       152        68       124 
```

The output would have 152 rows for each of the three species.

I thought `slice_sample()` would help, but it explicitly prevents using `n > n()`:

https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/be3e3a05fd0081cb53168d6aedb417d62139b75d/R/slice.R#L43-L44

The {caret} use case also has the subtle requirement that the output be a strict superset of the original table, i.e., all rows originally present must continue to be so (we can't randomly exclude some).

I think `reframe()` is the intended function here, but I don't see any good examples demonstrating how it'd be used, in particular how to operate on the full table as opposed to individual columns.

In {data.table}, I'd do:

```r
x[, by = .outcome, {
  out <- .SD
  if (.N < maxClass) {
    new_rows <- sample.int(.N, maxClass - .N, replace = TRUE)
    out <- rbind(out, .SD[new_rows])
  }
  out
}]
```

It's also pretty easy in {base}:

```r
do.call(rbind, lapply(split(x, ~.outcome), function(xx) {
  n = nrow(xx)
  if (n == maxClass) return(xx)
  new_rows <- sample.int(n, maxClass - n, replace = TRUE)
  rbind(xx, xx[new_rows, ])
}))
```

However, this has a _major_ caveat that [`split()` silently drops missing observations in `.outcome`](https://bugs.r-project.org/show_bug.cgi?id=18899) (that `split()` makes it harder to retain the storage type of the grouping column(s) is also noteworthy but more manageable). 

I can think of some approaches that do something like (1) filter to groups that require supplementation (2) generate new rows (3) `bind_rows()` back, but haven't gotten there completely & it does sound a bit onerous.

title: Feature request: detect and throw a warning when `isTRUE` or `isFALSE` is used within `case_when`

<sup>Created on 2025-05-26 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>


Should an order be defined for list columns, so that `arrange()` actually does something?
For reference, duckdb defines an order on list type which seems pretty natural and universal: https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/sql/data_types/list.html#comparison-and-ordering
> The LIST ordering is defined positionally using the following rules, where min_len = min(len(l1), len(l2)).
> 
> Equality. l1 and l2 are equal, if for each i in [1, min_len]: l1[i] = l2[i].
> Less Than. For the first index i in [1, min_len] where l1[i] != l2[i]: If l1[i] < l2[i], l1 is less than l2.

I believe the equivalent R definition would be something along those lines:
``` r
`%==%` <- function(x, y) {
  min_len <- min(length(x), length(y))
  sub <- seq(1, min_len)

  all(x[sub] == y[sub])
}

`%<%` <- function(x, y) {
  min_len <- min(length(x), length(y))
  sub <- seq(1, min_len)

  i <- head(which(x[sub] != y[sub]), n = 1L)

  if (length(i) < 1) {
    return(FALSE)
  } else {
    x[[i]] < y[[i]]
  }
}

`%<=%` <- function(x, y) {
  (x %<% y) || (x %==% y)
}

# One maybe wants to sort w.r.t. to the `%<=%` operator?
# Examples:

c(3, 1) %<=% c(1, 1)
#> [1] FALSE

c(1, 1) %<=% c(3, 1)
#> [1] TRUE

c(1, 3) %<=% c(3, 1)
#> [1] TRUE

c(1, 1) %<=% c(1, 1)
#> [1] TRUE
```

<sup>Created on 2025-05-26 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>


Should `arrange()` sort w.r.t. to `%<=%` when used on list columns?

title: Feature suggestion: .groups option for slice() (and friends)
description:
I frequently take a grouped dataframe, sort it in a desired way, and then take a slice(1)  to take the top row of the group.
This can be a good way to ensure that 'ties' in sorting don't lead to multiple rows for the grouping variables.
Invariably, I have to do an ungroup() afterwards.

When I use summarise(), I like to use .groups = 'drop'   (to not have so many functions in the pipe as if I'd used ungroup() )

Why not add .groups as an option to slice?

The default behaviour of slice() is to leave groups alone, so not quite like summarize, but I think the difference can easily be conceptually defended.

tldr:
`df |> group_by(colA, colB) |> arrange(colC) |> slice(1) |> ungroup()`
could be
`df |> group_by(colA, colB) |> arrange(colC) |> slice(1, .groups = 'drop')`

title: Move `reframe()` out of the experimental stage
Recommended way to split data by a variable, apply a function, and return a bound dataframe (i.e., a non-experimental `do()` replacement)
description:
Hi folks,

My question hinges on this sort of situation. Obviously this example is pretty artificial, but its a situation in which you have a function which acts on a dataframe, returns a dataframe, doesn't return grouping variables, but might need access to them.

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

fun <- function(x) {
  if (any(x$Species == "setosa")) {
    tail(x, n = 3) |> select(Petal.Length)
  } else {
    head(x, n = 3) |> select(Petal.Length)
  }
}

iris |>
  group_by(Species) |>
  do(fun(.))
#> # A tibble: 9 × 2
#> # Groups:   Species [3]
#>   Species    Petal.Length
#>   <fct>             <dbl>
#> 1 setosa              1.4
#> 2 setosa              1.5
#> 3 setosa              1.4
#> 4 versicolor          4.7
#> 5 versicolor          4.5
#> 6 versicolor          4.9
#> 7 virginica           6  
#> 8 virginica           5.1
#> 9 virginica           5.9
```

<sup>Created on 2025-03-01 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

`do()` can deal with this admirably, but I'm unsure what the modern equivalent is.

`purrr::map()` doesn't behave the same because it drops the group variables, so you don't know what is what:

```r
> purrr::map(
+   split(iris, ~Species),
+   fun
+ ) |>
+   dplyr::bind_rows()
  Petal.Length
1          1.4
2          1.5
3          1.4
4          4.7
5          4.5
6          4.9
7          6.0
8          5.1
9          5.9
```

`nest()` also doesn't really work because the nested dataframe has no access to the `Species` column:

```r
> iris |>
+   nest_by(Species) |>
+   mutate(data = list(fun(data)))
# A tibble: 3 × 2
# Rowwise:  Species
  Species    data            
  <fct>      <list>          
1 setosa     <tibble [3 × 1]>
2 versicolor <tibble [3 × 1]>
3 virginica  <tibble [3 × 1]>
Warning message:
There were 3 warnings in `mutate()`.
The first warning was:
ℹ In argument: `data = list(fun(data))`.
ℹ In row 1.
Caused by warning:
! Unknown or uninitialised column: `Species`.
ℹ Run dplyr::last_dplyr_warnings() to see the 2 remaining warnings. 
```

`group_modify()` is recommended by the `do()` documentation, but it is experimental, so I don't want to put it in packages until its stable. It also doesn't use `.by`, which may imply this isn't a function that's going to be taken forward? It seems to be the closest thing, however.

`reframe()` I believe can only act on columns, so I don't think that's quite right either? It is also "experimental".

The answer may lie in `pick()`, but I'm not quite sure how to apply it to this specific use case. It also seems to not 'nest' the grouping variables, so it has the same issue as the above `nest()` example.

So I'm at a bit of a loss as to what the new `do()` actually is!

Cheers.

title: mutate() doesn't seem to signal warning conditions properly
description:
`mutate()` doesn't seem to signal named warning conditions for calling handlers to pick up.

Example: function emits a custom condition, and that specific class can't be suppressed.

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

foo_warn <- function(x) {
  warning(my_warning)
  x
}

my_warning <- structure(
  list(message = "MY_WARNING", call = NULL),
  class = c("my_warning", "warning", "condition")
)

df <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 2)

suppressWarnings(
  mutate(df, x = foo_warn(x)),
  "my_warning"
)
#> Warning: There was 1 warning in `mutate()`.
#> ℹ In argument: `x = foo_warn(x)`.
#> Caused by warning:
#> ! MY_WARNING
#>   x y
#> 1 1 2

# my_warningis never signaled, handlers can't pick it up
withCallingHandlers(
  mutate(df, x = foo_warn(x)),
  my_warning = function(c) {
    stop("condition signaled")
  }
)
#> Warning: There was 1 warning in `mutate()`.
#> ℹ In argument: `x = foo_warn(x)`.
#> Caused by warning:
#> ! MY_WARNING
#>   x y
#> 1 1 2

# but removing the `warning` class is at least a work-around
# 
foo_cond <- function(x) {
  warning(my_condition)
  x
}

my_condition <- structure(
  list(message = "MY_CONDITION", call = NULL),
  class = c("my_condition", "condition")
)

withCallingHandlers(
  mutate(df, x = foo_cond(x)),
  my_condition = function(c) {
    stop("condition signaled")
  }
)
#> Error in (function (c) : condition signaled
```

title: Align the default case-sensitivity of `matches` with the regex default
description:
`matches` accepts a regex for pattern matching within `tidyselect` functions and, in my opinion, would therefore be more user-friendly if it had the same default case-sensitivity behaviour as regex. Right now, matches is not case sensitive. 

This issue proposes switching the default value of the `ignore.case` parameter from `TRUE` to `FALSE`. I'm happy to submit a pull request, but will wait to see how much traction this issue gets.

```r

attributes(df$datetime)
#> $class
#> [1] "POSIXct" "POSIXt"

title: case_when() Lacks Safe Handling for Unexpected Values
description:
Currently, `case_when()` does not provide a built-in way to validate categorical inputs and throw an error when an unexpected value is encountered. The function requires all return values to have the same type, making it impossible to safely use in cases where an unexpected value is encountered. The function is also incompatible in most cases with `stop()`.

This makes `case_when()` unsafe in cases where developers need both:
1. A normal transformation for known values
2. A hard error for unknown values

## Reproducible Example:
```
library(dplyr)


replace_func <- function(x) {
  
  case_when(
    x == "A" ~ 1,
    x == "B" ~ 2,
    x == "C" ~ 3,
    
    # If there is a different value I want the function to throw an error
    # and stop the execution
    .default = stop(paste0("Invalid value", x))
  )
  
data <- tibble(x = c("A", "B", "A", "C"))

# This will throw an error - even though all values are specified in the function
data %>% mutate(new_x = replace_func(x))
# Expected behavior would be to return something like:

# A tibble: 4 x 2
#   x     new_x
#   <chr> <dbl>
# 1 A         1
# 2 B         2
# 3 A         1
# 4 C         3


# But for it to fail if there is a value not specified in the function
data1 <- tibble(x = c("A", "B", "A", "C", "D"))


# This should throw an error because the default value is stop() and the value
# "D" is not specified in the function
data1 %>% mutate(new_x = replace_func(x))
```

Currently, the only alternatives for handling unknown values in `case_when()` are:

1. A manual check after executing `case_when()`, which is an imperfect solution with unnecessary complexity or
2. Leaving `.default = NA`, which can lead to silent failures—an unknown value that should have been handled explicitly might be mistakenly transformed into `NA` instead of triggering an error.

Neither of these solutions is ideal.

## Proposed Solution

I believe the default behavior should be something along the lines of `.default = stop(paste0("Unknown value: ", x))`. This would force users to explicitly handle unknown values within their program, ensuring safer data transformations. If users want to allow unknown values to default to `NA`, they should be required to specify it explicitly by using `.default = NA` or `TRUE ~ NA`. This approach would provide better safety by default, preventing unintended `NA` values from propagating due to missing mappings in `case_when()`.

Would love to hear your thoughts on this!

title: Possible memory leak involving warnings
description:
I recently updated my `dplyr` version (late to the party), and I'm hitting some increased memory usage. I've traced it back to how warnings are handled. Beginning in `dplyr 1.1.1`, I get the following output:
``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

identity <- function(x, warn) {
    if (warn) {
        warning("fake warning")
    }
    x
}

df <- tibble::tibble(e = rep(1, 1e8))

print(gc())
#>             used  (Mb) gc trigger   (Mb)  max used  (Mb)
#> Ncells    620941  33.2    1306337   69.8   1306337  69.8
#> Vcells 101049658 771.0  148096356 1129.9 101084366 771.3

df <- df %>% mutate(e = identity(e, warn = TRUE))
#> Warning: There was 1 warning in `mutate()`.
#> ℹ In argument: `e = identity(e, warn = TRUE)`.
#> Caused by warning in `identity()`:
#> ! fake warning

print(gc())
#>             used  (Mb) gc trigger   (Mb)  max used  (Mb)
#> Ncells    729780  39.0    1306337   69.8   1306337  69.8
#> Vcells 101287706 772.8  148096356 1129.9 102369359 781.1

rm(df)
print(gc())
#>             used  (Mb) gc trigger   (Mb)  max used  (Mb)
#> Ncells    729742  39.0    1306337   69.8   1306337  69.8
#> Vcells 101287654 772.8  148096356 1129.9 102369359 781.1
```

<sup>Created on 2025-01-31 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

If I restart R and rerun with `warn = FALSE`, the final memory usage is only 7.9 MB rather than 772.8 MB. Additionally, if I rewrite the mutate to avoid using a pipe via `df <- mutate(df, e = identity(e, warn = TRUE))`, the final memory usage is only 8.8 MB. Switching the pipe to `|>` also yields low memory usage. Under `dplyr 1.1.0`, the above reprex yields 18.8 MB.

I don't have a full appreciation for whether warnings would capture my environment, but I'm wondering if that's perhaps happening within either base R or dplyr's own record of warnings.
