Weirdly the issue is only occurring on macos checks and I'm wondering if this is bug, issue with how I'm using dplyr in code, GitHubActions issue, or something else?

In short, I having an issue with GithubActions checks for newest release of my CRAN package [scCustomize](https://github.com/samuel-marsh/scCustomize) (The PR with the GitHubAction checks can be found here https://github.com/samuel-marsh/scCustomize/pull/141).  The issues are coming from errors in running function examples and the error is only occurring on macos check (ubuntu and windows pass with no issues).  I originally made a posit post on this [see here](https://community.rstudio.com/t/github-actions-check-failing-due-to-example-only-on-mac/176868), but after some more debugging I'm thinking that something might be either wrong in my code or a bug in dplyr (again no idea why it is only occurring on one platform but maybe I'm missing something) or something else?

The error first occurred with function that has been present in package prior to this version and previous passed checks.  The full function can be found [here](https://github.com/samuel-marsh/scCustomize/blob/master/R/Object_Utilities.R#L623) but the relevant portion I believe is this piece of code:

```

    # sample_name is user supplied variable that is the name of column in meta_df that defines the groups
```

title: [Feature Request] Option to throw error if tables in join have shared column names other than join key
description:
Today, if two tables are joined and they have shared columns other than the join key, suffixes are automatically appended to disambiguate. For example:

```r
library(tidyverse)
dat <- as_tibble(mtcars) %>%
  distinct(mpg, wt, vs)
dat %>% left_join(dat, by = c('mpg', 'wt'))
#> # A tibble: 32 × 4
#>      mpg    wt  vs.x  vs.y
#>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1  21    2.62     0     0
#>  2  21    2.88     0     0
#>  3  22.8  2.32     1     1
#>  4  21.4  3.22     1     1
#>  5  18.7  3.44     0     0
#>  6  18.1  3.46     1     1
#>  7  14.3  3.57     0     0
#>  8  24.4  3.19     1     1
#>  9  22.8  3.15     1     1
#> 10  19.2  3.44     1     1
#> # ℹ 22 more rows
```

In many data pipelines, overlapping columns are unexpected and cause issues later in the pipeline. (I think this is why most SQL databases throw an error in this case, rather than automatically appending suffixes.) For such cases, it would be nice to have function-level or package-level options to throw an error.

title: Feature Request: Intuitive DataFrame Transposition Functionality in dplyr
description:
Brief description of the problem:

Transposing a DataFrame in dplyr currently requires a combination of pivot_longer() and pivot_wider() functions. This process is not as straightforward as using the base R t() function and can be confusing for users, especially those new to dplyr or coming from a base R background. An intuitive, one-step transposition function would greatly simplify the data manipulation process in dplyr.

Expected output:

A new function, possibly named transpose_df(), that allows users to transpose a DataFrame in a single step, mirroring the simplicity and ease of use of the base R t() function.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# Sample dataframe
df <- tibble::tibble(
  x = 1:3,
  y = 4:6,
  z = 7:9
)

# Current method for transposing in dplyr/tidyr
transposed_df <- df %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = "variable", values_from = "value")

# Print the transposed dataframe
print(transposed_df)

title: How to extend my code that works by group to all data
description:
Dear all, 
I'm trying to analyse the effect of "Factor1" and "Factor2" on the response variable "perf" by "location", and obtaining at the end my original dataset associated to the lsmeans and tukey groups letters. Here below the code I'm using that gives me exactly what I need but only by location, my need is : how can I extend it in a way my output combines results of all locations, i.e, output of lsmeans and CLD by location :

```r
library(multcomp)
library(lsmeans)
library(dplyr)
library(broom)

output <- as.data.frame(dataset)
output$perf <- as.numeric(output$perf)
output$factor1 <- as.factor(output$factor1)
output$factor2 <- as.factor(output$factor2)
output <- output %>% 
           group_by(location) %>% 
           mutate(row=row_number()) 

model <- lm(perf ~ factor1 + factor2, data = output)
lsmeans <- lsmeans(model, ~ factor1)
CLD = cld(lsmeans,
            alpha   = 0.05,
            Letters = letters,
            adjust  = "tukey")         

output <- left_join(output, CLD, by = "factor1")
```
Thank you in advance for your help !

title: `rename_with()` errors when no match/clarity of error message
description:
I thought I could use map over a list of data frames to rename them using `rename_with()` and a tidyselector like `matches()`, whether or not each data frame has a matching column name. Now it looks as though that is not longer possible (#6688). 

That's all fine and good. Now I see I can just use `rename()`, which does not error. But I think the error for `rename_with()` could be more clear by saying that there is no match. 

Lastly, I'm curious: why the difference in erroring vs. not between `rename()` and `rename_with()`?

``` r
library(tidyverse)

# No error
mtcars |> rename("joe" = matches("qwerty")) |> head(1)
#>           mpg cyl disp  hp drat   wt  qsec vs am gear carb
#> Mazda RX4  21   6  160 110  3.9 2.62 16.46  0  1    4    4

# Hinting error
mtcars |> rename_with(~ "joe", qwerty)

#> ! Can't subset columns that don't exist.
#> ✖ Column `qwerty` doesn't exist.
#> Backtrace:

#>   2. ├─dplyr:::rename_with.data.frame(mtcars, ~"joe", qwerty)

#>   5. │     ├─tidyselect:::with_subscript_errors(...)
#>   6. │     │ └─rlang::try_fetch(...)
#>   7. │     │   └─base::withCallingHandlers(...)
#>   8. │     └─tidyselect:::vars_select_eval(...)
#>   9. │       └─tidyselect:::walk_data_tree(expr, data_mask, context_mask)
#>  10. │         └─tidyselect:::as_indices_sel_impl(...)
#>  11. │           └─tidyselect:::as_indices_impl(...)
#>  12. │             └─tidyselect:::chr_as_locations(x, vars, call = call, arg = arg)
#>  13. │               └─vctrs::vec_as_location(...)

#>  15.   └─vctrs:::stop_subscript_oob(...)
```

title: Request for alias functions for relationship = '' join parameter
description:
Hi all!

I really love the new `relationship` parameter within dplyr join functions as it has streamlined a lot of my pre/post-join sanity checks.

I was coding today and found myself typing `relationship = ` for the seemingly thousandth time when I had the idea that an alias here would be really useful for me (and thus likely for others as well).  It'd be faster to write the code & would result in less unnecessary multi-line wrapping for simple joins.

Here's my proposal for consideration.

*one-to-one 4 additional character alias*
```r
left_join(..., relationship = 'one-to-one')
left_join_oto(...)
```

*one-to-many 4 additional character alias*
```r
left_join(..., relationship = 'one-to-many')
left_join_otm(...)
```

*one-to-many 4 additional character alias*
```r
left_join(..., relationship = 'many-to-one')
left_join_mto(...)
```

*many-to-many 4 additional character alias*
```r
left_join(..., relationship = 'many-to-many')
left_join_mtm(...)
```

I'd be happy to attempt a PR for this feature, but first would want to know if such a feature would be accepted provided it was coded properly with unit tests, documentation, etc.  I'd also be happy if someone else just implemented it, but happy to help anyway I can.

Thoughts on this proposed feature?  Dead on arrival or something that would be considered?

Thanks!
Jason

title: anti_join() error. Problematic argument: suffix
When `.unpack = TRUE`, `.names` should delay its column name uniqueness check
description:
Extracted from https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6933

Sometimes the function you apply in `across()` returns a tibble who's column names already uniquely identify that function (`TTR::TDI()` or `TTR::MACD()`), so you don't need to name the `list()` as that would be repetitive, and you don't need the `_1` or `_2` you get automatically.

It would be nice if you could set `.names = "{.col}_"` when `.unpack = TRUE` to handle this special case, but that runs the name uniqueness check too early. It creates two names called `var1_`, which do eventually get resolved _after_ the unpacking is done, and a second name uniqueness check is already done in `df_unpack()`, so I think we can skip the ones in `across_setup()` when `.unpack = TRUE`.

Easiest way to do this is the probably give `across_setup()` a `name_repair` argument that we can set to `"minimal"` when `.unpack = TRUE`.

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

df <- tibble(
  var1 = seq(1, 100, 1)
)

metric_a <- function(x) {
  tibble::tibble(a = x, a_info = x + 1)
}
metric_b <- function(x) {
  tibble::tibble(b = x, b_info = x + 1)
}

# dont need 1 and 2 here
df |>
  mutate(across(
    var1,
    list(
      \(.x) metric_a(.x),
      \(.x) metric_b(.x)
    ),
    .unpack = TRUE
  ))
#> # A tibble: 100 × 5
#>     var1 var1_1_a var1_1_a_info var1_2_b var1_2_b_info
#>    <dbl>    <dbl>         <dbl>    <dbl>         <dbl>

#>  4     4        4             5        4             5
#>  5     5        5             6        5             6
#>  6     6        6             7        6             7

#>  8     8        8             9        8             9
#>  9     9        9            10        9            10
#> 10    10       10            11       10            11
#> # ℹ 90 more rows

# this is also repetitive
df |>
  mutate(across(
    var1,
    list(
      a = \(.x) metric_a(.x),
      b = \(.x) metric_b(.x)
    ),
    .unpack = TRUE
  ))
```

title: Improve error message when the RHS of `case_when` has values of different data types.
description:
The `case_when` function does not do silent coercion when multiple data types are provided at the RHS of the tilde (the _to_ values). This is a design feature as stated in the docs: `all RHSs must evaluate to the same type of vector.`. In my opinion the error message thrown when the user does mistakenly provide multiple data types is too cryptic:

`must be a <dt1> vector, not a <dt2> vector.`

Where `<dt1>` is the first data type seen on the RHS and `<dt2>` the second data type seen. 

Where this especially bites me is when one of the values on the RHS is `NA`, combined with nonlogical values. As in the following example

```r
library(dplyr)
x <- tibble(a = 1:10)
x |> mutate(b = case_when(
  between(a, 3, 6) ~ NA,
  TRUE             ~ 'other',
))
```

This results in the error message `must be a logical vector, not a character vector.` It is easy to forget that `NA` is a logical (and not known to many R users in the first place I think). Therefore one does not spot the problem easily. Since there is no reference to the RHS in the error message, one is inclined to look for the problem on the LHS. Since predicates are spedified here one assumes easily something is wrong here and loses time debugging something that is not broken.

## Proposed alternative

There are two elements that can be improved I think. (1) Make a reference to the RHS (2) Note that multiple data types are provided instead of saying that `<dt2> ` must be of `<dt1>`. The latter depends on the order the data types were provided which is quite random. A proposed form would be.

`Multiple data types provided on the RHS, where only one is accepted. Data types provided: <dt1>, <dt2>`

title: The .keep= "unused" parameter of the mutate does not work correctly when the ifelse function (from the base) is called
description:
Hello,

I have detected that if the ifelse function (of the base) is used within a mutate and the .keep parameter is equal to "unused", in certain situations the columns called by the ifelse do not disappear.

For example, if the true value does not apply to any row, it generates that the column that is called in the true value does not disappear. This behavior does not happen when using the if_else function, however I think this is a bit confusing for the end user.

I understand that the if_else function evaluates the entire expression which causes .keep = "unused" to work correctly.

```
# Example ifelse --------------------------------

data <- data.frame(
  ROW = c(1,2,3,4),
  VALUE_1 = c("A","A","A","A"),
  VALUE_2 = c("B","B","B","A")
)

data %>%
  mutate(
    EXPRESION = ifelse(
      test = ROW > 4,
      yes = VALUE_1,
      no = VALUE_2
    ), .keep = "unused"
  ) 

Result:
  VALUE_1 EXPRESION
1       A         B
2       A         B
3       A         B
4       A         A

# Example if_else ------------------------------

data <- data.frame(
  ROW = c(1,2,3,4),
  VALUE_1 = c("A","A","A","A"),
  VALUE_2 = c("B","B","B","A")
)

data %>%
  mutate(
    EXPRESION = if_else(
      condition = ROW > 4,
      true = VALUE_1,
      false = VALUE_2
    ), .keep = "unused"
  ) 

Result:
  EXPRESION
1         B
2         B
3         B
4         A

```

Regards,

It would be neat if the group_*() functions (group_map(), group_modify() and group_walk()) included the .by syntax similar to the other dplyr functions! 

For example, in the case of:
```r
library(estimatr)

mtcars %>%
  group_by(am, vs) %>%
  group_map(~tidy(lm_robust(mpg ~ hp, data = .x))) %>%
  ungroup() # question asker forgot to include this (!)
```
It could instead be:
```r
library(estimatr)

mtcars |> group_map(~tidy(lm_robust(mpg ~ hp, data = .x)), .by = c(am, vs))
```
Keep up the great work! :-)

title: Add a `ptype` argument to `between()` since we can't make it cast to the type of `x` at this time
description:
The result of using `between()` in filtering is not equivalent to evaluating a conditional expression when working with ordered factors.

```{r}
> (x <- data.frame(Visit = c("Discharge", "Month 3", "Month 6", "Month 12", "Month 20")))
      Visit
1 Discharge
2   Month 3
3   Month 6
4  Month 12
5  Month 20

> class(x$Visit)
[1] "character"
```

Now let's make it an ordered factor with assumed levels (used later for other operations):
```{r}
> (x$Visit <- factor(x$Visit, levels = c("Baseline", "Discharge", "Month 3", "Month 6", "Month 12", "Month 20", "Premature"), ordered = TRUE))
[1] Discharge Month 3   Month 6   Month 12  Month 20 
Levels: Baseline < Discharge < Month 3 < Month 6 < Month 12 < Month 20 < Premature
```

When filtering using the conjunction of conditions it works
```{r}
> x %>% filter(Visit >= "Discharge" & Visit <= "Month 20")
      Visit
1 Discharge
2   Month 3
3   Month 6
4  Month 12
5  Month 20
```
When using the convenient between(), it doesn't
```{r}
> x %>% filter(between(Visit, "Discharge", "Month 20"))
```

title: reframe() is dropping columns when you use rowwise()
description:
### Minimal reprex
```r
library(dplyr)
quantile_df <- function(x, probs = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)) {
  tibble(
    val = quantile(x, probs, na.rm = TRUE),
    quant = probs
  )
}

# Actual Behavioiur: Removes the grouping columns and just returns cols from rowwise
starwars %>%
  rowwise() %>% 
  reframe(quantile_df(height)) %>%
  ungroup()
  # 261 rows, 2 cols from quantile_df

  rowwise() %>%
```

title: Improve na_if documentation re vctrs coercion rules
description:
**Brief description of the problem**

Using `na_if` it generated error messages that I found mystifying:

```r
> na_if("ID", -3333)
Error in `na_if()`:
! Can't convert `y` <double> to match type of `x` <character>.
Run `rlang::last_trace()` to see where the error occurred.
> na_if("ID", "-3333")
[1] "ID"
> na_if( 1, "-3333")
Error in `na_if()`:
! Can't convert `y` <character> to match type of `x` <double>.
Run `rlang::last_trace()` to see where the error occurred.
> na_if( 1, -3333)
[1] 1
```
Currently the `na_if(x, y)` documentation simply states:

"y is cast to the type of x before comparison."

so it sounds like it should be able, when doing `na_if("ID", -3333)`, to cast the numeric `-3333` to character before doing the comparison.  

So I was initially mystified by this behavior (above), but then it was explained to me that `na_if` is using {vctrs} under the hood, so it is using `vctrs` coercion rules.   As such, please consider extending the `na_if` documentation for the `na_if` function with a bit more text and relevant examples to explain and clarify this.

title: feature request: unmatched="error" for the left table (`x`) in the `left_join()`
description:
When performing `left_join()` it would be nice to have an option to throw an error in case one of the rows **in `x`** didn't have a match.

### Background
A common use-case is to have some kind of large metainformation table. You would like to join meta-information while making sure that every row of the original (left) table has exactly one match.

`unmatched="error"` in the `left_join()` will check if all the rows **in `y`** had a match.

### Example
```r
meta <- tribble(
  ~ Species, ~ Scientific.Name,
  "setosa", "Iris setosa",
  "virginica", "Iris virginica",
  # versicolor is missing
  "human", "Homo sapiens",
  "dog", "Canis lupus familiaris",
)
with_meta <- left_join(
  iris,
  meta,
  relationship = "many-to-one"
  # here we need something like unmatched = "x_error" , which will through an error because 
  # versicolor wasn't matched
)
# that's a work-around
stopifnot(any(is.na(with_meta$Scientific.Name)))
```

title: Usage of `overlaps()`, `closest()`, `between()`, and `within()` in join_by() triggers NOTE
description:
I'm using the new helpers `overlaps()`, `closest()`, `between()`, and `within()` in the `join_by()` function in my CRAN package. However, when I run R CMD CHECK, it generates the following NOTE:

```
no visible global function definition for 'closest'
```

Normally I would evade such a note by either importing the function into my package, prefixing the namespace, or using the `.data$` pronoun. None of these are possible, as `dplyr::overlaps()` doesn't exist (see also #6838) , and the `.data$` pronoun clearly shouldn't be used and also doesn't work.

One possible workaround is defining the helpers in `globalVariables`,but as Hadley noted this is a ["hideous hack"](https://stackoverflow.com/a/12429344), and I'd prefer to avoid it if possible. 

How can these helpers be used in `join_by()` without triggering a NOTE during CRAN checks?

title: The case for `filter(.missing = NULL, .how = c("keep", "drop"))`
description:
There have been quite a few requests in the past for an "anti filter", i.e. I want to specify a set of conditions that determine which rows to _drop_. Additionally, it has traditionally been somewhat difficult to explain that `filter()` is about specifying rows to _keep_; that isn't really explained clearly in the verb name. Also, we've also seen in the past that it is mildly confusing that `select()` is about columns and `filter()` is about rows, again, there isn't anything in the verb names to describe the difference.

---

One thing we could consider doing is to add two new very explicit verbs:
- `keep_rows(data, ..., by = , missing = )`
- `drop_rows(data, ..., by = , missing = )`

Where `keep_rows()` is equivalent to `filter()`, and `drop_rows()` is the opposite.

To be very clear, `filter()` would _never_ disappear. We would, however, consider superseding it in favor of these if they prove to be successful, which really only means we'd start using them in docs and workshops instead of `filter()`. We'd even consider not even superseding `filter()`, which many people find scary. Instead we'd just be aliasing `keep_rows()` as `filter()`.

The biggest annoyance when writing a "drop" style expression with `filter()` is that you first have to write a "keep" expression and then painfully invert it. i.e.:

"drop rows from `df` where `a` and `b` and `c` are `TRUE`"

``` r
library(dplyr)

df <- tibble(
  id = c(1, 2, 3),
  a = c(TRUE, NA, TRUE),
  b = c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  c = c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE)
)
df
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>      id a     b     c    
#>   <dbl> <lgl> <lgl> <lgl>
#> 1     1 TRUE  FALSE TRUE 
#> 2     2 NA    TRUE  TRUE 
#> 3     3 TRUE  TRUE  TRUE

# "keep rows where a and b and c are TRUE"
# this nicely drops NAs because they don't match our specified criteria
filter(df, a, b, c)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>      id a     b     c    
#>   <dbl> <lgl> <lgl> <lgl>
#> 1     3 TRUE  TRUE  TRUE

# "drop rows where a and b and c are TRUE"
# this AWFULLY drops NAs because of how filter() works!
# NA doesn't match our criteria so shouldnt be seen as something to drop
filter(df, !(a & b & c))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>      id a     b     c    
#>   <dbl> <lgl> <lgl> <lgl>
#> 1     1 TRUE  FALSE TRUE
```

Note that even the seemingly correct "drop" expression is actually wrong when it comes to handling missing values. It is fairly hard to get this right.

The `drop_rows()` version would be:

```r
df %>% drop_rows(a, b, c)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>      id a     b     c    
#>   <dbl> <lgl> <lgl> <lgl>
#> 1     1 TRUE  FALSE TRUE 
#> 2     2 NA    TRUE  TRUE 
```

Where `NA` isn't considered something you "drop" by default, but would be if `missing` was tweaked to whatever we decide means "treat a missing value like `TRUE`".

---

A few other notes:
- `missing` is from https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6560 and controls how missing values are treated. By default, both functions would treat an `NA` as `FALSE` (i.e. missing values are never kept or dropped), but could be made to treat them as `TRUE` or an error. Though I don't think `missing = c("keep", "drop", "error")` works uniformly for both verbs so we'd need to think of another parameterization.
- Both functions would support `if_all()` and `if_any()`, which I think form nice natural sentences. "drop rows if any are NA" sounds pretty good for `drop_rows(df, if_any(c(a, b), is.na))`. That is like `tidyr::drop_na()`.
- Neither would support `across()`, which we have been deprecating from `filter()` for a little while now.
- Both functions would combine multiple conditions using `&`, as that is typically the natural way to combine multiple conditions and you can always get `|` behavior with either an explicit `|` or by using multiple calls to the function. i.e. `df %>% drop_rows(x > 5 | y > 6)` is the same as `df %>% drop_rows(x > 5) %>% drop_rows(y > 6)` (and you can't do that split trick with `&`). `if_any()` can also work for `|` when you need to apply the same function to multiple columns.
- Both functions would support `by`

Some issues and questions related to this:
- https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6888
- https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/1527
- https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/741
- https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/1797
- https://stackoverflow.com/questions/45661377/delete-rows-based-on-multiple-conditions-with-dplyr

title: Unexpected/impractical behaviour of rowwise() in combination with mutate_all()
description:
When trying to apply a function using `mutate_all()` to each **row** of a data frame using `rowwise()`, it seems the function only considers individual values, rather than the complete row. 

Comparing column-wise with rowwise operations:
```
# Columnwise - considers the complete column when applying the function
library(dplyr)
head(mtcars) %>% mutate_all(rank)

>                   mpg cyl disp hp drat wt qsec vs am gear carb
> Mazda RX4         3.5 3.5  2.5  4  5.5  2  1.0  2  5    5  5.5
> Mazda RX4 Wag     3.5 3.5  2.5  4  5.5  3  2.5  2  5    5  5.5
> Datsun 710        6.0 1.0  1.0  1  4.0  1  4.0  5  5    5  2.0
> Hornet 4 Drive    5.0 3.5  5.0  4  2.0  4  5.0  5  2    2  2.0
> Hornet Sportabout 2.0 6.0  6.0  6  3.0  5  2.5  2  2    2  4.0
> Valiant           1.0 3.5  4.0  2  1.0  6  6.0  5  2    2  2.0

# Rowwise - considers only the individual values within the row when applying the function, hence always returning rank 1
library(dplyr)
head(mtcars) %>% rowwise() %>% mutate_all(rank)
```

title: Unexpected differences in `cur_group_id()` operations in vs. outside `mutate` calls
description:
Hello, I'm encountering unexpected behavior from `cur_group_id()`. In particular, I expected that operations within a `mutate()` call surrounding `cur_group_id()` would treat the output of `cur_group_id()` as a vector along the rows of the tibble.

In the below reprex, calling `duplicated(cur_group_id())` in the `mutate` call gives a different result than calling `cur_group_id()` in the `mutate` call, extracting the result, and then calling `duplicated`.

```r
library(tidyverse)
data(mtcars)

#   Pick a column to group by (that has repeated values)
mt_tibble = as_tibble(mtcars) |>
    group_by(cyl)

#  Call 'duplicated' outside the 'mutate' call
mt_tibble |>
    mutate(gid = cur_group_id()) |>
    pull(gid) |>
    duplicated() |>
    table()

## FALSE  TRUE 
##     3    29

# Call 'duplicated' inside 'mutate' call
mt_tibble |>
    mutate(gid = duplicated(cur_group_id())) |>
    pull(gid) |>
    table()

## FALSE 
##    32 
```

I'm interested to know if I'm fundamentally misusing `cur_group_id()`, since I'm not very experienced with it, but I also think that if this is considered expected behavior, it is probably counterintuitive for many users, and seems inconsistent with other `dplyr` behavior (for example, `mutate(n = n() * 2)` is a perfectly valid operation that elementwise doubles the values output by `n()`)

Thanks!

Best,

title: New function to drop instead of keep observations (anti filter)
description:
There are a couple of problems I regularly run into when subsetting data with multiple conditions. 

The first has been brought up several times ([including in this open issue](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6560)): `filter()` drops any observations where any of the variables used in the conditions is missing.

A less obvious issue is readability. I often have to drop observations where any of several conditions is true. Writing this using `filter()` usually requires complex use of negation and parentheses, even if there are no missings to be concerned about. Understanding and explaining these statements in my code is fraught to say the least.

I propose a new `dplyr` function called `drop_if()`. It would drop all rows meeting any condition specified. This would greatly reduce the need to use `!()` and would also keep observations that are missing any of the references variables in the resulting data set by default.

The way I wrote this out for now is straightforward to understand but likely not efficient from a computational standpoint (filter to keep observations matching the condition then using `anti_join()` to drop them from the original data set). 

```r
library(tidyverse)

mpg_miss <- mpg %>% 
  mutate(
    class = na_if(class, "pickup"),
    cty   = na_if(cty, 18)
  )

mpg_miss_rown <- mpg_miss %>% 
  mutate(rown = row_number())

# if we want to drop where class is "suv" or cty < 15, temp df of these
keep <- mpg_miss_rown %>% 
  filter(
    class == "suv" | cty < 15
  ) %>% 
  select(rown)

keep %>% 
  nrow()
## [1] 89

drop <- mpg_miss_rown %>% 
  anti_join(keep) %>% 
  select(-rown)
## Joining, by = "rown"

drop %>% nrow()
## [1] 145

# drops if class or cty is NA
mpg_miss %>% 
  filter(!(class == "suv" | cty < 15)) %>% 
  nrow()
## [1] 114

# annoying syntax but produces desired result
mpg_miss %>% 
  filter(!(class == "suv" | cty < 15) | (is.na(class) & !cty < 15) | (class != "suv" & is.na(cty)))  %>%
  nrow()
## [1] 145

## Not run:
# What syntax could look like:
mpg_miss %>% 
  drop_if(class == "suv" | cty < 15)
## End(**Not run**)
```

title: Unexpected behavior in `filter()` when column name matches an environment variable
description:
A friend and I have both encountered unexpected behavior from `filter()` and struggled to debug it until realizing that `filter()` was comparing a column against itself, instead of against a variable of the same name that had been defined elsewhere in the environment (for example, as a function argument).

```r
library(dplyr)

# mtcars has 32 rows originally
nrow(mtcars)
# > [1] 32

# should show that 11 cars have 4 cylinders
mtcars |> filter(cyl == 4) |> nrow()
# > [1] 11

# should also show that 11 cars have 4 cylinders
cyl <- 4
mtcars |> filter(cyl == cyl) |> nrow()
# > [1] 32
```

Possible solutions:

- `filter()` warns when comparing a column against itself (which would return all rows), much like it warns when using a single `=` instead of double equal `==`
- `filter()` first looks to the environment for a defined variable of the same name as the column when a column is possibly compared against itself

title: `if_else` being strict about object length
description:
I am trying to understand whether this is expected behaviour from `if_else`:

```r
x <- character(0)
if_else(!length(x), NA_character_, x)
#> Error in `if_else()`:
#> ! `false` must have size 1, not size 0.
#> Run `rlang::last_trace()` to see where the error occurred.
```

(I presume that 'size' means 'length' in this context, but I'm definitely no expert in the terminology that should be used here -- apologies if I'm misunderstanding the error message.)

Part of the reason why this is happening seems to be that, [quoting](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6728) @DavisVaughan, "the true and false arguments are always evaluated, regardless of whether their values are seen in the result." However, the example above is about length/size rather than type.

The same code works with base R:

```r
ifelse(!length(x), NA_character_, x)
#> NA

na_if_empty <- function(x) if(length(x)) x else NA_character_
na_if_empty(x)
#> NA
```

Is there any way to perform something like the above with `if_else`, or is the function deliberately strict on object length, and I should therefore use base R instead when I need to replace an 0-length string with `NA`?

title: Descending mixed multiple column ranking with `pick()` and `rank()`
description:
---
Hi I just would like to bring this up since I stumble upon this certain use case wonder what the development team thinks!
combine `pick()` and `rank()` family like `dense_rank()` can help me get the rank of row I wanted, but what if I want to descending order for some of the column? 
Right now the method I can think of are rather hacky 

```r
df <- tibble(
  Gene = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"),
  Percent_expressed = c(0.3,0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.1),
  Expression = c(3, 2, 10, 2, 1),
  p_val_adj = c(0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0.001, 0.005)
) %>% glimpse
```


### Scenario 1: Higher Expression and Percent_expressed have "higher" rank 
```r
# [Wrong way ..]
# A. Use "-column_name" will just remove the column inside `pick()`
df %>% mutate(rank = dense_rank(pick(-Expression, -Percent_expressed))) %>% arrange(rank) %>% glimpse

# [Cause Errors]
# B. Use desc per column will cause issue
df %>% mutate(rank = dense_rank(pick(desc(.$Expression), Percent_expressed))) %>% arrange(rank) %>% glimpse
# Caused by error in `pick()`:
# ! Problem while evaluating `desc(Expression)`.
# Caused by error in `obj_check_vector()`:
# ! object 'Expression' not found

# [Cause Errors]
# B2. or with .$Expression sill give error
df %>% mutate(rank = dense_rank(pick(desc(.$Expression), Percent_expressed))) %>% arrange(rank) %>% glimpse
# Caused by error in `pick()`:
# ! Selections can't have negative values.

# [Cause Errors]
# C. Use desc() outside pick() will double the length of the vector
df %>% mutate(rank = dense_rank(desc(pick(Expression, Percent_expressed)))) %>% arrange(rank) %>% glimpse
# Caused by error:
# ! `rank` must be size 5 or 1, not 10.

# [Works but hacky]
# D. The hacky way I think of is to wrap dense_rank outside dense_rank to work for me
df %>% mutate(rank = dense_rank(-dense_rank(pick(Expression, Percent_expressed)))) %>% arrange(rank) %>% glimpse
```

### Scenario 2: Higher Expression and Percent_expressed + lower p_val_adj have "higher" rank
```r
# [Works but hacky]
# E. And if we want mixed orders, e.g. descending in Expression and Percent_expressed, and ascending order
# I can think of is to create negative p_val_adj and rank on that
# This way can be cumbersome if we have many columns to rank on.
df %>% mutate(n_p_val_adj = -p_val_adj) %>% 
    mutate(rank = dense_rank(-dense_rank(pick(n_p_val_adj, Expression, Percent_expressed)))) %>% arrange(rank) %>%
    #select(-n_p_val_adj) %>% 
    arrange(rank) %>% 
    glimpse

# [Works but hacky]
# F. Currently, alternative implementation I can think of is arrange on each column and then use row_number()
df %>% arrange(p_val_adj, desc(Expression), desc(Percent_expressed)) %>% 
    mutate(rank = row_number()) %>% arrange(rank) %>% glimpse
```
Since `pick()` is relative new implementation as I can see from discussion, I wonder if `arrange()` like behavior that work with `desc()` would be part of the consideration?
Or if there's some simpler way to think about this I overlooked? Thanks!!

title: `case_when()` needs to throw a better error when conditions are matrices
description:
Please briefly describe your problem and what output you expect. If you have a question, please don't use this form. Instead, ask on <https://stackoverflow.com/> or <https://community.rstudio.com/>.

Please include a minimal reproducible example (AKA a reprex). If you've never heard of a [reprex](http://reprex.tidyverse.org/) before, start by reading <https://www.tidyverse.org/help/#reprex>.

---

I had some code that was passing matrices as the conditions to a `case_when` statement. Previously, `case_when` would implicitly convert these matrices to vectors, but at some point it stopped doing that. However, I don't think this was an intentional behavior change, because depending on how exactly one calls `case_when` on matrix conditions, it can produce one of several different error messages or return a value of the wrong length (see reprex below demonstrating 3 different behaviors). None of the error messages hint at the underlying problem, which made debugging this issue after a package update very difficult.

If passing matrices as the conditions to `case_when` is not an intended usage, I would expect it to produce an interpretable error message to that effect.

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(assertthat)

x <- matrix(rnorm(36), ncol = 6)

## Each of the following generates a different error
{
  y1 <- case_when(
    !is.finite(x) ~ "Invalid",
    .default = "Default"
  )
  assert_that(length(y1) == length(x))
}
#> Error: length(y1) not equal to length(x)

{
  y2 <- case_when(
    !is.finite(x) ~ "Invalid",
    x < 0 ~ "Negative",
    .default = "Default"
  )
  assert_that(length(y2) == length(x))
}
#> Error in `vec_slice()`:
#> ! Can't subset elements past the end.
#> ℹ Locations 8, 10, 13, …, 35, and 36 don't exist.
#> ℹ There are only 6 elements.
#> Backtrace:
#>     ▆
#>  1. ├─dplyr::case_when(...)
#>  2. │ └─dplyr:::vec_case_when(...)
#>  3. │   └─vctrs::vec_slice(value, loc)
#>  4. └─vctrs (local) `<fn>`()
#>  5.   └─vctrs:::stop_subscript_oob(...)
#>  6.     └─vctrs:::stop_subscript(...)
#>  7.       └─rlang::abort(...)

{
  y3 <- case_when(
    !is.finite(x) ~ "Invalid",
    x < 0 ~ "Negative",
    x > 0 ~ "Positive",
    x == 0 ~ "Zero"
  )
  assert_that(length(y3) == length(x))
}
#> Error in if (!any(are_unused)) {: missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

## Everything works fine if you convert x to a vector
{
  xvec <- as.vector(x)
  yvec <- case_when(
    !is.finite(xvec) ~ "Invalid",
    xvec < 0 ~ "Negative",
    xvec > 0 ~ "Positive",
    xvec == 0 ~ "Zero"
  )
  assert_that(length(yvec) == length(xvec))
}
#> [1] TRUE
```

title: `mutate` superseding `transmute` should allow ordering columns
description:
I recently noticed that `transmute` has been marked as superseded by `mutate(.keep="none")`. However, it turned out that `mutate` doesn't replicate column ordering behavior of `transmute`, but does something odd:

```r
> data.frame(a=1, b=2) %>% transmute(a, x=b*2, b)
  a x b
1 1 4 2
> data.frame(a=1, b=2) %>% mutate(a, x=b*2, b, .keep="none")
  a b x
1 1 2 4
```
With more complex examples, the ordering becomes pretty confusing and difficult to explain. I'm guessing this may have to do with the `.keep = "used"` use case resorting things. For `.keep = "none"`, explicit column ordering as given, replicating or approximating `transmute` behavior,  would be much more useful (e.g. order of first LHS mention or last LHS mention).

title: `case_when` within `mutate` loses variable labels
description:
Maybe this is expected/not a bug, but it seems that `case_when()` within `mutate()` loses variable labels, although `mutate()` alone or with `replace()` doesn't. Reprex:

``` r
suppressWarnings(suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr)))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(sjlabelled))

data <- readRDS(url("https://osf.io/d4mjk/?action=download"))

get_label(data$Status)
#>          Status 
#> "Response Type"

data <- data %>% 
  mutate(Status = Status + 1)

get_label(data$Status)
#>          Status 
#> "Response Type"

data <- data %>% 
  mutate(Status = replace(Status, Status == 1, 50))

get_label(data$Status)
#>          Status 
#> "Response Type"

data <- data %>% 
  mutate(Status = case_when(Status == 50 ~ 1))

get_label(data$Status)
#> NULL
```

<sup>Created on 2023-05-23 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>


Could it be because `case_when()` is vectorized? And given that I wish to preserve labels, what workaround would you recommend? Falling back to `replace()`? Thank you.

# Edit: 

Linked to #5762. Which suggested `recode()` as the workaround. However, `recode()` has been superseded by `case_match()`.

But `case_match()` does not seem to solve the issue:

``` r
suppressWarnings(suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr)))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(sjlabelled))

data <- readRDS(url("https://osf.io/d4mjk/?action=download"))

get_label(data$Status)
#>          Status 
#> "Response Type"

data <- data %>% 
  mutate(Status = case_match(Status, 1 ~ 50))

get_label(data$Status)
#> NULL
```

title: Adjusting to different behaviour between `case_match` and `recode`
description:
Since `recode` is being superseded, I'm looking at changing to `case_match`. I usually use it to reverse code an integer vector (e.g. 1 -> 5,  5 -> 1, etc.) and have found named list/vector useful but `case_match` doesn't accept the same. 
The named list approach is useful to include `recode` in other functions as named list are more straightforward to produce. 
How should I adapt here? 

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

x <- rep(1:5, 5)
#This still works
dplyr::recode(x, !!!setNames(1:5, 5:1))
#>  [1] 5 4 3 2 1 5 4 3 2 1 5 4 3 2 1 5 4 3 2 1 5 4 3 2 1
#This does not work
dplyr::case_match(x, !!!setNames(1:5, 5:1))
#> Error in `dplyr::case_match()`:
#> ! Case 1 (`!!!setNames(1:5, 5:1)`) must be a two-sided formula, not the
#>   number 1.

#>     ▆

#>  4.       └─base::mapply(.f, .x, .y, MoreArgs = list(...), SIMPLIFY = FALSE)

#>  7.             └─rlang::abort(message, call = error_call)
```

title: Possible regression re. use of glue in dplyr::across
description:
This is discussed in https://twitter.com/mjskay/status/1660770865087148032

Essentially, users are reporting errors when using `glue` inside an anonymous function given to `dplyr::across()`. This error did not previously exist.

On [my setup](https://twitter.com/jimjam_slam/status/1659392114994839553?s=20), with R 4.2.2 on macOS, and with dplyr 1.0.10 and glue 1.6.2, the following works to modify two columns:

```r
library(dplyr)
library(glue)
mtcars |> mutate(across(c(mpg, cyl), \(x) glue("Oh hai {x}")))
```

![image](https://github.com/tidyverse/glue/assets/6520659/2843bd11-13a7-408a-b100-1769c79529d9)

But [Matthew Kay reports](https://twitter.com/mjskay/status/1659381134273150977?s=20) that they get an error, unless they add dots to the anonymous function or save it to a variable before passing it to `across`:

![image](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/assets/6520659/f33ce5ec-a5f5-4cb9-bf2e-94e049bcba39)

[Cameron Patrick](https://twitter.com/camjpatrick/status/1659376009375027200?s=20) also gets an error on R 4.2.3 for Windows with dplyr 1.1.1 and glue 1.6.2 (the same version of glue as me). They get this using the purrr anonymous function syntax:

![image](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/assets/6520659/83c6b1c8-65d2-4b76-9801-ff93273e077c)


I'm not sure whether this is a problem with glue, dplyr or an interaction between the two, but as the version of glue between my successful reprex and Cameron's unsuccessful one isn't changed, I've chosen to file here.

title: Improve error message for joining ordered factors?
description:
Would it be possible to improve the error message that is displayed when one is trying to join ordered factors (ordinal data) with different levels?

```r

+                  D.2 = factor(c(4,5,3,1,2), ordered = TRUE),
+                  F.4 = c(5,4,3,2,1))
> df1$D.2
[1] 4 5 3 1 2
Levels: 1 < 2 < 3 < 4 < 5
> 
> df2 <- data.frame(D.1 = c(6,2,3,4,1),

+                                ordered = TRUE,
+                                levels = c(1,2,3,4,5,NA)))
> df2$D.2
[1] <NA> 3    3    5    1   
Levels: 1 < 2 < 3 < 4 < 5 < <NA>

Joining with `by = join_by(D.1, D.2)`

Run `rlang::last_trace()` to see where the error occurred.
```

title: case_when misbehaves if logical(0) in LHS
description:
Thanks for reading this report. Recently I encountered that when dealing with NULL, the behaviour of case_when function does not meet my expectation. Here is an example:
```r
#library(dplyr)
case_when(is.null(NULL) ~ 1, NULL == NA ~ 2, .default = 3)
```
Since the arguments are evaluated in order, the expected return value is ought to be 1 since the result of LHS in first arguments is TRUE, but it actually returns numeric(0). Here is a simpler example:
```r
#library(dplyr)
case_when(TRUE ~ 1, logical(0) == NA ~ 2, .default = 3)
```
Actually I'm not very sure whether it is a bug or just by design. If I'm wrong, please tell me.

description:

title: slice_sample() uses statistically incorrect sampling algorithms
description:
`slice_sample()` relies on `base::sample.int()` which in turn relies on incorrect sampling algorithms. The difficulty of obtaining appropriate unequal probability samples is obscure and is not known outside of survey statistics. I don't want to go into base R code although they have to fix that, too (somewhat more surprising given that Thomas Lumley, one of the core R people, is a survey statistician, at least part time). The appropriate algorithms are implemented in `sampling::UPmaxentropy()`.

```r
# example from Tille (2006)
set.seed(25)
uneq_p = c(0.07,0.17,0.41,0.61,0.83,0.91)
sim_uneq_p <- as.data.frame(matrix(rep(0,6*20000),ncol=6))
for (k in 1:nrow(sim_uneq_p)) {
  this <- sample.int(n=length(uneq_p),size=sum(uneq_p),prob=uneq_p)
  sim_uneq_p[k,this] <- 1
}
colSums(sim_uneq_p)/nrow(sim_uneq_p)
uneq_p
# done right
sim_uneq_p_done_right <- as.data.frame(matrix(rep(0,6*20000),ncol=6))
for (k in 1:nrow(sim_uneq_p_done_right)) {
   sim_uneq_p_done_right[k,] <- sampling::UPmaxentropy(uneq_p)
}
colSums(sim_uneq_p_done_right)/nrow(sim_uneq_p_done_right)
uneq_p
```

@krlmlr @DavisVaughan 

Code in `sampling` is (kinda) ugly, and the development most likely does not satisfy the `tidyverse` standards. I don't know if you want to rely on this as a dependency. Relevant parts may need to be taken over and internalized. (I have written the unequal probability sampling code from scratch in Stata, so I am closely familiar with the methodology and what it takes to code it.)

title: `setops` unexpectedly unnest complex columns
description:
Hi,

This bug pertains to all `setops`, but here is a reprex using `setdiff()`:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
a = data.frame(x=1:2, v=package_version(c("4.0", "2.0.0.0.0.0.0.8")))
b = data.frame(x=1:2, v=package_version(c("1.0", "3.0")))
x = dplyr::setdiff(a, b)
x
#>   x v....1 v....2 v....3 v....4 v....5 v....6 v....7 v....8
#> 1 1      4      0      0      0      0      0      0      0
#> 2 2      2      0      0      0      0      0      0      8

```

A little workaround in the meantime:

```r
to_package_version = function(x){
  if(is.package_version(x)) return(x)
  package_version(apply(x, 1, \(.x){
    i=max(which(.x>0), 2)
    paste(.x[1:i], collapse=".")
  }))
}

dplyr::setdiff(a, b) %>% 
  mutate(v=to_package_version(v))
#>   x               v
#> 1 1             4.0
#> 2 2 2.0.0.0.0.0.0.8
```

**EDIT:** 

This issue might have rather been posted on `vctrs` in the first place, as `vctrs::vec_set_difference(a, b)` has the same output. The number of 8 columns comes from an agnostic proxy in [vctrs/R/type-misc.R#L34](https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/8af47522399e449e16dbddb1c9b4676c2c143c5f/R/type-misc.R#L34).
Sorry for the crossposting, I should have checked better.

title: `.by` creates different row order as `group_by()`
description:
The new `.by` does not seem to sort the results of **`summarize()`** or **`reframe()`** by factor levels. This causes an inconsistency to `group_by()`:

```r
lev <- c("A", "B", "C")

X <- data.frame(x = 1:3, g = factor(rev(lev), levels = lev))

X %>% group_by(g) %>% summarize(mean(x))  # A B C
X %>% summarize(mean(x), .by = g)         # C B A
```

Introducing a `.sort` argument as suggested in https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6663 would be great!

title: group_by creates new/false columns when a named vector is used in an across(all_of()) selection
description:
I noticed recently that in dplyr (1.1.2), I receive some unexpected and unfortunate additional columns if I used a named vector in an `all_of` selection for `group_by`. I would have expected just the values of the vector to be returned as grouping variables, but I also get the names of the selection vector as additional columns. This causes some problems in my application and seems like an unintended side effect.

```r
library(dplyr)

df <- data.frame(
  a=sample(letters[1:3], size=20, replace=TRUE),
  id=rep(1:5, each=4),
  y=rnorm(20)
)

gcols <- c("a", "id") %>% setNames(c("a_col", "id_col"))

# peculiar
df %>% group_by(across(all_of(gcols))) %>%
  filter(row_number()==1L)

# expected
df %>% group_by(across(all_of(unname(gcols)))) %>%
  filter(row_number()==1L)
```

title: Performance regression for dplyr::rowwise() introduced in version 1.1.0
description:
It seems that a performance regression has been introduced for `dplyr::rowwise()` in `{dplyr}` version 1.1.0.

I give some reprexes below illustrating large differences in execution time when using this on v1.1 compared to v1.0.10.
 * A: Execution of the function `test_code`, which uses `dplyr::rowwise()`, is fast in v1.0.10: **1.86 seconds**.
 * B: The same example is much slower in v1.1.0: **51.5 seconds**.
   * B2: Execution time of a function called `test_code_without_rowwise`, which is modified not to use `dplyr::rowwise()` doesn't suffer these slowdowns: **0.337 seconds**.
 * C: Execution of the function `test_code`, which uses `dplyr::rowwise()`, is a similar duration in v1.1.1: **52.2 seconds**.

These seem to indicate that usage in `dplyr::rowwise` in v1.1.0+ is much slower than previous versions.

*Note that we are using collapsable sections to improve readability of the code below. The functions in the collapsable sections are part of the reprexes.*

A: Using `dplyr::rowwise()` in v1.0.10
---
Execution of the function `test_code`, which uses `dplyr::rowwise()`, is fast in v1.0.10: **1.86 seconds**.

Note that the timer starts after the package is installed.

<summary>**Click to show definitions of functions which are part of this reprex**</summary>

``` r
    rowwise() %>%
    mutate(
      col1 = recode(
```

title: Is it possible to NOT deprecate by = character() in _join - or how to rework the below code when it happens?
description:
The problem: I calculate hierarchical percentages, where a denominator for the current group is nominator for the parent group. The "top" level row is labelled 100% and is simply divided by itself*.

/ *because the exact value of N and Ntot is required to pass later into a procedure calculating the confidence interval for the %, so no - it cannot be just fixed at 1. /

Later I'm going to show you how the title of this issue relates to my problem. Not let's generate some data.
```
data <- structure(list(SOC = c("SOC1", "SOC1", "SOC1", "SOC1", "SOC2", 
"SOC2", "SOC2", "SOC3", "SOC3", "SOC1", "SOC1", "SOC1", "SOC2", 
"SOC5", "SOC5", "SOC10", "SOC11", "SOC11", "SOC1", "SOC1", "SOC1", 
"SOC1", "SOC2", "SOC2"), PT = c("PT1-1", "PT1-1", "PT1-2", "PT1-3", 
"PT2-1", "PT2-1", "PT2-2", "PT3-3", "PT3-4", "PT1-1", "PT1-1", 
"PT1-2", NA, "PT5-10", "PT5-2", "PT10-2", "PT11-1", "PT11-2", 
"PT1-1", "PT1-1", "PT1-2", "PT1-3", "PT2-1", "PT2-2"), ARM = c("SoC", 
"SoC", "SoC", "SoC", "SoC", "SoC", "SoC", "SoC", "SoC", "Arm1", 
"Arm1", "Arm1", "Arm1", "Arm1", "Arm1", "Arm1", "Arm1", "Arm1", 
"SoC", "SoC", "SoC", "SoC", "SoC", "SoC"), SIDE = c("LEFT", "LEFT", 
"LEFT", "RIGHT", "RIGHT", "RIGHT", "RIGHT", "RIGHT", "LEFT", 
"RIGHT", "RIGHT", "LEFT", "LEFT", "LEFT", "LEFT", "LEFT", "RIGHT", 
"RIGHT", "LEFT", "LEFT", "RIGHT", "LEFT", "RIGHT", "RIGHT")), row.names = c(NA, 
24L), class = "data.frame")
```
which gives (head):
```
> head(o)
   SOC    PT ARM  SIDE
1 SOC1 PT1-1 SoC  LEFT
2 SOC1 PT1-1 SoC  LEFT
3 SOC1 PT1-2 SoC  LEFT
4 SOC1 PT1-3 SoC RIGHT
5 SOC2 PT2-1 SoC RIGHT
6 SOC2 PT2-1 SoC RIGHT
.... and so on
```

Let's run some exemplary code, that calculates the denominators I use later in my code. It's sufficient here to share only this part of the code:

```{r}
# First, the grouping columns
> grp_cols <- c("ARM", "SOC")

# Now - the sequences of grouping columns, defining levels of the denominators.

> sequences_of_cols <- sapply(seq(from = length(grp_cols), to=1), function(s) grp_cols[seq(s)])
> sequences_of_cols <- c(sequences_of_cols, list(character(0))) # will make the "top" total

> sequences_of_cols
[[1]]
[1] "ARM" "SOC"

[[2]]
[1] "ARM"

[[3]]
character(0)  # this is for the top row. Using it facilitates my code a lot later with left_join()
 
# Now the code calculating the denominators per each level of grouping
> lapply(sequences_of_cols, 
        function(s) 
            data %>% 
            group_by(across(all_of(s))) %>%
            summarize(.groups = "drop") %>% 
            left_join( data %>%
                       group_by(across(all_of(head(s, -1)))) %>%
                           summarize(n_tot = n()),
                       by = head(s, -1))) 
[[1]]
# A tibble: 8 × 3
  ARM   SOC   n_tot
  <chr> <chr> <int>
1 Arm1  SOC1      9
2 Arm1  SOC10     9
3 Arm1  SOC11     9
4 Arm1  SOC2      9
5 Arm1  SOC5      9
6 SoC   SOC1     15
7 SoC   SOC2     15
8 SoC   SOC3     15

[[2]]
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  ARM   n_tot
  <chr> <int>
1 Arm1     24
2 SoC      24

[[3]]
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  n_tot
  <int>
1    24
```

I need exactly this format of the list.
See? The left_join() handles both non-empty vector of "parent" columns (minus the last one), and when it's empty - it just gives me the n_tot without the column names (that's why I couldn't join by anything).

And I would be very happy about this code, if it didn't tell me that: 

> "Using `by = character()` to perform a cross join was deprecated in dplyr 1.1.0."

which means this is unsafe and I cannot rely on it.
Theoretically I should conditionally use either left_join() or cross_join(), but this overcomplicates the above code :(

```{r}
> lapply(sequences_of_cols, 
+        function(s) 
+            data %>% 
+            group_by(across(all_of(s))) %>%
+            summarize(.groups = "drop") %>% 
+            {
+                x <- .
+                tmp <- data %>%  group_by(across(all_of(head(s, -1)))) %>% summarize(n_tot = n())
+                
+                if(length(head(s, -1)) > 0)  
+                    left_join(x, tmp, by = head(s, -1)) %>% return()
+                 else 
+                    tmp  %>% return()  # or cross_join(), if there were some other columns in the "x" I want to preserve
+            })
[[1]]
# A tibble: 8 × 3
  ARM   SOC   n_tot
  <chr> <chr> <int>
1 Arm1  SOC1      9
2 Arm1  SOC10     9
3 Arm1  SOC11     9
4 Arm1  SOC2      9
5 Arm1  SOC5      9
6 SoC   SOC1     15
7 SoC   SOC2     15
8 SoC   SOC3     15

[[2]]
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  ARM   n_tot
  <chr> <int>
1 Arm1     24
2 SoC      24

[[3]]
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  n_tot
  <int>
1    24
```
But those "inline {}" look a bit weird to me, moreover they don't seem to work with the new |> operator.

If only I could use the left_join() without the warning of deprecation, it would be great. Couldn't you leave this functionality for backward compatibility, especially that you provide now the explicit cross_join(), so people can use it easily without specifying by=character())?

Or maybe there is another way to achieve the same without this {} or creating helper functions like "my_join()" combining the two? The format of the list needs to be as shown, including the "top" row.

title: Inconsistent behavior of rolling join depending on the order of the arguments of `join_by`
description:
I ran into an issue that arises specifically when using a rolling join paired with an additional inequality condition. The resulting joined dataset differs depending on the order of the join criteria. It seems like to get the right result I need to put the `closest()` statement as the second one in `join_by()`.

In the reprex below I am looking for the next value that is above `x` by more than 1. To do so, I create a variable `y = x + 1` and then join on `x$b < y$a` to match my condition, and by `closest(x$id < y$id)` to get the closest next match. Depending on the order of the join criteria, I get different results.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
n <- 1e2
set.seed(123)
test <- tibble(id = 1:n, a = rnorm(n)) %>%
  mutate(b = a + 1)

res1 <- test %>%
  left_join(test,
            join_by(closest(x$id < y$id), x$b < y$a))

res2 <- test %>%
  left_join(test,
            join_by(x$b < y$a, closest(x$id < y$id)))

waldo::compare(res1, res2)
#> old vs new
#>              id.y       a.y      b.y
#> - old[1, ]     NA        NA       NA
#> + new[1, ]      3 1.5587083 2.558708
#>   old[2, ]      3 1.5587083 2.558708
#>   old[3, ]     NA        NA       NA
#>   old[4, ]      6 1.7150650 2.715065
```

title: `summarise()` warns about < 1 row when there are 0 groups
description:
`summarise()` now warns if more (or less) than 1 row per `summarise()` group is returned, however when the number of groups are 0 (e.g. in the case of a data frame with 0 rows), I would expect that 0 groups * 1 row = 0 so this warning would not be shown, i.e. this warning should only occur if the returned number of rows is different than the number of groups.

This is a convoluted, but minimal reprex...
``` r
library(dplyr)

packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '1.1.2.9000'

starwars %>% 
  filter(grepl("^D", species)) %>% 
  group_by(species) %>% 
  summarise(sex = unique(sex), .groups = "keep")
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#> # Groups:   species [2]
#>   species sex

starwars %>%
```

title: `coalesce()` silently coerces `NaN` to `NA`
description:
I was fixing [some Arrow test failures](https://github.com/apache/arrow/issues/35131) which are the result of the dev version of waldo correctly distinguishing between `NA_real_` and `NaN`, and came across this behaviour where `NaN` values are silently coerced by `dplyr::coalesce()` into `NA`s.  

I'm unsure if this is a bug or just a difference in implementations/interpretations, but the second row in the `cwx` column in the example below is making me think it could be a bug?

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(arrow)

df <- tibble(
  w = c(NaN, NaN, NA_real_),
  x = c(NA_real_, NaN, 3.3),
  y = c(NA_real_, 2.2, 3.3),
  z = c(1.1, 2.2, 3.3)
)

df %>%
  mutate(
    cw = coalesce(w),
    cz = coalesce(z),
    cwx = coalesce(w, x),
    cwxy = coalesce(w, x, y),
    cwxyz = coalesce(w, x, y, z)
  )
#> # A tibble: 3 × 9
#>       w     x     y     z    cw    cz   cwx  cwxy cwxyz
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1   NaN  NA    NA     1.1    NA   1.1  NA    NA     1.1
#> 2   NaN NaN     2.2   2.2    NA   2.2  NA     2.2   2.2
#> 3    NA   3.3   3.3   3.3    NA   3.3   3.3   3.3   3.3

df %>%
  arrow_table() %>%
  mutate(
    cw = coalesce(w),
    cz = coalesce(z),
    cwx = coalesce(w, x),
    cwxy = coalesce(w, x, y),
    cwxyz = coalesce(w, x, y, z)
  ) %>%
  collect()
#> # A tibble: 3 × 9
#>       w     x     y     z    cw    cz   cwx  cwxy cwxyz
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1   NaN  NA    NA     1.1   NaN   1.1  NA    NA     1.1
#> 2   NaN NaN     2.2   2.2   NaN   2.2 NaN     2.2   2.2
#> 3    NA   3.3   3.3   3.3    NA   3.3   3.3   3.3   3.3
```

title: `na_if()` throws an error on unknown levels of a factor
description:
Hi,

Since` dplyr 1.1.0`, `na_if()` is stricter about type stability.

While this might be a very good thing in most cases, it can get quite awkward when dealing with factors.

For instance, consider this example:

``` r
library(dplyr)
x=factor(letters)
na_if(x, "a")
#>  [1] <NA> b    c    d    e    f    g    h    i    j    k    l    m    n    o   
#> [16] p    q    r    s    t    u    v    w    x    y    z   
#> Levels: a b c d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z
na_if(x, "aa")
#> Error in `na_if()`:
#> ! Can't convert from `y` <character> to `x` <factor<754f0>> due to loss of generality.
```

<sup>Created on 2023-04-24 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

The breaking change is significant in a project where I have to deal with multiple factors with different levels but sharing a common NA level. 

`forcats::fct_na_level_to_value()` seems to work in place though. If this is the correct way to deal with factors, maybe it could be worth documenting?

title: Breaking changes between minor versions.
description:
This [commit](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/commit/178d168e29334d4d35563827cfb14cc6fa0cc076) was part of the recent 1.1.0 to 1.1.1 bump. I use version 1.1.1 and received a warning in some code that the `left_join` I was using on a tibble was many-to-many and it suggested I use `relationship='many-to-many'` to suppress the warning which I did. 

A colleague of mine uses dplyr version 1.1.0 and tried to run my code. The code broke because on his version `relationship` is not a valid parameter for `left_join`. 

I just wanted to bring this up because it's unexpected that a minor version bump could encourage the writing of backward incompatible code. My apologies for not going into more detail with a reprex but I expect that is not necessary in this case.

title: Documentation: misleading code sample in the `rowwise` vignette
description:
There are two code blocks, which are seemingly equivalent:

```r
rf %>% mutate(total = sum(c_across(where(is.numeric))))
```
and
```r
df %>% mutate(total = rowSums(pick(where(is.numeric))))
```

The problem is that the second one is summing up also the values from the `id` column.

The `rowSums` snippet is in [this chapter](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/rowwise.html#row-wise-summary-functions), the `sum` variant slightly above.

title: Consider allowing `.env$` in `join_by()`
description:
Motivated by https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6821

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

df1 <- tibble(
  X1 = c("chr1", "chr2"),
  a = c(1, 2)
)

df2 <- tibble(
  X2 = c("chr2", "chr3"),
  b = c(3, 4)
)

by.1 <- "X1"
by.2 <- "X2"

# The "old" way
# inner_join(df1, df2, by = setNames(by.2, by.1))

# This works but we don't typically encourage using `!!` in high level APIs
inner_join(df1, df2, by = join_by(!!by.1 == !!by.2))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   X1        a     b
#>   <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 chr2      2     3
 
# It might be nice to be able to do this, but it currently errors
inner_join(df1, df2, by = join_by(.env$by.1 == .env$by.2))
#> Error in `join_by()`:
#> ! The left-hand side of a `$` expression must be either `x$` or `y$`.
#> ℹ Expression 1 contains `.env$by.1`.
```

Some notes from talking with @lionel-:
- We have an equivalent-ish to `.data$` already with `x$` and `y$`. They don't have a `.` prefix because I attempted to match the original argument names
- So it seems like we are missing an equivalent to the `.env$` pronoun, and we may as well call it `.env$` here too
- It would look up in the `caller_env()` of `join_by()`, and I don't think `join_by()` would get an `env = caller_env()` argument to "pass the env through" unlike what is done in `glue()`.
- It would look up using `inherits = TRUE`, because it seems like tidy eval does this too, and we generally think that makes sense
- It would require the result to be a single string, or die trying. i.e. you can only use this to inject a single name from the environment, not to inject an entire expression

description:
I feel inequality operators `!=` or `<>`  should also be part of `join_by()`.  To understand the usage, let's see this question on stack overflow.  

---
The problem is simple enough - we have data of customer orders with `order_date` and `ship_date`.  If we want to find those orders where any customer orders before shipping of any of the previous order.  This question was put up on [stack overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/q/63975054/2884859).

We can now do it with `join_by` but we cannot get the `!=` inside here, so we will have to filter out those rows in next operation.


```r

                               "C"), order_id = structure(1:7, .Label = c("1", "2", "3", "4", 
                                                                          "5", "6", "7"), class = "factor"), order_date = structure(c(17897, 
                                                                                                                                      17901, 17912, 17901, 17902, 17903, 17905), class = "Date"), ship_date = structure(c(17926, 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                          17906, 17914, 17904, 17904, 17904, 17906), class = "Date")), row.names = c(NA, 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     -7L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))


library(dplyr)
#>

df %>% 
  inner_join(df, 
             by = join_by(customer_id == customer_id,
```

title: `filter()` when iterator and function's argument have the same name
description:
I'd like to filter a dataframe within a function based on a condition passed as an argument. If the argument is created as an iterator in a for-loop, and this has the same name of the dataframe variable to filter on, `{{` does not work as intended unless I first use the argument somehow. 

Consider 
```r
library(tidyverse)

f <- function(Species) {
    iris %>%
        filter(Species == {{ Species }}) %>%
        distinct(Species) %>%
        print()
}
```

This will work

```r
f(Species = "setosa")

#   Species
# 1  setosa
```

but this will not
```r
for (Species in c("setosa")) {
    f(Species = Species)
}

#      Species
# 1     setosa
# 2 versicolor
# 3  virginica
```

If I use the variable passed as argument (a `print` is just enough), then it works
```r
f2 <- function(Species) {
    print(Species) # <--- I added this

    iris %>%
        filter(Species == {{ Species }}) %>%
        distinct(Species) %>%
        print()
}

for (Species in c("setosa")) {
    f2(Species = Species)
}

# [1] "setosa"
#   Species
# 1  setosa
```

I realize that this is somehow a niche use case. Is this behavior as expected? Would you be able to help?

title: Create aliases for core verbs to help exiles from excel-land
description:
The meaning of `gather` and `spread` were self-explanatory. Until they weren't. Having been teaching R/tidyverse to people who have only previously worked with crazy formatted excel spreadsheets, the meaning of `filter`, `select` and friends is equally confusing to them. 

If you want to get certain columns then it is reasonable to `filter` out those columns. If you want to get certain rows it is reasonable to `select` those rows. If you want to change the order in which columns appear, it is reasonable to `arrange` the columns. And when you are used to keeping variables as rows rather than columns (as in common in excel since it often makes data entry easier) it takes a bit of mental effort to get your head around the fact that `mutate` works on columns.

My suggestion is to make the following set of aliases for common dplyr verbs:

```
summarise: summarise_df
filter: filter_rows
distinct: distinct_rows
slice: slice_rows
arrange: arrange_rows
pull: pull_col
select: select_cols
mutate: mutate_cols
transmute: transmute_cols
rename: rename_cols
```

These aliases wouldn't impact any existing code and would provide additional hints to learners reducing cognitive load. There are already plenty of other dplyr verbs that are phrases (`left_join`, `group_by`, `bind_cols`, etc) so it wouldn't be out of keeping with the current naming conventions.

Making these basic functions more self-explanatory clearly increases verbosity (though since it is just an alias, it is entirely opt-in from the user's point of view), but it would make it that little bit quicker for learners to start doing useful work with R and make those pedagogically all-important early wins that little bit faster and easier.

title: How to adjust to different behavior of across .fn argument passing in dplyr 1.1.1 vs. 1.0.10?
description:
I have a summarizing function that's similar to the function below. It allows the user to pass grouping variables, summary variables and any number of summary functions as arguments. 

```
# Allow user to choose summary function(s)
fnc = function(data, summary.vars=NULL, group.vars=NULL, 
               FUNS=c(mean=~mean(., na.rm=TRUE))) {

    group_by(across({{group.vars}})) %>%

                            .fn=FUNS,
```

title: `if_any` function not removing NAs in `filter` where `across` will remove NA
description:
In this example I am trying to remove rows that have any NA's. I tried using `if_any` but noticed that it doesn't work. Below is an example where I compare `across` and `if_any` where `across` does the job but results in a warning. I don't believe I am using the `if_any` function incorrectly and that is behavior seems to be a bug. I put my R version and package version in the reprex.

```r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

a <- c(1,NA,4,6)
b <- c(1,4,NA,6)

test <- tibble(a,b)

test %>% 
  filter(if_any(everything(), ~!is.na(.x)))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
```

title: Does join_by() support data masking?
description:
I am wondering if the link `` <[`data-masking`][rlang::args_data_masking]> `` should be added to `?join_by`.

That would help cases like mine where I'm using this anchor to build static analysis tools that know "there be ~dragons~ NSE here" inside calls that support NSE-only symbols (as do `select()`, `group_by()`, etc.).

But I also understand the data masking supported by `join_by()` is not as fully general as in other cases (e.g. the nod to pre-computing), so I am hesitating to just drop the link in and file a PR as it's not strictly an inconsistency.

If `join_by()` is an exception case (supports some NSE, but doesn't use the `args_data_masking` link), that's also fine.

title: `count()` and `add_count()` could be much faster
description:
Right now these eventually just do `summarise(n = n())` or `mutate(n = n())` at some point, but that can be very slow with many groups. We already have `vec_count()`, which should be much much faster than `count()` with many groups. We could also add some kind of vctrs primitive that works like a windowed count for `add_count()`, or just build on top of `vec_count()`'s result plus an additional call to `vec_match()`.

We'd have to think through how weighted counts would work, maybe `vec_count()` needs support for a weight argument (a double vector).

Motivation is something like this, and flights isn't even that big. Roughly 55k groups here.

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(nycflights13)

bench::mark(
  count(flights, dep_time, dep_delay),
  vctrs::vec_count(flights[c("dep_time", "dep_delay")]),
  check = FALSE
)
#> Warning: Some expressions had a GC in every iteration; so filtering is
#> disabled.
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   expression                                                 min  median itr/s…¹
#>   <bch:expr>                                            <bch:tm> <bch:t>   <dbl>
#> 1 count(flights, dep_time, dep_delay)                    419.6ms 441.4ms    2.27
#> 2 vctrs::vec_count(flights[c("dep_time", "dep_delay")])   17.3ms  21.5ms   42.7 
#> # … with 2 more variables: mem_alloc <bch:byt>, `gc/sec` <dbl>, and abbreviated
#> #   variable name ¹​`itr/sec`
```

Also need to handle the fact that `...` and `wt` are data-masking, probably with `add_computed_columns()` like `distinct()`.

title: `mutate()` drops column attributes
description:
I find it confusing and frustrating that `mutate()` (silently) drops column attributes such as column labels from haven - especially when very superficial changes are made to the columns (e.g. type conversion, many forcats-operations, etc). I would prefer it not to touch them at all. Could there at least be a global option for dropping or leaving attributes? For us working with real world data such labels are crucial for an effective workflow. 
Note: Similar issues have been raised before  (https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/pull/6102 and https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6689) but that seems to have been on data frame level attributes and/or related to grouped tbls. 

``` r
x <- mtcars
attr(x$cyl, which = "label") <- "The number of cylinders"
attributes(x$cyl)
#> $label
#> [1] "The number of cylinders"
x <-
  dplyr::mutate(x, cyl = as.character(cyl))
attr(x, "label")
#> NULL
```

title: Reconsider re-exports from rlang
description:
Can we start to un-export any of these https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/main/R/utils-tidy-eval.R?

Also, should we un-export `.data`? It doesn't belong on that help page, as noted in https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/pull/6801. We also don't export `.env` from dplyr, but those two are very closely related, and right now you can do `?dplyr::.data` but not `?dplyr::.env`.

title: dplyr v1.1.0 performance degradation when using group_by variables inside mutate/summarize transformations
description:
There is a considerable performance degradation in dplyr v1.1.0 in comparison to dplyr v1.0.10 when group_by variables are being used inside mutate / summarize transformation logic.

My expectation is that the performance should be on similar lines as dplyr v1.0.10.

Below is a reprex that benchmarks a mutate transformation using group_by variable on mpg dataframe on aforementioned dplyr versions.

**dplyr v1.0.10**

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(ggplot2)
library(microbenchmark)
microbenchmark(
  dplyr_1_0_10 = mpg %>%
    group_by(manufacturer, class, model) %>%
    mutate(
      cylr = case_when(
        manufacturer == "audi" & model == "a4 quattro" ~ first(cyl, order_by = desc(year)),
        T ~ cyl
      ),
      displr = case_when(
        manufacturer == "audi" & model == "a4 quattro" ~ first(displ, order_by = desc(year)),
        T ~ displ
      ),
      ctyr = case_when(
        manufacturer == "audi" & model == "a4 quattro" ~ first(cty, order_by = desc(year)),
        T ~ cty
      ),
      hwyr = case_when(
        manufacturer == "audi" & model == "a4 quattro" ~ first(hwy, order_by = desc(year)),
        T ~ hwy
      )
    ) %>%
    select(manufacturer, class, model, cylr, displr, ctyr, hwyr),
  unit = "milliseconds"
)
```

title: `filter(across())` warning isn't always triggered
description:
Between 1.0.7 and 1.1.0 `filter()` stopped taking matrices, per #5973. [NEWS for dplyr 1.0.8](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/main/NEWS.md#dplyr-108) reflects this change, but it also says there should be an informative message:

> - `filter()` forbids matrix results (#5973) and warns about data frame results, especially data frames created from `across()` with a hint to use `if_any()` or `if_all()`.

See reprex below:

Goal: Drop rows where _all_ columns other than `id` are `NA`s.

```r
# create df ––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

library(tibble)

df <- tribble(
  ~id, ~x,  ~y,
  1,   NA, "a",
  2,  "b",  NA,
  3,   NA,  NA,
  4,  "c", "d",
)

# new dplyr - 1.1.0 ––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

suppressMessages(library(dplyr))
packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '1.1.0'

# works
df |>
  filter(if_any(!id, ~!is.na(.)))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>      id x     y    
#>   <dbl> <chr> <chr>
#> 1     1 <NA>  a    
#> 2     2 b     <NA> 
#> 3     4 c     d

# doesn't work
df |>
  filter(!across(-id, is.na))
#> Error in `filter()`:
#> ℹ In argument: `!across(-id, is.na)`.
#> Caused by error:
#> ! `..1` must be a logical vector, not a logical matrix.

# old dplyr - 1.0.7 ––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

unloadNamespace("dplyr")
new_lib <- tempfile()
dir.create(new_lib)
withr::with_libpaths(new = new_lib, remotes::install_version("dplyr", "1.0.7"))
suppressMessages(library(dplyr, lib.loc = new_lib))
packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '1.0.7'

# works
df |>
  filter(if_any(!id, ~!is.na(.)))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>      id x     y    
#>   <dbl> <chr> <chr>
#> 1     1 <NA>  a    
#> 2     2 b     <NA> 
#> 3     4 c     d

# also works, but gives a different answer
df |>
  filter(!across(-id, is.na))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>      id x     y    
#>   <dbl> <chr> <chr>
#> 1     2 b     <NA> 
#> 2     4 c     d

unlink(new_lib, recursive = TRUE)
```

I believe, per the NEWS item, the message should be improved. I had a hard time deciphering the error given by 1.1.0 above, hence went the rabbit hole of trying to figure out what changed between the sessions.

title: Cannot drop columns that are used in group_by except for the last grouping variable
description:
It seems that if `group_by()` is used, then any of the variables except for the last one cannot be removed with `select()`.

```r
# this works, returns only "disp"
mtcars %>% group_by(cyl) %>% summarise(disp = mean(disp)) %>% select(-cyl)

# this works, returns "gear" and "disp"
mtcars %>% group_by(gear, cyl) %>% summarise(disp = mean(disp)) %>% select(-cyl) 

# this doesn't work as intended; returns "cyl" as well
mtcars %>% group_by(cyl, gear) %>% summarise(disp = mean(disp)) %>% select(-cyl)
```

After some testing, it looks like only the last variable used in the grouping can be dropped. `mtcars %>% group_by(cyl, gear, am, vs) %>% summarise(disp = mean(disp)) %>% select(disp)` only drops `vs`.

I could not find any information in the documentation about this behaviour. 

Using `ungroup()` does allow us to remove the columns. I see a very old issue about this https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/1030 but I don't see any reason given to why this is happening. It essentially ignores what the user wants to do, so I agree with the OP that perhaps a warning can be warranted, but I think that outright rejecting what the user wants to do is much too strict.

title: Calling `lubridate::as.period()` on an interval column errors within `mutate()` if the unit is "months".

title: Provide a function to prevent R CMD check "undefined global variable" warnings
description:
When using `dplyr` in an R package, `R CMD check` generates warnings that the column names used in `dblyr` functions are undefined global variables.

It would be very helpful to have a function similar to `dotty::dotify` (https://github.com/kevinushey/dotty/blob/main/R/dotify.R) that can be used to automatically call `utils::globalVariables` to prevent these messages.

---
Minimal example:

Create a dummy R package containing only a single function that used `dplyr`:

```r
f <- function() { get("iris") %>% filter(Species == "setosa") %>% select(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width) }
package.skeleton("dummy", list="f")
## Creating directories ...
## Creating DESCRIPTION ...
## Creating NAMESPACE ...
## Creating Read-and-delete-me ...
## Saving functions and data ...
## Making help files ...
## Done.
## Further steps are described in './dummy/Read-and-delete-me'.
unlink("dummy/man/f.Rd")
cat("Depends: dplyr\n", file=file("dummy/DESCRIPTION", "a"))
cat(
   c(
       'importFrom("stats", "filter")\n',
       'importFrom("dplyr", "%>%")\n',
       'importFrom("dplyr", "select")\n'
   ),
   file=file("dummy/NAMESPACE", "a")
)
```

Then run `devtools::check(dummy)` and note these lines:
```
  f: no visible binding for global variable ‘Species’
  f: no visible binding for global variable ‘Sepal.Length’
  f: no visible binding for global variable ‘Sepal.Width’
  Undefined global functions or variables:
    Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Species
```

The solution, adding the call `globalVariables(names=c("Species","Sepal.Length","Sepal.Width")` to the R package in, say `zzz.R`, resolves the problem, but generating and maintaining the appropriate list can be error prone and tedious.

Availability of a function, say `useDplyr()` that could be called from, say `zzz.R` to  "automagically" detect these and call `globalVariables()` would simplify things tremendously.
