title: Mutate dynamic assignment of column names works with both curly and curlycurly only in anonymous functions
description:
Dynamic assignment of column names works nicely with `"{}":=` syntax. Similarly, curlycurly `"{{}}":=` also works (or, if one has passes character vectors, `!! :=` works too).

When passing vectors to the argument with loops, both versions only work in non-anonymous functions. However, it does stop to work both ways when using pre-defined functions. Then, only the single-curly variation works. Is that intended? (I assume it has something to do with evaluation of promises?)
``` r
library(dplyr, warn = F)

## loops work both with curly and curlycurly in anonymous functions
lapply(2, function(n) {names(mutate(iris, "{n}" := Petal.Width * n))[6]})
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "2"
lapply(2, function(n) {names(mutate(iris, "{{n}}" := Petal.Width * n)[6])})
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "2"

## the whole thing does not work exactly the same with non-anonymous functions
multipetal_curly <- function(n) names(mutate(iris, "{n}" := Petal.Width * n))[6]
multipetal_curlycurly <- function(n) names(mutate(iris, "{{n}}" := Petal.Width * n))[6]

## works
lapply(2, function(i) multipetal_curly(n = i))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "2"
## doesn't work as expected - the column is named after the function argument
lapply(2, function(i) multipetal_curlycurly(n = i))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "i"
```

title: `group_by` adds column when unquote-splicing arguments
description:
Dplyr's `group_by` function adds columns when selecting them with an unquote-splice (`!!!`) or with the unquote operator (`!!`). This is inconsistent with other dplyr functions; the same arguments to `select` don't add the arguments.

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))

demo <- function(f, q) {
  starwars %>% 
    select(name, height) %>% 
    mutate(
      !!!q
    ) %>% 
    f(name, height, !!!names(q))
}

args <- quos(x = ifelse(height > 100, "1", "2"))


# `group_by` adds a new column with the name as a character vector
demo(group_by, args)
#> # A tibble: 87 × 4
#> # Groups:   name, height, "x" [87]
#>    name               height x     `"x"`
#>    <chr>               <int> <chr> <chr>
```

title: unexpected output when converting factors to integers with mutate after using bind_rows .id = [group name] on grouped data
description:
I do not fully understand why this happens, but I feel this is related to the group structure and that `bind_rows` does not fully replace this when creating an identifier column that has the same name as the previous group. 

The weird thing for me is that it works when mutating factors to integers in two different steps within the same mutate call, although I always thought that one does not need to create intermediaries. 

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = F)

iris2 <- group_by(iris, Species)

## fails when using bind rows and creating a column with the same name as a grouping column
iris2 %>%
  split(.$Species) %>%
  bind_rows(.id = "Species") %>%
  mutate(var_f =  as.integer(as.factor(Species))) %>%
  pull(var_f) %>% unique()
#> [1] 1

## it weirdly does not fail when doing two separate mutate steps
iris2 %>%
  split(.$Species) %>%
  bind_rows(.id = "Species") %>%
  mutate(var_f = as.factor(Species), 
         var_i = as.integer(var_f)) %>%
  pull(var_i) %>% unique()
#> [1] 1 2 3

## it works well with ungrouped data
iris2 %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  split(.$Species) %>%
  bind_rows(.id = "Species") %>%
  mutate(var_f =  as.integer(as.factor(Species))) %>%
  pull(var_f) %>% unique()
#> [1] 1 2 3
```

title: Upkeep for dplyr
`ungroup()` drops data frame attributes
description:
This is referring to **dataframe/tibble** attributes, not tibble *column* attributes. The CRAN install of dplyr 1.1.0 sometimes drops attributes:

```r
d = mtcars
attr(d, "foo") = "bar"
attr(d, "foo")
#> [1] "bar"

## preserved
d |> select(cyl) |> attr("foo")
#> [1] "bar"
d |> rename(cyl2 = cyl) |> attr("foo")
#> [1] "bar"
d |> arrange(cyl) |> attr("foo")
#> [1] "bar"
d |> group_by(cyl) |> attr("foo")
#> [1] "bar"
d |> mutate(mpg2 = mpg) |> attr("foo")
#> [1] "bar"
d |> transmute(mpg2 = mpg) |> attr("foo")
#> [1] "bar"
d |> filter(cyl == 1L) |> attr("foo")
#> [1] "bar"
d |> count(cyl) |> attr("foo") 
#> [1] "bar"
d |> bind_rows(d) |> attr("foo")
#> [1] "bar"
d |> bind_cols(select(d, cyl2 = cyl)) |> attr("foo")
#> [1] "bar"


## dropped
d |> group_by(cyl) |> ungroup() |> attr("foo")
#> NULL
d |> summarize(mpg = max(mpg)) |> attr("foo")
#> NULL
```

I can understand why it might make sense for `summarize()` to drop attributes (but then why does `count()` preserve them?), but I don't see why `ungroup(group_by(...))` should drop attributes unilaterally. Given that almost all `dplyr` verbs preserve the attribute, I'm wondering if this is a bug/regression.

There are a variety of issues regarding attributes but they are all closed.

- https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/2432
- https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/5132
- https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/3429

title: case_when() doesn't return NA for NA by default
description:
**The problem of `case_when()`'s `.default =`.** 
I think that current logic of `case_when()` is flawed in terms of how it handles `NA`. `case_when()` is positioned as a _"A general vectorised if-else"_ that _"allows you to vectorise multiple if_else() statements"_. So, I expect `case_when()` to behave the same way as `if_else()`/`ifelse()` if i put minimum options:

```
vec <- c(1L, 2L, NA_integer_)
> dplyr::if_else(vec == 1, "one", "not one")
[1] "one"     "not one" NA       
```
this behaviour is the same for the base R `ifelse()`
```
ifelse(vec == 1, "one", "not one")
[1] "one"     "not one" NA       
```
Non-vectorised if-else returns error for `NA`:

```
> if(vec[3] == 1) {"one"} else {"not one"}
Error in if (vec[3] == 1) { : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

```
However, naive attemption to reproduce the same results as for `if_else()`/`ifelse()` using `case_when(`) will fail:

```
> dplyr::case_when(
    vec == 1 ~ "one", # first condition is analog of "if"
    .default = "not one" # .default value is analog of "else"
)
[1] "one"     "not one" "not one"

```
...due to `NA` are considered `FALSE` by all conditions, BUT `.default =` value will be returned.
Thus, `NA` values need some special treatment. For example, to mimic `if_else()`/`ifelse()` behaviour we need to set up `is.na(vec) ~ NA`.

There is a note on this trick in docs for `case_when(`), however, it is not on the surface: inside description of `.default` = argument and only in one code example. So, the function works not the way many users (including me) expect it to work and not consistent with  `if_else()`/`ifelse()`. Finally, it contradicts the logic of `NA` handling in general: for missing value we don't know in which group a value behind the `NA` will fall and we cannot say that it belongs (or doesn't) to the `.default` group.

**I think of this possible solution**

in addition to `.default =` argument add `.na` = argument (the value that willl be returned in case of `NA` in condition) with default `.na = NA` that can be overwritten either by setting up `.na` = parameter or by `is.na(ver) ~ value`. The last one has prority over `.na = argument`.

title: treatment of expensive calls for a data subset in data pipeline
description:
Hi all,

I am given a dataset on which a certain subset of the data needs to be processed differently (the subset is defined by an additional variable).
Conceptually I could just use the following tidy solution:
```
data %>%
  select(group, input) %>%
  mutate(
    output =
      case_when(
        group == "subset" ~ call1(input),
        .default = call2(input)
      )
  )
```

From what I have understood, `call1` and `call2` are both first evaluated on the whole dataset and the final result is selected by testing the condition `group == "subset"`.

My issue comes in when the data with `group == "subset"` is quite small compared to its complement and `call1` is a very expensive call (and also does not scale so well with the number of observations). So one would like to really only evaluate `call1` for the particular subset, not for the whole dataset.

I worked around the issue by using the following construct:
```
bind_rows(
  data %>%
    select(group, input) %>%
    filter(group != "subset" | is.na(group)) %>%
    mutate(output = call2(input))
,
  data %>%
    select(group, input) %>%
    filter(group == "subset") %>%
    mutate(output = call1(input))
)
```
which does not seem very "tidy" to me.
Is there a recommended way (maybe using different verbs?) to treat this kind of scenario?

Thank you!

title: Isn't the `join_by()` DSL a new type of tidy evaluation ?
description:
It is not data masking, it's not tidy selection, but it's evaluated and it's tidy ? Should it be included as a 3rd type of tidy evaluation the ["Programming with dplyr" vignette](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/programming.html) ?

I love the "\<tidy-select>" and "\<data-masking>" hyperlinks in the doc, having these argument types named and knowing that tidy evaluation means one of those is very helpful to browse the doc and to teach.

`join_by()` 's `...` arg does not have this honour, maybe because it's the only function that uses this DSL, still I think it might be named for consistency and avoiding confusing re different kinds of NSE used in the tidyverse.

This [SO question](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/75531148/why-to-quote-in-dplyr-and-why-not-to-quote-in-dplyr), and more specifically Paul's answer,  made me request this.

title: Corner cases with `.data` and `.env`
description:
_Edit: updated the issue since I oversaw first that `.data` was also the first arg name._

These are artificial cases but since the `.data` and `.env` pronouns are used essentially for robustness and eliminating ambiguity I think maybe those might be dealt with and documented so we can count on this robustness a bit more. Moreover `.data` is not a completely absurd name for a data frame column.

``` r
library(dplyr, w=F)

# fails because of `.data` arg as it should, would fail also if there was a `.data` column
band_members %>% mutate(.data = 1)
#> Error in UseMethod("mutate"): no applicable method for 'mutate' applied to an object of class "c('double', 'numeric')"

# succeeds, but should it ?
band_members %>% mutate(.env = 1)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   name  band     .env
#>   <chr> <chr>   <dbl>
#> 1 Mick  Stones      1
#> 2 John  Beatles     1
#> 3 Paul  Beatles     1

# fails because looks in global env
band_members %>% mutate(.env = band_members, foo = .env$band)
#> Error in `mutate()`:
#> ℹ In argument: `foo = .env$band`.
#> Caused by error in `eval_bare()`:
#> ! object 'band' not found

# succeeds, looks in data
band_members %>% mutate(.env = band_members, foo = .env)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   name  band    .env$name $band   foo$name $band  
#>   <chr> <chr>   <chr>     <chr>   <chr>    <chr>  
#> 1 Mick  Stones  Mick      Stones  Mick     Stones 
#> 2 John  Beatles John      Beatles John     Beatles
#> 3 Paul  Beatles Paul      Beatles Paul     Beatles
```

<sup>Created on 2023-02-22 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

I believe the least surprising behaviour is to expect that `.env` and `.data` always refer to pronouns.

Since `mutate()` is already not accepting any data frame (refusing duplicate or empty names at least), it might refuse to create a column named ".data" or ".env", and maybe even refuse an input that would contain one, basically considering those corrupted.

(out of scope for dplyr but maybe these might even be refused in any function that uses `.name_repair` unless it's set to `"minimal"`)

title: recode() is superseded by case_match() but case_match() isn't exported from dplyr 1.0.10
description:
The [documentation for `recode()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/recode.html) states it's superseded by `case_match()`. However, `case_match()` is not available in dplyr 1.0.10.
```R
dplyr::case_match()
Error: 'case_match' is not an exported object from 'namespace:dplyr'
```

While the related `case_when()` is exported from dplyr, it fails to hello world in R 4.2.2.
```R
factorVec = factor(c("A", "B"))
case_when(factorVec == "A" ~ 1,
          factorVec == "B" ~ 2,
          .default = NA_real_)
Error in `case_when()`:
! Case 3 (`factorVec == "A" ~ 1`) must be a two-sided formula, not a double vector.
```
`recode()` handles the above without difficulty.
```R
recode(factorVec, 
       "A" = 1,
       "B" = 2,
       .default = NA_real_)
```

It seems like one of the two possibilities below should happen.

1) `case_match()` and `case_when()` are backed out and `recode()` revered from superseded status.
2) `case_match()`, `case_when()` are implemented so that `recode()` can be deprecated without forcing dplyr users into `if_else(if_else(if_else(...)))` stacks.

Assuming the latter, it seems unit test coverage for `case_match()` and `case_when()` needs to be expanded and I would suggest it cover more complex formulas and type conversions than the simple repexes here. `recode()` allows multiple terms, `exp()`, `log()`, and so on. It's desirable to retain that flexibility.

There may be additional issues in this area as it appears #6328 also added `vec_case_match()` but that's not exported from dplyr and isn't in the documentation.

title: mutate(across(x, lst(fn)) isn't able to access other columns
description:
I think this is a bug introduced in a recent update because it's breaking code I wrote a few months ago.

For this workflow:  `mutate(across(x, lst(fn))`, it seems that `fn` isn't able to access other dataframe columns.  It produces an error `object 'y' not found` where `y` is another dataframe column.

`across` works as intended by using `list` instead of `lst`.

Here is a minimal example.  I hope this is useful.

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.2.2
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag

#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '1.1.0'

df <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 2)

# ok.  I think this was fixed here: https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/5924
df %>% 
  mutate(across(x, lst(f1 = ~. + 1)))
#>   x y x_f1
#> 1 1 2    2

# fails
df %>% 
  mutate(across(x, lst(f2 = ~y + . + 1)))
#> Error in `mutate()`:

#> Caused by error in `across()`:
#> ! Can't compute column `x_f2`.

#> ! object 'y' not found

#> Backtrace:
#>      ▆
#>   1. ├─df %>% mutate(across(x, lst(f2 = ~y + . + 1)))
#>   2. ├─dplyr::mutate(., across(x, lst(f2 = ~y + . + 1)))
#>   3. ├─dplyr:::mutate.data.frame(., across(x, lst(f2 = ~y + . + 1)))
#>   4. │ └─dplyr:::mutate_cols(.data, dplyr_quosures(...), by)
#>   5. │   ├─base::withCallingHandlers(...)
#>   6. │   └─dplyr:::mutate_col(dots[[i]], data, mask, new_columns)
#>   7. │     ├─base::withCallingHandlers(...)
#>   8. │     └─mask$eval_all_mutate(quo)
#>   9. │       └─dplyr (local) eval()
#>  10. ├─dplyr (local) `<rlng_lm_>`(x)
#>  11. └─base::.handleSimpleError(`<fn>`, "object 'y' not found", base::quote(`<rlng_lm_>`(x)))
```

title: `cur_group_id()` gives wrong result when inside `summarize(mutate(...)`
description:
Here's a very weird bug I just encountered. The idea is that we want to run a function per group, which mutates that group to add a new column involving `i`, the current group ID. What should happen is that we get `"setosa1" "versicolor2" "virginica3"` as the ID is incremented per group, but in reality they are all fixed at 1. 

It's a very contrived example but it's the simplest way I've found to reproduce this bug. `dplyr::group_map` is probably a more elegant way to solve this but I dare not use experimental functions.

``` r
per_group = function(i, grp){
  dplyr::mutate(grp, name=paste0(Species, i))
}

iris |>
    dplyr::group_by(Species) |>
    dplyr::summarise(per_group(dplyr::cur_group_id(), dplyr::cur_data_all())) |>
    dplyr::pull(name) |>
    unique()
#> `summarise()` has grouped output by 'Species'. You can override using the
#> `.groups` argument.
#> [1] "setosa1"     "versicolor1" "virginica1"
```

<sup>Created on 2023-02-20 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

What is super interesting to me is that if we `force` the promise `i` to evaluate, it works correctly, which to me implies that the fault lies in handling promises:

``` r
per_group = function(i, grp){
  force(i)
  dplyr::mutate(grp, name=paste0(Species, i))
}

iris |>
    dplyr::group_by(Species) |>
    dplyr::summarise(per_group(dplyr::cur_group_id(), dplyr::cur_data_all())) |>
    dplyr::pull(name) |>
    unique()
#> `summarise()` has grouped output by 'Species'. You can override using the
#> `.groups` argument.
#> [1] "setosa1"     "versicolor2" "virginica3"
```

title: On `multiple` matches, and how we can improve
description:
After reading https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6717, I've gone back to the drawing board to see if we are missing something with how `multiple` works.

I am now convinced that we have gotten `multiple` slightly wrong, making it more painful than it should be. I think the intentions are right, the execution of what it warns on is just slightly off.

There are 4 types of joins worth considering in this discussion:
- `1-to-1`
- `many-to-1`
- `1-to-many`
- `many-to-many`

With equi-joins, `multiple` will warn on `1-to-many` and `many-to-many`, i.e. anything with `*-to-many` where something in `x` matches multiple rows in `y`.

My big proposal here is that:
- Warning on `many-to-many` is correct.
- Warning on `1-to-many` is _wrong_.

---

I think that `many-to-1` and `1-to-many` are both very useful and safe joins. But more importantly, these are essentially _symmetrical_ styles of joins, so it doesn't make much sense to warn on one of these and not the other. Most of the time, you actually see these listed online as _just_ `1-to-many`, with the opposite being inferred, because they are so similar. It's just a matter of how you frame your question.

Our original thought process was:

> It is confusing for users when a join results in more rows than there are in `x`.

This is what can happen in `1-to-many` and `many-to-many`, which explains our current behavior, but I think a more appropriate assertion is:

> It is confusing for users when a join can result in a (possibly cartesian) explosion of `nrow(x) * nrow(y)` rows.

This can only happen with `many-to-many`, and is worth guarding against because it typically means there is a misspecified join. This assertion is supported by three trustworthy references online:

- [IBM's database relationship guide](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/cdfsp/7.6.0?topic=structure-database-relationships) which says this about `many-to-many`, suggesting they aren't a good idea:
  > Each record in both tables can relate to none or any number of records in the other table. These relationships require a third table, called an associate or linking table, because relational systems cannot directly accommodate the relationship.

- [Stata's merge guide](https://www.stata.com/manuals13/dmerge.pdf) which does `m:m` merges slightly differently than we do, but the principle still stands, I think:
  > Because m:m merges are such a bad idea, we are not going to show you an example. If you think
that you need an m:m merge, then you probably need to work with your data so that you can use a
1:m or m:1 merge.

- [FileMaker Pro's help docs](https://fmhelp.filemaker.com/help/18/fmp/en/index.html#page/FMP_Help/many-to-many-relationships.html) which discuss how many-to-many relationships can always be replaced with a 3rd table that creates two 1-to-many relationships to that table.

---

I do think that `multiple = "error"` is still quite useful. It's really great when you want to enforce that you have a `1-to-1` or `many-to-1` style join where `y` is a kind of lookup table that contains extra information you want to bind on to `x` without changing its rows. That is a different use case than what we are discussing here.

---

Implementing what I'm suggesting here would silence the join warnings seen here:
https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6717#issuecomment-1428780577

I think that that user is doing "everything right," i.e. there is nothing wrong with those joins. Even the three-way join of:

```r
student_term <- left_join(student, term, by = join_by(student.id))
left_join(student_term, course, by = join_by(student.id, term))
```

is just two `1:many` joins, which I'm now convinced are normal and expected join types.

---

So how would we do this? I think we need an argument specifically targeting `many-to-many` joins, like:

```r
#> @param many Handling of many-to-many joins. These typically indicate
#>   a structural problem in your join or data.
#> 
#>   - `"ignore"`, allow many-to-many joins.
#>   - `"warning"`, warn on many-to-many joins.
#>   - `"error"`, error on many-to-many joins.
#> 
#>   If `NULL`, will default to `"warning"` for equi joins.
#> 
#>   Not applicable for non-equi joins (NOT SURE ABOUT THIS).

many = NULL / c("ignore", "warning", "error")
```

We'd then change `multiple` to have an unconditional default of `"all"`, and we'd quickly deprecate `"warning"` because it would no longer be meaningful in any way (you'd just use `"error"` if you were worried about that case).

And of course I'd have to figure out how to exactly detect the `many-many` case on the vctrs side.

This framing is also supported by a great data.table discussion about `allow.cartesian` https://github.com/Rdatatable/data.table/issues/4383. The `a)` case there aligns with what `multiple = "error"` catches, and their `b)` case aligns with what `many` would catch. They've essentially come to the same conclusion that I have about what is needed to guard against these effectively.

I also think this is something I'd eventually be comfortable making an error by default, which was one of our goals with `multiple`'s default originally.

title: if_else throws false must be a vector, not NULL. error for dplyr 1.1.0
description:
I posted an issue yesterday (#6728) but it was closed immediately after the first reply, which I felt was unjustified because my response and argument is not being replied to anymore because the issue is closed. I therefore would like to reopen it here again for a discussion, and I am hoping for a more fruitful solution.

Between dplyr 1.0.0 and 1.1.0, an undocumented (unless I oversaw it)  and breaking change has been included into `if_else` that I find not very useful personally and which forced me and others to go back to base R `ifelse`, and I wanted to learn what was the motivation for it. In essence, it seems "The `true` and `false` arguments are always evaluated, regardless of whether their values are seen in the result, which causes an error in dplyr 1.1.0 when `NULL` is involved. I'd appreciate a discussion why  this is a useful change, because it worked differently and "as expected" until dplyr 1.0.0. Thank you

title: if_else throws `false` must be a vector, not `NULL`. error for dplyr 1.1.0
description:
For dplyr v1.1.0, code that worked before now breaks:

```r
library(dplyr)
basename = NULL
dplyr::if_else(is.null(basename), "plot", basename)
# Error in `dplyr::if_else()`:
# ! `false` must be a vector, not `NULL`.
```
The message doesnt make sense to me here because even though `basename` is `NULL`, it never goes into the `false` block. The idea is here: Return a string with a folder name. If the user didnt set one (`basename = NULL`), return a default (`"plot"`), otherwise return whatever the user put there.

Is this a deliberate (breaking) change and if so, what's the rationale here?

title: `slice_sample` errors out if a column name in `.data` has the explicit name of `replace`
description:
Based on the fact that this being caused at the call to `base::sample.int()`, I suspect that it's attempting to absorb `.data$replace` (if present) before the actual replace argument in `slice_sample`.

Didn't see anyone with this issue on StackOverflow so I'm submitting here for review.

``` r
library(dplyr)
#>

(slice_sample(tibble(replace = 1:10), prop = 0.25))

#>  12. ├─rlang (local) local(...)
#>  13. ├─base::local(...)
```

title: dplyr verbs to ISO standards
description:
Less of an issue, but more of a question.

I have been a long-time `dplyr` user. At this point, there are probably no verbs that are more natural to me.

There are many clis, database languages, and data manipulation libraries that use ISO SQL or roll with their own grammar.

I have wondered why no ISO standard for `dplyr` verbs exists? I know a standard would encourage me to make an API layer supporting the grammar if I were to make another tool in a different language or framework.

I guess what I am trying to say is that the grammar is bigger than `dplyr` alone. Why not standardize the grammar for other tools to point to?

Here's the warning raised by the following code:


title: Is it possible to set an option to globally turn off the multiple matches warning on joins?
description:
`dplyr` 1.1 has a new argument `multiple` in the join functions that, by default, throws a warning if a row in `x` matches more than one row in `y`. You have to explicitly set `multiple="all"` in every join in order to silence the warning. According to the help, this default was chosen because multiple matches are "usually surprising." In the data I work with (education) multiple matches are the norm (students attend in multiple terms and take multiple courses in each term; instructors have multiple students, teach more than one course and perhaps multiple sections of a course, etc.). The constant warnings are really annoying, but it would likewise be annoying to have to explicitly set the `multiple` argument every time I do a join (including many, many joins across existing functions in our internal packages that would need to be updated). 

Ideally, the default would be not to warn. If you're not open to that change, is there any way to set an option at the top of a script that disables warnings related to multiple matches, and, if not, would you be willing to add such an option?

title: `na_if`: automatic type conversion to `date` fails
description:
When working with dates in a tibble, what I need to do quite often, is to aggregate those dates using `min` or `max` with the rule, that it should ignore `NA`s, but return `NA` if all inputs per aggregation group are `NA`. This is different from the default behavior of `min`/`max` which return `Inf`/`-Inf` respectively in this case. To workaround this, I used to wrap everything by `na_if` to convert `Inf`s to `NA`.

The recent update of dplyr breaks that code with error given in the reprex below: can't convert double to date. Explicit conversion by `as.Date(Inf)` seems to work. However, it seems that the documentation is saying that this should also work implicitely. That would make this a bug I guess.

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

lf <- tibble(date = c(Sys.Date(), Sys.Date(), NA, NA), n = c(1L, 1L, 2L, 2L))

# this used to work (not anymore with dplyr 1.1.0)
lf %>%
  summarize(
    na_if(min(date, na.rm = T), Inf),
    .by = n
  )
#> Error in `summarize()`:
#> ℹ In argument: `na_if(min(date, na.rm = T), Inf)`.
#> ℹ In group 1: `n = 1`.
#> Caused by error in `na_if()`:
#> ! Can't convert `y` <double> to match type of `x` <date>.

#> Backtrace:
#>      ▆
#>   1. ├─lf %>% summarize(na_if(min(date, na.rm = T), Inf), .by = n)
#>   2. ├─dplyr::summarize(., na_if(min(date, na.rm = T), Inf), .by = n)
#>   3. ├─dplyr:::summarise.data.frame(...)
#>   4. │ └─dplyr:::summarise_cols(.data, dplyr_quosures(...), by, "summarise")
#>   5. │   ├─base::withCallingHandlers(...)
#>   6. │   └─dplyr:::map(quosures, summarise_eval_one, mask = mask)
#>   7. │     └─base::lapply(.x, .f, ...)
#>   8. │       └─dplyr (local) FUN(X[[i]], ...)
#>   9. │         └─mask$eval_all_summarise(quo)
#>  10. │           └─dplyr (local) eval()
#>  11. ├─dplyr::na_if(min(date, na.rm = T), Inf)
#>  12. │ └─vctrs::vec_cast(x = y, to = x, x_arg = "y", to_arg = "x")
#>  13. └─vctrs (local) `<fn>`()
#>  14.   └─vctrs::vec_default_cast(...)
```

title: Warnings on built package are going silent
description:
Hello all, 
We have found that using dplyr inside a package does not issue any warnings. 
For example, if the following function is in the environment, it issues the warning.
```
library(dplyr)
test <- function(){
  a <- data.frame(ID=c(1,2,3,4))
  b <- data.frame(ID=c(1,1,2,2,3,3,4,4),LETTER=c("a","b","c","d","f","g","h","i"))
  c <- a %>% dplyr::left_join(b,by="ID")
} 
test()
```

> Warning message:
In dplyr::left_join(., b, by = "ID") :
  Each row in `x` is expected to match at most 1 row in `y`.
ℹ Row 1 of `x` matches multiple rows.
ℹ If multiple matches are expected, set `multiple = "all"` to silence this
  warning.

But if the function is added to a package and the function is called it does not issue the warning. 
We compiled the packaged in R Studio (Version 2022.12.0+353 (2022.12.0+353)) over Mac OS and Windows with R 4.2.2 and dplyr 1.1.0

But I don't understand how or why, especially as I can reproduce [this example from Hadley ](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6100#issuecomment-1353697847)that this shouldn't happen.

**This has the `$core` and `$tabyl_type` attributes:**

Do you know why these attributes are dropped compared to the comment I linked above?  And thoughts on whether this could/might be addressed on the dplyr side? title: `rename_with` with empty column selection fails w/ dplyr 1.1.0.
description:
Hi,

due to the size check in the new dplyr version, dplyr 1.1.0, renames with empty column selections don't work anymore (since it expects a vector of functions of size 0).
This is of course not a big problem when used interactively, since one can simply omit the whole statement.
But when used programmatically in a data pipeline it forces the programmer to always treat this case separately (if for instance the .cols argument is defined by external dynamical parameters).

I would expect this function to simply do nothing if no columns are selected, and not throw an error.


``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

tibble(col = c(1,3)) %>%
  rename_with(
    .cols = contains("test"),
    .fn = ~ paste0("blah.", .)
```

title: Use `==` in `closest` join
description:
`closest` only accepts inequality operators, but it would seem natural to have `==` (or some other operator) for joining with the _closest_ value, irrespective of whether it is higher or lower. 

---

Consider this minimal example (data taken from [this SO question](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/75359588/can-i-joint-2-dataframes-in-r-by-an-id-column-and-a-nearest-date-value)). This issue was also mentioned [here](https://community.rstudio.com/t/dplyr-1-1-0-new-rolling-join-feature-join-by-closest-value/154218/2). Inequality join with closest is okay, but equality join with closest are not working. 

```r
library(lubridate)
library(dplyr)
df1 <- data.frame(var2 = c("Dog", "Dog", "Cat"),
                  Date = dmy(c("01-01-2022","02-01-2022" , "07-12-2022")))
#   var2       Date
# 1  Dog 2022-01-01
# 2  Dog 2022-01-02
# 3  Cat 2022-12-07

df2 <- data.frame(Date = dmy(c("07-01-2022","04-12-2022" , "10-12-2022")))
#         Date
# 1 2022-01-07
# 2 2022-12-04
# 3 2022-12-10

df1 %>% 
  inner_join(df2, join_by(closest(Date <= Date)))
#    var2    Date.x     Date.y
# 1  Dog 2022-01-01 2022-01-07
# 2  Dog 2022-01-02 2022-01-07
# 3  Cat 2022-12-07 2022-12-10

df1 %>% 
  inner_join(df2, join_by(closest(Date == Date)))

# Error in `join_by()`:
#   ! The expression used in `closest()` can't use `==`.
# ℹ Expression 1 is `closest(Date == Date)`.
# Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.
```
Instead, it'd be nice to have a simple option for either direction:
```r
df1 %>% 
  inner_join(df2, join_by(closest(Date == Date)), multiple = "all")
#    var2    Date.x     Date.y
# 1  Dog 2022-01-01 2022-01-07
# 2  Dog 2022-01-02 2022-01-07
# 3  Cat 2022-12-07 2022-12-04
# 4  Cat 2022-12-07 2022-12-10
```

title: Speed of first() evaluated within grouped tibbles
description:
Using `dplyr 1.1.0` and `vctrs 0.5.2`, I'm noticing speed issues when evaluating `first` within grouped tibbles.

```r
df <- dplyr::group_by(tibble::tibble(x = 1:10000, grp = rep(1:100, 100)), grp)
bench::mark(
  first = dplyr::summarize(
    df,
    f = dplyr::first(x)
  ),
  indexed = dplyr::summarize(
    df,
    f = x[1]
  )
)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 first        7.44ms   7.98ms      119.    1.57MB     19.1
#> 2 indexed      1.01ms   1.06ms      901.   55.62KB     12.7
```

On `dplyr 1.0.10` with `vctrs 0.5.0`, the `first` benchmark is about 1.7 ms.

title: Mutate and summarize speed related to parentheses
description:
Using `dplyr 1.1.0` and `vctrs 0.5.2`, I'm noticing speed issues with `mutate` and `summarize` related to parentheses on the RHS.

```r
df <- tibble::tibble(x = 1:10000)
bench::mark(
  b1 = dplyr::summarize(
    df,
    res = (1 + 1)
  ),
  b2 = dplyr::summarize(
    df,
    res = 1 + 1
  )
)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 b1           1.47ms   1.53ms      625.    3.78MB     12.6
#> 2 b2           3.13ms   3.38ms      290.   546.9KB     15.6
bench::mark(
  b1 = dplyr::mutate(
    df,
    res = (1 + 1)
  ),
  b2 = dplyr::mutate(
    df,
    res = 1 + 1
  )
)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 b1           1.64ms   1.73ms      557.     363KB     14.9
#> 2 b2           3.23ms    3.5ms      279.     102KB     15.4
```

On `dplyr 1.0.10` with `vctrs 0.5.0`, all give the same result, ~1.5 ms. I'm using `tibble 3.1.8` for both tests. With more complicated aggregation expressions, I've seen 15x slowdowns.

title: `dplyr::if_else()` fails when `condition` is a labelled logical vector
description:
Starting with dplyr 1.1.0, [`dplyr::if_else()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/if_else.html) fails with a meaningless error message when `condition` is a **labelled** logical vector:

``` r
d <-
    mtcars |>
    dplyr::mutate(mileage = mpg > 20) |>
    labelled::set_variable_labels(mileage = "mileage dummy")

dplyr::if_else(d$mileage,
               "guzzler",
               "moderate")
#> Error in `dplyr::if_else()`:
#> ! `condition` must be a vector with type <logical>.
#> Instead, it has type <logical>.

#>     ▆
#>  1. └─dplyr::if_else(d$mileage, "guzzler", "moderate")
#>  2.   └─vctrs::vec_assert(x = condition, ptype = logical(), arg = "condition")
#>  3.     └─rlang::abort(...)
```

title: `bind_rows()` on a list of data.tables creates corrupt output
description:
when using bind_rows on a list of data.tables with keys, with either map_dfr or a do.call, the keys are not removed This is a problem, because the keys are not correct anymore, which means that later queries are using an index that is wrong. 

not sure if I should report this under data.table or dplyr, but since the issue is in bin_rows, I guess it is dplyr.

[here is the issue I filed under data.table](https://github.com/Rdatatable/data.table/issues/5587)




```


library(data.table)
library(dplyr)




data <- data.table(var1=c('a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f', 'g', 'h'), var2=c(rep(2016, 4), rep(2018, 4)), key=c('var1', 'var2'))


test1 <- lapply(c(2018, 2016), function(x) data[var2 %in% c(x-1, x)])


test2 <- do.call(bind_rows, test1)
# wrong 
test2[var1 %in% c('c', 'e'), .N]
# right
sum( test2$var1 %in% c('c', 'e') )


```

same thing  happens w. map_dfr,that uses bind_rows under the hood. This is how I found the issue. It is very common in my workflow, and I suspect I am not the one.


doing the same with rbind removes the keys, which is the expected behaviour - as the index from the key are no longer valid.


```

test2_rbind <- do.call(rbind, test1) 
# here it is fine - because the keys not there, giving a wrong picture of the structure of the DT
test2_rbind[var1 %in% c('c', 'e'), .N]

# when removing the keys, everything is fine. 
setkey(test2, NULL)
test2[var1 %in% c('c', 'e'), .N]


```



curiosly, using split() instead of lapply circumvents the issue - but this is not a solution, since typically you need to apply a function to the data, - splitting it and then recombining it with split() makes no sense. But I am including it here for completeness.


```


test1 <- split(data, data$var2)
test2 <- do.call(bind_rows, test1)
# right 
test2[var1 %in% c('c', 'e'), .N]

```

title: v1.1.0 runtime for case_when with grouping variable is slow
description:
Using `case_when` in a `mutate` call with a grouping variable is much, much slower in v1.1.0 compared to v1.0.10.  The code works but it's causing a tremendous slowdown in many of the packages I maintain (see [here](https://www.r-project.org/nosvn/R.check/r-devel-linux-x86_64-debian-clang/MassWateR-00check.html), many examples have elapsed time >5s).

title: Slow method dispatch / parameter evaluation
description:
I'm a devopsy/sysengineer type who has been tasked with taking machine learning models provided by data scientists and serving them up as web APIs. We have quite complex `dplyr` pipelines used to format, filter and aggregate data before being fed into model training, so during inference we pass a tiny subset through the same dplyr pipeline.

This data-prep stage is taking a very long time. After doing a bit of digging it appears to be related to the complexity of the queries used, the number of `dplyr` function calls and parameters passed to them. They're about 2 orders of magnitude slower than `data.table` even when called with lists or strings:

```r
$ radian
R version 4.1.3 (2022-03-10) -- "One Push-Up"
Platform: x86_64-w64-mingw32 (64-bit)        

r$> library(data.table)
    library(dplyr)
    library(microbenchmark)
    my_data <- structure(list(ChummerId = 1L, DateOfBirth = "1970-10-30T00:00:00", class = "data.frame", row.names = 1L)) # because dput
    my_data <- data.frame(my_data)

r$> slow <- function() { my_data %>% dplyr::select() }

r$> dog_slow <- function() { my_data %>% dplyr::select('DateOfBirth') }

r$> hog_slow <- function() { my_data %>% dplyr::select('DateOfBirth', 'ChummerId') }

r$> microbenchmark(slow(), times=10000)
Unit: microseconds
   expr min  lq   mean median     uq     max neval
 slow() 882 944 1085.2 967.45 1091.6 61982.7 10000

r$> microbenchmark(dog_slow(), times=10000)
Unit: milliseconds
       expr    min     lq     mean  median     uq     max neval
 dog_slow() 1.2256 1.3034 1.515808 1.35735 1.5519 78.1194 10000

r$> microbenchmark(hog_slow(), times=10000)
Unit: milliseconds
       expr    min     lq     mean median      uq     max neval
 hog_slow() 1.5661 1.6601 1.907114 1.7368 1.95965 63.0409 10000
```

For comparison:

```r

r$> my_select <- function(.data, columns, ...) { .data[columns] }

r$> my_selector <- function() { my_data %>% my_select(c('DateOfBirth', 'ChummerId')) }

r$> microbenchmark(my_selector(), times=10000)

          expr min   lq     mean median   uq    max neval
 my_selector()  15 15.9 20.42863   16.8 18.4 3232.1 10000
```

title: Advice in compatibility.html vignette is wrong
description:
The Compatibility vignette suggests that using `pkg::foo()` is an option instead of using `importFrom` in situations where there are namespace differences between the current and development versions of dplyr that a package author is trying to support.

The vignette claims this will raise a NOTE, but that this is largely harmless. Doing as advised in the vignette will actually raise a WARNING, however, not a NOTE, and this will fail checks on CI systems like GitHub Actions (causing an error) and will be a much harder sell on CRAN (and certainly slow down submissions as manual intervention will almost certainly be required for a WARNING).

For example, when trying to handle the deprecation in `summarise()` of results of more than one row per group and reimplementation of this in `reframe()`, using 

```r
...
#' @importFrom dplyr summarise
...
if (utils::packageVersion("dplyr") > "1.0.10") {
  dplyr::reframe(...)
} else {
  summarise(...)
}
...
```

Causes warnings:

```
* checking dependencies in R code ... WARNING
Missing or unexported object: 'dplyr::reframe'
```

~~I would suggest removing this suggestion, or at the very least correct it and include a big warning to unsuspecting users that WARNINGs will cause difficulties for CRAN.~~

description:

)

mutate(foo, y = {

title: Consider `.sort = FALSE` for `summarise()`, `reframe()`, and `slice_sample()`
description:
With the introduction of `.by`, we no longer sort group keys automatically. There are a whole host of good reasons for this as outlined here https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/5664#issuecomment-907232443, and I am mostly confident this is the right long term default for dplyr.

However, I am empathetic to the fact that users do often like to see their summary results sorted in ascending order. Right now, our recommendation is:

```r
df %>%
  summarise(..., .by = c(a, b, c)) %>%
  arrange(a, b, c) # could also come before `summarise()`
```

This is nice because you get the full power of `arrange()` including `desc()` and `.locale`.

I think we should _consider_ a `.sort` argument like:

```r
df %>%
  summarise(..., .by = c(a, b, c), .sort = TRUE)
```

- `.sort = FALSE` would be the default for reasons mentioned above.
- We'd document this as the 100% backwards compatible way to transition from `group_by()` to `.by` (even though most of the time the ordering isn't important).
- You must accept that you get _ascending order_ and the _C locale_. That makes it compatible with `group_by()`. If you need anything fancier, call `arrange()`.
- I do like that you won't have to repeat the group names.
- Obviously `.sort = TRUE` errors on unorderable types like clock's year-month-weekday.
- This would probably only be an argument for the `.data.frame` method, as opposed to the generic, because dbplyr probably won't want to enforce a sort order? Uncertain.

Basically, this leaves the idea of a `groupby + summarise` operation theoretically pure (because it shouldn't require orderable keys), but also gives users a convenient way to optionally opt in to sorted results.

---

There are 3 functions that would get this argument:
- `summarise()`
- `reframe()`
- `slice_sample()` (goes with #6662)

The following would not get `.sort` because they aren't about row ordering:
- `filter()`
- `mutate()`
- `slice()` and `slice_min/max/head/tail()` (after #6662 is changed)

title: `slice()` and `slice_head/tail/min/max()` should act like a `filter()` not a `reframe()`
description:
Note that this `filter()` call keeps the groups of `x` separated. i.e.  the groups of `2` and `1` are not aggregated together

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

df <- tibble(x = c(2, 1, 2, 2, 1), y = c(3, 2, 1, 2, 4))
df
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>       x     y
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     2     3
#> 2     1     2
#> 3     2     1
#> 4     2     2
#> 5     1     4

# Maintain group separation, we just take the first 2 per x group
df %>% filter(row_number() %in% 1:2, .by = x)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>       x     y
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     2     3
#> 2     1     2
#> 3     2     1
#> 4     1     4
```

`filter()` is simply about deciding which rows to keep, not about the ordering of the result.

I think that `slice()` and `slice_head/tail/min/max()` should function the exact same way. They currently do not:

``` r
# These both group the results by `x`.
# The difference is `.by` doesn't do an additional sort by `x`.
df %>% slice(1:2, .by = x)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>       x     y
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     2     3
#> 2     2     1
#> 3     1     2
#> 4     1     4

df %>% group_by(x) %>% slice(1:2)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#> # Groups:   x [2]
#>       x     y
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     2
#> 2     1     4
#> 3     2     3
#> 4     2     1
```

Slicing is purely about figuring out which rows to _keep_. It doesn't have anything to do with determining the order of said rows.

The current slice implementation is (implicitly) like a `reframe()` call instead.

``` r
df %>% reframe(.by = x, {
  data <- pick(everything())
  data[row_number() %in% 1:2,]
})
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>       x     y
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     2     3
#> 2     2     1
#> 3     1     2
#> 4     1     4
```

I think the way to practically make it work like a `filter()` is to change the implementation to build up a logical vector the same size as `.data` to slice with. That would retain the row ordering of `.data`.

---

The one `slice()` family exception to this is `slice_sample()`, which is not a filter. It can even generate more rows than you started with. Possibly this is a sign that `slice_*()` was an unfortunate prefix for that.

For this reason, `slice_sample()` should continue to aggregate groups together. It will just be slightly different, but that is okay.

title: `mutate(.by_row =)`, `reframe(.by_row =)`, and possibly `filter(.by_row =)`
description:
Related to https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/4723

With the introduction of `.by`, it seems reasonable to once again reconsider `rowwise()` as well. I think we are convinced that the _idea_ of rowwise is useful, but the implementation could possibly be improved. A few pain points:
- `rowwise()` is a form of persistent grouping, but you rarely want it on for more than 1 operation
- `ungroup()` is an odd verb for turning off rowwise behavior
- It still sucks that you need `summarise(model = list(lm(...)))`, i.e. the `list()` wrapping is manual
- Maintaining the `rowwise_df` class is difficult and error prone for us
- There are _very_ few times where rowwise behavior is actually useful. I think the two cases are `mutate()` and `reframe()`.

---

With that in mind, I'd like to suggest a two-part replacement for `rowwise()`:
- Two per-operation rowwise verbs, `mutate_row()` and `reframe_row()`. These become the _only_ two places in dplyr where rowwise behavior is applicable.
- Give `mutate()`, `summarise()`, `reframe()`, `mutate_row()`, and `reframe_row()` the ability to automatically wrap scalars in a list. i.e. if `vec_is(elt)` is `FALSE`, wrap automatically into a list. This means that value could _never_ exist in a data frame column as is, so there is no ambiguity about wrapping and it is fairly easy to explain.

Those two proposals result in the following new patterns:

```r
# dplyr 1.1.0
iris %>%
  tidyr::nest(.by = Species) %>%
  rowwise(Species) %>%
  mutate(model = list(lm(Petal.Length ~ Sepal.Length, data = data))) %>%
  reframe(broom::tidy(model))
   
# New 1:
# (note the lack of list(), and no persistant rowwise-ness)
# (note how we carry Species along in the reframe_row() call)
iris %>%
  tidyr::nest(.by = Species) %>%
  mutate_row(model = lm(Petal.Length ~ Sepal.Length, data = data)) %>%
  reframe_row(Species, broom::tidy(model))

# New 2:
# (note that even summarise() doesn't need manual list() wrapping)
iris %>%
  summarise(
    model = lm(Petal.Length ~ Sepal.Length, data = pick(everything())),
    .by = Species
  ) %>%
  reframe_row(Species, broom::tidy(model))

# All result in:

#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   Species    term         estimate std.error statistic  p.value
#>   <fct>      <chr>           <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 setosa     (Intercept)     0.803    0.344      2.34  2.38e- 2
#> 2 setosa     Sepal.Length    0.132    0.0685     1.92  6.07e- 2
#> 3 versicolor (Intercept)     0.185    0.514      0.360 7.20e- 1
#> 4 versicolor Sepal.Length    0.686    0.0863     7.95  2.59e-10
#> 5 virginica  (Intercept)     0.610    0.417      1.46  1.50e- 1
#> 6 virginica  Sepal.Length    0.750    0.0630    11.9   6.30e-16
```

This two part proposal has the very nice property that the difference between `mutate()` and `mutate_row()` becomes _purely_ about column access:
- `mutate()` accesses columns using `vec_slice()` / `[`
- `mutate_row()` accesses columns using `vec_slice2()` / `[[`

In other words, rowwise has _nothing_ to do with the output type of each column expression, and you still get useful results.

In terms of other invariants, there is one related to `vec_size()`:
- `mutate_row()` requires each expression to return an element of `vec_size() == 1`
- `reframe_row()` allows each expression to return an element of any size
- (the size invariant is enforced after list wrapping) 

Other niceties:
- It becomes very clear when you are doing a rowwise operation, because it is in the name of the verb (similar to `.by` being in the verb)
- Somewhat obvious, but it means rowwise behavior isn't persistent. You always have bare tibble in, bare tibble out, which greatly simplifies things.

---

Extra notes:
- Somewhat obvious, but `mutate_row()` and `reframe_row()` won't get `.by` because they operation "by row"
- We don't want to teach `.by` about rowwise behavior, like `.by = .row` or something. We want `.by` to be _pure_ tidyselect. Plus this special behavior would only apply for `mutate()` and `reframe()` and that would be very confusing.
- We do _not_ need `summarise_row()`. This would have the _exact_ same semantics as `mutate_row()`, but would just drop unused columns (which can mostly be done with `.keep` in `mutate_row()`). In particular `summarise_row()` and `mutate_row()` would both have to have the `vec_size() == 1` invariant from above, so we really don't need both.
- There is no need for `filter_row()`. The only useful thing I can think of is something like `filter_row(!is.null(model))` for filtering out `NULL` list elements. But you can do that way more efficiently with an ungrouped call to `filter(!funs::is_na(model))`.

`mutate_row()` and `reframe_row()` mostly have the semantics of the wrappers below, but this doesn't do the automatic list-wrapping of scalars:

```r
mutate_row <- function(.data, ...) {
  .data <- rowwise(.data)
  .data <- mutate(.data, ...)
  ungroup(.data)
}

reframe_row <- function(.data, ...) {
  .data <- rowwise(.data)
  reframe(.data, ...)
}
```

title: `distinct()` Grouping example is unclear and incomplete
description:
The #Grouping example [@](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/distinct.html) does not make it clear how groups affect `distinct()`. Grouping variables are only included if a variable is specified inside `distinct()`:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
df <- tibble(
  g = c(1, 1, 3),
  x = c(1, 1, 1),
  y = c(3, 1, 1)
) %>% 
  group_by(g)
## Includes g in variables used by distinct()
df %>% distinct(x)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#> # Groups:   g [2]
#>       g     x
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     1
#> 2     3     1
## Does not include g in variables used by distinct()
df %>% distinct()
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#> # Groups:   g [2]
#>       g     x     y
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     1     3
#> 2     1     1     1
#> 3     3     1     1
```

<sup>Created on 2023-01-24 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

I created this issue as I expected `distinct()` to include grouping variables whether or not arguments are specified inside `distinct()`.

title: `mutate` a new column using an external pointer to grouped data
description:

```r
    mutate(newVisit = ifelse(n < 6, paste(time[ind-1],time[ind], sep = "/"), time[ind]))
```

title: Add all_of() / any_of() selection helper example to documentation of `rename()`
description:
I recently found out that `all_of()` and `any_of()` can be used with a named vector inside `dplyr::rename()` to rename variables. This is a very helpful, though undocumented feature (see reprex below). I assume that this is intended behavior.

In that case, I wonder whether it might be worth adding to the documentation of `rename()` which doesn't mention the use of selection helpers so far.

Since the documentation of `tidyselect::all_of()` doesn't contain an example using a named vector this might also be an issue for the tidyselect repo. However, I think adding it to `rename()`would be helpful, since it is a common problem to rename columns based on  lookup vector which contains more names than the actual data.frame.

``` r
library(dplyr)

iris <- as_tibble(iris) # so it prints a little nicer

recode_vec <- c("Sepal_Length" = "Sepal.Length",
                "Non_existent_var" = "Non.existent.var" )

rename(iris, any_of(recode_vec))
```

title: Slow performance of `n_distinct()` on grouped dataframe when `na.rm=TRUE`
description:
Hi,

There is a slow performance of `n_distinct()`, but only on grouped dataframe on only when `na.rm=TRUE`.
There, the performance is around 10 times slower than `length(unique(na.omit(.x)))`.

Note that the allocated memory is higher than base R, even when `na.rm=FALSE`.

Here is a reprex with a benchmark:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(0)  
a = expand_grid(subjid=1:30, visit=1:10) %>% 
  mutate(x = runif(n(), 0, 100),
         x = ifelse(x>50, NA, x))

f1a = n_distinct   
f1b = function(.x) n_distinct(.x, na.rm=TRUE)   
f2a = function(.x) length(unique(.x))   
f2b = function(.x) length(unique(na.omit(.x)))   

f = function(fun){
  a %>% 
    group_by(subjid) %>% 
    mutate(n_x = fun(x)) %>% 
    pull() %>% table()
}
  
x = bench::mark(
  n_distinct = f(f1a),
  length_unique = f(f2a),
)
x2 = bench::mark(
  n_distinct_narm = f(f1b),
  length_unique_narm = f(f2b),
)

x
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression         min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>    <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 n_distinct      6.18ms   6.44ms      153.    1.65MB     6.39
#> 2 length_unique   5.85ms   6.01ms      165.  111.64KB     6.33
x2
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression              min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>         <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 n_distinct_narm     62.01ms  63.04ms      15.9   243.5KB     9.54
```

title: across() fails silently when using .funs (used in scoped mutate) instead of .fns
description:
[across](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/across.html#arguments)() uses `.fns =`  as the argument to supply an anonymous function. 
This is different than the [scoped mutate functions](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/mutate_all.html?q=mutate_at#arguments), which used `.funs =`, with an extra "u".

This causes some problems when rewriting code from scoped syntax `mutate_at(.funs = ~)` to the new `mutate(across(.fns = ~))`, because supplying the wrong argument in `across()` (namely, `.funs` instead of `.fns`) fails silently, as shown below.

``` r
library(tidyverse)

mtcars <- as_tibble(mtcars) %>% select(mpg)

# Using the named argument ".fns" applies the function, as expected
mtcars %>% mutate(across(mpg, .fns = ~ . * 1000))
#> # A tibble: 32 × 1
#>      mpg
#>    <dbl>
#>  1 21000
#>  2 21000
#>  3 22800
#>  4 21400
#>  5 18700
#>  6 18100
#>  7 14300
#>  8 24400
#>  9 22800
#> 10 19200
#> # … with 22 more rows

# Using the named argument ".funs" fails, silently
mtcars %>% mutate(across(mpg, .funs = ~ . * 1000))
#> # A tibble: 32 × 1
#>      mpg
#>    <dbl>
#>  1  21  
#>  2  21  
#>  3  22.8
#>  4  21.4
#>  5  18.7
#>  6  18.1
#>  7  14.3
#>  8  24.4
#>  9  22.8
#> 10  19.2
#> # … with 22 more rows
```

<sup>Created on 2023-01-12 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

As the argument is ignored, the result is no different than failing to supply any function at all.
(Supplying the function without naming the argument works as expected.)

Perhaps `across` should throw a warning when it does not detect an anonymous function being supplied?

title: Support a 0-length array result in summarize, when working on an empty DataFrame
description:
Currently, afaict dplyr handles summarizing an empty dataframe as follows:

* for each argument:
* apply the given calculation, using the empty dataframe
* use the result type to produce a new 0-length column, but ~~discard its value~~ (edit: grouped summarize discards the value, ungrouped summarize keeps it)
* if the result is length 0 or > 1, print a deprecation warning

This results in a sort of funky situation where operations like `+` raise a warning, because `integer() + 1` results in a 0-length array. I wonder if a 0-length result when summarizing an empty data.frame should not be deprecated? It seems like there is already some special behavior around empty frames, and some operations returning 0-length results is likely in this case :/.

``` r
library(tidyverse)

df <- tibble(a = integer())

integer() + 1
#> numeric(0)

df %>% summarize(b = sum(a))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>       b
#>   <int>
#> 1     0

df %>% summarize(b = a + 1)
#> Warning: Returning more (or less) than 1 row per `summarise()` group was deprecated in
#> dplyr 1.1.0.
#> ℹ Please use `reframe()` instead.
#> ℹ When switching from `summarise()` to `reframe()`, remember that `reframe()`
#>   always returns an ungrouped data frame and adjust accordingly.
#> # A tibble: 0 × 1
#> # … with 1 variable: b <dbl>
```

<sup>Created on 2023-01-10 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

related to https://github.com/machow/siuba/issues/467

**edit:** wait -- I just noticed ungrouped summarize keeps the value, but grouped summarize discards it...

``` r
library(tidyverse)

df <- tibble(a = integer())

df %>% group_by(a) %>% summarize(b = sum(a))
#> # A tibble: 0 × 2
#> # … with 2 variables: a <int>, b <int>
```

title: Joining columns with list content returns NULL instead of NA
description:
I noticed that, when joining data that has list content, unmatched rows in left_join() produce NULL values rather than the NA values common for all other datatypes. 

This potentially creates downstream issues, as replacing the NULLs with NAs for consistent behaviour is relatively expensive (go-to functions like na_if() usually struggle with this type of nested list column).

There may be a work-around in the join family I'm not seeing, but this does seem like unintended and incosistent behaviour.

Reprex:
```r
test_1 <- tibble(id = c("1611030457298161665", "1611079838563184641"))

test_2 <- tibble(id = "1611030457298161665", content = list(c("this", "is", "a", "list")))

test_3 <- tibble(id = "1611030457298161665", content = "not a list")

left_join(test_1, test_2, by = "id)

left_join(test_1, test_3, by = "id)
```
Results:
```
  id                  content  
  <chr>               <list>   
1 1611030457298161665 <chr [4]>
2 1611079838563184641 <NULL> 

  id                  content   
  <chr>               <chr>     
1 1611030457298161665 not a list
2 1611079838563184641 NA 
```

title: add recode unquote splicing example to case_match
description:
I see `case_match` is going to supersede `recode` and it looks to have some useful aspects e.g. the grouped LHS, but if I understand the examples correctly because of the 2-sided formulae it might not support unquote splicing (at least of a character vector) which for us is a major shortcut when using `recode`. 

It would be great if the example below from `?recode` where a named character vector is used for unquote splicing with `!!!` is also  included in the `case_match` examples. Assuming this isn't possible, can an example please be added to `case_match` to show how to recreate a similar pattern (e.g. perhaps we have to create a list of expressions or formulae with `paste` or `reformulate`, and then use rlang trickery like `parse_exprs`).
``` r
library(dplyr)
char_vec <- sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 10, replace = TRUE)
char_vec
#>  [1] "a" "b" "b" "c" "c" "a" "b" "c" "b" "a"
# Use a named character vector for unquote splicing with !!!
level_key <- c(a = "apple", b = "banana", c = "carrot")
recode(char_vec, !!!level_key)
#>  [1] "apple"  "banana" "banana" "carrot" "carrot" "apple"  "banana" "carrot"
#>  [9] "banana" "apple"
```

title: Consider `.default = NA` in `case_match/when()`?
description:
In https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/pull/6590#discussion_r1050807631, @hadley brought up that rather than `.default = NULL` we could use `.default = NA`

On one hand I see the appeal of `.default = NA`:
- No need to handle `NULL` specially in `vec_case_when()`
- Possibly more intuitive?

On the other hand, I like `.default = NULL` because:
- When I rewrite `vec_case_when()` in C, I will probably optimize for this case. We could initialize an output with `vec_init(size)` and then assign into it wherever we have a match. If `.default = NULL` then we are done and we don't need to do extra recycling or assignment to handle the default values.
- We use `if_else(missing = NULL)` already and `missing` maps directly to `default`. I feel like it makes sense to be consistent with that.
- `NULL` is our typical value for "I haven't specified this argument at all so give me its default behavior"
- It matches the default of `ptype` and `size` in `case_when/match()` and I liked that

Whatever is decided, we need to be consistent in:
- `vec_case_when()`
- `vec_case_match()`
- `case_when()`
- `case_match()`
- `if_else()`

title: `cross_join()` in place of `by = character()`
description:
Rationale for adding an explicit `cross_join()` function in favor of the existing `by = character()` method:

* I think `by = character()` is fairly unintuitive, and I’ve seen 2 cases recently where people didn’t even know it existed

* I think `by = character()` should really be an error. I think its current behavior of doing a cross join is actually a little scary. Like, supplying `c("x", "y")` matches on two _columns_, supplying `"x"` matches on one _column_, but `character()` all of the sudden matches all _rows_? Seems very odd to me.

* Importantly, currently only `inner_join(by = character())` is a _true_ cross join. SQL cross joins must result in `nrow(x) * nrow(y)` number of rows, and only the inner cross join does this in the edge case where one of the inputs has 0 rows (i.e. the left join would retain all x rows). I know this is edge case behavior, but the weirdness here feels worth resolving by just adding `cross_join()`

* I think it would be more straightforward for dbplyr and friends to convert `cross_join()` to SQL. Converting `left_join(by = character())` to SQL is probably quite odd.

* It would be nice that `cross_join()` wouldn’t have a `by` argument at all, making it very clear it doesn’t have anything to do with columns

* We could document `cross_join()` on its own help page, raising awareness of it

* `join_by()` wouldn’t have to support cross joins, which it currently does by allowing empty `join_by()` calls to be treated like cross joins. I could turn that into an error for 1.1.0 if we also added `cross_join()` at the same time, which would be much nicer than having to deprecate it slowly in the future.

title: `slice_sample()` and friends with `check_dots_empty()` in generic
description:
In https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/pull/6378 we moved `check_slice_dots()` into the generic of `slice_sample()` and friends. This check does two things:
- Checks for jointly missing `n` and `prop` plus a single unnamed value in `...` and errors if there is one
- Calls `check_dots_empty()`

Having the 2nd point in the generic is problematic for authors that provide methods for `slice_sample()` and friends with their own custom arguments. For example:

`tidyterra:::slice_sample.SpatRaster(.keep_extent = TRUE)`

`.keep_extent` is seen as an empty dot no matter what 

I think we could move the `check_dots_empty()` check into the `.data.frame` method, but keep the jointly missing typo check in the generic, and that would keep most of the checking benefits while allowing extension authors to add their own extra args.

(Note, check the PR against tidyterra to make sure it actually fixes it)

title: `left_join()` issues with `check_dots_used()`

Maybe we can move `check_dots_used()` into the `.data.frame` method, and at that point it should probably be changed to `check_dots_empty()`? This probably has other repercussions for method authors that call `NextMethod()`, but I think we should give it a try before giving up.

title: Feedback on `join_by()` helpers
description:
Following up on the [call for feedback on dplyr 1.1.0](https://www.tidyverse.org/blog/2022/11/dplyr-1-1-0-is-coming-soon/)...

The new `join_by()` function supports helpers `between()`, `within()`, and `overlaps()` for working with numeric ranges. I have two pieces of feedback on the `within()` helper:

* This function name is provided by base R, so roxygen is creating links from the [dplyr docs](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/dev/reference/join_by.html) to the [base R function](https://rdrr.io/r/base/with.html). This might cause some confusion for end users. I think these links can be prevented though.
* The name "within" has a lot of meanings in different scenarios, but the implementation is very specific to numeric ranges. I'm a bit worried we might be boxing ourselves into a corner if we want to provide more `join_by()` helpers in future. For example, "within" is often used to check membership (e.g., [`ipaddress::is_within()`](https://davidchall.github.io/ipaddress/reference/address_in_network.html)). I'm unfamiliar with your plans for `join_by()`, but I'm wondering if this should be renamed as `range_within()`?

Looking forward to the new release - congrats! 🎉

title: Suggested wording for `.by` documentation: "per-operation" instead of "temporary"
description:
Currently, `.by` documentation at [R/by.R](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/HEAD/R/by.R) calls `.by` temporary and `group_by()`. 

I think calling `.by` "temporary" only makes sense in the presence of, or as a newly developed alternative to `group_by()`. However, if you're learning dplyr today for the first time (or after this release is out) and you learn `.by` first instead of `group_by()`, and have never heard of `group_by()` or don't know how it works, the word "temporary" doesn't make as much sense, I think.

The [blog post](https://www.tidyverse.org/blog/2022/11/dplyr-1-1-0-is-coming-soon/#temporary-grouping-with-by) uses the following wording for data.table:

> This feature was inspired by [data.table](https://cran.r-project.org/package=data.table), which has always used per-operation grouping.

I like the term "per-operation" grouping better than temporary and I think it's easier to understand even if you don't know about `group_by()` behaviour.

I would suggest something like the following:

> There are two ways to group in dplyr:
>
> - Persistent grouping with `group_by()`
> - Per operation grouping with `.by`
>
> This help page is dedicated to explaining where and why you might want to use the latter. Grouping radically affects the computation of the dplyr verb you use it with, and one of the goals of `.by` is to allow you to place that grouping specification within the function that actually uses it. As an added benefit, with `.by` don't need to remember to `ungroup()` after `summarise()`, and `summarise()` won't message you about how it's handling the groups!

title: tolerance in `all_equal()`
description:
First I acknowledge the deprecation status :

> all_equal() allows you to compare data frames, optionally ignoring row and column names. It is deprecated as of dplyr 1.1.0, because it makes it too easy to ignore important differences.

Previously phrased as (with my emphasis):

> `all_equal()` allows you to compare data frames, optionally ignoring row and column names. It is questioning as of dplyr 1.0.0, because it seems to solve a problem ***that no longer seems that important***.

However `all_equal()` is very useful for my use case, which is basically:

> Given a workflow where data is collected from a data base and wrangled, adapt the wrangling to use dbplyr and collect as late as possible, without altering the transformations

dbplyr work might often shuffle the rows as row order is meaningless in data bases and I rely on `all_equal()` to test if my dbplyr translations are working with something like

```
data_old <- tbl(con, "name") %>% collect() %>% old_wrangling()
data_new <- tbl(con, "name") %>% new_wrangling() %>% collect()
all_equal(data_old, data_new)
```

However in my use case the numeric rounding is different depending on where I collect so `all_equal()` returns `FALSE` where waldo would say:

```
     old$praemie_b      | new$praemie_b          
 [1] 12.0000000000000   | 12.0000000000000   [1] 
 [2] 18.0000000000000   | 18.0000000000000   [2] 
 [3] 616.8000000000000  | 616.8000000000000  [3] 
 [4] 6847.8000000000002 - 6847.7999999999993 [4] 
 [5] 5308.1999999999998 - 5308.2000000000007 [5] 
 [6] 4618.1999999999998 - 4618.2000000000007 [6] 
 [7] 5776.1999999999998 - 5776.2000000000007 [7] 
 [8] 12.0000000000000   | 12.0000000000000   [8] 
 [9] 4127.3999999999996 | 4127.3999999999996 [9] 
[10] 18.0000000000000   | 18.0000000000000   [10]
```

With waldo I can set the tolerance to work around that but then I cannot shuffle rows anymore.

Could we either add a tolerance arg to `all_equal()` or an `ignore_row_order()` arg to waldo to solve this issue ?

---------

For lurkers : 

```
all_equal2 <- function(target, current, ignore_col_order = TRUE, ignore_row_order = TRUE, convert = FALSE, ..., digits = 6) {
  dplyr::all_equal(
    dplyr::mutate_if(target, is.numeric, round, digits) ,
    dplyr::mutate_if(current, is.numeric, round, digits),
    ignore_col_order, ignore_row_order, convert, ...
  )
}
```

title: Two suggestions for dplyr 1.1.0 .by with mutate
description:
.by is a great facility with mutate

Here are two things that would make it even better from my perspective:

- allow creation of an on-the-fly grouping variable -- for example

`df |> mutate(b=a / max(a), .by=stringr::str_starts(name, "south"))`

- alternatively, if a grouping variable can't be created on the fly, it would be nice to be able to create it in the same mutate statement, rather than in separate statements, for example:

`df |> mutate(southornot=stringr::str_starts(name, "south"), b=a / max(a), .by=southornot)`

rather than the following, which appears to be required now:

`df |> mutate(southornot=stringr::str_starts(name, "south")) |> mutate(b=a / max(a), .by=southornot)`

Thanks for considering it, and thanks for the big leap forward in dplyr.

title: Make `Joining with` message clickable to copy-to-clipboard
description:
Hi,

dplyr 1.1.0 seems like it is going to be great (I installed the dev version with `pak::[pak](http://pak.r-lib.org/reference/pak.html)("tidyverse/dplyr")`). I really like .by in summarise and mutate.

One small suggestion for messages related to the new join:

In the old join, if I leave out the "by" it gives a helpful message stating what it does by default, giving the ", by=" statement it used. This is nice because if I like it, I can copy it directly into code.

The new 1.1.0 message when "by" is left out is slightly different. For example, here is a typical message:

``` 
Joining with `by = join_by(mergevar)`
```

Notice that this does not have a comma and space before the "by", or else it would look like this:

``` 
Joining with `, by = join_by(mergevar)`
```

The advantage of the second message is that it can be copied into code without the two extra keystrokes the first one requires. Hardly a significant issue, but it could add up over thousands of people and many days.

Thanks for considering it.

title: `inner_join(unmatched =)` probably needs to support a string of length 2
description:
i.e. to be able to say `inner_join(unmatched = c("error", "drop"))` to error if any rows in `x` are going to be dropped, but ignore any dropped rows in `y`

This is the only join that would need this, as:
- `left_join()` can only have `unmatched` `y` rows
- `right_join()` can only have `unmatched` `x` rows
- `full_join()` can't have `unmatched` rows at all

---

This came up when working on the 1.1.0 blog post.

Let's look at our `employees` and `parties` example. The goal is to safely figure out which party each employee will be celebrated at:
- We can't match an employee's birthday to multiple parties (implying we need `multiple = "error"`)
- We can't drop an employee's birthday (implying we need `unmatched = "error"` for `employees` and one of `inner/right_join()` so `unmatched` would be triggered on `x`)
- We are okay if an unmatched party is dropped from the result, because we just care about the employee->party mapping being filled out (implying we need `unmatched = "drop"` for `parties` and this narrows us down to `inner_join()`). This can happen if, say, no employees have birthdays in Q4.

So really we need:

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(clock)
set.seed(12345)

parties <- tibble(
  q = 1:4,
  party = date_parse(c("2022-01-10", "2022-04-04", "2022-07-11", "2022-10-03"))
)

parties
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>       q party     
#>   <int> <date>    
#> 1     1 2022-01-10
#> 2     2 2022-04-04
#> 3     3 2022-07-11
#> 4     4 2022-10-03

employees <- tibble(
  name = wakefield::name(100),
  birthday = date_parse("2022-01-01") + (sample(365, 100, replace = TRUE) - 1)
)

employees
#> # A tibble: 100 × 2
#>    name       birthday  
#>    <variable> <date>    
#>  1 Seager     2022-08-26
#>  2 Nathion    2022-10-04
#>  3 Sametra    2022-06-13
#>  4 Netty      2022-05-12
#>  5 Yalissa    2022-05-28
#>  6 Mirai      2022-08-20
#>  7 Toyoko     2022-08-23
#>  8 Earlene    2022-04-21
#>  9 Abbegayle  2022-01-27
#> 10 Valyssa    2022-03-06
#> # … with 90 more rows

# employees |>
#   inner_join(
#     parties, 
#     join_by(between(birthday, start, end)),
#     unmatched = c("error", "drop"),
#     multiple = "error"
#   )
```

I thought a `right_join()` would suffice, but that answers a different question because it will add unmatched `y` rows onto the result, which means you can end up with a (possibly) unexpected number of rows (because the output number of rows doesn't match the number of rows in the `x` input). In particular, it doesn't match the 3rd bullet mentioned above about being fine with dropping unmatched parties

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(clock)
set.seed(12345)

parties <- tibble(
  q = c(1:4),
  party = date_parse(c("2022-01-10", "2022-04-04", "2022-07-11", "2022-10-03")),
  start = date_parse(c("2022-01-01", "2022-04-01", "2022-07-01", "2022-10-01")),
  end = date_parse(c("2022-03-31", "2022-06-30", "2022-09-30", "2022-12-31"))
)

parties
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>       q party      start      end       
#>   <int> <date>     <date>     <date>    
#> 1     1 2022-01-10 2022-01-01 2022-03-31
#> 2     2 2022-04-04 2022-04-01 2022-06-30
#> 3     3 2022-07-11 2022-07-01 2022-09-30
#> 4     4 2022-10-03 2022-10-01 2022-12-31

# Not sampling anything from the 4th quarter here
employees <- tibble(
  name = wakefield::name(100),
  birthday = date_parse("2022-01-01") + (sample(250, 100, replace = TRUE) - 1)
)

employees
#> # A tibble: 100 × 2
#>    name       birthday  
#>    <variable> <date>    
#>  1 Seager     2022-08-26
#>  2 Nathion    2022-01-21
#>  3 Sametra    2022-06-13
#>  4 Netty      2022-05-12
#>  5 Yalissa    2022-05-28
```

title: Feedback for alternate names for `reframe()`
description:
In https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/pull/6557 we implemented `reframe()`, which allows us to deprecate the `summarise()` feature that allowed it to return per-group results of size 0 or >1, as requested by https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6382

In https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6382, we had a large amount of discussion about the name of this new function. That issue also documents a number of assumptions about how this function should be used. We were never able to come up with a name that we were 100% happy with, but `reframe()` seemed like the least worst option.

It has some nice connections to `tibble::enframe()` and `tibble::deframe()` https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6382#issuecomment-1323866603

Until dplyr 1.1.0 is released, this issue will stay open to gather feedback about this name.

- Feel free to leave comments with additional suggestions
- Leave a 👍 reaction on this comment if you like this name
- Leave a 👎 reaction if you strongly disagree with this name
