title: `group_map` overrides default arguments to `.f` with group names when called with `...`
description:
Situation: `group_map.data.frame` is called from a function taking `...` arguments. `group_map` passes those `...` arguments to `.f`, i.e., the function being mapped. `.f` also accepts one or more named arguments with defaults, in addition to the data.frame and `...`.

I'd expect one of two possible behaviors here:

1. Grouping variables are not passed to `.f` via `...`; the `...` arguments to `.f` are the same as those passed to the outer function, or
2. Grouping variables are passed to `.f` via `...`; the `...` arguments to `.f` are the union of the grouping variables and the `...` arguments passed to the outer function (possibly with a warning or error if named arguments passed to the outer function conflict with reserved names for the grouping variables)

Either way, I'd expect default arguments to `.f` to be retained, unless they're overridden explicitly in the calls to `group_map` or the outer function. Instead, they're overridden by the grouping variable.

```r
library(dplyr)

data <- tibble(group = c(1, 1, 2, 2))

inner_function <- function(df, foo = 3:4, bar = 7:8, ...) {
    tibble(foo = foo, bar = bar, ...)
}

inner_function(data, foo = 5:6, baz = 9:10)

# # A tibble: 2 × 3
#     foo   bar   baz
#   <int> <int> <int>
# 1     5     7     9
# 2     6     8    10

outer_function <- function(df, ...) {
    data |>
        group_by(group) |>
        group_map(inner_function, ...)
}

outer_function(data, foo = 5:6, baz = 9:10)

# [[1]]
# # A tibble: 2 × 3
#     foo bar$group   baz
#   <int>     <dbl> <int>
# 1     5         1     9
# 2     6         1    10

# [[2]]
# # A tibble: 2 × 3
#     foo bar$group   baz
#   <int>     <dbl> <int>
# 1     5         2     9
# 2     6         2    10
```

Note that `bar`, a default argument to `inner_function`, is overridden by the `group` variable and isn't present in the output.

With a single grouping variable, `group_map` overrides the first argument to the inner function that isn't specified in the call to the outer function. So this modification results in the expected output:

```r
inner_function <- function(df, foo = 3:4, an_unused_argument = NULL, bar = 7:8, ...) {
    tibble(foo = foo, bar = bar, ...)
}

outer_function(data, foo = 5:6, baz = 9:10)

# [[1]]
# # A tibble: 2 × 3
#     foo   bar   baz
#   <int> <int> <int>
# 1     5     7     9
# 2     6     8    10

# [[2]]
# # A tibble: 2 × 3
#     foo   bar   baz
#   <int> <int> <int>
# 1     5     7     9
# 2     6     8    10
```

For completeness, note that `group_modify` exhibits similar behavior, since it wraps `group_map`.

title: `rename_with()` doesn't handle factors well
description:
`rename_with.data.frame()` has _unexpected_ results when `.fn` returns a `factor` -- or at least unexpected for me.  Documentation does _suggest_ that `.fn` should return a `character` vector, but I wouldn't expect factors to be coerced to integers first.

The coercion occurs within `[<-`, which could be replaced with `vec_slice()`?

https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/434caa2db5c1f48b9f0becc9295e547c1072260b/R/rename.R#L69

``` r
df <- data.frame(
  a = 1,
  b = 2,
  c = 3
)

foo <- function(x) {
  factor(toupper(x))
}

dplyr::rename_with(df, foo)
#>   1 2 3
#> 1 1 2 3


# name reassignment within rename_with.data.frame()
x <- c("a", "b", "c")
x[1:3] <- foo(x)
x
#> [1] "1" "2" "3"


# vctrs seems fine
x <- c("a", "b", "c")
vctrs::vec_slice(x, 2:3) <- foo(x[2:3])
x
#> [1] "a" "B" "C"
```

title: `filter(.missing = )` option to optionally retain missing values
description:
Currently, `filter()`:
- Retains `TRUE`
- Drops `FALSE` and `NA`
- This matches `subset()`

A number of requests have come up in the past desiring:
- Retains `TRUE` and `NA`
- Drops `FALSE`
- This matches `[`

Here are a few:
* https://stackoverflow.com/questions/46378437/how-to-filter-data-without-losing-na-rows-using-dplyr (17k views)
* https://stackoverflow.com/questions/32908589/why-does-dplyrs-filter-drop-na-values-from-a-factor-variable (8k views)
* https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6432 (august this year)
* https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6013
* https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/4478 (requesting more docs about this)
* https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/3196
* https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/812
* https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/1527 (more about drop(), but still related to NAs)
* My wife has brought this up to me at least 3 times

This is most apparently annoying when you have multiple columns to filter by

``` r
library(dplyr)

df <- tibble(
  x = c(TRUE, FALSE, NA, NA, NA),
  y = c(NA, TRUE, NA, NA, NA),
  z = c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, NA)
)
df
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   x     y     z    
#>   <lgl> <lgl> <lgl>
#> 1 TRUE  NA    TRUE 
#> 2 FALSE TRUE  TRUE 
#> 3 NA    NA    TRUE 
#> 4 NA    NA    FALSE
#> 5 NA    NA    NA

filter(df, x, y, z)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 3
#> # … with 3 variables: x <lgl>, y <lgl>, z <lgl>

filter(df, x | is.na(x), y | is.na(y), z | is.na(z))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   x     y     z    
#>   <lgl> <lgl> <lgl>
#> 1 TRUE  NA    TRUE 
#> 2 NA    NA    TRUE 
#> 3 NA    NA    NA
```

I propose a `.missing = c("drop", "keep", "error")` argument to `filter()` that would allow you to optionally keep rows with `NA`.

We'd have to carefully analyze the boolean algebra here to make sure we are being consistent. In particular I think we want to make sure these are the same if we do this, but I think they are:

```r
# these should be the same
filter(df, x, y, .missing = "drop")
filter(df, x & y, .missing = "drop")

# these should be the same
filter(df, x, y, .missing = "keep")
filter(df, x & y, .missing = "keep")
```

The `"drop"` case is probably already consistent because that is what we do today, and the `"keep"` case is probably like this, which seems consistent

``` r
na_to_true <- function(x) {
  x[is.na(x)] <- TRUE
  x
}

na_to_true(TRUE & NA)
#> [1] TRUE
na_to_true(TRUE) & na_to_true(NA)
#> [1] TRUE
```

---

When we do this, we should also think about whether `vec_pall()` or `vec_pany()` could be used in `filter()` in any way, since they are heavily optimized for performance.

title: Bug or inconsistent or illogical processing of "suffix" in consecutive joins.
description:
When joining tibbles with columns that have the same name but are not join columns, the `suffix` argument allows you to provide a scheme to rename the columns from the tibbles. However, when you perform consecutive joins there is an inconsistent behavior. The first join correctly applies the suffixes. The second does not. All subsequent ones appear to.

I was especially surprised that it wasn't just with piped joined. Saving the intermediate joins to variables gives the same effect.

My expected output from the `reprex` below is:

```
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>       A B1    B2    B3     B4   
#>   <int> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr>
#> 1     1 a     d     g     j    
#> 2     2 b     e     h     k    
#> 3     3 c     f     i     l
```

There may be a "reason" why `dplyr` behaves this way. But it is very confusing and, more importantly, would require an elaborate workaround to achieve the desired result.

``` r
library(tidyverse)

df1 = tibble(A=1:3, B=letters[1:3])
df2 = tibble(A=1:3, B=letters[4:6])
df3 = tibble(A=1:3, B=letters[7:9])
df4 = tibble(A=1:3, B=letters[10:12])

df1 %>%
inner_join(df2, by="A", suffix=c("1", "2")) %>%
inner_join(df3, by="A", suffix=c("", "3")) %>%
inner_join(df4, by="A", suffix=c("", "4"))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>       A B1    B2    B     B4   
#>   <int> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr>
#> 1     1 a     d     g     j    
#> 2     2 b     e     h     k    
#> 3     3 c     f     i     l


j12 = inner_join(df1, df2, by="A", suffix=c("1", "2"))
j12
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>       A B1    B2   
#>   <int> <chr> <chr>
#> 1     1 a     d    
#> 2     2 b     e    
#> 3     3 c     f
j123 = inner_join(j12, df3, by="A", suffix=c("", "3"))
j123
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>       A B1    B2    B    
#>   <int> <chr> <chr> <chr>
#> 1     1 a     d     g    
#> 2     2 b     e     h    
#> 3     3 c     f     i
j1234 = inner_join(j123, df4, by="A", suffix=c("", "4"))
j1234
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>       A B1    B2    B     B4   
#>   <int> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr>
#> 1     1 a     d     g     j    
#> 2     2 b     e     h     k    
#> 3     3 c     f     i     l
```

title: When all_of() variables are missing, only a generic error appears

title: A ptype stable `mutate()` ?
description:
Type stability is a big thing in the tidyverse, but `mutate()` allows us to freely override types, leading to potential mistakes (overriding dates or factors with character for instance), which might lead to errors down the line, silent in the worst case.

Would it make sense to allow `mutate()` to be stricter with an argument, or maybe have a different function `mutate_strict()` , or a subclass to enforce this behaviour ?

See below a draft using a `"safe"` subclass, I use `vctrs::vec_cast()` so we still have a level of flexibility in the input but the stability of the output's ptype is guaranteed. We can use `factor` or `list_of` when building the original object, and then we use simple `character` or `list` to update the object with no risk of corrupting the data.

``` r
library(dplyr, w = F)
mutate.safe <- function(.data, ...) {
  # convert dots to quosures so we can manipulate the expressions
  dots <- rlang::enquos(...)
  if(!all(names(dots) %in% names(.data))) rlang::abort("can't add columns to a safe tibble, did you mispell `...` ?")
  # edit the expressions, wrapping them into `vctrs::vec_cast()`
  dots <- purrr::imap(dots, ~ {
    # `arg = fun(my_expr)` becomes `arg = vctrs::vec_cast(fun(my_expr), ptype(arg))` 
    new_expr <- expr(vctrs::vec_cast(!!rlang::quo_squash(.x), vctrs::vec_ptype(!!rlang::sym(.y))))
    # if arg is a constant env is empty, we set to baseenv(so we can fetch `::`)
    env <- rlang::quo_get_env(.x)
    if (identical(env, emptyenv())) .x <- rlang::quo_set_env(.x, baseenv())
    rlang::quo_set_expr(.x, new_expr)
  })
  class(.data) <- setdiff(class(.data), "safe")
  out <- mutate(.data, !!!dots)
  class(out) <- c("safe", class(out))
  out
}
foo <- tibble(a= letters[1:2], b = c(1,2), c = factor(letters[1:2]), d = as.Date(c("2022-01-01", "2022-01-02")), e = vctrs::list_of(cars))
class(foo) <- c("safe", class(foo))

mutate(foo, f = 1) # we can't create a new colum
#> Error in `mutate()`:
#> ! can't add columns to a safe tibble, did you mispell `...` ?

mutate(foo, a = 1) # can't cast double to character
#> Error in `mutate()`:
#> ℹ In argument: `a = vctrs::vec_cast(1, vctrs::vec_ptype(a))`.
#> Caused by error:
#> ! Can't convert `1` <double> to <character>.


mutate(foo, b = 3:4) # casting integer to double
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   a         b c     d                       e
#>   <chr> <dbl> <fct> <date>     <list<df[,2]>>
#> 1 a         3 a     2022-01-01       [50 × 2]
#> 2 b         4 b     2022-01-02       [50 × 2]

mutate(foo, c = c("b", "b")) # casting character to factor with allowed levels
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   a         b c     d                       e
#>   <chr> <dbl> <fct> <date>     <list<df[,2]>>
#> 1 a         1 b     2022-01-01       [50 × 2]
#> 2 b         2 b     2022-01-02       [50 × 2]

mutate(foo, c = c("b", "d")) # can't cast because wrong levels
#> Error in `mutate()`:
#> ℹ In argument: `c = vctrs::vec_cast(c("b", "d"), vctrs::vec_ptype(c))`.
#> Caused by error:
#> ! Can't convert from `c("b", "d")` <character> to <factor<38051>> due to loss of generality.
#> • Locations: 2

mutate(foo, d = lubridate::as_datetime(c("2022-01-01", "2022-01-02"))) # datetimes are casted to date
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   a         b c     d                       e
#>   <chr> <dbl> <fct> <date>     <list<df[,2]>>
#> 1 a         1 a     2022-01-01       [50 × 2]
#> 2 b         2 b     2022-01-02       [50 × 2]

mutate(foo, d = c("2022-01-01", "2022-01-02")) # characters can't be casted to date
#> Error in `mutate()`:
#> ℹ In argument: `d = vctrs::vec_cast(c("2022-01-01", "2022-01-02"),
#>   vctrs::vec_ptype(d))`.
#> Caused by error:
#> ! Can't convert `c("2022-01-01", "2022-01-02")` <character> to <date>.

mutate(foo, e = list(iris)) # using list_of allowed us to prevent corrupting our data silently
#> Error in `mutate()`:
#> ℹ In argument: `e = vctrs::vec_cast(list(iris), vctrs::vec_ptype(e))`.
#> Caused by error:
#> ! Can't convert from `..1` <data.frame<
#>   Sepal.Length: double
#>   Sepal.Width : double
#>   Petal.Length: double
#>   Petal.Width : double
#>   Species     : factor<fb977>
#> >> to <data.frame<
#>   speed: double
#>   dist : double
#> >> due to loss of precision.

mutate(foo, e = list(head(cars))) # and we don't have to bother with list_of anymore if we feed the right format
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   a         b c     d                       e
#>   <chr> <dbl> <fct> <date>     <list<df[,2]>>
#> 1 a         1 a     2022-01-01        [6 × 2]
#> 2 b         2 b     2022-01-02        [6 × 2]
```

title: case_when failing due to variable format
description:
Hi,
the same general issue reported in this [SO question](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/71712964/dplyr-case-when-throws-error-names-attribute-1-must-be-the-same-length-as-the) and in the issue tracker under different forms ([1](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6362),[2](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6206)) seems to be still present in version `1.0.10` .
The weird thing is also data type conversion, because when I read in the csv with data I get `var2` and `var3` as both integer but when handling it with `dplyr` it causes the abovementioned issue in the case of `case_when`.
It happened the opposite as well, reading another file with `read.csv`, getting both values as `numeric` but making it work only after coercing both with `as.numeric` as well.

Here some data and code:
[bug_dataset.txt](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/files/10030025/bug_dataset.txt)

```
test = read.delim( file.path(working.folder,"bug_dataset.txt"),dec = "," )

str(test)

test = test %>%
  mutate(
    var2 = case_when(
      var3 == 1 & var2 == 0  ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ var2
    ) )


test_ok = test %>%
  mutate(
    var2 = as.numeric(var2),
    var3 = as.numeric(var3),
    var2 = case_when(
      var3 == 1 & var2 == 0  ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ var2
    ) )

str(test_ok)
```

title: incorrect ordering when having multiple `across` calls inside `arrange`
description:
There's something fishy here...
When having multiple `across` inside `arrange`, sometimes the ordering is correct and other times it is not:
``` r
  library(tidyverse)

  df <- tribble(
    ~other_text, ~categ_1, ~categ_2, ~points_1, ~points_2, ~total,
    "x",      "A",      "B",       22L,       20L,    42L,
    "z",      "A",      "B",       20L,       22L,    42L,
    "y",      "A",      "B",       22L,       20L,    42L

#> # A tibble: 3 × 6

#> 2 z          A       B             20       22    42
#> 3 y          A       B             22       20    42
  
  set.seed(3)
  purrr::map_lgl(1:20,
                 ~ identical(
                   df %>%
                     slice_sample(n = nrow(.)) %>%
                     arrange(desc(total),
```

title: if_any/if_all bug with NA_real_ evaluation in a mutate()
description:
I'm not sure if this is my old R/tidyverse version (4.1.2 (2021-11-01), tidyverse_1.3.2), but I'm encountering a strange apparent bug with `if_all()`/`if_any()` relating to inconsistent evaluations of `NA_real_`s and that propagating to new columns when I make changes to other evaluations in the same `mutate()`.

```r
library(tidyverse)

d = tribble(
  ~fold_change_a, ~fold_change_b, ~fold_change_c, ~p_value_a, ~p_value_b, ~p_value_c,
  1, 1.5, 0.8, 0.02, 0.1, 0.4,
  3, NA_real_, NA_real_, 0.005, NA_real_, NA_real_,
  NA_real_, 1, 1.8, NA_real_, 0.5, 0.024,
  5, 10, 8, 0.009, 0.004, 0.006
)
d %>%
  mutate(
    fold_gt2_all = if_all(starts_with("fold"), ~ . < 2),
    fold_gt2_any = !if_any(starts_with("fold"), ~ . >= 2),
    fold_other_1 = if_any(starts_with("fold"), ~ . < 2),
    fold_other_2 = if_all(starts_with("fold"), ~ . > 2),
  )
# A tibble: 4 × 10
#  fold_change_a fold_change_b fold_change_c p_value_a p_value_b p_value_c fold_gt2_all fold_g…¹ fold_…² fold_…³
#          <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl> <lgl>        <lgl>    <lgl>   <lgl>  
#1             1           1.5           0.8     0.02      0.1       0.4   TRUE         TRUE     TRUE    FALSE  
#2             3          NA            NA       0.005    NA        NA     FALSE        FALSE    TRUE    FALSE  
#3            NA           1             1.8    NA         0.5       0.024 NA           NA       TRUE    FALSE  
#4             5          10             8       0.009     0.004     0.006 FALSE        FALSE    TRUE    FALSE

d %>%
  mutate(
    fold_gt2_all = if_all(starts_with("fold"), ~ . > 2), #flipped to greater than
    fold_gt2_any = !if_any(starts_with("fold"), ~ . <= 2), #flipped to less than
    fold_other_1 = if_any(starts_with("fold"), ~ . < 2), #same as above
    fold_other_2 = if_all(starts_with("fold"), ~ . > 2), #same as above
  )
# A tibble: 4 × 10
#  fold_change_a fold_change_b fold_change_c p_value_a p_value_b p_value_c fold_gt2_all fold_g…¹ fold_…² fold_…³
#          <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl> <lgl>        <lgl>    <lgl>   <lgl>  
#1             1           1.5           0.8     0.02      0.1       0.4   FALSE        FALSE    TRUE    FALSE  
#2             3          NA            NA       0.005    NA        NA     NA           NA       NA      NA     
#3            NA           1             1.8    NA         0.5       0.024 FALSE        FALSE    TRUE    FALSE  
#4             5          10             8       0.009     0.004     0.006 TRUE         FALSE    TRUE    FALSE  
# … with abbreviated variable names ¹​fold_gt2_any, ²​fold_other_1, ³​fold_other_2
```
As you can see, in rows with NAs, I'm getting NA results that are sort of odd to me (I'm not sure why either both rows with NA are evaluating to NA or neither instead of one at a time), but at least it's semi-consistent. However, in the second example, you can see that the unchanged second columns have now had the NA propagated to them, despite the evaluation not changing. 

Interestingly, removing the NA result in the first evaluation fixes the propagation to the remaining columns as shown below:

```
d %>%
    mutate(
        fold_gt2_all = if_all(starts_with("fold"), ~ . > 2 | is.na(.)), #added the or condition
        fold_gt2_any = !if_any(starts_with("fold"), ~ . <= 2),
        fold_other_1 = if_any(starts_with("fold"), ~ . < 2),
        fold_other_2 = if_all(starts_with("fold"), ~ . > 2),
    )
# A tibble: 4 × 10
#  fold_change_a fold_change_b fold_change_c p_value_a p_value_b p_value_c fold_gt2_all fold_g…¹ fold_…² fold_…³
#          <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl> <lgl>        <lgl>    <lgl>   <lgl>  
#1             1           1.5           0.8     0.02      0.1       0.4   FALSE        FALSE    TRUE    FALSE  
#2             3          NA            NA       0.005    NA        NA     TRUE         FALSE    TRUE    FALSE  
#3            NA           1             1.8    NA         0.5       0.024 FALSE        FALSE    TRUE    FALSE  
#4             5          10             8       0.009     0.004     0.006 TRUE         FALSE    TRUE    FALSE  
# … with abbreviated variable names ¹​fold_gt2_any, ²​fold_other_1, ³​fold_other_2
```

Perhaps someone with the more recent version can test this to see if it's the old build's fault or if the issues have persisted.

title: Mismatch between actual and documented behaviour for `slice_sample()`
description:
`slice_sample()` throws an error, when a group has less rows than `n`, :

```r
library(dplyr)

mtcars$am[1] <- 2
mtcars %>%
  group_by(am) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 3)
## Error in `slice_sample()`:
## ! Problem while computing indices.
## ℹ The error occurred in group 3: am = 2.
## Caused by error in `sample.int()`:
## ! cannot take a sample larger than the population when 'replace = FALSE'
## Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.
```
Similarly, an error is thrown when `prop` is larger than 1:

```r
library(dplyr)

mtcars %>%
  group_by(am) %>%
  slice_sample(prop = 1.2)
## Error in `slice_sample()`:
## ! Problem while computing indices.
## ℹ The error occurred in group 1: am = 0.
## Caused by error in `sample.int()`:
## ! cannot take a sample larger than the population when 'replace = FALSE'
## Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.
```

However, the documentation says:

> If n is greater than the number of rows in the group (or prop > 1), the result will be silently truncated to the group size.

It seems that the actual and the documented behaviour do not match.

I'm using R 4.2.2 with dplyr 1.0.10 on Ubuntu 20.04.5.

title: Alternative `summarise()` groupings
description:
Related to
https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/14
https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/236
https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/4722

With the addition of `.by`, we now have less reliance on the `<grouped_df>` class in general. This means that it is probably a lot easier to add narrowly scoped grouping extensions that only affect specific verbs.

For example, `summarise()` could gain support for bootstrap summaries, sort of like what I did for strapgod https://github.com/DavisVaughan/strapgod. It could also gain support for rollup summaries, completing with syntax like `complete(x / (a * b))`, and maybe rolling window summaries.

The general idea is that instead of grouping by columns:

```r
df %>% summarise(mean = mean(x), .by = c(y, z))
```

you could do this instead to generate 5 replicates of the data and then summarise the mean of each replicate:

```r
df %>% summarise(mean = mean(x), .rows = bootstraps(5))
```

This theoretical `.rows` argument (name subject to change) would be mutually exclusive with `.by`. The implementation of `bootstraps()` would roughly look like:

```r
bootstraps <- function(n) {
  function (data) {
    # Use `data` and `n` to generate a `group_data()` structure,
    # i.e. with `n = 5` probably a `.bootstraps = 1:5` column and a `.rows = list(sample(5), sample(5), ...)` list col
    tibble(...)
  }
}
```

`.rows` would take either:
- A data frame containing a `group_data()`-like structure that identifies which rows of `data` go with each group, and what the keys are
- Or a function of 1 argument, the original data, which would generate that group-data like data frame.

Right now we think that the only verb that should have this argument is `summarise()`. This alternative grouping structure probably doesn't make a whole lot of sense for `mutate()`, `filter()`, `slice()`, etc.

This could be a solution to the fact that `.by` doesn't allow you to support `.drop = FALSE`. That `.drop` option is essentially only used with `summarise()`, so something like this could possibly replace it `summarise(df, .rows = no_drop(x, y))` which would internally just create the group-data structure that we already make with `compute_groups(drop = FALSE)`.

A list of potential extensions:
- `group(x, y, z)`, equivalent to `.by`
- `rollup(x, y)`
- `complete(x / (a * b))` Wilkinson-Rogers syntax
- `no_drop(x, y)`, for `.drop = FALSE`, but with a better name. or `group(x, y, z, .drop = FALSE)`, or only use Wilkinson-Rogers syntax
- `rolling(2)` for rolling summaries

title: `group_walk()` should gain `.keep` explicitly
description:
The Usage docs currently show

```r
group_map(.data, .f, ..., .keep = FALSE)

group_modify(.data, .f, ..., .keep = FALSE)

group_walk(.data, .f, ...)
```

and the `group_walk()` method doesn't have `.keep`, making you think `group_walk()` doesn't support `.keep`, but it does:

``` r
mtcars %>%
  group_by(vs) %>%
  group_walk(~print(head(.x, n = 1)), .keep = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 11
#>     mpg   cyl  disp    hp  drat    wt  qsec    vs    am  gear  carb
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1    21     6   160   110   3.9  2.62  16.5     0     1     4     4
#> # A tibble: 1 × 11
#>     mpg   cyl  disp    hp  drat    wt  qsec    vs    am  gear  carb
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1  22.8     4   108    93  3.85  2.32  18.6     1     1     4     1


mtcars %>%
  group_by(vs) %>%
  group_walk(~print(head(.x, n = 1)), .keep = FALSE)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 10
#>     mpg   cyl  disp    hp  drat    wt  qsec    am  gear  carb
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1    21     6   160   110   3.9  2.62  16.5     1     4     4
#> # A tibble: 1 × 10
#>     mpg   cyl  disp    hp  drat    wt  qsec    am  gear  carb
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1  22.8     4   108    93  3.85  2.32  18.6     1     4     1
```

So `group_walk()` should gain a `.keep` arg explicitly

title: cbind with a grouped_df and stringsAsFactors=FALSE results in an erroneous column being added
description:
> Originally discovered in https://github.com/glin/reactable/issues/283 but @glin traced it down to a potential bug in {dplyr}. If this doesn't feel like a bug, feel free to close

`cbind(..., stringsAsFactors = FALSE)` when provided a grouped_df() doesn't work correctly - it adds a `stringsAsFactors` column.

```r
cbind(x = "a", data.frame(y = 2), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
#   x y
# 1 a 2

cbind(x = "a", dplyr::grouped_df(data.frame(y = 2), "y"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
# # A tibble: 1 x 3
#   x         y stringsAsFactors
#   <chr> <dbl> <lgl>           
# 1 a         2 FALSE     
```

This feels like a bug because in the documentation for `cbind` it says that the parameter `stringsAsFactors` is supported, which suggests it shouldn't be treated as a column:

> For the "data.frame" method of cbind these can be further arguments to data.frame such as stringsAsFactors.

title: Avoid materialization of row names
description:
For duckdb, it is crucial that the row names are materialized only when really accessing the data. Currently, this happens in at least two undesired places. We can work around for now, but eventually this should be fixed.

The relational package implements a data frame wrapper that shows messages when data access is triggered. Eventually, this will be on CRAN so that we can use it in tests.

CC @hannes.

``` r
# remotes::install_github(“duckdblabs/relational”)

df <- data.frame(a = 1:3)

df1 <- relational::wrap_df(df)
#> 1
#> 2
dplyr:::dplyr_new_data_frame(df1)
#> ⚠️ DATAPTR()
#> [1] NA -3
#> ⚠️ DATAPTR()
#> [1] 1 2 3
#>   a
#> 1 1
#> 2 2
#> 3 3

df2 <- relational::wrap_df(df)
#> 1
#> 2
dplyr::dplyr_reconstruct(df2, df)
#> ⚠️ DATAPTR()
#> [1] NA -3
#> ⚠️ DATAPTR()
#> [1] 1 2 3
#>   a
#> 1 1
#> 2 2
#> 3 3
```

title: [FR] allow grouping from inside `mutate()`
description:
Hi,

With `dplyr` 1.0+, `across()` let us use a more compact syntax that I believe improved the quality of our code.

In the same wave of thought, it would be very nice to have a grouping syntax from inside `mutate()`.

For instance, I sometimes have to do something like this:

```r
x = mtcars %>% 
  group_by(cyl) %>% 
  mutate(mean_mpg_by_cyl = mean(mpg)) %>% 
  group_by(carb) %>% 
  mutate(mean_mpg_by_carb = mean(mpg)) %>% 
  group_by(vs) %>% 
  mutate(mean_mpg_by_vs = mean(mpg)) %>% 
  ungroup()

x %>% 
  filter(mean_mpg_by_carb>17 & mean_mpg_by_vs>20 & mean_mpg_by_cyl>19)
```

It would be so much more elegant to write (and DRY-proof) if there was some way to write it like this:

```r
x = mtcars %>% 
  mutate(
    mean_mpg_by_cyl = across(mpg, mean, .group_by=cyl),
    mean_mpg_by_carb = across(mpg, mean, .group_by=carb),
    mean_mpg_by_vs = across(mpg, mean, .group_by=vs),
  )
```

Do you think this would be feasible and in the scope of `dplyr`?

I know there will be some limitations, like what should be done with existing grouping, what should be done inside summarise (where different grouping makes little sense), and probably more, but I thought it was still worth the shot asking 😁

title: Group Sampling
description:
My goal is to return all of the rows in a random subset of the groups (the levels of a factor) of a data frame. 

#### Example: Palmer Penguins

Say I wish to randomly sample two of the three islands to sample, then take a random sample of 10 penguins from each. I could do it this way:

```r
library(dplyr)
library(palmerpenguins)
data(penguins)

set.seed(24)
clusters <- sample(levels(penguins$island), 2)

penguins %>%
  filter(island %in% clusters)) %>%
  group_by(island) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 10)
```

What I'd like to do is something like:

```r
penguins %>%
  group_sample(island, n = 2) %>%
  group_by(island) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 10)
```

#### Discussion

This may not merit a new function, but I figured it was worth asking about. `dplyr` natively allows for [stratified sampling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratified_sampling), which is terrific. It works just the way you'd expect:

```r
penguins %>%
  group_by(island) %>%
  slice_sample(10)
```

The use case here is essentially [cluster sampling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cluster_sampling). While filtering can get the job done, this operation strikes me as exactly a sampling operation, not a filtering one.

This came up while trying to map into dplyr verbs the study design used by the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP). They assess student learning outcomes on a sample of students drawn by:

1. within each of the 50 US states
2. taking a random sample of 100 schools and 
3. within each school
4. taking a random sample of 60 students.

Steps 1, 3, and 4 are implemented in one step in `dplyr`, but 2 is not, as far as I can figure.

```r
df %>%
  group_by(state) %>%
  ?group_sample?(school, n = 100) %>%
  group_by(school) %>% # assuming the previous verb doesn't tack on groups
  slice_sample(n = 60)
```

title: Unexpected slice_max behaviour. Turns mandatory arguments into optional arguments when run within a function
description:
Thanks for all your work on this package!!

# Problem
I found some extremely unexpected behavior of `slice_max` (at least for me!)

I was writing a function which took a mandatory argument 'topn', which I passed to `slice_max` within this function.

To my surprise, calling the function without setting `topn` threw no error. Reprex below


# Desired Behaviour
I'd have expected R to throw the error: ` Error in print(topn): argument "topn" is missing, with no default`


# Reprex: Unexpected Behaviour 
``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

# Define function that passes argument along to slice_max
foo <- function(topn){
  
  slice_max(mtcars, order_by = mpg, n = topn)
    
}

# Running function without arguments throws no error
foo()
#>                 mpg cyl disp hp drat    wt qsec vs am gear carb
#> Toyota Corolla 33.9   4 71.1 65 4.22 1.835 19.9  1  1    4    1
```

<sup>Created on 2022-10-22 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>


# Reprex: Example of expected behaviour
``` r
# Define function that passes argument along to slice_max
foo2 <- function(topn){
  print(topn)
  slice_max(mtcars, order_by = mpg, n = topn)
  
}

# Throws appropriate error since variable is 'used' in `print`
foo2()
#> Error in print(topn): argument "topn" is missing, with no default
```

<sup>Created on 2022-10-22 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>


# Why is this happening
As per 'normal' R behaviour, arguments which aren't used in the function are not 'required' - and thus no error is thrown

``` r
foo3 <- function(very_important_arg) {
  # very_important_arg never used, so is not required
  print('No error thrown :)')
}

foo3()
#> [1] "No error thrown :)"
```

<sup>Created on 2022-10-22 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>


The unexpected behavior here is that I assumed passing `topn` to `slice_max`, meant it would be considered as being 'used'. 

So my guess is its something to do with the argument evaluation works in the absense?

# Potential fixes

Bit of a shot in the dark, I don't know the dplyr source well at all so at the risk of showing my ignorance:

Would a `check_number` or `check_required` call to this argument lead to the expected behaviour?

title: Version of `na_if` that takes conditionals.
description:
I often have want to convert some of my data to NA, and keep the rest. If it is as simple as identifying a particular value, I can use `na_if`. If, instead, I want to use a conditional, I have to use `if_else`, which would not be a problem if I didn't then have to also keep track of what type of `NA` I have to use, since `if_else` is type strict.

(Apologies if this already exists...)

``` r
library(tidyverse)

ll <- LETTERS[1:5]

# Works
ll %>% na_if("A")
#> [1] NA  "B" "C" "D" "E"

# Does not work even with multiple values (which makes sense because it's designed to be parallelized along the vector). 
ll %>%  na_if(c("A","B"))
#> Error in `na_if()`:
#> ! `y` must be length 5 (same as `x`) or one, not 2.

# Fails due to type strictness.
ll %>% {if_else(. %in% c("A", "C"), NA, .)}
#> Error in `if_else()`:
#> ! `false` must be a logical vector, not a character vector.

# With type strictness.
ll %>% {if_else(. %in% c("A", "C"), NA_character_, .)}
#> [1] NA  "B" NA  "D" "E"

# `case_when` works but is much slower.
bench::mark(
  if_else = ll %>% {if_else(. %in% c("A", "C"), NA_character_, .)},
  case_when = ll %>% {case_when(!(. %in% c("A", "C")) ~ .)}
)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 if_else      29.5µs   31.9µs    26601.        0B    10.6 
#> 2 case_when    94.5µs  102.6µs     8525.    91.9KB     6.13
```

title: Output list of group_split() does not function as other lists
description:
The resulting list from using `group_by()` and `group_split()` does not function as a normal list, which caused me to [ask this question on SO](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/74133220/in-r-how-to-modify-re-assign-a-list-element-using-index).  Since the resulting list does not function in the same way as other lists, I think this might be a problem or at least pointing out to people smarter than me.

```r
df <- tibble(A = rep(paste("Group", c(1:3)),3), 
             B = seq(1, 18, 2),
             C = (1:9))

lst <- df %>% 
  group_by(A) %>% 
  group_split() 

# This doesn't work for assigning back to the list
for (j in 1:3){
  lst[[j]] <- lst[[j]] %>% 
    mutate(D = B * C)
}
lst

# This **DOES** work when converted with as.list()
lst2 <- as.list(lst)
for (j in 1:3){
  lst2[[j]] <- lst2[[j]] %>% 
    mutate(D = B * C)
}
lst2

# This **DOES** work created from base::split()
lst3 <- split(df, df$A)
for (j in 1:3){
  lst3[[j]] <- lst3[[j]] %>% 
    mutate(D = B * C)
}
lst3

```

title: `relocate()` fails with empty `.before`/`.after`
description:
First, apologies if this is fixed in the current dev version. I'm having trouble installing it.

## Issue 
Using `relocate()` with a `.before` or `.after` tidyselection matching no columns results in an error.

``` r
data <- tibble::tibble(x = 1, y = 2, z = 3)

# The unmatched tidyselection correctly has no affect on a simple relocate()
dplyr::relocate(data, y, dplyr::starts_with("junk"))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>       y     x     z
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     2     1     3

# Meanwhile, using .before or .after gives a cryptic error
dplyr::relocate(data, y, .before = dplyr::starts_with("junk"))
#> Warning in min(unname(tidyselect::eval_select(.before, .data))): no non-missing
#> arguments to min; returning Inf
#> Error in seq.int(from, to): 'to' must be a finite number
dplyr::relocate(data, y, .after = dplyr::starts_with("junk"))
#> Warning in max(unname(tidyselect::eval_select(.after, .data))): no non-missing
#> arguments to max; returning -Inf
#> Error in seq.int(from, to): 'from' must be a finite number

# Compare: when a nonexistent column is provided directly, we get an informative error
dplyr::relocate(data, y, .before = junk)
#> Error in `chr_as_locations()`:
#> ! Can't subset columns that don't exist.
#> ✖ Column `junk` doesn't exist.
dplyr::relocate(data, y, .after = junk)
#> Error in `chr_as_locations()`:
#> ! Can't subset columns that don't exist.
#> ✖ Column `junk` doesn't exist.
```

<sup>Created on 2022-10-17 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

## Past tests

Tests using the (deprecated?) `eval_relocate()` exist. See line 150 of test_relocate.R. Are these tests currently used? Are they passing or failing? (`dplyr:::eval_relocate()` gives me nothing; I don't know how to run these tests.)
https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/main/tests/testthat/test-relocate.R#L150

```r
test_that("Empty `before` selection moves columns to front", {
  data <- tibble(x = 1, y = 2, z = 3)
  expr <- expr(y)
  before <- expr(where(is.character))

  expect_identical(
    eval_relocate(expr, data, before = before),
    c(y = 2L, x = 1L, z = 3L)
  )
})

test_that("Empty `after` selection moves columns to end", {
  data <- tibble(x = 1, y = 2, z = 3)
  expr <- expr(y)
  after <- expr(where(is.character))

  expect_identical(
    eval_relocate(expr, data, after = after),
    c(x = 1L, z = 3L, y = 2L)
  )
})

```

## Desired behavior
If an error is desired behavior, a more helpful error message should be given, for example:
```r
data <- tibble::tibble(x = 1, y = 2, z = 3)
dplyr::relocate(data, y, .before = dplyr::starts_with("junk"))
#> Error in `relocate()`:
#> ! Can't relocate before columns that don't exist.
#> ✖ No columns match dplyr::starts_with("junk").
```
My personally preferred behavior would be for the `.before` to be ignored entirely:
```r
data <- tibble::tibble(x = 1, y = 2, z = 3)
dplyr::relocate(data, y, .before = dplyr::starts_with("junk"))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>       y     x     z
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     2     1     3
```

title: Test of inequality not typo-safe
description:
Today, one of my students wanted to check if two columns are not equal. Instead of using `!=` he wanted to use `!(x == y)` but forgot an `=`. Unfortunately, the output gave no warning that something is wrong. 

Sure, using `!=` would prevent this but then again my student is an absolute beginner and simply forgot about `!=`. Could happen to other beginners too. Is it possible to prevent these kind of mishaps? Or create a warning?

```r
data.frame(x = c(1L, 2L), y = c(3L, 2L)) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    test_equality = (x = y), # typo here but detectable that output is not correct Boolean
  )
# x y   test_equality
# 1 3   3
# 2 2   2


data.frame(x = c(1L, 2L), y = c(3L, 2L)) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    test_inequality = !(x = y), # typo here but Boolean output
  )
# x y   test_inequality
# 1 3   FALSE
# 2 2   FALSE
```

title: Issue with non equi joins, repeated column names, and `keep = FALSE`
description:
With non equi joins we allow the same column to be used in multiple expressions, because you need to do this to specify bounds correctly. Seems that doesn't play well with `keep = FALSE`.

This, of course, also affects `between()` because it generates expressions exactly like these

``` r
library(dplyr)

df1 <- tibble(x = 1)
df2 <- tibble(lower = 0, upper = 2)

# Fine (default)
left_join(df1, df2, join_by(x >= lower, x <= upper), keep = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>       x lower upper
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     0     2

# Hmm
left_join(df1, df2, join_by(x >= lower, x <= upper), keep = FALSE)
#> Error in `left_join()`:
#> ! Join columns must be unique.
#> ✖ Problem with `x`.

#> Backtrace:
#>     ▆
#>  1. ├─dplyr::left_join(df1, df2, join_by(x >= lower, x <= upper), keep = FALSE)
#>  2. └─dplyr:::left_join.data.frame(df1, df2, join_by(x >= lower, x <= upper), keep = FALSE)
#>  3.   └─dplyr:::join_mutate(...)
#>  4.     └─dplyr:::join_cols(...)
#>  5.       └─dplyr:::check_join_vars(by$x, x_names, by$condition, keep, error_call = error_call)
#>  6.         └─rlang::abort(bullets, call = error_call)
```

title: `nest_join()` upgrades
description:
In some recent exploration of `nest_join()`, I've decided that it is lacking some features that would make it more powerful and generic. They are:

- `nest = c("y", "x", "both")`, an argument that would decide which inputs should be nested. Right now, we can only get the behavior of `nest = "y"`, but `nest = "both"` is particularly useful to replace something like this `left_join(group_nest(x, g), group_nest(y, g), by = g)`. It would interact with the `name = NULL` argument.
  - `nest = "y"` or `nest = "x"`: `name = NULL` autonames based on the relevant input, otherwise can be a single string
  - `nest = "both"`: `name = NULL` autonames based on both inputs, otherwise must be a character vector of length 2

- `type = c("left", "right", "inner", "full")`, an argument that describes which type of join you'd like to do. Right now, `nest_join()` really only does the semantics of a left-join (keep all rows from x, drop unmatched rows from y). I think it would be pretty nice to be able to do all types of joins.

---

Context is with ivs, where it is often useful to apply something like `iv_set_intersect()` between columns across multiple tables and _by key_. You need to be able to do `nest = "both"` to get two list-columns, and then you can apply `rowwise() %>% summarise(iv = iv_set_intersect(x$iv, y$iv))` to that to apply the function per key.

This is the general idea that I want to make easier

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(ivs)
library(clock)

needles <- tibble(
  g = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2),
  lower = date_build(2019, 1, c(1, 5, 10, 12, 2, 8, 9)),
  upper = date_build(2019, 1, c(3, 7, 11, 14, 3, 11, 10))
) %>%
  mutate(range = iv(lower, upper), .keep = "unused")

haystack <- tibble(
  g = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2),
  lower = date_build(2019, 1, c(2, 4, 12, 6, 14)),
  upper = date_build(2019, 1, c(8, 11, 15, 9, 16))
) %>%
  mutate(range = iv(lower, upper), .keep = "unused")

needles
#> # A tibble: 7 × 2
#>       g                    range
#>   <dbl>               <iv<date>>
#> 1     1 [2019-01-01, 2019-01-03)
#> 2     1 [2019-01-05, 2019-01-07)
#> 3     1 [2019-01-10, 2019-01-11)
#> 4     1 [2019-01-12, 2019-01-14)
#> 5     2 [2019-01-02, 2019-01-03)
#> 6     2 [2019-01-08, 2019-01-11)
#> 7     2 [2019-01-09, 2019-01-10)
haystack
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>       g                    range
#>   <dbl>               <iv<date>>
#> 1     1 [2019-01-02, 2019-01-08)
#> 2     1 [2019-01-04, 2019-01-11)
#> 3     1 [2019-01-12, 2019-01-15)
#> 4     2 [2019-01-06, 2019-01-09)
#> 5     2 [2019-01-14, 2019-01-16)

nested_needles <- needles %>%
  group_by(g) %>%
  group_nest(.key = "needles")

nested_haystack <- haystack %>%
  group_by(g) %>%
  group_nest(.key = "haystack")

nested_needles
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>       g            needles
#>   <dbl> <list<tibble[,1]>>
#> 1     1            [4 × 1]
#> 2     2            [3 × 1]
nested_haystack
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>       g           haystack
#>   <dbl> <list<tibble[,1]>>
#> 1     1            [3 × 1]
#> 2     2            [2 × 1]

left_join(nested_needles, nested_haystack, by = join_by(g)) %>%
  rowwise(g) %>%
  summarise(range = iv_intersect(needles$range, haystack$range), .groups = "drop")
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>       g                    range
#>   <dbl>               <iv<date>>
#> 1     1 [2019-01-02, 2019-01-03)
#> 2     1 [2019-01-05, 2019-01-07)
#> 3     1 [2019-01-10, 2019-01-11)
#> 4     1 [2019-01-12, 2019-01-14)
#> 5     2 [2019-01-08, 2019-01-09)
```

title: Multiple `across` calls to `arrange` ignore subsequent `across` statements if first returns more than one column
description:
As noted in [this stack overflow question](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/73943949/sophisticated-formula-inside-arrange/73945836#73945836), using `across(starts_with(...))` in an `arrange()` call has odd behaviour when selecting more than one column.

See example below with two `across` calls looking for one or more columns. If the first `across` call returns more than one column, then these are ordered with the expected priority, but the second call to `across` is ignored. If the first `across` call returns one column, then the second evaluates fine.

``` r
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)

df <- tibble(a_1 = rep(3:1, each = 4),
             a_2 = rep(13:11, each = 4),
             b_1 = rep(24:21, each = 3),
             b_2 = 22:11)

df |> 
  arrange(across(starts_with("a_")),
          across(starts_with("b_")))

#> # A tibble: 12 × 4
#>      a_1   a_2   b_1   b_2
#>    <int> <int> <int> <int>
#>  1     1    11    22    14
#>  2     1    11    21    13
#>  3     1    11    21    12
#>  4     1    11    21    11

#>  6     2    12    23    17
#>  7     2    12    22    16

#>  9     3    13    24    22
#> 10     3    13    24    21
#> 11     3    13    24    20
#> 12     3    13    23    19

# `a_1` and `a_2` are correctly ordered; `b_1` and `b_2` have remained untouched within each stratum of `a_1`*`a_2`

df |> 
  select(-a_2) |> 
  arrange(across(starts_with("a_")),
          across(starts_with("b_")))

#> # A tibble: 12 × 3
#>      a_1   b_1   b_2
#>    <int> <int> <int>

#>  5     2    22    15

#>  7     2    23    17
#>  8     2    23    18
#>  9     3    23    19
#> 10     3    24    20
```

title: Error in error message when using `case_when` with `factor` on column that doesn't exist
description:
An error in `rlang::format_error_bullets` is raised when trying to use `case_when` in conjunction with `factor` for a column that doesn't exist, disambiguated with `.data`:

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))

starwars %>% 
  mutate(
    y = case_when(
      .data$x == "Some value" ~ "Option1",
      TRUE ~ "Option2"
    ) %>% factor(levels = c("Option1", "Option2"))
  )
#> Error in format_error_bullets(x[-1]): nms %in% c("i", "x", "") are not all TRUE
```

<sup>Created on 2022-10-03 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>


This error also happens if the required field is NULL:

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))

starwars %>% 
  mutate(
    x = NULL,
    y = case_when(
      .data$x == "Some value" ~ "Option1",
      TRUE ~ "Option2"
    ) %>% factor(levels = c("Option1", "Option2"))
  )
#> Error in format_error_bullets(x[-1]): nms %in% c("i", "x", "") are not all TRUE
```


But this error *doesn't* happen when `.data` isn't used:

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))

starwars %>% 
  mutate(
    y = case_when(
      x == "Some value" ~ "Option1",
      TRUE ~ "Option2"
    ) %>% factor(levels = c("Option1", "Option2"))
  )
#> Error: Problem with `mutate()` input `y`.
#> x object 'x' not found
#> ℹ Input `y` is ``%>%`(...)`.
```




Or, when the output of `case_when` isn't piped into `factor`:

``` r

# Without pipe
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))

starwars %>% 
  mutate(
    x = NULL,
    y = case_when(
      .data$x == "Some value" ~ "Option1",
      TRUE ~ "Option2"
    ),
    y = factor(y, levels = c("Option1", "Option2"))
  )
#> Error: Problem with `mutate()` input `y`.
#> x Column `x` not found in `.data`
#> ℹ Input `y` is `case_when(.data$x == "Some value" ~ "Option1", TRUE ~ "Option2")`.

```


May be related to #5466

title: Suggestion: filter raises warning on `filter(x, id == id)`
description:
A [twit](https://twitter.com/_ColinFay/status/1574751654590976002) by Colin Fay describes a common [papercut issue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paper_cut_bug) when using `dplyr::filter()`. 

A user writes the following code (notice the `id == id` inside the `filter()`):

```r
x <- function(data, id){
  data |> dplyr::filter(id == id)
}
```
where the user actually meant:

```r
x <- function(data, id){
  data |> dplyr::filter(id == .env$id)
}
```

And the behaviour they get is:

```r
x <- function(data, id){
  data |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(id))
}
```

I can't think of scenarios where `id == id` is useful:

- If the user meant `.data$id == .data$id`, I would suggest `!is.na(.data$id)` instead, as a more explicit expression.
- If the user meant `.data$id == .env$id`, the user is introducing a bug and should get a warning.

In either case a warning offering the two alternatives should probably be helpful, in my opinion.

title: Feature request: `dplyr::distinct`: add argument to keep last duplicate
description:
In survey-based research, we often have scenarios where some participants started a survey, then stopped for some reason (e.g., technical problem), and restarted shortly after. The *full* and correct answer is therefore the last one, not the first one. E.g.,

``` r
library(dplyr)
df <- data.frame(
  id = c(1, 1, 2),
  item1 = c(NA, 1, 1),
  item2 = c(NA, 1, 1),
  item3 = c(NA, 1, 1)
)
df
#>   id item1 item2 item3
#> 1  1    NA    NA    NA
#> 2  1     1     1     1
#> 3  2     1     1     1
```

If using `dplyr::distinct()`, which conceptually seems to be the perfect tool to deal with such duplicates, we end up removing the wrong duplicate:

``` r
df %>% 
  distinct(id, .keep_all = TRUE)
#>   id item1 item2 item3
#> 1  1    NA    NA    NA
#> 2  2     1     1     1
```

The ideal solution would be to either add a logical argument, e.g., `.keep_first`, `.keep_last`, with TRUE or FALSE, but those might be confusing because of `.keep_al`. So an alternative could be `.keep`, taking a character string either “first”, or “last”, with current default.

``` r
df %>% 
  distinct(id, .keep = "last")
```

    #>   id item1 item2 item3
    #> 2  1     1     1     1
    #> 3  2     1     1     1

Of course, there are other workarounds, such as using base R,

``` r
df[!rev(duplicated(rev(df$id))),]
#>   id item1 item2 item3
#> 2  1     1     1     1
#> 3  2     1     1     1
```

Or:

``` r
df %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  filter(row_number() == n()) %>% 
  ungroup()
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#> # Groups:   id [2]
#>      id item1 item2 item3
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     1     1     1
#> 2     2     1     1     1
```

But it just feels bad to have to use a workaround to `distinct` if the function exists already.

title: `group_by_prepare` with default `error_call` argument results in error
description:
The default values for arguments `caller_env` and `error_call` in `group_by_prepare` don't seem to work

`group_by_prepare` with default `error_call`
``` r
df <- data.frame(x = 1)
dplyr::group_by_prepare(df)
#> Error in is_missing(call): promise already under evaluation: recursive default argument reference or earlier problems?
```
<sup>Created on 2022-08-31 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

with `error_call` supplied but not `caller_env`, adding a column
``` r
df <- data.frame(x = 1)
dplyr::group_by_prepare(df, y = 3, error_call = call('fun'))
#> Error in initialize(...): promise already under evaluation: recursive default argument reference or earlier problems?
```
<sup>Created on 2022-08-31 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

The reason I noticed this is that `group_by_prepare(data.frame(x = 1))` works with CRAN dplyr but not dev dplyr, which causes `group_by` to fail in dtplyr if dev dplyr is installed.

It seems to be because `caller_env` is self-referencing in the function signature. I guess the users of this function would be package developers who can probably figure out what's going on and just supply the arguments, but it was a little confusing. Maybe these arguments could have no default to make the error more understandable (`argument "caller_env" is missing` rather than `promise already under evaluation`), or `caller_env` renamed to `.caller_env`.

https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/48431a541c16ad7f88bf2e2918013ae1dc82f480/R/group-by.r#L193-L199

``` r
fun <- function(caller_env = caller_env(2)) {
  print(caller_env)
}
fun()
#> Error in print(caller_env): promise already under evaluation: recursive default argument reference or earlier problems?
```

title: Replace `preceding()` and `following()` with `closest()`
description:
```r
preceding(x, y, inclusive = TRUE)  -> closest(x >= y)
preceding(x, y, inclusive = FALSE) -> closest(x > y)
following(x, y, inclusive = TRUE)  -> closest(x <= y)
following(x, y, inclusive = FALSE) -> closest(x < y)
```

This should be more intuitive for interactive exploration too, because you probably start out with `x >= y`, then realize you only care about the closest match, so you just wrap it in `closest()` rather than having to switch to `preceding()`

title: Add `merge` indicator after a join
description:
A prior iteration of this request was [closed and locked as old](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/2183), but the asserted rationale does not address the request. It would be very useful if the `dplyr` mutating join functions allowed for an option to create a variable indicating which observations were joined (or not) from each data frame. This is a feature available in Stata's `merge` command and in Pandas (`indicator = True`). It has been implemented in R through the `statar` package, but it would be great to have it included in the `dplyr` mutating join functions. 

The purported rationale for closing the earlier iteration of this feature request was that `tidylog` has solved the problem. The `tidylog` package is great, but it doesn't add any variables to the merged data frame, which was the initial feature request.

title: `filter` option to keep `NA`s
description:
Hey there,
I'd like to propose to add a parameter to `dplyr::filter` to specify how `NA`s are treated in the logical vector.
From the documentation: "Note that when a condition evaluates to NA the row will be dropped, unlike base subsetting with [."
While this is a good default behavior, it would be nice to be able to add, e.g. `.treat.nas=T` to the function call to emulate base R subsetting in a convenient way.

Use case / reprex: Looking for inconsistencies in data, you sometimes want to show NAs:
```r
tibble(col1 = 1:3, col2 = c(1, 1, NA)) %>% filter(col1 != col2)
```
This call only outputs row 2 but it would be nice to be able to obtain row 3 as well if desired.

Thanks and kind regards,
Mario

title: `safely()` and `%||%` equivalent for use inside `mutate()`
description:
I commonly work with datasets from different sources that use different names for the same variables, and I need to consolidate these into a common name.

Currently, I use a workflow with `tibble::has_name()`:

```r
library(tidyverse)
if (!has_name(mtcars, "MPG")) mutate(mtcars, MPG = MPG)
```

This is can be tedious with many variables and different schemes.

It would be really convenient if I could instead call variable names inside of `mutate()` and have a way for them to return `NULL` instead of error if the variables are missing. Something like:

```r
mutate(mtcars, MPG = safely(MPG) %||% mpg)
```

Could something like that be implemented?

title: `bind_rows` skips elements with empty sub lists
description:
When using `bind_row` to transform a list to a dataframe, it skips over elements with empty sub lists, even though those elements may have other important data points which might be bound. This could potentially result in missing key data points or loss of data.

```r
list_with_empty_lists <- list(
  list(index_id = "A",
       content = list(),
       content2 = "something important"),
  list(index_id = "B",
       content = list()),
  list(index_id = "C",
       content = list("foo")),
  list(index_id = "D",
       content = list("bar")),
  list(index_id = "E",
       content = list()))
  
                              
bind_rows(list_with_empty_lists)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  index_id content   content2
  <chr>    <list>    <chr>   
1 C        <chr [1]> NA      
2 D        <chr [1]> NA  

```
Expected result:

```
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  index_id content   content2
  <chr>    <list>    <chr> 
1 A        <NULL> "something important"  
2 C        <chr [1]> NA      
3 D        <chr [1]> NA  
```
I would classify this as an issue of the potential for loss data which goes against some general R philosophy/principle.

``` r
library(dplyr)
```

title: Reconsider `multiple` argument in `nest_join()`
description:
It seems like it should _always_ be set to `"all"` because this is the whole point of the nest join, and you dont have the Cartesian product issue because an invariant of the join is `nrow(x) == nrow(out)`.

See also https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/pull/6379#discussion_r940691828

Some precedence for this is `semi/anti_join()`, which don't have this argument and always set it to `"any"` internally

```
set.seed(1)
```

title: summarize() with multi-row returns
description:
As of dplyr 1.0.0, `summarize()` will create multiple rows per group, according to the length of the return value of the summary function. This new feature leads to unintended behavior if the vector return is accidental, and also can lead to data loss.

``` r
library(conflicted)
library(dplyr)

my_custom_summary_function <- function(n) {
  # Should return a scalar, but I accidentally return a vector
  rep(n, n)
}

tibble(n = 2:0) %>% 
  group_by(n) %>% 
  summarize(out = my_custom_summary_function(n), .groups = "drop") %>% 
  ungroup()
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>       n   out
#>   <int> <int>
#> 1     1     1
#> 2     2     2
#> 3     2     2
```

<sup>Created on 2022-08-01 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

Should we introduce a `.multi = c("allow", "require", "fail")` argument that supports the pre-1.0.0 strict mode of operation? Should `.multi = "fail"` even be the default?

``` r
library(conflicted)
library(dplyr)

my_custom_summary_function <- function(n) {
  # Should return a scalar, but I accidentally return a vector
  rep(n, n)
}

tibble(n = 2:0) %>% 
  group_by(n) %>% 
  summarize(out = my_custom_summary_function(n), .groups = "drop", .multi = "fail") %>% 
  ungroup()
## Error: `out` has length != 1 in groups 1, 3, use `.multi = "allow"` if this is intended
```

title: filter and select behave differently when passed strings with curly-curly
description:
Context: I'm writing a lesson for a data science course that includes an introduction to curly-curly notation for writing functions that encapsulate dplyr pipes.  

`filter()` and `select()` behave differently when a string (quoted column name) is passed instead of a bare.  Wrapping the variable reference in `if_all()` or `if_any()` works as expected, but seems more cumbersome than intended.  

Reprex: 
``` r
## Passing a string to select using curly-curly works same as passing a bare
foo = function(df, var) {
    dplyr::select(df, {{ var }})
}
identical(foo(mtcars, disp), 
          foo(mtcars, 'disp'))
#> [1] TRUE

## But passing a string to filter using curly-curly is interpreted as a string
## NB In the actual example, the filter condition is !is.na{{ var }}
bar = function(df, var) {
    dplyr::filter(df, {{ var }} > 300)
}
bar(mtcars, disp) |> nrow()
#> [1] 11
bar(mtcars, 'disp') |> nrow()
#> [1] 32

## Wrapping the condition in `if_all()` or `if_any()` works as expected, but seems unnecessarily complicated
bat = function(df, var) {
    dplyr::filter(df, dplyr::if_all({{ var }}, ~ . > 300))
}
bat(mtcars, disp) |> nrow()
#> [1] 11
bat(mtcars, 'disp') |> nrow()
#> [1] 11
```

title: Make `count()` more flexible?

title: Typer coercion causes uninformative error message when using mutate.
description:
`df1` has doubles in its numeric columns while `df2` has integers. The result of the case_when() statement in the second case coerces one set of results to doubles while the rest are kept as integers. This causes an obscure error message that does little to help identify the issue.

Using `start - 1L` fixes the second case as everything is kept as integers.

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

df1 <- tibble(
    type = c("+", "+", "-", "-"),
    start = c(1, 2, 3, 4),
    end = c(5, 6, 7, 8)
)

df1 %>%
    mutate(
        start = case_when(
            type == "+" ~ start - 1,
            type == "-" ~ end
        )
    )
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   type  start   end
#>   <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 +         0     5
#> 2 +         1     6
#> 3 -         7     7
#> 4 -         8     8

df2 <- tibble(
    type = c("+", "+", "-", "-"),
    start = c(1L, 2L, 3L, 4L),
    end = c(5L, 6L, 7L, 8L)
)

df2 %>%
    mutate(
        start = case_when(
            type == "+" ~ start - 1,
            type == "-" ~ end
        )
    )
#> Error in `mutate()`:
#> ! Problem while computing `start = case_when(type == "+" ~ start - 1,
#>   type == "-" ~ end)`.
#> Caused by error in `` names(message) <- `*vtmp*` ``:
#> ! 'names' attribute [1] must be the same length as the vector [0]
```

title: `relocate()` drops attributes attached to bare data frames
description:
Since this is mainly just using `x[i]` it should be using `dplyr_col_select()` internally, which patches the `[` method of base R data frames and data.table objects to retain attributes

``` r
library(dplyr)

df <- vctrs::data_frame(x = 1, y = 2)
attr(df, "foo") <- "bar"

out <- relocate(df, y, .before = x)

attr(out, "foo")
#> NULL
```

Since `mutate()` also uses `relocate()`, that should fix the same kind of issue that comes from `mutate()` + `.before`

``` r
library(dplyr)

df <- vctrs::data_frame(x = 1, y = 2)
attr(df, "foo") <- "bar"

out <- mutate(df, z = 3, .before = x)

attr(out, "foo")
#> NULL
```

title: `!is.numeric` doesn't work in `across`
description:
I am trying to summarise all columns that are not numeric, e.g. both characters and dates. However, using `summarise(across(where(!is.numeric), some_function))` doesn't work.
I'm at a loss - there may be something I've missed or maybe it's a bug?

Here's a reprex:

---

Let's first generate some data; both characters, dates and integers:

```r
abc <- tibble(
  a = c("a", "a", "b"),
  b = as_date(c("2022-06-27", "2022-06-28", "2022-06-27")),
  c = c(1,2,2)
  )
```

Then let's first inspect the modes of the data:
`mode(abc$a)` > `"character"`
`mode(abc$b)` > `"numeric"`
`mode(abc$c)` > `"numeric"`

So on first glance, the dates are numeric - however:
`is.numeric(abc$b)` > `FALSE`

And if we try to summarise using `is.numeric`, the dates are (as expected) not processed:

```r
abc %>% 
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), n_distinct))
```
```r
# A tibble: 1 × 1
      c
  <int>
1     2
```

...and of course neither with `is.character`:
```r
abc %>% 
  summarise(across(where(is.character), n_distinct))
```
```r
# A tibble: 1 × 1
      a
  <int>
1     2
```

So the logical thing is to just negate and use `!is.numeric`, but that throws an error:
```r
abc %>% 
  summarise(across(where(!is.numeric), n_distinct))
```
```r
Error in `summarise()`:
! Problem while computing `..1 = across(where(!is.numeric), n_distinct)`.
Caused by error in `across()`:
! invalid argument type
Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.
```

```r
library(dplyr)

# arrange() 
a_def_arr <- arrange(a_def, desc(x))
b_num_arr <- arrange(b_num, desc(x))
c_chr_arr <- arrange(c_chr, desc(x))

# order() ALWAYS reorders the rownames
a_def_ord <- a_def[order(a_def$x, decreasing = TRUE), ]
b_num_ord <- b_num[order(b_num$x, decreasing = TRUE), ]
c_chr_ord <- c_chr[order(c_chr$x, decreasing = TRUE), ]

# arrange() reinitialises them from 1 if rownames are numbers
row.names(a_def_ord) # [1] "3" "2" "1"

row.names(b_num_ord) # [1] "13" "12" "11"
```

title: group_by NULL
description:
If we use a NULL in a `group_by` it works, i.e. it ignores it, but if we name the NULL then it gives an error.

```
mtcars %>% group_by(vs, NULL) %>% tally # works.  NULL ignored.
mtcars %>% group_by(vs, am = NULL) %>% tally  # issues error message
```

It would be useful if the second above acted the same as the first so we could do this which works if `by_am` is TRUE but currently gives an error if `by_am` is FALSE.  It will work if `by_am` is FALSE if we don't name the argument but in that case it will give a name of `"if (by_am) am"` so we need to name it.

```
# gives error
by_am <- FALSE
mtcars %>% group_by(vs, am = if (by_am) am) %>% tally
```

There are some workarounds in this SO post https://stackoverflow.com/questions/72896135/how-can-i-use-dplyr-group-by-within-a-function-conditional-on-a-flag but a direct solution as above would be nice.

Also the `group_by` help page should make clear how it behaves with a NULL argument.

title: Feature Request: join_many_to_one() and join_one_to_one()
description:
Related to sfirke/janitor#427

I often need to perform join operations which confirm that the join is either 1:1 or many:1.  Is there interest in this and similar functions to confirmation the result of join operations?

The underlying idea is to ensure a connection between rows in a data.frame on both the left and right side of the join with a `join_controller()` function.  The `join_controller()` function ensures that a row is matched on the left or right data.frame:

* "any": Any outcome is acceptable; this overrides all other options.
* "all": Each row from the input must appear in the output at least one time.
* "unique": A row may appear in the output zero or one time.
* "missing": At least one row must not match in the new dataset (the values must be missing). This option is rarely used.
* "nomissing": All rows must match in the new dataset (the values must not be missing).

`join_one_to_one()` and `join_many_to_one()` are special cases of the above controls.

I've implemented it here: https://github.com/sfirke/janitor/pull/480

``` r
library(bsd.report)

join_many_to_one(
  data.frame(x=rep(1:2, 2)),
  data.frame(x=1:4, y=5:8)
)
#> Joining, by = "x"
#>   x y
#> 1 1 5
#> 2 2 6
#> 3 1 5
#> 4 2 6

join_many_to_one(
  data.frame(x=rep(1:2, 2)),
  data.frame(x=c(1, 1:3), y=5:8)
)
#> Joining, by = "x"
#>   x
#> 2 1
#> Error in join_control_detect(x = ret, control = x_control, detect_column = x[, : `x`: Rows are not unique in the new dataset. Keys for duplicated rows are above.

join_one_to_one(
  data.frame(x=rep(1:2, 2)),
  data.frame(x=1:4, y=5:8)
)
#> Joining, by = "x"
#> Error in join_control_detect(x = ret, control = y_control, detect_column = y[, : `y`: All rows were are not in the new dataset. Missing rows: 3, 4

join_one_to_one(
  data.frame(x=rep(1:2, 2)),
  data.frame(x=1:2, y=5:6)
)
#> Joining, by = "x"
#>   x
#> 3 1
#> 4 2
#> Error in join_control_detect(x = ret, control = y_control, detect_column = y[, : `y`: Rows are not unique in the new dataset. Keys for duplicated rows are above.

join_one_to_one(
  data.frame(x=1:2),
  data.frame(x=1:2, y=5:6)
)
#> Joining, by = "x"
#>   x y
#> 1 1 5
#> 2 2 6
```

title: Revisit injection properties of `!!` with grouped data frames
description:
A few of us find this behavior very odd, given how it works with `.env$` and when not injected

```r
library(dplyr)

xx <- 1:32
mtcars <- mtcars[1:3]

# This seems weird
mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  mutate(x = !!xx)
#> # A tibble: 32 × 4
#> # Groups:   cyl [3]
#>      mpg   cyl  disp     x
#>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <int>
#>  1  21       6  160      1
#>  2  21       6  160      2
#>  3  22.8     4  108      3
#>  4  21.4     6  258      4
#>  5  18.7     8  360      5
#>  6  18.1     6  225      6
#>  7  14.3     8  360      7
#>  8  24.4     4  147.     8
#>  9  22.8     4  141.     9
#> 10  19.2     6  168.    10
#> # … with 22 more rows

# Because these fail
mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  mutate(x = xx)
#> Error in `mutate()`:
#> ! Problem while computing `x = xx`.
#> ✖ `x` must be size 11 or 1, not 32.
#> ℹ The error occurred in group 1: cyl = 4.

mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  mutate(x = .env$xx)
#> Error in `mutate()`:
#> ! Problem while computing `x = .env$xx`.
#> ✖ `x` must be size 11 or 1, not 32.
#> ℹ The error occurred in group 1: cyl = 4.
```

I know this was talked about here https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6188#issuecomment-1102311640, but I feel like a constant value should always be recycled to the group size. Bypassing that and using the size of the whole data frame for an injected constant feels extremely strange.

I know recycling to the group size isn't particularly useful (the groups would have to be the same size if you are injecting a vector), but I feel like it is the more internally consistent thing to do and it should make the internal code easier to understand. Our argument is that if you want to inject something that is the same size as the data, then you should ungroup first.

title: `cur_group()` and size zero grouped data frame edge case bug
description:
This has to do with the number of rows returned by `group_data()`, and therefore by `group_keys()`

``` r
library(dplyr)

df <- tibble(x = integer())
gdf <- group_by(df, x)

mutate(df, y = cur_group())
#> # A tibble: 0 × 2
#> # … with 2 variables: x <int>, y <tibble[,0]>

mutate(gdf, y = cur_group())
#> Error in `mutate()`:
#> ! Problem while computing `y = cur_group()`.
#> Caused by error in `vec_slice()`:
#> ! Can't subset elements past the end.
#> ℹ Location 1 doesn't exist.
#> ℹ There are only 0 elements.

# Has 1 row
group_keys(df)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 0

# Has 0 rows
group_keys(gdf)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 1
#> # … with 1 variable: x <int>
```

We do this workaround when there are zero groups, but it only applies to the group rows

https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/55dfc1c5b49eae3f1b144ebe7d9fa2c3d79b1835/R/data-mask.R#L4-L8

It seems like we need to make a similar kind of patch to `group_keys()` as well

https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/55dfc1c5b49eae3f1b144ebe7d9fa2c3d79b1835/R/data-mask.R#L26

Maybe it should be set to `vec_init(group_keys(), n = 1)` if there are no groups? That would allow `cur_group()` to return a size 1 result,  which would then be recycled back to size 0

That would give this result, where you can see the initialized 1 row keys if you really want to

``` r
library(dplyr)

df <- tibble(x = integer())
gdf <- group_by(df, x)

mutate(gdf, y = print(cur_group()))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>       x
#>   <int>
#> 1    NA

#> # A tibble: 0 × 2
#> # Groups:   x [0]
#> # … with 2 variables: x <int>, y <tibble[,1]>
```

title: `rowwise()` size zero data frame edge case
description:
There is a weird edge case that occurs with size zero data frames and `rowwise()`. In these cases, a list-col is made up of just `list()`, meaning there aren't any elements in there to extract and use in the expression.

Practically, what ends up happening is that this `Rf_length(column) > 0` branch returns `FALSE`, so the list-column gets chopped, resulting in `list(list())`
https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/55dfc1c5b49eae3f1b144ebe7d9fa2c3d79b1835/src/chop.cpp#L20-L24

That results in weird bugs, like this one:

``` r
library(dplyr)

df <- tibble(x = list(1, 2, 3, 4))
df <- rowwise(df)

# Looks good
mutate(df, y = x + 1)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#> # Rowwise: 
#>   x             y
#>   <list>    <dbl>
#> 1 <dbl [1]>     2
#> 2 <dbl [1]>     3
#> 3 <dbl [1]>     4
#> 4 <dbl [1]>     5

# Now it is impossible to know type is in `x`
df <- df[0,]
df
#> # A tibble: 0 × 1
#> # Rowwise: 
#> # … with 1 variable: x <list>
df$x
#> list()

# In practice this ends up doing `x + 1` -> `list() + 1`, which is theoretically
# very different from the `x + 1` above
mutate(df, y = x + 1)
#> Error in `mutate()`:
#> ! Problem while computing `y = x + 1`.
#> Caused by error in `x + 1`:
#> ! non-numeric argument to binary operator
```

I think that `Rf_length(column) > 0` was added to help with this case, but I think it may have made things more confusing and less consistent, because you aren't accessing the "elements" of the list column, you are working on the whole list-col itself

title: `rowwise()` + `mutate()` doesn't respect rowwise-ness when copying a list-col
description:
I don't think this is expected. I would have expected the first to return an `x` column containing `c(1, 2, 3, 4)` as a double vector.

``` r
library(dplyr)

df <- tibble(x = list(1, 2, 3, 4))
df <- rowwise(df)

# `x` isn't accessed an element at a time
mutate(df, y = x)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
```

title: If `.keep = "unused"`, default `.after` to first used variable
description:
Often you use `.keep = "unused"` to "replace" a variable with a new name and value, and you want it in the same place. So I find myself using this pattern pretty commonly:

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
df <- tibble(x = 1, y = 2, z = 3)
df |>

    y_new = y * 10,
    .keep = "unused",
    .after = y
  )

```

title: Unify `group_by()` and `left_join()`?
description:
In an edge case when `by` does not exist, `group_by()` works for `NULL` but not `left_join()`, and `character()` works for `left_join()` but not `group_by()`. Life will be easy if the behavior of these two is consistent. For now I will refer to `merge()` from base and stick with `NULL`.

``` r
a <- tibble::tibble(x = 1)
b <- tibble::tibble(y = 2)
a |> dplyr::group_by(NULL) # This works
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>       x
#>   <dbl>
#> 1     1
a |> dplyr::group_by(character()) # This does not
#> Error in `dplyr::group_by()`:
#> ! Problem adding computed columns.
#> Caused by error in `mutate()`:
#> ! Problem while computing `..1 = character()`.
#> ✖ `..1` must be size 1, not 0.
a |> dplyr::left_join(b, by = NULL) # This does not
#> Error in `dplyr::left_join()`:
#> ! `by` must be supplied when `x` and `y` have no common variables.
#> ℹ use by = character()` to perform a cross-join.
a |> dplyr::left_join(b, by = character()) # This works again
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>       x     y
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     2
a |> merge(b, by = NULL) # This works
#>   x y
#> 1 1 2
```

title: dplyr 1.1.0 revdep tracker
`case_when()` error path isn't working correctly
description:
``` r
library(dplyr)

# check_type
case_when(TRUE ~ 1, TRUE ~ "x")
#> Error in names(message) <- `*vtmp*`: 'names' attribute [1] must be the same length as the vector [0]

case_when(TRUE ~ 1, TRUE ~ structure(1, class = "foo"))
```
