title: Mutate: `env` must be an environment
description:
Unfortunately, I don't have a reprex to share here as this seems to be a heisenbug - the more I try to get details, the less often it appears!

I'm running a large amount of code on a HPC environment, and I occasionally get the errors similar to the following:

```r
Error in mutate_cols(.data, ..., caller_env = caller_env()) : 
  Problem with `mutate()` column `Proportion`.
ℹ `Proportion = calculate_popprop(pop_data, Age, Age, NA_integer_, NA_character_)`.
✖ `env` must be an environment
ℹ The error occurred in row 4.
Caused by error:
! `env` must be an environment
```

The appearance of this bug seems to be completely arbitrary - when doing two runs with the same settings/seeding etc., I can have either, both, or neither fail.

`calculate_popprop()` is a custom function with the following definition:

```r
calculate_popprop <- function(df_,
                              value_age_min_,
                              value_age_max_,
                              value_sex_,
                              value_ltla19_) {

  # Check input validity -------------------------------------------------------

  lengths_max <- list(
    value_age_min_, value_age_max_, value_sex_, value_ltla19_
  ) %>%
    purrr::map_dbl(length) %>%
    max(., na.rm = TRUE)

  # Convert any NA inputs into vector format
  value_age_min_ <- ifelse(
    all(is.na(value_age_min_)),
    rep_len(NA_integer_, lengths_max), value_age_min_
  )
  value_age_max_ <- ifelse(
    all(is.na(value_age_max_)),
    rep_len(NA_integer_, lengths_max), value_age_max_
  )
  value_sex_ <- ifelse(
    all(is.na(value_sex_)),
    rep_len(NA_integer_, lengths_max), value_sex_
  )
  value_ltla19_ <- ifelse(
    all(is.na(value_ltla19_)),
    rep_len(NA_character_, lengths_max), value_ltla19_
  )

  vec_length <- list(
    value_age_min_, value_age_max_, value_sex_, value_ltla19_
  ) %>%
    purrr::map_dbl(length) %>%
    unique()

  # Check length of all entries are equal
  if (length(vec_length) != 1) {
    stop("Mismatch of input lengths!")
  }

  # Create vector of output values ---------------------------------------------

  proportion <- list(df_) %>%
    # Duplicate population distribution to match lengths of other inputs
    rep_len(vec_length) %>%
    # Filter distribution by input strata
    purrr::map2(
      value_age_min_, ~ dplyr::filter(.x, is.na(.y) | Age >= .y)
    ) %>%
    purrr::map2(
      value_age_max_, ~ dplyr::filter(.x, is.na(.y) | Age <= .y)
    ) %>%
    purrr::map2(
      value_sex_, ~ dplyr::filter(.x, is.na(.y) | Sex == .y)
    ) %>%
    purrr::map2(
      value_ltla19_, ~ dplyr::filter(.x, is.na(.y) | LTLA19 == .y)
    ) %>%
    # Calculate proportion within strata
    purrr::map_dbl(
      ~ dplyr::pull(.x, ProportionByGroup) %>% sum(., na.rm = TRUE)
    )

  # Return proportions ---------------------------------------------------------
  return(proportion)
}
``` 

If you need further details - such as about the usual/expected structure of the inputs etc. - I can try to provide this.

title: n_distinct sql translation in Spark 3 cast column into array and counts nulls
description:
The Spark 3 implementation of `n_distinct` translates differently than Spark 2. In Spark 2, `n_distinct` translates to SQL `count(distinct(...))` while Spark 3 translates to `count(distinct(array(...)))`. The former implementation does not count null/missing values while this one does. This causes our regression testing transitioning from Spark 2 to Spark 3 to fail as the counts are different. In my example, the expected distinct count is 6 but in Spark 3 it is 7.




SPARK 3.1
```r
library(sparklyr)
#> Warning: package 'sparklyr' was built under R version 4.0.5
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'sparklyr'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local", version = "3.1")
df <- data.frame(num = c(1,1,1,1,2,2,2,2),
 id = c('1-A', '1-B', '1-C', NA_character_, NA_character_, '2-A', '2-B', '2-C'))
sdf <- dplyr::copy_to(dest = sc,
                      df = df,
                      name = 'test',
                      overwrite = TRUE,
                      memory = FALSE) 
proof <- sdf %>% summarise(distinct_count = n_distinct(id)) 

proof
#> # Source: spark<?> [?? x 1]

#>            <dbl>

proof %>%
  show_query()
#> <SQL>

title: summarize(across(...), across(...)) and mutate(across(...), across(...))
description:
A `summarize()` call can contain more than one call to `across()`, which makes it more powerful than the `_at` and `_if` variants. I still wonder if we need to consider new columns when selecting columns with `across()`. 

## Example

Consider the following (contrived) example:

``` r
library(dplyr)

data <- tibble(my_summary = 0, xa = 1, xb = TRUE)

data %>%
  summarize(
    across(starts_with("x"), sum, .names = "{.col}_summary"),
    across(ends_with("_summary"), mean, .names = "{.col}_summary")
  )
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   xa_summary xb_summary my_summary_summary xa_summary_summary xb_summary_summary
#>        <dbl>      <int>              <dbl>              <dbl>              <dbl>
#> 1          1          1                  0                  1                  1
```

<sup>Created on 2022-05-01 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

The second `across()` call captures the summary columns created in the first `across()` call. I can't think of a practical use case.

## Proposal

Should we limit the columns selectable with `across()` to the original columns in `summarize()`, and perhaps also in `mutate()` (though the case is not as clear there)? In the above example, the `_summary_summary` columns would no longer be created.

## Motivation

Separation of `mutate()` into `build_mutate_spec()` and `mutate_spec()` (same for `summarize()`), so that backends need to implement only `mutate_spec()` and let dplyr do the rest.

title: should arrange() show a warning on empty or constant criteria?
description:
Should `arrange()` show a warning on empty or constant criteria?
It would warn over some common errors.

Arrange with no arguments:
```r
df1 %>%
  arrange()
```

Trying to arrange by column name:
```r
df1 %>%
  arrange("col1")
df1 %>%
  arrange(col1)
```

Trying to arrange by column position:
```r
df1 %>%
  arrange(1:3)
df1 %>%
  arrange(across(1:3))
```

It would be similar to the warning when `filter` contains an asignment, instead of a condition:
```r
df1 %>%
  filter(col1 = condition)
df1 %>%
  filter(col1 == condition)
```

title: `rowwise()` with a mutate() call with warnings is very slow
description:
As identified by @debruine here https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6236#issuecomment-1103972470 this issue is actually caused when mutate() is used after rowwise() and generates warnings.

This code takes ~11 seconds to run in a clean R session

```r
library(dplyr)
library(tictoc)
tic()
foo <- tibble(
  id = 1:800
) %>% 
  rowwise() %>% 
  mutate(group_b_mean = mean(NULL))
toc()
# 11.584 sec elapsed
```

Please note that weirdly the same code takes <1second when run with the {reprex} addin.

Many thanks to debruine for figuring this out.

description:

# Install my example package that reexports desc.

title: For *_join functions, requesting handling when argument "on" is specified in place of "by"
description:
As a heavy SQL user, I'm constantly using argument "on" instead of "by" in inner_join and left_join. These functions do echo what they're actually joining on, but it's easy to miss. I feel like these functions should stop you in your tracks if you try to use "on" or throw a warning and make the substitution.

Bit of a contrived example below, but in both cases it's clear the user is intending to join on "id" and not c("id", "x")

```r
library(dplyr)

df2 <- data.frame(id = c(1,2), x = c(3.4, 2.7), z = c(4.4, 5.4))

df %>% inner_join(df2, on="id")
df %>% inner_join(df2, by="id")
```

title: Using .after or .before within across
description:
With `across`, we can perform computations on several columns at the same time. However, the `.after` argument in `mutate` is outside of `across`, which means I can't handle the location of newly created columns individually. I can only put them in bulk either before or after a certain position.

Ideally, the `.after` or `.before` argument would run on each new column within across.

```
df <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 2, z = 3)

df |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(tidyselect::everything(), ~ . + 1, .names = "{.col}_new"))
```

This puts all new columns at the end of `df`. However, what would make sense in many case is to put the new columns behind the original ones, i.e. expected output would be:

```
# A tibble: 1 x 6
      x x_new     y y_new     z z_new
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1     1     2     2     3     3     4
```

title: Behaviour for duplicates in left/right Joins
description:
# Description 

When conducting a left join or a right join, if there are multiple matches, then extra rows are added to the dataset (see example below). While I completely appreciate that it is sensible for new rows to be created, having spoken to colleagues that use this feature, many are not aware that the joins behave in this way, and this 

# Reproducible Example

```r
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(magrittr)

left_df <- tibble::as_tibble(
    list(
        name = c("john", "lisa", "mark", "connor", NA),
        income = c(1000, 2000, 100000, 50, NA)
    )
)

right_df <- tibble::as_tibble(
    list(
        name = c("john", "lisa", "mark", "mark", NA),
        outgoings = c(300, 600, 20000, 10, NA)
    )
)

left_df %>% dplyr::left_join(right_df, by=c("name"="name"))
```

This gives the following output:
```
# A tibble: 6 x 3
  name   income outgoings
  <chr>   <dbl>     <dbl>
1 john     1000       300
2 lisa     2000       600
3 mark   100000     20000
4 mark   100000        10
5 connor     50        NA
6 NA         NA        NA
```
# Suggested Solution

I was going to try and add a simple warning/message to make it clear how these joins are behaving, something along the lines of:

``` r
warning("Multiple matches between left and right dataframe, new rows being created in left df.")
```
I just wanted to check whether this is something that would be useful to others before I start working on it. I hope that makes sense! Thanks for all of the work on this package, it has been so useful for me, I'd love an opportunity to help in any way I can! 😄

title: Add function to "chop" a tibble into segments (sub-tibbles), with predefined number of rows of each segment
description:
Hello, 
I'm wrangling an audio dataset that will be used for classification with torch. For that, "chopping" the dataset into segments is a useful thing to do (maybe there are more use cases). Wondering if anyone would be interested in implementing a dplyr function to accomplish this, which is just a repeated slicing of a given tibble. 

Here's the function I came up with:

```{r}

#' @title "Chop" data into segments. 
#' @description Iteratively slice (chop) a dataset into segments (sub-datasets)
#'  of predefined length. 
#' @return `output` list containing each segment sub-dataset.  
#' @param dataset, dataset to be "chopped"
#' @param nrow_per_segment, predefined N of rows of each segment
#' @param keep_remaining, logical indicating if remaining rows of `dataset` are
#'   to be kept, in the case where the number of segments is not a whole number.
#'   If TRUE (default), the last segment will contain the remaining rows. If 
#'   FALSE, remaining rows will be dropped. 


chop_data <- function(
  dataset, 
  nrow_per_segment, 
  keep_remaining = TRUE 
) {
  
  n_segments <- nrow(dataset) / nrow_per_segment
  n_segments_floor <- floor(n_segments)
  
  output <- list()   
  for (i in 1:n_segments_floor) {
    segment_head <- ((i - 1) * nrow_per_segment + 1)
    segment_tail <- (i * nrow_per_segment)
    
    output[[i]] <-  dataset %>%  
      slice(segment_head:segment_tail)
    
  }
  
  print(
    paste0(
      "chopped dataset into ", 
      n_segments_floor, 
      " segments"
    )
  )
  
  if (keep_remaining == TRUE) {
    output[[i + 1]] <- dataset %>% 
      slice(segment_tail:nrow(dataset))
    
    print(
      paste0(
        "Kept remaining rows inside an extra ", 
        nrow(output[[i + 1]]),
        " row segment"
      )
    )
  } 
  
  
  return(output)
   
}

```

The function's result can be checked by running
```{r}
library(tidyverse)

example <- chop_data(
  dataset = mpg, 
  nrow_per_segment = 20,
  keep_remaining = TRUE
)

```


Cheers

title: is it better to warn when change the factor levels in group_df?
description:
Sometimes we may think `group_df` is like a unified but separate ~~data.frame~~ (like a `list-data.frame`), where we mistake to change factor levels in the different group of this data. 

There're some questions in `stackoverflow`:
-https://stackoverflow.com/questions/57696639/reorder-factor-levels-within-group
-https://stackoverflow.com/questions/53698444/reorder-factor-not-working-on-grouped-data

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
df <- tibble::tibble(
    afct = factor(rep(c("f1", "f2"), times = 2), levels = c("f1", "f2")),
    group = rep(c("a", "b"), each = 2),
    weight = c(1, 2, 2, 1)
)

# we mistate to do this:
df %>%
    dplyr::group_by(group) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
        bfct = forcats::fct_reorder(afct, weight)
    ) %>%
    dplyr::pull(bfct)
#> [1] f1 f2 f1 f2
#> Levels: f1 f2

# what we need is like this: 
df %>%
    dplyr::group_by(group) %>%
    dplyr::group_split() %>%
    lapply(function(x) {
        x %>%
            dplyr::mutate(
                bfct = forcats::fct_reorder(afct, weight)
            ) %>%
            dplyr::pull(bfct)
    })
#> [[1]]
#> [1] f1 f2
#> Levels: f1 f2
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] f1 f2
#> Levels: f2 f1
```

title: `.by` argument as alternative to `group_by`
description:
_Edit:_ Updated to reflect @DavisVaughan's suggestion [here](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6214#issuecomment-1073887193).

Any thoughts on implementing a `.by` arg so that functions can operate by group without returning a `grouped_df`?

Basically this:

```r
df <- tibble(x = 1:3, y = c("a", "a", "b"))

df %>%
  mutate(pct = x/sum(x), .by = y)
```

would be equivalent to this:

```r
df %>%
  group_by(y) %>%
  mutate(pct = x/sum(x)) %>%
  ungroup()
```

title: varying samples sizes in slice_sample across groups
description:
---
I would like to humbly suggest the following feature, totally aware that you cannot design functions to everyones needs:

sample_n used to support size-arguments that differ across groups. slice_sample does not. In usecases for at least three organisations I found this feature quite useful, as taking stratified samples with varying sample-sizes was often required. This keeps me from adapting to the new slice_sample. Would you kindly consider adding this feature to slice_sample?
Thank you very much!

```r
library(dplyr)
library(palmerpenguins)

# currently not supported:
penguins %>% 
  mutate(n_samples = case_when(
    year == 2007 ~ 3L,
    year == 2008 ~ 2L,
    year == 2009 ~ 4L,
    TRUE ~ 0L
  )) %>% 
  group_by(year) %>%
   slice_sample(n = n_samples) # formerly sample_n(size = n_samples)
```

title: `relocate.data.frame()` shouldn't rely on `vec_unique()` retaining names
description:
Currently, `relocate()` relies on the fact that `vec_unique()` keeps names
https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/8abb54b60e40ef7c619156a12b14872cb2eb7989/R/relocate.R#L83-L85

We think we should actually drop names from the result of `vec_unique()`, since the returned names are reliant on the fact that only the _first_ encountered duplicate value is returned (this is also consistent with `unique()`). See https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/issues/1442 and https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/pull/1532 where we tried to implement this, but found that dplyr relies on this behavior currently.

---

One easy way to fix this is to use `vec_unique_loc()` to get the locations, and then `vec_slice()`, which will retain names.

That should work in the immediate term but it may be worth looking at the code to also see why we currently get names off the unique values, and if there is something else we should be doing instead, since that _feels_ unreliable.

title: Memory leak(?) in dplyr, magrittr, or one of dplyr's dependencies
description:
# Overview

Hi, when enabling GC torture, I sporadically get:

```r
Error in dplyr::mutate(., `:=`(!!targets[idx], 1)) : 
   'rho' must be an environment not promise: detected in C-level eval
```

I don't know if this happens in **dplyr**, **magrittr**, or one of the **dplyr** dependencies.


# Background

I've spent 3+ days and about ~30 hours to narrow in on a _rare_ SEGV_MAPERR segfault problem that involves dplyr, magrittr, and many more packages, resulting `*** caught segfault ***` and `address 0x559700000004, cause 'memory not mapped'` reported by R. Not all runs, but several runs also reported on `*** recursive gc invocation` (also from R).

While trying to narrow in on the problem and trimming down the code (the original code wasn't mine and was quite verbose; I noticed it while revdep check Bioconductor **mistyR**), I lost the segfault on the way, but ended up with sporadic `'rho' must be an environment not <...>: detected in C-level eval` errors:

```
  'rho' must be an environment not ...: detected in C-level eval
  'rho' must be an environment not pairlist: detected in C-level applyClosure
  'rho' must be an environment not pairlist: detected in C-level eval
  'rho' must be an environment not promise: detected in C-level applyClosure
  'rho' must be an environment not promise: detected in C-level eval
```

These only appear if I run with GC torturing, which suggests a memory leak.

My hope is that this is caused by the same underlying problem that triggers my original segfault issue.


# Reproducible example

Here's a script `crash.R` that reproduces the problem together with the `data.rds` file attached as a _fake_ ZIP file ([data.rds.zip](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/files/8191297/data.rds.zip)) to please GitHub (rename `mv data.rds.zip data.rds`).


```r
## Memory leak in magrittr, or dplyr, or?
##
## Example:
## $ R --quiet --no-environ --no-init-file --no-save
## > source("crash.R")
## Run #1
## * Step A
## * Step B
##   - Step 1 of 5
##   - Step 2 of 5
## Error in dplyr::mutate(., `:=`(!!targets[idx], 1)) : 
##   'rho' must be an environment not promise: detected in C-level eval
##
## Requirements:
##   install.packages("dplyr")
##
## Reproduces on:
## * R 4.1.2 (2021-11-01; x86_64-pc-linux-gnu)
##    - RStudio Cloud; Linux Ubuntu 20.04;
##      Running R via the RStudio *Terminal*
## * R 4.1.3 RC (2022-03-02 r81842; x86_64-pc-linux-gnu)
##    - Linux Ubuntu 18.04; built from source with
##      --enable-R-shlib --enable-memory-profiling

library(magrittr)

gctorture2(20L)

for (kk in 1:10) {
  cat(sprintf("Run #%d\n", kk))
  
  cat("* Step A\n")
  targets <- letters[1:11]
  data <- readRDS("data.rds")

  cat("* Step B\n")
  res <- mapply(data, seq_along(data), FUN = function(df, idx) {
    cat(sprintf("  - Step %d of %d\n", idx, length(data)))
    data.frame(feature = targets) %>%
      dplyr::left_join(df, by = "feature") %>%
      dplyr::mutate(!!targets[idx] := 1.0)
  })
}

cat("Done\n")
```

title: More informative error for `case_when()` failing due to not matching NA
description:
It seems that since recently mutate `case_when()` calls are more strictly evaluated with regard to the variable type (or it always was as strict and some other R or package update, now produces integer instead of double values). 
That's fine, but I think, ideally the error message would be more informative than `'names' attribute [1] must be the same length as the vector [0]`, especially for this borderline case where (depending on the data) the same code might produce either integers or doubles.

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attache Paket: 'dplyr'
#> Die folgenden Objekte sind maskiert von 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag

#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(magrittr)

tibble(a = c("yes", "no"), 
       b = as.integer(c(0,2))) %>% 
  mutate(b = case_when(a == "yes" ~ NA_real_, 
                       TRUE ~ b))

title: Clearer across() documentation for multiple .fns
description:
I've found the documentation for across() about the multiple function case more oblique than perhaps it could be, but I'm not familiar enough with all of its applications to be sure I'll get it right if I directly submit a change via pull. This applies to both the Roxygen comment on R/across.R and to a lesser degree the colwise vignette, vignettes/colwise.Rmd

The current text in the Roxygen comment is
>Functions to apply to each of the selected columns. Possible values are:
>    - NULL, to returns the columns untransformed.
>    - A function, e.g. mean.
>    - A purrr-style lambda, e.g. ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
>    - A list of functions/lambdas, e.g. list(mean = mean, n_miss = ~ sum(is.na(.x))

and in the vignette,

> The second argument, .fns, is a function or list of functions to apply to each column. This can also be a purrr style formula (or list of formulas) like ~ .x / 2. (This argument is optional, and you can omit it if you just want to get the underlying data; you’ll see that technique used in vignette("rowwise").)
> ...
> ### Multiple functions
>
> You can transform each variable with more than one function by supplying a named list of functions or lambda functions in the second argument:

The intuition that I'm only seeing referred to indirectly is that the provided functions *fan out* into multiple outputs, i.e. if you provided n columns and m functions you'd end up with n x m outputs. The Roxygen intro also refers to transformation in the singular, "across() makes it easy to apply the same transformation to multiple columns...", so it feels like the multiple-output case is de-emphasised. There are other possible interpretations for "Functions to apply to each of the selected columns", e.g. maybe the functions are applied in order, to a single output. (This is of course very achievable through other methods like `purrr::compose` or `. %>% ...` pipes or purrr lambdas, and not necessary for `across` to do, but it's not ruled out by the description.)

It's also not made entirely clear that an _unnamed_ list of functions `c(...)` is probably unusual, i.e. the reason a _named_ list is used is because the name determines the output name (depending on `.names`) - someone might use an unnamed list in an ad-hoc to test a range of transformations, but named lists match the intention behind the design of the function better. The vignette is clearer about this, and while Roxygen uses a named list as an example but leaves the choice unaddressed, i.e. it could just be a code style cue to make a lambda more readable. (I've primarily used across with `mutate`, so the rationale in the `summarise`-style example wasn't immediately obvious.)

My suggestion would be to emphasise that a separate output is produced for each function, e.g. a maybe clumsy alternative wording would be
> Functions to apply to each of the selected columns, where each transformation produces a separate output column based on the column and list names.

Again, I don't know for sure if this conflicts with any current or planned uses for the function. As far as I can tell across more or less enforces this as a constraint, i.e. requires unique names for each output (although of course transform functions can return NULL in order to _not_ produce a new output column. _Optionally_ producing output for a list of functions opens up some interesting variations I guess that vary a little from the n x m account.)

Mostly my sense was that the intention or purpose behind the argument was underspecified in the documentation, making it harder to understand the behaviour unless you already know the behaviour. Partly this could be a consequence of across being a fairly flexible tool so its 'meaning' can look a little different in different uses, but I think we can nudge the docs towards giving a quicker birds-eye view. Hopefully you can see where I'm coming from.

title: Dedicated function for selecting from current data
description:
Would it be useful to have a dedicated function (say, `pick()`) to select columns from the current data? Currently, `across()` with only a `.cols` argument serves this role.

I would see a dedicated function having at least three advantages:

1.  Nicer syntax for union selections: `pick(1, last_col())` vs. `across(c(1, last_col()))`.
2.  Better semantics. `across()` makes sense when there’s functions to apply, but less so when it’s used just for selecting columns. `pick()` seems intuitive for only selecting columns.
3.  Reuse existing patterns: `across(c(1:2, 4), mean)` vs. `map_df(pick(1:2, 4), mean)`. The first requires you to know that `across()` can select columns *and* apply a function, latter can re-use existing function application methods.

The last point is particularly important if/when `...` is deprecated in `across()` (\#6073), as funtionality would not be identical anymore. For example:

``` r
# With no ..., need to use an anonymous function for na.rm
across(c(1, 3:4), ~ mean(., na.rm = TRUE))

# Could be avoided with `pick()`
map_df(pick(1, 3:4), mean, na.rm = TRUE)
```

I would see the primary uses for this as:

1.  Replace `across()` in e.g. `group_by()` selections `group_by(across(c(1, 3:5)))` vs. `group_by(pick(1, 3:5))`. Big semantic and syntactic win, IMO.
2.  Passing arguments to functions that take data frame or matrix arguments. For example common questions about taking means or sums over rows in data frames. In my experience people don’t think to `apply(across(1:5), 1, f)`, but `apply(pick(1:5), 1, f)` might be more intuitive.

I could think of two ways to implement this as a wrapper:

``` r
pick <- function(...) {
  across(.cols = c(...))
}
```

Or:

``` r
pick <- function(...) {
  select(cur_data(), ...)
}
```

Although, particularly with the `across()` route, it would seem nicer to reverse the dependency and extract the relevant parts from `across()` into`pick()` instead.

I appreciate your consideration for this feature request.

title: cur_column() requires extra parentheses to work inside if_any() and if_all()
description:
Say I have a list filter functions that I want to run against a data frame. A natural way to do this would be to use `filter(if_all(...))`. This gives an error when you invoke `cur_column()` inside `if_all(...)`.

``` r
library(dplyr)
criteria <- list(
    Species = \(.x) paste(.x) < "v",
    Petal.Width = \(.x) .x < .3
)

# Error: cur_column() demands to be called inside across()
iris |>
    filter(
        if_all(
            names(criteria),
            ~ criteria[[cur_column()]](.x)
        )
    )
#> Error in `filter()`:
#> ! Problem while computing `..1 = criteria[[cur_column()]](Species) &
#>   ...`.
#> Caused by error in `cur_column()`:
#> ! Must be used inside `across()`.
```

However, if I simply add extra parentheses around the `if_all(...)`, everything works:

``` r
# OK: extra parens around (if_all(...cur_column()...))
iris |>
    filter(
        (if_all(
            names(criteria),
            ~ criteria[[cur_column()]](.x)
        ))
    ) |>
    with(table(Species)) # less verbose output
#> Species
#>     setosa versicolor  virginica 
#>         34          0          0
```

<details>

If I use `across(...)` instead of `if_all(...)`, it works without extra parentheses but this is deprecated. Fixing the warning was how I discovered this issue.

title: dplyr 1.0.8 on R 4.0 not working due to cli dependency issue
description:
dplyr 1.0.8 can be installed on R 4.0 but the dependency cli comes with an outdated version (2.4.0) while this version of dplyr requires a newer version of cli. 

Please read more here: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/71179648/r-shiny-app-deployed-on-r-4-0-3-fails-but-works-on-4-1-2-package-dependencies

Recommended solution: bump up the dependent version of R for 1.0.8 to 4.1 so it cannot be installed with 4.0

title: bang-bang operator does not work with constants having length >1 in grouped dataframes
description:
When using a `mutate()` statement on a grouped dataframe, using the `!!` operator for a constant of an appropriate length greater than 1 throws an error in version 1.0.8, but, not using the `!!` operator works.  This is a break from previous versions.

I first noticed the break moving from version 1.0.7 to 1.0.8, and, it appears it is still happening in the 1.0.8.9000.

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '1.0.2'

y <- c(1, 2)

# works with y and !!y
data.frame(x = c("a", "a", "b", "b")) %>%
  group_by(x) %>%
  mutate(numbers = y)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#> # Groups:   x [2]
#>   x     numbers
#>   <chr>   <dbl>
#> 1 a           1
#> 2 a           2
#> 3 b           1
#> 4 b           2

data.frame(x = c("a", "a", "b", "b")) %>%
  group_by(x) %>%
  mutate(numbers = !!y)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#> # Groups:   x [2]
#>   x     numbers
#>   <chr>   <dbl>
#> 1 a           1
#> 2 a           2
#> 3 b           1
#> 4 b           2

detach("package:dplyr", unload = TRUE)
library(dplyr, lib.loc = "../../Rlib_trashme")
#>

#> [1] '1.0.8.9000'

#> [1] "dd9a3b8be98c6e12bc15d7057e29a571ceab9215"

title: mutate() truncates output to the same number of observations as variables with "model.selection" object
description:
No problems using mutate() on "model.selection" objects in version 1.0.7, but in 1.0.8, regardless of what is being done inside the mutate function, the output observations are truncated to equal the number of variables. For example, when using mutate() to add a cumsum() column to a "model.selection" object with 256 observations and 14 variables, the resulting output is only 15 observations long (with now 15 variables). Same result for several attempts with different number of variables, the output observations are truncated to the length of the number of variables. Reprex here:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(MuMIn)

dat <- data.frame(R1 = sample(c(0,1), 50, replace = T),
                  V1 = c(1:50),  V2 = c(51:100),
                  V3 = rep(1:2, 25), V4 = rep(1:5, 10))

dat.global.mod <- glm(R1 ~ ., data=dat, family=binomial(link=logit), na.action = "na.fail")
dat_dredge <- dredge(dat.global.mod)
#> Fixed term is "(Intercept)"

# dimensions of model.selection object
dim(dat_dredge)
#> [1] 16 10
dat_dredge <- dat_dredge %>% mutate(cumulative_weight=cumsum(weight))

# dimensions of model.selection object after mutating and adding one variable (cumulative_weight)
# now observations are truncated to equal the number of variables
dim(dat_dredge)
#> [1] 11 11
```

<sup>Created on 2022-02-14 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

If I force the object to a data frame, it works just fine, but then I can't do any further modeling work with it.

Again, this worked fine with 1.0.7, but does this truncation behavior with 1.0.8. I don't believe this is an issue with MuMIN because that package hasn't been updated in nearly two years.

title: `slice_sample()` errors if `n` bigger than number of rows
description:
In the man page for `slice` functions, the description for the argument `n` states:

> If n is greater than the number of rows in the group (or prop > 1), the result will be silently truncated to the group size. If the proportion of a group size does not yield an integer number of rows, the absolute value of prop*nrow(.data) is rounded down.

The output of `slice_sample` used to be the same `data.frame` (with different ordering) if `n` is higher than the number of rows, but it is now returning an error.

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

tmp <- data.frame(x = c(rep('a',6), rep('b',4)), y = 1:10)
print(tmp)
#>    x  y

#> 2  a  2
#> 3  a  3
#> 4  a  4
#> 5  a  5
#> 6  a  6
#> 7  b  7

tmp %>% slice_sample(n = 15)
#> Error in `slice_sample()`:

tmp %>% group_by(x) %>% slice_sample(n = 15)

#> ! Problem while computing indices.

#> Caused by error in `sample.int()`:

title: change in behaviour for cur_data() and list columns
description:
It seems that there is a change in behaviour between version 1.0.7 and 1.0.8.

Version 1.0.7:
```r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
x <- tibble(a = list(e = list(d = tibble(b = 1)), e = list(d = tibble(b = 1))))

f <- function(x) {
    x$a$d$b
}

x %>% 
    rowwise() %>% 
    mutate(list(f(cur_data())))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#> # Rowwise: 
#>   a                `list(f(cur_data()))`
#>   <named list>     <list>               
#> 1 <named list [1]> <dbl [1]>            
#> 2 <named list [1]> <dbl [1]>
```
In version 1.0.8 this doesn't work the same:
```r
x %>% 
    rowwise() %>% 
    mutate(list(f(cur_data())))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#> # Rowwise: 
#>   a                `list(f(cur_data()))`
#>   <named list>     <list>               
#> 1 <named list [1]> <NULL>               
#> 2 <named list [1]> <NULL>
```
If you redefine the function `f` like so, it would result in the same as in 1.0.7:

```r
f <- function(x) {
    x$a[[1]]$d$b
}
```

title: Inconsistent error when not finding bangbanged function
description:
Using dev version

See below, the use case is I don't attach dplyr, use `dplyr::` notation and forget that I should namespace `sym` too, the error with `mutate()` is especially not helpful, but there is also an inconsistency between `transmute()` and `select()` 

``` r
dplyr::mutate(iris, !!sym("Sepal.Width"))
#> Error in local_error_context(dots = dots, .index = i, mask = mask): promise already under evaluation: recursive default argument reference or earlier problems?

dplyr::select(iris, !!sym("Sepal.Width"))
#> Error in `dplyr::select()`:
#> ! could not find function "sym"

dplyr::transmute(iris, !!sym("Sepal.Width"))
#> Error in sym("Sepal.Width"): could not find function "sym"
```

If we don't use `!!` errors are helpful and consistent.

``` r
dplyr::mutate(iris, foo("Sepal.Width"))
#> Error in `dplyr::mutate()`:
#> ! Problem while computing `..1 = foo("Sepal.Width")`.
#> Caused by error in `foo()`:
#> ! could not find function "foo"

dplyr::select(iris, foo("Sepal.Width"))
#> Error in `dplyr::select()`:
#> ! could not find function "foo"

dplyr::transmute(iris, foo("Sepal.Width"))
#> Error in `dplyr::transmute()`:

title: In `dplyr::filter()`, specifying a logical condition with `~ .` notation fails inside `purrr::map2()` but works otherwise
description:
Given this data frame
```r
my_mtcars <- tibble::rownames_to_column(mtcars, "cars")
```
those are the rows I want to keep:
```r
cars_to_keep <- c("Merc 240D", "Fiat X1-9", "Ferrari Dino")
```
and using `dplyr::filter()`, both of the following syntaxes work:
```r
# option a: specify `cars` colname explicitly
dplyr::filter(my_mtcars, cars %in% cars_to_keep)
# option b: use a selection helper and `~ .` notation
dplyr::filter(my_mtcars, across(contains("cars"), ~ . %in% cars_to_keep))
```

---
By contrast, when having a tibble with _list-columns_ (which suggests using `purrr:map2()` for filtering) only **option a** works
```r
# the data
higher_level_tibble <- 
  tibble::tibble(my_data         = list(my_mtcars),
                 the_cars_i_want = list(cars_to_keep))

# this works:
higher_level_tibble %>%
  dplyr::mutate(my_filtered_data = purrr::map2(.x = my_data, .y = the_cars_i_want, .f = ~dplyr::filter(.x, cars %in% .y)))

## # A tibble: 1 x 3
##   my_data        the_cars_i_want my_filtered_data
##  <list>         <list>          <list>          
## 1 <df [32 x 12]> <chr [3]>       <df [3 x 12]>  

# this doesn't:
higher_level_tibble %>%
  dplyr::mutate(my_filtered_data = purrr::map2(.x = my_data, .y = the_cars_i_want, .f = ~ dplyr::filter(.x, across(contains("cars"), ~ . %in% .y))))

## Error: Problem with `mutate()` column `my_filtered_data`.
## i `my_filtered_data = map2(...)`.
## x Problem with `filter()` input `..1`.
## i Input `..1` is `across(contains("cars"), ~. %in% .y)`.
## x the ... list contains fewer than 2 elements
```

---
The only way to make this work inside `dplyr::mutate()` & `purrr::map2()` is to replace the `~ .` notation inside `dplyr::filter()` with an anonymous function:
```r
higher_level_tibble %>%
  dplyr::mutate(my_filtered_data = purrr::map2(.x = my_data, .y = the_cars_i_want, .f = ~ dplyr::filter(.x, across(starts_with("cars"), function(x) x %in% .y))))

## # A tibble: 1 x 3
##   my_data        the_cars_i_want my_filtered_data
##   <list>         <list>          <list>          
## 1 <df [32 x 12]> <chr [3]>       <df [3 x 12]> 
```
Bottom line
---
How come `~ .` doesn't work but `function(x)` does when using `dplyr::filter()` inside `dplyr::mutate()` & `purrr::map2()`? This is particularly confusing as `~ .` does work outside of `purrr::map2()` context.

N.B.
See [this StackOverflow post](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/70772004/how-to-combine-filteracrossstarts-withfoo-logical-condition-with-mu/70773282#70773282) about the same issue.

title: Feature request to distinct() function
description:
This is more a feature request in the `distinct()` function than an issue. However, I find this function somewhat lacking, and introducing some additional features would simplify certain operations:

If for example you want to find duplicate entries in specific columns, but at the same time keep all columns (`.keep_all = TRUE`), the `distinct()` will only keep the first row. This isn't always desirable (I dare say it is quite often not). It could for some reason be that you want to keep another row, or you want the row merged by some formula. Supposedly, there are ways of adding data-masking functionality. However, this isn't necessarily very intuitive, and therefore adding some base operations (e.g. column means or column medians, column sums) would greatly simplify how to deal with duplicated entries in the data.

Example:
Currently, `distinct()` can only preserve only the first row:
```r
a <- data.frame(
    "x" = rep(1:3, each = 2),
    "y" = rep(1:3, each = 2),
    "z" = 1:6
)

# Original dataframe
a
A data.frame: 6 × 3
x	y	z
<int>	<int>	<int>
1	1	1
1	1	2
2	2	3
2	2	4
3	3	5
3	3	6

# Dataframe with duplicates removed
distinct(a, x, .keep_all = TRUE)
A data.frame: 3 × 3
x	y	z
<int>	<int>	<int>
1	1	1
2	2	3
3	3	5
```

Example of suggested functionality:
```R
# Duplicates removed by adding column means:
distinct(a, x, .keep_all = "colMeans")
A data.frame: 3 × 3
x	y	z
<int>	<int>	<int>
1	1	1.5
2	2	3.5
3	3	5.5

# Duplicates removed by adding column sums:
distinct(a, x, .keep_all = "colSums")
A data.frame: 3 × 3
x	y	z
<int>	<int>	<int>
1	2	3
2	4	7
3	6	11
```

title: Case_when and ifelse calculations not lazy
description:
---

If the evaluations are not lazy (e.g delays the evaluation of an expression until its value is needed), then the NaN warning for sqrt(-1) should only be produced once. However, since the calculations are done for all case, the sqrt(-1) NaN warning is produced twice. In best practice, the calculations should not be done if the left hand side logical test is not satisfied. 

How I wish lazy evaluations of the type described in [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lazy_evaluation) be implemented for case_when. This limits the type of things I can do with writing programs (e.g. less flexible). For examples, it forces me to use base R if  else conditional statements rather than using case_when.... I think this problem applies for the ifelse function as well. 

The code below produces two NaN warnings... 
```r
library(dplyr)

even_function <- function(y){sqrt(y) }
odd_function <- function(y){sqrt(y) + 1}

data.frame(x=1:10, y =-1:8) %>% 
  mutate( type = case_when( x %% 2 == 0 ~ even_function(y) ,
             TRUE ~ odd_function(y) ))

```
Warning: Problem with `mutate()` column `type`.
ℹ `type = case_when(x%%2 == 0 ~ even_function(y), TRUE ~ odd_function(y))`.
ℹ NaNs produced
Warning: Problem with `mutate()` column `type`.
ℹ `type = case_when(x%%2 == 0 ~ even_function(y), TRUE ~ odd_function(y))`.
ℹ NaNs produced

The behaviour is reproducible for ifelse as well. 
```{r}
test_data %>% 
  mutate( type = ifelse(x %% 2 == 0, even_function(y),  odd_function(y)    ))

```
Warning: Problem with `mutate()` column `type`.
ℹ `type = ifelse(x%%2 == 0, even_function(y), odd_function(y))`.
ℹ NaNs produced
Warning: Problem with `mutate()` column `type`.
ℹ `type = ifelse(x%%2 == 0, even_function(y), odd_function(y))`.
ℹ NaNs produced

title: Feature request: abritrary mutating/processing entire tibble in pipe
description:
Please briefly describe your problem and what output you expect. If you have a question, please don't use this form. Instead, ask on <https://stackoverflow.com/> or <https://community.rstudio.com/>.

Please include a minimal reproducible example (AKA a reprex). If you've never heard of a [reprex](http://reprex.tidyverse.org/) before, start by reading <https://www.tidyverse.org/help/#reprex>.

---

Quite often there is a need to call some function (which does something else than column/rowwise operations) for the entire tibble based on the value of a predicate. 

In my opinion it would be nice to this in the pipe - so I'm asking would it be possible to add this kind of functionality to dplyr (or some other tidyverse package)?

Here is the basic idea - kind of operation to mutate/process the entire tibble (you can most probably generalize this idea further):

```r
call_fun_for_tibble_if <- function(x, predicate, fun, ...) { if (predicate) fun(x, ...) else x }
```

In this manner this stupid example
```r
test_me <- function(x, verbose = T) {
  out <- tibble(a = LETTERS)
  if (verbose) print(out)
  out
}
```
would become
```r
test_me <- function(x, verbose = T) {
  tibble(a = LETTERS) %>%
    call_fun_for_tibble_if (verbose, print)
}
```

title: `nest_by()` changes ordering of the data
description:
For example, here is the original ordering of the data:

``` r
library(tidyverse)

unique(starwars$sex)
#> [1] "male"           "none"           "female"         "hermaphroditic"
#> [5] NA
``` 

`{tidyr}` workflow preserves it:

``` r
df_tidyr <- starwars %>%
  group_by(sex) %>%
  nest()

unique(df_tidyr$sex)
#> [1] "male"           "none"           "female"         "hermaphroditic"
#> [5] NA
``` 

`{dplyr}` workflow doesn't:

``` r
df_dplyr <- starwars %>%
  nest_by(sex)

unique(df_dplyr$sex)
#> [1] "female"         "hermaphroditic" "male"           "none"          
#> [5] NA
```

<sup>Created on 2022-01-07 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1.9000)</sup>

The documentation says:

> Data frame attributes are not preserved, because `nest_by()` fundamentally creates a new data frame.

But I am still not sure if this is really the expected behavior since I can't see any obvious reason why creating a nested dataframe should change the ordering of the data.

title: Possible improvement/implementation of quo(s) using across
description:
Hello,

This seems part question / part suggestion for enhancement. I've noticed that `mutate_*` verbs are now marked as superseded by `across()` and tidyselect friends. I've noticed though, that one of my use cases isn't readily met by across() where it was by `mutate_at`.

I say it's part question because perhaps the answer is that I shouldn't have been using mutate_at() in this way to begin with, so the exclusion is intentional.

Take the following example of a function where I use some quasiquotation to operate on columns that are passed un-quoted:

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

plus_one <- function(df, ...) {
  my_cols <- rlang::enquos(...)

  df <- df %>%
    mutate_at(vars(!!!my_cols), ~. + 1)
  
  return(df)
}

new_plus_one <- function(df, ...) {
    my_cols <- rlang::enquos(...)

    df <- df %>%
      mutate(across(vars(!!!my_cols), ~. + 1))
  
    return(df)
}

newer_plus_one <- function(df, ...) {
    my_cols <- rlang::enquos(...)

    df <- df %>%
      mutate(across(!!!my_cols, ~. + 1))
  
    return(df)
}

new_working_plus_one <- function(df, ...) {
    my_cols <- rlang::enquos(...)
    my_cols_str <- vapply(my_cols, rlang::as_name, character(1))

    df <- df %>%
      mutate(across(my_cols_str, ~. + 1))
  
    return(df)
}

# Works
a <- plus_one(mtcars, cyl, gear, carb)

# This fails, though, because across() doesn't seem to accept either quoted columns nor vars():
new_plus_one(mtcars, cyl, gear, carb)
#> Error: Problem with `mutate()` input `..1`.
#> i `..1 = across(vars(cyl, gear, carb), ~. + 1)`.
#> x Must subset columns with a valid subscript vector.
#> x Subscript has the wrong type `quosures`.
#> i It must be numeric or character.

# ...and so does this
newer_plus_one(mtcars, cyl, gear, carb)
#> Error: Problem with `mutate()` input `..1`.
#> i `..1 = across(cyl, gear, carb, ~. + 1)`.
#> x Problem with `across()` input `.fns`.
#> i `.fns` must be NULL, a function, a formula, or a list of functions/formulas.

# So I would do this now (though not without warning):
b <- new_working_plus_one(mtcars, cyl, gear, carb)
#> Note: Using an external vector in selections is ambiguous.
#> i Use `all_of(my_cols_str)` instead of `my_cols_str` to silence this message.
#> i See <https://tidyselect.r-lib.org/reference/faq-external-vector.html>.
#> This message is displayed once per session.

identical(a, b)
#> [1] TRUE
```

<sup>Created on 2022-01-06 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

Does this jive with your understanding of how across() should operate in this case?
If so, is there a preferred approach to handling this case under the new framework?

title: How can I handle "Can't recycle" errors on R?
description:
Out of personal curiosity, I was trying to run the code you find here below (copy-pasted from this website: _https://probabledistributions.com/2019/07/analysing-the-swedish-housing-market-in-r-part-one/_). It's a piece of code written to scrape and subsequently analyze data on the Swedish real estate market.

When trying to re-run the code, some errors pop up - presumably due to dplyr updates. Could anyone please help me re-writing the code so that it works on the most recent packages? I tried to tackle the errors in the following way:

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
**Error 1**

_Error in open.connection(x, "rb") : HTTP error 404._

**Attempted solution 1**

Change URL to updated/interested URL https://www.hemnet.se/salda/bostader?location_ids%5B%5D=18031&item_types%5B%5D=bostadsratt

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
**Error 2**

_Error: Problem with mutate() column sold_date. i sold_date = sold_date %>% gsub("såld", "", .) %>% trimws %>% date_converter. x could not find function "date_converter"_

**Attempted solution 2**

Remove lines of code creating the error (i.e. lines 30-33).

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
**Error 3**

_Error: Can't recycle ..1 (size 43) to match ..2 (size 34)._

**Attempted solution 3**

Tried to run an older version of dplyr (<1.0.0), but wasn't successful.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
My intuition tells me that there must be a way to easily run the original code without distorting it as much as I'm doing in my Attempted solutions, but I just can't wrap my head around it.

Thanks a lot for your precious help!

```r
if(!"pacman" %in% installed.packages()[,"Package"]) install.packages("pacman")

                 lubridate, gridExtra,ggsci, leaflet,htmltools)

    bind_cols %>%

get_hemnet_data(base_url = "https://www.hemnet.se/salda/bostader?page=",
                page_number = 100) -> test_scrape

test_scrape

page_max = 2000 ## we'll scrape 2k pages with 50 listings on each
page_range = 1:page_max ## range for loop

## an extra caution to not iterate in page order
scramble_page <- tibble(n = page_range, 
                          key = sample(n, length(page_range)))

base_url = "https://www.hemnet.se/salda/bostader?page="

for(i in 1:page_max){

  message("Retrieving page: ", j,
          " . Number ",i, " of ",length(page_range)) # Progress bar
  if(i == 1){
    first_pause = 0
  }else{
    first_pause = ceiling(runif(1,2,4)) 
  }
  message("Resting... ", first_pause, " seconds")
  Sys.sleep(first_pause) # Take a randomised break
  if((i %% 3) == 0){ # After every three scrapes... take another, longer, break
    sec_pause = ceiling(runif(1,3,6))
    message("Pausing a little... ", sec_pause, " seconds") 
    Sys.sleep(sec_pause) # Take another break
  }
  iter_scrape = NULL 
  possibleError <- tryCatch({
    get_hemnet_data(base_url = "https://www.hemnet.se/salda/bostader?page=",
                    page_number = j) %>% dplyr::select(-id) -> iter_scrape
    
  }
  ,
  error=function(e) {
    e
    print(paste("Error in Loop",i, ". Page:",j, ". Jumping to next page.",sep = ""))
  })
  if(is.null(iter_scrape))
    next()
  
  scrape_tbl = rbind(scrape_tbl, iter_scrape)
  print(paste("percent completed:",paste0(100*(i/length(page_range)),"%") ))
} 

scrape_tbl %>% glimpse()

title: Grouped data summarize() with zero-length value silently drops group
description:
When running summarize with a calculated summary value (`value_at_mask` in the example) drop the group rather than giving the expected error that the result must be length >= 1.  The reason for the issue below is that `value[mask]` for group 2 is zero-length.

The expected result from the call below would give an error indicating that `value_at_mask` must be length 1 or greater.

``` r
library(tidyverse)

d <-
  tibble(
    ID=1:2,
    mask=c(TRUE, FALSE),
    value=1:2
  )
d %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  summarize(
    value_min=min(value),
    value_at_mask=value[mask]
  )
#> `summarise()` has grouped output by 'ID'. You can override using the `.groups` argument.
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#> # Groups:   ID [1]
#>      ID value_min value_at_mask
#>   <int>     <int>         <int>
#> 1     1         1             1
```

title: include window_order() here
description:
I'd like to second @krlmlr 's suggestion from #5903 to include `window_order()` here in addition to `dbplyr`.  


Currently, this creates an edge case where dplyr can run on a remote connection (`tbl_sql`) but not natively in R. I realize this was intentionally created to address #2874 (regarding the use of `arrange()` on remote sources), but it feels like the converse case, support for `window_order()` in native dplyr, would also be logical.  


For example, this fails 
```r
library(tidyverse)
diamonds %>% dbplyr::window_order(cut) %>% group_by(cut) %>% summarise(m=mean(price))
```

Note too that the error message is somewhat cryptic:

```
Error in UseMethod("op_vars") : 
  no applicable method for 'op_vars' applied to an object of class "c('tbl_df', 'tbl', 'data.frame')"
```

i.e. it is not obvious that `op_vars` is being triggered by `dbplyr::window_order()` and not some other part of the pipeline.  At very least a more helpful error message (`window_order() is not defined for an object of class "c('tbl_df', 'tbl', 'data.frame'), did you mean to use arrange() instead?`) would help.  

Ideally though it seems we should be able to use `window_order` on R data.frames, as discussed in #5903.

title: Still cannot mutate a grouping column if using `across()`
description:
Hi,

Since https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/4709 and version 1.0.0, `mutate()` and `summarise()` allow modification of grouping variables, which is very useful.

However, while this works nice and clean using the standard syntax, I get an error when I try to use `across()`.

Indeed, as said in https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/5963, `?across()` tells us that:

> Because `across()` is used within functions like `summarise()` and `mutate()`, you can't select or compute upon grouping variables.

This feels a bit inconsistent, and if it is still a real limitation today (I hope not), I guess at least that the justification in the doc is inadequate.


Here is a little reprex anyway (I use the dev version of `dplyr`) :
``` r
library(tidyverse)
mtcars %>%
    head() %>% 
    group_by(cyl) %>%
    mutate(cyl=sum(cyl))
#> # A tibble: 6 x 11
#> # Groups:   cyl [3]
#>     mpg   cyl  disp    hp  drat    wt  qsec    vs    am  gear  carb

#> 6  18.1    24   225   105  2.76  3.46  20.2     1     0     3     1
mtcars %>%
    head() %>% 
    group_by(cyl) %>% #removing this line removes the error
    mutate(across(cyl, ~sum(.x)))

title: setdiff vs. setequal inconsitency when columns have different types
description:
It seems like `setequal` compares column types while `setdiff` doesn't.

```r
df1 <- data.frame(x=1)
df2 <- df1

# df1$x and df2$x are both of type `num`
setdiff(df1, df2) # --> will output 0-rowed data.frame
setequal(df1, df2) # --> will output TRUE

df2$x %<>% as.integer 

# df1$x is of type `num` while df2$x is of type `int`
setdiff(df1, df2) # --> will output 0-rowed data.frame
setequal(df1, df2) # --> will output FALSE
```

I can see how this could actually be the intended behavior. 
However, in that case a hint in the docs would be great.

title: Feature request: across2() and pacross() (new version)
description:
First, I know that implementing `pacross` as `purrr::pmap` for `purrr::map` has already been asked in issue #5703, but my idea is a bit different of what is explained there, so I will try.

After a join it is usual to get a data frame like the next.
```r
# Example data
df <- tibble(
  id   = 1:10,
  sex  = c("m", "m", "m", "f", "f", "f", "m", "f", "f", "m"),
  lds1.x= c(NA, 1, 0, 1, NA, 0, 0, NA, 0, 1),
  lds1.y = c(1, NA, 1, 1, 0, NA, 0, 3, NA, 1),
  lds2.x = c(2, 1, NA, 0, 0, NA, 1, NA, NA, 1),
  lds2.y = c(0, 2, 2, NA, NA, 0, 0, 3, 0, NA)
)
```
While the issue #5425 has not a solution, a natural next step would be
```r
df %>% 
    mutate(lds1 = coalesce(lds1.x, lds1.y), 
           lds2 = coalesce(lds2.x, lds2.y))
# A tibble: 10 x 8
      id sex   lds1.x lds1.y lds2.x lds2.y  lds1  lds2
   <int> <chr>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
 1     1 m         NA      1      2      0     1     2
 2     2 m          1     NA      1      2     1     1
 3     3 m          0      1     NA      2     0     2
 4     4 f          1      1      0     NA     1     0
 5     5 f         NA      0      0     NA     0     0
 6     6 f          0     NA     NA      0     0     0
 7     7 m          0      0      1      0     0     1
 8     8 f         NA      3     NA      3     3     3
 9     9 f          0     NA     NA      0     0     0
10    10 m          1      1      1     NA     1     1
```
It is not a problem, but if the pairs `.x`, `.y` are not only 2, but a lot, it seems that it would be better to do it programatically . It surely [I have to try yet] can be do it through the referred `purrr` functions but it would be nice to have the chance of using select helpers.

```r
df %>%
    mutate(pacross(.xcols = starts_with("lds") & ends_with(".x"),
                   .ycols = starts_with("lds") & ends_with(".y"),   
                   .names = c("lds1", "lds2"),
                    ~coalesce(.x, .y)))
```
An alternative to the option `.names`, would be to use something like `.pattern = "^lds\\d"`, with which even when the collections of columns would have not the same order (e.g. `lds1.x, lds2.x, lds2.y, lds1.y`), they would be matched by the pattern.

title: enquo with a SQL tbl
description:
The issue is using NSE with `enquo` on a `tbl` and the resulting SQL escaping does not lead to the desired result.

I'm unsure if there should be an "error" (as it is *valid SQL*) here but it led to some silent incorrect results due to escaping with a BigQuery `tbl` and using quosures.  I'm not sure if this should be in `rlang` (due to NSE) or here, but figured I'd start here.

# Setting up some random data
Here we will use some data with a column called `date`, which is the use case we ran into. 

``` r
library(bigrquery)
library(lubridate)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'lubridate'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     date, intersect, setdiff, union
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
start = as_date("2020-01-01")
dates = seq(start, start + 5, by = 1)
class(dates)
#> [1] "Date"

df = data.frame(
  date = dates,
  row = 1:length(dates), stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
```
The `df` object is a simple `data.frame` with a date column and another column (which we do not use).
```r
fields = bigrquery::as_bq_fields(as.data.frame(df))
print(fields)
#> <bq_fields>
#>   date <DATE>
#>   row <INTEGER>

ds = bq_test_dataset()
project = ds$project
dataset = ds$dataset
table = "tmp"
x = bq_table(project, dataset, table)
bq_table_create(x, fields = fields)
#> <bq_table> streamline-resources.TESTING_skvbvahxnc.tmp

con = DBI::dbConnect(
  bigrquery::bigquery(),
  project = project
)
bq_table_upload(x, values = df)
res = con %>%
  dplyr::tbl(paste0(dataset, ".", table))
res %>% 
  collect()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>   date         row
#>   <date>     <int>
#> 1 2020-01-01     1
#> 2 2020-01-02     2
#> 3 2020-01-03     3
#> 4 2020-01-04     4
#> 5 2020-01-05     5
#> 6 2020-01-06     6
```
Now the data is in `bigquery` and we can filter it.
Let's set up 2 functions, with the default of `time_field` being a string, which we will use `!!` without quosures in `filter_date`
```r
filter_date = function(data, time_field = "date") {
  out = data %>% 
    dplyr::filter(!!time_field >= "2020-01-02")
  result = out %>% show_query()
  print(result)
  out
}
```
and we will use `!!` with `enquo`.  If we use `quo`, it is the same behavior as `filter_date`
```
filter_date_enquo = function(data, time_field = "date") {
  out = data %>% 
    dplyr::filter(!!enquo(time_field) >= "2020-01-02")

title: Cannot interactively debug anymore inside mutate(across(...)) since v1.0.6
description:
Interactive debugging, using either `browser()` or RStudio breakpoints, is incredibly useful when you are not exactly sure of what you are currently doing inside `across()`.

However, there has been a breaking change recently in this feature.

```r
mtcars %>% 
    head() %>% 
    mutate(
        across(where(is.numeric), ~{
            print(.x)
            #browser()
            .x*2
        })
    )
```

When you run this code, the output is fine, both prints and results.

However, if you uncomment the `browser()` command and then ask for the value of `.x`, it will throw the following: `"Error: object '.x' not found"`. This means that interactive debugging is now unusable.

Reverting to `devtools::install_version("dplyr", "1.0.5")` solves the problem.

title: group_by() row order different when testing
description:
I'm having an issue where some tests are failing unexpectedly because the row order of a tibble during tests is different to when code is run interactively, where the code involves a `group_by() %>% summarise()`. Steps to create the problem:
* create a new package
* put the function `func()` as below into an R file
```r
func <- function(){
  tib <- tibble::tibble(name = c("b", "b", "A", "C", "A", "C"),
                        value1 = 1:6,
                        value2 = 3:8)

  tib %>%
    dplyr::group_by(name) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(sum1 = sum(value1),
                     sum2 = sum(value2))
}
```
* put the test as below into corresponding test file
```r
test_that("func output", {
  funcOutput <- func()
  expect_equal(tibble::tibble(name = c("A", "b", "C"),
                              sum1 = c(8, 3, 10),
                              sum2 = c(12, 7, 14)),
                funcOutput)
})

The issue appears to be that the sorting of the groups is putting lower-case group items below upper-case ones during tests, but otherwise sorting them alphabetically. title: data.frame attributes are preserved on `mutate()` but dropped on `group_by |> mutate`
description:
Reprex:
``` r
library(dplyr)
#>
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#>
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#>
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(purrr)
attr(mtcars, "test") <- "foo"
mtcars_grouped <- group_by(mtcars, cyl)

mtcars |>
  mutate(new_col = 1) |>
  attributes() |>
  pluck("test")
#> [1] "foo"

mtcars_grouped |>
  mutate(new_col = 1) |>
  attributes() |>
  pluck("test")
#> NULL

mtcars_grouped |>
  mutate(across(where(is.complex), as.character)) |>
  attributes() |>
  pluck("test")
#> NULL
# did nothing but still lost attrs on the base data.frame
```

It would be better if no attributes were lost with mutate. Feels weird in the last case where no mutate actually gets done.

However if `group_by() |> mutate()` must drop attributes, it's probably better that `mutate` does also. You can easily get tricked into thinking some code is going to work, but then it bombs when it accidentally gets passed some sticky groups. This happened to me today, 4 levels of package context up from where the mutate was.

title: `bind_rows()` strips out columns' "custom" attributes
description:
When I have two tibbles containing columns with "custom" attributes, they are stripped out during `bind_rows()`. Note that conventional attributes such as levels or class are retained as expected. I suspect that the issue lies in `dplyr_reconstruct()` phase, because the template is OK, but the function does not care about _column_ attributes at all:

``` r
library(tidyverse)

b <- a <- tibble(a = factor(letters[1:3]))

attr(b$a, "my_attr") <- attr(a$a, "my_attr") <- "don't loose this"

# those are OK

#>

#>

# where is my attribute?
bind_rows(a, b) %>% map(attributes)

title: bind_rows: allow coercion to type x when column is all NA's
description:
I am currently collecting data across well formatted xlsx files.

For a given numerical column some of these files only missing values, where as other files have numeric data in these.

The files with only missing values have this column set to character (because read_xlsx cannot know better), while for other files they correctly get the numeric or double type.

This gives me a problem when I try to bind_rows, as it stops with the error message that it can't combine character and double.

Could it be considered safe to coerce type when one side (either the exising data or the new data to be combined with existing data), is all NA's? Since it is very reasonable that that column originally was another type that was turned to NA with the input function used to read it?

In my particular case (biotech, reading data files from lab), I am dealing with 60 or so files, with 130 or so columns each.
I iteratively have to solve my problem one column at a time. For each column that triggers the above error, I have to add it to a list of columns that needs to be cast to numeric before-hand (even if they are all NA's), and then I retry bind_rows.

I am contemplating writing a function that will read all the files into a list of tibbles, check each column found in any one frame, check if it exists only as character, and if so all NA's, or at most as one other class in the set. A quite laborous and complex thing to do for something that could be available in a much simpler implementation as an option or even as default behaviour in bidn_rows perhaps?

title: Unexpected behavior of `{{ var }}` if variable name is declared in multiple namespaces
description:
The `{{ var }}` (curly-curly operator) behaves strangely when the variable name is used multiple times in different namespaces.

1. a global variable, which is passed to the function
2. a variable in function scope
3. a column in the data.frame
4. the variable is not referenced beforehand in the function

---

The following output shows that it depends on how you name the variable that is iterated over in the uppermost namespace.
If everythings works as expected, the output would always be `1` for 2015 and `100` vor 2016. But if I use the variablename `year` in the for-loop AND do not reference the function variable `year` beforehand, the curly-operator seems to compare the column `year` to itself, which is always `TRUE` -> Thus, using all rows in the dataset to calculate the mean of `50.5` instead of `1` or `100`

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

d <- list(year=c(2015,2015,2016,2016), val=c(1,1,100,100))
df <- as.data.frame(d)

years = c(2015, 2016)

calc_mean_curly <- function(df, year) {
  subdf <- df %>% filter(year == {{ year }})
  mean(subdf$val)
}

calc_mean_exclamation <- function(df, year) {
  subdf <- df %>% filter(year == !!year)
  mean(subdf$val)
}

calc_mean_curly_ref_first <- function(df, year) {
  year
  subdf <- df %>% filter(year == {{ year }})
  mean(subdf$val)
}

# strange namespace conflict?
for (year in years) {
  cat("YEAR: ", year, "\n")
  print(paste("curly =", calc_mean_curly(df, year)))
  print(paste("exclamation =", calc_mean_exclamation(df, year)))
  print(paste("curly, ref first =", calc_mean_curly_ref_first(df, year)))
}
#> YEAR:  2015 
#> [1] "curly = 50.5"
#> [1] "exclamation = 1"
#> [1] "curly, ref first = 1"
#> YEAR:  2016 
#> [1] "curly = 50.5"
#> [1] "exclamation = 100"
#> [1] "curly, ref first = 100"

# works fine
for (y in years) {
  cat("YEAR: ", y, "\n")
  print(paste("curly =", calc_mean_curly(df, y)))
  print(paste("exclamation =", calc_mean_exclamation(df, y)))
  print(paste("curly, ref first =", calc_mean_curly_ref_first(df, y)))
}
#> YEAR:  2015 
#> [1] "curly = 1"
#> [1] "exclamation = 1"
#> [1] "curly, ref first = 1"
#> YEAR:  2016 
#> [1] "curly = 100"
#> [1] "exclamation = 100"
#> [1] "curly, ref first = 100"
```

title: Opened in error
Error when using glue() in across() with lambda function (.x not found)
description:
Hi,

I came across this very specific bug today. I'm not sure whether it belongs to `glue`, to `dplyr` or to `rlang`. 

I'm guessing it's a matter of environment in `glue`, but don't hesitate to move this issue to a more appropriate place. 

If you use `glue()` in `mutate(across(...))` using a purrr-style lambda function, you get an error saying that `.x` is not found. However, if you use a regular function, there is no error.

library(glue)

mutate(iris, across(starts_with("Petal."),

mutate(iris, across(starts_with("Petal."),
                    function(.x)ifelse(.x>2, "", glue("{.x} (>2)")))) %>% head(1)

title: Unexpected behaviour of missing `{{var}}` in `across()`, `arrange()`, `group_by()`, etc.
description:
When used without tidyeval, `across()`, `arrange()`, `group_by()` can execute without a problem even if no arguments are passed to them. One would expect the same behavior with tidyeval, but this is not the case. Reprex below (also note that in the case of `arrange()`, the error messages are different in the two function calls, and it seems inconsistent):

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))

dat <- tibble(x = 1, y = 1)

f1 <- function(.data, order_by) {
  .data %>%
    arrange({{order_by}})
}

f2 <- function(.data, order_by) {
  .data %>%
    arrange(across({{order_by}}))
}

g1 <- function(.data, group_by) {
  .data %>%
    group_by({{group_by}})
}

g2 <- function(.data, group_by) {
  .data %>%
    group_by(across({{group_by}}))
}

dat %>% # works fine
  arrange()
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>       x     y
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     1

dat %>% # works fine
  arrange(across())
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>       x     y
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     1

dat %>% # works fine
  group_by()
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>       x     y
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     1

dat %>% # works fine
  group_by(across())
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#> # Groups:   x, y [1]
#>       x     y
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     1

dat %>% # does not work
  f1()
#> Error in mapply(.f, .x, .y, MoreArgs = list(...), SIMPLIFY = FALSE): zero-length inputs cannot be mixed with those of non-zero length

dat %>% # does not work
  f2()
#> Error in order(vec_order(proxy, direction = direction, na_value = if (desc) "smallest" else "largest")): argument 1 is not a vector

dat %>% # does not work
  g1()
#> Error in group_by(., {: argument "group_by" is missing, with no default

dat %>% # does not work
  g2()
#> Error in group_by(., across({: argument "group_by" is missing, with no default
```

title: Separate `transmute()` from `mutate(.keep = "none")`
description:
In #6035 we reworked `.keep` to be more consistent for `mutate()`. I still stand by this decision in the context of `mutate()`, but this has changed the behavior of `transmute()`, since that is currently `mutate(.keep = "none")`. Here is a good example that shows the change in behavior for both group-vars and modified non-group vars.

```r
library(dplyr)

df <- tibble(
  g1 = 1:3,
  g2 = 1:3,
  x = 1:3,
  y = 4:6
)

gdf <- group_by(df, g1, g2)

transmute(gdf, x = x + 1, z = x + 1, y = y + 1, g1 = g1 + 1)

# CRAN:
# - The column order supplied in `...` is kept.
# - Grouping vars not modified by `...` are kept at the front.

#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#> # Groups:   g1, g2 [3]
#>      g2     x     z     y    g1
#>   <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     2     3     5     2
#> 2     2     3     4     6     3
#> 3     3     4     5     7     4

# Current dev:
# The column ordering comes from:
# - Modified columns are altered in place
# - New columns are added at the end

#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#> # Groups:   g1, g2 [3]
#>      g1    g2     x     y     z
#>   <dbl> <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     2     1     2     5     3
#> 2     3     2     3     6     4
#> 3     4     3     4     7     5
```

It turns out that many people want `transmute()` to keep the current CRAN behavior because they use it for mixed selection and mutation and expect a specific column ordering from it.
- See https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6080#issuecomment-970170216
- See https://github.com/privefl/bigsnpr/pull/274#discussion_r749363632

We previously believed that `transmute()` had swapped between these two outputs over various dplyr releases, but this was actually not true, as seen in https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/6080#issuecomment-970433326. The current CRAN behavior has always been how `transmute()` works. In light of this, we believe we should retain the CRAN behavior of `transmute()` for the next dplyr release.

That said, `mutate(.keep = "none")` should retain its current dev behavior. This is an experimental argument, so changing it should not affect too many users. The dev behavior of `.keep = "none"` is overall more consistent with the rest of the `mutate()` options, makes it easier to predict the output when combined with `.before` and `.after`, and simplifies the implementation because it means that `.keep` never affects the column ordering, it is mainly about which columns get dropped (#6035 goes into this in great detail).

So, the action items are:
- Fix `transmute()` to revert to the CRAN behavior, which requires giving it its own implementation separate from `mutate()`
- Update the NEWS bullet to only mention the change in `.keep`
- Separate any comparison of `transmute()` and `.keep = "none"` in the documentation, making it clear how those are different

title: `mutate()` > `dplyr_col_select()`
description:
With the change in https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/pull/6035, `mutate.data.frame()` always end up calling `dplyr_col_select(out, cols_retain)` when before it did not in the `keep == "all"` case. 

I think it is better, however I believe this is what is breaking `fable tools` and then `fable` because: 

``` r
fabletools:::`[.mdl_df`
#> function (x, i, j, drop = FALSE) 
#> {
#>     out <- as_tibble(NextMethod())
#>     cn <- colnames(out)
#>     kv <- intersect(key_vars(x), cn)
#>     mv <- intersect(mable_vars(x), cn)
#>     if (n_keys(x) != length(kv)) {
#>         return(out)
#>     }
#>     build_mable(out, key = !!kv, model = !!mv)
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x7fe1da9332a8>
#> <environment: namespace:fabletools>
```

<sup>Created on 2021-11-15 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1.9000)</sup>

Because of this, `mutate.data.frame()` might return a `tibble` now, but used to return a `mdl_df` before. A workaround might be to do: `dplyr_reconstruct(dplyr_col_select(out, cols_retain), .data)` but it otherwise feel like this should be fixed in fabletools:::`[.mdl_df`. 

cc @DavisVaughan

title: Allow `.keep` in mutate() to support tidy selection
description:
Simplified example:

library(dplyr)

transmute_keep <- function(df, ..., .select){

# To keep simple am not including `.before` and `.after` args
mutate_keep <- function(df, ..., .keep = c("all", "used", "unused", "none")){

title: Chaining gsub() operations inside across gives warnings and incorrect output when using "~" notation, but correct output when using function(x) { } notation
description:
I'm trying to write a function that chains multiple `gsub()` operations on a single vector of values and uses `across` to operate on multiple columns. This works fine when I use an explicit anonymous function (i.e., `function(x) {...}`) inside `across`, but gives incorrect output when using the `~` notation to begin the function. I'm not sure if this is a bug or if I'm doing something wrong; I'm reporting it here in case it is a bug. Below is a reproducible example.

``` r
library(tidyverse)

d = tibble(a=LETTERS, b=letters, c=1:26)
```
Mutating with explicit anonymous function gives expected output
```
d %>% 
  mutate(across(matches("[ab]"),
                function(x) { 
                  gsub("[ABC]", "xyz", x) %>% 
                    gsub("([de]).*", "uvw", .)
                }))
#> # A tibble: 26 × 3
#>    a     b         c
#>    <chr> <chr> <int>
#>  1 xyz   a         1

#>  7 G     g         7
#>  8 H     h         8
#>  9 I     i         9

<sup>Created on 2021-11-06 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v1.0.0)</sup>

Partly I suppose because I'm expecting it to behave in the same way as `head()`.

When looking at the documentation, it looks like the idea is to force the user to choose between `n` and `prop`. One downside is that, when looking at the function definition, a user might think that both are required. 
``` r
slice_head(.data, ..., n, prop)
```
The other downside is that it might make the function harder to reason about. What happens if both `n` and `prop` are provided? At the moment it seems that `prop` gets silently ignored:

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = F)

mtcars %>% 
  head(n = 1, prop = 0.99)
#>           mpg cyl disp  hp drat   wt  qsec vs am gear carb
#> Mazda RX4  21   6  160 110  3.9 2.62 16.46  0  1    4    4
```

<sup>Created on 2021-11-06 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v1.0.0)</sup>

This seems similar to the [situation with `forecats::fct_lump()`](https://design.tidyverse.org/args-independence.html#cs-fct-lump). In that case, the solution would be to have new functions as follows:

``` r
slice_head_n(.data, n, ...)
slice_head_prop(.data, prop, ...)
slice_tail_n(.data, n, ...)
slice_tail_prop(.data, prop, ...)
```
These would make it clear what the intent of the function is. The arguments would all be required and so easy to reason about and there would be less chance of accidentally passing arguments to the dots. 

One downside of changing the arguments is it might complicate translations in dplyr's extensions. I'm not sure what the implications of that would be.
