title: Include example of using a data frame in `mutate()`
description:
From https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/5494#issuecomment-679990205:

> You can already do that in dplyr, just by returning a data frame:
> 
> ```
> library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
> 
> df <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 2)
> 
> my_f <- function(x) {
>   data.frame(x1 = x + 1, x2 = x * 2)
> }
> df %>% mutate(my_f(x))
> #>   x y x1 x2
> #> 1 1 2  2  2
> ```
> 
> Created on 2020-08-25 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0.9001)

I'm one of today's [lucky 10,000](https://xkcd.com/1053/). I've been using `dplyr` heavily for many years, and for some reason never knew that it was feasible (even desirable) to use unnamed expressions in `mutate`. I think this is one of the more under-sold capabilities of `mutate` and `summarize`. This was in response to a [SO comment](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/66763386/daily-correlation-in-r/66763782?noredirect=1#comment118019219_66763782).

I think it's absolutely useful to know that this works:

```r
mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  summarize(as.data.frame(cor.test(disp,hp)[c("estimate","p.value")]))
# # A tibble: 3 x 3
#     cyl estimate p.value
# * <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>
# 1     4    0.435   0.182
# 2     6   -0.514   0.238
# 3     8    0.118   0.687
```

And while it might seem obvious to some, I cannot find reference to this method in `?mutate` or any of the package `.Rd` files. (It *is* used in several of the tests.)

I can provide a PR, is there interest in adding a mention to this in `mutate` and `summarize` help docs?

title: `if_else()` only gives an error for inconsistent lengths of the first problematic argument
description:
In the following code, `if_else()` gives an error only indicating a problem for `true`, when `false` is also inconsistent with the length of `condition`.
``` r
dplyr::if_else(logical(3), true = character(2), false = character(4))
#> Error: `true` must be length 3 (length of `condition`) or one, not 2.
```
<sup>Created on 2021-03-22 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v1.0.0)</sup>

A user who came across this issue may have to run their code, fix the issue with `true`, and run the code again before discovering the issue with `false` (and this whole process again if `missing` is also inconsistent).

This issue occurs because each replacement's length is checked in `replace_with()`. If an extra step was added within `if_else()`, the lengths of `true`, `false`, and `missing` could be checked all at once. This would more closely match the behavior of `case_when()`, which uses `validate_case_when_length()` to report the lengths of all inconsistent conditions at the same time.

I'd be happy to submit a PR if this would be beneficial.

title: row_number() function needs to describe intended use case
description:
The primary use of `row_number()` is to get the current row's number in a data frame or tibble. This view is reinforced by books (e.g., https://www.tidytextmining.com/tidytext.html), a search on Github (e.g., https://github.com/search?l=R&q=%22row_number%22&type=Code), and the function's own name.

I propose putting `row_number()`'s into its own documentation page. The new page should focus on the function's intended use.

While `row_number()` may be implemented as a ranking function, that is an implementation detail. Since the intent of `row_number()` is not to rank vectors, examples demonstrating its use as a vector-ranker should be omitted. Those who are interested in these kinds of implementation details would be best served inspecting `row_number()`'s code.

title: rowSums on grouped data very slow when many groups
description:
rowwise operation, e.g., rowSums, is super slow when performed on grouped data with many many groups. It may be worth to internally `ungroup` first before performing the actual computation?  


``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'

#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#>

set.seed(42)
id <- as.character(round(rnorm(250000), 6))
tf <- c(TRUE, FALSE)
a <- sample(tf, 250000, replace = T)
b <- sample(tf, 250000, replace = T)
foo <- data.frame(id, a, b) %>% group_by(id)

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
grouped = foo %>%
  mutate(sum = rowSums(across(.funs = as.integer))),

title: Suggestion: concise switch-style case function implementation
description:
Brief description of the **suggestion**:

In many languages, there is a `case_when`-like conditional clause. Instead of requiring a full Boolean condition and output pair, it accepts a single input like `inputValue`. Each condition thereafter is assumed to be an exact match or "fall-through" case. 

It has a number of forms depending on the language:

- **SAS:**  `select-when`
- **SQL:** (some flavors)  `case var when comparator then`
- **Java** and **C++**: similar to `switch`

From SAS and SQL, this function is a nice was to create mutually exclusive categories with the first matching condition to output just like `case_when`.  In C++/Java this is a programmatic flow command more comparable to `if` than `if_else` or `case_when`. 

Here is a `case_when` as dplyr currently handles this situation, and the more parsimonious `switch-case` style statement. 

**dplyr `case_when`**
```r
inputObject <- tibble( shape = c( 'triangle', 'trapezoid', 'hexagon', 'pentagon', 'square', 'rectangle') )

inputObject %>%
mutate( vertices = case_when( shape == "triangle" ~ 3,
shape %in% c( 'square', 'rhombus', 'rectangle', 'parallelogram', 'trapezoid', 'quadrilateral') ~ 4,
shape == 'pentagon' ~ 5, 
shape == 'hexagon' ~ 6 ) )
```

**SQL `case` secondary implementation**
In some implementations of SQL there are two forms of the `CASE` statement. One is testing a specific variables against possible values (what I am suggesting to add to dplyr) and the other is arbitrary Boolean statements.  Here these two styles are described in the TERADATA SQL documentation [Using CASE Expressions to Optimize Query Design](https://docs.teradata.com/r/kmuOwjp1zEYg98JsB8fu_A/LMPRZogKY199S9IXIdCBOQ)
```sql

SELECT CASE shape 
WHEN 'triangle' THEN 3
WHEN 'square' THEN 4
WHEN 'pentagon' THEN 5
...
WHEN 'octagon' THEN 8 END as vertices
FROM inputObject;
```


**Suggested `switch` (loosely based on C++/Java)**
```c++
inputObject %>%
mutate( vertices = switch( shape,
case 'triangle': 3, 
case 'square':
case 'rhombus':
case 'rectangle':
case 'parallelogram':
case 'trapezoid':
case 'quadrilateral': 4,
case 'pentagon': 5
case 'hexagon': 6) )
```


This could even be further condensed and with tildes to be more stylistically similar: 

```r
inputObject %>%
mutate( vertices = switch( shape,
case 'triangle' ~ 3, 
case c( 'square', 'rhombus', 'rectangle', 'parallelogram', 'trapezoid', 'quadrilateral') ~ 4,
case 'pentagon' ~ 5,
case 'hexagon' ~ 6,
default ~ 9) )
```

It is still a case_when in form and function, the only difference being that it assumes an equal sign or an %in% relationship between the first parameter and the ... case-statements which then result in the value output. Switches are nice for recoding itemized questionnaires and Likert scales. 

**SAS style `SELECT-WHEN`**
SAS syntax uses SELECT-WHEN in its data step programming to handle these situations. 

Example pulled from SAS blog: [https://blogs.sas.com/content/iml/2016/06/20/select-when-sas-data-step.html](https://blogs.sas.com/content/iml/2016/06/20/select-when-sas-data-step.html)

```sas
/* example of using the SELECT statement */
data Heart / view=Heart;
set sashelp.heart;
select (Smoking_Status);
   when ('Non-smoker')        Smoking_Cat=1;
   when ('Light (1-5)')       Smoking_Cat=2;
   when ('Moderate (6-15)')   Smoking_Cat=3;
   when ('Heavy (16-25)')     Smoking_Cat=4;
   when ('Very Heavy (> 25)') Smoking_Cat=5;
   otherwise                  Smoking_Cat=.;
end;
run;
```




**Numeric Data in Switches:**
There is a language (maybe Java?) that additionally handles ranges when a switch is used with numeric types (and can conceivably be used with any numeric-like format such as dates). There is a caveat with numeric types that the -Inf and Inf ends would need to be used, and to avoid inclusion, exclusion, ambiguous, a direction of such as 40 - <50 years of age, 50 - <60 years. That would look something like this:

_Integer Example_
```r
inputTable <- tibble( inputAge = c( 6, 57, 83, 12, 15 ) )

inputTable %>%
mutate( ageCategory = switch( inputAge,
case -Inf - 17: Child,
case 18 - 65: Adult,
case 66 - Inf: Senior) )
```

_Real Example_
The problem with real numbers is knowing which side of the interval is inclusive and which is exclusive. A parameter **inclusivity** which specifies left or right can handle the continuity problem with real numbers instead of discrete integers as above. 
```r
expectantMoms <- tibble( daysFromConception = c( 6, 57, 83, 12, 15 ) )

expectantMoms %>%
mutate( trimester= switch( daysFromConception %/% 7, inclusivity = "left", 
case 0:13: 1,
case 13:24: 2,
case 24:Inf: 3 ) )
```


**Dates, Intervals, and other Numeric-like types**
```r

tblDates <- tibble( inputDate = c( 2021-01-06, 2021-03-10, 2021-04-01, 2021-11-09) )

tblDates %>%
mutate( season2021 = switch( inputDate, 
case intervalSpring:
case ymd_hms( 2021-03-20 05:37:00 ) [syntax tbd maybe : colon or - dash] ymd_hms( 2021-06-20 23:31:59 ): 
"Spring",

case intervalSummer:
case ymd_hms( 2021-06-20 23:32:00 ) : ymd_hms( 2021-09-22 15:20:59):
"Summer",

case intervalFall:
case ymd_hms( 2021-09-22 15:21:00 ) : ymd_hms( 2021-12-21 10:58:59):
"Fall",

case intervalWinter:
case ymd_hms( 2021-12-21 10:59:00 ) : ymd_hms( 2021-09-22 15:20:59):
"Winter") )
```

title: Add slice_min_max (complementing slice_min and slice_max)
description:
Hi,

I come with a minor feature request for convenience with a possible implementation: 

Have you considered worth having a `slice_min_max` function to complement `slice_min` and `slice_max`?

I find `slice_min_max()` function convenient to explore the most extreme values of a variable and apparently I'm not alone, since I also found an implementation of `slice_min_max` at Shona Wilde's  ["personal functions package"](https://github.com/shonawilde/shonarrr/blob/master/R/slice_min_max.R) (and we chose the same function name!).

Here is a suggestion of what could be added to the documentation of `slice.R` and a simple implementation.:

```r
#' * `slice_head()` and `slice_tail()` select the first or last rows.
#' * `slice_sample()` randomly selects rows.
#' * `slice_min()` and `slice_max()` select rows with highest or lowest values
#'   of a variable.
#' * `slice_min_max()` combines the respective outputs of `slice_min()` and `slice_max()`, returning `2*n` rows.

slice_min_max <- function(...) {
  bind_rows(
    slice_min(...),
    slice_max(...)
  )
}

```

I could provide a pull request adding that function, if you agree. (And a similar approach could be used on `slice_head_tail()`). Otherwise feel free to close this issue. :+1:  I'll keep using that function on my scripts.

Thanks for your time

title: names when joining multiple data frames
description:
When joining multiple data frames getting good names nicely is surprisingly
involved code-wise.  The code below adds the data frame name as a suffix to 
each column except the columns joined by.

That isn't too bad but if we wanted to only put the data frame names as suffixes 
on those columns whose name actually appears in more than one data frame  
(as opposed to every column except the ones joined by) then it would 
involve substantially more code.  (In the example below that means that 
instead of var2.c being the column name that that column
would have the name var2 since the name var2 occurs only once among the 3 data frames.)
See https://stackoverflow.com/questions/66461873/use-dataframe-name-as-suffix-when-joining-several-data-frames/66463627#66463627
for several solutions and note how much code there is.

Some feature that would make this easier would be nice to have.

```R
# This suffixes each column's data frame name to that column's 
# name (except id) seems. It more complex than desirable but if we
# were to add the requirement that columns that appear just
# once among the three data frames not be suffixed then it
# would get even more involved code-wise.

library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(tibble)

a <- tibble(id = 1:5, var=letters[1:5])
b <- tibble(var=letters[11:15], id=1:5)
c <- tibble(id = 1:5, var=letters[16:20], var2="a")

# join a, b &  c adding originating data frame name as suffix except for id
lst(a, b, c) %>%
  map2(names(.), ~ rename_with(.x, function(x) paste(x, .y, sep = "."), -id)) %>%
  reduce(left_join, by = "id")
```
giving:
```
# A tibble: 5 x 5
     id var.a var.b var.c var2.c
  <int> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> 
1     1 a     k     p     a     
2     2 b     l     q     a     
3     3 c     m     r     a     
4     4 d     n     s     a     
5     5 e     o     t     a     
```

title: group_by failing on columns without an order relation (e.g. complex numbers)
description:
Consider this simple example where a `data.frame` is grouped by a variable which is a complex number:
```r
data.frame(g = complex(real = c(1, 1, 2, 2), 
                       imaginary = c(5, 5, 6, 7)),
           d = 1:4) %>% 
    group_by(g)
```
It result in an error:
```
rlang::last_trace()
<error/rlang_error>
Invalid type returned by `vec_proxy_compare()`.
Backtrace:
    █
 1. ├─`%>%`(...)
 2. ├─dplyr::group_by(., g)
 3. └─dplyr:::group_by.data.frame(., g)
 4.   └─dplyr::grouped_df(groups$data, groups$group_names, .drop)
 5.     └─dplyr:::compute_groups(data, vars, drop = drop)
 6.       └─dplyr:::vec_split_id_order(group_vars)
 7.         ├─vctrs::vec_slice(split_id, vec_order(as.data.frame(split_id$key)))
 8.         └─vctrs::vec_order(as.data.frame(split_id$key))
 9.           └─vctrs:::order_proxy(...)
```

I presume that the problem arises from the code trying to call `vctrs::vec_proxy_compare` on a data type without `<`, `<=` (order) relation.
In my opinion grouping operation should be possible on any type with a `==` (equivalence relation in the mathematical sense) defined. `==` is much more general and easier to define than `<`.
Ordering of the grouping variable, while often useful, is not crucial for most grouping purposes.

PS. Base R `order` is defined for `complex` type.

title: %notin% operator implementation
description:
The negation of `%in%` operator is something very handy that allows a clear and concise syntax, however it is missing on base R.

Would you consider implement that in `dplyr`?

[tidytable package](https://github.com/markfairbanks/tidytable) implemented it and can also be created with simply ``` `%notin%`  <- base::Negate(`%in%`) ```.

Nonetheless, it would be far easier and more suitable to have `%notin%` natively loaded together with `dplyr` or `tidyverse`.

Thank you

title: appending classes to date variables makes summarise fail
description:
If you append a class to Date variables and then try to summarise them the code fails with the error below. It is interesting because you can append the new class you want to work with in front of the date class and the summarise will work fine.  However, if you append the new class to the end the below code does not work. This is relevant because I was trying to determine if adding new classes to a variable would interfere with other R functions. Additionally the logic below seems inconsistent in the fact that order shouldn't matter if the new class was before or after the original date class. 

```R
library(dplyr)
packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '1.0.4'

# data frame with date column
df_date <- data.frame(dates = rep_len(Sys.Date(), 5))

# this works
df_date %>%
  dplyr::summarise_at(vars(dates), min)
#>        dates
#> 1 2021-02-27

# adding another class to the column, and the summarize still works
class(df_date$dates)
#> [1] "Date"
class(df_date$dates) <- c("not_a_class", "Date")
df_date %>%
  dplyr::summarise_at(vars(dates), min)
#>        dates
#> 1 2021-02-27

# put the fake class at the end, and the min() fn works and summarise fails
class(df_date$dates) <- c("Date", "not_a_class")
min(df_date$dates)
#> [1] "2021-02-27"
df_date %>%
  dplyr::summarise_at(vars(dates), min)
# Error: Problem with `summarise()` input `dates`.
# x `vec_cast.Date.Date()` is implemented at C level.
# This R function is purely indicative and should never be called.
# i Input `dates` is `.Primitive("min")(dates)`.
# Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.
```

title: Should the across help file also cater to the 'apply to dataframe` use case?
description:
I had difficulty with compactly expressing a mutate that wanted the result column to be a function of several input columns, to be selected via tidy select.

Eventually @jennybc linked me to: https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/rowwise.html#row-wise-summary-functions

Which demonstrated I can do something fairly clean like this:

```r
col_prod2 <- function(.df) {​​​​​
    .df %>%
      reduce(.f = `*`)
  }​​​​​

risk_matrix %>%
  mutate(interest_level = col_prod2(across(ends_with("level"))))
```

`across` was the first thing I looked at, but the help file is geared entirely to the `apply to each column` usecase, which was enough to convince me to stop investigating it. Maybe the help file should contain an example from the linked vignette?

title: dplyr 1.0.4 introduces grouping bug
description:
Dplyr is exhibiting strange, non-deterministic behavior on version 1.0.4. In the example below, running the first pipe causes the second one to error, whereas if you start with the second one it runs without error. From what I can tell, the error is because something is remembering the grouping of the first pipe, and when the second pipe has a different number of groups, it causes an error. This is only present when I use both a non-across step in mutate (using the `n()` function) and an `across` step.

I have tested this on dplyr 1.0.3 and do not experience the same error.

---


```r
library(dplyr)

mtcars %>% filter(cyl>=6) %>% 
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  mutate(num=n(),
         across(carb, ~.x*10))

mtcars %>% filter(cyl<6) %>% 
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  mutate(num=n(),
         across(carb, ~.x*10))
```

title: Should num_range select helper work together with e.g. ends_with or get an additional argument "suffix = "?
description:
I was just puzzled when I tried to select certain columns of my data frame that a) start with a letter, followed by a number (for which the `num_range` helper would be ideal) and b) also end with a certain string, e.g. "_rec" (for which `ends_with` would be perfect).

However, using this approach, a data frame with 0 columns is returned. I guess that num_range is only suited for full matches, however the help function doesn't say a word about it and I also think num_range would benefit from an option to not only add a prefix, but also a suffix.

```
# Data
df <- data.frame(x1 = c(1, 2),
                 x2 = c(3, 4),
                 x3 = c(5, 6),
                 x4y = c(7, 8),
                 x1_rec = c(9, 10),
                 x2_rec = c(11, 12),
                 x4y_rec = c(13, 14))

#   x1 x2 x3 x4y x1_rec x2_rec x4y_rec
# 1  1  3  5   7      9     11      13
# 2  2  4  6   8     10     12      14

# Code that should work, but doesn't
df %>% select(num_range("x", 1:2) & ends_with("_rec"))

# data frame with 0 columns and 2 rows

# Expected output
#   x1_rec x2_rec
# 1      9     11
# 2     10     12
```

What I could imagine is really just an extension of the num_range function, e.g.:
```

num_range(prefix = "x",
          range = 1:2,
          suffix = "_rec")
```

title: Error: Internal error in `vec_slice_impl()`: Unexpected `NULL`
description:
This is a similar issue to that raised by https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/5189 that @hadley closed.  Since that issue didn't have a reprex, and this is an issue which didn't previously exist using this code with this API, I think it's worth another look.

@DavisVaughan replied here that advising the API to fix the NULL might be one course of action https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/5189#issuecomment-625444956

This is previously functional code that now seems to throw an error when an API provides variables that are read as NULL, as I can no longer use bind_rows to move from a list to a data frame. Previous iterations of this code worked fine, so not sure what the change is - as far as I can tell, the API was not altered from previous versions. The last time I know for sure that this code ran without this error was early 2019, and I am only just revisiting it now for a new project.

A quick reproduction of the error:

---
```r

library(httr)
library(tidyverse)
#reproducible example with a form from Kent Marketing Petroleum Survey
# The code is used recursively build the set of feasible options in a series of drop-down menus from 
 https://charting.kentgroupltd.com/

kent_report_types<-function(product_id=1){
  # for testing, use product_id=1
  #product_id=1
  #For Each Product ID, get a report type
  #Product Report Types
  report_types<-content(POST(
    url = "https://charting.kentgroupltd.com/Charting/GetReportTypes",
      query = list(
      ProductID= product_id
    )
  ))
  
  #what I used to be able to do and would like to be able to do again
  #report_types %>% bind_rows() %>% filter(Value!=0)
  
  #now, that creates this error
#> report_types %>% bind_rows() %>% filter(Value!=0)
#Error: Internal error in `vec_slice_impl()`: Unexpected `NULL`.
# Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.

  # what I have to do now to work around it
  text<-sapply(report_types, function(x) x[[4]])
  value<-sapply(report_types, function(x) x[[5]])
  report_types<-tibble(text,value) %>% filter(value!=0) %>% mutate(product_id=product_id)
  report_types
}

#run the function
kent_report_types(1)
```

As far as I can tell, the API has not changed from when I wrote the original version of this code using bind_rows, but the API definitely sends a NULL variable:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/30224429/107549691-5ffe6380-6b8d-11eb-824b-9fd56f6c63c0.png)

I'd welcome any suggestions of a better work-around or a way to omit the NULL types from the list at reading.

title: add Bayesian option to slice_sample? (possible new feature)
description:
`slice_sample` is an effective way to bootstrap samples, both individually and in blocks when used in connection with `group_by`.

However, one of the most common misconception of bootstrapped samples, particularly when used to form intervals, is that they somehow represent probabilities, which they usually don't. However, there is often no good reason _not_ to output probabilities when you can, particularly given the frequent similarity in results and the reality that you might as well give readers what they want.

This is easily done using the Bayesian version of the bootstrap and it requires only 1-2 lines of additional code that would assign and normalize positive numbers to form a Dirichlet distribution over the rows of the existing sample, which is then sampled from with replacement treating the normalized positive numbers as weights. Because the Dirichlet forms a prior distribution, we end up with a true distribution and resulting probabilities.

As suggested [here](https://www.baseballprospectus.com/news/article/64534/an-updated-system-of-park-factors-and-volatility/), we can perform a Bayesian sample with `slice_sample` by adding code like this:
``` 
df.2<- df.1 %>%
        dplyr::mutate(
### generate random positive weights ###
           exp_rand = rexp(nrow(df.1), 1),
### normalize to a Dirichlet distribution ###
           samp_weights = exp_rand / sum(exp_rand)) %>%
### sample from the new Dirichlet, with replacement ###
        dplyr::slice_sample(., prop = 1, 
                          weight_by=samp_weights, 
                          replace=TRUE)
```
The additional normalization is arguably unnecessary since I believe `slice_sample` normalizes anyway, but it's good to show your work.

Although this is simple enough to add by hand, I suspect it something many users will be afraid to code or even be aware of themselves, and having a flag available inside the function like `Bayesian = TRUE`  would probably be much easier for them.

Just a suggestion.

title: Preservation of NULL row names adds work to mutate/summarize pipes
description:
I feel a common unit of work is to group by a categorical variable, calculate a summary measure on the continuous variables, then change the grouping variable to row names so that the data frame is entirely numeric (for some other downstream analyses). Possibly because of #5503 this workflow now requires an additional unit of work in reprex below.

I expected `column_to_rownames()` to just work after the call to `summarize()`. I see scenarios where the need to preserve row names is needed but here `has_rownames()` detects them after `summarize()` even though they're the same as a data frame with NULL row names (just row number). Do I simply need to add the pipe to  ``` `rownames<-`(NULL)``` now to adapt to the new changes?

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(tibble)

# Medians for each species
iris_med <- iris %>% 
  group_by(Species) %>% 
  summarize(across(where(is.double), median))

# Error because summarize() preserved rownames
iris_med %>% column_to_rownames("Species")
#> Error: `.data` must be a data frame without row names.

# Verified it has row names
iris_med %>% has_rownames()
#> [1] TRUE

# It's just row numbers
rownames(iris_med)
#> [1] "1" "2" "3"

# But these are the same ones as when NULL
identical(
  rownames(iris_med),
  `rownames<-`(iris_med, NULL) %>% rownames()
)
#> [1] TRUE

# Need to add this line to every call before column_to_rownames()
iris_med %>% 
  `rownames<-`(NULL) %>% 
  column_to_rownames("Species")
#>            Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width
#> setosa              5.0         3.4         1.50         0.2
#> versicolor          5.9         2.8         4.35         1.3

title: mutate(across()) only works in its own mutate statement--cannot have multiple mutations in one listed 'mutate'
description:
Updating from before, Thanks for the comment @yutannihilation , updating my error below, the issue still exists once a function is introduced. This **does** work in dplyr 1.0.3, but **not** 1.0.4.

After creating/applying a function,
mutate works when "across" is used in separate statement.
Mutate does **NOT** work when "across" is used in _same_ mutate statement

---


```r
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)


# originally, including across within a sequence of mutates under one mutate statement  
# will work ----
mtcars %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = 'Car_Name') %>%
  tibble() %>% 
  mutate(add_stuff = gear + carb, 
         across(where(is.character), toupper))

# and so will separating each statement as its own mutate
mtcars %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = 'Car_Name') %>%
  tibble() %>% 
  mutate(add_stuff = gear + carb) %>%  
  mutate(across(where(is.character), toupper))



# Now create a function to apply ----
testSplit <-  function(data, .selectedVars, .columnToTotal, .keepJustWeights = T, .keepTotal = F) {
  
  #make grand total
  dfWeights <-  data %>% 
    add_count(wt = {{.columnToTotal}}, name = 'total') %>% 
    mutate(Weight = {{.columnToTotal}}/total) 
  
  #find amount of each group
  dfSummed <- dfWeights %>% 
    group_by(across(c({{.selectedVars}},total))) %>% 
    summarise(across(c(Weight,{{.columnToTotal}}), ~ sum(.x,na.rm=TRUE))) %>% 
    ungroup()
  
  #remove total and .columnToTotal
  if (.keepJustWeights) {
    
    dfSummed %>%
      select({{.selectedVars}}, Weight)
    
    #keep all calculated columns
  } else if (.keepTotal) {
    
    dfSummed %>%
      select({{.selectedVars}}, Weight, {{.columnToTotal}}, total)
    
  } else{
    
    #remove total column, keep rest
    dfSummed %>%
      select({{.selectedVars}}, Weight, {{.columnToTotal}})
    
  }
}


# Apply the function and it will return a value  ----
cars <- mtcars %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = 'Car_Name') %>%
  tibble() %>% 
  testSplit(.selectedVars = c(cyl), 
            .columnToTotal = qsec)

# return the set  
cars




# now the original mutation on the original set won't work ----
mtcars %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = 'Car_Name') %>%
  tibble() %>% 
  mutate(add_stuff = gear + carb, 
         across(where(is.character), toupper))

# but it will still work if each statement receives its own "mutate" function in the pipe
mtcars %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = 'Car_Name') %>%
  tibble() %>% 
  mutate(add_stuff = gear + carb) %>%  
  mutate(across(where(is.character), toupper))

title: group_by / summarise very slow together with bit64::integer64 columns
description:
I was surprised to see how much slower it is to operate on integer64 columns compared to int / string columns. The reprex below shows this for a small example. In my real use case the version with integer64 columns hadn't terminated after half an hour, whereas it did in a few seconds when I would convert it to strings before.

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(bit64))

df <- tibble(x = 1, x64 = integer64(1), xstr = "1", y = sample(10000, 1000000, replace = T))

system.time(df %>% group_by(y) %>% summarise(x = x[1]))
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   0.071   0.007   0.078
system.time(df %>% group_by(y) %>% summarise(xstr = xstr[1]))
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   0.059   0.009   0.068
system.time(df %>% group_by(y) %>% summarise(x64 = x64[1]))

title: if_all() and if_any() return unexpected results when the tidy select function doesn't find columns
description:
I was playing around with the new `if_any()` and `if_all()` functions and I accidentally used `mtcars` instead of `iris` in the following code.

```r
big <- function(x) x > mean(x)

mtcars %>%
    mutate(
        category = case_when(
            if_all(contains("Width"), big) ~ "both big",
            if_any(contains("Width"), big) ~ "one big",
            TRUE ~ "small"
        )
    )
```

I'd expect all of these to return `"small"` but using the latest version of the code installed from GitHub, the column `category` returns `"both big"` for the whole column. I think this is incorrect since there are no columns in `mtcars` containing `"Width"`?

title: Side effects of the conversion of count() to a generic
description:
This is an extension off of a conversation from the RStudio Community - https://community.rstudio.com/t/subtle-difference-on-rownames-between-two-count-ed-tibbles/95090

#5538 implemented `count()` as a generic. With this change,  dplyr >= 1.0.3 is exhibiting some odd (to me) behavior in regards to rownames and tibbles. It appears that tibbles that are passed in to `count()` are returned with some different attributes that cause rownames to be printed. If the output of `count()` is explicitly cast as a tibble, rownames are not printed (as expected). Strangely, the results of these two operations pass a base `identical()` test but fail an `identical(attrib.as.set = FALSE)` test, although I don't see any difference in the results of `attributes()`  call on both of the resulting objects. It also appears that the `bad` object in my reprex returns a true from `tibble::has_rownames()`, this exists even if I explicitly pass a `rownames = FALSE` to my `as_tibble()` call.

The net result of this is that some objects in an analysis workflow are displayed in an `html_notebook` with rownames and others are not. There may be other side effects that I'm not aware of here.

Expected behavior: bare tibbles as generated by `count()` are printed without rownames

---
``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
bad <- mtcars %>% tibble::as_tibble() %>% count(disp)
good <- mtcars %>% count(disp) %>% tibble::as_tibble()
identical(bad, good, attrib.as.set = FALSE)

title: Referencing other columns inside mutate/summarise across is broken in 1.0.4
description:
In dplyr 1.0.3 you can reference other columns in the same data-frame/tibble group by name. This functionality is broken in 1.0.4

To reproduce, the following example works in 1.0.3

    storms %>% mutate(across(c('wind', 'pressure'), function(x) {
      return(x/lat)
    }))

In 1.0.4, running the above example results in the following error message

> \>rlang::last_error()
> <error/dplyr:::mutate_error>
> Problem with `mutate()` input `..1`.
> x object 'lat' not found

i.e. we can't reference other columns by name. A possible workaround is to use `cur_data()$name_of_column` but this is slower as the following benchmark demonstrates:

    library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = F)
    
    df <- tibble(cbind.data.frame(
      grp_1 = sort(rep(1:250, 4)),
      grp_2 = rep(1:4, 250), 
      matrix(rnorm(1000 * 100), nrow = 1000)))
    
    bench::mark(iterations = 100,
                filter_gc = FALSE,
                use_cur_data = df %>% summarise(across(is.numeric, function(x) {
                  rows = cur_data()
                  mask = (rows$grp_1 %% 2) == 0
                  return(mean(x[mask] / rows$grp_2[mask]))
                })),
                direct_reference = df %>% summarise(across(is.numeric, function(x) {
                  mask = (grp_1 %% 2) == 0
                  return(mean(x[mask] / grp_2[mask]))
                }))) %>%
      select(expression, min, median, `itr/sec`, `gc/sec`)

which results in the following output

    # A tibble: 2 x 5
      expression            min   median `itr/sec` `gc/sec`
      <bch:expr>       <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl>    <dbl>
    1 use_cur_data       17.2ms  18.29ms      51.1    10.7 
    2 direct_reference   8.12ms   8.59ms     108.      9.76

TL;DR In dply 1.0.3, using `cur_data()$column_name` to reference columns instead of directly using the column names can be considerably slower. In 1.0.4 referencing columns by name, not using cur_data, is currently broken.

title: tidyselect + where VS if_any/if_all, and error messages
description:
Number one, extremely happy to have the new features for `filter` and/or `mutate()` with `if_any`/`if_all`!!! This feature was not something I expected but am so excited to have!!!

🥳 

There is one problem I'd like to raise and one question:

**Problem**: The error message for using `if_any()` without a column selector results in some potentially bad recommendations (related to my question as well).

**Question**: What is the "correct" way of `select`-ing columns based on values *within* that column?

---

While I understand the use of `if_any` with `filter()`, I'm also interested in the similar option for `select()`. when cleaning data or working with "wide" data that I'm putting into a table I fairly often want to `select()` specific columns that *contain* a specific value/string/range/etc. IE just knowing it's numeric or text is not sufficient, but rather I'm interested in specifics of the column's contents.

I have a reprex below that shows some of my testing steps in trying to answer this question.

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(palmerpenguins)
#> Warning: package 'palmerpenguins' was built under R version 4.0.2


# Filter specific columns 

ex1 <- penguins %>% 
  filter(if_any(contains("bill"), ~.x == 39.1| .x == 18.7))

ex1
#> # A tibble: 6 x 8
#>   species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_… body_mass_g sex  
#>   <fct>   <fct>           <dbl>         <dbl>            <int>       <int> <fct>
#> 1 Adelie  Torge…           39.1          18.7              181        3750 male 
#> 2 Adelie  Biscoe           37.7          18.7              180        3600 male 
#> 3 Adelie  Dream            39            18.7              185        3650 male 
#> 4 Chinst… Dream            45.4          18.7              188        3525 fema…
#> 5 Chinst… Dream            51.5          18.7              187        3250 male 
#> 6 Chinst… Dream            50.2          18.7              198        3775 fema…
#> # … with 1 more variable: year <int>

# I realize this is a toy example 
# that could be solved by normal filter
ex2 <- penguins %>% 
  filter(bill_length_mm == 39.1| bill_depth_mm == 18.7)

all.equal(ex1, ex2)
#> [1] TRUE

# Skip tidyselect ---------------------------------------------------------

# What happens when you don't indicate tidyselect or colname?
# Throws a useful error but in this case leads down
# a not very useful path
penguins %>% 
  filter(if_any(~.x == 39.1))
#> Error: Problem with `filter()` input `..1`.
#> x Formula shorthand must be wrapped in `where()`.
#> 
#>   # Bad
#>   data %>% select(~.x == 39.1)
#> 
#>   # Good
#>   data %>% select(where(~.x == 39.1))
#> ℹ Input `..1` is `if_any(~.x == 39.1)`.

# So then let's follow the recommendation of:
# data %>% select(where(~.x == 39.1))
# this fails because it's not vectorized I believe?

penguins %>% 
  select(where(~.x == 39.1))
#> Error: `where()` must be used with functions that return `TRUE` or `FALSE`.

# Still fails with everything() indicated
penguins %>% 
  select(where(if_any(everything(), ~.x == 39.1)))
#> Error: `across()` must only be used inside dplyr verbs.

# Use base::any ---------------------------------------------------------

# So for this behavior, I want to select a specific column
# by values present in that column
# this WILL work if you use base::any() without any extra work!!!
# But I wanted to make sure this is a good idea?

penguins %>% 
  select(where(~any(.x == 36.7, na.rm = TRUE)))
#> # A tibble: 344 x 1
#>    bill_length_mm
#>             <dbl>
#>  1           39.1
#>  2           39.5
#>  3           40.3
#>  4           NA  
#>  5           36.7
#>  6           39.3
#>  7           38.9
#>  8           39.2
#>  9           34.1
#> 10           42  
#> # … with 334 more rows
```

title: Unexpected result when using `case_when()` in grouped summarize
description:
Brief description of the problem

``` r
library(tidyverse)
data <- tribble(
  ~id, ~corr, ~period,
  1, 0, "a",
  1, 0, "b",
  2, 0, "a",
  2, 1, "b",
  3, 1, "a",
  3, 0, "b",
  4, 1, "a",
  4, 1, "b"
)
data %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  summarise(
    resp_period = case_when(
      sum(corr) == 0 ~ "none",
      sum(corr) == 1 ~ period[corr == 1],
      sum(corr) == 2 ~ "both"
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>      id resp_period
#>   <dbl> <chr>      
#> 1     2 b          
#> 2     3 a          
#> 3     4 both       
#> 4     4 both
```

<sup>Created on 2021-02-03 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v1.0.0)</sup>

The result `tibble` is expected as 

```r
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>      id resp_period
#>   <dbl> <chr>      
#> 1     1 none          
#> 2     2 b       
#> 3     3 a       
#> 4     4 both
```
Seemingly, `case_when()` is not so useful in this case. What is the workaround? What's more, this might be the side-effect of the new `summarise()` behavior since `dplyr 1.0.0`.

title: group_by() seems to crash interactivity when used with plotly and crosstalk

description:

#>

#> This message is displayed once per session.
#> # A tibble: 150 x 5
#>    Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species

As a user, this is straightforward. 

But, in the context of a package function, this adds a new `tidyselect` dependency since `where` is currently [not](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/master/R/select-helpers.R) re-exported from `dplyr`.

as_tibble(iris) %>% filter(if_all(where(is.numeric), ~ !is.na(.)))

To appease `_R_CHECK_EXCESSIVE_IMPORTS_` check from `CRAN`, I'd prefer if `dplyr` re-exports this function, so that one doesn't have to add both `dplyr` and `tidyselect` to `Imports`.

title: rows_update function fails when data has duplicated matching ids
description:
When updating rows in a data frame with `rows_update`, if currently fails if the data frame has duplicated matching ids. However, this should be of no concern to the `rows_update` function since it's purpose (to my understanding) is to update certain values in the data based on finding the id. And if the id occurs several times in the data, the `rows_update` should just update them all.
At least I'd say there shoudl be an optional parameter in the function that let the user decide if they want to see an error or have the matching happen several times.

```
df <- data.frame(id = c("A", "A", "B"),
                 x  = c(1, 2, 3))

lookup <- data.frame(id = c("A", "B"),
                     x = c(9, 8))

df %>%
  rows_update(., lookup, by = "id")
```

This throws an error:

`Error: `x` key values are not unique.`

Expected outcome:

```
  id x
1  A 9
2  A 9
3  B 8
```

title: On the dev feature if_any/if_all (this is not a bug)
description:
Hi!
I just installed the dev version of `dplyr` to test the new feature produced after #5660.

I run the examples using the next data:
```r
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
df <- data.frame(
    "ID" = c("asdf","vfdkun", "seifu", "seijd", "qweri"),
    "elephant_zoo" = c(1,1,1,2,0), #Should not be useful there
    "rhino_zoo" = c(1,2,3,1,0), #Should not be useful there
    "hippo_zoo" = c(1,1,0,0,0),
    "elephant_wild_A" = c(0,0,1,1,3),
    "rhino_wild_A" = c(0,0,4,3,1),
    "elephant_wild_B" = c(0,0,0,0,0),
    "rhino_wild_C" = c(0,0,1,5,7),
    "hippo_wild_B" = c(0,0,0,0,0)) %>% 
  column_to_rownames(var = "ID")
df

asdf              1         1         1               0            0               0            0
vfdkun            1         2         1               0            0               0            0
seifu             1         3         0               1            4               0            1
seijd             2         1         0               1            3               0            5
qweri             0         0         0               3            1               0            7
       hippo_wild_B
asdf              0
vfdkun            0
seifu             0
seijd             0
qweri             0
```
It works as expected, since it works inside `filter`:
```r

       hippo_wild_B
asdf              0
vfdkun            0
seifu             0
seijd             0
```
But I hoped that it worked beyond that, which is not the case:
```r
df %>%
    mutate(ZOO = 
               case_when(if_any(contains("zoo"), ~`>`(.,0)) ~ "zoo", 
                         TRUE ~ "F"))
Error: Problem with `mutate()` input `ZOO`.
x LHS of case 1 (`if_any(contains("zoo"), ~. > 0)`) must be a logical vector, not a `tbl_df/tbl/data.frame` object.
ℹ Input `ZOO` is `case_when(if_any(contains("zoo"), ~. > 0) ~ "zoo", TRUE ~ "F")`.
Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.
```
So not a single logical vector outside `filter`... Let's try
```r
df %>%
    mutate(ZOO = 
               case_when(pull(if_any(contains("zoo"), ~`>`(.,0))) ~ "zoo", 
                         TRUE ~ "F"))
       elephant_zoo rhino_zoo hippo_zoo elephant_wild_A rhino_wild_A elephant_wild_B rhino_wild_C hippo_wild_B ZOO
asdf              1         1         1               0            0               0            0            0 zoo

seifu             1         3         0               1            4               0            1            0   F
seijd             2         1         0               1            3               0            5            0   F
qweri             0         0         0               3            1               0            7            0   F
```
The result is incorrect. Indeed:
```r
df %>%
    mutate(ZOO = pull(if_any(contains("zoo"), ~`>`(.,0))))
       elephant_zoo rhino_zoo hippo_zoo elephant_wild_A rhino_wild_A elephant_wild_B rhino_wild_C hippo_wild_B   ZOO
asdf              1         1         1               0            0               0            0            0  TRUE
vfdkun            1         2         1               0            0               0            0            0  TRUE
seifu             1         3         0               1            4               0            1            0 FALSE
seijd             2         1         0               1            3               0            5            0 FALSE
qweri             0         0         0               3            1               0            7            0 FALSE
```
Let's see:
```r
df %>%
    mutate(ZOO = if_any(contains("zoo"), ~`>`(.,0)))
       elephant_zoo rhino_zoo hippo_zoo elephant_wild_A rhino_wild_A elephant_wild_B rhino_wild_C hippo_wild_B
asdf              1         1         1               0            0               0            0            0
vfdkun            1         2         1               0            0               0            0            0
seifu             1         3         0               1            4               0            1            0
seijd             2         1         0               1            3               0            5            0
qweri             0         0         0               3            1               0            7            0
                                                                                                                                                                           ZOO
asdf                                                                                                                                   \033[38;5;246m# A tibble: 5 x 3\033[39m
vfdkun                                                                                                                                        elephant_zoo rhino_zoo hippo_zoo
seifu  \033[38;5;250m*\033[39m \033[3m\033[38;5;246m<lgl>\033[39m\033[23m        \033[3m\033[38;5;246m<lgl>\033[39m\033[23m     \033[3m\033[38;5;246m<lgl>\033[39m\033[23m    
seijd                                                                                                                 \033[38;5;250m1\033[39m TRUE         TRUE      TRUE     
qweri                                                                                                                 \033[38;5;250m2\033[39m TRUE         TRUE      TRUE     
Warning message:
In format.data.frame(if (omit) x[seq_len(n0), , drop = FALSE] else x,  :
  corrupt data frame: columns will be truncated or padded with NAs
```
Ough!!!

It would be nice to have these functions beyond `filter`. Meanwhile, we wil go on using `any_cols` as in #4770.

Thank you!

title: Feature request: across2() and pacross()
description:
I found myself in a situation today where I wished there was an `across2()` or `pacross()` version of `across()` similarly to the way there are `map2()` and `pmap()` versions of `purrr::map()`. Here is a reproducible example to illustrate my situation.

I am given patient data that includes the Patient Health Questionnaire (phq). I've been asked to dichotomize each of the phq columns. I've also been given column labels and value labels and asked to add them to the new columns in the data frame.

```r
# Example data
df <- tibble(
  id   = 1:10,
  sex  = c("m", "m", "m", "f", "f", "f", "m", "f", "f", "m"),
  phq1 = c(3, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 3, 0, 1),
  phq2 = c(1, 2, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 3, 0, 1),
  phq3 = c(2, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 3, 0, 1),
  phq4 = c(0, 2, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 3, 0, 1)
)
```

```{r}
# Column labels
phq_var_labs <- c(
  'Little interest or pleasure in doing things dicot',
  'Felling down, depressed, or hopeless dicot',
  'Trouble falling or staying asleep, or sleeping too much dicot',
  'Feeling tired or having little energy dicot'
)

# Value label
phq_val_labs <- c(
  'Not at all and several days' = 0, 
  'More than half the days and nearly every day' = 1
)
```
Of course, I can easily create the new dichotomized variables using `mutate()` and `across()`.

```{r}
df %>% 
  mutate(
    across(
      .cols = phq1:phq4,
      .fns  = ~ case_when(
        .x  < 2 ~ 0,
        .x >= 2 ~ 1
      ),
      .names = "{col}_dicot"
    )
  )
```
However, I wasn't able to come up with a tidyverse iterative solution that I liked. Here is the best solution I was able to come up with:

```{r}
# Dichotomize the values
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      .cols = all_of(phq_8_vars),
      .fns  = ~ case_when(
        .x  < 2 ~ 0,
        .x >= 2 ~ 1
      ),
      .names = "{col}_dicot"
    )
  )

# Add column and value labels
for(i in seq_along(phq_8_vars)) {
  d <- paste0(phq_8_vars[[i]], "_dicot")
  attr(all_visits[[d]], "label") <- phq_8_var_labs[[i]]
  attr(all_visits[[d]],"labels") <- phq_8_val_labs
}
```

In my case, and perhaps others, it would be handy to be able to do something like:

```{r}
df <- df %>% 
  mutate(
    across2(
      .cols = phq1:phq4,
      .y    = phq_var_labs,
      .fns  = function(x, .y) {
        v <- case_when(
          x  < 2 ~ 0,
          x >= 2 ~ 1
        )
        attr(v, "label")  <- .y
        attr(v, "labels") <- phq_val_labs
        v
      },
      .names = "{col}_dicot"
    )
  )
```

title: Multi-join suffixes
description:
Hi,

I want to merge several data.frames with some common columns and append a suffix to the column names to keep track from where does the data for each column come from. 

I can do it easily with the suffix term in the first full_join, but when I do the second join, no suffixes are added. I can rename the third data.frame so it has suffixes, but I wanted to know if there is another way of doing it using the suffix term.

Here is an example code:
```
x = data.frame(col1 = c("a","b","c"), col2 = 1:3, col3 = 1:3)
y = data.frame(col1 = c("b","c","d"), col2 = 4:6, col3 = 1:3)
z = data.frame(col1 = c("c","d","a"), col2 = 7:9, col3 = 1:3)

> df = full_join(x, y, by = "col1", suffix = c("_x","_y")) %>% 
  full_join(z, by = "col1", suffix = c("","_z")) 

> df
  col1 col2_x col3_x col2_y col3_y col2 col3
1    a      1      1     NA     NA    9    3
2    b      2      2      4      1   NA   NA
3    c      3      3      5      2    7    1
4    d     NA     NA      6      3    8    2
```
I was expecting that col2 and col3 from data.frame z would have a "_z" suffix. I have tried using empty suffixes while merging two data.frames and it works.

I can work around by renaming the columns in z before doing the second full_join, but in my real data I have several common columns, and if I wanted to merge more data.frames it would complicate the code. This is my expected output.

```
> colnames(z) = paste0(colnames(z),"_z")

> df = full_join(x, y, by = "col1", suffix = c("_x","_y")) %>% 
  full_join(z, by = c("col1"="col1_z"))

> df
  col1 col2_x col3_x col2_y col3_y col2_z col3_z
1    a      1      1     NA     NA      9      3
2    b      2      2      4      1     NA     NA
3    c      3      3      5      2      7      1
4    d     NA     NA      6      3      8      2
```

I have seen other [similar problems][1] in which adding an extra column to keep track of the source data.frame is used, but I was wondering why does not the suffix term work with multiple joins.

PS: If I keep the first suffix empty, I can add suffixes in the second join, but that will leave the col2 and col3 form x without suffix.

```
> df = full_join(x, y, by = "col1", suffix = c("","_y")) %>% 
  full_join(z, by = "col1", suffix = c("","_z"))

> df
  col1 col2 col3 col2_y col3_y col2_z col3_z
1    a    1    1     NA     NA      9      3
2    b    2    2      4      1     NA     NA
3    c    3    3      5      2      7      1
4    d   NA   NA      6      3      8      2
```

I might be missing why this is not working the way I expected, but in principle it should be very simple to add a suffix to the "newly added" columns.

Thanks!

  [1]: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/65152352/suffixes-when-merging-more-than-two-data-frames-with-full-join

title: `rows_patch(x, y, ...)` shows unhelpful error message when `nrow(y) > nrow(x)`
description:
When I try to patch a data frame (`x` in the below example) using another data frame with more rows (`y`), an error is thrown with an unhelpful message. It took some time to figure out that the row number difference was the source of the error. `rlang::last_error()` and `rlang::last_trace()` didn't help.

Is there any reason a data frame *should not* be patched by a data frame with more rows? I could be missing some theory here. If there *is* a good reason why this should not be allowed, can I add that to the documentation for `rows_patch()` and friends?

y = data.frame(id = c(1, 3, 5, 7), foo = c("a", "c", "e", "g"))

title: Example in documentation for arrange is incorrect
description:
The [documentation](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/arrange.html) for `1.0.2` states that "embracing" works for `arrange()`, see quote from examples section:

```
# use embracing when wrapping in a function;
# see ?dplyr_data_masking for more details
tidy_eval_arrange <- function(.data, var) {
  .data %>%
    arrange({{ var }})
}
```

However, this does not work unless `across()` is used, see simple example below.

```r
var <- "disp"

# Expected to work according to docs
mtcars %>% select({{ var }}) %>%  arrange({{ var }})

# This is what works in 1.0.2
mtcars %>% select({{ var }}) %>%  arrange(across({{ var }}))

```

title: Is there a reason why the tally() generic doesn't have ... ?
description:
Making `tally()` generic is breaking {mosaicCore} (as did the introduction of the non-generic `tally()` years ago).  I created a work-around so that {dplyr} and {mosaic} could co-exist.  I need to come up with a new work-around now that `tally()` is generic.  So I've been looking at the new generic.

I'm seeing that the `dplyr::tally()` generic doesn't include `...` as an argument and does include other arguments that could probably be left to the specific methods, contrary to the advice in section 7.1 of https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-exts.pdf. I'm wondering why.

title: Error: Problem with `mutate()` input `..1`. x Can't subset columns that don't exist.
description:
Hi all,

The issue arises when I create a data frame from another using group by and summarise. I do the same again, but using the across() function in group_by.

here is the output from reprex:
```r
data1 = data.frame(a = c(rep('A',4),
                         rep('B',5),
                         rep('D',2)),
                   b = rnorm(11),
                   c = c(rep(T, 5),
                         rep(F,6)),
                   d = c(rep('T',3),
                         rep('F',2),
                         rep('G',6))
                   )

data2 = data1 %>% 
  filter(c == TRUE) %>% 
  distinct(b, .keep_all = T) %>% 
  group_by(a, d) %>%  
  summarise(count = n()) 
#> Error in data1 %>% filter(c == TRUE) %>% distinct(b, .keep_all = T) %>% : could not find function "%>%"

group_vars = c('a','d')

data3 = data2 %>%
  mutate(d = 'All') %>% 
  group_by(across(group_vars)) %>% 
  summarise_all(sum, na.rm = T) 
#> Error in data2 %>% mutate(d = "All") %>% group_by(across(group_vars)) %>% : could not find function "%>%"
```

Here is the error:
Error: Problem with `mutate()` input `..1`.
x Can't subset columns that don't exist.
x Column `a` doesn't exist.
i Input `..1` is `across(vars)`.
i The error occurred in group 1: a = "A".
Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.

I also notice that data2 only recognizes a single group "a" rather then both "a" and "b".

> data2
# A tibble: 3 x 3
# Groups:   a [2]
  a     d     count
  <chr> <chr> <int>
1 A     F         1
2 A     T         3
3 B     F         1

A work around has been using the older:
group_by_at(vars(any_of(group_vars))) %>% 
instead of the group_by(across()) statement

Thanks in advance for any help or insight you may have.

title: `rows_*()` functions should be able to use different joins keys in `x` and `y`
description:
Currently, rows_* functions like `rows_update` require an unnamed character string for the `by` parameter, which makes it impossible to dynamically pass id column names. *_join functions, however, allow for a named by-vector so that names can be passed dynamically (see here for some reference: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/65688508/tidyverse-join-two-data-sets-with-dynamic-column-names-for-by-column).

It would be desirable if the rows_* function also allow for named vectors. 

```
library(tidyverse)
x <- data.frame(a1 = c(1, 2, 3))
y <- data.frame(a2 = c(1, 2, 4),
                new = c("a", "b", "c"))

z <- data.frame(a2  = 3,
                new = "d")

x_name <- "a1"
y_name <- "a2"

# works
x_new <- x %>%
  left_join(., y, by = setNames(y_name, x_name))

# doesn't work
x_new %>%
  rows_update(., z, by = setNames(y_name, x_name))

# Error: `by` must be unnamed.
```

title: Bind_rows cannot combine bit64::integer64 with other types
description:
The `bind_rows()` function is nice in that it allows some differences in types. For example, a `numeric` column can be combined with an `integer` column without problem. However, this is not the case for `bit64::integer64` types. For example:

```r
library(dplyr)

# This works:
bind_rows(tibble(a = as.numeric(1)), 
          tibble(a = as.integer(2)))
# # A tibble: 2 x 1
#         a
#   <dbl>
#   1     1
#   2     2

# This fails:
bind_rows(tibble(a = as.numeric(1)), 
          tibble(a = bit64::as.integer64(2)))
# Error: Can't combine `..1$a` <double> and `..2$a` <integer64>.
# Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.
```

For consistency, it would be nice if `bit64::integer64` could be treated similar to other numeric types.

title: Lazy evaluation bug in `mutate`/`transmute` ?
description:
This is inspired from [this SO post ](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/65591282/an-object-inside-map-function-is-not-recognized-another-case ). I have made a smaller and simpler example. 

Consider this data : 

```r
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)

data <- data.frame(i1 = 1:3, i2 = 3:1)
data
#    i1 i2
#1   1  3
#2   2  2
#3   3  1
```

Now let's say I want to add a new column `temp` to above dataframe which is going to be list of dataframes. I try : 


1) 
```
data %>% mutate(t1 = map(i1, ~data %>% mutate(!!paste0('col', .x) := 1)))
```

This returns

>Error in paste0("col", .x) : object '.x' not found


But it works if I use this without `mutate` : 

2. 
```
map(data$i1, ~data %>% mutate(!!paste0('col', .x) := 1))

#[[1]]
#   i1 i2 col1
#1  1  3    1
#2  2  2    1
#3  3  1    1

#[[2]]
#  i1 i2 col2
#1  1  3    1
#2  2  2    1
#3  3  1    1

#[[3]]
#   i1 i2 col3
#1  1  3    1
#2  2  2    1
#3  3  1    1
```


It also works with `mutate` when we write a separate function to do the same thing. 

3.
```
fun_group <- function(i){
  data %>% mutate(!!paste0('col', i) := 1)
}

data %>% mutate(temp = map(i1, fun_group)) 
```

So why does 1 fail whereas 2 and 3 work fine. I have tried various modifications to the above to understand the reason but I failed to understand why it behaves differently. Tried changing `data` with `mtcars`, changing `mutate` with `transmute` but the error is still there.

title: grouped mutations err (instead of warn) in 0-row tibble
description:
`group_by` on a 0-row dataframe causes failure on subsequent table modifications. The same `mutate` 'works' when un-grouped.

```r
iris0 <- iris %>% slice(0) %>% as_tibble()

## raises warnings, but works:
iris0 %>% mutate(foo = min(Sepal.Length))
#> Warning: Problem with `mutate()` input `foo`.
#> ℹ no non-missing arguments to min; returning Inf
#> ℹ Input `foo` is `min(Sepal.Length)`.
#> Warning in min(Sepal.Length): no non-missing arguments to min; returning Inf
#> # A tibble: 0 x 6
#> # … with 6 variables: Sepal.Length <dbl>, Sepal.Width <dbl>,
#> #   Petal.Length <dbl>, Petal.Width <dbl>, Species <fct>, foo <dbl>

## errs:
iris0 %>% group_by(Species) %>% mutate(foo = min(Sepal.Length))
#> Error: Can't subset elements that don't exist.
#> x Location 1 doesn't exist.
#> ℹ There are only 0 elements.
```

I think the default behavior seen in the non-grouped (i.e. working) code above is the correct behavior: if the original data being mutated has 0 rows, ignore the new input. `min(double(0))` returns a length-1 scalar (`Inf`), and this seems consistent with adding new values to a dataframe if they're length-1 or of equal length to the existing data (i.e. `n()`) ... in this case the new scalar value is 'recycled' to length-0: `Inf[0]` yields `numeric(0)`.

title: `mutate()` recycles output when passed a non-vectorized function
description:
Applying a non-vectorized function to one column ("column A") results in a new column ("column B") comprising only the value of the function applied to the first element of column A. 

```r
library(magrittr)
data(mtcars)
mtcars$make_model <- rownames(mtcars)
mtcars %>%
  dplyr::mutate(make = strsplit(make_model, ' ')[[1]][1]) %>%
  head()
```

```

3 22.8   4  108  93 3.85 2.320 18.61  1  1    4    1        Datsun 710 Mazda

6 18.1   6  225 105 2.76 3.460 20.22  1  0    3    1           Valiant Mazda

While I'm not convinced that this is `mutate()`'s problem more than it is e.g. `strsplit()`'s problem (I'm thinking of the warning used by `if()`), it might be great if `mutate()` could detect this and warn that output is being recycled.

title: Upgrade past dplyr 1.0.0 to either 1.0.1 or 1.0.2 causes order of magnitude slowdown in group_by mutate()
description:
dealing with max(na.rm=T) in a mutate statement when grouping by **2 columns** slows down by an order by magnitude from version 1.0.0 to 1.0.1

---

Orders of magnitude difference in time to complete between version 1.0.0 to 1.0.2. When the tibble is very large (thousands or hundreds of thousands of rows) the time explodes. Requires a session restart between installing versions to reproduce the example to ensure the old packages are unloaded and new version is loaded.

library(devtools)
library(rstudioapi)

packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '1.0.0'
install_version("dplyr", version = "1.0.0", repos = "http://cran.us.r-project.org", upgrade = "never", quiet = TRUE)
restartSession()
```

title: *_join functions don't preserve labels in labelled vectors when one of the joined data sets contains more or less labels than the other
description:
When having labelled vectors like from `haven` package, these labels are not preserved in joining functions if the labels between the two to-be-merged data sets are not 100% identical. However, it is common that to-be-merged data sets might have additional (or fewer) labels, but should still be preserved.

E.g assume a usual social science survey where you have one data set for Jan/Feb/March and this information is stored in a labelled column. Now, you have a new survey with data from April, again labelled in a respective column. When joining these two data sets, it would be preferable to keep the lables if they are consistent, clear and non-overlapping.

So if data set 1 has labels like 1 = Jan, 2 = Feb, 3 = Mar; and data set 2 has labels 4 = Apr, labels should be preserved and merged (or there should be at least a parameter to turn on this feature).

```
library(tidyverse)
library(haven)

old <- data.frame(id = c(1, 2, 3),
                  x  = haven::labelled(x      = c(1, 2, 3),
                                       labels = c("first" = 1, "second" = 2, "third" = 3))) %>%
  as_tibble()
```
```
# A tibble: 3 x 2
     id          x
  <dbl>  <dbl+lbl>
1     1 1 [first] 
2     2 2 [second]
3     3 3 [third]
```
```
new <- data.frame(id = c(4),
                  x  = haven::labelled(x      = c(4),
                                       labels = c("first" = 1, "second" = 2, "third" = 3, "fourth" = 4))) %>%
  as_tibble()
```
```
# A tibble: 1 x 2
     id          x
  <dbl>  <dbl+lbl>
1     4 4 [fourth]
```

Now, `full_join(old, new)` deletes the labels.

```
Joining, by = c("id", "x")
# A tibble: 4 x 2
     id     x
  <dbl> <dbl>
1     1     1
2     2     2
3     3     3
4     4     4
```

whereas the expected output would be

```
# A tibble: 4 x 2
     id          x
  <dbl>  <dbl+lbl>
1     1 1 [first] 
2     2 2 [second]
3     3 3 [third]
4     4 4 [fourth]
```

In brief, [hacksaw](https://github.com/daranzolin/hacksaw) is a goofy little package that suits my programming and table-making habits. It has a variety of `*_split` function built off of common dplyr verbs, e.g. `filter_split`, `select_split`, etc.

title: group_by() assigns group indices in different order than they appear in data
description:
Simple example:
```r
library(dplyr)
d = tibble(id = c("B", "A"))
d.grp = group_by(d, id)
mutate(d.grp, grp.id = cur_group_id())
## # A tibble: 2 x 2
## # Groups:   id [2]
##   id    grp.id
##   <chr>  <int>
## 1 B          2
## 2 A          1
```
There are some cases where it it is convenient for the group IDs be ordered by how they appear in the data. What is the reasoning behind the decision to order the grouping by some other logic (in this case, I assume alphabetically)? Currently, the only way to guarantee that the group indices are in the order of the data is to first `arrange()` the data before grouping, which can be expensive.

title: Segfault from C stack overflow in zero-length slicing when withr::defer() is used
description:
The following does segfault
```r
f3 <- function(...) {
  withr::defer(2)
  integer(1) 
  message('reaching this')
  data <- dplyr::slice(mtcars, integer(1))
}

f3()
#> reaching this
#> R session aborted in Rstudio, or Error: segfault from C stack overflow when ran via testthat.
```

You can also remove `integer(1)` and `message('reaching this')` and the same segfault occurs. 

The following similar commands that either don't use `withr::defer()` or zero-slice explicitly with `0L` instead of `integer(1)` (which are identical, i.e. `identical(integer(1), 0L)` returns `TRUE`)  don't segfault:
```r
f1 <- function(...) {
  withr::defer(2)
  data <- dplyr::slice(mtcars, 0L)
}

f1()


f2 <- function() {
  data <- dplyr::slice(mtcars, integer(1))
}

f2()
```

A reproducible example ran on CI/CD and output logs can be found in this [package](https://github.com/lorenzwalthert/segfault.dplyr.testthat/blob/main/tests/testthat/test-segfault.R) and the associated [GitHub Actions](https://github.com/lorenzwalthert/segfault.dplyr.testthat/runs/1594813013#step:5:93) for released R and current CRAN.

Wasn't sure if this issue belongs here or to the withr repo, so feel free to move it. Errors don't occur when slicing with `[`, so there is a dplyr component to it.

title: give `*_join()` more control on duplicated and unmatched rows
description:
As @lionel- nicely proposed in #3967 it would be great to have more control on what the `*_join()` functions do on duplicated or unmatched rows. Proposed arguments:

* `.unmatched = c("keep", "drop", "error")`
* `.duplicates = c("error", "product")`

for example a 1:1 join would then simply be `.unmatched = "error"` and `.duplicates = "error"`.

As the arguments should rather be added to the existing `*_join()` functions the "keep" and "drop" options for `.unmatched` don't really make sense for all joins. Rather, one would have

`left/right/full_join()` -> `.unmatched = c("keep", "error")`
`inner_join()` -> `.unmatched = c("drop", "error")`

title: Need an easy way to calculate group "subtotals"
description:
`dplyr` makes it easy to perform grouped calculations via `group_by()`, but it is tedious and error-prone to calculate (sub)totals for grouping variables, especially when there are many grouping variables.  I have created [a function that makes this process easy and painless](https://github.com/jrf1111/TCCD/blob/master/R/with_subtotals.R), and I think it would be a very helpful supplement to `group_by()`.  See example below.

```r

library(tidyverse)
library(data.table)

#desired function
test <- mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl, am) %>%
  with_subtotals() %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_mpg = mean(mpg)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# the old, long, and error prone way
test2 <- data.table::rbindlist(
  list(
    mtcars %>%
      group_by(cyl, am) %>%
      summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_mpg = mean(mpg)
      ) %>%
      ungroup(),

    mtcars %>%
      group_by(cyl) %>%
      summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_mpg = mean(mpg),
        am = "total_"
      ) %>%
      ungroup(),

    mtcars %>%
      group_by(am) %>%
      summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_mpg = mean(mpg),
        cyl = "total_"
      ) %>%
      ungroup(),


    mtcars %>%
      summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_mpg = mean(mpg),
        am = "total_",
        cyl = "total_"
      ) %>%
      ungroup()
  ),
  use.names = TRUE
)


test <- test %>% arrange_all()
test2 <- test2 %>% arrange_all()

all.equal(test, test2, check.attributes = FALSE) # TRUE
```

I'll start a PR if maintainers like this idea.

title: c_across combines levels of incompatible factor variables without message
description:
The new `c_across()` is exactly what i needed just now and i'm delighted to have found it. However, it took me a while to diagnose a problem with a calculation i was performing that involved converting factor columns to integers and taking their sum (see reprex below). While in most cases the factors had the same levels, in one case some levels were differently coded. (In practice, this can occur by accident or because categorical variables with different groups are being combined into meaningful scores.) I inferred that this caused the row vector to be redefined as a single factor variable with a concatenated vector of levels, which then took larger values when converted to integers. As a result, the row sums were much larger than their intended values.

While i think that this is appropriate behavior, i think it would preempt confusion to print an informative message when multiple factor variables with different levels are concatenated using `c_across()`. (This may only be an issue when someone is doing arithmetic on the result.) Incidentally, i've written a package that combines factors in this way (and currently does not print such a message), so i'd be interested in any general guidance folks have.

``` r
suppressMessages(library(dplyr))
#> Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.0.2
# tibble with incompatible factor columns
d <- tibble(
  a = factor(letters[1:3][c(1, 3, 2)], levels = letters[1:3]),
  b = factor(letters[4:6][c(2, 1, 3)], levels = letters[4:6])
)
# expected or desired sum
d %>%
  mutate_all(as.integer) %>%
  mutate(c = a + b)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#>       a     b     c
#>   <int> <int> <int>
#> 1     1     2     3
#> 2     3     1     4
#> 3     2     3     5
# sum using `c_across()` due (evidently) to factors being combined with
# concatenated levels
d %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(c = sum(as.integer(c_across(c(a, b)))))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#> # Rowwise: 
#>   a     b         c
#>   <fct> <fct> <int>
#> 1 a     e         6
#> 2 c     d         7
#> 3 b     f         8
```

<sup>Created on 2020-12-13 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

I could not find an existing issue about this, and the behavior was the same after CRAN and `master` branch installations.

title: Function for reduced chi squared
description:
---

I am wondering if dplyr can add a function to calculate the reduced chi squared for linear or non linear model objects. 
Here is some of my personal attempt to constructing such a function. 

---

**Description**

The reduced chi-square statistic is used to show the goodness of model fitting. 
This function is to calculate the reduced chi-squared of a fitted model. 
It is based on the R *summary()* function which doesn't directly provide a reduced chi-square for the model fitted. 

**Input (Arguments)**

- `y`: a list of numeric value the response in the model, can be a column of an existing tibble. 
  - _Justification_: in model fitting, we usually have a response variable and one or several variables as input. The `y` here is the response variable and we use it to calculate the chi-squared value. 
- `model`: a fitted model either by linear fitting or non-linear fitting. 
  - _Justification_:  the fitted model will provide the fitted value involved in the calculation of chi-squared value. It also shows the number of variables involved in the model and this will be used to calculate the degree of freedom of the model. 
- ...

**Output**

This function returns a numeric value which is the reduced chi-square of the fitted model. 

```r
r.chi_cal <- function(y, model){
  if(!is.numeric(y)) {
    stop('I am so sorry, but this function only works for numeric response variable\n',
         'You have provided an object of class: ', class(y)[1])
  }
  
  if(class(model) != 'lm' & class(model) != 'nls') {
    stop('I am so sorry, but this function only works for linear or nonlinear least-squares models\n',
         'You have provided an object of class: ', class(model)[1])
  }
  
  se <- summary(model)$sigma
  chisq_val <- sum(((y - predict(model)) / se) ^ 2)
  df <- length(y) - summary(model)$df[1] + 1
  r.chi_val <- chisq_val / df
  r.chi_val
}
```

title: surpising `summarize` output when re-using variable name
description:
The `summarize` function has suprising behaviour when re-using a variable name, e.g.:

```r
foo <- tribble(
  ~a, ~b, ~c,
  0 ,  0,  1,
  0 ,  0,  2,
  0 ,  1,  3,
)
foo %>% group_by(a, b) %>%
  summarise(c=mean(c), c_sum=sum(c), c_len=length(c), n=n(), .groups = "drop")
```
```txt
# A tibble: 2 x 6
      a     b     c c_sum c_len     n
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <int> <int>
1     0     0   1.5   1.5     1     2
2     0     1   3     3       1     1
```
Notice the incorrect result of `c_sum` and `c_len`, due to `c` being updated after the `c=mean(c)` statement.
You could say I should've seen this coming, since other functions like `mutate` also work this way, but I believe the typical tidyverse user may trip up on this.
To me this seems like a typical use case in data science, e.g. for averaging out values over time intervals or such.

Maybe this situation should at least trigger a warning?
