title: `bind_rows()` has unpredictable behavior with `NA`, `NULL`, and zero-length values in list
description:
I'm sure there are some design decisions in the way `bind_rows()` handles `NA`, `NULL` and zero-length list elements when creating the final `tbl_df`. However, I would like to note the differences between `dplyr::bind_rows()`, `do.call(rbind, .)` and `data.table::rbindlist()` because it appears that {dplyr} has the most undesirable and unpredictable behavior of all 3 options.

In all of the test cases below I would, at minimum, expect the result to have 2 rows and 2 columns. Ideally, it would also preserve the column order based on the elements and replace all zero-length elements with NA (i.e. `NULL` and zero length vectors like `integer(0)` or `character(0)`).

``` r
library(data.table, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
```

**Happy path test case (preserves all elements as-is)**
``` r
first_list <- list(a = "A", b = 1)
second_list <- list(a = "B", b = 2)
l <- list(first_list, second_list)

bind_rows(l)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   a         b
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 A         1
#> 2 B         2

do.call(rbind, l)
#>      a   b
#> [1,] "A" 1
#> [2,] "B" 2

rbindlist(l, fill=TRUE)
#>    a b
#> 1: A 1
#> 2: B 2
```

**All NA elements in a list (row)**
``` r
first_list <- list(a = NA, b = NA)
second_list <- list(a = "B", b = 2)
l <- list(first_list, second_list)

# preserves first row
bind_rows(l) 
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   a         b
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 <NA>     NA
#> 2 B         2

# preserves first row
do.call(rbind, l) 
#>      a   b 
#> [1,] NA  NA
#> [2,] "B" 2

# preserves first row
rbindlist(l, fill=TRUE) 
#>       a  b
#> 1: <NA> NA
#> 2:    B  2
```

**All NULL elements in list**
``` r
first_list <- list(a = NULL, b = NULL)
second_list <- list(a = "B", b = 2)
l <- list(first_list, second_list)

# drops first row
bind_rows(l) 
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   a         b
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 B         2

# preserves first row and retains NULL values
do.call(rbind, l) 
#>      a    b   
#> [1,] NULL NULL
#> [2,] "B"  2

# drops first row
rbindlist(l, fill=TRUE)
#>    a b
#> 1: B 2
```

**A single NULL element**
``` r
first_list <- list(a = NULL, b = 1)
second_list <- list(a = "B", b = 2)
l <- list(first_list, second_list)

# preserves first row, but flips column order
bind_rows(l) 
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>       b a    
#>   <dbl> <chr>
#> 1     1 <NA> 
#> 2     2 B

# preserves first row and retains NULL value
do.call(rbind, l) 
#>      a    b
#> [1,] NULL 1
#> [2,] "B"  2

# preserves first row and returns NA value in place of NULL
rbindlist(l, fill=TRUE) 
#> Warning in rbindlist(l, fill = TRUE): Column 1 ['a'] of item 1 is length 0. This
#> (and 0 others like it) has been filled with NA (NULL for list columns) to make
#> each item uniform.
#>       a b
#> 1: <NA> 1
#> 2:    B 2
```

**A single length zero element**
``` r
first_list <- list(a = character(0), b = 1)
second_list <- list(a = "B", b = 2)
l <- list(first_list, second_list)

# drops first row
bind_rows(l) 
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   a         b
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 B         2

# preserves first row
do.call(rbind, l)
#>      a           b
#> [1,] Character,0 1
#> [2,] "B"         2

# preserves first row and returns NA in place of zero-length element
rbindlist(l, fill=TRUE) 
#> Warning in rbindlist(l, fill = TRUE): Column 1 ['a'] of item 1 is length 0. This
#> (and 0 others like it) has been filled with NA (NULL for list columns) to make
#> each item uniform.
#>       a b
#> 1: <NA> 1
#> 2:    B 2
```

title: n_distinct freezes on large table group_by-summarise
description:
Hi!

I encountered the problem with dplyr 1.0.0. If I try to do group_by and then calculate distinct combintations with function n_distinct (in summarise) the calculation freezes. The problem exists only on large tables (~50 mln rows) and dplyr version 1.0.0.
Everything works if either dplyr 0.8.5 or table is small. Memory is not full, process is running but nothing happened
I am using RStudio Server 1.3.959

```r
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(123)
table_size <- 50000000

       date = sample(x = seq(as.Date('2020/07/01'), as.Date('2020/07/18'), by="day"), size = table_size, replace = TRUE),
       column_3 = sample.int(n = 100, size = table_size, replace = T),
       column_4 = sample.int(n = 100, size = table_size, replace = T),

table_tbl %>% group_by(column_1, date, column_3, column_4, column_5) %>% 
  summarise(ndist = n_distinct(column_6, column_7)            )
```

title: group_by drops column attributes
description:
EDIT: @hadley identified the underlying issue is with grouping rather than summarize. See his post below While creating new columns using `mutate` or `summarize`, I'd like to be able to add the `label` attribute to each column so that I can add additional context to my columns at the time of creation. A useful [stackoverflow post](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/27347548/r-assign-variable-labels-of-data-frame-columns) supplied info on how to do this with `mutate`, however I've found that summarize drops the column attributes after creation (please see reprex below).
Having labels makes my data so much more understandable, and allows my customers (also R users) to get everything they need when using `view`/`View`: --- Brief description of the problem: While `mutate` and an ungrouped `summarize` maintain column attributes such as `label`, a grouped `summarize` does not. ``` r library(magrittr) library(tibble) library(dplyr) #> #> Attaching package: 'dplyr' #> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats': #> #> filter, lag #> The following objects are masked from 'package:base': #> #> intersect, setdiff, setequal, union library(Hmisc) #> Loading required package: lattice #> Loading required package: survival #> Loading required package: Formula #> Loading required package: ggplot2 #> #> Attaching package: 'Hmisc' #> The following objects are masked from 'package:dplyr': #> #> src, summarize #> The following objects are masked from 'package:base': #> #> format.pval, units mtcars = tibble::as_tibble(mtcars) # Mutate works as expected mtcars %>% dplyr::mutate(mpg_hp_ratio = mpg/hp %>% structure(label = 'Miles per Gallon to Horse Power Ratio')) %>% dplyr::pull() %>% Hmisc::label() #> [1] "Miles per Gallon to Horse Power Ratio" # Ungrouped summarize works as expected mtcars %>% dplyr::summarise(mpg_hp_ratio = mpg/hp %>% structure(label = 'Miles per Gallon to Horse Power Ratio')) %>% dplyr::pull() %>% Hmisc::label() #> [1] "Miles per Gallon to Horse Power Ratio" # Grouped summarize does not keep the label mtcars %>% dplyr::group_by(cyl) %>% dplyr::summarise(mpg_hp_ratio = mean(mpg)/mean(hp) %>% structure(label = 'Average Miles per Gallon to Horse Power Ratio')) %>% dplyr::pull() %>% Hmisc::label() #> `summarise()` ungrouping output (override with `.groups` argument) #> [1] "" ``` Created on 2020-07-20 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)

title: Include update and conflict options in join commands
description:
Hi, 

It would be great if join commands had the possibility to update values. 

For example, I am working with data frame "m" and want to update the "x" values for some NA cases using another data frame "y".  Join commands will generate two columns x.x and x.y. Then, I would have to mutate values to update variables in this new, larger data.frame. 

However, if there was an update = T option, the new data.frame could automatically update NA values from the master data-set with the columns that have the same name in the using data set. Then, no new columns will be generated, I will be working in a smaller data-set and there would be no need to do any extra steps. 

There could also be a conflict option to also manage the cases in which there are values in both the master and using data set. For example, if conflict = F, then when there are values in both master and using values then master data is retained, and nothing is changed in the column for rows that are present in master and using data. However, if conflict = T then the data from the using data set is retained. 

In STATA this is part of the  [merge](https://www.stata.com/manuals13/dmerge.pdf) command. Some people have been asking the same and making some workarounds [example](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/51572462/update-replace-values-in-dataframe-with-tidyverse-join). 
 
Thank you once again for dplyr.

```r
m <- data.frame(id  = c(1,2,3), x = c(4, 4, NA))
u <- data.frame(id  = c(1,2,3), x = c(5, 5, 5))

# Current results
m %>% full_join(u, by = "id")

# With update = T we want:
data.frame(id  = c(1,2,3), x  = c(4,4,5))

# With update = T and conflict = T we want:
data.frame(id  = c(1,2,3), x  = c(5,5,5))
# With update = T and conflict = F we want:
data.frame(id  = c(1,2,3), x  = c(4,4,5))


```

title: Mutate Drops Row Names
description:
---

Hey! I know that row names on tibbles are deprecated (which I disagree with but that is beside the point) but I think that for now, given that someone wants to continue using this deprecated feature, functions like mutate should not drop rownames in cases by default where the user wants to keep them.  There are constructs outside of the tidyverse that still use rownames; for example the bioconductor object 'eset' uses them in important ways and there are tools that take esets and not more modern bioconductor objects.   So if I want to use tibbles and dplyr verbs when constructing esets I have to do inconvenient workarounds, or not use dplyr.   So what I want is for tidyverse functions to preserve rownames wherever possible, even though I know it is not possible with certain things (like joins where rows are added). 


Here is a simple example: 
```r
library(tidyverse)
small_tibble <- mpg[1:3,1:3]
rownames(small_tibble) <- c("snap","cracke","pop")
print(rownames(small_tibble)) #setting rownames was successful
small_tibble_mutated <- small_tibble %>% mutate(displ = displ^2)
print(rownames(small_tibble_mutated)) #rownames disappeared
```

title: Control duplicate rows in joins
description:
It would be incredible if you could specify which kind of duplicates in the join variable(s) is(are) acceptable as in [the STATA merge command](https://www.stata.com/manuals13/dmerge.pdf). 

This means having the possibility to decide whether it's ok to have: 
- Duplicates in the join variables of the master data but not in the join variables of the using data (a m:1 join)
- Duplicates in the join variables of the using data but not in the join variables of the master data (a 1:m join)
- Duplicates in both cases (an m:m join)
- No duplicates (a 1:1 join)

I work in education, and some times data-sets were poorly digitized because some students appear to have been enrolled in more than one school (duplicates in the join variable).  When that happens both in the master and using data, those students multiply exponentially in the resulting data-frame, as it happens now with, for example, left_join.  You may not want that. Also, if you are not cautious enough, you may not pay attention to duplicate students, that "ninjaly" add more observations to your results. 

STATA used to have the same issue and only had two commands "merge" or "join" somehow similar to R, and did not let you decide when duplicates are acceptable (i.e duplicate information in the using data when merging students to school characteristics, school id is the join variable) and when it may not be acceptable (i.e duplicate information in the master and using data when merging a student list to a student characteristic, student id is the join variable). At some point, they made that feature feasible and it's great because it allows you to merge and make quality control in one single step. 

Thank you for your time and amazing work. Hope this helps.

title: c_across behaviour surprising (to me) due to everything() auto update
description:
Since `c_across()` is quite recent, I wanted to share an observation.
In the following, I would have expected "small" to be 1.
```r
> data.frame(x = c(1, 2), y = c(30, 40)) %>%
+   rowwise() %>%
+   mutate(big   = sum(c_across() >= 10),
+          small = sum(c_across() < 10))
# A tibble: 2 x 4
# Rowwise: 
      x     y   big small
  <dbl> <dbl> <int> <int>
1     1    30     1     2
2     2    40     1     2
```
In hindsight, I understand why this is happening: `c_across()` takes `everything()` as `cols` and during the second call "big" is added to content of `everything()`.

This can obviously be avoided by setting "x:y" in the calls to `c_across()` to bypass the calls to `everything()`.

Yet, I wonder if you did really want that multiple calls to `everything()` within a single mutate do update their scope.

title: NULL in group_by
description:
With reference to https://stackoverflow.com/questions/62898859/how-can-i-use-dplyr-across-programmatically-on-no-variables/62901180#62901180 compute_mean1 gives an error but compute_mean2 and compute_mean3 give the expected answer.   compute_mean1 uses across and fails, coimpute_mean2 uses group_by_at and works while compute_mean3 is the same as coimpute_mean1 but also has the argument .add=TRUE and gives the expected answer. Surely this should work even if .add = FALSE.

```
compute_mean1 <- function(df, grouping) { # compute grouped mean with across()
  df %>% 
    group_by(across(all_of(grouping))) %>% 
    summarise(y = mean(y), .groups = "drop")
}

compute_mean2 <- function(df, grouping) { # compute grouped mean with group_by_at()
  df %>% 
    group_by_at(grouping) %>% 
    summarise(y = mean(y), .groups = "drop")
}

compute_mean3 <- function(df, grouping) { # compute grouped mean with across()
  df %>% 
    group_by(across(all_of(grouping)), .add = TRUE) %>%
    summarise(y = mean(y), .groups = "drop")
}

library(dplyr)

my_df <- tibble("x" = c("a", "a", "b", "b"), y = 1:4)

compute_mean1(my_df, NULL)

compute_mean2(my_df, NULL)

compute_mean3(my_df, NULL)
```

title: Different output for new mutate(across()) compared to "old" mutate_at()
description:
I'm trying to convert multiple columns using dplyr 1.0.0 with the new mutate(across()) function. Using the "old" `mutate_at()` function produces the expected outcome -- the combination of `mutate()` and `across()` not. Here is a reproducible example (actually the one where I encountered the issue):

I'm using the tidytuesday dataset on coffee ratings for week 28. There are 3 columns that contain numeric information on the altitude where coffee beans originate (all starting with "altitude_"). The column `unit_of_measurement` is a character that is either "m" for meter or "ft" for feet. 

The goal is to transform the 3 altitude variables from ft to m when `unit_of_measurement == "ft"`.  Using the "old" `mutate_at` function works just fine (3.28084 is the value I use to transform 1 ft to 1 m).

Translating this to the new `mutate(across())` combination as outlined [here](https://www.tidyverse.org/blog/2020/04/dplyr-1-0-0-colwise/#why-across), I'm getting a strange output.

The columns were not transformed but instead, a new column was added called ".funs". 

I'm not sure if I have missed something when transforming to `mutate` for dplyr 1.0.0 or if this is a bug.

Any help would be much appreciated! :)

# dependencies
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytuesdayR)

# load the data
tt <- tidytuesdayR::tt_load("2020-07-07")

coffee_ratings <- tt$coffee_ratings
coffee_ratings_red <- coffee_ratings %>%
  select(starts_with("altitude_"), unit_of_measurement)
coffee_ratings_red %>% 
  print(n = 20)
#> # A tibble: 1,339 x 4

title: Possible inconsistence of across inside mutate
description:
Hi!

I try to get the name of a variable inside `mutate`. My goal is transform that variable by using it to get a value from another data frame. I have something like
```r
mtcars %>%
    mutate(mpg = !!as.character(strdata[which(strdata$var == "mpg"),]$question))
```
and I want to do something to get `"mpg"` in the dots in the next code:
```r
mtcars %>%
    mutate(across(c(mpg), ~!!as.character(strdata[which(strdata$var == ...),]$question)))
```
To test this, first I tried:
```r
> mtcars %>%
+   mutate(mpg = deparse(substitute(mpg)))
   mpg cyl  disp  hp drat    wt  qsec vs am gear carb
1  mpg   6 160.0 110 3.90 2.620 16.46  0  1    4    4
2  mpg   6 160.0 110 3.90 2.875 17.02  0  1    4    4
3  mpg   4 108.0  93 3.85 2.320 18.61  1  1    4    1
4  mpg   6 258.0 110 3.08 3.215 19.44  1  0    3    1
5  mpg   8 360.0 175 3.15 3.440 17.02  0  0    3    2
6  mpg   6 225.0 105 2.76 3.460 20.22  1  0    3    1
...
```
so, until here, all works as expected. But next, I get the inconsistence:
```r
> mtcars %>%
+   mutate(across(c(mpg), ~deparse(substitute(.))))
   mpg cyl  disp  hp drat    wt  qsec vs am gear carb
1  ..1   6 160.0 110 3.90 2.620 16.46  0  1    4    4
2  ..1   6 160.0 110 3.90 2.875 17.02  0  1    4    4
3  ..1   4 108.0  93 3.85 2.320 18.61  1  1    4    1
4  ..1   6 258.0 110 3.08 3.215 19.44  1  0    3    1
5  ..1   8 360.0 175 3.15 3.440 17.02  0  0    3    2
6  ..1   6 225.0 105 2.76 3.460 20.22  1  0    3    1
...
```
so I get `..1` instead of `mpg`. Is it expected? Is it some way to get variable name inside `across`?

Thank you!

title: Dealing with the new `summarise` messages as a package developer
description:
I'm developing a package that uses dplyr and it's `summarise()` function. With the release of dplyr 1.0, `summarise()` now sends a message every time it is used without the `.groups` argument. 

I _could_ add `.groups = "drop_last"` to each instance of `summarise()`, but I'm a little worried that since the lifecycle of this argument is labeled "experimental" that I'll need to change it again relatively soon. Is this safe to use?

I also checked, and when used in a package, `summarise()` doesn't seem to raise any messages like it would normally. If this is intentional, is this (very cool) feature documented anywhere?  I can't seem to find it, but it might be helpful to let package developers know about it.

title: dplyr 1.0.0 left_join freezes R
description:
Recently updated to `dplyr 1.0.0` on my local machine. If I try and left_join even a small `data.frame`, R freezes and I have to use `pkill rsession` to restart Rstudio. The strange part is, the behaviour is only present on my local machine, not an EC2 instance I spun up. 

Someone else also might have encountered this issue, here is a small reproducible example to test:

```r
library(dplyr)
library(vroom)
taxonomy <- vroom("https://publicdata314.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/taxonomy.csv")

#> Rows: 10
#> Columns: 6
#> Delimiter: ","
#> chr [4]: unit_name_1, unit_name_2, complete_name, kingdom_name
#> dbl [2]: tsn, kingdom_id

vernaculars <- vroom("https://publicdata314.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/vernaculars.csv")

#> Rows: 10  
#> Columns: 4
#> Delimiter: ","
#> chr [3]: vernacular_name, language, approved_ind
#> dbl [1]: tsn

# Freezes on local machine
taxonomy %>% 
  left_join(vernaculars)
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/12710800/87243633-d12f3a00-c437-11ea-8f84-a935f38ba522.png)

Things I have tried:

* Reinstall Rstudio
* Reinstall `Rccp`
* Install dplyr from `github`

For now I have resorted to installing an older version:

```r
packageurl <- "http://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/dplyr/dplyr_0.8.5.tar.gz"
install.packages(packageurl, repos=NULL, type="source")
```

title: Getting started vignette should use `!` to negate the selection instead of `-`
description:
dplyr 1.0.0 introduced boolean operators, but it seems they are not advertised. At least, since `-` is no more documented, the vignette should use `!` instead.

c.f. https://tidyselect.r-lib.org/reference/language.html

If this sounds good, I'm happy to create a pull request for this.

title: Should there be a is_rowwise_df() function?
description:
A row-wise data frame is implicitly grouped by row, but is not a `grouped_df`. This makes it so that `is_grouped_df()` returns `FALSE` when passed a row-wise data frame, and that is consistent. However, I can't seem to find an equivalent function for the `rowwise_df` class. Should there be a `is_rowwise_df()` function?

```r
library(tidyverse)
rdf <- rowwise(diamonds)
is_grouped_df(rdf)
#> [1] FALSE
is(rdf, "rowwise_df")
#> [1] TRUE
```

title: Possible bug in rowwise()?
description:
Hi, I am not sure I am missing something, of it this is really a bug. I have noticed that `rowwise()` is not working well with `ggplot2`. For example, if I have three rows, and I map columns of this row to my plot function, I am retrieving only the last plot in all the rows.

``` r

plot_this <- function(.data, x, y, label) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_point(data = .data, aes(mpg, hp)) +
    geom_point(aes(x = {{ x }}, y = {{ y }}), color = "red", size = 4) +
    geom_text(aes(x = {{ x }}, y = {{ y }}, label = {{ label }}), color = "white", fontface = "bold")
}

df <- tibble(
  data = list(mtcars),

#> # A tibble: 2 x 2

title: distinct() error with sticky geom column

library(maps)

county_sf %>% distinct(vars(ID))

I would expect this to return all rows that have distinct IDs, ignoring 'geom' and not failing with an error.

title: Package clash with fRegression
description:
Hello,

I would like to report a possible bug when using tidyverse together with the fRegression package. fRegression or its dependent packages seems to overwrite some functionalities of tidyverse, possibly dplyr, so it does no work properly.

```r
library(tidyverse)
data(diamonds)
test <- diamonds %>% filter(price > 100) # works
library(fRegression)
test <- diamonds %>% filter(price > 100) # produces an error
```
Is there a workaround for that issue available?

title: bind_rows with lists in v1.0.0 very slow
description:
I was noticing this when running code which uses `purrr:map_dfr()`, where `dplyr::bind_rows()` is used with the list output of `purrr:map()`. This operation is much slower under dplyr v1.0.0 compared to dplyr v0.8.5

I have tried to create a reprex but had to run it twice because of the different dplyr versions required to show the issue. And I have used `microbenchmark` to show runtimes. And sorry the warnings are in german and I took out my username in the session info.

Summary: `dplyr::bind_rows()` with a list under v1.0.0 takes nearly 1400 times the runtime

My current solution is using a tibble instead of a list but that's not always possible for me, still slower than the list in v0.8.5 and I wonder if this is a bug or not.

title: Inconsistent and unpredictable behaviour from group_by with .drop=FALSE
description:
The effect of the `.drop=FALSE` argument to `group_by` depends on whether the grouping variables are explicitly factors or not.

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts=FALSE)

mtcars %>%
  
  group_by(gear, am, .drop=FALSE) %>%
  
  summarise(count=n(), .groups="drop")
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>    gear    am count
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <int>
#> 1     3     0    15
#> 2     4     0     4
#> 3     4     1     8
#> 4     5     1     5

mtcars %>%
  
  mutate(am=as.factor(am)) %>%
  
  group_by(gear, am, .drop=FALSE) %>%
  
  summarise(count=n(), .groups="drop")
#> # A tibble: 6 x 3
#>    gear am    count
#>   <dbl> <fct> <int>
#> 1     3 0        15
#> 2     3 1         0
#> 3     4 0         4
#> 4     4 1         8
#> 5     5 0         0
#> 6     5 1         5
```

<sup>Created on 2020-06-30 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

Since all grouping variables are either explicitly or impicitly factors, I would expect similar behaviour in each case (unless there are additional values encoded in `levels` but not seen in the data, which is not the case here).

Some combinations of implicit and explicit factors give very strange results (note that there are no `NA`'s in `mtcars`):

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts=FALSE)

mtcars %>%
  
  mutate(am=as.factor(am)) %>%
  
  group_by(gear, am, cyl, .drop=FALSE) %>%
  
  summarise(count=n(), .groups="drop")
#> # A tibble: 12 x 4
#>     gear am      cyl count
#>    <dbl> <fct> <dbl> <int>
#>  1     3 0         4     1
#>  2     3 0         6     2
#>  3     3 0         8    12
#>  4     3 1        NA     0
#>  5     4 0         4     2
#>  6     4 0         6     2
#>  7     4 1         4     6
#>  8     4 1         6     2
#>  9     5 0        NA     0
#> 10     5 1         4     2
#> 11     5 1         6     1
#> 12     5 1         8     2
```

<sup>Created on 2020-06-30 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

To be absolutely clear, you can recover the intended and expected behaviour in these cases by converting all of the grouping variables to explicit factors:

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts=FALSE)

mtcars %>%
  
  mutate(gear=as.factor(gear), am=as.factor(am)) %>%
  
  group_by(gear, am, .drop=FALSE) %>%
  
  summarise(count=n(), .groups="drop")
#> # A tibble: 6 x 3
#>   gear  am    count
#>   <fct> <fct> <int>
#> 1 3     0        15
#> 2 3     1         0
#> 3 4     0         4
#> 4 4     1         8
#> 5 5     0         0
#> 6 5     1         5

mtcars %>%
  
  mutate(gear=as.factor(gear), am=as.factor(am), cyl=as.factor(cyl)) %>%
  
  group_by(gear, am, cyl, .drop=FALSE) %>%
  
  summarise(count=n(), .groups="drop")
#> # A tibble: 18 x 4
#>    gear  am    cyl   count
#>    <fct> <fct> <fct> <int>
#>  1 3     0     4         1
#>  2 3     0     6         2
#>  3 3     0     8        12
#>  4 3     1     4         0
#>  5 3     1     6         0
#>  6 3     1     8         0
#>  7 4     0     4         2
#>  8 4     0     6         2
#>  9 4     0     8         0
#> 10 4     1     4         6
#> 11 4     1     6         2
#> 12 4     1     8         0
#> 13 5     0     4         0
#> 14 5     0     6         0
#> 15 5     0     8         0
#> 16 5     1     4         2
#> 17 5     1     6         1
#> 18 5     1     8         2
```

title: pull() equivalent to accept expressions
description:
`pull()` only accepts a a column name/position as argument, what makes it equivalent to `$` or `'[['()`, except for quotation.
Most of the times I use `pull()` after a `transmute()` or `mutate()` call. In fact, even in `pull()`'s documentation, the example does the same:

```r
df %>%
  mutate(z = x * y) %>%
  pull()
}
```

It cannot accept an expression such as `pull(x*z)` because it would break the current implementation, e.g., `pull(-x)` would be ambiguous. Would it be interesting to have a single function equivalent to a `mutate() %>% pull()` chain?

title: `all_equal()` lacks a `name_repair` parameter
description:
Since dplyr 1.0, I get messages about "new names" when comparing dataframes with columns having non-universal names:

```r
mtcars2 <- dplyr::rename(mtcars, "m p g" = mpg)

dplyr::all_equal(target = mtcars2,
                 current = mtcars2)
#> New names:
#> * `m p g` -> m.p.g
#> New names:
#> * `m p g` -> m.p.g
#> [1] TRUE
```
<sup>Created on 2020-06-23 by the reprex package (v0.3.0)</sup>

I'd like to avoid these name conversion but `all_equal()` doesn't know a `name_repair` (or `.name_repair`) argument as e.g. `tibble::as_tibble()` does.

Internally, `dplyr::all_equal()` calls the unexported `dplyr:::equal_data_frame()` which calls `dplyr::as_tibble()` with a hard-coded `.name_repair = "universal"`.

I guess this argument could just be exposed all the way through `all_equal()` which would allow me to avoid these name conversions, right? Any objections? I'd be happy to submit a PR for this if that is approved.

title: Odd behaviour with ifelse() and grouped mutate()
description:
Continuing a discussion from [this RStudio Community thread](https://community.rstudio.com/t/mutate-multiple-columns-if-grouping-variable-has-all-observations-missing/70206/4). The OP was attempting to modify rows within each group if all the rows for that group were `NA` (leave them as-is otherwise).

Seemed like a pretty straightforward application of `ifelse()`. But this attempt generates an incorrect result for group C (values should be returned as-is since it contains only 1 `NA`).

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

df <- tibble(num = c(NA, NA, 1, 1, NA, 1), 
             grp = c("A", "A", "B", "B", "C", "C"))

df %>% 
  group_by(grp) %>% 
  mutate(num = ifelse(sum(is.na(num)) == n(), 999, num))
#> # A tibble: 6 x 2
#> # Groups:   grp [3]
#>     num grp  
#>   <dbl> <chr>
#> 1   999 A    
#> 2   999 A    
#> 3     1 B    
#> 4     1 B    
#> 5    NA C    
#> 6    NA C
```

But breaking down the `mutate()` call into two sub-steps works.

``` r
df %>% 
  group_by(grp) %>% 
  mutate(lgl_test = sum(is.na(num)) == n(),
         num = ifelse(lgl_test == TRUE, 999, num))
#> # A tibble: 6 x 3
#> # Groups:   grp [3]
#>     num grp   lgl_test
#>   <dbl> <chr> <lgl>   
#> 1   999 A     TRUE    
#> 2   999 A     TRUE    
#> 3     1 B     FALSE   
#> 4     1 B     FALSE   
#> 5    NA C     FALSE   
#> 6     1 C     FALSE
```

However, `dplyr::if_else()` hints at what's going wrong. It seems that the comparison isn't performed element-wise because `num` is of length 2 (the group size).

``` r
df %>% 
  group_by(grp) %>% 
  mutate(num = if_else(sum(is.na(num)) == n(), 999, num))
#> Error: Problem with `mutate()` input `num`.
#> x `false` must be length 1 (length of `condition`), not 2.
#> i Input `num` is `if_else(sum(is.na(num)) == n(), 999, num)`.
#> i The error occured in group 1: grp = "A".
```

Breaking down into two steps works as with `ifelse()`.

``` r
df %>% 
  group_by(grp) %>% 
  mutate(lgl_test = sum(is.na(num)) == n(),
         num = if_else(lgl_test == TRUE, 999, num))
#> # A tibble: 6 x 3
#> # Groups:   grp [3]
#>     num grp   lgl_test
#>   <dbl> <chr> <lgl>   
#> 1   999 A     TRUE    
#> 2   999 A     TRUE

df <- tibble(

my_summarise <- function(df, group_var) {

    group_by(!!group_var) %>%
    summarise(a = mean(a))
}

my_summarise(df, quo(g1))

##

my_summarise <- function(df, group_var) {
  group_var <- enquo(group_var)
  print(group_var)
  
  df %>%
    group_by(!! group_var) %>%
    summarise(a = mean(a))
}

my_summarise(df, g1)

##

my_mutate <- function(df, expr) {
  expr <- enquo(expr)
  mean_name <- paste0("mean_", quo_name(expr))
  sum_name <- paste0("sum_", quo_name(expr))
  
  mutate(df,
         !! mean_name := mean(!! expr),
         !! sum_name := sum(!! expr)
  )
}

my_mutate(df, a)

title: Feature Request: Make bind_rows() gives more specific errors
description:
When binding a long list of data.frames with many columns each, it would help if error messages gave information about both what tables were giving the error and what columns in the tables were causing the problems.

The error message below of:

```
Error: `x` must be a vector with type <double>.
Instead, it has type <double>.
```

does not indicate what the problem is under the surface.  A few different items here would help:

* Please make the errors with `bind_rows()` indicate which column has the error.  (That took a long time to track down because I had about 50 columns.)
* Please make errors with `bind_rows()` indicate which input tables are giving the error.  (That also took a long-ish time to track down because in addition to having about 50 columns, I was binding a list of 15 different data.frames.)
* ~~This appears to be an issue binding doubles with different attributes.  I couldn't make a reprex that didn't use `hms()` rapidly, but if `A2 <- 1`, then there was no error.  I know that handling attributes can be a difficult question, but I don't think that the code I have below should cause an error (at least since currently `double` is coerced to a `hms` as is indicated by the warning).~~
    * As I was writing this issue, I realized that the error message is coming from `hms()`, so I will open that part over there.  But, the first two hold because the `bind_rows()` error message being more specific could have helped save significant troubleshooting time.

library(hms)
library(dplyr)

title: Suggestion: Add argument `keep_grouping_vars` to cur_data()
description:
The new `cur_data()` in `dplyr` is fantastic. However, it does not yet serve as a full replacement of `do`. Why? According to its docu, it excludes the grouping variables. I suppose this is to ensure that the same variable name does not appear twice in the resulting data.frame. 

Would it be possible to add an argument `keep_grouping_vars = FALSE` to `cur_data` where this could be overwritten?

Here is an example:

```
library(dplyr)

iris %>% 
  group_by(Species) %>% 
  summarize(should_by_five = ncol(cur_data()))

# Output
  Species    should_by_five
  <fct>               <int>
1 setosa                  4
2 versicolor              4
3 virginica               4
```

This is my suggestion:

```
iris %>% 
  group_by(Species) %>% 
  summarize(should_by_five = ncol(cur_data(keep_grouping_vars = TRUE)))
```

The current workaround:

```
iris %>% 
  group_by(Species) %>% 
  summarize(should_by_five = ncol(bind_cols(cur_group(), cur_data())))
```

title: Does if_else always evaluate both 'true' and 'false' regardless of 'condition'?
description:
It appears to me that `if_else` evaluates both the `true` and `false` arguments, and then returns only the one that matches the `condition` argument. This differs from `ifelse` which appears to only evaluate the `true` or `false` argument that matches the `condition` argument. 

This is a problem if `if_else` is being used to avoid evaluating an expression that is know to fail in certain situations. Is this necessary to ensure "that `true` and `false` are the same type."? What would be a `tidyverse` way of handling this? 

``` r

x <- list("a", 1, 2, "b")

sapply(x, function(x) ifelse(is.numeric(x), x + 1, NaN)) 
#> [1] NaN   2   3 NaN
sapply(x, function(x) dplyr::if_else(is.numeric(x), x + 1, NaN))
#> Error in x + 1: non-numeric argument to binary operator
```

title: Disallow grouping by column named `.rows`
description:
with a clean error message.

## Original post

I'm not sure if this is really a bug but may warrant a warning message / change in the documentation.

In the documentation for the [`tibble`](https://tibble.tidyverse.org/reference/tibble.html) function one of the examples says

```r
# Use := to create columns with names that start with a dot:
tibble(.rows = 3)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 0
tibble(.rows := 3)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 1
#>   .rows
#>   <dbl>
#> 1     3
```
However if a user actually creates a tibble with a column named `.rows` then grouping will later cause an error

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(rlang, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

# this doesn't work
dat <- tibble(x = 1:10, .rows := rep(c("bob", "george"), 5))
dat %>% group_by(.data$.rows)
#> Error: Column name `.rows` must not be duplicated.

# changing to another name beginning with a dot will work
dat <- tibble(x = 1:10, .cows := rep(c("bob", "george"), 5))
dat %>% group_by(.data$.cows)
#> # A tibble: 10 x 2
#> # Groups:   .cows [2]
#>        x .cows 
#>    <int> <chr> 
#>  1     1 bob   
#>  2     2 george
#>  3     3 bob   
#>  4     4 george
#>  5     5 bob   
#>  6     6 george
#>  7     7 bob   
#>  8     8 george
#>  9     9 bob   
#> 10    10 george
```

I'm not sure if this can be protected against but if not maybe it would be useful to have a warning next to the example.

title: unexpected column order when moving multiple columns with relocate and .after=last_col()
description:
When selecting multiple columns with `relocate`, I would expect them to end up at the new location in the order I specified them in. This usually works, but it behaves unexpectedly in one particular case: when using (`after=last_col()`) and the last column is part of the columns to be relocated.

```r
df <- tibble(x=1, y=2, z=3)
relocate(df, y, z, .after=x) # x, y, z
relocate(df, z, y, .after=x) # x, z, y
relocate(df, y, z, .after=last_col()) # x, z, y << unexpected
relocate(df, z, y, .after=last_col()) # x, z, y
```
I might be off with my expectation here, but at least going by semantics ("move a bunch of columns to the end"), I feel like this specification should work...

title: coalesce() function "Must subset elements with valid subscript vector"
description:
Hi,

I have historically been able to wrap the coalesce() function with a function that will identify suffixed columns in a dataframe and coalesce accordingly.
However, after updating to v.1.0.0, the functionality appears to be broken due to the following exception:
"Must subset elements with a valid subscript vector."



---

Brief description of the problem

```r
library(dplyr)

coalesce_df_fields <- function(df, suffix_a, suffix_b) {
  suffix_a <- paste0('(',suffix_a,')$')
  suffix_b <- paste0('(',suffix_b,')$')

  fields_a <- data.frame(fields_a = colnames(df)[grepl(suffix_a, colnames(df))]) %>%
    mutate(root = gsub(suffix_a, '', fields_a))
  
  fields_b <- data.frame(fields_b = colnames(df)[grepl(suffix_b, colnames(df))]) %>%
    mutate(root = gsub(suffix_b, '', fields_b)) %>%
    filter(fields_b != 'not_in_sf')
  
  colname_ref <- fields_a %>% full_join(fields_b, by = 'root')
  ## LOOP: Need to create new field "root" in df that coalesces "fields_a" and "fields_b" values
  df[colname_ref$root] <- coalesce(df[colname_ref$fields_a], df[colname_ref$fields_b])
  
  return(df)
  
}

## use case of the function:

sample_df <- data.frame(id = c('a', 'b', 'c', 'd'),
                 int_x = c(NA, 5, NA, 8),
                 char_x = c('14', NA, 'hello', 'what'),
                 int_y = c(100, 389, 90, 9),
                 char_y = c('this', 'should', 'fill', 'in'))

df <- coalesce_df_fields(sample_df, '_x', '_y')

```

title: case_when() evaluating all RHS expressions except only the ones matching LHS
description:
According to one example in the function documentation

```r
# case_when() evaluates all RHS expressions, and then constructs its
# result by extracting the selected (via the LHS expressions) parts.
# In particular NaN are produced in this case:
y <- seq(-2, 2, by = .5)
case_when(
  y >= 0 ~ sqrt(y),
  TRUE   ~ y
)
```
Wouldn't it be better to only evaluate the RHS for the instances where the LHS is TRUE and then paste these evaluations together? 

If there are five cases evenly distributed across the vector, this means five times more computations. Yes, vectorization is fast, but it's faster to not do computations one is not interested in anyway.

title: Replacing group_by_at(NULL) using across
description:
([I posted it  also to stackoverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/62277996/replacing-group-by-atnull-using-across?noredirect=1#comment110151810_62277996))

Before, I used `group_by_at` to group by a vector of strings or by NULL:
```r
library(tidyverse)

grouping_1 <- c("cyl", "vs")
grouping_2 <- NULL

mtcars %>% group_by_at(grouping_1) 
mtcars %>% group_by_at(grouping_2) 
```
The help of `group_by_at` indicates that the function is superseded and that `across` should be used instead. But, grouping by NULL gives an error

```r

```

For me, `group_by_at` used in the way described has been useful because in my functions I can use the same code without checking every time whether the grouping argument is empty (NULL) or not.

title: Right outer join reorders by LHS (unexpected behavior)
description:
In the earlier version, `right_join` maintained the RHS order. 
Since `dplyr` version 1.0.0, `right_join` reorders the resulting tibble according to the LHS's `by` argument. 

Reprex: Let's say I want to attach the matching rows of tibble `df_1` to the shorter tibble `df_2` by common elements of the variable `Letrs`:
```r 
library(tidyverse)
(df_1 <- tibble(Stri = replicate(26,paste0(sample(letters,1),sample(1:40,1))), 
                Letrs = rev(letters)[1:26]))
# # A tibble: 26 x 2
#    Stri  Letrs
#    <chr> <chr>
#  1 m37p  z    
#  2 t2p   y    
#  3 t37w  x    
#  4 o27p  w    
#  5 f26a  v    
#  6 t39x  u    
#  7 o30p  t    
#  8 u14w  s    
#  9 h40q  r    
# 10 y3t   q    
# # ... with 16 more rows

(df_2 <- tibble(Letrs = letters[1:10], 
                Nmbrs = seq(10)) )
# # A tibble: 10 x 2
#    Letrs Nmbrs
#    <chr> <int>
#  1 a         1
#  2 b         2
#  3 c         3
#  4 d         4
#  5 e         5
#  6 f         6
#  7 g         7
#  8 h         8
#  9 i         9
# 10 j        10
```


In earlier versions, I got a result like this: 
```r
# # A tibble: 10 x 3
#    Stri  Letrs Nmbrs
#    <chr> <chr> <int>
#  1 l2q   a         1
#  2 i4n   b         2
#  3 i38d  c         3
#  4 n3c   d         4
#  5 n3r   e         5
#  6 t19v  f         6
#  7 w6y   g         7
#  8 k33f  h         8
#  9 k21b  i         9
# 10 j5y   j        10
```
Since 1.0.0, however, `right_join` reorders resulting table by LHS: 
```r
right_join(df_1, df_2, by = "Letrs")
# # A tibble: 10 x 3
#    Stri  Letrs Nmbrs
#    <chr> <chr> <int>
#  1 j5y   j        10
#  2 k21b  i         9
#  3 k33f  h         8
#  4 w6y   g         7
#  5 t19v  f         6
#  6 n3r   e         5
#  7 n3c   d         4
#  8 i38d  c         3
#  9 i4n   b         2
# 10 l2q   a         1
```
This does not change the result with regards to content: If ordered by the variable `Stri`, for example, both tibbles are identical. 

If this happens on purpose, I missed it in the release notes.

title: Can't use 'recover' with dplyr 1.0.0. How to interactively debug?
description:
I've noticed that `recover = TRUE` is now seemingly unusable with dplyr.

For example this code
```r
library(tidyverse)

mtc <- mtcars

set.seed(1111)
rand_na <- function(vec) {
  index_na  <- rdunif(15, a = 1, b = length(vec))
  vec[index_na] <- NA
  vec
}

mtc$cyl <- rand_na(mtcars$cyl)

mtc %>%
  group_by(carb) %>%
  nest() %>%
  mutate(model = map(data, ~lm(mpg ~ cyl + hp + wt,
                               data = .x)))
```

Produces this stack of frames:

```r
Enter a frame number, or 0 to exit

 2: withVisible(eval(quote(`_fseq`(`_lhs`)), env, env))

10: mutate.data.frame(., model = map(data, ~lm(mpg ~ cyl + hp + wt, data = .x))
11: mutate_cols(.data, ...)
12: tryCatch({
    for (i in seq_along(dots)) {
        not_named <- (is.null(d
13: tryCatchList(expr, classes, parentenv, handlers)
14: tryCatchOne(expr, names, parentenv, handlers[[1]])
15: value[[3]](cond)
16: stop_dplyr(i, dots, fn = "mutate", problem = conditionMessage(e), parent = 
17: abort(bullets, class = "dplyr_error", error_name = error_name, error_expres
18: signal_abort(cnd)
```

And I haven't been able to actually find the call to `lm` burried in there, since I seem to hit some c code in `mutate_cols` that breaks the chain.

Just shy of a year ago I made a [video of myself debugging this error with recover](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M5n_2jmdJ_8&t=730s). So we can look at what the stack of frames was then:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9996346/83993364-8c2a6a80-a996-11ea-8ace-1ce608d72047.png)

And we can see, I had access to `lm` and `lm.fit`, where the error is occurring.

IMHO this is a real shame as `recover` was a really efficient technique for jumping to the source of an error and tinkering with offending code to understand why it was breaking. In the latest `dplyr` we do get a handy error message:

In this case it might be enough, but in more complex cases, like the second error I debug in the video, and the case I just had today it won't be. 

I'm looking at writing a lot of code, overloading other people's functions, and messing around with environments to get to a situation where I can debug an error right at the point it fails.

I had a look at `rlang::last_error` and it seems like it almost has all the pieces I'd need to re-run the offending function with debugOnce. So that got me thinking that maybe `rlang` could bring this facility back with something like `rlang::debug_last_error`. That might be jumping the gun though. Maybe I am just stuck in the old way of doing things.

Is there another  pathway to get to interactive debugging with `dplyr`, like what I was doing with `recover`?

title: Group_nest and nest_by class, problem with pivot_longer
description:
I'm not sure if this is an expected behavior of `group_nest` and `nest_by`. They generate a different class than "list ()", compared to nest (). There is generally no "problem" with this, but I have recently encountered problems using `pivot_longer` or `pivot_wider`. It seems to recognize the classes generated by `group_nest` and `nest_by` as strange.

Here a reprex:

``` r
library(tidyverse)

# 1. Using group_nest()
df <- mtcars %>% 
  group_nest(cyl) %>% 
  mutate(
    data2 = map(data, 
                ~ filter(.x, hp >= 95))
  )

df %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = data:data2,
    names_to = "type_data",
    values_to = "df"
  )
#> Error: Can't combine `data` <list_of<
#>   tbl_df<
#>     mpg : double
#>     disp: double
#>     hp  : double
#>     drat: double
#>     wt  : double
#>     qsec: double
#>     vs  : double
#>     am  : double
#>     gear: double
#>     carb: double
#>   >
#> >> and `data2` <list>.

# 2. Using nest_by()
df2 <- mtcars %>% 
  nest_by(cyl) %>% 
  mutate(
    data2 = list(filter(data, hp >= 95))
  )

df2 %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = data:data2,
    names_to = "type_data",
    values_to = "df"
  )
#> Error: Can't combine `data` <list_of<
#>   tbl_df<
#>     mpg : double
#>     disp: double
#>     hp  : double
#>     drat: double
#>     wt  : double
#>     qsec: double
#>     vs  : double
#>     am  : double
#>     gear: double
#>     carb: double
#>   >
#> >> and `data2` <list>.

# 3. Using nest()
df3 <- mtcars %>% 
  group_by(cyl) %>%  
  nest() %>% 
  mutate(
    data2 = map(data, 
                ~ filter(.x, hp >= 95))
  )

df3 %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = data:data2,
    names_to = "type_data",
    values_to = "df"
  )
#> # A tibble: 6 x 3
#> # Groups:   cyl [3]
#>     cyl type_data df                
#>   <dbl> <chr>     <list>            
#> 1     6 data      <tibble [7 × 10]> 
#> 2     6 data2     <tibble [7 × 10]> 
#> 3     4 data      <tibble [11 × 10]>
#> 4     4 data2     <tibble [4 × 10]> 
#> 5     8 data      <tibble [14 × 10]>
#> 6     8 data2     <tibble [14 × 10]>
```

title: Global option for .groups argument to summarise
description: There’s a new message that prints when no explicit value is supplied for the .groups argument to summarise(). It would be great to have a global option to choose the default, then suppressing the warning thereafter so users don’t have to go through and set it explicitly throughout their codebase.

title: slice_sample() behaving differently than sample_n()
description:
A really useful feature of `sample_n()` is the ability to vary `size` by the grouping variable(s):

```r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '1.0.0'

set.seed(123223)

starwars %>%
  select(name, sex, homeworld) %>%
  add_count(sex, homeworld, name = "number") %>%
  group_by(sex, homeworld) %>%
  sample_n(size = case_when(
    number %in% 1:4 ~ 1,
    number >= 5 ~ 2
  )) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(desc(number), homeworld)
#> # A tibble: 64 x 4
#>    name                sex    homeworld number
#>    <chr>               <chr>  <chr>      <int>
#>  1 Owen Lars           male   Tatooine       6
#>  2 Darth Vader         male   Tatooine       6
#>  3 Jar Jar Binks       male   Naboo          5
#>  4 Rugor Nass          male   Naboo          5
#>  5 Finn                male   <NA>           5
#>  6 Yoda                male   <NA>           5
#>  7 Dormé               female Naboo          3
#>  8 BB8                 none   <NA>           3
#>  9 Bail Prestor Organa male   Alderaan       2
#> 10 Wedge Antilles      male   Corellia       2
#> # … with 54 more rows
```

Switching to `sample_n()`'s successor `slice_sample()` yields a different number of rows:

```r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '1.0.0'

set.seed(123223)

starwars %>%
  select(name, sex, homeworld) %>%
  add_count(sex, homeworld, name = "number") %>%
  group_by(sex, homeworld) %>%
  slice_sample(n = case_when(
    "number" %in% 1:4 ~ 1,
    "number" >= 5 ~ 2
  )) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(desc(number), homeworld)
#> # A tibble: 75 x 4
#>    name              sex    homeworld number
#>    <chr>             <chr>  <chr>      <int>
#>  1 Cliegg Lars       male   Tatooine       6
#>  2 Biggs Darklighter male   Tatooine       6
#>  3 Palpatine         male   Naboo          5
#>  4 Rugor Nass        male   Naboo          5
#>  5 Qui-Gon Jinn      male   <NA>           5
#>  6 Finn              male   <NA>           5
#>  7 Dormé             female Naboo          3
#>  8 Padmé Amidala     female Naboo          3
#>  9 R4-P17            none   <NA>           3
#> 10 BB8               none   <NA>           3
#> # … with 65 more rows
```

`sample_n()` is behaving as I would expect: returning one sample per combination of `sex` and `homeworld` when said combination occurs between 1 and 4 times; and two samples per combination when there are 5 or more occurrences.

Maybe I'm doing something wrong, but `slice_sample()` is returning two samples for all combinations of `sex` and `homeworld`, regardless of the number of times said combination occurs, except for combinations which only occur once, which can only return one sample.

title: Default behavior of count() seems to have changed in 1.0.0
description:
Noticed that the default behavior of count() has changed in 1.0.0 but wasn't listed as a breaking change in the release notes

0.8.5
``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '0.8.5'
tibble(x = 1:3, n = 3:1) %>% count(x)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>       x     n
#>   <int> <int>
#> 1     1     1
#> 2     2     1
#> 3     3     1
```
1.0.0
``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '1.0.0'
tibble(x = 1:3, n = 3:1) %>% count(x)
#> Using `n` as weighting variable
#> ℹ Quiet this message with `wt = n` or count rows with `wt = 1`
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>       x     n
#>   <int> <int>
#> 1     1     3
#> 2     2     2
#> 3     3     1
```

title: Behaviour of the new `nest_by()` function
description:
I am playing with the new version of dplyr and I am facing an error when using the new `nest_by()` function. The first two versions of the code work, but fail on the third one. Is it expected?

``` r
library(tidyverse)

iris %>% 
  group_by(Species) %>% 
  nest() %>% 
  mutate(n = map_int(data, nrow))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#> # Groups:   Species [3]
#>   Species    data                  n
#>   <fct>      <list>            <int>
#> 1 setosa     <tibble [50 × 4]>    50
#> 2 versicolor <tibble [50 × 4]>    50
#> 3 virginica  <tibble [50 × 4]>    50

iris %>% 
  group_nest(Species) %>% 
  mutate(n = map_int(data, nrow))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#>   Species                  data     n
#>   <fct>      <list<tbl_df[,4]>> <int>
#> 1 setosa               [50 × 4]    50
#> 2 versicolor           [50 × 4]    50
#> 3 virginica            [50 × 4]    50

iris %>% 
  nest_by(Species) %>% 
  mutate(n = map_int(data, nrow))
#> Error: Problem with `mutate()` input `n`.
#> x Result 1 must be a single integer, not NULL of length 0
#> ℹ Input `n` is `map_int(data, nrow)`.
#> ℹ The error occured in row 1.
```

I discovered that I can avoid using `map_int()` and it will work.

``` r
iris %>% 
  nest_by(Species) %>% 
  mutate(n = nrow(data))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#> # Rowwise:  Species
#>   Species                  data     n
#>   <fct>      <list<tbl_df[,4]>> <int>
#> 1 setosa               [50 × 4]    50
#> 2 versicolor           [50 × 4]    50
#> 3 virginica            [50 × 4]    50
```

title: 'scalar chr' type cannot be joined to a 'chr' type
description:
Hello,

I have a code which has been working for a long time. However, now I recreated the image and dplyr was updated to 1.0.0

I have a list which is turned to a tibble by bind_rows and then this tibble is joined to another one by `unique_id` variable. After the 1.0.0 update, bind_rows turns the type of `unique_id` to `'scalar' chr`. When this tibble is joined I get: 


>   tibbleFromListWithBindRows <- initialList %>% 
       map("desiredValues") %>% 
       bind_rows

> resultNeeded <- initialilTibble %>% 
         right_join(
           tibbleFromListWithBindRows,
           by = "unique_id"
         )

    Error: Can't join on `x$unique_id` x `y$unique_id` because of incompatible types.
    ℹ `x$unique_id` is of type character.
    ℹ `y$unique_id` is of type scalar.

> class(tibbleFromListWithBindRows$searchId)
[1] "scalar"    "character"
> typeof(tibbleFromListWithBindRows$searchId)
[1] "character"


In order to fix this I did: 

> resultNeeded <- initialilTibble %>% 
         right_join(
           tibbleFromListWithBindRows %>%
              mutate(unique_id = as.character(unique_id)),
           by = "unique_id"
         )

However, this seems like an ugly fix. Is this behavior intended, and if yes, why?

Also, where did these scalar types came from? 
I cannot find any documentation of them being mentioned in the release [notes](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/releases/tag/v1.0.0).

P.S. Sorry for not being able to include a reproducible example. I tried but failed.

title: select() does not preserve attributes for data frames
description:
According to the documentation, `select()` should preserve attributes ("Data frame attributes are preserved." in section Value). However, this seems to work only for tibbles, not for data frames. This is an reproducible example:

```
mtcars_df <- mtcars
attr(mtcars_df, "test") <- TRUE
mtcars_tib <- as_tibble(mtcars_df)
attr(mtcars_df, "test")
attr(mtcars_tib, "test")

attr(dplyr::select(mtcars_df), "test")
attr(dplyr::select(mtcars_tib), "test")
```

With dplyr 0.8.5, all the four calls of `attr()` return `TRUE` as expected. But with dplyr 1.0.0, `attr(dplyr::select(mtcars_df), "test")` returns `NULL`.

The result does not change, if some columns are selected.

title: Error in dplyr 1.0.0 when using mutate on objects extending data.frame
description:
Since `dplyr 1.0.0`, when you use `mutate` on custom objects that inherit from `data.frame`, an error is thrown depending on the place of `data.frame` on the list of classes.

If `data.frame` is the last class in the list, the function performs normally, else, it throws this surprising error message: 

> Error: `x` must be a vector, not a `data.frame/myobject2` object.

Using `as.data.frame` beforehand has no effect but using `as_tibble` makes it right again.

Here is a reproducible example:

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
tmp=iris
class(tmp) = c("myobject", "data.frame")
tmp %>% mutate(Sepal.Length=Sepal.Length*2) %>% head(2)
#>   Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species
#> 1         10.2         3.5          1.4         0.2  setosa
#> 2          9.8         3.0          1.4         0.2  setosa
class(tmp) = c("data.frame", "myobject2")
tmp %>% mutate(Sepal.Length=Sepal.Length*2) %>% head(2)
#> Error: `x` must be a vector, not a `data.frame/myobject2` object.
tmp %>% as.data.frame %>% mutate(Sepal.Length=Sepal.Length*2) %>% head(2)
#> Error: `x` must be a vector, not a `data.frame/myobject2` object.
class(tmp) = c("myobject", "data.frame", "myobject2")
tmp %>% mutate(Sepal.Length=Sepal.Length*2) %>% head(2)
#> Error: `x` must be a vector, not a `myobject/data.frame/myobject2` object.
tmp %>% as.data.frame %>% mutate(Sepal.Length=Sepal.Length*2) %>% head(2)
#> Error: `x` must be a vector, not a `data.frame/myobject2` object.
tmp %>% as_tibble %>% mutate(Sepal.Length=Sepal.Length*2) %>% head(2)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 5
#>   Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species
#>          <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <fct>  
#> 1         10.2         3.5          1.4         0.2 setosa 
#> 2          9.8         3            1.4         0.2 setosa
```

title: Weird behaviour with dplyr 1.0 while modifying NA level of a factor
description:
Hi,

I have found, after upgrading to dplyr 1.0, that there is a weird behaviour in the interaction between group_by and mutate.

The thing is that while working with dplyr 0.8.5 I had a dataset which I grouped by date and then modified the NA level of another variable to finally make a plot. It worked nicely (besides the warnings that you can see in the reprex below, I wasn't aware of them till I made the reprex because the code was originally in an rmarkdown file with warnings set to off).

When I upgraded to dplyr 1.0 (and R 4.0) the levels of the variable where not correctly ordered (look at the legend in the first plot in the R 4.0 reprex).

I solved the problem by putting the mutate sentence before the grouping sentence, I don't understand why grouping should modify the action of fct_explicit_na() because I think that the lattter just substitutes NA for some other string.

I realize that to modify the factors before grouping the dataset may be more logical, but there is a clear different behaviour between the two versions of dplyr (I'm blaming dplyr for the issue but  maybe it is also due to the R 4.0 upgrade). 

In brief, with dplyr 0.8.5 the job was done right but with warnings but with dplyr 1.0 the job is incorrectly done and without warnings so I think that this may compromise the reproducibility of some projects or analysis.

Maybe the only weird behaviour was mine while ordering the sentences in the pipeline to get the plot.

Don't you think that the newer version should at least warn the user about this issue?

title: filter() removes variable labels
description:
Since upgrading to R 4.0, `dplyr::filter` now strips the variable labels. This is similar to [this previous issue](https://github.com/larmarange/labelled/issues/39). However, I have only found the problem to occur with `filter`. Other `dplyr` functions like `group_by`, `mutate`, and `select` all preserve the value labels.

---

I'm running R version 4.0.0 and dplyr version 0.8.5.

```r
# some labelled data
labelled_df <- structure(list(sex = structure(c(1, 2, 2, 2, 1, 2), 
                                              label = "Sex", 
                                              labels = c(Male = 1,
                                                         Female = 2), 
                                              class = "haven_labelled"), 
                              educ6 = structure(c(2, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2), 
                                                label = "Education with 6 categories", 
                                                labels = c(`LT HS` = 1, HS = 2, 
                                                           `Some Col` = 3, AA = 4, BA = 5, `Post-BA` = 6), 
                                                class = "haven_labelled"), 
                              age = structure(c(29, 28, 82, 72, 75, 60), 
                                              format.stata = "%9.0g")), 
                         row.names = c(NA, -6L),
                         class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))


# The problem, dplyr::filter strips the labels
labelled_df %>%
  filter(sex == 1)

# select works fine
labelled_df %>%
  select(1:2)

# group_by and summarize work fine too
labelled_df %>%
  group_by(sex) %>%
  summarise(age = mean(age))

# it's possible to use labelled:copy_labels_from as a workaround
labelled_df %>%
  filter(sex == 1) %>%
  labelled::copy_labels_from(labelled_df)
```

title: group_by / summarise on empty data frame behaves weirdly.
description:
A `group_by() %>% summarise()` on an empty tibble creates a 1-row tibble and some warnings.
I'd expect it to just return a 0-row tibble with the grouping variable.

This would be useful in a case where we want to aggregate results but don't know a priori whether there are any matching rows to aggregate.

As-is, the case `nrow(.) == 0` needs special treatment.

NB I did not test this in the development version yet.

library(dplyr)

title: count() has had major breaking changes
description:
Count used to work twice in a row to find out how many count values you had, eg:

Counting a combination of vars, and then counting the n would produce a result that told you how many times you had a count of, say, 1 or 2, etc.

Ie, you'd get this:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/25590353/82705497-fcb25700-9c34-11ea-850c-dc8a7da71803.png)

However, now you get an error:

``` r
require(tidyverse)
#> Loading required package: tidyverse

mtcars %>% 
  count(cyl, gear) %>% 
  count(n)
#> Using `n` as weighting variable
#> Error: Column `n` is already present in output.
#> ℹ Use `name = "new_name"` to pick a new name.
```

And if you give the second count a name so as to avoid the conflict, it auto-weights, so the result still is not what was produced originally.

``` r
require(tidyverse)
#> Loading required package: tidyverse

mtcars %>% 
  count(cyl, gear) %>% 
  count(n, name = "nn")
#> Using `n` as weighting variable
#>    n nn
#> 1  1  2
#> 2  2  6
#> 3  4  4
#> 4  8  8
#> 5 12 12
```

While I get that there are ways around this, it seems like an unexpected assumption that a weight should be applied, and it also requires a lot of recoding old things.

title: General lead/lag function (allow negative numbers)
description:
I am suggesting creating a general lead/lag function that can take in both positive and negative integers and generate leads and lags respectively. I understand the idea of not allowing negative integers in the current format, to catch potential user errors, but this situation also duplicates code for what is essentially a single function, just separated in two. I propose an example in the following reprex.

``` r
suppressMessages(library(dplyr))
library(purrr)

# I want to create versions of the same dataset where a variable is in leads or lags

# current method
mtcars_leads <- map(0L:3L, ~mtcars %>% mutate(shift_wt = lead(wt, n = .x)))
mtcars_lags <- map(1L:3L,  ~mtcars %>% mutate(shift_wt = lag(wt, n = .x)))
final_list <- map(c(rev(mtcars_lags), mtcars_leads), ~.)

# desired general function
leadlag <- function(x, n, ...) {
  
  # insert appropriate argument and type checking
    
  # core function
    if (n >= 0) {
      return(lead(x, n, ...))
    }
    
    if (n < 0) {
      return(lag(x, abs(n), ...))
    }
}

# single line for same function, avoids code duplication
final_list_desired <- map(-3L:3L, ~mtcars %>% mutate(shift_wt = leadlag(wt, n = .x)))

# check they are identical
identical(final_list, final_list_desired)
#> [1] TRUE
```

title: Variable labels get dropped by mutate
description:
Mutate does not preserve variable labels specified using the labelled package, making it more cumbersome to work with variable labels in a dplyr workflow. Admittedly, this is an interaction between two packages, but they are both part of the tidyverse, so very often used together I would imagine.

This seems to apply to mutate functions in general, which is a bummer, given how convenient in-place processing using mutate_at or the new across() syntax.

Using base R notation instead of mutate confirms that the issue is not with the intermediate functions but with mutate. In other words, assignment to columns using base R preserves the variable labels as expected. Demonstration below:

```r
library(dplyr)
library(labelled)

# Mutate drops haven_labelled variable labels, but this seems wrong
f <- factor(c("yes", "yes", "no", "no", "don't know"))
value_labels <- c("yes" = 1, "no" = 2, "don't know" = 9)
dat <- tibble(responses = to_labelled(f,value_labels)) %>% 
  set_variable_labels(responses="Variable labels get dropped by mutate")
dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(responses_mut = to_factor(responses))

# Assignement using base R notation does not drop labels
dat$responses_base <- to_factor(dat$responses)
sapply(dat,var_label)
#> $responses
#> [1] "Variable labels get dropped by mutate"
#> 
#> $responses_mut
#> NULL
#> 
#> $responses_base
#> [1] "Variable labels get dropped by mutate"

# This seems to apply to mutate_* functions in general
# (note that the variable label now dropped from responses_base)
dat %>% 
  mutate_if(is.factor,to_labelled) %>%
  sapply(var_label)
#> $responses
#> [1] "Variable labels get dropped by mutate"
#> 
#> $responses_mut
#> NULL
#> 
#> $responses_base
#> NULL

# It also applies to the new across() notation
# (note that the variable label now dropped from responses_base)
dat %>% 
  mutate(across(is.factor,to_labelled)) %>%
  sapply(var_label)
#> $responses
#> [1] "Variable labels get dropped by mutate"
#> 
#> $responses_mut
#> NULL
#> 
#> $responses_base
#> NULL
```

title: Using across in group_by on previously grouped data exhibits strange behavior
description:
When using `across()` within `group_by()` on a data frame, the behavior isn't as expected if variables selected through `across()` are existing grouping columns of the data frame. This seems to be because the column selection seems to exclude grouped columns by default. Because of this, `group_by()` using `across()` mimics more the behavior of `mutate_at()` rather than `group_by_at()`.

```r
## works
mtcars %>%
  group_by(across(c(mpg:hp)))
#> # A tibble: 32 x 11
#> # Groups:   mpg, cyl, disp, hp [31]

## works since drat not in across selection
mtcars %>%
  group_by(drat) %>%
  group_by(across(c(mpg:hp)))
#> # A tibble: 32 x 11
#> # Groups:   mpg, cyl, disp, hp [31]

mtcars %>%
  group_by(hp) %>%
  group_by(across(c(mpg:hp)))
#> Note: Using an external vector in selections is ambiguous.
#> i Use `all_of(hp)` instead of `hp` to silence this message.
#> i See <https://tidyselect.r-lib.org/reference/faq-external-vector.html>.
#> This message is displayed once per session.
#> Error: Problem with `mutate()` input `..1`.
#> x Can't subset columns that don't exist.
#> x Locations 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, etc. don't exist.
#> i There are only 10 columns.
#> i Input `..1` is `across(c(mpg:hp))`.
#> i The error occured in group 1: hp = 52.
```
When using selection helpers, the grouping will just silently exclude previously grouping variables, unless the selection is empty.
```r
mtcars %>%
  group_by(hp) %>%
  group_by(across(contains("p")))
#> # A tibble: 32 x 11
#> # Groups:   mpg, disp [31]

mtcars %>%
  group_by(across(c(mpg:hp))) %>%
  group_by(across(contains("p")))
#> Error: `vars` must be a character vector.
```

title: Cartesian Products and cross_join() for unequal joins
description:
Currently it appears that a cartesian product can only be created with a full_join using a dummy variable for the by clause. There are times that I need to just cross-join...  Just simple deck of cards type processing: 14 numbers ( A, K, Q,, J, 10 - 2) x Suits ( C, D, H, S ) for A Clubs, K Clubs .... 2 Spades.

It seems that `joins` don't current support unequal relationships such as greater than or between. I would like to be able to cross-join and then apply a filter to do relationships such as a dataset with intervals 0 - 30, 31 - 60, and 61 - 90 days and show me every event with event_day < cut point or between 31 - 60 for example.  

I use this type of logic a lot in medical and insurance claims data where I need to look queries like "all events which occurred prior to 30-, 60-, 90- days and then summarize say sum of all costs at each point within a department".

As SQL supports these in the left_ , right_ and inner_joins, I would naturally do something like: 

```
SELECT cutpoint, sum( cost_var )
FROM ( SELECT event_id, cost_var, cutpoint
            FROM tblCuts 
             LEFT JOIN tblEvents by event_day <= day)
GROUP BY cutpoint; 
```

Here's a dataset for a reprex

tblEvents
id cost_var event_day department
1 90.00 3 A
1 120 43 B
1 0.09 45 C
1 1290,10 92 A

tblCuts
cut_day department depart_id_cd manager
30 A 123 smith
30 B 456 jones
30 C 789 love
60 A 123 smith
60 B 456 jones
60 C 789 love
90 A 123 smith
90 B 456 jones
90 C 789 love

I need days before the interval end date and department group_by accumulations assuming there is other data about the the department on the tblCuts that I also need to process. 

Is there a way to do this which I am unaware of without adding a dummy "fake" join variable to a full_join and then apply my filter for the condition when the two variables are on the same data row? 

*** Note: ***
This is a toy example as I legally can't use my data or code to make reprex for you so I make up toy examples of the problem to get at the root of my need. I'm very sorry as sometimes the toy is easily solved and the real situation involves more complex data / inputs. Offering a simple solution to the toy problem that doesn't  that are easier processed with the crosses that are like the ones here and have other confidential data.

title: protect from [ implementations
description:
I'm pretty sure package neuropsychology starts failing now because of `[.describe` from Hmisc: https://github.com/harrelfe/Hmisc/blob/261eb05a15a4b5373b1374ad96f409d6c7dbcb3f/R/describe.s#L525

```r
'[.describe' <- function(object, i, ...)
{
  at <- attributes(object)
  object <- '['(unclass(object),i)
  structure(object, descript=at$descript,
            dimensions=c(at$dimensions[1], length(object)),
            class='describe')
}
```

I can and I will send a pr to @harrelfe so that the class correctly restores, instead of just "describe", but perhaps in `mutate_cols()` we can assert that what `out[keep]` gives back is still a data frame and shout if not ?

`mutate.data.frame()` : 

```r
mutate.data.frame <- function(.data, ...,
                              .keep = c("all", "used", "unused", "none"),
                              .before = NULL, .after = NULL) {
  keep <- arg_match(.keep)

  cols <- mutate_cols(.data, ...)
  out <- dplyr_col_modify(.data, cols)

  .before <- enquo(.before)
  .after <- enquo(.after)
  if (!quo_is_null(.before) || !quo_is_null(.after)) {
    # Only change the order of new columns
    new <- setdiff(names(cols), names(.data))
    out <- relocate(out, !!new, .before = !!.before, .after = !!.after)
  }

  if (keep == "all") {
    out
  } else if (keep == "unused") {
    unused <- c(names(.data)[!attr(cols, "used")])
    keep <- intersect(names(out), c(unused, names(cols)))
    out[keep]
  } else if (keep == "used") {
    used <- names(.data)[attr(cols, "used")]
    keep <- intersect(names(out), c(used, names(cols)))
    out[keep]
  } else if (keep == "none") {
    keep <- c(
      # ensure group vars present
      setdiff(group_vars(.data), names(cols)),
      # cols might contain NULLs
      intersect(names(cols), names(out))
    )
    out[keep]
  }
}
```

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

df <- neuropsychology::personality %>% 
  select(where(is.numeric)) %>% 
  psych::describe() %>%

title: select/rename - Duplicate names no longer allowed?
description:
In R 3.5.3 with dplyr 0.8.3 I was able to rename variables to have duplicate names. I was making result summary tables comparing means by group using the following pattern:

```r

library(foreach)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(kableExtra)
nanmean = function(x) mean(x, na.rm=T)
nansd = function(x) sd(x, na.rm=T)

res <- foreach(x = c("mpg","hp"), .combine = rbind) %do% {
  fmla = list(as.formula(mtcars[,x] ~ as.factor(mtcars[,"am"])))
  test = "t.test"
  out = try(do.call(what=test,
                    args=fmla),
            silent=T)
  
  data.frame(predictor = x, stat = out$statistic, p = out$p.value)
}

res$predictor <- as.character(res$predictor)

out.table <- mtcars %>%
  mutate(am = ifelse(am == 1, "manual", "auto")) %>% 
  select(am, mpg, hp) %>%
  group_by(am) %>%
  summarise_all(list(n = ~sum(!is.na(.)), mean = ~sprintf("%0.2f", nanmean(.)), sd = ~sprintf("%0.2f", nansd(.)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(am),
               names_to = c("Variable",".value"),
               names_pattern = "(.*)_(.*)") %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c("Variable"),
              names_from = c("am"),
              values_from = c("n","mean","sd"), names_repair = "minimal") %>%
  inner_join(res, by = c("Variable" = "predictor")) 

# finalize pretty table formatting
out.table %>%
  select(Variable,
         n = "n_auto", mean = "mean_auto", sd = "sd_auto",
         n = "n_manual", mean = "mean_manual", sd = "sd_manual",
         p) %>%
  kableExtra::kable(format = "html", escape = F, digits=2, booktabs = T, linesep="", align=c(rep("l",1), rep("r",7))) %>%
  kableExtra::add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Automatic" = 3, "Manual" = 3, " ")) 
```

In R 3.6.3 and dplyr 0.8.5 the last `select()` won't run and returns an error "Error: Names must be unique" because I am intentionally setting duplicate column names. 

Is this intended or a newly introduced bug?

title: Conversion problem from "funs_()" to "list(~)"
description:
---
I modified the example by [drsimonj](https://gist.github.com/drsimonj/2038ff9f9c67063f384f10fac95de566) to make lagged data for 
panel data. 

When replacing the deprecated *funs_()* with *list(~)* I get an error message.

---
This is the code including the error message:

```r

# Make data
  N  <- 10
  TS <- 30
  
  cross_id     <- sort(LETTERS[rep(seq(1,N, 1), TS)])
  tim_id        <- rep(seq(1,TS, 1), N)
  
  data_set      <- tibble(cross_id, tim_id)     %>%
                          group_by(cross_id)          %>%
                          mutate(x_1 = rnorm(TS)) %>%
                          mutate(x_2 = rnorm(TS)) 

# Lags  and lag function
  nr_lags         <- 1:2
  lag_names       <- paste("lag", nr_lags,  sep = "_")
  lag_functions   <- stats::setNames(paste("dplyr::lag(., ", nr_lags, ")"), lag_names)

# Works fine with deprecated  'funs_'
  data_set %>%
          dplyr::group_by(cross_id)            %>%
          dplyr::mutate_at(vars(x_1, x_2), funs_(lag_functions))
  
# Error message with 'list(~)'                 
  data_set %>%
          dplyr::group_by(cross_id)            %>%
          dplyr::mutate_at(vars(x_1, x_2), list(~lag_functions))
  

Error: Problem with `mutate()` input `x_1`.

title: Summarise_at/_if summarize_at/if >1 times for multiple column sets
description:
Issue described (with solutions) [here](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/48944369/using-dplyr-summarize-with-different-operations-for-multiple-columns) but I feel like this would be an excellent feature, contingent on it not being too nightmarish to program.

Currently summarise_at/summarise_if/summarize_at/summarize_if can only be used once, on a single selection of column variables. It's easy to conceive cases when one might want to, e.g. group by date, and summarise mean values for all numeric columns, but the first value for character columns.
Conceptually this would also open the door for selecting the same columns multiple times for different operations e.g. min mean max on the same set. Though this may already be handled elsewhere, this would be a neat way of simplifying feature extraction using dplyr.

```r
iris %>%
group_by(Species) %>%
summarise_at(matches(".Length"), mean, na.rm = T,
             matches("Sepal"), min, na.rm = T)
```

title: dplyr::rename with fixed new-names and old-names given by length-1 named vectors gives wrong names
description:
A one-line reprex of this behavior is:

``` r
dplyr::rename(data.frame(old = 1), new = c(dud = "old"))
#>   new...dud
#> 1         1
```

This is an issue if we have a function where data.frames with myriad names have their names changed to certain "standard" names. In the case below, I have a standard column-name `foo`, but a data.frame's called it `bar` instead, so we call the following function to give it the standard name

``` r
standardize <- function(df, fooName) {
  dplyr::rename(df, foo = !!fooName)
}

standardize(data.frame(bar = 1), "bar")
#>   foo
#> 1   1
```

<sup>Created on 2020-05-07 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

This works just fine.

However, if, for whatever reason, the value passed to `fooName` is a length-1 named vector, we get the behavior shown at the start:

``` r
name <- c(buzz = "bar")
standardize(data.frame(bar = 1), name)
#>   foo...buzz
#> 1          1
```

The vector's name is clumsily suffixed to the desired name with an ellipsis. Is this expected behavior? I'm currently solving this by using `foo = unname(fooName)`, which works, but wonder if this is just a bug.

title: Rowwise calculations with haven_labelled objects don't work with the new vctrs approach under the hood
description:
Calculating the rowwise mean across columns doesn't work if the two columns are haven_labelled objects.

```r
library(tidyverse)

# data
test <- structure(list(Q16_1 = structure(c(1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 
1), label = "Q16_1 MYLABEL 1", labels = c(`Not Selected` = 0, 
Selected = 1), class = "haven_labelled"), Q16_2 = structure(c(1, 
1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0), label = "Q16_2 MYLABEL 2", labels = c(`Not Selected` = 0, 
Selected = 1), class = "haven_labelled")), class = c("tbl_df", 
"tbl", "data.frame"), row.names = c(NA, -10L))
```

Previously, I used a pmap approach that worked nicely 
```r
# Works
test %>%
  mutate(x = pmap_dbl(select(., num_range(prefix = "Q16_", range = 1:2)), ~mean(c(...), na.rm = TRUE)))
```

Trying to switch to dplyr's rowwise + c_across approach fails with an error
```r
#Doesn't work
test %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(x = mean(c_across(num_range(prefix = "Q16_", range = 1:2))))
```

```
Error: `mutate()` argument `x` must return compatible vectors across groups.
i `x` is `mean(c_across(num_range(prefix = "Q16_", range = 1:2)))`.
```

It only works if I change the type of my two columns to numeric before calculating the mean.
```r
# Works
test %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(Q16_1 = as.numeric(Q16_1),
         Q16_2 = as.numeric(Q16_2)) %>%
  mutate(x = mean(c_across(num_range(prefix = "Q16_", range = 1:2))))
```
