title: Accessible helper for run length encoded style groups
description:
This has been discussed in various issues and forums, notably:

- https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/237, suggesting `group_by_adj()` (suggesting pre-ordered adjacency);
- https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/1534;
- https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/1661; and
- https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/4445 (most recent)

One key difference is that some of those discussions focused on a new `group_by_*` verb, where I suggest having just a helper function is sufficient to scratch the itch sufficiently. Lacking safeguards and sanity checks, it could be as straight-forward as:

```r
rle_group <- function(...) {
  yy <- rle(paste(...))
  rep(seq_along(yy$lengths), yy$lengths)
}

df <- data.frame(x = c(0, 0, 1, 0), y = c(2, 2, 2, 2))
df %>%
  group_by(grp = rle_group(x, y))
# # A tibble: 4 x 3
# # Groups:   grp [3]
#       x     y   grp
#   <dbl> <dbl> <int>
# 1     0     2     1
# 2     0     2     1
# 3     1     2     2
# 4     0     2     3
```

The under-inspiring `Groups: grp` may not be as informative as [Romain's previous suggestion](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/237#issuecomment-35085223) of

```lang-r
> df <- data.frame( x = 1, a = rep(c(1,2), each = 4), b = rep( letters[1:2], each = 2), stringsAsFactors = TRUE )
> gdf <- grouped_df_adj_impl( df, list( quote(x), quote(a), quote(b) ), FALSE )
> summarise(gdf, n = n() )
Source: local data frame [4 x 4]
Groups: x, a

  x a b n
1 1 1 a 2
2 1 1 b 2
3 1 2 a 2
4 1 2 b 2
```

(where the `Groups: x, a` is more useful), it still enables the grouping.

This comes up frequently enough on StackOverflow that I think its utility is justified. I think the implementation could be innocuous enough to not impact other verbs.

The use of `paste` enables "one or more" columns, and happens to side-step `rle`'s avoidance of `factor`. It does add overhead, so a more performant variant might be supported (that does not omit `factor`s). I'd think a variant of [Hadley's initial suggestion](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/237#issuecomment-34117419) (Rcpp-based) could be adapted to handle one-or-more.

I'd be willing to start on a PR if maintainers support the concept.

title: `group_split()`'s `keep` argument should be `.keep`
description:
Because `...` is passed on to `group_by()` which has mutate-like semantics.

```r
library(dplyr)

df <- data.frame(x = 1:2)

group_split(df, y = 1:2)
#> [[1]]
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       x     y
#>   <int> <int>
#> 1     1     1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       x     y
#>   <int> <int>
#> 1     2     2
#> 
#> attr(,"ptype")
#> # A tibble: 0 x 2
#> # … with 2 variables: x <int>, y <int>

group_split(df, keep = 1:2)
#> [[1]]
#>   x
#> 1 1
#> 2 2
#> 
#> attr(,"ptype")
#> integer(0)
```

Would also align better with `nest_by()`

title: relocate .after doesn't play nicely with subclasses
description:
Attached is a minimal package that shows the problem. Load it, then run

```r
registerS3method("relocate", "foo", packagefileprob:::relocate.foo,
      envir = asNamespace("dplyr")) # normally the package would do this on onLoad

tmp <- structure(data.frame(a=1,b=2), class = c("foo", "data.frame"))
relocate(tmp, b, a) # fine
relocate(tmp, a, .after = b) # dies
```

My output:

```
> relocate(tmp, b, a) # fine
got to relocate.foo
  b a
1 2 1
> relocate(tmp, a, .after = b) # dies
got to relocate.foo
Error: object 'b' not found
```

This seems to come from somewhere deep within `tidyselect::eval_sym`, but don't ask me to debug this wizardry.

title: Strange issue when Spectrum and dplyr are loaded together
description:
Here is a strange problem that I ran into today. In RStudio with R 4.0 on both Mac and Linux, If I load the following packages together: 

```r
library(dplyr)
library(Spectrum)
```

and then try to run any function starting with "wrap", e.g.:

```r
wrap_test <- function() {
  "test"
}

wrap_test()
```

after using the RStudio autocomplete feature (tab) to complete the function's name, the R session freezes and starts using 100% of my CPU. I could not figure out what the issue was but I could reproduce it on my Mac and my Linux machines. I'm guessing some weird interaction between Spectrum and dplyr. I'll cross-post this on the Spectrum Github page.

title: slice_max() inconsistency with prop argument
description:
Love the systematization of the `slice()` variants, well done! 

Check this out:


``` r
tb <- tibble(x = sample(5))


tb %>% slice_min(x, prop = .40)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>       x
#>   <int>
#> 1     1
#> 2     2

tb %>% slice_max(x, prop = .40)
#> # A tibble: 0 x 1
#> # … with 1 variable: x <int>
```
I assume that's unintentional, since when you use the `n` parameter, you get the expected:
```r
tb %>% slice_min(x, n = 2)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>       x
#>   <int>
#> 1     1
#> 2     2

tb %>% slice_max(x, n = 2)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>       x
#>   <int>
#> 1     5
#> 2     4
```
And when you use the older `top_frac()` you get the same expected:
```r
tb %>% top_frac(.40, x)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>       x
#>   <int>
#> 1     5
#> 2     4
```
I haven't had time to look into the internals of `slice_max.data.frame()`, but thought I'd point it out since I know y'all are looking to get it out the door soon.

title: Allow aggregate functions within `arrange`
description:
Inspired by [this Stack Overflow question](https://stackoverflow.com/q/61503447/903061), perhaps `arrange` should allow aggregate functions.

Want: order groups by aggregate function

Attempt:

```
mtcars %>% 
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  arrange(mean(mpg))
# Error: incorrect size (1) at position 1, expecting : 32
```

Workaround:

```
mtcars %>%
  mutate(cyl = forcats::fct_reorder(factor(cyl), mpg, .fun = mean)) %>%
  arrange(cyl)

## or (more literally)

mtcars %>% 
  group_by(cyl) %>% 
  mutate(mean_mpg = mean(mpg)) %>%
  arrange(mean_mpg) %>%
  select(-mean_mpg)
```

Could `arrange` recycle length-one inputs up to the group size? Would make it more consistent with `filter` and `mutate`.

title: different behaviour between filter and arrange on group operations
description:
filter () could be used to filter out groups, e.g.

`mtcars %>% group_by (cyl)  %>% filter (mean (mpg) > 18)
`

will remove groups based on cyl, that have mean(mpg) less than 18

at the same time f I try to arrange groups based on mean (mpg)

`mtcars %>% group_by (cyl)  %>% arrange (desc(mean (mpg)))
`

I get an error. So filter() makes implicit assumption that I want to operate on groups, but arrange() does not. Is this on purpose?

title: Is `slice(df, numeric(0))` an undocumented feature or UB?
description:
I sometimes use `slice(df, 0)` to obtain an empty data.frame with preserved column structure. I just realized that this behavior is not documented.

``` r
library(dplyr)

# Convenient
slice(mtcars, 0)
#>  [1] mpg  cyl  disp hp   drat wt   qsec vs   am   gear carb
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

# And similar to base R behavior
mtcars[0,]
#>  [1] mpg  cyl  disp hp   drat wt   qsec vs   am   gear carb
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
```

<sup>Created on 2020-04-23 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

The doc only mentions positive or negative indices:

> Integer row values. Provide either positive values to keep, or negative values to drop. The values provided must be either all positive or all negative. Indices beyond the number of rows in the input are silently ignored.

So if `0` is silently ignored, the call is equivalent to `slice(mtcars, numeric(0))`

Is `slice(mtcars, numeric(0))` effectively undefined behavior that one should not rely upon, or is it an undocumented feature of `slice`?

I looked at the tests for `slice` and none checks that slicing with an empty index vector gives an empty data.frame with preserved column structure.

The closest was:

```R
test_that("slice skips 0 (#3313)", {
  d <- tibble(x = 1:5, y = LETTERS[1:5], g = 1)
  expect_identical(slice(d, 0), slice(d, integer(0)))
  # Truncated
}
```

title: parallelization causes enexpr to produce different output
description:
`enexpr` generates different output depending on if I use parallelization or not. The parallelized output seems unusable; it's just a "piece" object of the "name" class. A simple reprex: ```r library(dplyr) # very simple function that uses `enexpr` f <- function(x){ enexpr(x) } f(10 * z) # generates list of enexpr-ized values c('10 * z', '2 * z') %>% plyr::llply(f) # generates list of "piece" of the "name" class doParallel::registerDoParallel(2) c('10 * z', '2 * z') %>% plyr::llply(f, .parallel=TRUE) ``` I also tried parallelizing with `furrr` and got the same result. I noticed this when creating functions that utilize [tidytable](https://github.com/markfairbanks/tidytable), which relies on `enexpr`. A more relevant reprex versus that shown above: ```r library(dplyr) library(tidytable) # not very useful, but simple function to subset a data.table make_subsets = function(to_filter, filter_col, dt){ to_filter = enexpr(to_filter) filter_col = enexpr(filter_col) dt_filter(dt, !!filter_col == !!to_filter) } # works when run without parallelization c('setosa', 'versicolor', 'virginica') %>% plyr::llply(make_subsets, filter_col = Species, dt = iris_df) # doesn't work due to `enexpr` generating different output doParallel::registerDoParallel(2) c('setosa', 'versicolor', 'virginica') %>% plyr::llply(make_subsets, filter_col = Species, dt = iris_df, .parallel=TRUE) ```

title: Binding Issue
description:
I came across what I believe is a bug in the dev version of dplyr 0.8.99.9002 (maybe rooted in vctrs; didn't go too far with the hunting).

I believe if you try to row bind two tibbles and one contains a primary/default class that isn't tibble it will throw an error.  Reading in from `readr::read_csv` is a case of this that creates a class `"spec_tbl_df" "tbl_df"      "tbl"         "data.frame"`.  If you use this on the toy example below the columns in both tables appear to be compatable (numeric and character).  I would expect that if you have 2 data.frames, regardless of other classes, when you use `bind_rows`, so long as the column classes are the same or coercable, then the bind should work.

```
library(readr)
library(dplyr)

xy <- read_csv("x,y\n1,2\n3,4", col_types = "dc")
xy2 <- tibble(x = 3.4, y = 'd')

## > sapply(xy, class)
##           x           y 
##   "numeric" "character" 
## > sapply(xy2, class)
##           x           y 
##  "numeric" "character" 


dplyr::bind_rows(xy, xy2)
## > dplyr::bind_rows(xy, xy2)
## Error: Can't convert <spec_tbl_df<
##   x: double
##   y: character
## >> to <data.frame<
##   x: double
##   y: character
## >>.
## Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.
## In addition: Warning message:
##  Error: Can't convert <spec_tbl_df<
##   x: double
##   y: character
## >> to <data.frame<
##   x: double
##   y: character
## >>.
## Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred. 

xy %>% 
    class
## [1] "spec_tbl_df" "tbl_df"      "tbl"         "data.frame"

## This works with no error
dplyr::bind_rows(as_tibble(xy), xy2)
```

title: Coalesce returns wrong units for "difftime" class object
description:
I was using `dplyr::coalesce` with `difftime` objects, and I discovered that instead of finding the first non-missing value, it converts an NA `difftime` to a `difftime` with a value of 1 second.

In the example below, `coalesce(y, x)` should return `Time difference of 1 hours` not `Time difference of 1 secs`

```r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#>

library(lubridate)

#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, union
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     date, intersect, setdiff, union

x <- difftime(as_datetime('2020-01-01 01:00:00'), as_date('2020-01-01'))

y <- difftime(as_date('2020-01-01'), NA)

x
#> Time difference of 1 hours

y
#> Time difference of NA secs

coalesce(x, y)
#> Time difference of 1 hours

coalesce(y, x)
#> Time difference of 1 secs
```

title: Small improvements for erroring expressions
description:
I think this:

```
Error: `filter()` argument `..1` errored.
ℹ `..1` is `!is.na(SWD)`.
✖ object 'SWD' not found
```

would be slightly clearer by indicating that `..1` is the user input in the `i` bullet:

```
Error: `filter()` argument `..1` errored.
ℹ Input `..1` is `!is.na(SWD)`.
✖ object 'SWD' not found
```

By the way for vctrs we discussed the idea of standardising on "input" rather than "argument", as the former sounds a little less technical. So the header could use input as well:

```
Error: `filter()` input `..1` errored.
ℹ Input `..1` is `!is.na(SWD)`.
✖ object 'SWD' not found
```

Finally, not a big deal but I think "errored" looks a bit strange and could be improved, though I'm not sure how. Maybe one of these:

```
Error: A problem occurred with `filter()` input `..1`.
Error: There is a problem with `filter()` input `..1`.
Error: Problem with `filter()` input `..1`.
```

Maybe the last one? It's very short yet user friendly.

```

title: pipe operator fails when passing a dataframe to data.table::as.data.table
description:
Hi all, 
I'm running into an issue with dplyr pipes and data.table.
Specifically, the following code block fails:
``` 
x <- data.frame(x=1)
x %>% data.table::as.data.table

Error in .::data.table : unused argument (as.data.table)
```

However, this code block succeeds:
```
x <- data.frame(x=1)
library(data.table)  
x %>% as.data.table
```

I've found this behavior on both R-3.6.1 and R-3.6.3, with dplyr-0.8.3/0.8.4/0.8.5, and data.table-1.12.8.
Perhaps easiest to test: a brand new install of R-3.6.3 on mac reproduces the issue.

title: bind_rows on tibble with extra class breaks
description:
I have a function that returns a tibble. I add an extra class to the tibble so I can use autoplot.myclass etc. This works fine. 

I need to use `bind_rows` to combine two such tibbles. This worked fine in ‘0.8.5’ but breaks in '0.8.99.9002'. I think the problem arises when there is a factor with different levels in each tibble.

Here is a minimal reprex

``` r
library("dplyr")
packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '0.8.99.9002'
a <- tibble(a = factor("a"))
b <- tibble(a = factor("b"))
bind_rows(a, b) #works
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>   a

#> 2 b

class(a) <- c("myclass", class(a))
class(b) <- class(a)
bind_rows(a, b) #fails

title: between() support for character vectors
description:
Hello, rerequesting a feature that doesn't look like it was ever made available.

---

`between` currently (v0.8.5) only supports numeric inputs, and not character.

```
Error: Not compatible with requested type: [type=character; target=double].
```

I found this earlier closed issue #2995 which was closed in favor of an issue opened for `vctrs`.

I followed to the `vctrs` issue, which looks like it got moved to the [r-lib/funs](https://github.com/r-lib/funs/) repository: https://github.com/r-lib/funs/issues/26

Which I can see was closed with this commit implementing such a function with `vctrs`: https://github.com/r-lib/funs/commit/057146f5d90d9173530f2e5b169b6218c7af4be8

But as far as I can tell, [r-lib/funs](https://github.com/r-lib/funs/) is not actually a package that is available on CRAN for people to easily use. (There is not much documentation so I'm not exactly sure what that package is.)

So support for character inputs to `between` is still a missing feature for dplyr users. 

I understand that I can copy the small amount of code there is and define a custom function, but I believe there is still good reason to want dplyr to support it in the existing function with that name that works for numeric inputs.

Thank you!

title: segfault with rowwise and mutate when vector > length 1 returned
Allow summarise() to explicitly control grouping
description:
The current grouping behaviour causes much confusion, and it's not correct now that summary expressions can return multiple values and rowwise is back to life. I now think the way to fix this is to add a `.groups` argument that could take any of the following values:

* `NULL` (default) = `"drop_last"` + message displaying the new grouping vars
* `"drop_last"`: current behaviour
* `"drop"`: returns ungrouped tibble
* `"keep"`: preserves existing grouping
* `"rowwise"`: one group per row

`summarise()` is the only verb that operates on "groups" (rather than rows or columns), so is the only function that needs this option.

cc @MilesMcBain

title: Summarising across a difftime variable on a grouped dataframe has very poor performance
description:
Running a `summarise()` across a difftime variable on a grouped dataset has exceptionally poor performance. This is noticeable in that the poor performance doesn't occur in base R or data.table and also doesn't occur in dplyr if you cast the variable to numeric. 

Re-producible example below (using dplyr 0.8.5)



```r
n <- 2000000
library(dplyr)
library(data.table)

a = as.Date('2018-01-01')
b = as.Date('2019-01-01')

dat_num <- tibble(
    patientid = sample( 1:50000, replace = TRUE, size = n ),
    value = difftime(b, a, unit = "days")  %>% as.numeric()
)

dat_date <- tibble(
    patientid = sample( 1:50000, replace = TRUE, size = n ),
    value = difftime(b, a, unit = "days") 
)



### Dplyr - numeric (quick)
system.time({
    dat_num %>%
        group_by(patientid) %>%
        summarise( m = max(value))
})

### Dplyr - difftime (takes forever to run) 
system.time({
    dat_date %>%
        group_by(patientid) %>%
        summarise( m = max(value))
})


### Base R - numeric (quick)
system.time({
    tapply( X = dat_num$value, dat_num$patientid, max)
})

### Base R - difftime (quick)
system.time({
    tapply( X = dat_date$value, dat_date$patientid, max)
})


### data.table - numeric (quick)
system.time({
    x <- as.data.table(dat_num)
    x[, .(m = max(value)), by = patientid]
})

### data.table - difftime (quick)
system.time({
    x <- as.data.table(dat_date)
    x[, .(m = max(value)), by = patientid]
})

```

title: Is there a reason why there is no is_distinct?
description:
I wonder if it would make sense to have a function called `is_distinct()`. It would work like `duplicated()` but with all the `tidyverse` goodness of finding distinct cases by considering unique combinations in several columns. I already typed one up and happy to put it in a PR:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
df <- data.frame(col1 = c(1:3, 1, 4, 4),
                 col2 = c(1, 1:3, 4, 4))
is_distinct <- function(...) {
  columns <- map(enquos(..., .named = TRUE), rlang::eval_tidy)
  data <- as_tibble(columns, .name_repair = "minimal")
  
  loc <- vctrs::vec_unique_loc(data)
  
  out <- logical(nrow(data))
  out[loc] <- TRUE
  out
}
df %>% mutate(unique_case = is_distinct(col1, col2))
#>   col1 col2 unique_case
#> 1    1    1        TRUE
#> 2    2    1        TRUE
#> 3    3    2        TRUE
#> 4    1    3        TRUE
#> 5    4    4        TRUE
#> 6    4    4       FALSE
```
Sometimes I want to know which columns were duplicated before removing them (e.g., to assess whether cases differed in another column). But maybe there is already a solution for this which I couldn't find.

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

title: Use predicate functions in `across` similar to `mutate_if`
description:
Previously, we could provide predicates to `mutate_if` (and `summarize_if`) like:

```r
iris %>%
  mutate_if(~"virginica" %in% .x, paste0, "_")
#>   Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species
#> 1          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2 setosa_
#> 2          4.9         3.0          1.4         0.2 setosa_
#> 3          4.7         3.2          1.3         0.2 setosa_
#> 4          4.6         3.1          1.5         0.2 setosa_
#> 5          5.0         3.6          1.4         0.2 setosa_
#> 6          5.4         3.9          1.7         0.4 setosa_
```
However, using `across`, we are restricted to the tidy-select framework, so either with an `is_` function:
```r 
is_virgin <- function(x) {
  "virginica" %in% x
}

iris %>%
  mutate(across(is_virgin, paste0, "_"))
```
Or column specification:
```r
iris %>%
  mutate(across(which(sapply(., function(x) "virginica" %in% x)), paste0, "_"))
```
Given that `across` is replacing scoped verbs, including `mutate_if` and `summarize_if`, the use of a predicate function would be useful. The former example can be time consuming and confusing when doing multiple `mutate_if` style operations, and the latter is not ideal even for a single use. I think it would be useful to pass in anonymous functions directly, just as the named function can be, in the same syntax as in `mutate_if`. 
```r
iris %>%
  mutate(across(~"virginica" %in% .x, paste0, "_"))
```
I see this isn't likely as it's not able to combine with other tidy select operators, so could this be a use case for a tidy helper that takes anonymous functions and can be combined with other helpers. For lack of a better naming idea, something like `matches_pred`:
```r
iris %>%
  mutate(across(matches_pred(~"virginica" %in% .x), paste0, "_"))
```

title: mutate_if "breaks" when used for normalisation
description:
When a transformation is applied across columns with a predicate selection, the value of the updated columns is used instead of the original value before the update has completed. Presumably, this behaviour is not expected and leads to unintended results.

Here is an example in which we would like to "normalise" `Sepal.Length`, `Sepal.Width` etc. to `Sepal.Width`:

```r
iris %>% head

#   Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species
# 1          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2  setosa
# 2          4.9         3.0          1.4         0.2  setosa
# 3          4.7         3.2          1.3         0.2  setosa
# 4          4.6         3.1          1.5         0.2  setosa
# 5          5.0         3.6          1.4         0.2  setosa
# 6          5.4         3.9          1.7         0.4  setosa

iris %>% mutate_if(is.numeric, ~ . / Sepal.Width) %>% head

#   Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species
# 1     1.457143           1          1.4         0.2  setosa
# 2     1.633333           1          1.4         0.2  setosa
# 3     1.468750           1          1.3         0.2  setosa
# 4     1.483871           1          1.5         0.2  setosa
# 5     1.388889           1          1.4         0.2  setosa
# 6     1.384615           1          1.7         0.4  setosa
```

Only  the first and the second column are correctly updated. After `Sepal.Width` is "self-normalised", this value (1) is used for `Petal.Width` and `Petal.Length`.

It might be a matter of debate if this behaviour is a "feature" or a "bug", but as the result is solely dependent on the position of the column (the column order), this is rather a bug …

title: first() and last() are only able to select single columns
Confusing error message inside `c_across()`
description:
I am using `rowwise()` and `c_across()` and encountered a confusing error message. Here is a toy case of my situation. I was counting the number of columns containing several strings. The selection inside the second `c_across()` captures the first variable that was `mutate`d, so it is trying to combine character and integer columns. 

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(stringr)
tibble(ai = c("a", "b", "a"), 
       bi = c("b", "b", "b"), 
       ci = c("a", "b", "c"), 
       d = c("a", "b", "a")) %>% 
  rowwise() %>% 
  mutate(ai_count = sum(str_detect(c_across(contains("i")), pattern = "a")),
         bi_count = sum(str_detect(c_across(contains("i")), pattern = "b")))
#> Error: `mutate()` argument `bi_count` must return compatible vectors across groups.
#> i `bi_count` is `sum(str_detect(c_across(contains("i")), pattern = "b"))`.
```

<sup>Created on 2020-04-09 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>


The error message `Error: `mutate()` argument `bi_count` must return compatible vectors across groups.` is confusing here. It seems to suggest it's a problem across the groups/rows, but it's actually an issue with concatenating variables of different types within the same group. Could this error message be made clearer here?

I also am rather confused as to why this errors at all. I would have expected `c_across()` to have similar coercion behavior as `c()` and to coerce the integer values to charcter.

title: `bind_rows()` and row names in case of `.id = NULL`
description:
In current development version if `.id` is not supplied (as by default) in `bind_rows()`, it forces new row names into output. I believe, this is consistent with underlying `vec_rbind()` (as it states [here](https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/5c69793052047bb5a395b6caadc00a2c32113843/R/bind.R#L35-L37)), but it is a surprise for 'dplyr' user.

I would also argue that creating row names in case of `.id = NULL` is a little bit excessive behavior.

Reprex of current situation:

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE, quietly = TRUE)
packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '0.8.99.9002'

bind_rows(list(a = tibble(x = 1:2))) %>% row.names()
#> [1] "a1" "a2"
```

title: Ungrouping after grouping converts data.frame to tbl_df
description:
A sequence of grouping and ungrouping operations changes the class of an object to `tbl_df` even if initially it was `data.frame`. Is it intended behavior? ```r iris %>% class ## [1] "data.frame" iris %>% rowwise %>% ungroup %>% class ## [1] "tbl_df" "tbl" "data.frame" ``` This issue is similar to those reported [here](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/1328) and [here](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/936), but in this case, the initial class is `data.frame` and I expect it to remain unless I change it explicitly to `tbl_df`. --- The consistency of classes is important for maintaining of the existing code, where `data.frame`-style behaviour is expected. Here is **an example** of how the existing code might be affected: several columns are to be assigned with matrix. The results for initial data.frame and for grouped/ungrouped data.frame are different. ```r df <- data.frame(var1 = 1:2, var2 = 3:4, var3 = 5:6) class(df) ## [1] "data.frame" dt <- df %>% rowwise %>% ungroup class(dt) ## [1] "tbl_df" "tbl" "data.frame" m <- matrix(1, nrow = 2, ncol = 2) # Expected output for a data.frame df[, c(1, 3)] <- m # > df # var1 var2 var3 # 1 1 3 1 # 2 1 4 1 # Unexpected output for the data.frame which has been quietly converted dt[, c(1, 3)] <- m # > dt # # A tibble: 2 x 3 # var1[,1] [,2] var2 var3[,1] [,2] # # 1 1 1 3 1 1 # 2 1 1 4 1 1 ```

title: name of first argument differs across functions
description:
While working on the [tidylog](https://github.com/elbersb/tidylog) package, I realized that the first argument of tibble-centric functions is often different: For instance, for `filter`, the first argument is called `.data`, while for `filter_all` (I know, it's deprecated), the first argument is called `.tbl`. There is also `x` for `top_n` and `tbl` (no dot!) for `sample_n`. In tidyr, mainly `data` seems to be used.

This may be a bit late for dplyr 1.0.0, but it would be really nice to have these consistent across functions. Of course, a change might produce a lot of breaking code, so maybe this is too minor an issue to take on.

title: Error when default value in lag() and lead() is of different class
"Error: Only bare vectors have shapes" when pivoting after str_glue()
description:
I think there might be a bug when using `pivot_wider()` just after `str_glue()`. 
The errors says `Error: Only bare vectors have shapes.` but it disappears if we add `as.character()` after `str_glue()`.

Here is a minimal example:
``` r
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(1)
iris$id_col <- sample(1:4, NROW(iris), replace = TRUE)

# Doesn't work
iris %>% 
  mutate(NEW = str_glue("{Species}")) %>% 
  pivot_wider(id_cols = id_col, names_from = NEW, 
              values_from = Sepal.Length,
              values_fn = list(Sepal.Length = length))
#> Error: Only bare vectors have shapes.

# Works when adding as.character() after str_glue()
iris %>% 
  mutate(NEW = str_glue("{Species}"),
         NEW = as.character(NEW)) %>% # <- New line
  pivot_wider(id_cols = id_col, names_from = NEW, 
              values_from = Sepal.Length, 
              values_fn = list(Sepal.Length = length))
#> # A tibble: 4 x 4
#>   id_col setosa versicolor virginica
#>    <int>  <int>      <int>     <int>
#> 1      1     16         11        11
#> 2      4      7         13        13
#> 3      3     11         11        14
#> 4      2     16         15        12
```

description:

```

title: Suggestion: remember() and recall()
description:
I would like to suggest two new functions: `remember()` and `recall()`. The idea is to (temporarily) save values to the global environment that can later be used in the same command. This way, saved values can be used in functions like `ggplot()` following after a series of pipes, without having to save the value using an intermediate command.

For example (schematic):

```r
data %>%
  filter(...) %>%
  remember(rows = nrow(.)) %>%
  group_by(...) %>%
  summarise(...) %>%
  ggplot() +
  labs(subtitle = paste("Number of observations:", recall(rows)))
```

For the field of epidemiology (and probably other fields as well) it is important to state e.g. the number of observations to be able to interpret the data, but you could think of endless ways of using this. I would now do:

```r
obs <- data %>%
  filter(...) %>%
  nrow()

data %>%
  filter(...) %>%
  group_by(...) %>%
  summarise(...) %>%
  ggplot() +
  labs(subtitle = paste("Number of observations:", obs))
```

This means the initials transformations (that could be very complex) have to be run twice. Another option is then of course:
```r
my_complex_transformation <- data %>%
  very_complex_stuff(...)

obs <- my_complex_transformation %>%
  nrow()

my_complex_transformation %>%
  group_by(...) %>%
  summarise(...) %>%
  ggplot() +
  labs(subtitle = paste("Number of observations:", obs))
```

WIth `remember()` and `recall()`, this process would be more convenient and very flexible.

----

The functions code:
```r
remember <- function(.data, ...) {
  dots <- list(...)
  for (i in seq_len(length(dots))) {
    assign(x = names(dots)[i],
           value = dots[[i]],
           envir = globalenv())
  }
  .data
}

recall <- function(x, delete = TRUE) {
  x_name <- deparse(substitute(x))
  x_val <- x
  if (delete == TRUE) {
    rm(list = x_name, envir = globalenv())
  }
  x_val
}
```

title: Can't bind cols with custom class
description:
Updated to latest `tibble` and `dplyr` dev versions.

I can't bind the columns of two tibbles when one of them has an additional custom class. This worked before updating.

Possibly related to https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/5066 , https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/issues/972

``` r
d1 <- tibble::tibble("a" = c(1,2,3))
d2 <- tibble::tibble("b" = c(1,2,3))
class(d2) <- c("clazz", class(d2))
class(d2)
#> [1] "clazz"      "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
dplyr::bind_cols(d1, d2)
#> Error: No common type for `..1` <tbl_df<>> and `..2` <clazz<>>.
```

title: Error: 'vec_as_subscript' is not an exported object from 'namespace:vctrs'
description:
See https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/5048. Now I am getting this error again, except for vec_as_subscript instead of vec_as_subscript2. I've reinstalled vctrs, made sure my packages were up to date, and it still seems like this hasn't truly been solved. 

This occurred when trying to run a chunk of code containing standard tidyverse functions like filter, gather, etc. The only solution is to close the session and start a new one. The only libraries being loaded are tidyverse, lubridate, and janitor. 

I hope this is fixed soon because this is starting to occur more frequently and interfere with my work.

title: Found the following significant warnings:   Warning: `select_()` is deprecated as of dplyr 0.7.0.
description:
I maintain the [depmap Bioconductor package](https://github.com/UCLouvain-CBIO/depmap) which fully depends on dplyr. I wanted to get a head start to update the package in line for the dplyr 1.0 release. After installing the development version of dplyr, I have updated the code in the vignettes in the depmap package to be line with the scheduled dplyr 1.0 changes, however I still get the same warning when checking the package: 

```
* checking whether package ‘depmap’ can be installed ... WARNING
Found the following significant warnings:
  Warning: `select_()` is deprecated as of dplyr 0.7.0.
  Warning: `filter_()` is deprecated as of dplyr 0.7.0.
```

Do you know why this error is being displayed? I find this confusing because nowhere in my package are the select_`*`() or filter_`*`() functions utilized, only the plain vanilla  select() or filter() functions as shown below in an example:

```
rnai %>% dplyr::select(entrez_id, cell_line,  gene_name, dependency) %>%
                dplyr::filter(entrez_id == "4780")
```

Could this error be cause by not using the .data pronoun in the select() or filter() functions?

title: `group_map()` family behavior is inconsistent with empty data frame
description:
`group_map()` family invokes the closure when the input data frame is empty:

```r
tibble() %>% group_walk(~ { print("hello!") })

tibble(x=integer()) %>% group_by(x) %>% group_walk(~ { print("hello!") })
```

I consider this to be inconsistent behavior since `group_map()` otherwise does not invoke the closure for empty groups, this is not how purrr `map()` behaves either, and ultimately, runs contrary to the usual `map` semantics in FP.

title: Row-wise grouped operations produce an unnecessary warning
description:
Using a function from `group_map()` family on a `rowwise()` grouped data frame will produce the warning "keep is ignored in group_split(<rowwise_df>)" as of 792f9b1f96373dc1ee90a613ebba8c5aec4e7269:

```r
library(dplyr)

iris %>% rowwise() %>% group_walk(~ {})
```

    Warning message:
    keep is ignored in group_split(<rowwise_df>) 

It seems that the problem is in this line: https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/792f9b1f96373dc1ee90a613ebba8c5aec4e7269/R/group_map.R#L127

I suggest to change it to something like:

```r
chunks <- if(missing(keep)) {
   group_split(.data)
 }) else { 
   group_split(.data, keep = isTRUE(keep))
}
```

title: dplyr dev `sample_frac()`
description:
I'm not sure if it's an existing `tibble` problem or a  new dplyr dev issue. But it breaks the `sugrrants` unit test, which checks `sugrrants::frame_calendar()` should return identical results regardless of input data row ordering.

With dplyr `v0.8.5`,

``` r
set.seed(2020L)
iris_tbl <- dplyr::as_tibble(iris)
all.equal(iris_tbl, dplyr::sample_frac(iris_tbl))
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(iris, dplyr::sample_frac(iris))

#> [2] "Component \"Sepal.Width\": Mean relative difference: 0.1701105" 
#> [3] "Component \"Petal.Length\": Mean relative difference: 0.4865935"

title: Export `any_of()` and `all_of()` select-helpers
description:
The description for `tidyselect::one_of()` in ver 1.0.0 states:
> one_of() is retired in favour of the more precise any_of() and all_of() selectors.

So I was a bit surprised to find that these functions are not being exported in `select-helpers.R` like the other functions are.

This seems to only be a problem in package development, where trying to use `dplyr::any_of()` fails (because it isn't exported like `one_of()` is).

When trying to prepare a downstream dependency for the 1.0 release, I was getting inconsistent results from my checks. I think I've narrowed down the problem to this code, which can reliably cause a segfault when using valgrind.

For my purposes, I think I can avoid by coercing the list to a data.frame, but still felt worth mentioning here.

```r
library(dplyr)

df <- data.frame(x = 1:2)
attr(df, "something") <- list("something")

new_col <- list(y = 3:4)
df <- bind_cols(df, new_col)

df <- as_tibble(df)

df %>%
  mutate(new_var = as.character(x))
```

title: mutate_if predicate function doesnt seem to be able to handle different settings for `.`
description:
Consider this fake data
```
smooth_data <- data.frame(`s(gam_variable_1_output)` = c(1.004, 1.345, 1.460, 1.540),
                          `s(gam_variable_2_output)` = c(1, 1, 1, 1),
                          grouping_variable_1 = c(1,2,3,4),
                          grouping_variable_2 = c("a", "b", "a", "b"),
                          grouping_variable_3 = c(500, 500, 500, 500),
                          stringsAsFactors = FALSE) 
```

I want to apply a function to all of the smooth variables (variables that begin with "s(") only if the levels of that smooth variable arent 1 unique value.

Something like this should be accomplished through the following
```
smooth_data %>%
mutate_if(.predicate = funs(length(unique(.)) != 1 & grepl("s\\(", quo_name(quo(.)))),
          ~2) # we'll use this to keep it simple
```
Such that this should result in the following (I removed the rownames / numbers from R output)
```
s(gam_variable_1_output)
                       2
                       2
                       2
                       2
s(gam_variable_2_output)
                       1
                       1
                       1
                       1
grouping_variable_1       grouping_variable_2       grouping_variable_3
                  1                       "a"                       500
                  2                       "b"                       500
                  3                       "a"                       500
                  4                       "b"                       500
```
But the function doesnt work.
If we want to split the predicate up, then we see something interesting.

```
#### FIRST PART OF CONDITIONAL: only look at variables that arent a single value
## THIS WORKS
smooth_data %>% mutate_if(funs(length(unique(.)) != 1), ~2)

## ^ THAT IS THE SAME AS THIS; THIS WORKS
smooth_data %>% mutate_if(~length(unique(.)) != 1, ~2)

## THIS DOES NOT WORK
smooth_data %>% mutate_if(length(unique(.)) != 1, ~2)


#### SECOND PART OF CONDITIONAL: only look at variables that have name including `s(`
## THIS WORKS
smooth_data %>% mutate_if(grepl("s\\(", names(.)), ~2)

## THIS THROWS ERROR (BECAUSE OF `names(.)`)
smooth_data %>% mutate_if(~grepl("s\\(", names(.)), ~2)

## THIS DOES NOT WORK
smooth_data %>% mutate_if(~grepl("s\\(", quo_name(quo(.))), ~2)

## WHICH IS THE SAME AS THIS
smooth_data %>% mutate_if(funs(grepl("s\\(", quo_name(quo(.)))), ~2)

## AND THIS THROWS ERROR (BECAUSE .predicate NEEDS ~)
smooth_data %>% mutate_if(grepl("s\\(", quo_name(quo(.))), ~2)
```

This is interesting because it suggests to me that my main line of code cant run since the first part of the conditional needs to be in the funs() setting, while the second part cannot be in the funs() setting. This isnt an answer to the question but I think it clearly shows the problem with `mutate_if`

title: Explore using more explicit column referencing
description:
https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/30363bf501349be8536f9e332f1ce8846883c46b/R/group_data.R#L44

This illustrated a bug in a package I maintain - it extends `[`, but we did not realize `[` with a single argument does column reference.

``` r
obj <- tibble::tibble(col1 = c(1,2), col2 = c(3,4))

obj[0]
#> # A tibble: 2 x 0
obj[1]
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>    col1
#>   <dbl>
#> 1     1
#> 2     2
obj[1,]
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>    col1  col2
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     3
obj[,1]
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>    col1
#>   <dbl>
#> 1     1
#> 2     2
```

<sup>Created on 2020-03-22 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>


I wonder whether using `[,0]` would be a "better" or more explicit practice here, or if it makes a difference. 🤷‍♂ 

I have fixed the bug in my package now, but it definitely threw me for a loop!! Wanted to mention it in case others are affected.

title: summarize performance drop off with many groups
description:
I am testing out the dev version of dplyr and have noticed some performance regressions when using summarize with a large number of groups. Calling `n()` with a large number of groups produces a ~400x increased runtime, whereas using `max()` has ~10x increased runtime. 

Performance on `0.8.5`

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '0.8.5'

set.seed(42)
many_grps <- data.frame(grp = sample(1:1e5,
                                     1e6,
                                     replace = TRUE),
                        val = runif(1e6)) %>% 
  group_by(grp)
n_groups(many_grps)
#> [1] 99997

set.seed(42)
few_grps <- data.frame(grp = sample(1:100,
                                    1e6,
                                    replace = TRUE),
                       val = runif(1e6)) %>% 
  group_by(grp)
n_groups(few_grps)
#> [1] 100

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(summarize(many_grps, n = n()),
                               summarize(many_grps, m = max(val)),
                               summarize(few_grps, n = n()),
                               summarize(few_grps, m = max(val)),
                               times = 5,
                               unit = 'ms')
#> Unit: milliseconds
#>                                expr       min        lq      mean    median
#>       summarize(many_grps, n = n())  2.474665  2.531869  2.786606  2.743778
#>  summarize(many_grps, m = max(val)) 17.693114 19.297248 22.774355 20.640482
#>        summarize(few_grps, n = n())  0.144234  0.154476  0.182271  0.175776
#>   summarize(few_grps, m = max(val))  8.792012 10.393226 11.908963 10.482098
#>         uq       max neval cld
#>   3.037315  3.145401     5 a  
#>  27.791042 28.449888     5   c
#>   0.190168  0.246701     5 a  
#>  14.835186 15.042294     5  b
```

title: possible circularity when installing dplyr 1.0 with devtools
description: Hi.  Romain asked me to post this.  I tried to install dplyr from github using `devtools::install_github()` to resolve expected CRAN package incompatibilities with dplyr 1.0.0.  However, head of master currently needs rlang_0.4.5.9000, and devtools imports rlang, which can't be re-installed while in use. (I can't use devtools to update rlang for the same reason.)  Happy to post the output if helpful.  And apologies in advance if I've missed an obvious workaround.  I'm not seeing a solution on SO for "install devtools dependencies from github".

title: Change documentation of `vars()` so it's consistent with ggplot2 usage
description:
The documentation of `vars()` labels it as superseded and states it is not needed anymore. I think this will be confusing if ggplot2 users try to look it up and have dplyr loaded as well:
https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/ee6d931c46fbb9efe3030f67bd49c63b3b578497/R/colwise.R#L87-L108

I suggest to just keep the following, and maybe add a sentence about ggplot2? (Not sure where we stand with cross-package help references at this time.)
``` r
#' Select variables 
#' 
#' This helper is intended to provide equivalent semantics to 
#' [select()]. It is used for instance in scoped summarising and 
#' mutating verbs ([mutate_at()] and [summarise_at()]).
#' 
#' Note that verbs accepting a `vars()` specification also accept a 
#' numeric vector of positions or a character vector of column names. 
#' 
#' @param ... <[`tidy-select`][dplyr_tidy_select]> Variables to include/exclude 
#'   in mutate/summarise. You can use same specifications as in [select()]. 
#'   If missing, defaults to all non-grouping variables. 
#' @seealso [all_vars()] and [any_vars()] for other quoting 
#'   functions that you can use with scoped verbs. 
#' @export 
```

title: Please support classed atomic vectors in tidy framework
description:
Support for classed atomic vectors in dplyr is very important for various use cases. It has long been very helpful and powerful that this could be done with Tidyverse packages.

The way this worked prior to dplyr 1.0, it was great for both readability (`x` and `y` below were not masked as opaque list columns for example), but far more importantly, only with the necessary classes on these atomic vectors could functions be meaningfully applied to them so that analysis and data manipulation could be done in a tidy framework. For example below, without the classes, it seems I basically can't use the tidyverse for this any longer. Am I missing some work around?

```r
library(dplyr)
library(tabr)

x <- as_vector_time("c e_g c'e_'g'")
x
<Noteworthy string>
  Format: vectorized time
  Values: c <e_g> <c'e_'g'>

# transpose notes by two semitones, then recover pitch interval
tibble(x = x) %>% 
  mutate(y = transpose(x, 2), interval = pitch_interval(x, y))
# A tibble: 3 x 3
  x          y          interval
  <notwrthy> <notwrthy>    <int>
1 c          d                 2
2 e_g        fa                2
3 c'e_'g'    d'f'a'            2

# slightly different example; this is a lag function, not element-wise
x <- as_vector_time("a, c e r r c a, g#, a ac'e'")
x
<Noteworthy string>
  Format: vectorized time
  Values: a, c e r r c a, g#, a <ac'e'>

tibble(pitch = x) %>% mutate(scale_interval = scale_diff(pitch))
# A tibble: 10 x 2
   pitch      scale_int
   <notwrthy> <chr>    
 1 a,         NA       
 2 c          m3       
 3 e          M3       
 4 r          NA       
 5 r          NA       
 6 c          M3       
 7 a,         m3       
 8 g#,        m2       
 9 a          m9       
10 ac'e'      P1  
```

The above examples are using the current release of dplyr. With the upcoming v1.0, I get errors like `mutate() argument pitch errored.` It seems like it has to do with the vectors having classes.

Tibbles can still hold these objects, e.g., `tibble(pitch = x)` works fine alone and I can even mutate `pitch`, as long as the function does not create another classed atomic variable. E.g., the second example will still work because it creates a character variable.

`tibble(pitch = x) %>% mutate(pitch2 = pitch)` works as well. 

But not `tibble(pitch = x) %>% mutate(pitch2 = x)`

Going forward, it seems any such variables would have to be pulled out of tibbles, manipulated, and  then reinserted into a new tibble, just to have them in a tibble (and all done with the `tibble` call). But actually analyzing and manipulating the data "the tidy way" becomes impossible for all such data structures. Is it necessary to remove such a broad functionality? This was one of the beauties of using tibbles and a tidy framework when working with classed atomic objects.

title: Unclear Error When Merging with Incompatible Classes
description:
I'm testing some underlying issues with my package that are showing up with the upcoming version 1.0.0.

I was trying to track down an issue with a `full_join()` call, and I got an error:  "Error: No common type for `needles$Subject` <double> and `haystack$Subject` <ordered<2bdd1>>."  I had no idea what that meant at first since neither `needles` nor `haystack` appear in my code.  The previous message was much clearer, and it would be nice to have that message or a similar one back for 1.0, "Error: Can't join on 'A' x 'A' because of incompatible types (integer / factor)"

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

  tibble(A=factor(1:3), B=LETTERS[1:3]),

)

title: case_when evaluates function on rows not selected by logical expression
description:
When using `case_when` within a `mutate` call, I expect a function to be evaluated only on the rows that are selected by the logical expression in the two-sided formula. But when I evaluate a function like `log`, it seems to be being passed the entire column such that it elicits a warning message. This is the case even if the logical expression only picks out positive numbers.

Here is a minimally reproducible example:

```
adf <- tibble(type = rep(c('to_log', 'not_to_log'), each = 5),
              value = c(runif(5, .01, 1), runif(5, -1, -.01)))

mutate(adf, case_when(value > 0 ~ log(value),
                      value <= 0 ~ value))

mutate(adf, case_when(type == 'to_log' ~ log(value),
                      type == 'not_to_log' ~ value))
```

With an unexpected warning message from `log`:

```

title: Feature request: sample_n samples UP TO n rows
description:
I want to take up the old issue #3681 by @kevinmneal:

> Let's say I have a dataframe with several groups, with varying numbers of samples (rows) in each group. I'd like to be able to sample up to 10 rows from each group. However, some groups have fewer than 10 samples, and so the function returns an error (will only sample 10, and no fewer, from each group), with a suggestion to sample with replacement. Sampling with replacement will, of course, not return 10 unique samples from groups with 10 or more available, and so my desired condition of subsampling my dataframe to up to 10 samples per group is not met.

It has been closed with a rather cryptic remark.  I believe that at least a workaround should be documented here.  I could also offer to work on this: the proposal would be to add a logical option `allow_smaller_sample` to `sample_n`, which is `FALSE` by default.  If it is true, the returned sample either has the correct size or is either everything (per group).

title: summarise() and st_union() causes an error when there a Polygons and Multipolyons
description:
---

summarise() with st_union produces an error with the developer version. The following example works with the CRAN version but not with the developer version. The error is that the type is not the same (Polygon vs. Multipolygon). I do not now if this is intendit in the new version or if this is an error in the dev version.

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)

chapters = read_sf("https://benjaminschlegel.ch/charts/chaptermap/chapters.geojson")
chapters = st_make_valid(chapters)

chapters$Chapter = str_replace_all(chapters$Chapter, "-", "/")
chapters$Chapter2020 = ifelse(
  chapters$Chapter %in% c("Aarau", "Olten"), 
  "Aarau/Olten", 
  ifelse(
    chapters$Chapter %in% c("Bülach", "Winterthur/Schaffhausen"), 
    "Winterthur/Schaffhausen/Bülach",
    chapters$Chapter
  ))

chapters = chapters %>% group_by(Chapter2020) %>% 
  summarise(geometry = st_union(geometry)) %>% ungroup()
```

title: case_when: support tibble on RHS
description:
Sometimes it is useful to return multiple values from a `case_when()` call (e.g. a name of a property and a short description). Currently, this only works indirectly by wrapping the RHS in an extra list:

``` r
library(dplyr, quietly = TRUE, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

x <- rep.int(c(TRUE, FALSE), times = 5)
case_when(
  x ~ list(tibble(a = 1, b = 1)),
  !x ~ list(tibble(a = 0, b = 2))
) %>% 
  bind_rows()
#> # A tibble: 10 x 2
#>        a     b
#>  * <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1     1     1
#>  2     0     2
#>  3     1     1
#>  4     0     2
#>  5     1     1
#>  6     0     2
#>  7     1     1
#>  8     0     2

#> 10     0     2
```

<sup>Created on 2020-03-17 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

  x ~ list(tibble(a = 1:10, b = 1:10)),
  !x ~ list(tibble(a = -(1:10), b = 2*(1:10)))
) %>%

title: ntile() distributes remainders across buckets differently in dplyr vs database
description:
Hi!  👋   I'm seeing slight differences in the way `ntile()` distributes "remainders" across buckets in dplyr versus in the database I'm using (Redshift). 

For example, when we divide mtcars (32 rows) into 5 buckets, the two remainders are distributed into bucket 1 & 3 (arrows mine).

``` r
library(dplyr)

mtcars_dplyr <- mtcars %>% 
  mutate(bucket = ntile(mpg, 5)) %>% 
  select(mpg, bucket)

mtcars_dplyr %>% count(bucket)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 2
#>   bucket     n
#>    <int> <int>
#> 1      1     7 <-----
#> 2      2     6
#> 3      3     7 <-----
#> 4      4     6
#> 5      5     6
```

<sup>Created on 2020-03-17 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

When I do the same in the database, the remainders get distributed to the buckets in order. The [Oracle docs](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/B19306_01/server.102/b14200/functions101.htm) describe it this way:

> The remainder values (the remainder of number of rows divided by buckets) are distributed one for each bucket, starting with bucket 1. 

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)

mtcars_db <- tbl_memdb(mtcars)

mtcars_db <- mtcars_db %>%
  mutate(bucket = ntile(mpg, 5)) %>%
  select(mpg, bucket) %>%
  collect()

mtcars_db %>% count(bucket)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 2
#>   bucket     n
#>    <int> <int>
#> 1      1     7 <-----
#> 2      2     7 <-----
#> 3      3     6
#> 4      4     6
#> 5      5     6
```

title: mutate doesn't work with `fs::fs_bytes()`.
description:
The `fs_bytes` class is missing a vctrs implementation, so that `mutate` (and probably some other dplyr operations) give an error.

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
tibble(size = 1) %>% 
  mutate(size = fs::fs_bytes(size))
#> Error: `mutate()` argument `size` errored.
#> ℹ `size` is `fs::fs_bytes(size)`.
#> x Can't find vctrs or base methods for concatenation.
#> vctrs methods must be implemented for class `fs_bytes`.
#> See <https://vctrs.r-lib.org/articles/s3-vector.html>.
```

title: Allow bind_rows() to evaluate "." in a pipe
description:
When working with a dataset that has multiple "types" of records that need to be dealt with in a pipe, it would be nice to have a way to "split" paths. I.e. in my pipe, provide two or three "branches" where I can behave differently and then merge the dataset back together again.

`bind_rows()` is very close to providing this behavior, but it does not allow piping with the `.` within its arguments. I'm not sure if this is even feasible, but is something that I have used in various other functions with success (`join` variants, etc.), and seems to work with named variables.

Alternatively, some other way to "split" a pipe into branches would be nice.

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))

nrow(iris)
#> [1] 150

# works for doubling rows
iris %>%
  bind_rows(., .) %>%
  nrow()
#> [1] 300

# fails for piped arguments with "."
iris %>%
  bind_rows(
    . %>% filter(Sepal.Length < 5),
    . %>% filter(Sepal.Length >= 5)
  )
#> Error: Argument 2 must be a data frame or a named atomic vector

# works with a named variable
bind_rows(
  iris %>% filter(Sepal.Length < 5),
  iris %>% filter(Sepal.Length >= 5)
) %>%
nrow()
#> [1] 150
```

title: GitHub news out of sync with CRAN
description: GitHub has 0.8.4 listed as the development version, while 0.8.5 is on CRAN. Further, the changes in the GH news for 0.8.4 are not present on CRAN. I think the GH news should be updated to reflect the CRAN releases and their associated small changes, and the dev version bumped to 0.8.6.

title: issue with do() and group_modify() with dplyr 0.8.5
description:
When I downloaded the newest version of dplyr, the following code produced an error. When I re-installed the 0.8.3 version, the code snippet runs fine. 

```r
# install.packages("devtools")
# devtools::install_github("meghapsimatrix/simhelpers")

library(simhelpers)
library(dplyr)

welch_res %>%
  group_by(n, mean_diff, method) %>% # grouping 
  do(calc_absolute(.,  estimates = est, true_param = mean_diff)) %>% # run the function
  mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 5) %>% # rounding
  kable() 
```

Here is the error from the 0.8.5 version: 
```
Error: 'vec_as_subscript' is not an exported object from 'namespace:vctrs'
```

I ran the code one line at a time and the error pops up when I run the do() function. 

The code should run as shown in this vignette: https://meghapsimatrix.github.io/simhelpers/articles/MCSE.html

I just want to know if there are any issues with do() or group_modify() functions in the upcoming dplyr version 🐱 

Thank you!

title: mutate crashes R if assigning new variable(s) and removing variables at once
description:
The issue happens with the latest dplyr on GitHub.
dplyr 0.8.3 is okay.

Here is an example.

```r
reprex::reprex(
  dplyr::mutate(data.frame(x = 1, y = 1), z = 1, x = NULL, y = NULL)
)
# Error: <callr_status_error in get_result(output = out, options):
# callr subprocess failed: could not start R, exited with non-zero status, has crashed or was killed>
```

Following works fine

``` r
dplyr::mutate(data.frame(x = 1, y = 1), x = NULL, y = NULL)
#> data frame with 0 columns and 1 row
dplyr::mutate(data.frame(x = 1, y = 1), z = 1, y = NULL)
#>   x z
#> 1 1 1
dplyr::mutate(data.frame(x = 1, y = 1), x = NULL, y = NULL, z = 1)
#>   z
#> 1 1
```

description:
Hi,

library(dplyr)

title: across() argument names and argument order
description:
I’ve just read the [blog post about dplyr 1.0.0](https://www.tidyverse.org/blog/2020/03/dplyr-1-0-0-is-coming-soon/) and couldn’t wait to get my hands on `across()` – it looks great\! I did some quick testing and ran into a couple of issues with the arguments:

  - Should `across()`'s argument names be prefixed with dots to avoid `...` collisions? Partial argument name matching is a particularly nasty problem otherwise.
  - Should the `names` argument be moved after `...` so that it’s easier to pass positional arguments to `fns` like you would in `purrr::map()` et al? It doesn’t seem like it would ever really be a good idea to pass `names` by position, anyway.

<!-- end list -->

``` r
library(tidyverse)

tbl <- tibble(
  x = c("a", "a", "b", "c"),
  y = c("a", "b", "b", "c")
)

# this is what I was after:
mutate_at(tbl, vars(x, y), fct_lump, n = 1)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   x     y    
#>   <fct> <fct>
#> 1 a     Other
#> 2 a     b    
#> 3 Other b    
#> 4 Other Other

# unfortunate partial match collision:
mutate(tbl, across(c(x, y), fct_lump, n = 1))
#> Error: Column 2 must be named.
#> Use .name_repair to specify repair.
mutate(tbl, across(x, fct_lump, n = 1))
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>   x     y     `1`  
#>   <chr> <chr> <fct>
#> 1 a     a     a    
#> 2 a     b     a    
#> 3 b     b     b    
#> 4 c     c     c

# workaround:
mutate(tbl, across(c(x, y), fct_lump, n = 1, names = "{col}"))
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   x     y    
#>   <fct> <fct>
#> 1 a     Other
#> 2 a     b    
#> 3 Other b    
#> 4 Other Other

# this is a pretty common pattern I use to modify
# a column without having to type out the name twice
mutate_at(tbl, vars(x), str_c, "_foo")
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   x     y    
#>   <chr> <chr>
#> 1 a_foo a    
#> 2 a_foo b    
#> 3 b_foo b    
#> 4 c_foo c

# but alas:
mutate(tbl, across(x, str_c, "_foo"))
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>   x     y     `_foo`
#>   <chr> <chr> <chr> 
#> 1 a     a     a     
#> 2 a     b     a     
#> 3 b     b     b     
#> 4 c     c     c
```

title: Feature request: annotated mutates (show definition of columns)
description:
One advantage excel has over dplyr/data.table/pandas/SQL is that non-technical users can click on to each cell and see the cell definition. This is useful to allow our non-technical managers/external stakeholders to understand what are the transforms done on the data. 

One middle ground for dplyr might be annotated columns, eg the following

---

```r
library(tidyverse)  # version 1.2.1


mutate_annotated <- function(.data, ...) {
  arg_vars <- enquos(...)
  my_labels <- map(arg_vars, rlang::as_label)
  .data <- .data %>% mutate(...)
  for(col_name in names(my_labels)) {
    attr(.data[[col_name]], 'label') <- sprintf('= %s', my_labels[[col_name]]) 
  }
  .data
}

display_annotated <- function(df, to_excel = FALSE) {
  my_labels <- map(df, function(x) ifelse(!is.null(attr(x, 'label')), attr(x, 'label'), ''))
  if (to_excel) {
    my_labels <- map(my_labels, function(x) str_c(" ", x))
  }
  df_display <- bind_rows(as_tibble(my_labels), df %>% mutate_all(as.character))
  df_display
}

display_annotated_alternate <- function(df, to_excel = FALSE) {
  my_labels <- map(df, function(x) ifelse(!is.null(attr(x, 'label')), attr(x, 'label'), ''))
  my_labels <- as.character(my_labels)
  if (to_excel) {
    my_labels <- str_c(' ', my_labels)
  }
  colnames(df) <- str_c(colnames(df), my_labels, sep = '\n')
  df
}


df <- tibble(a = c(1, 2), b = c(3, 4)) %>% 
  mutate_annotated(
    c = a + b,
    d = c/b,  
    e = d - lag(d, 1)
  )

display_annotated(df, to_excel = TRUE) %>% write_delim("clipboard-16384", delim = '\t', na = '')
```

above output copied to clipboard and pasted to excel becames:

a | b | c | d | e

  |   | = a + b | = c/b | = d - lag(d, 1)
1 | 3 | 4 | 1.333333 |  
2 | 4 | 6 | 1.5 | 0.166667

Please let me know if this seems promising or if there are other better ways to do this... I would imagine a similar thing can be done for summarise(). Of course, this gets tricky once users do renames, but not impossible.

title: across() performance slow compared to scoped variant
description:
I ran into an issue where `across()` takes a bit of time on large grouped calculations, but the retired `summarize_if()` variant runs much faster. I cooked up a simple example below.

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = F)

df <- tibble(cbind.data.frame(
                   grp_1 = as.character(sort(rep(1:250, 4))),
                   grp_2 = as.character(rep(1:4, 250)), 
                   matrix(rnorm(1000 * 100), nrow = 1000)))

bench::mark(
  iterations = 10,
  filter_gc = FALSE,
  
  `summarize(across(is.numeric, diff))` =   {
    df %>% 
      group_by(grp_1,grp_2) %>% 
      summarize(across(is.numeric, diff))
  },
  `summarize_if(is.numeric, diff)` = {
    df %>% 
      group_by(grp_1,grp_2) %>% 
      summarize_if(is.numeric, diff)

) %>%

If you are seeing this error in code that used to work, the most likely cause is a change dbplyr 1.4.0. Previously
`df$x` or `df[[y]]` implied that `df` was a local variable, but now you must make that explict with `!!` or `local()`,

title: mutate_all() and multi-line purrr-style function
description:
Hello! It looks like mutate_all may exhibit inconsistent behaviour when purrr-like functions with multiple operations are passed inside of brackets. In the output below, using this type of input function results in unexpected output, whereas creating the same function in the working environment or explicitly writing it as an anonymous function works great. 

``` r
library(dplyr)

df = data.frame(x = c("A", "B"), y = c(NA_character_, "B"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# this should change column y from c(NA, B) to c(--, B)
fill_na <- function(.x){
  .x[is.na(.x)] <- '--'
  .x
}

# works great!
mutate_all(df, fill_na)
#>   x  y
#> 1 A --
#> 2 B  B

# works less great
mutate_all(df,
  .funs = ~ {
    .x[is.na(.x)] <- '--'
    .x
  }
)
#>   x y
#> 1 A A
#> 2 B B

# using explicit function fixes it
mutate_all(df,
  .funs = function(.x){
    .x[is.na(.x)] <- '--'
    .x
  }
)
#>   x  y
#> 1 A --
#> 2 B  B
```

title: Option to choose the separator in summarise_all [feature request]
description:
When you use `summarise_all`, it can often be interesting to pivot the result, for instance for plotting purpose.

Here is something similar to what I usually do:

```r
iris %>% 
  group_by(Species) %>% 
  summarise_all(list(mean=mean, sd=sd)) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols=-Species, names_to = c("variable", "fun"), names_sep="_")   
```
Unfortunately, I often find myself dealing with variable names having underscores inside (as it is the recommended way in the tidyverse IIRC). Of course, this leads to this kind of errors, where the pivoting cannot know which underscore is supposed to be used:

```r
iris %>% 
  group_by(Species) %>% 
  rename_all(~str_replace_all(.x, "\\.", "_")) %>% 
  summarise_all(list(mean=mean, sd=sd)) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols=-Species, names_to = c("variable", "fun"), names_sep="_") 
```

There are some workarounds but they don't always work. If it was possible to explicitly choose the separator, I could write something like this and it should work every time:

```r
iris %>% 
  group_by(Species) %>% 
  rename_all(~str_replace_all(.x, "\\.", "_")) %>% 
  summarise_all(list(mean=mean, sd=sd), sep="__") %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols=-Species, names_to = c("variable", "fun"), names_sep="__") 
```

Alternatively (or even additionally, as it may handle other cases), `pivot_longer` could have a `use_last_only` option to force it to only use the last occurrence of a said separator.

title: across() needs to pass ... to `fns`
Unable to refer to the name of the column being acted on with new mutate syntax
description:
The code below attempts to perform a `mutate_at` with the function using the name of column being acted on to determine the outcome. 

With the previous syntax, using `quo_name(quo(.))` within `funs()` would return the name of the column being acted on. With the new syntax, this just returns a literal dot. 

``` r
# Load packages
library(magrittr)
library(tidyverse)

# Initialise data frame
template_df <- tibble::as_tibble(list("subject_ids"=c("S01", "S02", "S03", "S04"))) %>% 
                      dplyr::mutate(attr_path="", 
                                    attr_url="",
                                    attr_date="",
                                    attr_random=c("a", "12", "8", "3"))

mappings <- list(pre_path="/path/to/subject_info/prefix",
                 pre_url="s3://path/to/aws/prefix",
                 pre_date="26th Feb 2020")

valid_samples <- c("S01", "S03", "S04")


populate_df <- function(x, column_name, subject_id, valid_samples, mappings){
  # Return the right attribute based on the column
  pre_key = str_replace(column_name, "^attr_", "pre_")
  # Check sample is valid
  if(! subject_id %in% valid_samples){
    # We return nothing if no valid
    return("")
  }
  #print(c(x, column_name))
  # Conditional return depending on what column this is
  if(column_name %in% c('attr_date')){
    # If this is a date, return the date plus the time
    return(paste(mappings[pre_key], Sys.time()))
  } else if(column_name %in% c('attr_path', 'attr_url')){
    # If this is a path, return the path prefix plus the subject id
    return(file.path(mappings[pre_key], subject_id))
  } else {
    # Not sure what column this is, or what to do with it 
    # so we'll return the previous value
    return(x)
  }
}

# The old way - works
template_df %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  dplyr::mutate_at(vars(starts_with("attr_")), 
                   funs(populate_df(x=., 
                                    column_name=quo_name(quo(.)), 
                                    subject_id=.data$subject_ids,
                                    valid_samples=valid_samples,
                                    mappings=mappings))) %>%
  ungroup()
#> Warning: funs() is soft deprecated as of dplyr 0.8.0
#> Please use a list of either functions or lambdas: 
#> 
#>   # Simple named list: 
#>   list(mean = mean, median = median)
#> 
#>   # Auto named with `tibble::lst()`: 
#>   tibble::lst(mean, median)
#> 
#>   # Using lambdas
#>   list(~ mean(., trim = .2), ~ median(., na.rm = TRUE))
#> This warning is displayed once per session.
#> # A tibble: 4 x 5
#>   subject_ids attr_path           attr_url        attr_date          attr_random
#>   <chr>       <chr>               <chr>           <chr>              <chr>      
#> 1 S01         "/path/to/subject_~ "s3://path/to/~ "26th Feb 2020 20~ "a"        
#> 2 S02         ""                  ""              ""                 ""         
#> 3 S03         "/path/to/subject_~ "s3://path/to/~ "26th Feb 2020 20~ "8"        
#> 4 S04         "/path/to/subject_~ "s3://path/to/~ "26th Feb 2020 20~ "3"

# Alternative new way 1 - list with ~fun syntax
template_df %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  dplyr::mutate_at(vars(starts_with("attr_")), 
                   list(~ populate_df(x=., 
                                      column_name=quo_name(quo(.)),

title: Pass through fields with summarize - feature request
description:
Please briefly describe your problem and what output you expect. If you have a question, please don't use this form. Instead, ask on <https://stackoverflow.com/> or <https://community.rstudio.com/>.

Please include a minimal reproducible example (AKA a reprex). If you've never heard of a [reprex](http://reprex.tidyverse.org/) before, start by reading <https://www.tidyverse.org/help/#reprex>.

---
## Problem Statement

The `group_by` -> `summarize` pairing is used quite a lot to both reduce the number of rows and columns in your dataset to bring you do the fields you care about. However, there are cases where additional fields may provide information that while are not required for this summarization at this step, provides useful information down stream.  I was able to come up with three cases of work around that I have deployed myself to get around this problem. The most common one I have seen in the wild is the first case I highlight in my reprex; adding additional fields to the group_by.
---

# Demo
``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(tibble)

sample_df <- tribble(
  ~keyvar1,   ~keyvar2,    ~info1,    ~info2, ~sample, ~measure1, ~measure2,
  "subj_id1",  "test1",  "group1",  "gemini",       1,        1,          2,
  "subj_id1",  "test1",  "group1",  "gemini",       2,        2,        1.5,
  "subj_id1",  "test2",  "group1",  "gemini",       1,       45,         62,
  "subj_id1",  "test2",  "group1",  "gemini",       3,       40,         66,
  "subj_id2",  "test1",  "group2",  "taurus",       1,        2,        2.5,
  "subj_id2",  "test1",  "group2",  "taurus",       2,      1.8,          1,
  "subj_id2",  "test2",  "group2",  "taurus",       1,       44,         55,
  "subj_id2",  "test2",  "group2",  "taurus",       3,       43,         20
) 


# Current setup has three ways to get around needing varisbles to be passed
# to later data.frames

# 1. listing non-key fields in group_by
# advantage: easy to add the "non-key" fields
# disadvantage: can lead to confusion when reading code what the key variables are
# not sure if there is a increase in processing time
sample_df_aggregated_extra <- sample_df %>% 
  group_by(keyvar1, keyvar2, info1, info2) %>% 
  summarize(
    measure1 = mean(measure1),
    measure2 = mean(measure2)
  )

# 2. using "unique" in summarize
# advantage: clear which fields are key or passed through
# disadvantage: time consuming and not in the spirit of DRY
sample_df_aggregated_unique <- sample_df %>% 
  group_by(keyvar1, keyvar2) %>% 
  summarize(
    info1 = unique(info1),
    info2 = unique(info2),
    measure1 = mean(measure1),
    measure2 = mean(measure2)
  )

# 3. using joins and temporary objects
# advantage: clear which fields are key or passed through
# disadvantage: time consuming and requires another step
sample_df_aggregated_simple <- sample_df %>% 
  group_by(keyvar1, keyvar2) %>% 
  summarize(
    measure1 = mean(measure1),
    measure2 = mean(measure2)
  )

final_sample_df_aggregated <- sample_df %>% 
  distinct(keyvar1, keyvar2, info1, info2) %>% 
  left_join(sample_df_aggregated_simple, by = c("keyvar1","keyvar2"))


testthat::expect_equal(
  sample_df_aggregated_extra,
  sample_df_aggregated_unique
)

testthat::expect_equal(
  sample_df_aggregated_extra,
  final_sample_df_aggregated
)
```
<sup>Created on 2020-02-23 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

## Request/Proposal

 Would it be possible to add an argument to either group_by or summarize, or maybe a "keep" function for within "group_by" that allows for the identification of "tag-along" fields that are
advantageous to keep but at the current grouping add no information. 

I tried to see if there was any past issues that addressed this and I didn't come across any. I apologize if this is a duplicate.

```r

## Keep field in summarize. A bit clunky
sample_df_aggregated_unique <- sample_df %>% 
  group_by(keyvar1, keyvar2) %>% 
  summarize(
    info1 = unique(info1),
    info2 = unique(info2),
    ..keep = c(measure1,measure2)
  )

## using a helper function, similar to `match` and the other var helper funcs.
sample_df_aggregated_unique <- sample_df %>% 
  group_by(keyvar1, keyvar2, keep(measure1,measure2)) %>% 
  summarize(
    info1 = unique(info1),
    info2 = unique(info2),
  )
```

title: Mutate on a column of exprs produces a list rather than updates the columns
description:
Another weird case from using expr in a tibble (I do appreciate doing this throws up problems)...

If you mutate a normal column using .data, you affect each row in the table using that row's value. (demonstrated in the example using column x, from which we produce x2. So far so normal.

If you mutate where our .data variable is an expression column however, in this case column y, we get returned a list of values for the entire column, which is then placed in each row.

``` r
library(rlang)
test <- tibble::tibble(x =c("A", "B"), y = c(expr(a), expr(b)))
dplyr::mutate(test, x2 = paste(x, "A"))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   x     y      x2   
#>   <chr> <list> <chr>
#> 1 A     <sym>  A A  
#> 2 B     <sym>  B A
dplyr::mutate(test, y2 = expr_text(y))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   x     y      y2        
#>   <chr> <list> <chr>     
#> 1 A     <sym>  list(a, b)
#> 2 B     <sym>  list(a, b)

<sup>Created on 2020-02-20 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>
```

title: Order seems important when using !grepl in filter
description:
I've encountered a problem using !grepl in the filter command in dplyr. In the work I am doing, the use of  ! is important. I'm removing the Chatham Islands from a data.frame, which will be linked later in my code

Works (grepl): 
SIAreasNoDups2013 <- AreasNoDups2013 %>%
   filter(AU2013_V1_ >= 580200 | grepl("Chatham", AU2013_label))

Doesn't work (!grepl):
SIAreasNoDups2013 <- AreasNoDups2013 %>%
   filter(AU2013_V1_ >= 580200 | !grepl("Chatham", AU2013_label))

Doesn't work (!grepl):
SIAreasNoDups2013 <- AreasNoDups2013 %>%
  filter(!grepl("Chatham", AU2013_label) | AU2013_V1_ >= 580200)

Works:
SIAreasNoDups2013 <- AreasNoDups2013 %>%
  filter(!(grepl("Chatham", AU2013_label) | AU2013_V1_ < 580200))

The data is from a public file, so I have uploaded it to my repository. I'm new to using GitHub so let me know if you can't access this file: https://github.com/programgirl/TestData/blob/master/AreasNoDups2013.rds

title: sample_n() is slow because of slice()?
description:
I realized that `sample_n` was the bottleneck of my simulations, and was shocked by how much slower it is than base `sample`+subsetting. Turns out this is due to `slice` (which I understand is being called) being much slower than base `[` for me.

Example with a tibble since this [issue ](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/4312) suggested it as a fix

```r
df <- data.frame(A = rep('A', 20), C = seq(1:20))
df2 <- dplyr::as_tibble(df)

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  
  'sample_n'     = {dplyr::sample_n(df2,size = 1,weight = C)},
  
  'sample+['     = {df2[sample(1:20, size = 1, prob = df2$C),]},
  
  'sample+slice' = {dplyr::slice(df2, sample(1:20, size = 1, prob = df2$C))}
  
)

# Unit: microseconds
# expr         min    lq    mean   median   uq   max   neval
# sample_n     149.1 155.5 162.925 159.70 163.65 342.9   100
# sample+[     31.0  37.3  42.335  42.65  44.70  80.3    100
# sample+slice 127.5 132.9 138.887 135.45 138.50 324.1   100
```

Also happens without sampling

```r
microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  
  '['     = {df2[5,]},
  'slice' = {dplyr::slice(df2, 5)}
  
)

# Unit: microseconds
# expr  min    lq    mean median     uq   max neval
# [     22.6  25.4  29.572  30.55  32.55  60.1   100
# slice 104.9 108.2 114.078 110.40 112.80 280.3  100
```
Using R 3.6.1, dplyr 0.8.3
Am missing something ? Thanks!

title: Should relocate() inform when .before/.after is not specified?
description:
Like joins do when `.by` is not specified, could `relocate()` show a concise message about what's happening when neither `.before` or `.after` is specified? Something like `Relocating, .before = 1`?

Without reading the docs, it doesn't seem obvious that the selected columns should be moved to the left-hand side, and having the message would protect against misspellings of the argument names.

For example, I tried the following, and it took me a while to figure out why "it wasn't working"; i.e. that I had forgotten the dot prefix from `.after`:
``` r
library(dplyr)

df <- tibble(a = 1, b = 1, c = 1, d = "a", e = "a", f = "a")
df %>% relocate(f, after = is.numeric)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   f         a     b     c d     e    
#>   <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr> <chr>
#> 1 a         1     1     1 a     a
```

Just like with the join message, it would be simple enough to explicitly specify `.before = 1` to suppress the message, while still having the shorthand for when you don't care about it.
