```
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2

#> 1 name1 north
#> 2 name2 north
```

title: sample_frac wrong on grouped data without indices attribute (e.g. after a summarise)
description:
This works as I expect:
```r
> expand.grid(a=1:5,b=1:5) %>% group_by(a,b) %>% summarise %>% group_by(a) %>% sample_frac(0.2)
# A tibble: 5 x 2
# Groups:   a [5]
      a     b
  <int> <int>
1     1     1
2     2     4
3     3     1
4     4     3
5     5     4
```

I should be able to remove the group_by(a) in the call above, because coming out of the summarise(), it's already grouped by a.  But something goes very wrong when I do so:

```r
> expand.grid(a=1:5,b=1:5) %>% group_by(a,b) %>% summarise %>% sample_frac(0.2)
# A tibble: 0 x 2
# Groups:   a [0]
# ... with 2 variables: a <int>, b <int>
```

The only difference between the two cases is the absence of the "indices" attribute in the former case.  We can verify that stripping indices reproduces the broken behavior:

```r
> expand.grid(a=1:5,b=1:5) %>% group_by(a,b) %>% summarise %>% group_by(a) %>% structure(indices=NULL) %>% sample_frac(0.2)
# A tibble: 0 x 2
# Groups:   a [0]
# ... with 2 variables: a <int>, b <int>
```

title: Use different alias for funs(), do() and source data reference
description:
Hello,

Dplyr use . as reference to the manipulated element in `*_all, *_if, *_at`, etc... function, as reference to the manipulated rows with `do()` and as reference to the source data in almost every dplyr function.

Wouldn't be useful to define different aliases for different purposes? for example `.x, .rows, .data`, so that something like this (totally invented example) is possible:

```R
Data %>% 
    group_by(Age) %>% 
    do({
        Other.Data %>% filter(Age == DF$Age) %>%
            mutate_at(vars(matches('Foo')), funs(.x > rowMeans(.rows))) %>% 
            mutate(Bar = sum(Bar > mean(.data$Bar)))
    })
```
Would prevent me to define alias before and avoid errors.

Thanks

title: Feature request: inner join on character and factor columns
description:
Currently when you join a character vector and a factor together the join works, but the joined column is converted into a character vector. This is definitely what you would want for most joins, but an inner join seems like it should (or at least could) have the result be a factor. By the definition of an inner join all of the results should be levels of the factor column, so it is hard to imagine situations where the user would prefer the output to be a character over a factor.

For example

```r
library(tidyverse)
base_data <-
  data_frame(raw_string = c("a","b","c","d"), 
             raw_value  = c( 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ))
lookup_info <-
  data_frame(fancy_string = factor(c("a","b")),
             fancy_other_thing =   c(100,200))
       
inner_join(base_data, lookup_info, by = c("raw_string"="fancy_string"))
```

Gives the warning
```r
Column `raw_string`/`fancy_string` joining character vector and factor, coercing into character vector
```

But the column could be a factor with the levels of `fancy_string`.

title: Error: The LHS of `:=` must be a string or a symbol
description:
I am running the following code which is supposed to create a column name produced by summarize using paste. 

```
> data <- data.frame(A=c("A","B","C"), B=c(1,2,3))
> data %>% group_by(A) %>% summarize(paste("hello","world",sep="_"):= n())
Error: The LHS of `:=` must be a string or a symbol
```
Although paste evaluates to "character".  The code below works.

```
data <- data.frame(A=c("A","B","C"), B=c(1,2,3))
dD<- paste("hello","world",sep="_")
data %>% group_by(A) %>% summarize(dD:= n())
```

I am guessing this is related to NSE since not a bug but is there a way to make it work?

title: Feature Request: imap_at*
description:
Ran into an interesting problem where I have a `tibble` and a list of columns -> values-that-mean-missing which does not span all columns of the tibble. The goal is to make the proper NA-substitutions in that tibble subject to the list of values-that-mean missing.

It's easy enough to do this for a small number of values, but it'd be nice to use `purrr` iterators here.

Here's a reprex:
``` r
library(tidyverse)

mt_tbl <- as_tibble(mtcars)

na_vals <- list(
  cyl = 6,
  disp = 160
)

# naive way
naive <- mt_tbl %>%
  mutate(
    cyl = na_if(cyl, na_vals$cyl),
    disp = na_if(disp, na_vals$disp)
  )

naive
#> # A tibble: 32 x 11
#>      mpg   cyl  disp    hp  drat    wt  qsec    vs    am  gear  carb
#>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1  21      NA   NA    110  3.9   2.62  16.5     0     1     4     4
```

title: Feature Request (or Documentation and Error Message Request): Vectorize between
description:
`between` currently appears to only support scalar values for `left` and `right`.  It would be helpful to have `left` and `right` optionally vectorized such that any of the following would work:

``` r
library(dplyr)                    
#> Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 3.4.4
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
between(1:5, c(1, 3:6), c(1, 3:6))
#> Error in between(1:5, c(1, 3:6), c(1, 3:6)): Expecting a single value: [extent=5].
between(1:5, 1, c(1, 3:6))        
#> Error in between(1:5, 1, c(1, 3:6)): Expecting a single value: [extent=5].
between(1:5, c(1, 3:6), 1)        
#> Error in between(1:5, c(1, 3:6), 1): Expecting a single value: [extent=5].
```

If this is not reasonable, it would help if both the documentation and error messages were updated.  The documentation for `left` and `right` currently says "Boundary values", but it would be more accurate to say "Boundary scalar values".  The error would be more helpful if it indicated where the single value were expected:  "Expecting a single value for 'left': [extent=5]" and "Expecting a single value for 'right': [extent=5]"

title: Using qualified functions inside filter or arrange results in 'object not found' error for SQL
description:
For an SQL backend, using `desc()` or `between()` inside an `arrange` or `filter`, respectively, returns an error if the functions are qualified.

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
lf <- dbplyr::lazy_frame(x = 1, y = 1, 
                         src = dbplyr::simulate_dbi())

# Works
lf %>% 
  arrange(desc(y)) %>% 
  show_query()
#> <SQL> SELECT *
#> FROM "df"
#> ORDER BY "y" DESC
lf %>% 
  filter(between(y, 0, 1)) %>% 
  show_query()
#> <SQL> SELECT *
#> FROM "df"
#> WHERE ("y" BETWEEN 0.0 AND 1.0)

# Doesn't work
lf %>% 
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(y)) %>% 
  dplyr::show_query()
#> Error in dplyr::desc(y): object 'y' not found
lf %>% 
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::between(y, 0, 1)) %>% 
  dplyr::show_query()
#> Error in dplyr::between(y, 0, 1): object 'y' not found
```

title: Reinstate support for filtering and arranging lubridate Periods and Intervals
description:
Support for `filter()`ing and `arrange()`ing columns of class `Period` and `Interval` was [recently dropped](https://community.rstudio.com/t/am-i-crazy-having-issues-with-dplyr-filter/7710) from `dplyr`. The ability to work with these types is useful, so I'd like the feature reinstating.

(By 'useful', I mean in particular that there are DataCamp courses depending upon this feature. For example, [Working with Dates and Times in R](https://campus.datacamp.com/courses/working-with-dates-and-times-in-r/arithmetic-with-dates-and-times?ex=11).)

---

To reproduce:

```r
library(dplyr)                        
library(lubridate)                    
x <- data_frame(                      
  start = as.Date("2000-01-01") + 0:19, 
  finish = as.Date("2001-01-01") + 19:0,
  interval = start %--% finish          
)                                     
x %>%                                 
  arrange(interval)                     
#> Error in arrange_impl(.data, dots): Column `interval` classes Period and Interval from lubridate are currently not supported.
                                      
x %>%                                 
  filter(interval > 0)                  
#> Error in filter_impl(.data, quo): Column `interval` classes Period and Interval from lubridate are currently not supported.
```

title: feature request: case_when() TRUE should translate to ELSE
description:
sql translation of case_when() has no else clause
---
case_when works just fine with dataframes. Using it in a database environment, I'm missing the possibility of defining an else-clause:

```r
translate_sql(case_when(
  height > 200 | mass > 200 ~ "large",
  species == "Droid"        ~ "robot",
  TRUE                      ~  "other"
))
```
translates to:
`(...) WHEN (TRUE) THEN ('other') END`
whereas it should translate to:

title: n_distinct() on sqlite with more columns returns an error
description:
---
When I use a connection to a sqlite on disk, the verb n_distinct() returns an error if there are two or more columns. Same code, if I select just one column or collect data before counting record, it works properly.

```r
# remove objects
rm(list =  ls())

# require packages
require(dplyr)
require(dbplyr)
require(RSQLite)

# create a sqlite db and connect to it
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")

# copy data into sqlite
copy_to(con, mtcars)
  
# point to table 
my_tbl <- tbl(con, "mtcars")

# n_distinct with one column (THIS WORKS)
my_tbl %>% group_by(gear) %>% summarise(n_distinct(mpg))

# if I use the local (or collected) data it is ok (THIS WORKS)
my_tbl %>% collect() %>% group_by(gear) %>% summarise(n_distinct(mpg, cyl))

# n_distinct with two columns (THIS DOES NOT WORKS)
my_tbl %>% group_by(gear) %>% summarise(n_distinct(mpg, cyl))

## Error in result_create(conn@ptr, statement) : 
## wrong number of arguments to function COUNT()
```
The code is correctly translated into Sql

```r
# Show query
my_tbl %>% group_by(gear) %>% summarise(n_distinct(mpg, cyl)) %>% show_query()

## SELECT `gear`, COUNT(DISTINCT `mpg`, `cyl`) AS `n_distinct(mpg, cyl)`
## FROM `mtcars`
## GROUP BY `gear`
```

title: Non-standard evaluation with n_distinct
description:
The following examples crash unexpectedly:

```r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts=FALSE)
df = head(iris)
b = TRUE
summarize(df, n = n_distinct(Sepal.Length, na.rm = T))
summarize(df, n = n_distinct(Sepal.Length, na.rm = b))
summarize(df, n = n_distinct(Sepal.Length, na.rm = (TRUE||TRUE)))
```

But the following examples work as expected:

```r
n_distinct(df$Sepal.Length, na.rm = T) # outside of summarize/mutate/...
summarize(df, m = mean(Sepal.Length, na.rm = T)) # using mean instead of n_distinct
summarize(df, b = between(T, FALSE, TRUE))  # using another dplyr function instead of n_distinct
summarize(df, n = n_distinct(Sepal.Length, na.rm = !!T)) # bang bang
summarize(df, n = n_distinct(Species, na.rm = !!(TRUE||TRUE))) # bang bang

# perhaps the most surprising:
nd = n_distinct
summarize(df, n = nd(Sepal.Length, na.rm = T))
```

Could `n_distinct` have the same behaviour as `mean` or the other?

title: multiple test affected by group_by
description:
I am wandering if anyone forget to add "ungroup" before doing multiple test correction like me?
code like this:

```r
wilcT.res = Expression %>%
  group_by(gene_id) %>%
  do(broom::tidy(wilcox.test(.$Exp~.$Group))) %>%
  mutate(q = p.adjust(p.value,'BH'))
```

This will do multiple test correction for each gene (which means actually no multiple test correction is done). Not sure if needs to at least add a warning message here?

The right way to do it in my thought:

```r
wilcT.res = Expression %>%
  group_by(gene_id) %>%
  do(broom::tidy(wilcox.test(.$Exp~.$Group))) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(q = p.adjust(p.value,'BH'))
```

title: Feature request: sample_n samples UP TO n rows
description:
Let's say I have a dataframe with several groups, with varying numbers of samples (rows) in each group. I'd like to be able to sample up to 10 rows from each group. However, some groups have fewer than 10 samples, and so the function returns an error (will only sample 10, and no fewer, from each group), with a suggestion to sample with replacement. Sampling with replacement will, of course, not return 10 unique samples from groups with 10 or more available, and so my desired condition of subsampling my dataframe to up to 10 samples per group is not met.

There is at least one clunky solution on stackoverflow ( https://stackoverflow.com/questions/41666714/sampling-different-numbers-of-rows-by-group-in-dplyr-tidyverse ), but it is best implemented with few groups. I have 50+ groups where I don't immediately know the actual group size, so this is not ideal. Would it be easy to make sample_n more flexible, where "size" is UP TO that value, instead of absolutely that value?

title: relational tibbles - does it need to be joined?
description:
I work with relatively large datasets: the main tibble is a tidy, long tibble (millions of rows) with three columns: Sample, Hash, number of occurrences. Each row is an observation. In order to plot, model, etc, I need to group samples according to their metadata, and hence there is another tibble with as many rows as samples (~100 rows and ~10 columns: Site, Month,...).

Let's say that I want to plot a boxplot of the number of unique sequences per sample at each site. A workflow will look like

```r
require(RCurl)
library(tidyverse)

long_tibble<- read_csv(file = getURL("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ramongallego/dplyr_question/master/example_long_tible.csv") )

factor_tibble <- read_csv (file = getURL("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ramongallego/dplyr_question/master/example_factor_tible.csv"))

together<- left_join(long_tibble, factor_tibble) 

ggplot (data = together, aes (x= Site, y = nunique)) + 
  geom_boxplot(data = together %>%
 group_by(sample, Site) %>%
 summarise(nunique = n_distinct(Hash)))

```
My question is - and apologies if this is not the right forum to ask it - is whether I need to join all data in a unique tibble, or if I can tell tidyverse to look for the group_by grouping outside the tibble. 

My guess is that for every new column added to the long table we increase the size of the file by a lot so I was wondering which is the most 'tidy' way of dealing with relational tibbles

title: Order DataFrame using DataFrameVisitors
sample_n is slow with many groups + Date columns
description:
I was trying to randomly sample some rows in a grouped data frame using `sample_n` and found unusually slow performance. ~~I checked `Rprof` and found that upwards of 90% of the CPU time was being spent on `[.Date`, even when the date column wasn't a grouping variable.~~

~~I found a simple approach based on `mutate` and `filter` that can be orders of magnitude faster for my specific case, although it would take some work to make it as flexible as the current `sample_n` implementation. If you're interested, I could look into possibly doing that work as a PR.~~

This was partially fixed in 0.7.5, but date columns still make the operation very slow, as discussed in my comment below.

```r
library(dplyr)                                                            
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
set.seed(1)                                                               
                                                                          
# Make a medium-sized data frame with many groups                         
n = 5e3 # Number of times to repeat the alphabet in column `x`            
z = data_frame(                                                           
  x = rep(letters, n), 
  y = sample(rep(1:n, 26)),                                                 
  z = rnorm(26 * n)                                                         
) %>%                                                                     
  group_by(x, y)                                                            
                                                                          
# 1: Randomly sampling one row from each group can be fast with              
# `mutate` and `filter`                                                   
system.time(                                                              
  z %>%                                                                     
    mutate(n = sample(1:n())) %>%                                             
    filter(n == 1)                                                            
)                                                                         
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   2.348   0.040   2.433
                                                                          
# 2: randomly sampling with sample_n is much slower                          
system.time(                                                              
z %>%                                                                     
  sample_n(size = 1))                                                                         
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>  15.118   0.146  15.546
                                                                          
# 3: randomly sampling with sample_n is even slower when one column is a date
system.time(                                                              
z %>%                                                                     
  mutate(date = as.Date("2018-06-13")) %>%                                  
  sample_n(size = 1)                                                        
)                                                                         
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>  53.131   0.629  55.649
```

I'm using R 3.4.4 and dplyr ~~0.7.4~~ 0.7.5

title: Suggestion: Multi replace function
description:
I was thinking of this function that would act as this multi replace function. It would replace multiple values depending on values in a different data structure. I'm sure this has a proper name, but I'm running into a chicken and egg problem.

This suggestion is best displayed with an example: Supposed you have a data.frame where one of the variables Is a mix between good values and bad values that you have the correct corresponding good values for. In this example Is there a mix between full country names and iso codes. It would be a pain to set up all the necessary ifelse statements.

``` r
df <- data.frame(num = 1:10,
                 name = c("Canada", "MX", "Ireland", "DK", "US",
                          "Sweden", "Australia", "Canada", "Canada", "Canada"),
                 stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

index <- data.frame(from = c("MX", "DK", "US", "DE"),
                    to = c("Mexico", "Denmark", "United States", "Germany"),
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
```

We would like the `df` data.frame to be all full country names. The following `all_replace` is an adhoc example of the function.

``` r
library(dplyr)
all_replace <- function(tbl, reference, tbl_match, ref_match, ref_out) {
  by_vector <- ref_match
  names(by_vector) <- tbl_match
  joined_df <- left_join(tbl, reference, by = by_vector)
  
  ifelse(is.na(joined_df[[ref_out]]), 
         joined_df[[tbl_match]], 
         joined_df[[ref_out]])

}
```
Which when used would result in the following:

``` r
df %>%
  mutate(name = all_replace(., index, "name", "from", "to"))
#>    num          name
#> 1    1        Canada
#> 2    2        Mexico
#> 3    3       Ireland
#> 4    4       Denmark
#> 5    5 United States
#> 6    6        Sweden
#> 7    7     Australia
#> 8    8        Canada
#> 9    9        Canada
#> 10  10        Canada
``` 

I don't know if this kind of function is within the scope of `dplyr` but I feel like it is a problem that occurs for time to time.

title: dplyr left_join only outputs the left column from the "by" condition.
description:
I have noticed that dplyr::left_joins only preserve one of the join variable columns. All columns not used in the join are preserved from both sides.  This is behavior is not what I would expect based on the docs:

https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/join.html 
> left_join()
return all rows from x, and _**all columns from x and y**_. Rows in x with no match in y will have NA values in the new columns. If there are multiple matches between x and y, all combinations of the matches are returned.

There are fine workarounds for this (like duplicated the join column before the join).  But it seems cleaner to return all columns and then let people select down if they want to.

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
#Column y is not represerved post join 
#(in SQL you can have both the right and left columns in the select list)
df1 <- data.frame(x=1:10)
df2 <- data.frame(y=c(2,5,8),z=c(1,2,3))
dplyr::left_join(df1, df2, by=c("x"="y")) 
#>     x  z
#> 1   1 NA
#> 2   2  1
#> 3   3 NA
#> 4   4 NA
#> 5   5  2
#> 6   6 NA
#> 7   7 NA
#> 8   8  3
#> 9   9 NA
#> 10 10 NA
```

title: nest_join returns tibble of NA values for alternating joins on repeated identifiers
description:
My understanding is that `nest_join(.) %>% unnest()` should be equivalent to `inner_join(.)`. When I nest join a table with a repeated identifier, every other joined table contains only NA values. The `inner_join(.)` procedure returns what I would expect.

The reprex below demonstrates this behavior. I do not know why `nest_join` returns NA values in the first printed tibble.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
first <- tibble(x = rep(1, 4))
second <- tibble(x = 1, y = 1:4)
first %>%
  nest_join(second) %>%
  unnest()
#> Joining, by = "x"
#> # A tibble: 16 x 2
#>        x     y
#>    <dbl> <int>
#>  1     1     1
#>  2     1     2
```

title: MS SQL mutate(ifelse()) translation not working
description:
Duplicate issue filed under dbplyr before I realized I should file here. https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/issues/93

I'm running into an issue when using mutate and ifelse (or if) on a SQL Server backend. The following sample query:
```
df <- tbl(con, in_schema("schema", "table_name")) %>%
   mutate(field = ifelse(field %in% c('test1', 'test2', 'test3'), 'string1', 'string2') %>%
   collect()
```

... will give the following translation:

```
SELECT CASE WHEN (("field" IN ('test1', 'test2', 'test3')) = 'TRUE') THEN ('string1') 
            WHEN (("field" IN ('test1', 'test2', 'test3')) =  'FALSE') THEN ('string2') 
            END AS "field"
```

Which will return an error. The correct translation should be:

```
SELECT CASE WHEN ("field" IN ('test1', 'test2', 'test3')) THEN 'string1' 
            WHEN ("field" NOT IN ('test1', 'test2', 'test3')) THEN 'string2' 
            END AS "field"
```

Will correcting this in the mssql_if function create any issues in other queries, or is there a better way to do mutate(ifelse()) in mssql?

https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/477480e3c488fe6338ce5f142142d280dd61487b/R/db-odbc-mssql.R#L225

title: recursive nest_by
description:
Would some sort of recursive nest_by make sense ? @hadley 

I would not implement it like this, but here's the idea (needs nest_by_* from #3628)

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

data <- tibble(x = rep(1:2, each=4), y = rep(1:4, each = 2), a = 1:8, b = letters[1:8])

recursive_nest <- function(.data, .vars){
  if(length(.vars) == 0L ) {
    .data
  } else {
    recursive_nest( nest_by_at(.data, .vars), head(.vars, -1))
  }
}
```

title: nest_by
description:
so that `nest_by(...)` is equivalent to `group_by(...) %>% nest()` 

Here is a draft implementation in R: 

``` r
library(tidyverse)

nest_by <- function(.data, ..., .key = "data"){
  key_var <- quo_name(enexpr(.key))
  g <- group_by(.data, ...)
  rows <- group_rows(g)
  
  to_nest <- select(ungroup(g), setdiff(tbl_vars(g), group_vars(g)))
  
  g %>% 
    group_data() %>% 
    select(-.rows) %>% 
    mutate( !!key_var := map(rows, ~to_nest[.x,, drop = FALSE]) )
  
}
```

title: All-NA argument in `coalesce` throws error unless all other arguments are type logical

```
dplyr::coalesce(NA, 1)

dplyr::coalesce(1, NA)
# Error: Argument 2 must be type double, not logical
dplyr::coalesce(NA, TRUE)
# [1] TRUE
dplyr::coalesce(NA_real_, 1)
# [1] 1
```

If this error is intentional, I can write a PR with a test to expect this error. If it's not, I can write a PR to skip type checking for all-NA arguments.

title: copy_to: out of disk space error message unclear
description:
## Update (II)

The whole original issue below turned out to boil down to me running out of
disk space when writing the second table with the big indexes.
Closing my R session freed some space which is why it did work in the new session.

I'll leave the issue open as I *really* think a more clear error message
would be appropriate but feel free to close as wontfix as this is 
probably caused by upstream (sqlite) and should then better be fixed there.

---
## Original issue

A word of warning: I am new to the whole DBI world so I am not sure how to
further narrow-down this issue by myself.

I am working on porting existing `dplyr`-based code from writing tibbles to
disk and reading them into memory via `saveRDS`/`readRDS` to using an SQLite
backend.

I have several big tibbles (up to ~ 1e7 x 10) that I want to write to a local
SQLite database using `copy_to`:

```r
# use temporary database file (no NFS!)
tmp.sqlite <- tempfile(fileext = ".sqlite")

# open connection
tmp.db <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = tmp.sqlite)

# write first tibble
tibble.one %>%
  copy_to(dest = tmp.db, name = "tibble.one", temporary = FALSE,
          indexes = list("column.one", "column.three", "column.six"),
          overwrite = TRUE)

# close connection
dbDisconnect(tmp.db)

# some more code
# ...

# re-open connection
tmp.db <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = tmp.sqlite)

# write second tibble
tibble.two %>%
  #head(1e5) %>%
  copy_to(dest = tmp.db, name = "tibble.two", temporary = FALSE,
          indexes = list("column.two", "column.three", "column.five"),
          overwrite = TRUE)

# close connection again
dbDisconnect(tmp.db)
```

While this works fine for `tibble.one` it fails for `tibble.two` with the
following error:

```
Error in result_create(conn@ptr, statement) :
  cannot rollback - no transaction is active
```

When I uncomment the `head(1e5)` line it works.
When I try with `head(1e6)` it sometimes works but sometimes doesn't.
With `head(5e6)` it worked once but failed many times.

I am working on a sharable data set that reproduces the error but there are
many unknowns for me and I figured I might be doing something fundamentally
wrong and someone could point me in the right direction.

I considered asking a Q/A on SO but at any rate I consider this a bug as the
error message is not helpful at all and I posted it here as my guess is
`dplyr::copy_to` generates invalid/unstable SQL code for some inputs.

---
## Update (I)

I simplified my actual `tibble.two` and ensured it still failed every attempt
of using `copy_to` on the whole data.

I then saved the tibble via `saveRDS` to a webserver.

I copy/pasted the code I used before and added a few lines to load the data
from the URL:

```r
library(dplyr)
library(RSQLite)

# set seed to issue number
set.seed(3615)

# load problematic tibble
url("https://bimsbstatic.mdc-berlin.de/rajewsky/mschilli/tibble2.Rds") %>%
  gzcon %>%
  readRDS -> tibble.two

# create SQLite connection on tmpfile (no NFS!)
tmp.sqlite <- tempfile(fileext = ".sqlite")
tmp.db <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = tmp.sqlite)

# try to write problematic tibble
tibble.two %>%
copy_to(dest = tmp.db, name = "tibble.two", temporary = FALSE,
        indexes = list("col1", "col2", "col3"),
        overwrite = TRUE)

# try to write part of problematic tibble
tibble.two %>%
slice(sample(1:n(), 1e6)) %>%
copy_to(dest = tmp.db, name = "tibble.two.part", temporary = FALSE,
        indexes = list("col1", "col2", "col3"),
        overwrite = TRUE)

# close database connection
dbDisconnect(tmp.db)
```

Running this in a new R session, I was not able to reproduce the issue anymore.

title: move to 1-based indices for `.rows`
description: grouped data frames use 0-based indices in the metadata, mostly because the attributes used to be an internal implementation detail. Now with #3489 and functions like `group_data()` and `group_rows()` the metadata is more user facing, so we should switch to 1-based indices.

title: Compatibility with grouped data frames created with dplyr <= 0.7.5
description:
We might still see old-style grouped data frames if a user deserializes a file that has been created with dplyr <= 0.7.5 (perhaps unintentionally, e.g. when using a *knitr* cache).

Reference: https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/pull/3595#issuecomment-391994182.

title: Regression bug in 0.7.5: can't select a column from a dataframe if any column is NA
description:
This worked in 0.7.4 and errors in 0.7.5:

```
df <- data.frame(x=1, y=2, z=3)
colnames(df) <- c("x","y")
dplyr::select_(df, "x")
# Error in select_impl(.data, vars) : Column `3` cannot have NA as name
```

You may argue that the second line is bad code, but I don't think dplyr should break trying to select from that dataframe

title: Repeated window function returns incorrect result
description:
Dplyr database query appears to fail when the same window function is called twice

The following query is meant to find up to the first four unique destinations (by calendar date/time) for each carrier, in the `nycflights13::flights` dataset:

```r
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr)
library(nycflights13)

localdb <- src_postgres(dbname = 'dbname',
                        host = 'localhost',
                        port = 5432,
                        user = 'user',
                        password = 'password')

copy_to(localdb, flights, "flights",
        temporary = FALSE, 
        indexes = list(
          c("year", "month", "day"), 
          "carrier", 
          "tailnum",
          "dest"
        )
)

# Has row_number() twice
incorrect <- tbl(localdb, 'flights') %>%
  group_by(carrier, dest) %>%
  arrange(carrier, dest, time_hour) %>%
  filter(row_number() == 1L) %>%
  group_by(carrier) %>%
  arrange(carrier, time_hour) %>%
  filter(row_number() < 5L) %>%
  select(carrier, dest, time_hour) %>%
  collect()

head(incorrect, 10)
```

title: scoped functions won't work with tbl_lazy when the function is created by ~
description:
This fails (if I use `funs()` instead of `~`, it works):

``` r
library(DBI)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
dbWriteTable(con, "mtcars", mtcars)

tbl(con, "mtcars") %>%
  dplyr::summarise_all(~ any(is.na(.)))
#> Error in (function (..., .x = ..1, .y = ..2, . = ..1) : object 'mpg' not found
```

The error comes from here: https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/81419cab7d831e5a9d7e4279a4f893fa5750e8a1/R/tbl-lazy.R#L124

The root cause seems that `partial_eval()` won't accept expressions that generate a function in-place:

``` r
library(dbplyr)

q1 <- rlang::quo((function(x) is.na(x))(a))
q2 <- rlang::quo(is.na(a))

partial_eval(q1, vars = "a")
#> Error in (function(x) is.na(x))(a): object 'a' not found

partial_eval(q2, vars = "a")
#> <quosure>
#>   expr: ^is.na(a)
#>   env:  global
```

Another example here:

``` r
add_n <- function(n) {
  function(x) x + n
}

q3 <- rlang::quo(add_n(1)(a))

partial_eval(q3, vars = "a")
#> Error in add_n(1)(a) : object 'a' not found
```

The fix would probably come around here, but I didn't come up with the proper way of distinguishing the expression that generates function or not.

https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/ae86fb351bf3511aa73f622946db3a9ed7469fc4/R/partial-eval.r#L96

title: Inconsistency self join and pipping
description:
I ran into an issue trying to self join on a table. 

```r
iris %>%
  left_join(., . %>% select(Species, x = Sepal.Width), by = c("Species" = "Species"))
```
The code produced the following error -

> Error in UseMethod("tbl_vars") : 
  no applicable method for 'tbl_vars' applied to an object of class "c('fseq', 'function')"

I could not find this issue else where. After sometime playing around with it, I noticed the error went away if i put the ```.``` inside the ```select``` statement.

```r
iris %>%
  left_join(., select(., Species, x = Sepal.Width), by = c("Species" = "Species"))
```

 I do not know if this is intentional or a bug, so I though I would share.

I'm using dplyr v0.7.5 and ran into the same error testing v0.7.0.

Thanks,
Dustin

title: Suggestion for .id in bind_rows
description:
When you bind 2 tibbles, you can create an .id column to keep track of the original tibble they came from. If you want to add a third tibble to the newly created tibble, bind_rows creates a new .id variable, even if the name specified is the same. 

So my suggestion would be, if the .id column already exists, to get the counter continuing from where the last tibble left it

title: first() does not work without explicit x argument in a chain inside mutate
description:
When using `first()` (or `last()`) in a chain inside a `mutate()` (or `filter()`) command, the `x` argument has to be explicitly set. This is easy to work around in numerous ways, but the behavior seems strange, so maybe it points to something not quite right.

examples (using R v3.5.0 and dplyr v0.7.5)...
```r
library(dplyr)

mutate(tibble(v1 = 5:6), v2 = 1:4 %>% first())
# Error in mutate_impl(.data, dots) : bad value

clonefirst <- first
mutate(tibble(v1 = 5:6), v2 = 1:4 %>% clonefirst())
# # A tibble: 2 x 2
#      v1    v2
#   <int> <int>
# 1     5     1
# 2     6     1

mutate(tibble(v1 = 5:6), v2 = 1:4 %>% first(.))
# # A tibble: 2 x 2
#      v1    v2
#   <int> <int>
# 1     5     1
# 2     6     1

mutate(tibble(v1 = 5:6), v2 = 1:4 %>% nth(1))
# # A tibble: 2 x 2
#      v1    v2
#   <int> <int>
# 1     5     1
# 2     6     1

mutate(tibble(v1 = 5:6), v2 = 1:4 %>% `[[`(1))
# # A tibble: 2 x 2
#      v1    v2
#   <int> <int>
# 1     5     1
# 2     6     1

mutate(tibble(v1 = 5:6), v2 = first(1:4))
# # A tibble: 2 x 2
#      v1    v2
#   <int> <int>
# 1     5     1
# 2     6     1

1:4 %>% first()
# [1] 1

first(1:4)
# [1] 1
```

title: diff() by groups is applied globally instead of by group under Linux
description:
I am trying to calculate the diff() over a column in a data.frame by grouping the rows. This works fine under Windows and MacOS. Under Linux Mint 18 (Xenial), the behavior is as shown below for R versions 3.3 as well as 3.4.

Instead of calculating the diff() over entries of each group, hence having NA for the first element of each group, the diff() is applied globally as shown below. The same result can be observed when using `c = a - lag(a)`, indicating, that it is not an issue with the diff() function.

```r
A <- data.frame(a = c(1, 3, 5, 8), b = c(1, 1, 2, 2))

3    5.    2.    2.
4    8.    2.    3.
```

Expected output would be

```r
# A tibble: 4 x 3

      a     b     c
```

title: sample_frac() sample size
description:
I would like to raise the issue about the sample size returned by `sample_frac()`.  Here is a simple example of current behaviour:

```r
library(dplyr)
sample_frac(data.frame(x = 1:3), size = 0.5)
#>   x
#> 2 2
#> 1 1
```

The frame has 3 elements, but the function always returns 2 rows, implying a true sampling probability of of 2/3 over repeated sampling, not 1/2. This is because `dplyr:::sample_n_basic()` rounds the size to be sampled up or down to an integer.

I believe it would be more appropriate for the sample size to be random in these cases, so that the long-run performance of the sampling mechanism evaluates exactly to the expected sample size (even if this is fractional).

Here is what I have in mind (for `dplyr:::sample_n_basic`):
```r
# determine size stochastically such that E[nrow(result)] = fraction
expected_size <- size * n
size <- floor(expected_size) + rbernoulli(1, expected_size - floor(expected_size))
```

What are the developers' opinions on this matter? Can this be implemented (perhaps via an additional argument `random_size = FALSE` to ensure backwards compatibility)?

description:
I scheduled the Rscript which takes data from MS SQL Server and performs regression. The script takes only new data.
For example, today was loaded 100 obs from 01.01.2017-03.03.2017,script conducted the regression on this data.

Tomorrow will be loaded 100 obs from 04.03.2017-04.06.2017 and script will work with this obs and not from 01.01.2017 -04.06.2017.

I asked at this forum the question,how to make that R only works with data that have a fresh date and got this useful answer,
where we create last date log and take the data older than it.
If anyone is interested, here the link
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/50275618/create-sql-expression-in-r-for-certain-condition

    # READ DATE FROM LOG FILE
    log_dt <- readLines("/path/to/SQL_MaxDate.txt", warn=FALSE)
    
    # QUERY WITH WHERE CLAUSE
    sql <- paste0("SELECT Dt, CustomerName, ItemRelation, SaleCount, 
                          DocumentNum, DocumentYear, IsPromo
                   FROM dbo.mytable WHERE Dt > '", log_dt, "'")
    
    df <- sqlQuery(dbHandle, sql)
    
    # RETRIEVE MAX DATE VALUE
    max_DT <- as.character(max(df$Dt))
    
    # ...here code for regression, now, it's not important for this question
    
    # WRITE DATE TO LOG FILE
    cat(max_DT, file="/path/to/SQL_MaxDate.txt")

The question:My Scheduler runs 1 time per day, but it happens that the data in the SQL database does not load every day, it can loaded for example 1 time of 3 days and so on. 
Can R make a check?
If R determines that there is no new data( there is no fresh date), then the script does not start?
If R  determines("see") that there is new data, it runs script.
I.E. for example, last date when Rscript ran ,was 12.05.2018, and 13.05.2018 Rscipt was run by schedule, but  on this date nothing was loaded in sql, R "see" that there is no new date, and it will work with same last date and it doesn't run. And R must do this checking everytime when running, is there new date or not.
Is it possible to do or no?

``` r
library(tibble)
```

title: Feature Request: Allow matches to Invert the Result (and Generally Allow Access to grep)
description:
I have cases where I need to do operations like "group by all columns with names that do not start with 'Is_'".  The most logical way that I can think to do that is to add a `...` argument to `matches` that is passed to `grep_vars`.  With that, the full power of `grep` is exposed without notable additional code and in a backward-compatible way.

``` r
library(dplyr)                                                                    
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
                                                                                  
matches_augmented <- function(match, ignore.case=TRUE, vars=current_vars(), ...) {
stopifnot(rlang::is_string(match), nchar(match) > 0)                              
dplyr:::grep_vars(match, vars, ignore.case = ignore.case, ...)                    
}                                                                                 
                                                                                  
d <- data.frame(A=1, B=2, Is_Foo=rep(1:2, 2), Is_Bar=rep(3:4, each=2))            
                                                                                  
# Without setting vars, I get an error "Error: Variable context not set"          
d_new <-                                                                          
d %>%                                                                             
group_by_at(matches_augmented("Is_", invert=TRUE, vars=names(.)))                 
                                                                                  
print(d_new)                                                                      
#> # A tibble: 4 x 4
#> # Groups:   A, B [1]
#>       A     B Is_Foo Is_Bar
#>   <dbl> <dbl>  <int>  <int>
#> 1    1.    2.      1      3
#> 2    1.    2.      2      3
#> 3    1.    2.      1      4
#> 4    1.    2.      2      4
```

title: Why do dplyr verbs remove all (non-class) attributes?
description:
I know about class attributes from Issue #719, but I do not understand why other attributes are removed. Preserving them would be more friendly to pkg authors who may wish to invent functions that fit in the pipeline between dplyr verbs, but need their own attributes.

```r
d <- data.frame(a=1:3)
attr(d,"foo") <- "bar"
d %<>% mutate(a=a/2)
attributes(d)$foo
```
The above gives `NULL`. 

My `simputation` pkg simply records the attributes at entry and re-adds them in the end. Clearly, `dplyr` verbs do something like that with the attribute used for grouping. So why not for others?

title: Results of Postgres Count function returned as Integer64
description:
Invoking the `COUNT` function of PostgreSQL returns a dataframe with the count column having type `S3: integer64` instead of a regular integer. This data type is not aggregated correctly by dplyr verbs and cannot be plotted by ggplot2.

The reprex is a bit artificial given that it requires a backend database:

```r
sql("SELECT
        created_at,
        count(*) AS count_col
FROM some_table
GROUP BY 1") %>%
  tbl(src = my_source) %>%
  collect(n = Inf)
```
In this case `count_col` is of type `S3: integer64`.

This happens even when using dplyr verbs:

```r
tbl(my_source, "some_table") %>%
    count()
```

Prior to this, the column type would be integer which can be handled by all dplyr verb and ggplot2.

Not sure if this is a Postgres-specific issue or if it occurs in other DBs as I don't have access to MySQL, etc...

title: Feature Request: Chatty dplyr/summarize message when group by is changed
description:
Proposal: give a message back to the user when `summarize` changes the grouping

Background:
I just spent many hours trying to understand some `dplyr` behavior which I ultimately traced back to the throughly documented feature where `dplyr` drops the last `group_by` element after `summarize` is run. I notice that I am not the only one being surprised by this:

#3315 dplyr::summarise removes a grouping variable
#2963 data is still grouped after a summarize (but not by original set of columns

I've seen more but these two popped up in a quick search. The reason this was so confusing to me was that I had explicitly set the grouping and all my experience with R and SQL didn't prepare me for the system to silently change something I had explicitly set. I notice that in other functions when dplyr does helpful things or makes assumptions it's pretty chatty about it. For example, when I do: 

```
inner_join(data.frame(a=1) ,data.frame(a=1) )
```
dplyr chattily reminds me that it's making an assumption about my join preference, thus warning me not to be surprised:
```
Joining, by = "a" 
```
I would love to see that same sort of chattiness when the `group_by` is changed automagically. Something like:
```
group_by reset to (groupA, broupB) after summarize()
```

cheers, 

JD

description:
The auto naming fails on some esoteric uses of `.data`: 

``` r

library(dplyr)

#> Error: Can't convert a call to a string
```

Problem is in `tidy_text` : 

```r
tidy_text <- function(quo, width = 60L) {
  expr <- quo_get_expr(quo)
  if (is_data_pronoun(expr)) {
    as_string(node_cadr(node_cdr(expr)))

    quo_text(quo, width = width)
  }
}
named_quos <- function(...) {
  quos <- quos(...)
  exprs_auto_name(quos, printer = tidy_text)
}
```

Can either: 
- make `is_data_pronoun` more robust, perhaps using the `quo_is_variable_reference` from #3537 and so fall back to `quo_text(quo, width = width)`. I can easily do that. 
- do some sort of substitution instead of `as_string` but whatever is in `[[` might involve the columns

title: inconsistency between dplyr and dbplyr summarise_at when variable names reused
description:
When `summarise_at` uses a variable in `.vars` that it also uses in `.funs`, the result is different in dplyr and dbplyr, and I think the dbplyr result is the right one -- though there's a case for just making it an error. 

```r
library(dplyr)
library(MonetDBLite)
library(DBI)
mydb <- dbConnect(MonetDBLite::MonetDBLite())
DBI::dbWriteTable(mydb, "mtcarsdb", mtcars)
mtcars.db = tbl(mydb, "mtcarsdb")

## wrong
mtcars %>% summarise_at(vars(cyl,disp,hp,drat), funs(sum(. *  cyl * mpg)))
## right
mtcars.db %>% summarise_at(vars(cyl,disp,hp,drat), funs(sum(. *  cyl * mpg)))
## also right
mtcars %>% mutate(cyl1=cyl) %>% summarise_at(vars(cyl,disp,hp,drat), funs(sum(. *  cyl1 * mpg)))

# intended result
with(mtcars, cbind(cyl * cyl * mpg,
                     disp * cyl * mpg,
                     hp * cyl * mpg,
                     drat * cyl * mpg) %>% colSums())
```

It looks as though in R the variable `cyl` is updated before it is used for the 2nd through 4th sums, but in SQL it isn't.

title: arrange .by_group Argument Should Be Dropped for non-grouped_df Classes (or give a clearer error)
description:
When accidentally trying to arrange a regular data.frame with `arrange`, I got a difficult to interpret error:

"Error in arrange_impl(.data, dots): incorrect size (1) at position 2, expecting : 2"

The issue was that I wasn't using a `grouped_df`; it was just a regular `data.frame`, and the `.by_group` argument only has meaning with the `grouped_df` class.

Theoretically, someone could have a column named `.by_group`, so I understand not having a general catch for that as an argument that is usually ignored.  When the quosure is named `.by_group`, it is a logical value of length 1, and it is not the same length as everything else, it would be helpful at the `arrange_impl` (or somewhere higher in the stack) gave a more useful error message indicating that the user probably didn't mean to use the argument (or maybe a warning and then ignore the argument).

``` r
library(dplyr)                                                              
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
                                                                            
# When not grouped, the ".by_group" argument is interpreted as a column when
# it reaches arrange_impl                                                   
data.frame(foo=1:2, bar=2) %>%                                              
arrange(foo, .by_group=TRUE)                                                
#> Error in arrange_impl(.data, dots): incorrect size (1) at position 2, expecting : 2
                                                                            
data.frame(foo=1:2, bar=2) %>%                                              
group_by(bar) %>%                                                           
arrange(foo, .by_group=TRUE)                                                
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#> # Groups:   bar [1]
#>     foo   bar
#>   <int> <dbl>
#> 1     1    2.
#> 2     2    2.
```

title: `case_when` quietly inserts NA when not all cases are covered
description:
Hi there,

I've noticed that `case_when`, while very useful, will insert `NA` quietly when the given cases do not cover all of the values in the column.

Is this the preferred way for the function to work? I'd prefer if it inserted NAs noisily, just in case I think that I've covered all of the cases but failed to do so. 

Another situation is when I am writing code on a bunch of sample rows to save time, then when I scale up to the full dataset I'd like it to fail noisily if there was an edge case that I failed to observe in my sample dataset.

Or more likely if I misspelled one of the cases, I'd like to know that it inserted `NA`s when I intended for all of the values to be filled in.

```r
# This code inserts NAs in the Species column, but raises no warnings
iris %>%
  mutate(Species = case_when(
    Species == "Setosa" ~ "Setosa",
    Species == "Versicolour" ~ "Versicolour"
    # Virginica not given
    )
```

Instead of no warning, I'd like some kind of warning to be raised. It might be useful if it could say how many `NA`s were inserted, but really I just want to know if any were inserted at all.

I'm happy to put in a pull request if I can get agreement that this is something that should be fixed.

Cheers

title: hybrid all or nothing
description:
meta issue to discuss the hybrid all or nothing.  
problems caused by hybrid : #2080

Currently the hybrid evaluation can be used in two ways. 

 - to handle the whole expression, i.e. `summarise(df, x = mean(y))` 

`mean(y)` is identified as something that can be handled internally, because we know `mean` and we know that `y` is a variable from the data. This is where hybrid eval really is useful

 - hybrid folding, to handle part of the expression, e.g. `summarise( df, x = mean(y) + 1)`

Here we do not know how to deal directly with `mean(y) + 1`, so what happens is a sort of hybrid folding where we traverse the expression and hunt for things that can be handled. This happens in each group, and is the source of most of the hybrid related problems. 

The idea would be to remove the hybrid folding entirely which would
- simplify the code base
- potentially make hybrid more aggressive/useful for the use case we keep, esp if this happens in parallel to #2311

Trying to select specific row indices with `dplyr::slice()` from a DB connection returns an error:
> Error in UseMethod("slice_") : 
>  no applicable method for 'slice_' applied to an object of class "c('tbl_dbi', 'tbl_sql', 'tbl_lazy', 'tbl')"

Reproducible example:

```{r}
library(dbplyr)
library(dplyr)
library(RSQLite)
data(iris)

# Put it into a SQLITE database
con <- dbConnect(SQLite(), ":memory:")
dbWriteTable(con, "iris", iris)

tblcon <- tbl(con, "iris")

### This doesn't work
tblcon %>% slice(1:10)

> Error in UseMethod("slice_") :
```

title: Numeric rounded unexpectedly when joining within SQL
description:
I have an issue where integers (classed as numerics) that have 16 significant figures get rounded to 15 significant digits when using the `dplyr` interface with databases via `tbl`. Here is an example of the observed behaviour (tmp_con is a `src:  postgres 9.5.3`  object created by `src_postgres`):

```
library(RPostgreSQL)
dbGetQuery(tmp_con$con, 'select * from tmp_double_precision_test')
# secs_elapsed
# 1             4104.538
# 2 1363392673615939.000
```

Now, observe the following behaviour when accessing this table via `tbl`:

```
tmp_df_out_1 <- 
    tbl(tmp_con, 'tmp_double_precision_test') %>%
    collect() %>%
    as.data.frame
tmp_df_out_1
# > tmp_df_out_1
# secs_elapsed
# 1             4104.538
# 2 1363392673615939.000
```

So far so good. Now let us do a within-SQL join:

```
tmp_df <- data.frame(id =  1363392673615939, secs_elapsed = 5)
tmp_df_out_2 <- 
    tbl(tmp_con, 'tmp_double_precision_test') %>%
    full_join(tmp_df, copy = T) %>%
    collect() %>%
    as.data.frame()

tmp_df_out_2
# secs_elapsed               id
# 1             4104.538               NA
# 2 1363392673615940.000               NA
# 3                5.000 1363392673615940

```

The values have been rounded. I have noticed this behaviour with Oracle as well. I on `dbplyr_1.2.1` and `dplyr_0.7.4`.


The `postgres` table in question is created with:

```
CREATE TABLE public.tmp_double_precision_test
(
  secs_elapsed numeric
)
WITH (
  OIDS=FALSE
);
ALTER TABLE public.tmp_double_precision_test
  OWNER TO postgres;

insert into tmp_double_precision_test (secs_elapsed) VALUES (4104.538);
insert into tmp_double_precision_test (secs_elapsed) VALUES (1363392673615939);
```

title: `dplyr::arrange()` with the `.by_group=TRUE` parameter set produces SQL with an error
description:
This is a cross post from the RStats Community, where I initially posted it: https://community.rstudio.com/t/dplyr-arrange-by-group-true-fails-with-sql-backend/7232

I've either got a misunderstanding or a bug... I *think* it's a bug. 

It seems that `dplyr::arrange()` with the `.by_group=TRUE` parameter set produces SQL with an error. Here's how to reprex it:

On the DB (Redshift in my case) set up a dummy table:

```
drop TABLE sandbox.testorder; 

CREATE TABLE sandbox.testorder (
    grp varchar(255),
    n  DOUBLE PRECISION
);

INSERT INTO sandbox.testorder (grp , n) VALUES ('a',3.3);
INSERT INTO sandbox.testorder (grp , n) VALUES ('a',1.1);
INSERT INTO sandbox.testorder (grp , n) VALUES ('b',2.2);
INSERT INTO sandbox.testorder (grp , n) VALUES ('b',4.4);
```
Then from `R` (presuming a connection to the DB called `con` and already loaded `dbplyr` 

```
testorder  <- tbl(con, "testorder")

testorder %>%
  group_by( grp ) %>%
  arrange( n, .by_group=TRUE) ->
out_test

show_query(out_test)
```
which generates the following SQL:
```
SELECT *
FROM "testorder"
ORDER BY "n", TRUE
```

which fails if I try to `collect(out_test)` with the following error:
```
Error in postgresqlExecStatement(conn, statement, ...) : 
  RS-DBI driver: (could not Retrieve the result : ERROR:  non-integer constant in ORDER BY
```
the rub seems to be the `,TRUE` there at the end. If I remove it, I get the followable runnable SQL:
```
SELECT *
FROM "testorder"
ORDER BY "n"
```

My guess is that the routine that generates the SQL has a glitch. Looks like it's just passing `, TRUE` instead of adding in the `group by` variables.

title: Proposal: keep_levels() with validation
description:
An issue I've faced many times is filtering a `data.frame`/`tibble` based on "levels" (unique values or factor levels) of a column. A common (?) pattern for this is to create a logical vector of presence/absence of the levels compared to a vector of acceptable levels, which `filter` then accepts ```r filter(iris, Species %in% c("setosa")) ``` The problem with this is that while `filter` and `%in%` are both doing their jobs correctly, together they can introduce an unexpected result ```r filter(iris, Species %in% c("virginica", "samosa")) ``` One might reasonably expect an error in the attempted filter to levels not present in the data, in the same way that `select` fails loudly if a column is not present ```r select(iris, Species, Spaceship) #> Error in FUN(X[[i]], ...) : object 'Spaceship' not found ``` The easiest way to get into this situation is to misspell a level, in which case it will (silently) not be in the filtered result ```r filter(iris, Species %in% c("selosa", "virginica")) %>% {unique(.$Species)} #> [1] virginica #> Levels: setosa versicolor virginica ``` Neither `filter` nor `%in%` is at fault here, but the intent of the code is lost because the implementation is not specific enough: `filter` does not perform "filter to the rows which contain X" but rather "filter to the rows for which some condition is `TRUE`" and delegates that responsibility of identifying those to `%in%`. `%in%` knows nothing of the intent so it responds faithfully with "X is not in this vector". I propose a new function `keep_levels` (and its counterpart `discard_levels`) which takes three main arguments rather than two: the levels to be kept/discarded are explicitly provided rather than providing a logical vector upfront. This alleviates the unexpected result by validating that the levels are indeed present ```r keep_levels(iris, Species, c("selosa", "virginica")) #> Error: Level(s) not present in Species: "selosa" ``` I have a prototype in the following gist (or expand below), though it is unlikely to be constructed the way `dplyr` would implement it and is not optimised to the C-level https://gist.github.com/jonocarroll/7f35eefb35f77aaefce527f0b16b034f It does however perform unquoting with `rlang` and provides informative error messages on failure. Would this prototype be welcome as a PR? If so, I will write the tests formally and submit it. [Original motivation](https://twitter.com/carroll_jono/status/971093803099541504):

Source of today's mild heart-attack: I have categories W, X_Y, and Z in some data. Intending to keep only the second two:

data %>% filter(g %in% c("X Y", "Z")

Did you spot that I used a space instead of an underscore? I sure as heck didn't, and filtered excessively to just Z.

— Jonathan Carroll (@carroll_jono) March 6, 2018
Prototype: ```r #' Keep only certain groups/levels of a column #' #' @param .d a data.frame or tibble #' @param .g column containing groups/levels to be kept or discarded #' @param .l groups/levels to be kept or discarded as character vector #' #' @return a data.frame or tibble with the same or fewer rows after filtering #' @export #' @importFrom rlang enquo #' #' @seealso discard_levels #' #' @examples #' keep_levels(iris, Species, "setosa") keep_levels <- function(.d, .g, .l) { g <- validate_level_inputs(.d, rlang::enquo(.g), .l) .d[.d[[g]] %in% .l, ] } #' Discard certain groups/levels of a column #' #' @param .d a data.frame or tibble #' @param .g column containing groups/levels to be kept or discarded #' @param .l groups/levels to be kept or discarded as character vector #' #' @return a data.frame or tibble with the same or fewer rows after filtering #' @export #' @importFrom rlang enquo #' #' @seealso keep_levels #' #' @examples #' discard_levels(iris, Species, "setosa") discard_levels <- function(.d, .g, .l) { g <- validate_level_inputs(.d, rlang::enquo(.g), .l) .d[! .d[[g]] %in% .l, ] } #' Validate levels to be kept/discarded #' #' Performs the following validations: #' - input .d is data.frame-alike #' - input .g is a column of .d #' - .l is/are present in .d$.g #' #' Failure of any of these validations results in an error. #' #' @inheritParams keep_levels #' @importFrom rlang quo_name #' #' @return column to be filtered as a character string (name) validate_level_inputs <- function(.d, .g, .l) { stopifnot(inherits(.d, "data.frame")) g <- rlang::quo_name(.g) if(! g %in% names(.d)) { stop(paste0("\"", g, "\" column not present in input data"), call. = FALSE) } levels_present <- .l %in% unique(.d[[g]]) if (!all(levels_present)) { stop(paste0("Level(s) not present in ", g, ": \"", toString(.l[which(!levels_present)]), "\""), call. = FALSE) } g } ```

title: Better tracebacks
description:
When a complex expression inside `mutate()` or most other verbs fails, the traceback is not informative:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
f <- function(x) if (x < 3) 5 else g()
g <- function() stop("oops")
tibble(a = 1:10) %>% group_by(a) %>% mutate(b = f(a))
#> Error in mutate_impl(.data, dots): Evaluation error: oops.
```

> Created on 2018-04-12 by the [reprex package](http://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.0).

It does contain the error message, but not the location. I wonder if the traceback can be made available.

If not, we could fix this by creating unrolled optimized R code in the C++ part, which then is passed to the R evaluator, and then transforming the results in C++ again:

```r
mutate <- function(.data, ...) {
  code <- unroll_mutate(.data, !!!quos(...))
  res <- eval(code)
  apply_mutate(.data, res)
}
```

title: Don't support overriding n() for now
description:
Earlier, there was no way to use `n()` in a package and pass `R CMD check` because *dplyr* wasn't exporting `n()`:

> older dplyr did not export `n()`, so other packages needed a biding to avoid CRAN issues (https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/3500#issue-313527497)

Currently, only two CRAN packages are affected, but I'd like to suggest to stop using `n()` from the user's environment for now, show a message to that effect, and change this later.

title: Unpredictable handling of attributes
description:
I'm wondering about the behaviour of attributes in dplyr. It is sometimes nice to be able to assign an attribute, e.g. 'label', to a variable when it is being defined. However, these attributes sometimes vanish.
In the exampel below, attributes assigned within `data_frame` and `mutate` are kept, but not within the `group_by` and `mutate` combination. 

```r
require(dplyr)
data_frame(x = 1:4 %>% structure(label = 'Id')) %>%
    mutate(gr = rep(letters[1:2], 2) %>% structure(label = 'Group')) %>%
    group_by(gr) %>%
    mutate(z = mean(x) %>% structure(label = 'Mean x, by Group')) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    str()
## Classes 'tbl_df', 'tbl' and 'data.frame':	4 obs. of  3 variables:
##  $ x : atomic  1 2 3 4
##   ..- attr(*, "label")= chr "Id"
##  $ gr: atomic  a b a b
##   ..- attr(*, "label")= chr "Group"
##  $ z : num  2 3 2 3
```

I know there have been related issues with attributes (e.g. #1984 and #2752).

title: mutate crashes instead of throwing errors
description:
`mutate` (and other dplyr verbs) seem to be very fragile recently.  When there is an error inside the call, they crash the R session rather than giving a graceful error.  I can't trace this back to a particular update, but I don't think it has always been this way.  I experience this both in Rstudio and in the R console. It makes it hard to find errors, because there is no information about what went wrong.

```r
library(dplyr)

x <- tibble(a = -1:3)

### Variable does not exist
with(x, a + b)
#Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'b' not found

mutate(x, c = a + b)
#terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::bad_alloc'
#  what():  std::bad_alloc
#Aborted (core dumped)

### Function call throws an error
with(x, list(rep(1, times = a)))
#Error in rep(1, x$a) : invalid 'times' argument
mutate(x, c = list(rep(1, times = a)))
#terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::bad_alloc'
```

title: n_distinct not counting negative integer64 values
description:
I've been using dplyr to aggregate some info from a database. Some of the columns are being read in as integer64, and some of these are negative. I'm finding that n_distinct counts all negative integer64 numbers as a single number.

A minimal example is as follows, with the expected answer being 41, but n_distinct gives us 22:
```r
> library(bit64)
> library(dplyr)
> x = as.integer64(-20:20 * 10^9)
> n_distinct(x)
[1] 22
> length(unique(x))
[1] 41
```

An example using only negative numbers is as follows:
```r
> x = as.integer64(-20:-1 * 10^9)
> n_distinct(x)
[1] 1
> length(unique(x))
[1] 20
```

title: round in mutate should print rounded values to console
description:
When using `round` in `mutate`, the output printed to the console does not show rounded values. Is this by design? 

This is undesirable because the user will see unrounded values and conclude that the function has not worked as expected. I see that when we `View` the output that the values do show as rounded.

```r
library(tidyverse)
runif(1) %>% 
  enframe() %>% 
  mutate(rounded = round(value, 2))

# A tibble: 1 x 3
   name value rounded
  <int> <dbl>   <dbl>
1     1 0.566   0.570
```

But when we `View` the output we do see the rounded values:

```
library(tidyverse)
runif(1) %>% 
  enframe() %>% 
  mutate(rounded = round(value, 2)) %>% View
```

title: translation of setdiff for Oracle should be MINUS
description:
It appears that **`dbplyr`** is translating `dplyr::setdiff()` as `EXCEPT`. For Oracle Database, the corresponding operator is `MINUS`. The translation is accordingly not working. As best I can tell, this is a **`dbplyr`** issue.

<details>
The variables `dbq`, `uid`, and `pwd` store the TNS service name, username, and password, respectively. The table `DUAL` should exist in the `SYS` schema for all versions of Oracle Database. I would expect `setdiff(tbl, tbl)` to return the empty set, but instead it throws an error. The final query modifies the auto-generated SQL from **`dbplyr`** to replace `EXCEPT` by `MINUS`, and returns the expected result.

```r
con <- DBI::dbConnect(drv = odbc::odbc(), Driver = "Oracle in instantclient_12_2", 
  Dbq = dbq, uid = uid, pwd = pwd)

tbl <- dplyr::tbl(con, "DUAL")
dplyr::setdiff(tbl, tbl)
#> Error: <SQL> 'SELECT * FROM (SELECT *
#> FROM ((SELECT *
#> FROM "DUAL")
#> EXCEPT
#> (SELECT *
#> FROM "DUAL")) "ebzdgbnsmd") "zzz2" WHERE ROWNUM <= 10'
#>   nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: HY000: [Oracle][ODBC][Ora]ORA-00907: missing right parenthesis
#> 

qry_except <- "SELECT *
FROM (
SELECT *
FROM (
(SELECT * FROM \"DUAL\")
EXCEPT
(SELECT * FROM \"DUAL\")
) \"xqcikplkqs\"
) \"zzz13\"
WHERE ROWNUM <= 10"

DBI::dbGetQuery(con, qry_except)
#> Error: <SQL> 'SELECT *
#> FROM (
#> SELECT *
#> FROM (
#> (SELECT * FROM "DUAL")
#> EXCEPT
#> (SELECT * FROM "DUAL")
#> ) "xqcikplkqs"
#> ) "zzz13"
#> WHERE ROWNUM <= 10'
#>   nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: HY000: [Oracle][ODBC][Ora]ORA-00907: missing right parenthesis
```

title: Messages after transmute_all() et al.
description:
`transmute()` should give a message if it adds a grouping variable, just like `select()`. No message after #3409, a message was given in 0.7.4:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
tibble(a = 1:2, b = 1) %>% 
  group_by(b) %>% 
  transmute(a)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#> # Groups:   b [1]
#>       b     a
#>   <dbl> <int>
#> 1    1.     1
#> 2    1.     2
```

`transmute_xxx()` should give a message if they do not change a grouping variable that would otherwise fit the criteria. This is new behavior.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
tibble(a = 1:2, b = 1) %>% 
  group_by(b) %>% 
  transmute_all(funs(`-`))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#> # Groups:   b [1]
#>       b     a
#>   <dbl> <int>
#> 1    1.    -1
```

title: Unexpected behavior in filter when not unquoting the quosure
description:
## Context

I was writing a blogpost about tidyeval, with as an example a very simple function based on `filter`.  

To stress the "two steps process" (`enquo` then `!!`), I wanted to build a function without `!!` to show the returned error. 

## Issue

It seems that `filter` doesn't return an error when we "forget" to unquote the quosure. 

```
#Doesn't throw an error (as could be expected) 
custom_filter <- function(df, col, threshold){
  col <- enquo(col)
  filter(df, col > threshold)
}

custom_filter(iris, Sepal.Length, 2)
[1] Sepal.Length Sepal.Width  Petal.Length Petal.Width  Species     
<0 lignes> (ou 'row.names' de longueur nulle)
```

And  
```
# Throws an error (as expected) : 
custom_select <- function(df, col){
  col <- enquo(col)
  select(df, col)
}
custom_select(iris, Species)
Erreur : `col` must resolve to integer column positions, not formula 
```

After a quick private conversation with @romainfrancois  on Slack, he pointed out that it seems to be due to the behavior of formulas:

```
> col <- quo(col)
> col < 2
[1] TRUE
> col > 2
[1] FALSE
> col <- quote(~col)
> col < 2
[1] TRUE
> col > 2
[1] FALSE
``` 

It seems that formulas and quosures can be evaluated against a number, leading to an unexpected behavior in filter when we forget to `!!` a quosure. 

This might be more an rlang issue, so just let me know and I'll move this issue on the rlang repo if needed.

title: case_when is inefficient
description:
As currently constructed, `case_when` is inefficient. First it evaluates the RHS of each of the formulas, then it picks the one to actually return based on the LHS. If the code on the RHS for some of the options takes awhile to evaluate, this will be much slower than necessary, and much slower than using if/if else logic.

It seems trivial to change the implementation so that the LHS is evaluated first, and the RHS is only evaluated for the one case that the function will return.

Compare:

```
t0 <- Sys.time()
res <- case_when(TRUE  ~ "A",
                 FALSE ~ {Sys.sleep(5); "B"})
t1 <- Sys.time()
res <- if (TRUE) "A" else if (FALSE) {Sys.sleep(5); "B"}
t2 <- Sys.time()

t1 - t0
t2 - t1
```

The former takes 5 unnecessary seconds.

title: db_explain.DBIConnection writes bad syntax for Oracle
description:
I'm trying out using `dplyr` on an Oracle OCI database connection built with `ROracle` (class `OraConnection`) and I ran into a problem with `explain()`.

Simplified version of what I tried is 

    con <- [make my usual DBI connection]
    remote_data <- con %>%
      tbl('DUAL') %>%
      explain

Which throws an error:

    Error in .oci.GetQuery(conn, statement, data = data, prefetch = prefetch,  : 
      ORA-00905: missing keyword

I was able to isolate the problem to the general-purpose [`db_explain.DBIConnection`](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/c0e51957a2fbeb4fe7bc93f0ed677d6d33e14828/R/dbi-s3.r#L122).

For the above query, that generates the SQL

    EXPLAIN SELECT *
    FROM "DUAL"

Which I tried running directly in Oracle and confirmed got the same error. 


I found something that works [in the Oracle documentation](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/B19306_01/server.102/b14211/ex_plan.htm#g42231), but I don't have the experience to say if this is the true desired output for the `explain()` function here.

First, in SQL directly I'm going for this:

    EXPLAIN PLAN FOR SELECT * FROM "DUAL";
    SELECT PLAN_TABLE_OUTPUT FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY());

To produce that in R, using a variation on the code in `db_explain.DBIConnection`

    remote_data <- tbl(con, 'DUAL')
    
    # explain() calls remote_query_plan() which calls db_explain.DBIConnection() with these params:
    con <- remote_con(remote_data)
    sql <- db_sql_render(remote_con(remote_data), remote_data$ops)
    
    # here is my replacement for the code in db_explain.DBIConnection()
    exsql <- build_sql("EXPLAIN PLAN FOR ", sql, con = con)
    dbSendQuery(con, exsql)
    expl <- dbGetQuery(con, 'SELECT PLAN_TABLE_OUTPUT FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY())')
    out <- utils::capture.output(print(expl))
    
    paste(out, collapse = "\n")


Here's what that looks like using `writeLines(out)`:

    1                                                             Plan hash value: 272002086
    2                                                                                       
    3             --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    4             | Id  | Operation         | Name | Rows  | Bytes | Cost (%CPU)| Time     |
    5             --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    6             |   0 | SELECT STATEMENT  |      |     1 |     2 |     2   (0)| 00:00:01 |
    7             |   1 |  TABLE ACCESS FULL| DUAL |     1 |     2 |     2   (0)| 00:00:01 |
    8             --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    9                                                                                       
    10                                                                                  Note
    11                                                                                 -----
    12    - automatic DOP: Computed Degree of Parallelism is 1 because of parallel threshold


Not sure if that is what this function should produce, but hopefully it helps.

title: Joins lose custom attributes
description:
Much like #3259, the join functions also lose custom attributes. We use attributes to save the query to the object it produced:
```r
my_get_data_function <- function(query) {
  data <- db_function_to_connect_and_collect_and_so_forth(sql(query))
  attr(data, "qry") <- sql(query)
  data
}
qry <- function(object) {
  q <- attributes(object)$qry
  if (!is.null(q)) {
    q
  } else {
    cat("No query found.\n")
  }
}
```

So, for example with `dplyr` data:
```r
library(dplyr)
attributes(band_members)
# $names
# [1] "name" "band"
# 
# $class
# [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
# 
# $row.names
# [1] 1 2 3

# save this attributes to this dataset:
attr(band_members, 'qry') <- sql("SELECT * FROM tbl1")
attributes(band_members)
# $names
# [1] "name" "band"
# 
# $class
# [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
# 
# $row.names
# [1] 1 2 3
# 
# $qry
# <SQL> SELECT * FROM tbl1

# and here it vanishes:
band_members %>% left_join(band_instruments) %>% attributes()
# Joining, by = "name"
# $class
# [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
# 
# $row.names
# [1] 1 2 3
# 
# $names
# [1] "name"  "band"  "plays"
```

Is this intended? Especially for `left_join`, we would like to keep the attributes of `x`.

title: Feature Request: function to add "totals" as an indexed group for summarizing
description:
(this is a generalization and extension of #1253)

This function would add a group to a grouped_df, called "Total" (or maybe a user-specified name), that has all row numbers in its index.  Once this group is added to the tibble, summarise functions would treat it like any other group.

Hypothetical example:
```
mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  add_totals_group() %>%
  summarise(avg_mpg = mean(mpg),
            n = n())

# A tibble: 4 x 3
  cyl   avg_mpg     n
  <chr>   <dbl> <int>
1 4        26.7    11
2 6        19.7     7
3 8        15.1    14
4 Total    20.1    32
```

The actual code to produce this hypothetical result is:
```
rbind(
  mtcars %>%
    group_by(cyl) %>%
    summarise(avg_mpg = mean(mpg),
              n = n()),
  mtcars %>%
    summarise(avg_mpg = mean(mpg),
              n = n()) %>%
    mutate(cyl = "Total")
)
```

I started working on it but ran into internal dplyr validation checks that don't like my "corrupt" grouped_df.  Here's my non-working attempt to tinker with the group indices:
```
add_totals_group <- function(dat){
  cur_indices <- attr(dat, "indices")
  attr(dat, "indices")[[length(cur_indices) + 1]] <- seq(nrow(dat))
  attr(dat, "group_sizes") <- c(attr(dat, "group_sizes"), nrow(dat))
  attr(dat, "biggest_group_size") <- nrow(dat)
  attr(dat, "labels") <- rbind(rep("Total", ncol(dat)))
  dat
}
```

title: Confusing error message across many dplyr verbs when improperly indexed
description:
(re [this Tweet](https://twitter.com/hadleywickham/status/952259891342794752))

I frequently get error messages of the following variety:

 `Error in filter_impl(.data, quo) : Result must have length 87, not 0`.

`Error in mutate_impl(.data, dots) : 
  Column `color` must be length 20 (the group size) or one, not 177`

This usually happens when I inadvertently use `df$col` instead of `col` to name a variable that I have either mutated or grouped by further up in a pipeline. 

Reprex below:  

```r
starwars <- starwars %>%
  mutate(age_bracket = case_when(
    birth_year < 21 ~ "kids",
    birth_year >= 18 & birth_year < 65 ~ "adults",
    TRUE ~ "Senior citizen discounts for Yoda & friends, woo"
  )) %>%
    filter(starwars$age_bracket == "kids")
```
```
Error in filter_impl(.data, quo) : Result must have length 87, not 4
```

It was much more common (and perplexing) when I was new to the tidyverse and accustomed to indexing variable names with `df$`.

I'm not sure what the most succinct and helpful error message would be. I like the new "Did you use %>% instead of +?" in ggplot, but I'm not sure how broad this error structure is (I've seen it for multiple dplyr verbs, and it's the same error if the df is indexed in other ways too. (e.g. `df[[14]]`). I would support "you probably have some stray `$`s in your pipeline, you Silly Billy", but I assume that's too specific. 

Thanks!

title: unquote fails in `bind_rows`
description:
When I unquote variables in any processing chain embedded in `bind_rows` it fails with various errors, depending on the context, for example:

```
`Error: `quote(var)` must resolve to integer column positions, not a symbol`
```

See more also here: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/47230211/dplyr-how-to-unquote-in-bind-rows

```r
require(dplyr)

f1 <- function(d, var){

    qvar <- enquo(var)

    d1 <- d %>% group_by(!!qvar) %>% summarize_all(first)
    d2 <- d %>% group_by(!!qvar) %>% summarize_all(first)

    bind_rows(d1, d2)

}

f2 <- function(d, var){

    qvar <- enquo(var)

    bind_rows(
        d %>%  group_by(!!qvar) %>% summarize_all(first),
        d %>%  group_by(!!qvar) %>% summarize_all(first)
    )
}

d <- data.frame(
    x = c(rep('a', 3), rep('b', 3)),
    y = seq(6)
)

f1(d, x) # works

f2(d, x) # fails
```

title: Rethink definition of variables in the result of a join
description:
Simplify name generation and resolution of clashes:

1. Use variables, remove rhs variables for equi-joins (but not for generic joins)
1. Add suffixes to remaining variables of the same name in lhs and rhs
1. Combine variables: join variables, remaining lhs variables, remaining rhs variables
1. Apply `tibble::set_tidy_names()`.

For *dplyr*, the result should be two lists that can be unquote-spliced into `select()`. The C++ side then only needs to know the number of join variables and return the result,  For *dbplyr*, something similar to the current `join_vars()` implementation would be useful. Need to think about a data structure that supports both, and export the function that computes the join variables.

Useful for/part of #2240.
