title: Unexpected error yield by `case_when()`
description:
Sorry for any ambiguity, but I don't know how to interpret this issue in a more clear way.

`case_when()` yields an error in the following code:

```r
set.seed(1)                                                 
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))          
tibble(tmp1 = sample(c(T, F), size = 32, replace = T),      
tmp2 = sample(c(T, F), size = 32, replace = T),             
tmp3 = sample(c(T, F), size = 32, replace = T)) %>%         
mutate(tmp = apply(cbind(tmp1, tmp2, tmp3), 1, function(x) {
case_when(                                                  
all(x == F) ~ "N",                                          
any(x == T) ~ "Y"                                           
)                                                           
}))                                                         
#> Error in mutate_impl(.data, dots): Evaluation error: object 'x' not found.
```

If I use `if-else` statement instead of `case_when()`, it works as expected:

```r
set.seed(1)                                                 
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))          
tibble(tmp1 = sample(c(T, F), size = 32, replace = T),      
tmp2 = sample(c(T, F), size = 32, replace = T),             
tmp3 = sample(c(T, F), size = 32, replace = T)) %>%         
mutate(tmp = apply(cbind(tmp1, tmp2, tmp3), 1, function(x) {
if (all(x == F)) {                                          
"N"                                                         
} else if(any(x == T)) {                                    
"Y"                                                         
}                                                           
}))                                                         
#> # A tibble: 32 x 4
#>    tmp1  tmp2  tmp3  tmp  
#>    <lgl> <lgl> <lgl> <chr>
#>  1 T     T     F     Y    
#>  2 T     T     T     Y    
#>  3 F     F     T     Y    
#>  4 F     F     F     N    
#>  5 T     F     T     Y    
#>  6 F     T     F     Y    
#>  7 F     F     T     Y    
#>  8 F     T     F     Y    
#>  9 F     F     T     Y    
#> 10 T     F     T     Y    
#> # ... with 22 more rows
```

If I define the anonymous function outside of `apply()`, and pass that function to `apply()`, it also works as expected:

```r
set.seed(1)                                           
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))    
f <- function(x) {                                    
if (all(x == F)) {                                    
"N"                                                   
} else if(any(x == T)) {                              
"Y"                                                   
}                                                     
}                                                     
tibble(tmp1 = sample(c(T, F), size = 32, replace = T),
tmp2 = sample(c(T, F), size = 32, replace = T),       
tmp3 = sample(c(T, F), size = 32, replace = T)) %>%   
mutate(tmp = apply(cbind(tmp1, tmp2, tmp3), 1, f))    
#> # A tibble: 32 x 4
#>    tmp1  tmp2  tmp3  tmp  
#>    <lgl> <lgl> <lgl> <chr>
#>  1 T     T     F     Y    
#>  2 T     T     T     Y    
#>  3 F     F     T     Y    
#>  4 F     F     F     N    
#>  5 T     F     T     Y    
#>  6 F     T     F     Y    
#>  7 F     F     T     Y    
#>  8 F     T     F     Y    
#>  9 F     F     T     Y    
#> 10 T     F     T     Y    
#> # ... with 22 more rows
```

Or, if `apply()` is called outside of `mutate()`, it also works as expected (though the output is not a data frame):

```r
set.seed(1)                                          
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))   
cbind(tmp1 = sample(c(T, F), size = 32, replace = T),
tmp2 = sample(c(T, F), size = 32, replace = T),      
tmp3 = sample(c(T, F), size = 32, replace = T)) %>%  
apply(1, function(x) {                               
case_when(                                           
all(x == F) ~ "N",                                   
any(x == T) ~ "Y"                                    
)                                                    
})                                                   
#>  [1] "Y" "Y" "Y" "N" "Y" "Y" "Y" "Y" "Y" "Y" "Y" "Y" "N" "Y" "Y" "Y" "Y"
#> [18] "N" "Y" "Y" "Y" "Y" "Y" "Y" "Y" "Y" "Y" "Y" "N" "Y" "Y" "Y"
```

The behavior of the first example is inconsistent and unexpected. Is it a bug or am I missing anything?

title: recode_factor does not handle !!!
description:
A code snippet like this

```r
dplyr::recode_factor(x, !!! layer_key)
```
produces an error that says !level_key is an invalid argument type

This is the result of a question on https://community.rstudio.com/t/using-recode-factor-with-quasi-quotation/5761/5

Here is a repro

``` r
library(magrittr)
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
set.seed(100)
x <- sample(head(LETTERS, 3), 10, replace = TRUE) %>% factor
x
#>  [1] A A B A B B C B B A
#> Levels: A B C
level_key <- list("Be", "Cool", "Amigo") %>% set_names(c("B", "C", "A"))    # set factor re-level 
level_key2 <- list(B = "Be", C = "Cool", A = "Amigo")

dplyr::recode_factor(x, !!!level_key)
#> Error in !level_key: invalid argument type
```

Created on 2018-03-03 by the [reprex package](http://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.0).

The problem is the use of c(...) inside of rcode_factor. Here is my analysis of the problem.

The problem is buried inside of recode_factor. It is that only functions that are implemented to use quosures can properly interpret `!!!`

Here is where the problem is in recode_factor:

``` r
dplyr:::recode_factor
#> function (.x, ..., .default = NULL, .missing = NULL, .ordered = FALSE) 
#> {
#>     recoded <- recode(.x, ..., .default = .default, .missing = .missing)
# ----------------------------The . problem is with c() ----
#>     all_levels <- unique(c(..., recode_default(.x, .default, 
#>         recoded), .missing))
#>     recoded_levels <- if (is.factor(recoded)) 
#>         levels(recoded)
#>     else unique(recoded)
#>     levels <- intersect(all_levels, recoded_levels)
#>     factor(recoded, levels, ordered = .ordered)
#> }
#> <environment: namespace:dplyr>
```
Created on 2018-03-03 by the [reprex package](http://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.0).


The problem is in the Combine, `c()`, function.  Although in `!!! layer_key` `!!!` looks like an operator or in !!!(layer_key)  it looks like a function it is neither. 

It depends on the function getting the `!!!` layer_key in an `...` argument to do something like enquo(...) so that standard evaluation is bypassed. It is enquo(or one of it's friends) that interprets `!!!` to turn a list into individual dot arguments.

But c() is a primitive function so it just does standard evaluation of `!!! level_key` which, in effect, produces a syntax kind of error.

Here is an example of a function that tries to use `!!!` with `c()`

``` r

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))
f2 <- function(...) {
    c(...)
}
level_key <- list("Be", "Cool", "Amigo") %>% set_names(c("B", "C", "A"))    # set factor re-level 

f2(!!! level_key)
#> Error in !level_key: invalid argument type
```

Created on 2018-03-03 by the [reprex package](http://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.0).

I don't see a workaround for this.

title: Postgres table creation not behaving like RPostgreSQL
description:
I need to modify the postgres connection ever so slightly to avoid a warning and undesired behavior in a greenplum database. If I don't provide a "distributed by" clause upon table creation the data is loaded according to the first column of the data provided. 

With PostgreSQL I am able to accomplish this with the first code chunk below. However, the corresponding approach does not work with the PqConnection 
class from RPostgres.

RPostgreSQL (works as expected and distributes randomly):

```r
#' @importFrom assertthat assert_that
#' @importFrom rlang is_string
#' @importFrom dbplyr build_sql as.sql
#' @export
db_create_table.PostgreSQLConnection <- function(con, table, types, temporary = TRUE, ...) {
  assertthat::assert_that(rlang::is_string(table), is.character(types))

  field_names <- escape(ident(names(types)), collapse = NULL, con = con)
  fields <- sql_vector(
    paste0(field_names, " ", types),
    parens = TRUE,
    collapse = ", ",
    con = con
  )
  sql <- dbplyr::build_sql(
    "CREATE ", if (temporary) sql("TEMPORARY "),
    "TABLE ", dbplyr::as.sql(table), " ", fields,
    " DISTRIBUTED RANDOMLY",
    con = con
  )

  DBI::dbExecute(con, sql)
}
```
RPostgres(not implemented... so uses first column for distribution as per db default):

```r
#' @importFrom assertthat assert_that
#' @importFrom rlang is_string
#' @importFrom dbplyr build_sql as.sql
#' @export
db_create_table.PqConnection <- function(con, table, types, temporary = TRUE, ...) {
  assertthat::assert_that(rlang::is_string(table), is.character(types))

  field_names <- escape(ident(names(types)), collapse = NULL, con = con)
  fields <- sql_vector(
    paste0(field_names, " ", types),
    parens = TRUE,
    collapse = ", ",
    con = con
  )
  sql <- dbplyr::build_sql(
    "CREATE ", if (temporary) sql("TEMPORARY "),
    "TABLE ", dbplyr::as.sql(table), " ", fields,
    " DISTRIBUTED RANDOMLY",
    con = con
  )

  DBI::dbExecute(con, sql)
}
```

title: Combining group_by and anti_join lead to erratic behavior of sample_n
description:

```r
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(42)

mtcars <- mtcars %>% mutate(name = rownames(mtcars))
green_cars <- mtcars %>% filter(mpg > 20)
brown_cars <- mtcars %>%
  group_by(carb) %>%
  anti_join(green_cars, by = 'name')
brown_cars %>% sample_n(1)
brown_cars %>% slice(1:n()) %>% sample_n(1)
brown_cars %>% sample_n(1)
```

The first execution of `brown_cars %>% sample_n(1)` returns 
```r
# A tibble: 0 x 12
```

title: Documentation: dplyr::filter note about base subsetting.
description:
From `help(filter)` (for `dplyr`):

> [dplyr::filter] Unlike base subsetting, rows where the condition evaluates to NA are dropped.

I believe `base::subset()` does drop rows where the condition is `NA`.

```r
library("dplyr")
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
subset(mtcars, NA)
#>  [1] mpg  cyl  disp hp   drat wt   qsec vs   am   gear carb
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
filter(mtcars, NA)
#>  [1] mpg  cyl  disp hp   drat wt   qsec vs   am   gear carb
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
```

The `[ ]` operator does not drop with `NA`, but I think many readers will take "base subsetting" to mean `base::subset`.

```r
> colnames(data.frame(goodname = dplyr::tibble(badname = "test")[, "badname"]))
```

title: filter can not use inline pull

``` r
                     ":memory:")
table <- dplyr::copy_to(db,
                        data.frame(idx = 1:5))
t2 <- dplyr::copy_to(db,
                        data.frame(idx = 1:2))
```

title: tbl impl for Teradata does not support cross schema query
description:

title: group_by_at() doesn't handle existig grouping correctly
description:
`group_by_at(tbl)` is confused if `tbl` is already a grouped tibble and new grouping uses some of variables that were used in this previously existing grouping. Instead of overwriting this existing grouping (as `group_by()` does by default) it returns tibble grouped only by variables that wern't used in previosuly defined grouping (and throws a warning about nonexistence of variables common for existing and newly defined grouping).

```r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Dołączanie pakietu: 'dplyr'
#> Następujące obiekty zostały zakryte z 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag

#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

# some grouped tibble
tbl = tibble(gr1 = rep(1:2, 4), gr2 = rep(1:2, each = 4), x = 1:8) %>%
  group_by(gr1)

# doesn't work
tbl %>%
  group_by_at(vars(one_of("gr1", "gr2"))) %>%
  summarise(xSum = sum(x))
```

title: Teradata ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) issue
description:
Hi all, thanks for all your work on the Teradata translations for dbplyr. One issue I've come across is that ROW_NUMBER() window functions generated by dbplyr produce errors.

For example, if I run this code:
```r
flights %>% 
  select(record_id, record_create_dt, acct_num, dep_dt, origin) %>% 
  group_by(record_id, record_create_dt, acct_num) %>% 
  mutate(rn = row_number()) %>% 
  show_query()
```

this is SQL generated:
```sql
SELECT "record_id", "record_create_dt", "acct_num", "dep_dt", "origin"
	,row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY "record_id", "record_create_dt", "acct_num", "dep_dt") AS "rn"
FROM (SELECT "record_id", "record_create_dt", "acct_num", "dep_dt", "origin"
FROM cdw.flights) "iljxeikdep"
WHERE (("dep_dt" = '2017-01-21') AND ("origin" = 'DEN'))
```

But it generates the following error:
```r
Error in new_result(connection@ptr, statement) : 
  nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1344: 42000: [Teradata][ODBC Teradata Driver][Teradata Database] Syntax error: expected something between the word 'dep_dt' and ')'.
```

However, I then tweaked the generated SQL to add an ORDER BY clause within the OVER (PARTITION BY ...) parenthetical and ran it directly in Teradata:
```sql
SELECT "record_id", "record_create_dt", "acct_num", "dep_dt", "origin"
	,row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY "record_id", "record_create_dt", "acct_num", "dep_dt" ORDER BY "record_id", "record_create_dt") AS "rn"
FROM (SELECT "record_id", "record_create_dt", "acct_num", "dep_dt", "origin"
FROM cdw.flights) "iljxeikdep"
WHERE (("dep_dt" = '2017-01-21') AND ("origin" = 'DEN'))
```
and it ran without error.

I'm not exactly sure why the dbplyr translated code didn't run while my altered code did, but it could be related to the fact that Teradata recognizes ROW_NUMBER() as an ordered analytical function and requires ordering criteria within the window function. Or maybe I'm missing an obvious solution. Any help would be greatly appreciated. Thanks again!

If I specify in the `if_else` command `TRUE` and `FALSE` explicitly, I get an error, If I use 1 and 0, everything runs fine.
My guess is that TRUE and FALSE are not enclosed in ticks. I manually changed the SQL statement to use `THEN ('TRUE')` and `THEN ('FALSE')` which worked.

```r
library(odbc)
library(tidyverse)
#> -- Attaching packages -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- tidyverse 1.2.1 --
#> v ggplot2 2.2.1     v purrr   0.2.4
#> v tibble  1.4.2     v dplyr   0.7.4

#> x dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
#> x dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
serverName <- "prosim2045.bku.db.de\\GV"
databaseName <- "UnITbox"
connection <- dbConnect(odbc(),
                        driver = "SQL Server",
                        server = serverName,
                        database = databaseName,
                        encoding = "latin1")
tbl_mtcars <- copy_to(connection, mtcars, name = "##temptable")
testmutate <- tbl(connection, "##temptable") %>%
    mutate(disp2 = if_else(disp > 100 & disp < 200, TRUE, FALSE))
testmutate %>% show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT "mpg", "cyl", "disp", "hp", "drat", "wt", "qsec", "vs", "am", "gear", "carb", CASE WHEN ((CONVERT(BIT, IIF("disp" > 100.0, 1.0, 0.0)) & CONVERT(BIT, IIF("disp" < 200.0, 1.0, 0.0))) =  'TRUE') THEN (TRUE) WHEN ((CONVERT(BIT, IIF("disp" > 100.0, 1.0, 0.0)) & CONVERT(BIT, IIF("disp" < 200.0, 1.0, 0.0))) =  'FALSE') THEN (FALSE) END AS "disp2"
#> FROM "##temptable"
testmutate %>% collect()
#> Error: <SQL> 'SELECT "mpg", "cyl", "disp", "hp", "drat", "wt", "qsec", "vs", "am", "gear", "carb", CASE WHEN ((CONVERT(BIT, IIF("disp" > 100.0, 1.0, 0.0)) & CONVERT(BIT, IIF("disp" < 200.0, 1.0, 0.0))) =  'TRUE') THEN (TRUE) WHEN ((CONVERT(BIT, IIF("disp" > 100.0, 1.0, 0.0)) & CONVERT(BIT, IIF("disp" < 200.0, 1.0, 0.0))) =  'FALSE') THEN (FALSE) END AS "disp2"
#> FROM "##temptable"'
```

```r
#> FROM "##temptable"
```

title: Connecting to a Netezza source causes crash using newest `dbplyr`
description:
I use a combination of packages to pull data from a Netezza database server into R, and write data back to the same server: `dplyr`, `odbc`, and `dbplyr`.  This technique no longer works if I use the latest version of `dbplyr` (1.2.0). Specifically, using `copy_to` function causes a crash (i.e. a fatal error).  Using `dbplyr` version 1.1.0 does not cause a crash.

To reproduce, you will need an ODBC connection to a Netezza database server. I called the DSN of the connection "NetezzaDSN".  (I'm on Windows).

Reproducing using the package `dbtest`:
```
# Using R 3.4.2
library(dplyr)
library(dbtest) # github version 0.1.0
library(odbc) # version 1.1.5
library(dbplyr) #version 1.2.0
con = dbConnect(odbc(), dsn = “NetezzaDSN”) # Using driver NetezzaSQL
test_connection(con) # --> fatal error
``` 

Reproducing using the function `copy_to` :
 
```
library(dplyr)
library(odbc)
library(dbplyr)
con = dbConnect(odbc(), "NetezzaDSN")
data(mtcars)
copy_to(con, mtcars, name = "test_table", temporary = FALSE, analyze = FALSE)
```

title: arrange_at(vars(...)) chokes if a variable is used for grouping, arrange(...) does not
description:
The function `arrange_at(.)` throws an 'object not found' error if a variable is used for sorting which is set as grouping variable.

Examples which work:

```r
mtcars %>% arrange(cyl)
## [Sorted output of mtcars]

# Same meaning, using arrange_at
mtcars %>% group_by(cyl) %>% arrange_at(vars(cyl))
## [Sorted output of mtcars]
``` 

However, if the data frame is grouped, only the first version works:

```r
mtcars %>% group_by(cyl) %>% arrange(cyl)
## [Sorted output of mtcars]
# Same meaning,  but does not work:
mtcars %>% group_by(cyl) %>% arrange_at(vars(cyl))
## Error in overscope_eval_next(overscope, expr) : object 'cyl' not found
```

If a grouped data frame is returned to non-grouped state, both approaches work again:

```r
mtcars %>% group_by(cyl) %>% group_by() %>% arrange_at(vars(-cyl))
## [Sorted output of mtcars]
```

This is confusing if I want, for example, sort a wide data table containing one name column and many data dimensions by all columns except the name. I need to use 

```r
widedata %>% arrange_at(vars(-NameColumn))
```

If `widedata` is a result of a prior operation involving grouping, I must explicitly remove the grouping. This would be OK, if technically needed but I think at least the error message 

    Error in overscope_eval_next(overscope, expr) : object '.....' not found

should be replaced by something like 

    Error: cannot arrange_by by a column used for grouping

Or, if technically feasible, of course it would be more awesome if arrange_at did not care about grouping!

title: Ungrouped filter()/mutate() if only "creation" or "mutating" functions are used
description:
If a filter or mutate expression isn't affected by the grouping, we can process it all at once, without splitting in groups:

```r
iris %>% group_by(Species) %>% filter(Petal.Width < 1.3)
```

is the same as

```r
iris %>% filter(Petal.Width < 1.3) %>% group_by(Species)
```

and should be processed as such. This should be accompanied with a message (and a way to turn off that message or to enforce grouped processing), for cases where we misclassify the filter or mutate expression.

This only works if *all* filtering or mutating expressions only use "creation" or "mutating" functions, see http://r4ds.had.co.nz/transform.html#mutate-funs.

title: select_helpers do not work with summarize_at
description:
The documentation of `summarize_at` says:

    summarise_at(), mutate_at() and transmute_at() allow you to select columns using the same name-based select_helpers just like with select().

The `select_helpers` documentation gives the following example:

```r
> iris <- tbl_df(iris)
> select(iris, starts_with("Petal"))
```

However, the following analogue gives an error message:
```r
> mutate_at(iris, starts_with("Petal"), sum)
Error: Variable context not set
```

To make it work:
```r
> mutate_at(iris, starts_with("Petal", vars = names(iris)), sum)
```

title: Using `slice()` with a row number vector which includes 0 results in wrong output
description:
If one uses `slice()` with a row number vector which includes 0 *and* other row numbers, wrong output is produced. Here’s a repexp:

``` r
library(dplyr)

# Example data
d = tibble(x = 1:5, y = LETTERS[1:5])

# This command works fine (returns a zero-row subset)
slice(d, 0)
#> # A tibble: 0 x 2
#> # ... with 2 variables: x <int>, y <chr>

# But these commands give incorrect output
slice(d, c(0, 1))
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       x y    
#>   <int> <chr>
#> 1    NA <NA>
slice(d, c(0, 1, 2))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>       x y    
#>   <int> <chr>
#> 1    NA <NA> 
#> 2     1 A
slice(d, c(-1, 0))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>       x y    
#>   <int> <chr>
#> 1     3 C    
#> 2     4 D    
#> 3     5 E
slice(d, c(0, -1))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>       x y    
#>   <int> <chr>
#> 1     3 C    
#> 2     4 D    
#> 3     5 E

# Subsetting using base R functions works fine, i.e. gives the expected output
d[0, ]
#> # A tibble: 0 x 2
#> # ... with 2 variables: x <int>, y <chr>
d[c(0, 1), ]
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2

d[c(0, 1, 2), ]
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
```

title: select() works with a vector of variable names
description:
`select()` works with vector of variable names but I think it shouldn't. Let me show why:

```r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union


## This is confusing. Shouldn't this give an error?
a <- tibble(c = 21:25, a = 1:5, b = 11:15)
bb <- c("a", "b")
a %>% select(bb)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 2
#>       a     b
#>   <int> <int>
#> 1     1    11
#> 2     2    12
#> 3     3    13
#> 4     4    14
#> 5     5    15

## This is the expected behavior
a <- tibble(c = 21:25, a = 1:5, b = 11:15)
b <- c("a", "b")
a %>% select(b)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 1
#>       b
#>   <int>
#> 1    11
#> 2    12
#> 3    13
#> 4    14
#> 5    15
```

It may be confusing for the user to have different results depending of the name of her object.

My suggestion is to give an error and force the user to write `a %>% select(one_of(bb))`

title: Multi-group summarise() followed by mutate() causing problems
description:
__Update:__ I made a much simpler reprex that still captures the problem. Scroll to the bottom.

This is really a call for help more than a real issue as I truly cannot figure out what is happening.

This is a lengthy issue, so I apologize for that, but I think it had to be to make a full reprex.

The main issue comes from doing this:

1) Extend a tibble as a new class `tbl_test`. Use the `reconstruct()` idea so it works with existing `dplyr` functions, and allow for `grouped_tbl_test` objects as well.

2) Group the `tbl_test` object by multiple groups. Below, I group by `symbol` and `date`.

3) Perform a `summarise()`. One of the groups is lost, but the other is not. Things look okay.

4) Immediately perform a `mutate()` (or any other function like it) on the result from 3. The class and attributes are lost, but more importantly, it seems like _the object that is passed to `mutate()` is actually modified itself_ (as if by reference). The `tbl_test` class on the object passed to the `mutate()` is lost somehow. 

I would appreciate any advice on this. The code below is a simplified form of how `tibbletime` works, and it affects that too. I've tried stepping through with the debugger, but can't pin down what is happening. Thanks!

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(tibbletime)
options(tibble.print_min = 5) 
```

``` r
# Reconstruct 
reconstruct <- function(new, old) {
  UseMethod("reconstruct", old)
}

reconstruct.tbl_test <- function (new, old) {
  
  # Check subclass, if the new thing is a grouped_df, then
  # it should also be grouped_tbl_test
  subclass <- NULL
  if(inherits(new, "grouped_df")) {
    subclass <- "grouped_tbl_test"
  }
  
  new_tbl_test(new, attr(old, "my_attr"), subclass = subclass)
}
```

``` r
# New creation function
new_tbl_test <- function(x, my_attr, ..., subclass = NULL) {
  
  # If reconstruct.tbl_test added grouped_tbl_test as a subclass, then we should append
  # c(grouped_tbl_test, tbl_test, grouped_df)
  # as subclasses so that the final result is 
  # c(grouped_tbl_test, tbl_test, grouped_df, tbl_df, tbl, data.frame)
  subclass <- c(subclass, "tbl_test")
  if("grouped_tbl_test" %in% subclass) {
    subclass <- c(subclass, "grouped_df")
  }
  
  tibble::new_tibble(
    x,
    my_attr = my_attr,
    subclass = subclass
  )
}
```

``` r
# This is how you would extend the functions using reconstruct()
mutate.tbl_test <- function(.data, ...) {
  reconstruct(NextMethod(), .data)
}

summarise.tbl_test <- function(.data, ...) {
  reconstruct(NextMethod(), .data)
}

group_by.tbl_test <- function(.data, ..., add = FALSE) {
  reconstruct(NextMethod(), .data)
}
```

``` r
# Some setup and initial tests

data(FANG)

# Make a tbl_test and check if things are working
FANG_test <- FANG %>%
  new_tbl_test(my_attr = "new_attr")

FANG_test
#> # A tibble: 4,032 x 8
#>   symbol date        open  high   low close   volume adjusted

#> # ... with 4,027 more rows
attr(FANG_test, "my_attr")
#> [1] "new_attr"
class(FANG_test)
#> [1] "tbl_test"   "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"

# Make a grouped_tbl_test and check if things are working
FANG_test_grouped <- FANG_test %>%
  group_by(symbol, date)

FANG_test_grouped
#> # A tibble: 4,032 x 8
#> # Groups: symbol, date [4,032]
#>   symbol date        open  high   low close   volume adjusted
#>   <chr>  <date>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>

# Can we just do multiple normal mutate() with this? Yes, no problem
FANG_test_grouped_mut <- FANG_test_grouped %>%

FANG_test_grouped_mut %>% class

```

## The problem

``` r

# Summarise the two-level grouped tbl_test
FANG_test_grouped_summarized <- summarise(FANG_test_grouped, mean = mean(adjusted))
```

title: Documentation of filter() return "value" is perhaps incorrect?
description:
The documentation of `filter()` specifically says that the return value is *"an object of the same class as `.data`"* ([link](http://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/filter.html#value)). This is not true, any additional classes are dropped. I know this may be the desired behavior of filter and other functions, as this has been discussed in several issues and hasn't been changed, but then the documentation should perhaps be adjusted accordingly? 

```r
##### example tbl #####                         
tbl <- tibble::tibble(a = 1:3, b = letters[1:3])
tbl                                             
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>       a b    
#>   <int> <chr>
#> 1     1 a    
#> 2     2 b    
#> 3     3 c
##### set a custom class #####                  
class(tbl) <- append(class(tbl), "test")        
class(tbl)                                      
#> [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame" "test"
##### use filter to remove 3rd row #####        
tbl <- dplyr::filter(tbl, a < 3)                
tbl                                             
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>       a b    
#>   <int> <chr>
#> 1     1 a    
#> 2     2 b
##### now the custom class is gone #####        
class(tbl)                                      
#> [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
```

Personally, I like to just "tag" objects with a small ID or string now and then without having to create custom object systems and methods and what not

title: Join functions rename columns whose clash should be resolved by `by` parameter
description:
It seems this change happened recently and it breaks enough from previous behavior that I thought I should bring it up.

I commonly want to join two tables pulled from an SQL database, each with an `id` column and the `left` table having a `right_id` column with the foreign key to the `right` table.

``` r
(left <- data.frame(id = 11:14, right_id = 1:4, x = letters[1:4]))
#>   id right_id x
#> 1 11        1 a
#> 2 12        2 b
#> 3 13        3 c
#> 4 14        4 d
(right <- data.frame(id = 1:4, y = LETTERS[1:4]))
#>   id y
#> 1  1 A
#> 2  2 B
#> 3  3 C
#> 4  4 D
```

Previously (with 0.7.4 on CRAN), `left_join(left, right, by = (right_id = 'id'))` would not modify the clashing column names if they were resolved by the joining columns -- so the above would return a table with the column `id` from the `left` table. 

Currently (tested with f49115b), `left_join` considers the column names to have clashed even if specified in the `by` argument, so that the `id` column from the `left` table is returned as `id.x` after the join.

``` r
left_join(left, right, by = c(right_id = "id"))
#>   id.x right_id x y
#> 1   11        1 a A
#> 2   12        2 b B
#> 3   13        3 c C
#> 4   14        4 d D
```

This can be handled by specifying `suffix` or by renaming the column after the join, but this seems like more code than necessary.

``` r
left_join(left, right, by = c(right_id = "id"), suffix = c("", ".right"))
#>   id right_id x y
#> 1 11        1 a A
#> 2 12        2 b B
#> 3 13        3 c C
#> 4 14        4 d D
left_join(left, right, by = c(right_id = "id")) %>% rename(id = id.x)
#>   id right_id x y
#> 1 11        1 a A
#> 2 12        2 b B
#> 3 13        3 c C
#> 4 14        4 d D
```

title: Oracle: copy_to with overwrite fails
description:
I am trying to send a table to an Oracle Database via ODBC ,overwriting if it already exists.
The copy_to method in Oracle via ODBC fails when overwrite=TRUE because "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS" isn't valid syntax in Oracle.

Example (without specific credentials), tested with Oracle 11.2:
```
con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), ...)
dplyr::copy_to(con, iris, overwrite=TRUE)
#> Error: <SQL> 'DROP TABLE IF EXISTS iris'
#> nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: HY000: [Oracle][ODBC][Ora]ORA-00933: SQL command not properly ended
dplyr::copy_to(con, iris, overwrite=TRUE)
#> Error in connection_begin(conn@ptr) : Double begin
```

Expected result:
The table iris is loaded to the database, being overwritten if it already exists.

Actual Result:
There is an error, and the connection can no longer be used (it seems the transaction isn't aborted on failure).

I also tried using ROracle but copy_to seems to fail when attempting to start a transaction:

```
con <- DBI::dbConnect(DBI::dbDriver("Oracle"), ...)
dplyr::copy_to(con, iris)
#> Error in (function (classes, fdef, mtable)  : 
#>  unable to find an inherited method for function 'dbBegin' for signature '"OraConnection"'
```

title: as.integer64 compability for SQL SERVER
description:
Currently, when converting from R to a SQL Server query, d[b]plyr incorrectly handles "as.integer64" This is the function I would expect to use if I want to cast as a bigint within SQL Server. What ends up happening is dplyr uses "AS.INTEGER64" as a SQL Command

1. In SQL SERVER create an example table
```sql
CREATE TABLE Example (Number int)
```

2. In R using dbplyr, try and query the table after casting Number as an integer64
```r
tbl(con,"Example") %>%
  mutate(Number64 = as.integer64(Number))
```

3. This yields:
```
Error: <SQL> 'SELECT  TOP 10 "Number", AS.INTEGER64("Number") AS "Number64"
FROM "Example"'
  nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: 42000: [Microsoft][ODBC Driver 13 for SQL Server][SQL Server]Incorrect syntax near the keyword 'AS'.
```

Which wouldn't happen if the SQL Query was the correct:
```
SELECT TOP 10 Number, CAST(Number AS BIGINT) AS NUMBER64
FROM EXAMPLE
```

title: Database filter on DBIConnection no longer works with latest development version of DBI
description:
I'm trying to build a dynamic SQL query using dplyr (latest dev version installed with devtools::install_github) and filter on a DBIConnection.

I get the following error:
```
    Error in getMethod("dbQuoteString", c("DBIConnection", "character"), asNamespace("DBI")) : 
    no method found for function 'dbQuoteString' and signature DBIConnection, character
```

After investigation, I found that the dbQuoteString methods have recently been modified in DBI, and
setMethod("dbQuoteString", c("DBIConnection", "character") has been removed:
https://github.com/r-dbi/DBI/commit/6c111b7f49632b03eff5f934ec9691f57f5f9702#diff-6d14eaf8cb28fc7edffaeb9d1337c374

I can workaround the issue by downgrading DBI to v0.7-12 (instead of 0.7-13):
devtools::install_github("rstats-db/DBI@v0.7-12")

```r
library(DBI)
library(plyr)
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:plyr':
#>
```

With version v0.7-13 of DBI, the following methods are available:
```r
showMethods("dbQuoteString")

```

By downgrading to version v0.7-12, the following methods are available (which solves the error):

```r
#> conn="DBIConnection", x="character"
#> conn="DBIConnection", x="SQL"
```

Note: I'm reporting this here instead of the DBI project because I assume dplyr needs to be updated to work with the latest DBI. If this was an unintended breaking change in DBI, I could report the issue in DBI instead.

title: What's going on when mutate RHS is a data frame?
description:
Recently I came across a use case where a colleague wanted to duplicate a column via mutate, but refer to the target column programmatically. In the course of doing this, I checked to see what would happen if I used `[` rather than `[[`, and found that not only did `mutate` not fail, but I got a strange result:

```r
library(dplyr)

my_col <- "base_col"

df <- data.frame("a" = c(1, 2),
                 "b" = c(2, 3),
                 "base_col" = c(3, 4))

# this works fine
df %>% mutate(new_col = .[[my_col]])
#>   a b base_col new_col
#> 1 1 2        3       3
#> 2 2 3        4       4

# what's going on here?
df %>% mutate(new_col = .[my_col])
#>   a b base_col new_col. new_col.
#> 1 1 2        3        3        3
#> 2 2 3        4        4        4
```
`mutate` is receiving a `data.frame` here:

```r
> df[my_col]
  base_col
1        3
2        4
```
...but it isn't obvious why the column gets added twice or where the periods are coming from. 

I think the right behaviour here is probably to fail, unless I'm missing something?

title: Filtering grouped data is slow
description:
EDIT: I've added a much simpler example at the top.

I've found that filtering grouped data is slow when there are many groups, even when the filter condition is orthogonal to the grouping.

It's possible I'm hoping for too much intelligence here -- that dplyr can detect when the grouping is relevant for the filtering condition(s).

Example:

```R
dat <- tibble(
  g = rep(1:1e5, length.out = 1e6),
  x = rnorm(1e6)
)

system.time({
  dat %>% filter(x > 0)
})
#  user  system elapsed 
# 0.012   0.000   0.012 

system.time({
  dat %>% 
    group_by(g) %>%
    filter(x > 0)
})
#  user  system elapsed 
# 2.325   0.016   2.344 
```

EDIT: Original example below:

I have a gist here with data:
https://gist.github.com/wch/15bce85635d7e035126681f81900fa47

To reproduce, clone the gist, enter the directory, and run this code:

```R
x <- readRDS("x.rds")
# # A tibble: 102,524 x 4
# # Groups: Package, Version [60,215]
#    Package Version type         n
#    <chr>   <chr>   <chr>    <int>
#  1 A3      0.9.1   Depends      2
#  2 A3      0.9.1   Suggests     2
#  3 A3      0.9.2   Depends      2
#  4 A3      0.9.2   Suggests     2
#  5 A3      1.0.0   Depends      2
#  6 A3      1.0.0   Suggests     2
#  7 abbyyR  0.1     Imports      2
#  8 abbyyR  0.2     Imports      5
#  9 abbyyR  0.2.1   Imports      5
# 10 abbyyR  0.2.1   Suggests     2
# # ... with 102,514 more rows

system.time({
  x %>% filter(Package == "shiny", Version == "1.0.5")
})
#  user  system elapsed 
# 7.385   0.107   7.588 

system.time({
  x %>% ungroup() %>% filter(Package == "shiny", Version == "1.0.5")
})
#  user  system elapsed 
# 0.003   0.001   0.004 
```

title: Feature Request: Port CRAN's fuzzyjoin Funtions to dplyr
description:
I would suggest porting some of CRAN's fuzzyjoin package functions to dplyr (With proper Contribution Acknowledgement):

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/fuzzyjoin/index.html

Of special interest is "fuzzy_join" function, which allows to do SQL queries such as these:
```
SELECT
    REPLACE(PATH, 'W:\\', '\\\\naswoav.usr.corp.gamesa.es\\WO_AV_DATA\\') AS PATH
  FROM
    dispoin.t_DISPOIN_DIR AS A
    INNER JOIN dispoin.t_scadas AS B
      ON
        A.PATH LIKE CONCAT('%', ScadaCode, '%')
        AND (A.PATH LIKE '%2016%' OR A.PATH LIKE '%2017%')
        -- También se puede usar  A.PATH REGEXP '2016|2017';
        AND A.PATH NOT LIKE '%Data_10M%'
        AND A.PATH NOT LIKE '%rejectAL%'
        AND A.PATH NOT LIKE '%REPROCESSED_FILES%'
        AND A.PATH NOT LIKE '%GA677_201308_AL.csv.s3542017.zip%';
```

title: Can't source code example from internals vignette
description:
Brief description of the problem

When I try to source this piece of code from [vignettes that describes the internals](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/master/vignettes/internals/hybrid-evaluation.Rmd) I get the error attached beneath the code piece, which says that I need the header file `plogr.h`

```C++
#include <dplyr.h>
// [[Rcpp::depends(dplyr,BH)]]

using namespace dplyr ;
using namespace Rcpp ;

// the class that derives from Result through Processor
class Hitchhiker : public Processor<INTSXP,Hitchhiker>{
public:
  
  // always returns 42, as it is the answer to everything
  int process_chunk( const SlicingIndex& ){
    return 42 ;    
  }
} ;

// we actually don't need the arguments
// we can just let this handler return a new Hitchhiker pointer
Result* hitchhiker_handler( SEXP, const ILazySubsets&, int ){
  return new Hitchhiker ;        
}

// registration of the register, called from R, so exprted through Rcpp::export
// [[Rcpp::export]]
void registerHitchhiker(){
  registerHybridHandler( "hitchhiker", hitchhiker_handler );    
}

/*** R

  n  <- 10000
df <- group_by( tbl_df( data.frame( 
    id = sample( letters[1:4], 1000, replace = TRUE ), 
    x  = rnorm(n)
) ), id )
  summarise( df, y = hitchhiker() )
```

title: Feature request: raise error for bad group_by column name
description:
With the new tidyeval setup, some dplyr verbs can take strings as arguments. For example, `select(mtcars, "cyl")` works as expected, no extra `!!` or `sym` needed. That's not true for `group_by` (or many of the other dplyr verbs).  
However, I would love for dplyr to raise an error when an inappropriate column name is provided. I've found this mistake is particularly easy to make with rlang's quoting/unquoting/symbol-creating.

"Inappropriate" is a little nebulous here, since `group_by` can accept arbitrary R code for in-memory operations. A heuristic that gets most of the way there would be to check if the `group_by` expression resolves to a character vector whose length is not equal to the number of rows.

What do you think?

```r
library(dplyr)
x <- "cyl"

# This is great, raising an error as expected:
group_by(mtcars, x)
#> Error in grouped_df_impl(data, unname(vars), drop) :
#>  Column `x` is unknown

# I think this is the correct way to have dplyr interpret values:
group_by(mtcars, !!rlang::sym(x))
#> # A tibble: 32 x 11
#> # Groups:   cyl [3]
#>      mpg   cyl  disp    hp  drat    wt  qsec    vs    am  gear  carb
#>  * <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1  21.0  6.00   160 110    3.90  2.62  16.5  0     1.00  4.00  4.00
# ...

# Oh no, we silently added a new, constant column with a weird name!
# This is the one I would like to raise an error.
group_by(mtcars, !!x)
#> # A tibble: 32 x 12
#> # Groups:   "cyl" [1]
#>      mpg   cyl  disp    hp  drat    wt  qsec    vs    am  gear  carb `"cyl"`
#>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>
#>  1  21.0  6.00   160 110    3.90  2.62  16.5  0     1.00  4.00  4.00 cyl
# ...

# Same as previous, it'd be nice to have an error here too.
group_by(mtcars, "cyl")

# But it's hard because you currently can write code like this:
group_by(mtcars, signif(mpg, 1))            #  3 groups
group_by(mtcars, 1:32)                      # 32 groups
group_by(mtcars, c(letters, letters[1:6]))  # 26 groups
```

This is spiritually similar to https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/3140.

title: Aggregating vectors with NA values very slow
description:
I just learned that working with NaNs of type `long double` comes with a 250x performance penalty on my system (Ubuntu, recent Intel CPU):

``` r
x_na <- rep(NA_real_, 1e5)
x_zero <- rep(0, 1e5)

options(digits = 3)
microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  sum(x_na),
  sum(x_zero),
  any(is.na(x_na)),
  any(is.na(x_zero))
)
#> Unit: microseconds
#>                expr     min      lq    mean  median    uq   max neval cld
#>           sum(x_na) 23102.6 23536.9 24134.3 23926.6 24522 29359   100   b
#>         sum(x_zero)    86.7    89.4    99.3    93.6   103   185   100  a 
#>    any(is.na(x_na))    97.5   143.9   240.2   151.6   165  2731   100  a 
#>  any(is.na(x_zero))   179.4   210.1   262.5   219.0   234  2120   100  a
```

> Created on 2018-01-06 by the [reprex package](http://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.1.1.9000).

On an old iMac I'm still seeing a 70x slowdown.

This is important, because a user may inadvertently create a column full of `NA` values and try to aggregate it.

This also affects the hybrid handlers in dplyr. I'm using GCC on Ubuntu, and I have tried various compiler switches to no avail. A coarse search hasn't found anything useful: https://www.startpage.com/do/search?query=r+sum+vector+na+slow.

Adding and storing a value to a `long double` NaN just seems slow ([code](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/cf542082bcaf408c81d2f4b8c60fe9714989514e/inst/include/dplyr/Result/Mean.h#L72-L75)). Reference: https://randomascii.wordpress.com/2012/04/21/exceptional-floating-point/.

Can you replicate? Should our hybrid `mean()` and `sum()` should check for `NA` every 1000 iterations or so?

title: dbplyr - Oracle SQL Translation does not accommodate Oracle timestamps.
description:
When using `dplyr` with a remote Oracle database the SQL translation does not correctly accommodate for Oracle `timestamp` datatypes. Specifically, filtering a tibble pointed at an Oracle table on a date time field (Oracle type `timestamp`, Tibble type `<dttm>`) results in a rejected query.

Date-time strings can be converted to Oracle `timestamp` with the `to_timestamp` function combined with an appropriate formatting string as outlined here: https://docs.oracle.com/cd/B19306_01/server.102/b14200/functions193.htm

I connected to the external database by using the `ROracle` package with the workaround specified here:
https://db.rstudio.com/databases/oracle/#dplyr-translation



```r
sql_translate_env.OraConnection <- dbplyr:::sql_translate_env.Oracle
sql_select.OraConnection <- dbplyr:::sql_select.Oracle
sql_subquery.OraConnection <- dbplyr:::sql_subquery.Oracle 

con <- dbConnect(dbDriver("Oracle"), 
                 dbname = "Database", 
                 user = rstudioapi::askForPassword("User")), 
                 password = rstudioapi::askForPassword("PW"))

table <- tbl(con, in_schema("SCHEMA","TABLE"))

results <- table %>%
  select(
    string,
    dateTime
  ) %>%
  filter(dateTime > Sys.time() - (10*60)) %>%
  show_query()
#> <SQL>
#>SELECT *
#>FROM (SELECT "string" AS "string", "dateTime" AS "dateTime"
#>FROM (SCHEMA.TABLE) ) "limdezpiqk"
#>WHERE ("dateTime" > SYS.TIME() - (10.0 * 60.0))
```
I would expect the SQL to look more like the following:

```r
#> <SQL>
#>SELECT *
#>FROM (SELECT "string" AS "string", "dateTime" AS "dateTime"
#>FROM (SCHEMA.TABLE) ) "limdezpiqk"
#>WHERE ("dateTime" > TO_TIMESTAMP('2018-01-04 12:32:24 CST', 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS TZD'))
```

title: Implement view
group_by is sorting and does not maintain original order
description:
It seems that dplyr's group_by does sort, at least for character, integer and numeric. It does maintain order for factor. Tested with dplyr 0.7.4:
```R
set.seed(4)
char   <- sample(LETTERS[1:20],40,replace = TRUE)
int    <- sample(1L:20L,40,replace = TRUE)
double <- sample(runif(20),40,replace = TRUE)

x <- tibble(char,int,double,fact=factor(char,levels = unique(char)))

# All group_by results are sorted except the factor
group_by(x,char) %>% do(.[1,'char'])
group_by(x,int) %>% do(.[1,'int'])
group_by(x,double) %>% do(.[1,'double'])
group_by(x,fact) %>% do(.[1,'fact'])

# If group_by does not sort, the first indices should contain the first element (zero-based)
# This is only true for the factor
g <- group_by(x,char);attr(g,'indices')[[1]]
g <- group_by(x,int);attr(g,'indices')[[1]]
g <- group_by(x,double);attr(g,'indices')[[1]]
g <- group_by(x,fact);attr(g,'indices')[[1]]
```
Not sure why group_by is sorting. It seems like it's unnecessary including the additional computational effort. This would make the behavior more like the base function ```unique``` or dplyr function ```distinct```, which does not sort either.

Sometimes sorting is nice, so perhaps it could be an option. If the behavior remains as is, perhaps we can add a sorting note to the group_by documentation. 

See for older discussion (but with incorrect finding/conclusion) #2159

title: Feature Request:  Preferred Column Values After Merge
description:
I often want to join two data.frames and then select the "best" result from the output columns.

This happens when I may have two sources of information with partially overlapping information.  One source may be more reliable than the other, so I would prefer to use source 1 if it has a value.  If source 1 doesn't have a value, I'd prefer to use the other source.

The function below does what I'm looking for, and I think it would fit in well in dplyr.  If of interest, I can generate a pull request with this and tests.

```r
#' Following a join, select non-missing values from one source
#' removing the other and combining duplicated column names.
#'
#' @param x The previously-joined data.frame (or similar)
#' @param suffix_order The column name suffixes to combine in preference
#'   order.  Values with the first suffix that are not missing will be
#'   kept.  Values missing with the first suffix will be replaced with
#'   values from the second suffix.
#' @param missing_values Either a vector or a list.  If a vector, all
#'   columns will be compared to the vector.  If a list, then column
#'   names will be matched to list names (and if not all column names.
#' @param duplicated_columns Column names (without the suffix) that are
#'   duplicated.  If not provided, they will be auto-detected.
#' @return A data.frame (or similar; input class is not changed) with
#'   \code{duplicated_columns} combined into one based on preference
#'   order.
#' @examples
#' # Missing values are substituted
#' full_join(data.frame(A=1, B=2, C=3),
#'           data.frame(A=4, B=5, C=6), by="A") %>%
#'   join_prefer()
#'
#' # Non-missing values (C==7) are kept
#' full_join(data.frame(A=c(1, 4), B=c(2, NA), C=c(3, 7)),
#'           data.frame(A=4, B=5, C=6), by="A") %>%
#'   join_prefer()
#'
#' # Not all columns must be operated on
#' full_join(data.frame(A=c(1, 4), B=c(2, NA), C=c(3, 7)),
#'           data.frame(A=4, B=5, C=6), by="A") %>%
#'   join_prefer(duplicated_columns="B")
#'
#' # Nonstandard missing values may be used
#' full_join(data.frame(A=c(1, 4), B=c(2, NA), C=c(3, 7)),
#'           data.frame(A=4, B=5, C=6), by="A") %>%
#'   join_prefer(missing_values=7)
#'
#' # Multiple missing values may be used
#' full_join(data.frame(A=c(1, 4), B=c(2, NA), C=c(3, 7)),
#'           data.frame(A=4, B=5, C=6), by="A") %>%
#'   join_prefer(missing_values=c(NA, 7))
#'
#' # Missing values can be specific to a column
#' full_join(data.frame(A=c(1, 4), B=c(2, NA), C=c(3, 7)),
#'           data.frame(A=4, B=5, C=6), by="A") %>%
#'   join_prefer(missing_values=list(B=NA))
#'
#' # Nonstandard missing values can be specific to a column
#' full_join(data.frame(A=c(1, 4), B=c(2, NA), C=c(3, 7)),
#'           data.frame(A=4, B=5, C=6), by="A") %>%
#'   join_prefer(missing_values=list(B=5))
#' @export
join_prefer <- function(x, suffix_order=c(".x", ".y"),
                        missing_values=NA,
                        duplicated_columns=NULL) {
  trim_suffix <- function(nm, suffix) {
    mask_match <- grepl(suffix, nm, fixed=TRUE)
    if (any(mask_match)) {
      gsub(suffix, "", nm[mask_match], fixed=TRUE)
    } else {
      character(0)
    }
  }
  if (is.null(duplicated_columns)) {
    if (is.list(missing_values)) {
      duplicated_columns <- names(missing_values)
    } else {
      trimmed_columns_1 <- trim_suffix(names(x), suffix_order[1])
      trimmed_columns_2 <- trim_suffix(names(x), suffix_order[2])
      duplicated_columns <- intersect(trimmed_columns_1, trimmed_columns_2)
    }
  }
  expected_columns <- c(paste0(duplicated_columns, suffix_order[1]),
                        paste0(duplicated_columns, suffix_order[2]))
  if (any(mask_missing_columns <- !(expected_columns %in% names(x)))) {
    stop("All duplicated_columns with suffix must be names of columns of x.  The following are not found: ",
         paste(expected_columns[mask_missing_columns], collapse=", "))
  }
  if (is.list(missing_values)) {
    if (!all(mask_not_found <- names(missing_values) %in% duplicated_columns)) {
      stop("Some names of missing_values are not duplicated_columns: ",
           paste(names(missing_values)[mask_not_found], collapse=", "))
    } else if (!all(mask_not_found <- duplicated_columns %in% names(missing_values))) {
      stop("Some duplicated_columns are not in the names of missing_values: ",
           paste(duplicated_columns[mask_not_found], collapse=", "))
    }
  }
  if (length(duplicated_columns)) {
    for (nm in duplicated_columns) {
      colname_1 <- paste0(nm, suffix_order[1])
      colname_2 <- paste0(nm, suffix_order[2])
      x[[nm]] <- x[[colname_1]]
      current_missing <-
        if (is.list(missing_values)) {
          missing_values[[nm]]
        } else {
          missing_values
        }
      mask_missing <- x[[colname_1]] %in% current_missing
      x[[nm]][mask_missing] <- x[[colname_2]][mask_missing]
      # Drop the duplicated column names
      x[[colname_1]] <- x[[colname_2]] <- NULL
    }
  } else {
    message("No duplicated columns found.")
  }
  x
}
```

title: Reduce time to error when collecting results of SQL query with duplicated column names
description:
When collecting the results of an SQL query with duplicated column names, it would be nice if you got the warning as soon as possible so you don't waste time having to rerun long queries after fixing the column names.

I will often write and test out queries in DataGrip or another SQL client and then move it into R, in the SQL client duplicate column names are fine, but for good reason dplyr doesn't allow this, warning:

`Error: Columns [COLUMN NAMES] must have unique names`

and then dumping the result.

```r
sql("SELECT
   main.id,
   main.phone,
   others.phone
FROM consumers main
INNER JOIN consumers others ON others.id = main.id") %>%
  tbl(src = my_source) %>%
  collect(n = Inf)
```

It would be nice to have dplyr warn the user, automatically assign column names (phone_v1, phone_v2) and collected the results into a tibble, or in lieu of that immediately warn the user upon executing the command if possible.

description:
For convenience in data analysis, I think it's a good idea to add `na.rm` as a parameter to the function `pull()` and let it obviously default to FALSE.
```r
pull(.data, var = -1, na.rm = FALSE)
```

I really like this new function by the way!

title: bind_rows() using tibbles with attributes loses attributes
description:
I assume this is very similar to #2457.

Using `bind_rows()` on two tibbles where either one has extra attributes removes all extra attributes. Perhaps an approach similar to #1692 can be taken where the attributes of the first are kept? Ideally I would like `bind_rows()` to be generic but I've read all the problems associated with that.

My use case is in `tibbletime`. My `print.tbl_time()` method relies on one of the attributes. Because the `tbl_time` class is kept after using `bind_rows()`, but the attributes are lost, this causes problems. It causes other problems too, but this shows up immediately.

``` r
library(dplyr)

iris_tbl <- as_tibble(iris)

attr(iris_tbl, "my_attr") <- "important thing"

# The classes of the first object are kept due to #1692
class(iris_tbl) <- c("my_new_class", class(iris_tbl))

iris_doubled <- iris_tbl %>%
  bind_rows(iris_tbl)

  attributes()
```

title: if_else converts matrix into vector (unlike base::ifelse)
description:
If `m` is the matrix: 

    m <- matrix(1:4, 2, 2)

then the following returns a matrix of the same size: 

    ifelse(m < 3, 1, 0)

while dplyr's `if_else` returns a vector: 

    dplyr::if_else(m < 3, 1, 0)

I would expect the latter to return a matrix too.

title: summarise shouldn't force base R functions like sum and mean
description:
The `summarise` function forces the use of base R functions, instead of the expected behaviour that it would use loaded ('active') functions from the own environment.

```r
# (from another package:)
#' @inherit base::mean
#' @export
mean <- function(x, ..., na.rm = TRUE) {
  base::mean(x, ..., na.rm = na.rm)
}

library(dplyr)
df <- tibble(group = LETTERS[1:10], 
             score = c(runif(3, 0, 1), 
                       NA,
                       runif(6, 0, 1)))

mean(df$score) # now na.rm = TRUE by default
# [1] 0.5479927

df %>% summarise(m = mean(score))
# # A tibble: 1 x 1
#       m
#   <dbl>
# 1    NA

> df %>% summarise(m = mean(score, na.rm = TRUE))
# # A tibble: 1 x 1
#       m
#   <dbl>
# 1    0.5479927
```
Why not use functions from ones own environment? This `mean` function comes from another package, which I deliberately loaded, so I would expect it to work in all my code. But apparently, the `summarise` function is an exception. I think you should not force the use of base R functions like `base::mean` in dplyr.

You might think that package developers just shouldn't overwrite functions like `mean`, but even dplyr does this (like `intersect`, `setdiff`, `setequal`, `union`). That too gives other results than when only base R was loaded, just like you would expect. Hence, you loaded dplyr. Now I ask you to let `summarise` use the latest loaded functions, not just base R. Another example: if I would write a function to overwrite `sum` to solve #3189, it wouldn't be used by `summarise` at default, even when my package was loaded after dplyr.

title: dplyr::recode will not work when %>% from tibble
description:
I expected dplyr::recode to recode a column when using df %>% recode(column...) with a tibble, similar to mutate. Instead, it produces the following error: 

> Error in UseMethod("recode") : no applicable method for 'recode' applied to an object of class "c('tbl_df', 'tbl', 'data.frame')"

```r
df <- tibble(x = 1:3,
             y = letters[1:3])

df %>%
  dplyr::recode(x,
                `1` = "a",
                `2` = "b",
                `3` = "c")
```

However, it works with the following alternatives. 

```r
  dplyr::recode(df$x,
                `1` = "a",
                `2` = "b",
                `3` = "c")
```
```r
df %>%
  mutate(x=dplyr::recode(x,
                `1` = "a",
                `2` = "b",
                `3` = "c"))
```

It would be great if recode could work with a tibble directly from %>% without using mutate or calling the df. This would help chaining arguments after recode with fewer commands. There are probably some unforseen complications with this that I am not aware of.

title: Edgecase handling of pull() with inexistent columns
description:
In some situations where the column to select does not exist, the supplied value is `NULL` or similar, it would be nice if `dplyr::pull()` could return something similar to what subsetting operations in base R or in tibble return (instead of an error), so no extra handling of these cases has to be done by the user. If `dplyr::pull()` does not behave like that by design, please ignore this issue.

Base R does this:
``` r
reprex::reprex_info()
#> Created by the reprex package v0.1.1.9000 on 2017-12-07

library(dplyr)

mtcars$abcd
#> NULL
mtcars[["abcd"]]
#> NULL
mtcars[,character(0)]
#> data frame with 0 columns and 32 rows
mtcars[character(0), ]
#>  [1] mpg  cyl  disp hp   drat wt   qsec vs   am   gear carb
#> <0 Zeilen> (oder row.names mit Länge 0)
```

Using S3 methods for tibbles, we get
```r
tbl <- as_tibble(mtcars)
tbl$abcd
#> Warning: Unknown or uninitialised column: 'abcd'.
#> NULL
tbl[["abcd"]]
#> NULL
tbl[,character(0)]
#> # A tibble: 32 x 0
tbl[character(0), ]
#> # A tibble: 0 x 11
#> # ... with 11 variables: mpg <dbl>, cyl <dbl>, disp <dbl>, hp <dbl>,
#> #   drat <dbl>, wt <dbl>, qsec <dbl>, vs <dbl>, am <dbl>, gear <dbl>,
#> #   carb <dbl>
```
However, with `dplyr::pull()` we always seem to get an error:
```r
pull(tbl, character(0))
#> Error: `var` must evaluate to a single number or a column name, not a character vector
pull(tbl, NULL)
#> Error: `var` must evaluate to a single number or a column name, not NULL
pull(tbl, "abc")
#> Error: Strings must match column names. Unknown columns: abc
```

title: duplicate colnames gives uninformative error when joining with tibbles
description:
Tibbles don't allow for duplicate column names at creation:

    > data_frame(x = 1:2, x = 3:4)
    Error: Column `x` must have a unique name

The `_join` functions throw informative errors when join key is duplicate and x is a regular `data.frame`

    > x <- data.frame(x = 1:2, x = 3:4)
    > colnames(x) <- c("x", "x")
    > inner_join(x, data.frame(x = 1:2))
    Error: Column `x` must have a unique name

However, via the same back door the column names of a `tibble` can get duplicated. When trying to join then the error is no longer informative.

    > x <- data_frame(x = 1:2, x2 = 3:4 )
    > colnames(x) <- c("x", "x")
    > inner_join(x, data_frame(x = 1:2))
    Joining, by = "x"
    Error in inner_join_impl(x, y, by$x, by$y, suffix$x, suffix$y, check_na_matches(na_matches)) : 
       Column `` is unknown

If possible, I think the best option here is close the back door route and throw an error at the second line of the last code block. Otherwise an informative error seems desired.

title: Inconsistency in LHS when using quosures compared to using literal column names
description:
I *think* I noticed a small inconsistency when using quosures vs. using literal column names between `filter` and `summarise`: for `filter` it's fine to use LHS = `(!!<quosure)` while for `summarise` it needs to be `!!quo_name(!!<quosure>)`.

I understand that there's a structural difference regarding the expected LHS between the two functions, but since using the literal column *name*  works for both in the "direct"/non-quosure approach, I thought this might be worth mentioning.

```r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attache Paket: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

# Using literal column names -----
mtcars %>% filter(disp > 150) %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  summarise(mpg = mean(mpg))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>     cyl   mpg
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     6 19.75
#> 2     8 15.10

# Using quosures -----
my_pipe <- function(df, filter_lhs, filter_rhs, group_var, summarize_var) {
  filter_lhs <- enquo(filter_lhs)
  filter_lhs_name <- quo_name(filter_lhs)
  group_var <- enquo(group_var)
  summarize_var <- enquo(summarize_var)
  summarize_var_name <- quo_name(summarize_var)

  df %>%
    filter((!!filter_lhs) > filter_rhs) %>%
    group_by(!!group_var) %>%
    summarise(!!summarize_var := mean(!!summarize_var))
}

mtcars %>% my_pipe(filter_lhs = disp, filter_rhs = 150,
  group_var = cyl, summarize_var = mpg)
#> Error: LHS must be a name or string

# Using quosures second approach -----
my_pipe <- function(df, filter_lhs, filter_rhs, group_var, summarize_var) {
  filter_lhs <- enquo(filter_lhs)
  filter_lhs_name <- quo_name(filter_lhs)
  group_var <- enquo(group_var)
  summarize_var <- enquo(summarize_var)
  summarize_var_name <- quo_name(summarize_var)

  df %>%
    filter((!!filter_lhs) > filter_rhs) %>%
    group_by(!!group_var) %>%
    summarise(!!summarize_var_name := mean(!!summarize_var))
    # summarise(!!summarize_var := mean(!!summarize_var))
    ## --> would be in-line with the way it needs to be done for 'filter' but
    ## fails
}
```

title: escaping numerics which are whole numbers should look like integers
description:
The current behaviour of escape() when applied to a numeric vector of whole numbers is to add a trailing '.0'. However, this can cause issues in some cases, for instance when dealing with PostgreSQL bigint columns which are usually drawn in to R as numerics.

In my case, I have a very large SQL table _big_table_ (~250 000 000 rows) with an indexed bigint column _customer_number_. I have a specific value `c = 37256083835234` of _customer_number_ for which I want to pull all records in _big_table_ as follows:
```r
tbl(db, "big_table") %>% filter(customer_number == c) %>% collect()
```

However, looking at the generated SQL query the 'where' filter generated is `customer_number == 37256083835234.0`, which forces PostgreSQL to perform a sequential scan over _big_table_, turning each customer_number into a double before doing the comparison, instead of simply doing an index scan, which it does if I generate and execute the SQL query as follows:
```r
dbGetQuery(db, paste("select * from big_table where customer_number =", c))
```

This behaviour would be avoided if small enough whole number numerics were output without any decimal point and digits thereafter, looking like integers, either by default or as an option. This does mean that the DB might need to do some conversions from bigints to doubles, but I think that is preferable to behaviour like this.

title: pmin and pmax fail in mutate connected to SQL Server
description:
Occasionally, I will need to use pmin or pmax to replace values above or below a threshold, for instance:

```r
require(dplyr)
data_frame(X = 1:10) %>%
  mutate(Y = pmax(X,5))
```

However, when I use dbplyr to try and do this using a SQL Server table, I get the following error:

```r
tbl(con,"OrderInfo") %>%
  mutate(Test = pmax(Revenue,0))
```

```
Error: <SQL> 'SELECT  TOP 10 "CustomerId", "OrderId", "ClientOrderId", "Channel", "OrderDate", "Revenue", "Cost", MAX("Revenue", 0.0) AS "Test"
FROM "OrderInfo"'
  nanodbc/nanodbc.cpp:1587: 42000: [Microsoft][ODBC Driver 13 for SQL Server][SQL Server]The MAX function requires 1 argument(s). 
```

As you can see, the SQL code generator assumes that I want to do a pairwise MAX, however SQL Server does not support that (only taking the maximum over a single column).

A cursory Stack Overflow search suggests that to do this operation a [case statement could be used](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/6585160/i-want-to-set-negative-numbers-in-a-view-to-zero-and-any-positive-should-remain). I think either the SQL code generator should either be updated to do this, or an error should be generated at the time of calling the mutate.

title: Non-signalling incorrect calculation in dbplyr based mutate
description:
The following `dbplyr` based `mutate()` has a non-signalling error (that is an incorrect result that is not brought to user attention by an exception).  Examining with `show_query()`: it appears that only 4 of the 5 assignments in the `mutate()` are translated to `SQL`, and one is silently lost.  I know there are related issues filed on complex `mutate()`'s throwing exceptions (and fixes in the works for such), but this kind non-signalling data corruption is important to research and may reveal a different corner-case.  This code may seem complicated, but it is common user code when the user attempts to simulate a per-row conditional assignment.

``` r
library("dplyr")
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '0.7.4'

my_db <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
d <- copy_to(my_db, 
             data.frame(val = c(0, 5),
                        a_1 = "",
                        a_2 = ""), 
             'd')

# all values in a_1 and a_2 should
# be "treatment" or "control" after
# the following statement.  
# That is not the case.
mutate(d,
       cond = val>2,
       a_1 = ifelse( cond, 
                     'treatment', 
                     a_1),
       a_2 = ifelse( cond, 
                     'control', 
                     a_2),
       a_1 = ifelse( !( cond ), 
                     'control', 
                     a_1),
       a_2 = ifelse( !( cond ), 
                     'treatment', 
                     a_2))
#> # Source:   lazy query [?? x 4]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.19.3 [:memory:]
#>     val     a_1  cond       a_2
#>   <dbl>   <chr> <int>     <chr>
#> 1     0 control     0 treatment
#> 2     5             1   control
```

title: Suggest adding example for intended use of !!! in recode
description:
Unquote-splicing as feature of recode in [0.7.0](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/master/NEWS.md#other). It would be helpful for the documentation to include an example of the intended way to use this feature. I suggest this:

``` r

library(tidyverse)
#> -- Attaching packages --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- tidyverse 1.2.1 --
#> v ggplot2 2.2.1     v purrr   0.2.4
#> v tibble  1.3.4     v dplyr   0.7.4
#> v tidyr   0.7.2     v stringr 1.2.0
#> v readr   1.1.1     v forcats 0.2.0
#> -- Conflicts ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ tidyverse_conflicts() --
#> x dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
#> x dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()

x <- sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 10, replace = TRUE)
dplyr::recode(x, a = "Apple")
#>  [1] "Apple" "b"     "Apple" "b"     "Apple" "b"     "c"     "b"    
#>  [9] "Apple" "b"

fruits <- c("Apple", "Banana", "Carrot")
fruit_lookup <- set_names(fruits, tolower(str_sub(fruits, 1, 1))) %>% as.list

recode(x, !!!fruit_lookup)
#>  [1] "Apple"  "Banana" "Apple"  "Banana" "Apple"  "Banana" "Carrot"
#>  [8] "Banana" "Apple"  "Banana"
```

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))

x <- sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 10, replace = TRUE)
dplyr::recode(x, a = "Apple")

#>  [9] "c"     "c"

fruits <- c("Apple", "Banana", "Carrot")
fruit_lookup_chr <- set_names(fruits, tolower(str_sub(fruits, 1, 1)))

recode(x, !!!fruit_lookup_chr)
#> Error: Only lists can be spliced
```

title: joining with class interval
description:
This is my first time posting on GitHub so I apologize in advance if I am missing needed information or if I am doing anything incorrectly. I also want to thank the developers for making an amazing package! 

I ran into a possible bug when joining a data frame that contained an interval class column (lubridate). The interval class seems to be joined by position, not via the "by" variable. I think this is related to [2432](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/2432), but I did not see this specific case described. Using merge produces the correct data frame.

Appreciate your support!

``` r
library(lubridate)
library(dplyr)
library(reprex)

df1 <- data.frame(id = seq(from = 1, to = 10, by = 1),
                  interval_start = seq.Date(from = ymd("2017-03-01"), to = ymd("2017-03-10"), by = 1))

df1 <- df1 %>%
  mutate(interval_end = interval_start + days(10)) %>%
  mutate(ten_d_interval = interval(start = interval_start, end = interval_end))

df2 <- data.frame(id = c(1,2,3,4,5,10,9,8,7,6),
                  letters = letters[1:10])

df2_join_df1 <- inner_join(df2, df1, by = "id")

# incorrectly joined df, see bottom five rows
df2_join_df1
#>    id letters interval_start interval_end                 ten_d_interval
#> 1   1       a     2017-03-01   2017-03-11 2017-03-01 UTC--2017-03-11 UTC
#> 2   2       b     2017-03-02   2017-03-12 2017-03-02 UTC--2017-03-12 UTC
#> 3   3       c     2017-03-03   2017-03-13 2017-03-03 UTC--2017-03-13 UTC
#> 4   4       d     2017-03-04   2017-03-14 2017-03-04 UTC--2017-03-14 UTC
#> 5   5       e     2017-03-05   2017-03-15 2017-03-05 UTC--2017-03-15 UTC
#> 6  10       f     2017-03-10   2017-03-20 2017-03-06 UTC--2017-03-16 UTC
#> 7   9       g     2017-03-09   2017-03-19 2017-03-07 UTC--2017-03-17 UTC

#> 10  6       j     2017-03-06   2017-03-16 2017-03-10 UTC--2017-03-20 UTC

df2_merge_df1 <- merge(df2, df1, by = "id")

# correcty merged df
df2_merge_df1
```

title: as.data.frame() does not respect column order for DB backends
description:
`as.data.frame()` does not respect column order for DB backends (or at least is not stable, or does not use the same column order as `colnames()`).  A lot of code depends on column order, so I would consider this a bug (regardless of the documented or not-documented invariants of `as.data.frame()`).  The issue occurs with more than one DB data provider (`RSQlite` and `Sparklyr`) and seems to change if a `compute()` is issued.

With the issue any code of the following form may be wrong.

```r
cn <- colnames(d)
dL <- as.data.frame(d)
```

As it will not be equivalent to:

```r
dL <- as.data.frame(d)
cn <- colnames(dL)
```

`knitr` currently [has such code](https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/1462), and is producing erroneous reports.

Right or wrong I think users expect stable column order.

Included `reprex` is long as the issue is subtle, yet important (and we need to establish issue on more than one backend).

``` r
reprex::reprex_info()
#> Created by the reprex package v0.1.1.9000 on 2017-11-21

packageVersion("knitr")
#> [1] '1.17'
packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '0.7.4'
packageVersion("dbplyr")
#> [1] '1.1.0'
packageVersion("sparklyr")
#> [1] '0.6.4'
packageVersion("rlang")
```

title: Support everything() in transmute()
description:
Following the discussion [here](https://community.rstudio.com/t/conceptual-reason-for-transmute/2984/9), it would be useful to be able to use everything() in transmute so that cases where I want to just add a couple of columns at the start of the tibble are dealt with.

This would then be possible:

```r
library(dplyr)
myTibble <- tibble(
                        c = c(1, 2, 3), 
                        d = c(5, 6, 7)
                     )

fullTibble <- myTibble %>% 
                         transmute(

                                 b = c + 2, 
                                 everything()
                         )
```

I'd actually rather be able to do this with select and remove need for transmute, but if not, then transmute would be next best thing.

title: S4 definitions of "sql" and "ident" classes
description:
This line: https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/d310ad1cef1c14d770c94e1a9a4c79c888f46af6/R/src_dbi.R#L179
has a couple of issues.
1. According to `dbplyr::ident()`, the S3 "ident" class derives directly from "character", not "sql". 
2. It seems that d(b)plyr assumes that objects of class "ident" (and the same applies to "sql", defined the line above) are actually character vectors, not just of class "character", i.e., there are `is.character()` checks. That means that any S4 class that would derive from "ident" would need to jump through some hoops to both have a character vector as its prototype _and_ derive from "ident" (currently a virtual class with a dummy S4 object as its prototype). A simple solution is to pass `ident()` as the prototype for the old class, i.e.,
```
setOldClass(c("ident", "sql", "character"), ident())
```
That might necessitate moving the class definitions to the dbplyr package. So I guess the general moral of the story is that any old class that wants to be implemented by a base type needs to provide a prototype. In S4, there is a difference between deriving from a class and actually inheriting the implementation of the class.

Here are some additional findings:
1. This line:
https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/3cc019dc1121480c44dbde65d60a19d6194b40c4/R/ident.R#L29
in dbplyr is not going to do anything right now, since `setOldClass()` defines classes lazily. If they already exist (from dplyr), they are not changed.
2. This:
https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/3cc019dc1121480c44dbde65d60a19d6194b40c4/R/ident.R#L24
for some reason returns a "sql" object instead of a "ident" object in the zero length case, so that will need to be fixed for the suggestion mentioned above to work.

title: Support more advanced patterns in matches()
description:
I tried to use matches() to match a slightly complex regular expression but it didn't support it so I had to use stringr instead. It seems that matches() uses grep rather than stringr.


```r
test <- tibble(
                       hh15_test = c(1,2,3), 
                       hh02_test = c(3,3,3), 
                       hh3_test=c(4,4,5), 
                       blah = c(1,2,3)
)

#Doesn't work
select(test, matches("(hh1)|(^(?!hh))"))

#Error in grep(needle, haystack, ...) : 
#  invalid regular expression '(hh1)|(^(?!hh))', reason 'Invalid regexp'

#Works
select(test, str_subset(current_vars(), "(hh1)|(^(?!hh))"))

      <dbl> <dbl>
#1         1     1
#2         2     2
#3         3     3
```

title: case_when semantics
description:
Hello,

`case_when` is great. As I've been using it more and more, I have two minor requests for changes that I think would make it easier to use.

can `case_when` get fall-through for missing supplied values similar to `base::switch`?

example usage:
``` r
x <- letters[1:5]
case_when(
   x == "a" ~ "case a", 
   x == "b" ~ , 
   x == "c" ~ "case b or c", 
            ~ "all other cases")
```
would give
``` r
[1] "case a"    "case b or c"   "case b or c"   "all other cases"   "all other cases"
```
Essentially what I'm proposing is that `case_when` supplies a `TRUE` on the left hand side if the last argument has a missing left hand side, and for earlier arguments missing a right hand side, the logical vector(s) on the left hand side keep getting `reduce`'d with `|` until an argument with a supplied right-hand-side is encountered.

title: Unexpected lubridate interval behavior when filtering dataframe via dplyr
description:
**Background**
I posted this on [SO](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/47276296/unexpected-lubridate-interval-behavior-when-filtering-dataframe-via-dplyr) as well, since I'm not entirely certain this is a bug - perhaps just my ignorance. 

I am creating a `lubridate` interval vector using a dataset similar to that which is available in the following chunk: 

```r
    dat <- readr::read_rds(url("https://github.com/mienkoja/stack_stash/blob/master/dat.rds?raw=true"))
    
    dat_mod <- dplyr::mutate(dat, interval = lubridate::interval(lubridate::ymd(start_combo)
                                                                 ,lubridate::ymd(stop_combo)))
```
**Problem**

If I try to filter the object via `dplyr`, I get an unexpected interval returned: 

```r
    dplyr::filter(dat_mod, id == 7000)
    
    ## A tibble: 1 x 4
    #     id start_combo stop_combo                       interval
    #  <int>       <dbl>      <dbl>                 <S4: Interval>
    #1  7000    20170802   20170816 2016-10-11 UTC--2016-10-25 UTC
```

**My own investigation**

Every interval (viewed via `dplyr::filter`) appears to be the same length as the expected interval, but all anchored (incorrectly) to 2016-10-11 UTC.

I suspect this is a `dplyr::filter` bug as I can search by bracket notation and get the expected result. 

```r
    dat_mod[dat_mod$id == 7000, ]
    
    ## A tibble: 1 x 4
    #     id start_combo stop_combo                       interval
    #  <int>       <dbl>      <dbl>                 <S4: Interval>
    #1  7000    20170802   20170816 2017-08-02 UTC--2017-08-16 UTC
```
 
Also, this does not appear to be an artifact of what is getting displayed in the output. If I assign the filtered object to a new object, the incorrect interval is preserved: 
 
```r
    dat_mod2 <- filter(dat_mod, id == 7000)
    dat_mod2
    ## A tibble: 1 x 4
    #     id start_combo stop_combo                       interval
    #  <int>       <dbl>      <dbl>                 <S4: Interval>
    #1  7000    20170802   20170816 2016-10-11 UTC--2016-10-25 UTC
```

title: translate_sql, as.character in combination with %in%
description:
dbplyr
version 1.1.0

If I use %in% in combination with as.character, translate_sql generates SQL that is not valid for sqlite
```r
library(RSQLite)
library(dbplyr)
db = dbConnect(SQLite(), ':memory:')

translate_sql(booklet_id %in% as.character(1:4), con=db )
#> <SQL> "booklet_id" IN CAST((1, 2, 3, 4) AS TEXT)
```
In postgres and possibly other dbms this would be accepted but not in sqlite where it should be:

"booklet_id" IN( CAST(1 AS TEXT), CAST(2 AS TEXT), CAST(3 AS TEXT), CAST(4 AS TEXT))

(running it through partial_eval and translate_sql_ gives the exact same problem)

Thanks for the very nice package by the way!

title: dplyr::copy_to(overwrite = TRUE) causes PostgreSQL to issue a spurious warning
description:
dplyr::copy_to(overwrite = TRUE) causes PostgreSQL to issue a spurious warning.  When deep in larger scripts are procedures this has been causing users to question the correctness of results as they do not have enough context to know which "tables did not exist" and what effect that has had on a larger process.  In context it looks like an unconditional drop was issued, perhaps there is a conditional drop that will not trigger this issue?

Below is a `reprex` showing the effect (using the dev version of `reprex` to capture the message).
