title: feature request : add `merge` indicator after a merge in dplyr
description:
Hello there, 

Congrats for the great work here! I have a suggestion to make.

Is there a way to get the equivalent of a `_merge` indicator variable after a merge in `Dplyr`? 

Something similar to **Pandas'** `indicator = True` option that essentially tells you how the merge went (how many matches from each dataset, etc).

Here is an example in `Pandas`

```
import pandas as pd

df1 = pd.DataFrame({'key1' : ['a','b','c'], 'v1' : [1,2,3]})
df2 = pd.DataFrame({'key1' : ['a','b','d'], 'v2' : [4,5,6]})

match = df1.merge(df2, how = 'left', indicator = True)
```

Here, after a `left join` between `df1` and `df2`, you want to immediately know how many rows in `df1` found a match in `df2` and how many of them did not

```
match
Out[53]: 
  key1  v1   v2     _merge
0    a   1  4.0       both
1    b   2  5.0       both
2    c   3  NaN  left_only
```

and I can tabulate this `merge` variable: 

```
match._merge.value_counts()
Out[52]: 
both          2
left_only     1
right_only    0
Name: _merge, dtype: int64
```

I don't see any option available after a, say, left join in `Dplyr`

```
key1 = c('a','b','c')
v1 = c(1,2,3)
key2 = c('a','b','d')
v2 = c(4,5,6)
df1 = data.frame(key1,v1)
df2 = data.frame(key2,v2)

> left_join(df1,df2, by = c('key1' = 'key2'))
  key1 v1 v2
1    a  1  4
2    b  2  5
3    c  3 NA
```

Am I missing something here? 

Originally posted on SO http://stackoverflow.com/questions/40110644/dplyr-is-there-a-merge-indicator-available-after-a-merge. 

The solution provided by the user is nice, but I believe this should be be an option implemented directly in `dplyr` merge. Having control over how the match went is fundamental.

What do you think?
Thanks!

title: class of element in data_frame is dropped when subsetting with `[`
description:
## tl;dr

```
dat <- c("a", "b")

d.f <-        data.frame('dat' = dat, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
d_f <- dplyr::data_frame('dat' = dat)

# Fails: "Error: d.f[, 1] not equal to d_f[, 1]"
testthat::expect_equal(d.f[, 1], d_f[, 1])

# Passes
testthat::expect_equal(d.f$dat, d_f$dat)

# Problem with dropped class, when subsetting with '['
# class(d.f[, 1]): "character"
# class(d_f[, 1]): "tbl_df" "tbl" "data.frame"
```
## Long Version

I want to test the class of a column in a `data_frame`. If I subset with `[` the class of the column is dropped. So I can't test for class `character` (which I need to).

It seems as if this is related to [tibble #155](https://github.com/tidyverse/tibble/issues/155) and [dplyr #1984](https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/issues/1984).

To show this, I create a base `data.frame` and a dplyr `data_frame` with one column containing the two values `a` and `b`. If I subset the column with `[, 1]`, the classes are not the same. **But** if I subset with `$names` the classes are equal.

```
# create data
std <- data.frame('names' = c('a', 'b'), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
dpl <- data_frame('names' = c('a', 'b'))
```

If I subset with `std[, 1], dpl[, 1]` I get

```
Elements:
[1] "a" "b"
# A tibble: 2 × 1
  names
  <chr>
1     a
2     b

Class of elements:
[1] "character"
[1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
```

But if I subset with `std$names, dpl$names` the result is as expected

```
Elements:
[1] "a" "b"
[1] "a" "b"

Class of elements:
[1] "character"
[1] "character"
```

Here is the rather lengthy code to reproduce the example.

```
library(dplyr)
library(testthat)

# helper
helper <- function(x1, x2) {
    cat('\nElements:\n')
    print(x1)
    print(x2)
    cat('\nClass of elements:\n')
    print(class(x1))
    print(class(x2))
}

# create data
std <- data.frame('names' = c('a', 'b'), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
dpl <- data_frame('names' = c('a', 'b'))

cat('\nA: Subset with "["')
x1 <- std[, 1]
x2 <- dpl[, 1]
helper(x1, x2)

cat('\n\nB: Subset with "$"')
y1 <- std$names
y2 <- dpl$names
helper(y1, y2)

cat('\n\nC: Subset with "$" AND "["')
z1 <- std$names[1]
z2 <- dpl$names[1]
helper(z1, z2)

# And some tests
# '[' fails
expect_equal(x1, x2)
expect_equal(class(x1), class(x2))

# '$' works
expect_equal(y1, y2)
expect_equal(class(y1), class(y2))

# '$' and '[' works
expect_equal(z1, z2)
expect_equal(class(z1), class(z2))
```

title: Using reactive variable inside dplyr verb with pool on Shiny application
description:
I have some input and have reactive value bind to them update when user click an action button. I use dplyr with pool to retrieve data from an external database.

Below is my `working` code to update a reactive data frame:

```
  date_from <- eventReactive(input$btn_update, {
    return(format(input$date_time[1], "%Y-%m-%d"))
  })

  date_to <- eventReactive(input$btn_update, {
    return(format(input$date_time[2], "%Y-%m-%d"))
  })

  daily_active_users <- eventReactive(input$btn_update, {
    from <- date_from()
    to <- date_to()
    return(collect(
      src_pool(pool_instance) %>% tbl("daily_active_user") %>%
        filter(time >= from, time <= to) %>%
        arrange(time) %>%
        mutate(net_change = dau - lag(dau)) %>%
        mutate(net_change = if_else(is.na(net_change), 0, net_change))
    ))
  })
```

Since I have many reactive data frame depends on date_from, and date_to, I want to achieve something like below (to reduce code duplication):

```
  daily_active_users <- eventReactive(input$btn_update, {
    return(collect(
      src_pool(pool_instance) %>% tbl("daily_active_user") %>%
        filter(time >= date_from(), time <= date_to()) %>%
        arrange(time) %>%
        mutate(net_change = dau - lag(dau)) %>%
        mutate(net_change = if_else(is.na(net_change), 0, net_change))
    ))
  })
```

But when running, it raise the error like:

```
LINE 6: WHERE (("time" >= DATE_FROM()) AND ("time" <= DATE_TO()))) "...

HINT:  No function matches the given name and argument types. You might need to add explicit type casts.
```

I switch to use `filter_` but it raise other error: 

```
comparison (5) is possible only for atomic and list types
```

Is there any better practice for my case since I have many reactive data frame; thus I will have duplicated code for the part:

title: Replacement of table in remote src by copy_to function
description:
It would be really useful having support (e.g. an additional parameter) for the replacement of an existing table in a remote src when using the dply::copy_to function. Currently, execution stops when the corresponding table exists (dplyr::db_has_table check). Depending on the additional parameter, the table can be dropped (possibly using CASCADE) and re-created in the same transaction block. 

However, there's an issue with this procedure and concurrent sessions: When trying to access a large remote table (tested in PostgreSQL) while the table is re-created in another process, the operation is delayed (as expected) but finally results in an error:

ERROR:  could not open relation with OID 321732

While the table is deleted and re-created, other processes try to access the old OID, which doesn't exist any more when the first transaction is finished. 

I have tried to drop and re-create columns instead of dropping the entire table. However, in PostgreSQL, this results in references to dropped columns (e.g. ........pg.dropped.1........ when executing DBI::dbListFields) and the table returned by dplyr::tbl() contains additional rows filled with NAs (likely the rows from the old dropped columns).

Creating views on the original table (which is then dropped and re-created) results in the same problem with missing OIDs...

Is there a way to circumvent this issue with the old/new OID?

title: Summarise nth & order_by crashes R (on Windows)
description:
A combination of 'summarise', 'nth', and 'order_by' crashes R on Windows (but not Mac).

Make sample data

``` r
library(dplyr)

set.seed(42)

# Simulate data
# obs is the total number of observations
# ninds is the number of unique individuals
obs <- 25000
ninds <- 5000

# Simulate BP data
id <- sample(1:ninds,obs,replace=TRUE)
SBP <- as.integer(rnorm(obs, 120, 15))
DBP <- as.integer(rnorm(obs,90,10))

# Put all into a data frame, adding a value for the visit number
bppheno <- data_frame(id,SBP,DBP) %>% 
  group_by(id) %>% 
  mutate(visit=row_number())
```

The following statement crashes R 3.3.1 on Windows (but not Mac). [dplyr 0.5.0]

``` r
bppheno_characteristics <- bppheno %>%
  dplyr::group_by(id) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(N_BP=n(), FIRST_SBP_DPLYR=first(SBP, order_by=visit))
```

The following variant without the wrapper does not crash R (on Windows)

``` r
bppheno_characteristics <- bppheno %>%
  dplyr::group_by(id) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(N_BP=n(),FIRST_SBP_RAW=SBP[[order(visit)[1]]])
```

Also, the following variant (explicitly calling dplyr::first) does not crash R (on Windows)

``` r
bppheno_characteristics <- bppheno %>%
  dplyr::group_by(id) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(N_BP=n(), FIRST_SBP_DPLYR=dplyr::first(SBP, order_by=visit))
```

title: Error with joins when using numeric and integer ID columns with column attributes
description:
When I try to join on an integer column with a numeric column, if the joining columns have attributes added to them it gives an **incompatible types (integer / numeric)** error. 
Example:

```
require(dplyr)
df1 <- data.frame(V1 = c(1, 2, 3), V2 = letters[1:3])
df2 <- data.frame(V1 = 1:3, V3 = LETTERS[1:3])
full_join(df1, df2)
# (Runs correctly)
attr(df1$V1, "foo") <- "bar"
full_join(df1, df2)
# Joining, by = "V1"
# Error: Can't join on 'V1' x 'V1' because of incompatible types (integer / numeric)
```

Also note that plyr::join does not give an error in the same situation:  

```
require(plyr)
df1 <- data.frame(V1 = c(1, 2, 3), V2 = letters[1:3])
df2 <- data.frame(V1 = 1:3, V3 = LETTERS[1:3])
plyr::join(df1, df2)
# (Runs correctly)
attr(df1$V1, "foo") <- "bar"
plyr::join(df1, df2)
# (Runs correctly)
```

I use column attributes quite a lot so it would be good if this didn't give an error. I think this might be related to #228.

title: preserve order of original dataset when using group_by()?
description:
Feel free to let me know that this is _not_ a bug. I was just puzzled by the re-ordering of my grouped column. I specifically converted to `character` in my input df in order to not have to constantly re-order the columns for plotting in `ggplot2`. This isn't the original data, but here's a reproducible example:

```
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1)
dat <- data.frame(lett = rep(letters[3:1], each = 3), vals = rnorm(9, 5, 2))

## get rid of default factor application to character col
dat$lett <- as.character(dat$lett)

## get means by lett column
dat_means <- dat %>% group_by(lett) %>% summarise(ave = mean(vals))
dat_means
```

Result, even without factors:

```
# A tibble: 3 × 2
   lett      ave
  <chr>    <dbl>
1     a 6.201023
2     b 5.736213
3     c 4.147707
```

My actual data contains month names, so consider that `"c", "b", "a"` is already the correct monthly order. What I expected/hoped for was that the groups could be fed into `summarise()` as they appear in the data frame. Otherwise, to get it to play nicely with `ggplot2` I've just been going back to factors since I can easily specify an order. This:

```
lett_orders <- unique(dat$lett)

dat_means$lett <- factor(dat_means$lett, levels = lett_orders)

```

It would be nice not to re-specify the ordering I already have in the data source to the results of `dplyr`'s `group_by()` whenever I use it.

Is there a defacto way to not have to do this? Or what is the suggested route to get back to the ordering that appears in the original data set for, say, plotting discrete variables in the correct order?

title: Documentation problem and request re arrange & 0.5
description:
I am not quite sure of this, but it appears to me that the vignette has not kept up with all the changes made in version 0.5. In particular, the 0.5 documentation says that arrange ignores grouping, while the vignette says that arrange sorts first by group. I am guessing that you want the vignette to match the current version. There are other 0.5 changes you may or may not want to check -- I think the original version mentioned nearly all the helper verbs then in place, but I do not believe this is still true.

Also, a related **documentation** (not functional change) request: It seems clear that different people have different intuitions about how arrange should work. I am one of those whose intuitions match with the "arrange affects all the row-related verbs equally" rational. But this is not another request for change. I assume you have thought about these things more deeply than I, and have selected the current set of rules for reasons that are good and sufficient. However, as someone who has not followed the controversy blow by blow, I am not sure what those good and sufficient reasons are. So my request is, either in the vignette or in the manual, one or two sentences about the rationale for the current rule would make it easier for me to understand that rule, remember it, and use it effectively; and I think this may be true for many of those whose intuitions run that way.

title: Feature Request: swap_if(), conditional swapping of values between columns
description:
Made a mistake in a partial dataset of a very manual experiment (costly to redo) and realized I needed a conditional swap between two columns. 

I envision it looking something like this in practice. I wish I could figure out how to include it in a mutate(), but it requires returning two columns at once. 

``` r
dt %>%
    swap_if(., condition, Column1, Column2)
```

My attempt at implementation leaves a lot to be desired and is hacked entirely from if_else/replace_with in dplyr. 

``` r
library(tidyverse)

dt <- tibble(V1=c(1,2,4), V2=c("a","a","b"), V3=c(2,3,1))

swap_if<- function (condition, val1, val2, missing = NA) 
{
    if (!is.logical(condition)) {
        stop("`condition` must be logical", call. = FALSE)
    }
    out1 <- val1[rep(NA_integer_, length(condition))]
    out2 <- val2[rep(NA_integer_, length(condition))]

    out1[condition & !is.na(condition)] <- val2[condition & !is.na(condition)]
    out2[condition & !is.na(condition)] <- val1[condition & !is.na(condition)]

    out1[!condition & !is.na(condition)] <- val1[!condition & !is.na(condition)]
    out2[!condition & !is.na(condition)] <- val2[!condition & !is.na(condition)]

    tibble(out1, out2)
}

#swaps, but want to use in a mutate call
swap_if(dt$V2=="b", dt$V1, dt$V3)
```

title: Summarising verbs with variable-length outputs
description:
A new dplyr family of verbs for variable-length output may be useful.
- Like `summarise()` it would discard all input columns except for the grouping variables. This allows the output to have a different number of rows than the input.
- Unlike `summarise()`, it would not require length 1 results and would only check for equal length within group. Grouping columns would be recycled to these lengths.

It could be called `condense()`, though it's only condensing in the sense that it get rids of non-grouping variables. May need a better name.

Ungrouped data frame: check squared constraint

``` r
mtcars %>% condense(col = 1:5, other = 5:1)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 2
#>     col other
#>   <int> <int>
#> 1     1     5
#> 2     2     4
#> 3     3     3
#> 4     4     2
#> 5     5     1

mtcars %>% condense(col = 1:5, other = 2:1)
#> Error: results must have same length
```

This gives us immediately:

``` r
mtcars %>% condense_all(summary)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 11
#>           mpg         cyl        disp          hp        drat
#>   <S3: table> <S3: table> <S3: table> <S3: table> <S3: table>
#> 1        10.4        4.00        71.1        52.0        2.76
#> 2        15.4        4.00       121.0        96.5        3.08
#> 3        19.2        6.00       196.0       123.0        3.70
#> 4        20.1        6.19       231.0       147.0        3.60
#> 5        22.8        8.00       326.0       180.0        3.92
#> 6        33.9        8.00       472.0       335.0        4.93
#> # ... with 6 more variables: wt <S3: table>, qsec <S3: table>, vs <S3:
#> #   table>, am <S3: table>, gear <S3: table>, carb <S3: table>
```

For a grouped data frame, we'd check the square constrain within groups:

``` r
grouped <- mtcars %>% group_by(am)

grouped %>%
  condense(
    col = rep(mean(cyl), times = round(mean(cyl))),
    other = rep(length(col), length(col))
  )
#> # A tibble: 12 x 3
#>       am   col other
#>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1      0  6.95     7
#> 2      0  6.95     7
#> 3      0  6.95     7
#> 4      0  6.95     7
#> 5      0  6.95     7
#> 6      0  6.95     7
#> 7      0  6.95     7
#> 8      1  5.08     5
#> 9      1  5.08     5
#> 10     1  5.08     5
#> 11     1  5.08     5
#> 12     1  5.08     5

grouped %>%
  condense(
    col = rep(mean(cyl), times = round(mean(cyl))),
    other = rep(length(col), length(col) - 1)
  )
#> Error: results must have same length within groups
```

Relevant discussion: hadley/dplyr#154

```
x = rbind(x, data.frame(flag = 2, uin = 2, val = 3)) 
```

This is what x looks like:

```
  flag uin val
1    1   1   2
2    2   2   3
```

I want to sum up the `val` and the `val` with `flag == 2`, so I write 

```
x %>% summarize(val = sum(val), val.2 = sum(val[flag == 2]))
```

and the result is 

```
   val val.2
1   5    NA
```

But what I expect is that `val.2` is 3 instead of `NA`.

For more information, if I calculate the conditional summation first then the total summation, it comes out with the correct answer:

```
x %>% summarize(val.2 = sum(val[flag == 2]), val = sum(val))
  val.2 val
1     3   5
```

Moerover, if I only calculate the conditional summation, it works fine too:

```
x %>% summarize(val.2 = sum(val[flag == 2]))
  val.2
1     3
```

title: Bug in conditional assignment using ifelse within mutate
description:
I am baffled by this bug. Here's some example code:

```
set.seed(1000)

df <- data.frame(Day = 1:100, 
                 Equity = rbinom(100, 1, 0.5), 
                 Bond = rbinom(100, 1, 0.5), 
                 Gold = rbinom(100, 1, 0.5))
str(df)

# Method 1: Incorrect calculation of weights
dfWeights <- df %>% 
                mutate(Total = (Equity + Bond + Gold)) %>% 
                mutate(EquityWeight = ifelse(isTRUE(all.equal(Total, 0)), 0, Equity/Total),
                       BondWeight = ifelse(isTRUE(all.equal(Total, 0)), 0, Bond/Total),
                       GoldWeight = ifelse(isTRUE(all.equal(Total, 0)), 0, Gold/Total))
dfWeights %>% filter(Total == 3)

# Method 2: Incorrect calculation of weights
dfWeights <- df %>% 
                mutate(Total = (Equity + Bond + Gold)) %>% 
                mutate(EquityWeight = ifelse(identical(Total, 0L), 0, Equity/Total),
                       BondWeight = ifelse(identical(Total, 0L), 0, Bond/Total),
                       GoldWeight = ifelse(identical(Total, 0L), 0, Gold/Total))
dfWeights %>% filter(Total == 3)

# Method 3: Correct calculations
dfWeights <- df %>% 
                mutate(Total = (Equity + Bond + Gold)) %>% 
                mutate(EquityWeight = ifelse(Total == 0, 0, Equity/Total),
                       BondWeight = ifelse(Total == 0, 0, Bond/Total),
                       GoldWeight = ifelse(Total == 0, 0, Gold/Total))
dfWeights %>% filter(Total == 3)

```

I wish to avoid using Method 3 because Total could be a floating point number in real world. But calculations from both methods 1 & 2 are incorrect even though upon checking individual cases, they are correct.

title: arrange column values after group_by (bug?)
description:
I had an interview today, and they asked me a very simple question:

> _A data frame with three columns (id, class_id, score), class_id is a factor with three levels (1, 2, 3), want to find out top 5 scores of each class_id._

I thought this is easy, I can do it in dplyr! But when I actually did it, what I get is different from what I expected.

Here is a simple simulation:

```
set.seed(123)
score <- data.frame(id = 1:900, class_id = rep(c(1, 2, 3), 300),
                    score = rnorm(900, mean = 60, sd = 15))
```

My first thought was using `top_n`:

```
library(dplyr)
score %>%
        group_by(class_id) %>%
        top_n(5, score)
```

It actually gives me the correct result, it's just the scores are not ordered in a very nice way, so I'm thinking it would be nice if I sort the scores in desc order within each group, but that's where I got confused.

```
score %>%
        group_by(class_id) %>%
        top_n(5, score) %>%
        arrange(desc(score))
```

By doing so, the result is totally different, it seems like the whole data frame is sorted by the score column in desc order, and it completely ignores the group_by and top_n clause.

This is different from what I remembered before, so I googled it, and l found #491 here, it seems that this issue should've been solved about two years ago...

So I tried a different way to get what I want, and a very strange thing happened (well, at least it is strange to me...).

If I do this:

```
score %>%
        group_by(class_id) %>%
        arrange(desc(score))
```

It won't arrange score in desc order within each class_id group, instead the whole data frame was sorted by the score column in desc order.

But if I take one step further, it will actually give me the perfect result I wanted:

```
score %>%
        group_by(class_id) %>%
        arrange(desc(score)) %>%
        slice(1:5)
```

Isn't this weird? I'm using dplyr version 0.5.0

description:
This is weird one (at least it seems to me).  I've reproduced this in a few different contexts, but `mtcars` suffices.  I'll print out a couple rows because it helps to see the problem.

Nothing surprising there.  But using `mutate_if` with a minus sign in `funs()`, and referencing a column in the middle of the tibble, updates the tibble to the left, but not the right of the referenced column.

title: wrong result when trying to join by columns with different character encoding
description:
It seems that, when joining data.frames (or tibbles),
the comparison of key columns should previously convert the character strings to a common encoding:

``` r
    df1 <- data_frame(tipo  = c("Física", "Psíquica", "Sensorial"),
                         n_Ben = c(13, 5, 3))
    df2 <- df1

    df1$tipo <- iconv(df2$tipo, to="UTF-8")
    Encoding(df1$tipo)
    # [1] "UTF-8"   "UTF-8"   "unknown"
    Encoding(df2$tipo)
    # [1] "latin1"  "latin1"  "unknown"
    all.equal(df1$tipo, df2$tipo)
    # [1] TRUE

    merge(df1, df2)
    #        tipo n_Ben
    #1    Física    13
    #2  Psíquica     5
    #3 Sensorial     3
```

But `inner_join` gives a wrong result:

``` r
    inner_join(df1, df2)
    # Joining, by = c("tipo", "n_Ben")
    # # A tibble: 1 × 2
    #        tipo n_Ben
    #       <chr> <dbl>
    #1 Sensorial     3
```

If we convert implicitly the columns to UTF-8 before the join operation, the result is correct.
For example:

``` r
    inner_join(df1 %>%
                 mutate_if(is.character, str_trim),
               df2 %>%
                 mutate_if(is.character, str_trim))
    # Joining, by = c("tipo", "n_Ben")
    # # A tibble: 3 × 2
    #        tipo n_Ben
    #       <chr> <dbl>
    #1    Física    13
    #2  Psíquica     5
    #3 Sensorial     3
```

The error happens on Windows (where the default encoding is "latin1"):

title: Disconnector/finalizer for SQLite connections
description:
Why is there no `disco` specified for sqlite connections?

As defined [here](https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/blob/master/R/src-sqlite.r#L106), `src_sqlite` returns:

``` r
src_sql("sqlite", con, path = path)
```

while [here](https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/blob/master/R/src-mysql.r#L105), `src_mysql` returns:

``` r
src_sql("mysql", con,
    info = info, disco = db_disconnector(con, "mysql"))
```

and similarly [here](https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/blob/master/R/src-postgres.r#L109), `src_postgres` returns:

``` r
src_sql("postgres", con,
    info = info, disco = db_disconnector(con, "postgres"))
```

(I also don't know why there is no `info` param to `src_sqlite`, but that is not as important to me as having a finalizer for all db connections.)

The `db_disconnector` function only requires that the underlying driver be DBI-compliant (in this case, has an implementation for `dbDisconnect`). From [here](https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/blob/master/R/dbi-s3.r#L270):

``` r
db_disconnector <- function(con, name, quiet = FALSE) {
  reg.finalizer(environment(), function(...) {
    if (!quiet) {
      message("Auto-disconnecting ", name, " connection ",
        "(", paste(con@Id, collapse = ", "), ")")
    }
    dbDisconnect(con)
  })
  environment()
}
```

This is clearly true for `RSQLite`. So is there another reason that these type of connections are not disconnected/finalized?

title: Misleading results when using identical() within mutate()
description:
I'm guessing it has something to do with the way vectorization works within `mutate` and there's probably a reason for the way it's implemented, but IMO this can lead to pretty/dangerous results.

Consider the following example:

`dat <- data.frame(x = 1:4, y = c(1, 2, 10, NA))`

I'd like to check if `y` differs from `x`:

```
mutate(dat, diff = x != y)
# x  y  diff
#1 1  1 FALSE
#2 2  2 FALSE
#3 3 10  TRUE
#4 4 NA    NA
```

Has "problems" with `NA`, so I turned to `identical`:

```
mutate(dat, diff = !identical(x, y))
# x  y diff
#1 1  1 TRUE
#2 2  2 TRUE
#3 3 10 TRUE
#4 4 NA TRUE
```

Hm, that's kinda strange >> investigated and found out it had to do with diverging data types:

```
class(dat$x)
# [1] "integer"
class(dat$y)
# [1] "numeric"
```

So let's take care of aligning that:

```
dat$x <- as.numeric(dat$x)
dat$y <- as.numeric(dat$y)
```

Now, I would intuitively think that `mutate` would give me the same result as this:

```
sapply(1:nrow(dat), function(ii) {
  !identical(dat[ii, "x"], dat[ii, "y"])
})
# [1]  FALSE FALSE TRUE TRUE
```

But it still gives me this:

```
mutate(dat, diff = !identical(x, y))
# x  y diff
#1 1  1 TRUE
#2 2  2 TRUE
#3 3 10 TRUE
#4 4 NA TRUE
```

while I'd expect this 

```
# x  y diff
#1 1  1 FALSE
#2 2  2 FALSE
#3 3 10 TRUE
#4 4 NA TRUE
```

Wouldn't you aggree that this is at best misleading/dangerous if not even completely undesired?

title: (Potential) Bug with date time operations
description:
Hello,

I ran into an unexpected outcome today. It looks like what should be a 'time' column is coerced into a 'date' class based on the return type of the first row.

Minimal reproducible example.

``` r
x <- data.frame(date = seq(ymd(20160725), ymd(20160801), "1 day")) %>% mutate(hour = row_number() - 1)

# This returns date_time as class date
x %>% mutate(date_time = date + dhours(hour))
```

This returns the following ...

``` r
        date hour  date_time
1 2016-07-25    0 2016-07-25
2 2016-07-26    1 2016-07-26
3 2016-07-27    2 2016-07-27
4 2016-07-28    3 2016-07-28
5 2016-07-29    4 2016-07-29
6 2016-07-30    5 2016-07-30
7 2016-07-31    6 2016-07-31
8 2016-08-01    7 2016-08-01
```

The following returns the desired outcome

``` r
# This returns date_time as class time
x %>% arrange(hour %>% desc) %>% mutate(date_time = date + dhours(hour))
```

``` r
        date hour           date_time
1 2016-08-01    7 2016-08-01 07:00:00
2 2016-07-31    6 2016-07-31 06:00:00
3 2016-07-30    5 2016-07-30 05:00:00
4 2016-07-29    4 2016-07-29 04:00:00
5 2016-07-28    3 2016-07-28 03:00:00
6 2016-07-27    2 2016-07-27 02:00:00
7 2016-07-26    1 2016-07-26 01:00:00
8 2016-07-25    0 2016-07-25 00:00:00
```

And here is a second work around

``` r
# Second workaround
x %>% mutate(date_time = as.POSIXct(date) + dhours(hour))
```

While I can definitely see how and why this would happen, the difference in class return was unexpected. Wanted to report in case this behavior is undesired.

Thank you,
-Chris

title: tbl_sql: Can't dynamically mutate variable
description:
Example:

``` r
pg <- src_postgres(...)
tbls <- list()
for(y in 2000:2010) {
    tbls[[paste(y)]] <- tbl(pg, paste0("data_", y))) %>% mutate(year=y)
}
tbls <- lapply(tbls, collect)

tbls
$`2000`
Source:   query [?? x 2]
Database: postgres 9.4.5 [***]
   id  year
<int> <dbl>
    1  2010
    2  2010
...
$`2001`
Source:   query [?? x 2]
Database: postgres 9.4.5 [***]
   id  year
<int> <dbl>
    1  2010
    2  2010
...
```

As of `dplyr 0.5` year is always set to `2010` (last iteration of for loop), before (`0.4.3`) y was correctly resolved for each list object (`2000, 2001, ..., 2010`). 

It seems that `collect()` now uses `y` from the global environment to form the sql query when executed instead of `mutate()` replacing it with the value during the loop.

title: "bind_rows" does not discard names from null values
description:
When given a list containing `NULL`s and `data.frame`s, bind_rows will keep the names of the `NULL`-valued entries in the list, and silently drop names from the end of the list.

Quick example, tested using R 3.1.1 and dplyr 0.5.0. This results in `virginica` entries incorrectly being labelled as `versicolor` by bind_rows.

``` r
library(dplyr)
data(iris)

iris_list = iris %>% group_by(Species) %>% sample_n(3) %>% split(.$Species)
iris_list["versicolor"] = list(NULL)
bind_rows(iris_list, .id="bind_rows_id")
```

I came across this bug using `purrr::map` with a function which returned either a data.frame or NULL. This behaviour appears to be new since 0.4.x

title: [SQL] Backends without intrinsic support for logical columns
description:
mutate() to a constant TRUE or FALSE currently breaks with hard-to-identify errors. In SQLite:

``` r
> memdb_frame(a = 1) %>% mutate(b = TRUE) %>% sql_render()
<SQL> SELECT `a`, TRUE AS `b`
FROM `vcdulhlkre`
> memdb_frame(a = 1) %>% mutate(b = TRUE)
Source:   query [?? x 2]
Database: sqlite 3.11.1 [:memory:]

Error: no such column: TRUE
```

I think this can be fixed in `escape.logical()`, the information how to treat logical constants can be encoded in the `sql_variant()`, perhaps with a "special" function similarly to `__dplyr_colwise_fun`.

Surprisingly, logical expressions are auto-coerced to numbers with SQLite:

``` r
> memdb_frame(a=1) %>% mutate(b = 2 == 2)
Source:   query [?? x 2]
Database: sqlite 3.11.1 [:memory:]

      a     b
  <dbl> <int>
1     1     1
```

From my experience this also affects SQL Server,  CC @imanuelcostigan.

title: Using %in% with databases fails when there is only one element on the rhs of %in%
description:
The MWE is as follows: 

``` r
library(dplyr)

src <- lahman_sqlite()

# playerIDs is a vector, this works
playerIDs <- c("bemisha01", "bendech01")
tbl(src, "Batting") %>% 
  filter(playerID %in% playerIDs) %>% 
  explain()
# <SQL>
#   SELECT *
#   FROM `Batting`
# WHERE (`playerID` IN ('bemisha01', 'bendech01'))

# playerIDs is a scalar, it does not
playerIDs <- "bemisha01"
tbl(src, "Batting") %>% 
  filter(playerID %in% playerIDs) %>% 
  explain()
# <SQL>
#   SELECT *
#   FROM `Batting`
# WHERE (`playerID` IN 'bemisha01')
```

According to [this code](https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/blob/d2a34e7112fe479d2ba3d8aef16735407eb751a1/R/translate-sql.r#L204-L206) `%in%` is transformed into the SQL `IN` operator regardless of the size of the elements on the right hand side of the %in% operator. 

This is a problem when working programmatically when the length of `playerIDs` may vary.

I did a little research, and my test showed that the process "hangs" at `vars <- db_query_fields(src$con, x)`, in `op_base_remote()`. It seems like `db_query_fields` request the whole table in my case.

It works as I expected if I replace `db_query_fields(src$con, x)` by `db_query_fields(src$con, build_sql(x, " limit 1"))`

An interest finding is that `db_query_fields.DBIConnection()` works well if I run it step-by-step, like

``` r
conn <- MonetDBLite::src_monetdb("db_name")
con <- conn$con
sql <- sql("select * from \"target_table\"")

# mimic the flow in db_query_fields()
sql_select(con, sql("*"), sql_subquery(con, sql), where = sql("0 = 1")) %>% 
  DBI::dbSendQuery(conn = con) %>% 
  DBI::dbFetch(0)

# output like this in my console
#  [1] col1  col2  col3 ...
# <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
```

Update:
I ran the same on Windows today. No issue.

title: when adverb
description:
Conditional `when` which translate to: "when this is true, do that, otherwise leave input unchanged". E.g.:

``` R
mtcars %>% when(., minify, . %>% sample_n(10) %>% select(-cyl) %>% mutate(mpg = mpg + 10))
```

If `minify` is TRUE, we get a sample of 10 cars and fuel economy magically increases.
If `minify` is FALSE, we get the original `mtcars`. 

Here is my definition, which uses NSE and exploits the `%>%` operator.

``` R
when <- function(.data, .predicate, .chain) {
  if( .predicate ) {
    .data %>% substitute(.chain)
  } else { .data }
}
```

Or, for example, to convert an arbitrary object to a tibble

``` R
tibblfy <- function(.data, var="rowname") {
  when( .data, !is.tibble(.data), . %>%  rownames_to_column(var) ) %>% as_tibble
}
```

``` R
mtcars %>% tibblfy("Car Name") %>% tibblfy("Car Name")
```

This doesn't fail because of the condition check.


title: USING clause in SQL variants
description:
I believe this is related to the root cause of #2022 #1997.

Per http://troels.arvin.dk/db/rdbms/ the `USING` clause is available in:

| Database | USING |
| --- | --- |
| PostgreSQL | yes |
| DB2 | no |
| MSSQL | no |
| MySQL | yes |
| Oracle | yes |
| Informix | no |

These days I spend most days in Hive and Spark and they also do not support `USING`.

The method `sql_join.default` contains `USING`. In libraries that relied on `dplyr v0.4` the workaround I saw was to use `dplyr::auto_names` to extract the column names and then construct the variable list to keep as the column names of `x` and `y` minus the join keys of `y`.  I cannot seem to find a way of querying the column names anymore within a custom `DBI` `sql_join` method.  Is there any new functionality in `dplyr` that can be used to fix joins for the other SQL variants?

In order to get around this I wrapped the left and right sub queries with a table alias and then explicitly referenced the fully qualified column names in the join result set.  I was able to do this in the sql_join() function of the connection subclass where x and y were references to an object that contained the unformatted SQL query components including the list of column names (eg: auto_names(x$select)).

The internals of this seems to have changed quite a lot between dplyr 0.4.3 and up, so I can no longer do this.  Is there any other way that  I can influence the qualification of join result set columns without ending up doing something crude like parsing the SQL of the subqueries to find what columns they generate etc?

In the first I'm calculating the cdf of some values using ecdf. This works fine until I try to subtract 1. In the second example, I'm trying to pass variables into a wilcox.test and getting the same error. Both problems are fixed if I write a wrapper function first. Is this a known issue? Is there something that predicts this behavior?

``` r
#dplyr 0.5.0
library(dplyr)

test_data = data.frame(
  grp = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 4),
  y = rnorm(8), stringsAsFactors = F
)

#this works
test_data %>% group_by(grp) %>%
  mutate(
    cdf = ecdf(y)(y)
  )

test_data %>% group_by(grp) %>%
  mutate(
    mean_y = mean(y) - 1
  )

#this throws an error:  Error: object 'y' not found 
test_data %>% group_by(grp) %>%
  mutate(
    surv = 1 - ecdf(y)(y) 
  )

#but this works

# example with wilcox.test

test_data2 = data.frame(
  grp = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 4),
  grp2 = rep(c("C", "D"), 4),
  y = rnorm(8), stringsAsFactors = F
)

test_data2 %>% group_by(grp) %>%
  mutate(
    p_value = 1 - wilcox.test(y)$p.value
  )

# Error: object 'y' not found 
test_data2 %>% group_by(grp) %>%
  mutate(
    p_value = wilcox.test(y ~ grp2)$p.value
  )

wilcox_fun = function(outcome, group) wilcox.test(outcome ~ factor(group))$p.value
```

title: Inconsistent handling of compound assignment pipe operator

title: Problems in handling encodings on Windows
description:
Hi, this would be related to #866 and #1555, but seems to be somewhat different.
### Example

Basically encodings are shown as "unknown" on Windows with Japanese locale. For example:

```
> x <- transform(iris, test = Sepal.Length + 10, テスト = Petal.Width * 10)
> Encoding(names(x)) # All "unknown"
[1] "unknown" "unknown" "unknown" "unknown" "unknown" "unknown" "unknown"
```

However if we use `mutate` to create new variables, non-English column names are in UTF-8:

```
> x.dp <- iris %>% mutate(test = Sepal.Length + 10, テスト = Petal.Width * 10)
> Encoding(names(x.dp)) # Non-english column is now in UTF
[1] "unknown" "unknown" "unknown" "unknown" "unknown" "unknown" "UTF-8"  
```

It does not happen if we make the same variable by `data_frame`:

```
> data_frame(test = 1:3, テスト = 1:3) %>% names %>% Encoding
[1] "unknown" "unknown"
```

`select` can handle UTF-8 variables:

```
> select(x.dp, テスト) %>% head(3)
  テスト
1      2
2      2
3      2
```

However `group_by` fails:

```
> x.dp %>% group_by(テスト) %>% head(3)
Error: unknown column 'テスト' 
```

The data made by `transform` has no problem on this:

```
> x    %>% group_by(テスト) %>% head(3)
Source: local data frame [3 x 7]
Groups: テスト [1]

  Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species  test テスト
         <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl>  <fctr> <dbl>  <dbl>
1          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2  setosa  15.1      2
2          4.9         3.0          1.4         0.2  setosa  14.9      2
3          4.7         3.2          1.3         0.2  setosa  14.7      2
```
### Problem

At first I thought that this is a problem in `group_by` function, but the fundamental problem seems to be that the column names created by `mutate`  are in UTF-8 encoding.


title: Suggestion: interjection function(s)
description:
Admittedly this is simple enough to just write and source every time it's wanted, but perhaps there's some more sophistication to add to it. Also, apologies if this already exists and I simply failed to find it.

I'd be interested in a simple function, mainly for interactive use, that is able to print a message in the middle of a chain. This would take data as an input as normal, print a `message` to the console, then output the data unmodified to the rest of the chain. A nearly trivial version might be 

```
say <- function(.data, .message) {
  message(.message)
  return(.data)
}
```

which I would use as:

```
mtcars %>% 
   group_by(cyl) %>% 
   say("caution, grouped data!") %>% 
   summarise(abc = mean(mpg))

caution, grouped data!
#> Source: local data frame [3 x 2]
#> 
#>     cyl      abc
#>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1     4 26.66364
#> 2     6 19.74286
#> 3     8 15.10000
```

or involving the data somehow:

```
mtcars %>% 
   group_by(cyl) %>% 
   say(paste(nrow(.), "data points")) %>% 
   summarise(abc = mean(mpg))

32 data points
#> Source: local data frame [3 x 2]
#> 
#>     cyl      abc
#>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1     4 26.66364
#> 2     6 19.74286
#> 3     8 15.10000
```

"`interject`" seems like a more appropriate name but it's not as simple as "`say`". "`interrupt`" would have been nice if it weren't for the other meaning within R.

An improvement on this would allow interjecting with an interstitial cut of the data within the chain, such as

```
peek <- function(.data, .message, .expr, ...) {
  message(.message)
  print(do.call(.expr, list(.data, ...)))
  return(.data)
}
```

(no doubt this requires some `lazyeval` treatment of `...` but that's above my pay grade). This would play out as

```
mtcars %>%
  peek("checkpoint 1", head, n=10) %>%
  filter(cyl < 6) %>%
  peek("checkpoint 2", head, n=3) %>%
  summarise(meanMPG = mean(mpg))

checkpoint 1
#>                    mpg cyl  disp  hp drat    wt  qsec vs am gear carb
#> Mazda RX4         21.0   6 160.0 110 3.90 2.620 16.46  0  1    4    4
#> Mazda RX4 Wag     21.0   6 160.0 110 3.90 2.875 17.02  0  1    4    4
#> Datsun 710        22.8   4 108.0  93 3.85 2.320 18.61  1  1    4    1
#> Hornet 4 Drive    21.4   6 258.0 110 3.08 3.215 19.44  1  0    3    1
#> Hornet Sportabout 18.7   8 360.0 175 3.15 3.440 17.02  0  0    3    2
#> Valiant           18.1   6 225.0 105 2.76 3.460 20.22  1  0    3    1
#> Duster 360        14.3   8 360.0 245 3.21 3.570 15.84  0  0    3    4
#> Merc 240D         24.4   4 146.7  62 3.69 3.190 20.00  1  0    4    2
#> Merc 230          22.8   4 140.8  95 3.92 3.150 22.90  1  0    4    2
#> Merc 280          19.2   6 167.6 123 3.92 3.440 18.30  1  0    4    4
checkpoint 2
#>    mpg cyl  disp hp drat   wt  qsec vs am gear carb
#> 1 22.8   4 108.0 93 3.85 2.32 18.61  1  1    4    1
#> 2 24.4   4 146.7 62 3.69 3.19 20.00  1  0    4    2
#> 3 22.8   4 140.8 95 3.92 3.15 22.90  1  0    4    2
#>    meanMPG
#> 1 26.66364
```

The advantage of this would be the ability to see what's happening in the middle of a chain without having to comment out various parts. This could also be useful for inspecting where a chain is up to for lengthy processing. When it's time to clean up the code, it's as simple as commenting out the `say`/`peek` lines.

I haven't added any considerations for edge-cases such as missing arguments, etc... as it's just a spur-of-the-moment thought.

title: Error with non-ASCII characters in column names with `summarise_each`
description:
When using a non-ASCII character and a non-valid character (space, parenthesis, etc.) in a column name and `check.names=TRUE`, the non-ASCII character is not replaced, the non-valid one is replaced and summarise_each is lost. Examples:

``` r
library(dplyr)
x <- 1:10

d <- data.frame(foo=x, `foo º`=x)
summarise_each(d, funs=funs(mean(., na.rm=T)))
# NO

d <- data.frame(foo=x, `foo é`=x)
summarise_each(d, funs=funs(mean(., na.rm=T)))
# NO

d <- data.frame(foo=x, `foo º`=x, check.names=F)
summarise_each(d, funs=funs(mean(., na.rm=T)))
# OK

d <- data.frame(foo=x, `foo é`=x, check.names=F)
summarise_each(d, funs=funs(mean(., na.rm=T)))
# OK

d <- data.frame(foo=x, `fooé`=x)
summarise_each(d, funs=funs(mean(., na.rm=T)))
# OK

d <- data.frame(foo=x, `foo `=x)
summarise_each(d, funs=funs(mean(., na.rm=T)))
# OK

d <- data.frame(foo=x, `foo )`=x)
summarise_each(d, funs=funs(mean(., na.rm=T)))
# OK
```

```
    ) "jttsguvcce"
    ORDER BY "n" DESC
) "tnsoliurid" ;
```

The inside subquery ("tnsoliurid") returns an ordered table but the `select * from` lost order on Netezza (not with Postgresql) because it has no ORDER BY clause.

Before 0.5.0, query was :

```
SELECT "EVT", "n" FROM 
  (SELECT "EVT", count(*)::integer AS "n" FROM "DQ_AUD" GROUP BY "EVT") AS "zzz1" 
ORDER BY "n"
```

title: *_if .predicate function semantics
description:
I've been checking out the 0.5.0 updates (which are awesome) and noticed an incongruity in the "Summarise and mutate multiple columns" family. While `funs()` has long allowed abbreviated anonymous functions with `.` to `.funs`, e.g.

``` r
mtcars %>% summarise_each(funs(mean(.) < 4))
#     mpg   cyl  disp    hp drat   wt  qsec   vs   am gear carb
#1 FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE
```

and now `vars()` enables a parallel process, where `.predicate` is used (`summarise_if`, `mutate_if`, `select_if`), it is very much limited to either a function name, as in the docs:

``` r
by_species <- iris %>% group_by(Species)
by_species %>% summarise_if(is.numeric, mean)
# Source: local data frame [3 x 5]
#
#      Species Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width
#       <fctr>        <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl>
#1     setosa        5.006       3.428        1.462       0.246
#2 versicolor        5.936       2.770        4.260       1.326
#3  virginica        6.588       2.974        5.552       2.026
```

or a full-on anonymous (or saved) function:

``` r
mtcars %>% summarise_if(function(x){mean(x) < 4}, mean)
#       drat      wt     vs      am   gear   carb
#1 3.596563 3.21725 0.4375 0.40625 3.6875 2.8125
```

which leaves `.predicate` taking a more limited set of function notations than `.funs`, which seems arbitrary and somewhat limiting. Thus, is possible to add a predicate-specific helper parallel to `funs()` and `vars()` allowing `.` notation like `funs()`, enabling something like:

``` r
mtcars %>% summarise_if(ifs(mean(.) < 4), mean)
```

(I suppose `preds()` would be more parallel than `ifs()`, but it just sounds scary.) Or is this pointless, because everything eventually going to move to `purrr`'s `~.x` style notation anyway?

title: na_if: Support multiple values that are replaced with NA
description:
The additions in 0.5 are great!! A lot of dataset contain multiple missing codes for a single variable though and I think it would be much more useful if the user could pass multiple values to `na_if`. For example, `1:10 %>% na_if(2, 4)` or even `1:10 %>% na_if(1:5, 10)` would both be useful. Maybe it's not desired because `na_if` is supposed to work like `NULL_IF` but I do think it's much more useful. So I propose modifying  `na_if` or adding a function `na_codes` that supports multiple values. Of course, `na_if(1:5, 5:1)` would lead to different results. If this is desired, I could submit a pull request.

Here are two example implementations:
#### Version 1 with support for vectors

```
na_codes <- function(x, ...) {
    x[x %in% c(...)] <- NA
    x
}
1:10 %>% na_codes(1:5, 10)
letters %>% na_codes("a", "b", c("z", "y"))
```
#### Version 2 without support for vectors

```
na_codes2 <- function(x, ...) {
    for(y in list(...))
        x[x == y] <- NA
    x
}
1:10 %>% na_codes(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10)
letters %>% na_codes("a", "b", "z", "y")
```
#### Performance comparison

Version 1 is slower but also supports vector arguments. Version 2 is as fast as `dplyr::na_if` with support for multiple arguments.

```
library("rbenchmark")
x <- rbinom(1e6, size = 1, prob = 0.5)
benchmark(dplyr::na_if(x, 1), na_codes(x, 1), na_codes2(x, 1))
#                test replications elapsed relative user.self sys.self user.child sys.child
#1 dplyr::na_if(x, 1)          100   2.870    1.000     2.138    0.468          0         0
#2     na_codes(x, 1)          100   4.895    1.706     4.150    0.518          0         0
#3    na_codes2(x, 1)          100   3.098    1.079     2.318    0.481          0         0
```

title: Lead/lag inside dplyr mutate results in inexplicable error when using functions to create default
description:
The default value in dplyr's lead and lag works fine when a constant as coded for it, but returns an error message saying it expects a single value if I try to use a function or select the first element of a different field in the data frame. Here is the code I am using:

```
library(dplyr)

# Create simple data frame to illustrate the problem
argh <- data.frame(
  tourID = c("123", "123", "123", "456", "456"),
  tour_start = c(8.16, 8.16, 8.16, 10.1, 10.1),
  travel_time = c(12.8, 29.5, 37.7, 45.8, 51.7),
  stop_duration = c(44.2, 12.3, 0, 212.3, 0)
)

# Try to use R evaluation of function to get default for lag(depart)
eh <- group_by(argh, tourID) %>%
  mutate(depart = 0, arrive = lag(depart, default = min(tour_start)))

# Try to use first() instead
eh <- group_by(argh, tourID) %>%
  mutate(depart = 0, arrive = lag(depart, default = first(tour_start)))
```

Note that the intent here is to use the value of tour_start specific to each tourID as the default value for lag(depart), which is defined in the mutate statement. However, using either min(tour_start) or first(tour_start) for the default value results in:

```
Error: expecting a single value
```

Both min() and first() unambiguously return a single value. Thus, there is a bug in dplyr, or the documentation and error message should be updated to state that you can only use constants for default values. The latter would be tragic if true, for it would greatly reduce the utility of dplyr. So I'm hoping that neither is applicable, and that I'm simply doing something stupid. Any ideas on how to get this to work?

I'm using dplyr_0.4.3 running under R 3.2.4 on OS X El Capitan 10.11.5.

title: Encoding problems on Windows caused by character -> symbol -> character roundtrip
description:
Some of the encoding problems (e.g., grouping) seem to be caused by converting `character` to `symbol` and back. On Linux (UTF-8 locale):

```
> "ä" %>% Encoding
[1] "UTF-8"
> "ä" %>% as.name %>% as.character %>% Encoding
[1] "UTF-8"
> "ä" %>% iconv(to = "latin1") %>% as.name %>% as.character %>% Encoding
[1] "unknown"
> "ä" %>% iconv(to = "latin1") %>% as.name %>% as.character %>% enc2utf8
[1] "<e4>"
```

On Windows (latin-1 locale):

```
> "ä" %>% Encoding
[1] "latin1"
> "ä" %>% as.name %>% as.character %>% Encoding
[1] "latin1"
> "ä" %>% iconv(to = "UTF-8") %>% as.name %>% as.character %>% Encoding
[1] "unknown"
> "ä" %>% iconv(to = "UTF-8") %>% as.name %>% as.character %>% enc2utf8
[1] "Ã¤"
```

On Windows, [one test fails](https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/blob/e87f6dd7181b143dba2ad26d13ec1fb8bbd902d0/tests/testthat/test-group-by.r#L240-L245) because of that.

So, currently we should suggest using ASCII (or at least native-encoded) column names, and _not_ fiddle with the encoding, in particular not set it to UTF-8 on Windows.

A lot of internal dplyr logic seems to be based on the `symbol` type, I don't see a quick solution here.

title: recode suggestions
description:
In my experience, the current version of `recode` is a little bit inflexible and I figured I'd make some suggestions which I think could help improve it. If you agree (perhaps has to be @lionel-), I could eventually make a pull request if you'd like.
#### Why?

As an example, imagine that you'd like to convert a likert scale to NPS (group 1 = 0 to 6, group 2 = 7 to 8, group 3 = 9 to 10). Currently, this would be very tedious:

``` R
v <- 1:10
recode(v, `0` = "detractor", `1` = "detractor", `2` = "detractor",  `3` = "detractor", etc.
```
#### Reverse order of recodes

To make any of the following suggestions possible, one would have to switch the way new values and old values are specified. Currently it is `old_value = new_value`. Reversing this means that we could supply multiple `old_value`'s (or logical vectors as indicies) to recode to `new_value`. 
#### 1. Recode multiple values

With the above in place, users could specify multiple values to recode to the same `new_value`:

``` R
v <- 1:3
# We could write:
recode(v, low = 1:2, high = 3)
#> low low high

# Instead of:
recode(v, `1` = "low", `2` = "low", `3` = "high")
#> low low high
```
#### 2. Accept logical vectors

If `recode` accepted logical vectors (same length as `.x`), users could specify the subsets to be recoded directly, and we would be able to do the following:

``` R
v <- 1:3
recode(v, low = v <= 2, high = v == 3)
#> low low high
```
#### 3. Allow dot notiation

The above might be tedious if `v` had a really long name to begin with, so another suggestion might be to allow a `.`-notation as a reference to `.x` and replace it before evaluating the call. This would allow:

``` R
verylongname <- 1:3
recode(verylongname, low = . <= 2, high = . == 3)
#> low low high
```

To make this possible, the current version of recode would have to be renamed to `recode_` and then we'd need another implementation of `recode` which uses lazyeval. 
#### Thanks

I might have missed obvious ways to do the above, or perhaps some sort of limitation if `recode` is meant to work with all kinds of backends? If not, hopefully the suggestions make sense/can be of use.

-Kristian

title: Poor performance for group_by & do for larger n and incorrect progress bar
description:
In the current release of dplyr 0.4.3 when running the code below, the time to finish grows N(o^3). Also for larger n (loops), the progress bar is incorrect. It shows that it is done, but then just seems to hang at the end, until the call completes (which can be much later).

``` r
## Syntetic data example

f_do <- function(df) {
  data.frame(x2=sum(df$x2),stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}

loops <- seq(1e4,10e4,by=1e4)
time  <- vector(mode = 'numeric',length(loops))
for (i in 1:length(loops)) {
  dat <- data.frame(x1=1:loops[i],x2=floor(runif(loops[i],1,10)))
  t <- system.time(r <- group_by(dat,x1) %>% do(f_do(.)))
  time[i] <- t['elapsed']
}
ggplot2::qplot(loops,time)
ggplot2::qplot(loops,time^(1/3))
```

The progress bar indication seems to grow linearly with the number of loops (as it should), but the actual time to finish grows N(o^3). A number of loops goes up, the time it seems to hang after the progress bar is complete grows.

I can't seem to reproduce the problem in the current Development/Master version, so perhaps the problem is already addressed, but I could not find a matching issue.

title: In tally_ and count_, support programmatic specification of wt
description:
Passing the name(s) of variables (as character) "just works" in most underscored ("programmatic") dplyr functions. For example:

```
tally(group_by_(my_data, "foo"), wt = bar)
```

But, it looks like this has yet to be supported in `tally_` (and hence, also in `count_`).

Proposed: these should also work:

```
tally_(my_data, wt = "bar")
count_(my_data, vars = "foo", wt = "bar")
```

Happy to construct test cases, pull request, etc. but not sure if this might be intended behavior — or if/how it intersects with the intended behavior of `lazyeval::interp` (relied upon by `tally_`).

title: Use dbExecute for non-query SQL commands
description: `dbExecute()` is available in DBI > 0.4-2. This should be called rather than `dbGetQuery()` in methods that execute SQL commands that do not return result sets. E.g. in `db_create_index()`, `db_save_query()`, etc.

title: Export db_create_indexes
description: Backends that require implementations of copy_to need to be able to access db_create_indexes. As this is not currently exported, backends will need to take a copy of this into their own code base. This seems unnecessary as there is nothing backend specific about this (simple for loop wrapper of db_create_index)

title: Documentation needs to be cleaned up
description:
A few things in no particular order based on my use to updated my dplyr backend to SQL Server:
- There are references to non-existent functions like `sql_commit()` and like in documentation and vignettes. These should be cleaned up.
- The DBI "shim" docs should be improved in following respects: identify which are really thin wrappers around DBI methods; which are **not** shims around DBI methods (e.g. `db_create_index()`); and overlapping with previous points, whether or not they have default methods specified for new backends to use and if so, what SQL statements are necessary for these to run effectively.

I'll add to this list as I go along.

title: median() fails if it produces numeric and integer vectors
description:
This is a rather elusive one, which does unfortunately affect the current development version, dplyr_0.4.3.9001. I trust it is related to #1908.
## Repex:

**Problem demonstration**

This works (notice the values in the dataframe):

```
test <- data.frame(id = rep(1:4, each = 2),
                   value = as.integer(c(NA, NA, 2, 3, 3, 5, 21, 0)))

median.mutate <- test %>% 
                 group_by(id) %>% 
                 mutate(median = median(value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% 
                 print()
#>
Source: local data frame [8 x 3]
Groups: id [4]

    id value median
    <int> <int>  <dbl>
1     1    NA     NA
2     1    NA     NA
3     2     2    2.5
4     2     3    2.5
5     3     3    4.0
6     3     5    4.0
7     4    21   10.5
8     4     0   10.5
```

But `median.mutate` will fail with each of the following dataframes, in which the only change is the number/position of NAs. The error returned is:  
**`Error: incompatible types, expecting a numeric vector`**

```
test <- data.frame(id = rep(1:4, each = 2),  # one NA only
                   value = as.integer(c(NA, 6, 2, 3, 3, 5, 1, 1)))

test <- data.frame(id = rep(1:4, each = 2),  # original + 1 additional NA
                   value = as.integer(c(NA, NA, 2, 3, 3, 5, NA, 1)))

test <- data.frame(id = rep(1:4, each = 2),  # two NAs at random positions
                   value = as.integer(c(NA, 5, 2, 3, 3, 5, NA, 1)))

test <- data.frame(id = rep(1:4, each = 2),  # two NAs at the end
                   value = as.integer(c(4, 3, 2, 3, 3, 5, NA, NA)))

test <- data.frame(id = rep(1:4, each = 2),  # one NA in random position
                   value = as.integer(c(4, 3, 2, 3, NA, 5, 1, 3)))

test <- data.frame(id = rep(1:4, each = 2),  # random group filled with NAs
                   value = as.integer(c(4, 3, 2, 3, NA, NA, 1, 3)))
```

What's really perplexing is that using `do` instead works with all of them, and so does the same chain, if instead of `median` one uses `mean` (this is why I believe it's related to #1908)

```
# Work with all of the above
median.do <- test %>% 
             group_by(id) %>% 
             do(mutate(., median = median(value, na.rm = TRUE))) %>% 
             print()

# Using 'mean' instead of 'median' also works with all of the above
mean.mutate <- test %>% 
                 group_by(id) %>% 
                 mutate(mean = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% 
                 print()
```

Many thanks in advance for looking into this.

description:
Dear Hadley and contributors,

I've stumbled upon a problem whereby using `mutate` on a grouped dataframe in which there is a group containing `NA` values only results in erroneous calculation for **other groups** too. The behaviour certainly seems to be inconsistent with other functions in `dplyr`, and also base R. 

I believe the issues is related to #489 from 10 July 2014 and that it is a bug. Please see the details below and many thanks for your help in advance,

Peter

**Data**

```
test <- data.frame(id = rep(1:4, each = 2),
                            value = c(NA, NA, 2, 3, 3, 5, 21, 0))

id value

5  3     3
6  3     5
7  4    21
8  4     0
```

```
               group_by(id) %>%
```

**Alternatives, which do work**

Using `do`:

```
    Source: local data frame [8 x 3]
```

description:

title: summarise_all() column name fixed formatting option
description:
Currently, the format of the output column names produced by `summarise_all()` depends on the number of number of columns in the input, as well as the number of aggregation functions used (I belive the logic for this is located in the `colwise_()` function). This is good for interactive use, but it would be useful to have a way to fix the output format (preferably as input column name underscore aggregation function, e.g. `mpg_mean`) for non-interactive use where the number of columns/functions might vary.

Below are some examples of how the column names vary. Each example produces the `mean()` of `mpg`, but calls it something different depending on what other columns/functions are used.
1. If only one aggregation function is used, then the output column names are the same as the input column names:

``` r
mtcars %>% 
  summarise_all(funs_('mean'))
#>        mpg    cyl     disp       hp     drat      wt     qsec     vs
#> 1 20.09062 6.1875 230.7219 146.6875 3.596563 3.21725 17.84875 0.4375
#>        am   gear   carb
#> 1 0.40625 3.6875 2.8125
```
1. If multiple aggregation functions are used, but only one column is selected, then the output column names are the same as the function names:

``` r
mtcars %>% 
  select_(.dots = c('mpg')) %>% 
  summarise_all(funs_(c('mean', 'sum')))
#>       mean   sum
#> 1 20.09062 642.9
```
1. If multiple aggregation functions are used, and multiple columns are selected, then the output column names are the input column names underscore the aggregation function names:

``` r
mtcars %>% 
  select_(.dots = c('mpg', 'cyl')) %>% 
  summarise_all(funs_(c('mean', 'sum')))
#>   mpg_mean cyl_mean mpg_sum cyl_sum
#> 1 20.09062   6.1875   642.9     198
```

title: group_by, slice, arrange issue
description:
Not sure if this is expected, but couldn't find anything in help files to discuss it.    Apologies in advance if this is a "feature" and not a bug.

```
#Runs
mtcars %>% group_by(cyl) %>% slice(1:5) %>% 
  do(mod = lm(mpg ~ wt + gear + hp, data = .))

#Source: local data frame [3 x 2]
#Groups: <by row>
#
#    cyl     mod
#  (dbl)   (chr)
#1     4 <S3:lm>
#2     6 <S3:lm>
#3     8 <S3:lm>

#Fails with both simple arrange() and arrange(desc())
mtcars %>% group_by(cyl) %>% arrange(desc(mpg)) %>% slice(1:5) %>% 
  do(mod = lm(mpg ~ wt + gear + hp, data = .))

#Code fails with error
#Error in lm.fit(x, y, offset = offset, singular.ok = singular.ok, ...) : 
#  0 (non-NA) cases

#Ungroup/regroup solves the problem
mtcars %>% group_by(cyl) %>% arrange(desc(mpg)) %>% slice(1:5) %>% ungroup %>% group_by(cyl) %>% 
  do(mod = lm(mpg ~ wt + gear + hp, data = .))

#Source: local data frame [3 x 2]
#Groups: <by row>
#
#    cyl     mod
#  (dbl)   (chr)
#1     4 <S3:lm>
#2     6 <S3:lm>
#3     8 <S3:lm>
```

I'm not expecting them to be the same results between the two different examples, but just trying to identify where the problem occurs and it is with the combination of arrange and slice while grouped.

title: Integer not automatically coerced to double
description:
This might be a won't fix, but I thought I'd float the balloon anyway.

Consider:

```
library(dplyr)
data_frame(
  id = c(1,2,3,4,5,6),
  value = c(1L,2L,3L,NA,NA,NA),
  group = c("A","A","A","B","B","B")
) %>% 
  group_by(group) %>%
  mutate(value = ifelse(is.na(value),0,value))
```

Which fails.  

Versus:

```
data_frame(
  id = c(1,2,3,4,5,6),
  value = c(1L,2L,3L,4,NA,NA),
  group = c("A","A","A","B","B","B")
) %>% 
  mutate(value = ifelse(is.na(value),0,value)) %>%
  group_by(group)
```

Which does not fail.

As a matter of linguistic parsing one might not expect different outcomes based on ordering.  Is there a reason dplyr can't coerce the returns from the group_by operation to share in the most general common data type (as done elsewhere in R) so that both functional orders yield successful results?

title: Add UNION ALL
description:
There is no verb for `UNION ALL` in `dplyr`. For R data frames, `bind_rows()` likely works. Even if rows are unique `UNION` generally does not yield the same result as `UNION ALL` (e.g., rows get resorted).

If `union_all(x, y)` were implemented it could be translated as `SELECT * FROM x UNION ALL SELECT * FROM y` for SQL and (I guess) `bind_rows(x, y)` for R. (An alternative might be to have `bind_rows(x, y)` translate into `SELECT * FROM x UNION ALL SELECT * FROM y` if `x` and `y` are in an SQL source.)

``` r
# version 1: where the constituent dates have class "chron"
bb = data_frame(

bb %>% 
  mutate(interval = interval(a, b)) %>% 
  mutate(int_overlaps(interval, dplyr:::lag(interval)))

bb = data_frame(
  a = as.POSIXlt(strptime(c("2011-03-27 01:30:00", "2011-03-27 01:31:00"), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), tz = "UTC"),
  b = as.POSIXlt(strptime(c("2011-03-27 01:33:00", "2011-03-27 01:34:00"), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), tz = "UTC")
```

title: Working with large database tables *much* slower with 0.4.3.9000
description:
Suppose `some_table` is a table in PostgreSQL with several gigabytes of data. Code like the following is superfast in `dplyr` version `0.4.3`, but very slow in `dplyr` version `0.4.3.9001`. It seems that something is causing the running of a query that materializes the whole table somehow (though it's not clear where it's being put).

``` r
library(dplyr)
pg <- src_postgres()
some_table <- tbl(pg, sql("SELECT * FROM some_table"))

some_table %>%
    mutate(new_var=some_function(some_field)) %>%
    print(n=100)
```

This breaks a pretty snazzy workflow in which data tables are built up in R with little concern for the size of the underlying tables (in straight-up SQL, `LIMIT` might be used to similar effect).

I have confirmed that reverting to `dplyr` version `0.4.3` solves the issue (no other changes). It is hard to spot any difference in the generated SQL based on the output of `explain()`. And it is difficult to supply a minimal reproducible example given the "several gigabytes of data" dimension.

Is this a known issue?

title: Make `/` behave in SQL as it does in R
description:
See #1799 (now closed).

There we discussed the fact that `/` will behave differently in SQL from how it behaves in R. This breaks a nice feature of `dplyr`, which is that analysis can be moved from R to SQL as it proceeds with little or no changes to code. I suggested that `/` should get translated so as to behave the same in both places:

---

@hadley responded: "Hmmm, that's not a bad idea, but what should it get translated to?"

---

I suggested that translating `/` as `%* 1.0 /%` might work:

```
> pg <- src_postgres()
> stuff <- tbl(pg, sql("SELECT 5 AS a, 2 AS b"))
> stuff
Source: postgres 9.5.2 [igow@localhost:5432/crsp]
From: <derived table> [?? x 2]

       a     b
   (int) (int)
1      5     2
..   ...   ...
> stuff %>% mutate(c = a %/% b)
Source: postgres 9.5.2 [igow@localhost:5432/crsp]
From: <derived table> [?? x 3]

       a     b     c
   (int) (int) (int)
1      5     2     2
..   ...   ...   ...
> stuff %>% mutate(c = a %* 1.0 /% b)
Source: postgres 9.5.2 [igow@localhost:5432/crsp]
From: <derived table> [?? x 3]

       a     b     c
   (int) (int) (dbl)
1      5     2   2.5
..   ...   ...   ...
```

I'm not sure if it was intended to close this issue along with the original "too esoteric" issue from #1799, so I am making this a new one (perhaps to be closed again) just in case.

title: NATURAL JOIN when there are no common elements is not allowed by dplyr
description:
In the following query tables `sdata` and `fdata` have no common columns, but PostgreSQL will happily execute the query:

```
# EXPLAIN SELECT *
     FROM fdata 
     INNER JOIN sdata 
     ON fyear >= byear AND fyear < eyear;
                                  QUERY PLAN                                   
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Nested Loop  (cost=0.00..50886.88 rows=322722 width=40)
   Join Filter: ((fdata.fyear >= sdata.byear) AND (fdata.fyear < sdata.eyear))
   ->  Seq Scan on fdata  (cost=0.00..28.50 rows=1850 width=16)
   ->  Materialize  (cost=0.00..33.55 rows=1570 width=24)
         ->  Seq Scan on sdata  (cost=0.00..25.70 rows=1570 width=24)
(5 rows)
```

One way (in principle) to do this in `dplyr` would be

```
fdata %>%
    inner_join(sdata) %>%
    filter(fyear >= byear, fyear < year)
```

But this gives the complaint `Error: No common variables. Please specify `by` param.`

A workaround suggested in my answer [here](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/37289405/dplyr-left-join-by-less-than-greater-than-condition) works as follows:

```
fdata %>% 
    mutate(dummy=TRUE) %>%
    inner_join(sdata %>% mutate(dummy=TRUE)) %>%
    filter(fyear >= byear, fyear < eyear) %>%
    select(-dummy)
```

Note that the `dummy` variable comes for free in SQL (PostgreSQL, at least); see [here](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/37289405/dplyr-left-join-by-less-than-greater-than-condition) for evidence.

But a more elegant approach would exist if `dplyr` allowed a join of two tables without common fields. The documentation claims "if [`by` is] `NULL`, the default, `join` will do a natural join ..." but note that 

``` sql
SELECT *
FROM fdata 
NATURAL JOIN sdata 
WHERE fyear >= byear AND fyear < year;
```

works fine in SQL (PostgreSQL). 

I can see merit in not allowing users to do a Cartesian product of two tables accidentally due to unanticipated absence of common columns. But I wonder if there isn't an elegant way to get this if that is what is intended.

title: Mutate behaves differently in R and in database
description:
In SQL, `mutate` using an existing variable name adds another variable of the same name; in R, it replaces the variable.

Sample code:

``` r
library(dplyr)
pg <- src_postgres()
stuff <- tbl(pg, sql("SELECT 5 AS a, 2 AS b"))

stuff %>%
    mutate(a = a * 2)

stuff %>%
    collect() %>%
    mutate(a = a * 2)

stuff %>%
    mutate(a = a * 2) %>%
    explain()
```

Similar code, but for SQLite:

``` r
library(dplyr)
pg <- src_sqlite(path = tempfile(), create = TRUE)
stuff <- tbl(pg, sql("SELECT 5 AS a, 2 AS b"))

stuff %>%
    mutate(a = a * 2)

stuff %>%
    collect() %>%
    mutate(a = a * 2)

stuff %>%
    mutate(a = a * 2) %>%
    explain()
```

It seems that by tweaking the SQL, it should be possible to mimic the behaviour of `mutate` on R-side `tbl_df` objects.

description:
`tbl_df` object inherits `data.frame` class, but it's behaviour is inconsistent with the generic R object:

```
library(dplyr)

dat <- data.frame(
  chr = letters[1:5],
  num = 1:5,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

dat2 <- tbl_df(dat)

class(dat[, 1])
## [1] "character"
class(dat2[, 1])
## [1] "tbl_df"     "data.frame"

is.character(dat[,1])
## TRUE
is.character(dat2[,1])
## FALSE
```

Imagine a real-life situation that dplyr is used at some part of the code, after that at some point automated checks are made against columns:

```
for (i in 1:ncol(dat2)) {
   if( is.character(dat2[, i]) ) {
      warning("Not a char!")
   }
}
```

User shouldn't expect anything strange from such code, but if dplyr was used that it would not return expected output.

The daily workaround for this problem is to add `%>% as.data.frame()` at the end of EVERY dplyr code, but this is inconvenient.

title: failure to report error when piping with no input

x %>% mutate

It should, perhaps, rather produce an error stating that no argument had been given? Not sure why it should produce a print instead, as it most likely would not be the intention of the coder to print the tbl using a no-argument pipe.

title: Performance suffers when comparing to double
description:
Here is the issue in a nutshell: Adding `L` in the second query (i.e., making the value an integer) allows PostgreSQL to use the index. Omitting it (so it gets passed as a numeric/floating point) makes performance just awful. (This is really a PostgreSQL issue that pops up when running from `dplyr` rather than an issue with `dplyr` per se.)

```
> dsf %>% 
+     filter(permno==21793) %>%
+     select(date, ret) %>%
+     explain()
<SQL>
SELECT "date" AS "date", "ret" AS "ret"
FROM (SELECT * FROM crsp.dsf) AS "zzz12"
WHERE "permno" = 21793.0


<PLAN>
Seq Scan on dsf  (cost=0.00..3281261.04 rows=443932 width=12)
  Filter: ((permno)::numeric = 21793.0)
> dsf %>% 
+     filter(permno==21793L) %>%
+     select(date, ret) %>%
+     explain()
<SQL>
SELECT "date" AS "date", "ret" AS "ret"
FROM (SELECT * FROM crsp.dsf) AS "zzz12"
WHERE "permno" = 21793


<PLAN>
Index Scan using dsf_permno_idx on dsf  (cost=0.57..323.47 rows=6280 width=12)
  Index Cond: (permno = 21793)
```

I'm not sure how this should be handled. Should the documentation point this out and encourage use of `L` when the columns being considered are integers? Or should something more automatic take place?

It is interesting to note that in SQL, the `WHERE` clause is simply `WHERE "permno" = 21793`, so this might be a "gotcha" for people naively translating the SQL to `filter(permno==21793)`.

``` R
drop_na <- function(data, ...){

    }
    filter(data, f)
}
```

title: POSIXlt-related segfault
description:
Last night I was working with some dates/times and I (incorrectly) thought I needed them in POSIXlt format because of some time zone issues.  Along the way, I stumbled on a non-deterministic segfault and managed to create a reprex (below).

The short version is that I can insert a POSIXlt into an existing tbl_df, and that some functions (like `bind_rows`) will try to work with the invalid result without checking its column classes. The segfault's probability of occurring seems to increase with the size of the tibble and also seems more likely to happen when the corrupted tibble is printed than when it's merely computed or stored.

I think that there are three mutually-compatible ways to defend against this:

1) tibble could be more aggressive about checking for the creation of invalid columns (e.g. with checks inside assignment functions, where possible).  I don't know how much can be done about `$<-` though, since it's primitive.

2) increase the number of dplyr functions that check `white_list.h` for invalid column classes

3) It might be possible to do some kind of bounds check to determine when dplyr will try to access unmapped memory and stop it at that level, but I don't know enough C++ to know.

title: Filter is slower with multiple rules at once vs multiple filter statements
description:
This may be a common and well known behavior but I find that a filter with multiple rules can be much slower than several filters each with one rule. 

In this toy example the multi-filter version is twice as fast. In most cases I imagine this is not an issue since it would be fast enough. In a big Shiny app online, though, I was finding that if I did couple of filters I could get the speed down substantially (10x). 

``` r
dat<-data.frame(country = sample(LETTERS, 30000000, replace=TRUE), 
                country2 = sample(LETTERS, 30000000, replace=TRUE),
              data = rnorm(30000000))

ptm <- proc.time()[3]
x <- filter(dat, country=="A")
x <- filter(x, country2=="B")
proc.time()[3]-ptm
#2.28

ptm <- proc.time()[3]
x <- filter(dat, country=="A",  country=="B")
proc.time()[3]-ptm
#4.65
```

title: combine() result varies by input lengths
description:
I get different results from `combine()` depending on the lengths of the elements inside the input list:

``` r
library(dplyr)
yes <- list(alpha = letters[1:3], omega = letters[25:26])
combine(yes)
#> [1] "a" "b" "c" "y" "z"
no <- list(alpha = letters[1:3], omega = letters[24:26])
combine(no)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "a" "b" "c"
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "x" "y" "z"
```

which I found because sometimes I can't unnest things with tidyr:

``` r
library(tidyr)
x <- c(alpha = "a.b.c", omega = "x.y.z")
data_frame(x) %>% 
  mutate(letters = strsplit(x, "\\.")) %>% 
  unnest(letters)
#> Error: incompatible number of rows (2, expecting 6)

x <- c(alpha = "a.b.c", omega = "y.z")
data_frame(x) %>% 
  mutate(letters = strsplit(x, "\\.")) %>% 
  unnest(letters)
#> Source: local data frame [5 x 2]
#> 
#>       x letters
#>   <chr>   <chr>
#> 1 a.b.c       a
#> 2 a.b.c       b
#> 3 a.b.c       c
#> 4   y.z       y
#> 5   y.z       z
```

_UPDATE: I should be concrete about the numerology of failure: AFAICT `combine()` is a no-op when the list contains atomic vectors, all of length `n`, but works as you'd expect as long as vector length varies._

title: semi_join on factors with different levels produces inconsistent results
description:
Hi y'all,

Firstly, apologies in advance for what is likely a headache in the making, and a sincere thank you for the work you do.

I found a somewhat disconcerting bug while looking at [this SO question](http://stackoverflow.com/q/36634304/4497050) where `self_join` produces different results called on the exact same data in the exact same way. It only seems to happen when joining on two factors with different levels (joining when already character works as expected), and did not (apparently) happen to @jaimedash on the SO question. I've tried to document what follows as thoroughly as I can (apologies for the length!), as I have no idea if it will exhibit the same behavior tomorrow, nor whether this behavior is fully reproducible or a fillip of my current configuration.

It began like so:

``` r
> library(dplyr)
>
> table1 <- data.frame(id=c(1:7), animal=c("cat","cat","dog","dog","parakeet","lion","duck"))
> table2 <- data.frame(id=c(1:4), animal=c("cat","dog","parakeet","duck"))

> semi_join(table1, table2, by = "animal")
  id   animal
1  1      cat
2  2      cat
3  3      dog
4  5 parakeet
Warning message:
    In semi_join_impl(x, y, by$x, by$y) :
    joining factors with different levels, coercing to character vector
```

...which is not what I expected, so I update my installed packages in case it was a known bug (`install.packages(c("sp", "testthat"))`), building from source. Doubting that made a difference, I try again:

``` r
> semi_join(table1, table2, by = "animal")
  id   animal
1  1      cat
2  6     lion
3  2      cat
4  3      dog
5  5 parakeet
Warning message:
    In semi_join_impl(x, y, by$x, by$y) :
    joining factors with different levels, coercing to character vector
```

...which is not just still wrong, it is _differently wrong_. After getting that same wrong result a couple times, I manually rebuild the data.frames as character to make sure `self_join` works, and it does:

``` r
> table1 <- data.frame(id=c(1:7), animal=c("cat","cat","dog","dog","parakeet","lion","duck"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
> table2 <- data.frame(id=c(1:4), animal=c("cat","dog","parakeet","duck"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
> semi_join(table1, table2, by = "animal")
  id   animal
1  1      cat
2  2      cat
3  3      dog
4  4      dog
5  5 parakeet
6  7     duck
```

...which is the expected result. Reloading them as factor, I now get a _third_ incorrect result:

``` r
> semi_join(table1, table2, by = "animal")
  id   animal
1  1      cat
2  6     lion
3  2      cat

5  3      dog
6  5 parakeet
Warning message:
    In semi_join_impl(x, y, by$x, by$y) :
```

After looking at the structures of the tables—without reloading or altering them—I try again, and it goes back to the second incorrect result:

``` r
> str(table1)
'data.frame':   7 obs. of  2 variables:
 $ id    : int  1 2 3 4 5 6 7

'data.frame':   4 obs. of  2 variables:

[1] "cat"      "dog"      "duck"     "lion"     "parakeet"
> levels(table2$animal)
[1] "cat"      "dog"      "duck"     "parakeet"
> semi_join(table1, table2, by = "animal")
  id   animal
1  1      cat

3  2      cat
4  3      dog
5  5 parakeet
Warning message:
In semi_join_impl(x, y, by$x, by$y) :
  joining factors with different levels, coercing to character vector
```

Run to work, come back, try rebuilt as character (fine), the as factors, and I get incorrect result 1. Trying with one as factor and the other character returns the correct result. More reloading gets me a fourth incorrect version:

``` r
> semi_join(table1, table2, by = "animal")
```

title: SQLite type conversion on first element when pulling data to R
description:
When pulling data from sqlite database to R, it seems to decide the column class based on the first element. This means if I have a decimal(18,4) type on a column, but the first element is 18, then it will convert to integer.

Example:
So in the sqlite database I have the following column:
4|Low|decimal (18, 4)|0||0

The first 5 rows are:
sqlite> SELECT Low FROM daily LIMIT 5;
18
22.5
24.55
24.1301
24.38

Now pulling this into R, we get the following result:
tbl(db,sql("SELECT Low FROM daily LIMIT 5"))
Low
1  18
2  22
3  24
4  24
5  24

If we offset the first row we get the expected numeric dbl class:
tbl(db,sql("SELECT Low FROM daily LIMIT 5 OFFSET 1"))

Low
1 22.5000
2 24.5500
3 24.1301
4 24.3800
5 24.0600

Is this intended? If so, what is the best way to prevent this?

EDIT: As a workaround, we can multiply the column by 1.0:
con %>% tbl(sql("SELECT Low*1.0 FROM daily"))
Low*1.0
(dbl)
1  18.0000
2  22.5000
3  24.5500
4  24.1301
5  24.3800

Still, maybe having a way of forcing the table column types when pulling to R would be a preferred way of doing this.

title: spread() and gather() for SQL sources
description:
~~spread() needs specification of the new column names. This ensures that the resulting schema is known to dplyr.~~ spread() needs compute() anyway, unique values can be fetched into memory.
