title: cannot find "median" in `summerise_`
description:
We can use `summarise_` in those pesky situations in Shiny when we want to select a function to apply to a dataframe. This often works just fine, like below; 

```
ChickWeight %>% 
  group_by(Diet) %>% 
  summarise_("mean(weight)")
```

Here the string `mean(weight)` gets handled appropriately and we get a nice summary back for every `Diet`. The mean works just fine, the median function however gives an odd error; 

```
ChickWeight %>% 
  group_by(Diet) %>% 
  summarise_("median(weight)")
```

This returns a `Error: could not find function "median"` error. The normal `summarise` (without `_`) does work and other aggregation functions seem to work as well. Any idea what might be causing this? 

I also notice that the `summarise_` approach does not seem to work on user defined functions. Is `dplyr` using internal Rcpp functions when it sees `mean`/`var`/`max`/`min`? If thats the case it might need to have `median` added.

title: Window functions not translated to sql correctly after group_by() followed by an aggregation
description:
In the current master branch of dplyr, window functions include PARTITION BY in the query after a group_by statement followed by an aggregation although they shouldn't. As expected, the aggregation drops the grouping variable but PARTITION BY is still included in the sql statement. 

Since SQlite doesn't support windows function I haven't been able to reproduce this using memdb_frame. 

This works as expected: 
`library(nycflights13)
flights_sqlite <- copy_to(db, flights, temporary = TRUE, indexes = list(
  c("year", "month", "day"), "carrier", "tailnum"))
flights_sqlite %>% group_by(carrier) %>%  mutate(rank = rank(desc(sumdelay))) %>% show_query()
`

```
<SQL>
SELECT "year", "month", "day", "dep_time", "dep_delay", "arr_time", "arr_delay", "carrier", "tailnum", "flight", "origin", "dest", "air_time", "distance", "hour", "minute", rank() OVER (PARTITION BY "carrier" ORDER BY "sumdelay" DESC) AS "rank"
FROM "flights"
```

This pipeline should drop PARTITION BY from the query: 
`flights_sqlite %>% group_by(carrier) %>% summarise(sumdelay = sum(arr_delay)) %>% mutate(rank = rank(desc(sumdelay))) %>% show_query()`

```
<SQL>
SELECT "carrier", "sumdelay", rank() OVER (PARTITION BY  ORDER BY "sumdelay" DESC) AS "rank"
FROM (SELECT "carrier", SUM("arr_delay") AS "sumdelay"
FROM "flights"
GROUP BY "carrier") "pjwhowndgm"
```

If I specify multiply groups the translation to sql works fine: 
`flights_sqlite %>% group_by(carrier, year) %>% summarise(sumdelay = sum(arr_delay)) %>% mutate(rank = rank(desc(sumdelay))) %>% show_query()`

```
<SQL>
SELECT "carrier", "year", "sumdelay", rank() OVER (PARTITION BY "carrier" ORDER BY "sumdelay" DESC) AS "rank"
FROM (SELECT "carrier", "year", SUM("arr_delay") AS "sumdelay"
FROM "flights"
GROUP BY "carrier", "year") "fxffgnvxvt"
```

title: Standard Evaluation “could not find function”
description:
Standard Evaluation, according to the [NSE vignette](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dplyr/vignettes/nse.html), understands three forms of quoted expressions:

> 1. With a formula, `~ mean(mpg)`.
> 2. With `quote()`, `quote(mean(mpg))`.
> 3. As a string: `"mean(mpg)"`.

It is understood that these three are different, because formulae capture the environment. Nevertheless, I’m puzzled why the following yields different results:

``` r
library(dplyr)

mtcars %>% rowwise() %>% summarize_(x = ~prop.test(mpg, disp)$p.value)
mtcars %>% rowwise() %>% summarize_(x = quote(prop.test(mpg, disp)$p.value))
```

I’d expect the same result for both. Instead, I only get the expected result (a `tbl_df` of p-values) for the first statement; for the second statement, I get:

> Error: could not find function "prop.test"

The only reason for this that I can think of is that `prop.test` is defined in `package:stats`, and maybe for some weird reason that package (though attached) isn’t visible from wherever the expression is evaluated). However, this doesn’t seem to be the case, because other functions from within the same package _are_ found:

``` r
mtcars %>% summarize_(x = ~sd(mpg))
mtcars %>% summarize_(x = quote(sd(mpg)))
```

These two lines yield the same result. What causes the difference in behaviour between the call to `prop.test` and the call to `sd`?

title: update_with
description:
I'm doing an analysis that requires a lot of manual corrections to the original dataset. I keep tables of changes that mirror the original (see example in code) and then I use the code below to impute the original values. Probably niche, but who am I to decide. Here's my code:

``` R
library(dplyr)
library(lazyeval)

update_with = function(data, update, by) {

  # columns to be updated
  # (cols(data) intersect cols(update)) -- by
  orig_order = colnames(data)
  update_cols =
    setdiff(intersect(colnames(data), colnames(update)), by)

  # left join update
  data = data %>% left_join(update, by=by)

  print(update_cols)

  # mutate one by one
  for(col in update_cols) {
    col.x = paste(col, "x", sep=".")
    col.y = paste(col, "y", sep=".")

    update = interp( ~ifelse( is.na(y), x, y)
                   , x=as.name(col.x)
                   , y=as.name(col.y))

    data = data %>% mutate_( .dots = setNames(list(update), col) ) %>%
      select( -one_of(c(col.x,col.y)) )
  }

  data[,orig_order]
}


a = data.frame(x = 1:100,y = 5, z = 1:50)
b = data.frame(x = 1:10, y = 0)

a %>% update_with(b, by="x")

```

title: dbSendQuery doesn't act consistently with all drivers; may force full extraction
description:
#### Situation
- Redshift returns _all_ results immediately when you invoke `dbSendQuery`. It does not wait for `dbFetch`.
- Invoking `head` on a `tbl_sql` will invoke `collect`, and thus `dbSendQuery`.
- Large tables will ... try to return all their rows. If the table is large enough, R will run out of RAM and crash. 
- This is a breaking change from the previous version of dplyr, which employed a `limit` clause.
#### Story

I'm using `dplyr` to connect to a Postgres-type database (Redshift) and pull everything into a nice, neat report. It's a great experience.

Now, I happened to want a _very_ recently added feature (`union_all`), and, since I like to live dangerously, I updated this afternoon :)

However, upon rendering my Rmarkdown document, it hung on `head(tmp_table)`. For a very long time.

After leaving it alone for an hour, I decided to check the running queries table in Redshift. It turns out it was running `select * from tmp_table`. The only problem is that the table has > 12 billion rows. 
#### Workaround

I've just [stolen most of the collect function](https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/blob/ec74316dcfb7a91002d8465d0d548498296946d4/R/tbl-sql.r#L387) and added a `LIMIT` clause manually.

``` r
dhead <- function(table, n = 10){
  if (n < 0 | n == Inf){
    n = -1
  }
  query = sprintf("%s LIMIT %s", sql_render(table), n)
  res = dbSendQuery(table$src$con, query) 
  on.exit(dbClearResult(res))
  dbFetch(res, n) %>%
    return
}
```

title: Improve compilation time
description:
On my four-core machine, dplyr compiles in just above one minute. Tried precompiled headers, but this doesn't reduce compilation time much.

The compiler state after including `dplyr.h` is roughly 200 MB; ~~this means that it essentially doesn't matter how large a `.cpp` module is. The only thing that can help is to reduce the number of modules by merging some of the smaller ones into larger ones. A amalgamation ("unity build", like sqlite) would build fastest, but the code doesn't support this yet because of inconsistent `using namespace` statements~~.

Current lines per module:

```
    19 strings_addresses.cpp
    20 test.cpp
    27 distinct.cpp
    37 init.cpp
    42 address.cpp
    50 between.cpp
    69 arrange.cpp
    74 group_indices.cpp
    74 matrixToDataFrame.cpp
    76 window.cpp
    80 select.cpp
   115 summarise.cpp
   148 combine_variables.cpp
   283 bind.cpp
   295 filter.cpp
   303 api.cpp
   384 join.cpp
   616 RcppExports.cpp
  2085 dplyr.cpp
```

Compile time per module follows. Not surprising, dplyr.cpp takes the longest time and should probably be even split.

title: Trying to extract list elements from newly created list in summarise() crashes R
description:
The following code consistently crashes R:

```
library(dplyr)
d = data_frame(gr=c(1,1,2,2), x=1:4)
d %>%
  group_by(gr) %>%
  summarise(ki=list(t.test(x)$conf.int),
            low=ki[1], high=ki[2])
```

Note that the list have to be created in the same `summarise()` operation to cause the crash. The following works fine (i.e., doesn’t crash R):

```
d2 = d %>%
  group_by(gr) %>%
  summarise(ki=list(t.test(x)$conf.int))
d2 %>% summarise(low=ki[1], high=ki[2])
d2 %>% group_by(gr) %>% summarise(low=ki[1], high=ki[2])
```

(I observe the problem with dplyr 0.4.3 in R 3.2.3 on Windows.)

title: count does not use current group_by (unintuitive)
description:
Hi, 

Currently `count` does not 'respect' `group_by` statements, which is not intuitive (I observed this multiple times when training novice R/dplyr users).

Example:

``` R
data(diamonds, package="ggplot2")
diamonds %>% count(cut)

diamonds %>% group_by(cut) %>% count # gives total count, not group_by

# Source: local data frame [1 x 1]
#
# n
# (int)
#1 53940

diamonds %>% group_by(cut) %>% count(clarity) # gives count by clarity (but not cut)

# Source: local data frame [8 x 2]
# 
# clarity     n
# (fctr) (int)
#1      I1   741
#2     SI2  9194
#3     SI1 13065
#4     VS2 12258
# ...
```

I know that one way to 'fix' this is to use `tally` and to expand the group_by statement, however I will submit a PR in which `count` expands the current grouping.

title: mutate_ and lubridate::parse_date_time SE not working together as expected
description:
Consider:

``` R
df <- frame_data( ~ start_date,
                    "07/15/2015 15:39", 
                    "07/15/2015 15:42")

df_NSE <- df %>% 
          mutate(response_date = parse_date_time(start_date, orders ="mdY hm"))
```

I would have thought that something like the following would be a standard-evaluation equivalent:

``` R
var_name <- "start_date"
df_SE_expected_to_work <- df %>% 
          mutate_(response_date = ~parse_date_time(var_name, orders ="mdY hm"))
```

but this just throws a warning and just has blank rows for the response_date column:

``` R
Warning message:
All formats failed to parse. No formats found. 
```

I tried many variations even with interp, just to make sure it wasnt my understanding of NSE such as this one:

``` R
df_SE_interp_expected_to_work <- df %>% 
          mutate_(response_date = interp(~parse_date_time(var_name, orders ="mdY hm"), var_name = var_name))
```

but i get the same outcome

I was able to hack a working solution for both cases:

``` R
df_SE_working <- df %>% 
          mutate_(response_date = ~parse_date_time(df[[var_name]], orders ="mdY hm"))
df_SE_interp_working <- df %>% 
          mutate_(response_date = interp(~parse_date_time(df[[var_name]], orders ="mdY hm"), var_name = var_name))
```

title: Is there a typo in the dplyr inner join documentation?
description:
The documentation of dplyr's inner join states

> inner_join: return all rows from x where there are matching values in **x**, and all columns from x and y. If there are multiple matches between x and y, all combination of the matches are returned.

Is that bolded x a typo? I thought it was supposed to return all rows in x where there are matching values in y. I'm not really sure what the former means otherwise.

title: left_join() on postgres tbl duplicates join variables in some cases
description:
Somehow, somewhere a recent change to the development version of dplyr breaks left_join() for tables created with tbl() for database objects created with src_postgres().

It's been pretty hard to create a reproducible example. Say I have three tbl objects. 

my_db <- tbl(src_postgres("nycflights13"), "flights")
tbl1 <- tbl(my_db, sql("select year, origin, tailnum, carrier from flights"))
tbl2 <- tbl(my_db, sql("select year, origin, tailnum, carrier from flights"))
tbl3 <- tbl(my_db, sql("select \* from (values (1, 'UA'), (2, 'AA'), (3, 'B6')) as t (num,carrier)"))

This works fine: 

```
tbl1 %>% left_join(tlb2, by = c("carrier" = "carrier"))
From: <derived table> [?? x 7]

   year.x origin.x tailnum.x carrier year.y origin.y tailnum.y
    (int)    (chr)     (chr)   (chr)  (int)    (chr)     (chr)
1    2013      EWR    N14228      UA   2013      EWR    N14228
2    2013      EWR    N14228      UA   2013      LGA    N24211
3    2013      EWR    N14228      UA   2013      EWR    N39463
```

This does not: 

```
tbl1 %>% left_join(tlb3, by = c("carrier" = "carrier"))
From: <derived table> [?? x 6]

    year origin tailnum carrier   num carrier
   (int)  (chr)   (chr)   (chr) (int)   (chr)
1   2013    EWR  N14228      UA     1      UA
2   2013    LGA  N24211      UA     1      UA
3   2013    JFK  N619AA      AA     2      AA

```

This issue is that in the first example, I get column carrier back only once. In the second example dplyr returns the carrier column twice. This is problematic because when adding a bunch of operations and then collecting the data, postgres complains that the column reference to carrier is ambiguous. 

Btw, I could have used tbl1 %>% left_join(tlb3, by = "carrier") in this case but that doesn't change the result.

This did not happen in previous dplyr versions I have been using.

title: filtering and summarizing in group_by for postgres gives error with out adding a collect
description:
With a data.frame this works as expected:

```
z <- data.frame(a=c(1,1,1,2,2,2,3,3,3), b=c(1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9))
z %>% group_by(a) %>% filter(row_number() <=2) %>% summarize(k = paste(as.character(b), collapse=";"))
```

gives

```
 Source: local data frame [3 x 2]

       a     k
   (dbl) (chr)
 1     1   1;2
 2     2   4;5
 3     3   7;8
```

But with a postgres backend, it fails

```
data_repo <- src_postgres(...)
x <- copy_to(data_repo, z), name="x", temporary=T)
a <- x %>% group_by(a) %>% filter(row_number() <=2) %>% summarize(k = paste(as.character(b), collapse=";"))
a$query$sql
a %>% compute
```

gives

```
SELECT "a", "k"
 FROM (SELECT "a", string_agg(CAST("b" AS TEXT), ';') AS "k"
 FROM (SELECT "a", string_agg(CAST("b" AS TEXT), ';') AS "k", row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY "a") AS "zzz329"
 FROM "x") AS "zzz330"
 WHERE "zzz329" <= 2.0
 GROUP BY "a") AS "zzz331"
Source: postgres 9.4.6 [<user>@<host>]
 From: <derived table> [?? x 2]

 Error in postgresqlExecStatement(conn, statement, ...) :
   RS-DBI driver: (could not Retrieve the result : ERROR:  column "x.a" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function
 LINE 3: FROM (SELECT "a", string_agg(CAST("b" AS TEXT), ';') AS "k",...
                      ^
 )
```

It looks like the problem is the `string_agg` is applied twice, where it should only be applied in the outer `SELECT`, as this query gives the right result.

```
SELECT "a", "k"
FROM (
     SELECT "a", string_agg(CAST("b" AS TEXT), ';') AS "k"
     FROM
        (SELECT
                "a",
                "b",
                row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY "a") AS "zzz329"
        FROM "x") AS "zzz330"
     WHERE "zzz329" <= 2.0
     GROUP BY "a") AS "zzz331";
```

With this in mind, adding a `collapse` call between the filter and summarize does the trick.

```
a <- x %>% group_by(a) %>% filter(row_number() <=2) %>% collapse %>% dplyr::summarize(k = paste(as.character(b), collapse=";"))
a$query$sql
a %>% collect
```

gives

```
 <SQL> SELECT "a", "k"
 FROM (SELECT "a", string_agg(CAST("b" AS TEXT), ';') AS "k"
 FROM (SELECT "a", "b"
 FROM (SELECT "a", "b", row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY "a") AS "zzz332"
 FROM "x") AS "zzz333"
 WHERE "zzz332" <= 2.0) AS "zzz334"
 GROUP BY "a") AS "zzz335"
 Source: local data frame [3 x 2]

       a     k
   (dbl) (chr)
 1     1   1;2
 2     2   4;5
 3     3   7;8
```

title: Better semantics for dataframeable objects
description:
After thinking about https://github.com/hadley/purrr/issues/179, I wonder if we could improve the semantics of dataframeable objects in `bind_rows()` by taking a vector viewpoint rather than a list viewpoint.

If we think about vectors, the current behaviour is not consistent because `bind_rows()` effectively binds columns together:

``` r
col_vectors <- list(
  a = c(1, 2),
  b = c(3, 4)
)

row_vectors <- list(
  c(a = 1, b = 3),
  c(a = 2, b = 4)
)
```

``` r
bind_rows(row_vectors)
#> Error: cannot convert object to a data frame

bind_rows(col_vectors)
#> Source: local data frame [2 x 2]
#>
#>       a     b
#>   (dbl) (dbl)
#> 1     1     3
#> 2     2     4
```

I think it'd be more intuitive to go the `rbind()` and `cbind()` way, and treat vectors differently depending on the direction of the binding. `bind_rows()` would require vectors with inner names and `bind_cols()` would require vectors with outer names.

Advantages:
- Arguably more intuitive if we think about vectors rather than lists.
- Better behaviour down the line, e.g. `map_df()`
- This would be compatible with splicing the input as suggested in PR #992.

The latter would add a lot of flexibility. `bind_cols()` and `bind_rows()` would accept indistinctly data frames, named vectors, and lists of data frames and named vectors.

cc @jennybc

title: summarise_each_, mutate_each_ require vars and that all variables be named
description:
#1170 plus more

`summarise_each_` and `mutate_each_` require that `vars` must be specified. If one of the variable names is `NA`, it is impossible to successfully specify `vars`. Example below plays out same w/ either function.

``` r
library(dplyr)
x <- frame_data(
  ~colA, ~colB,
  1,   4,
  3,   6
)
# this works
# x %>% summarise_each_(funs(median), c("colA", "colB"))
x %>% summarise_each_(funs(median))
#> Error in colwise_(tbl, funs_(funs), vars): argument "vars" is missing, with no default

title: Conditional mutate
description:
Say I have a data frame:

```
x <- data.frame(a=c(1,2,3,4,NA,6))
```

I want to replace all na values by 2 and limit the values at 4 in this data frame.
The limiting I could do by using pmin e.g.

```
y <- x %>% mutate(b=pmin(a,4))
```

In the more difficult cases I could fall back on the _ifelse()_ function.

```
y <- x %>% mutate(b=ifelse(is.na(a),2,a))
```

However the _ifelse()_ function has some serious drawbacks since it drops the attributes. Therefore you cannot do this with POSIXct objects and other types that depend on attributes.

A possible suggestion to overcome this issue and provide a more generic method could be to introduce a new keyword, similar to group_by. This keyword subsets the rows on which to apply the next operations in the same way that filter does but without throwing those rows out. E.g.:

```
y <- x %>% 
  mutate(b=a) %>% 
  subset(is.na(a)) %>% 
  mutate(b=2) %>% 
  subset(b>4) %>% 
  mutate(b=4)

   a b
1  1 1
2  2 2
3  3 3
4  4 4
5 NA 2
6  6 4
```

Some use cases:
- NA replacement
- More general value replacement
- Data cleaning

Some stackoverflow posts:
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/24459752/can-dplyr-package-be-used-for-conditional-mutating
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/22337394/combine-mutate-with-conditional-values

title: Use of rle inside mutate or group_by
description:
In reference to https://stackoverflow.com/questions/35246453

There seems to be an issue when using `rle` inside `mutate` or `group_by` on a regular `data.frame`/`tbl_df` in a dplyr pipe. Here's an example:

```
dat <- data.frame(x=c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2), y=1:7)
```

These approaches do not work:

```
#1
dat %>% 
    tbl_df %>% 
    group_by(yy = with(rle(x), rep(seq_along(lengths), lengths))) %>%
    summarize(mean(y))
Error: cannot coerce type 'closure' to vector of type 'integer'

#2 without "with()"
dat %>%
    group_by(rep(seq_along(rle(x)$lengths), rle(x)$lengths)) %>%
    summarize(mean(y))
Error: invalid Indextyp 'closure'
```

Interestingly, it works when `dat` is converted to a `tbl_dt`:

```
dat %>% 
    tbl_dt %>% 
    group_by(yy = with(rle(x), rep(seq_along(lengths), lengths))) %>%
    summarize(mean(y))
Source: local data table [4 x 2]
     yy mean(y)
  (int)   (dbl)
1     1     2.0
2     2     4.5
3     3     6.0
4     4     7.0
```

Another option that also works for `tbl_df`s but is less convenient is the use of `{}`:

```
dat %>%
    group_by(yy = {yy = rle(x); rep(seq_along(yy$lengths), yy$lengths)}) %>%
    summarize(mean(y))
Source: local data frame [4 x 2]

     yy mean(y)

title: order_by/arrange with multiple variables in window function
description:
``` r
tbl(kpc, 'jgt') %>% 
  group_by(pev_id)  %>% 
  arrange(mes_critere, inf_critere) %>% 
  mutate(ordre=row_number()) %>% sql
```

leads to 

``` r
(...)
row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY "pev_id" ORDER BY ("mes_critere", "inf_critere")) AS "ordre"
(...)
```

Idem when using `order_by` in `mutate`.

With [Netezza](https://github.com/philippechataignon/dplyrnz) , this syntax is incorrect and must be :
`row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY "pev_id" ORDER BY "mes_critere", "inf_critere") AS "ordre"`

Both syntax are admitted by Postgresql but the last is in the documentation and I don't think parentheses are in the standard.

Proposed patch:

```
--- a/R/over.R
+++ b/R/over.R
@@ -12,7 +12,7 @@ over <- function(expr, partition = NULL, order = NULL, frame = NULL) {
       sql_vector(partition, collapse = ", "))
   }
   if (!is.null(order)) {
-    order <- build_sql("ORDER BY ", sql_vector(order, collapse = ", "))
+    order <- build_sql("ORDER BY ", sql_vector(order, collapse = ", ", parens=F))
   }
   if (!is.null(frame)) {
     if (is.numeric(frame)) frame <- rows(frame[1], frame[2])
```

title: Add partition function
description:
``` R
partition <- function(n, probs) {
  if (abs(sum(probs) - 1) > 1e-6) {
    stop("`probs` must sum to 1.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  idx <- findInterval(
    seq(0, 1, length = n), 
    c(0, cumsum(probs)), 
    rightmost.closed = TRUE
  )
  names(probs)[sample(idx)]
}
```

title: bind_rows Not Equivalent to rbind
description:
The [blog](http://blog.rstudio.org/2015/01/09/dplyr-0-4-0/) states "If `x` is a list of data frames, `bind_rows(x)` is equivalent to `do.call(rbind, x)`"

However, consider:

```
dataList <- list(data.frame(A = 1:5, row.names = 0:4), data.frame(A = 6:7, row.names = 88:89))
do.call(rbind, dataList)
bind_rows(dataList)
```

`bind_rows` changes the row numbers, unlike `rbind` which preserves the user's numbering, so the two approaches are not entirely equivalent.

It also converts factors to characters when the levels are unequal, unlike `rbind`.

title: rowwise is broken for 'list' objects
description:
Might be related to #1491 and hybrid evaluation, but this a different issue.

This is a little involved (it took me quite a while to figure out the REPEX), so hang on:
When we assign a list object in a mutate call after a rowwise it seems that the values which depends on other columns are reassigned after all calls have been done to the last value of the column variable. It's one of the extremely weird bugs that only our dear `R` can produce.
The best real-world example would be fitting models with different parameters, but I cooked you a small repex:

```
ft <- function(test) {
  res <- list(tt = test, tt2 = !!test)
  test2 <- test
  res$tt3 <- test2
  return(res)
}

data.frame(prob = c(F,F,F,T)) %>% tbl_df %>% rowwise() %>% 
  mutate(model = list(ft(prob)),
         probFromModel = model[["tt"]],
         probAssignedFromModel = model[["tt3"]],
         probComputedFromModel = model[["tt2"]])
# Source: local data frame [4 x 5]
# Groups: <by row>
#   
#   prob     model probFromModel probAssignedFromModel probComputedFromModel
# (lgl)     (chr)         (lgl)                 (lgl)                 (lgl)
#1 FALSE <list[3]>          TRUE                  TRUE                 FALSE
#2 FALSE <list[3]>          TRUE                  TRUE                 FALSE
#3 FALSE <list[3]>          TRUE                  TRUE                 FALSE
#4  TRUE <list[3]>          TRUE                  TRUE                  TRUE
```

We can see that (i) the "test" value is right when it is evaluated, (ii) computed values (copied) are okay (iii) any value that are "shallowed" copied (even the re-assignment) are prone to the bug.

The function is here to test re-assignment, but doing something like `model = list(list(tt=...))` works the same.

Seems like a bug around hybrid evaluation and the fact that we might want to enforce some kind of deep-copy of the arguments.

title: Would it be a good idea for dplyr verbs to propagate NULL data frames?
description:
I just wonder whether perhaps one could make dplyr verbs to act more like base R and propagate NULL data frames instead of throwing an error. Here is a simple example:

``` r
  # Assume you sometimes have no data
  # and df is NULL
  df = NULL

  # Base R does not throw errors quickly
  # but conveniently propagates NULL
  df[df$a==1,]
  ## NULL

  # dplyr verbs are not as tolerant...
  filter(df, a==1)
  ## Error in UseMethod("filter_") : 
  ## no applicable method for 'filter_' applied to an object of class "NULL"
```

Returning NULL instead of an error could probably be easily implemented by adding functions like:

``` r
filter_.NULL = function(...) return(NULL)
```

While this is not a big issue, I would find NULL propagation quite convenient, since one can get rid of some case distinctions and dplyr would probably behave more like base R.

Conceptually it also seems sound to me to return NULL:
If I filter something from NULL, it seems intuitive that the result is NULL.
If I arrange NULL the result should also be NULL.
If I mutate NULL the result should also be NULL.
... and so on...

title: Cannot specify column names by string for summarise_()
description:

``` r
group_by(mtcars, cyl)
```

does the same thing as:

``` r
someColumn <- 'cyl'
group_by_(mtcars, someOtherColumn)
```

However, `summarise_` does not seem to do this. The following works:

``` r
summarise(mtcars, mean(disp))
```

But this does not:

``` r
someColumn <- 'disp'
summarise_(mtcars, mean(someColumn))
```

The latter produces a warning (basically hinting that it couldn't match the column names), and returns NA for the summary.

It would be really useful if `summarise_` would behave like `group_by_` in allowing column names to be specified via character variables. (If this is what it's supposed to be doing, it currently isn't, and this is a bug. If not, it would be a welcome feature!) :)

title: is_row_wise option for filter?
description:
filtering a data frame with many groups can often be unnecessarily slow because filter has no way of knowing if the filtering condition is row-wise, and so it repeats each filtering operational within each group.

ungrouping solves the problem, but this may not be obvious to many users.

would it make sense to add an argument to filter to give users control over this option, or at least to add a note in the documentation about this?

sample code below demonstrates the issue.

``` r
# create a dummy dataframe with 100,000 groups and 1,000,000 rows
# and partition by group_id
df <- data.frame(group_id=sample(1:1e5, 1e6, replace=T),
                 val=sample(1:100, 1e6, replace=T)) %>%
      group_by(group_id)

# filter rows with a value of 1 naively
system.time(df %>% filter(val == 1))

#   user  system elapsed
#  1.447   0.017   1.476

# ungroup before filtering for a huge speedup
system.time(df %>% ungroup() %>% filter(val == 1))

#   user  system elapsed
#  0.007   0.003   0.010
```

title: summarise issue with POSIXct
description:
The issue here is that `LAST_DAY` column should be a `POSIXct` object and not an `int` (as opposed to what the value of `LAST_DAY` should be, 2015-12-01 or -02).

                 event=c("a","a","b","b"))

df %>% group_by(event) %>% summarise(FIRST_DAY=min(FIRST_DAY), LAST_DAY=max(FIRST_DAY)) -> df_summary

title: Using tbl_dt on grouped tbl_dt silently ungroups (and vice versa).
description:
Creating a tbl_dt from  a grouped tbl_df silently ungroups the result.
Similarly, creating a tbl_df from a grouped tbl_dt silently ungroups the result.
This behavior seems odd given the general tendency not to ungroup;
I would have expected the group information to stay. 

```
x_df <- data_frame ( g = rep(c("a", "b", "c" ), each = 5), v = 1:15)
x_dt <- x_df %>% tbl_dt()

x_df %>% group_by(g) %>%              groups()
x_df %>% group_by(g) %>% tbl_dt() %>% groups()

x_dt %>% group_by(g) %>%              groups()
x_dt %>% group_by(g) %>% tbl_df() %>% groups()
```

title: joining to NULL
description:
All of the joins error if one of the inputs is `NULL`, whereas `base::merge()` returns a 0-row data frame with variables taken from the non-`NULL` input, if such exists, or with 0 columns, if it's also `NULL`. If this is how it's supposed to be, then just close this.

``` r
library(dplyr)
inner_join(NULL, iris)
#> Error in UseMethod("inner_join"): no applicable method for 'inner_join' applied to an object of class "NULL"
merge(NULL, iris)
#> [1] Sepal.Length Sepal.Width  Petal.Length Petal.Width  Species     
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
merge(NULL, NULL)
#> data frame with 0 columns and 0 rows
```

title: Problems with filter() and "!=" and "|" operators
description:
Sorry, I'm not sure if this is a bug, and, if it is, whether it already has been reported. I'm having problems using `filter` with the `!=`  and `|` logical operators.

```
    n <-  c(2, 3, 5) 
    s <-  c("aa", "bb", "cc") 
    b <-  c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE) 
    df <-  data.frame(n, s, b) 
```

This filters correctly, so the problem isn't with `==`

```
    df %>% 
        filter(s == "aa" | b == FALSE)
```

This filters correctly, so the problem isn't with `!=` by itself

```
df %>% 
    filter(s != "aa")
```

This filters correctly, so the problem isn't with `&` and `!=`

```
df %>% 
    filter(n != 2 & b != TRUE)
```

Problem begins here. This filters for `n` but not for `b`

```
    df %>% 
    filter(n != 2 | b != TRUE)
```

This doesn't filter any of the variables

```
df %>% 
    filter(s != "aa" | b != FALSE)
```

```
R version 3.2.3 (2015-12-10)
Platform: x86_64-apple-darwin13.4.0 (64-bit)
Running under: OS X 10.10.5 (Yosemite)
dplyr_0.4.3 
```

I originally tested this with Cran version but just tested it with developer's version as well and had the same problems.

title: Using an expression to compute the new name in rename
description:
This works to rename the `demand` column to `demand2`. Note we are using plyr's `rename`, not dplyr's `rename`:

```
library(dplyr)
num <- 2
BOD %>% plyr::rename(list(demand = paste0("demand", num)))  # ok
```

Since dplyr's `rename` uses new = old vs. plyr which uses old = new there is no easy way to do the above with dplyr's `rename`.   This is pretty ugly but anyways it gives an error message:

```
library(dplyr)
num <- 2
BOD %>% do({ L <- setNames(list("demand"), paste0("demand", num)); rename_(., L) }) # bad
```

Also the following gives an error message since one cannot provide an expression where a name goes:

```
library(dplyr)
num <- 2
BOD %>% rename(list(paste0("demand", num) = demand))  # bad
```

Actually neither plyr's `rename` nor dplyr's `rename` are fully general since plyr can only easily handle expressions in the new name and dplyr in the old name.  `renameCol` in the doBy package can handle expressions in both the old and the new name as it uses the syntax `renameCol(indata, src, tgt)` where `src` and `tgt` are character vectors of names and either of these or both can be complex expressions.

```
# rename column named paste0(base, num) to toupper(base)
# (In this case it renames column x2 to X)
library(dplyr)
base <- "x"
num <- 2
anscombe %>% doBy::renameCol(paste0(base, num), toupper(base))
```

title: option to clean/normalize data.frames?
description:
(Migrated from [rvest #116](https://github.com/hadley/rvest/issues/116).) When `dplyr` is used with `rvest`, some HTML tables do not provide sufficient information to generate legitimate data.frames in R. Specifically, the following will fail: ``` r library(dplyr) library(rvest) HTML <- read_html('
Var1
12
') HTML %>% html_node('table') %>% html_table() %>% tbl_df() ## Error: All columns must be named ``` The discussion started with a suggestion to add an option to `html_table` to check the column header names, but it has shifted to putting the data.frame validation into `dplyr`. Perhaps something like: ``` r #' Check validity/format of a data.frame or tbl. #' #' Ensure the data.frame or tbl has legitimate and optionally unique column names. #' @param x data.frame #' @param check.names logical, whether to check/fix the column names #' @param unique logical, force column names to be unique (\code{TRUE}) or #' allow duplicates (\code{FALSE}); ignored if \code{check.names} is \code{FALSE} #' @return data.frame, with optionally different column names #' @export fix_df <- function(x, check.names=TRUE, unique=TRUE) { if (check.names) { col_names <- make.names(colnames(x), unique=unique) colnames(x) <- col_names } x } ``` Use case, taking from the `rvest` example above: ``` r HTML %>% html_node('table') %>% html_table() %>% fix_df() %>% tbl_df() ## Source: local data frame [1 x 2] ## Var1 X ## (int) (int) ## 1 1 2 ``` Perhaps, since it is currently just working on column names, it should be named `fix_df_names` or even `fix_df_colnames`.

title: lag inconsistent with base R and clobbers all other uses of lag
description:
`lag` in dplyr clobbers `lag` in base R and also any lag methods.   To make it worse it clobbers it with a function that works differently from `lag` in R reversing the notation of lead and lag.

lag in dplyr should be renamed to Lag or some other name which will not conflict with core R and other packages.

A warning is issued when dplyr is loaded but this inconsistency is so egregious that I don't think that that is sufficient.

Try the following and note the difference.

```
lag(ts(1:4))
library(dplyr)
lag(ts(1:4))
```

Note that zoo and dyn work consistently with R.  lag.xts works the opposite way that R works but at least it just adds an xts method and does not interfere with other methods.  dynlm provides L which is like lag but in the opposite direction which seems ok because it uses a different name.

title: filter() errors when header has empty cell, common with data exported with write.csv
description:
I have same problem as this StackO post: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/31385976/error-attempt-to-use-zero-length-variable-name.  The first response by _hackR_ gave me the clue to look at how `read_csv` and `filter` are related. It appears that filter errors when data that includes rownames without header is read in after `read_csv`; a column of rownames without headers commonly occurs with csv created using `write.csv`. Thus, `readr` reads that column in without a header, and then `filter` errors on the empty header cell while search for the column name to subset by.

In such cases, using read_csv(...) [-1] or read.csv() will get rid of the problem. But maybe there's a filter solution that takes these into account. I've posted this same response at the StackO link.

``` r
# write_csv to read_csv or read.csv
# both work fine with filter
mtcars %>% readr::write_csv("~/Desktop/test.csv")
test_r <-  readr::read_csv("~/Desktop/test.csv") %>% filter(hp>100)
test.r <-  read.csv("~/Desktop/test.csv") %>% filter(hp>100)

# write.csv introduces a column of rownames w/o a header
# and read_csv doesnot add a header but read.csv imputes an X
# thus when filter works on read.csv imports, it has all headers with filled cells
# but filter after read_csv has an empty header cell
mtcars %>% write.csv("~/Desktop/test1.csv")
test1_r <- readr::read_csv("~/Desktop/test1.csv") 
test1_r %>% str() 
test1_r %>% filter(hp>100)

test1.r <- read.csv("~/Desktop/test1.csv")
test1.r %>% str() 
test1.r%>% filter(hp>100)


#error occurs at
#> test1_r %>% filter(hp>100)
Error in filter_impl(.data, dots) : 
  attempt to use zero-length variable name
```

title: non overwriting update set where
description:
In this SO post: 

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/34096162/dplyr-mutate-replace-on-a-subset-of-rows/34096575

it is pointed out that there is no good way to `mutate` on a subset of rows.  In SQL it would be done with something like `update mytable set a = 1, b = 2 where c > 0`  and a, b, c are columns in  mytable.  For dplyr a non-overwriting version would be needed to maintain the functional flavor.

One answer at that link proposes %<>% from magrittr but this is overwriting and not really consistent with the functional nature of dplyr.  

In an answer at the same link, I had posted code and a test run for `mutate_cond` (data frames only) which is like `mutate` but also adds a condition such that the mutate only operates on rows satisfying that condition.

I had also posted there code and a test run for `mutate_last` (data frames only) which is used within `group_by` and is like `mutate` except it only acts on the last group (whereas ordinary `mutate` acts on every group).  Since TRUE > FALSE if we group by a condition it only acts on rows satisfying that condition.   

Yet another another possibility would be to allow `mutate` to specify which group or groups are to be acted on or to have a variation of `mutate` that does this.   Alternately `group_by` could specify which groups are to be acted upon or a `filter`-like command could restrict subsequent commands until it was cancelled.

Something along the above lines would be nice to add to dplyr and would make dplyr more expressive in such cases.

title: choices: new function to be used from within mutate and transmute functions
description:
During creation of new variable using mutate function based on values of other variables, we usually use `ifelse` function as below

```
mutate(df, col2 = ifelse(col1 > 10, "val1", "val2")
```

The problem occurs when there are multiple criteria based on which values are to be assigned to a given variable

```
mutate(df, col2 = ifelse(col1 > 10, "val1", 
                            ifelse(col1 > 100, "val2", 
                            ifelse(col1 > 1000, "val3", "val4"))
```

The above function quickly gets messy and is difficult to comprehend and maintain.

I saw the above discussion in one of the issues (I am not able to trace it out now) and am suggesting a new function `choices` to be used within `mutate` and `transmute` function with the form below which can circumvent the above problem

```
mutate(df, col2 = choices("val1" ~ (col1 > 10), 
                                         "val2" ~ (col1 > 100),
                                         "val3" ~ (col1 > 1000),
                                          escape = "val4"))
```

The implementation of the function is in the [gist link](https://gist.github.com/sumprain/e53e21e58548229bd2d9)

Is it possible to include the code in the package?

Will it be possible to link this issue with the ongoing discussion?

Thanks a lot and keep up the exemplary work going.

title: group_by(), mutate(), and ifelse() give wrong results when combined with factor()
description:
I've run into a situation where in combination with `group_by()`, `mutate(factor(ifelse()))` gives incorrect results. This might be related to at #1036 (and possibly other issues), which is caused by the combination of group_by/mutate, and varying return types from ifelse. However, here I don't understand how ifelse return types could vary, as there are no missing values and data is always character.

The problem goes away if I use `ungroup()`, so the grouping plays a role. For that reason, I first show the issue, and below that, also go through the grouping stage so that it can be reproduced. That's why the whole issue is a bit long. Please bear with me.
## Issue itself

I have a data frame of Stanley Cup Playoff results by series. One column contains the name of the away team, another the name of the home team, and a third one the name of the winning team. I want to detect whether the winner is the home or away team, i.e. to obtain a character vector where each element is either "away" or "home". This is of course easy to do with `ifelse(winner == away, "away", "home")`.

But since the vector will be used as the outcome variable in model training, ultimately I need it as a factor. But if I (within a `mutate()`) wrap the `ifelse()` in a `factor()`, the results are incorrect:

``` r
series
```

```

```

``` r
series <- series %>%
  mutate(winner_character=ifelse(winner == away, "away", "home"),
  winner_factor=factor(ifelse(winner == away, "away", "home")))

```

```

  away   70    0

```

``` r

  filter(winner_character != winner_factor)
```

```

So, in 147/165 = 89% cases it goes right, but in 18 cases the factor gives the wrong result.

In #1036, the problem was inconsistent types for NA returned by ifelse(): logical NA vs numeric NA. But here there are no NAs.
## Workaround 1

If I `ungroup()`, the problem goes away:

``` r
series <- series %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(winner_character=ifelse(winner == away, "away", "home"),
  winner_factor=as.factor(ifelse(winner == away, "away", "home")))
table(series$winner_character, series$winner_factor)
```

```

  away   70    0
  home    0   95
```

Anybody have an idea what I can do further?
## How data frame `series` was generated

For reproducibility, below is how the `series` data frame was generated, including the grouping (the example data file is attached at the bottom):

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(readr)

games <- read_tsv("https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/files/46354/playoffs.txt")

```

It's a table of NHL playoff game results.

I want to group that by series to detect who was the series winner. First, define a function to pick a team:

``` r
team <- function(x) { # x is a character vector of team names
  # when picking a winner, pick the most frequently occurring team
  counts <- sort(table(x), decreasing=TRUE)
  if ((length(counts) > 1) && (counts[1] > counts[2]))
    return(names(counts)[1])
  # but when detecting the away/home team, they can occur an equal number of
  # times, and it that case we want to pick the one that occurs first
  x[1]
}
```

Now, group by series and detect the overall winner and home/away team for each series):

``` r
series <- games %>%
  group_by(season, round, series) %>%
  summarise(away=team(away), home=team(home), winner=team(winner))

Now we have the `series` data frame that was used in the beginning.
## Workaround 2

There is also another way to circumvent the problem. Instead of grouping by `season`, `round`, and `series`, we can concatenate all three together and use that for grouping:

``` r
games2 <- games %>%
  mutate(series=paste(season, round, series, sep="/")) %>%
  select(series, away, home, winner)
series2 <- games2 %>%
  group_by(series) %>%
  summarise(away=team(away), home=team(home), winner=team(winner))
series2 <- series2 %>%
  mutate(winner_character=ifelse(winner == away, "away", "home"),
  winner_factor=factor(ifelse(winner == away, "away", "home")))
table(series2$winner_character, series2$winner_factor)
```

```
       away home
  away   70    0
  home    0   95
```

Again, the problem goes away. So, for some reason the problem occurs when grouping has been done over three variables(character, integer, integer), but not when with only one (character), or when `ungroup()` is used.

title: Somewhat unexpected "invalid subscript type 'double'" when using $
description:
Dear all,

I wanted to add a new column to a data frame with a constant value from a list:

``` r
someVariable <- list(a = 3, b = 5)
dplyr::mutate(mtcars, newColumn = someVariable$a) %>% head
```

This works.

But if a variable of the same name ("a") is present, I get an error:

``` r
someVariable <- list(a = 3, b = 5)
a <- 10
dplyr::mutate(mtcars, newColumn = someVariable$a) %>% head
Error: invalid subscript type 'double'
```

A fix consists in encapsulating the offending call with I():

``` r
someVariable <- list(a = 3, b = 5)
a <- 10
dplyr::mutate(mtcars, newColumn = I(someVariable$a)) %>% head()
```

(edit: this fix might not be advisable as `newColumn` is of class `AsIs` and not of the expected `double`. To avoid the issue, simply store the value into a new variable and use this new variable instead of `someVariable$a` in the call to `dplyr::mutate`.)

This is reminiscent of bug #421 , which is closed.

Whether it's something to fix or not, I leave it up to you but it was a bit maddening to debug (in my case, the variable 'a' was only sometimes present in the global environment, so my tests were passing when run from a separate environment, but not always when run from the console.).

thanks.

title: Better syntax for mutate() than nested "ifelse" functions
description:
All of the dplyr functions make R code more readable except for one pretty common case, conditionally assigning variable values with mutate(). The current syntax is something like:
 `df <- mutate(df, newvar = ifelse(oldvar %in% c("a", "b", "c"), "group1", ifelse(oldvar %in% c("d", "e", "f"), "group2", ifelse(oldvar %in% c("g", "h", "i"), "group3", NA))))`

I saw a question on StackOverflow that gave a much better solution, borrowing from the "mosaic" package: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/24459752/can-dplyr-package-be-used-for-conditional-mutating?rq=1

``` library(mosaic)
df <- mutate(df, newvar = derivedFactor(
  "group1" = oldvar %in% c("a", "b", "c"),
  "group2" = oldvar %in% c("d", "e", "f"),
  "group3" = oldvar %in% c("g", "h", "i"),
  .default = NA
))
```

Could something like this be the default syntax, please? 

Data frame for testing: `df <- data.frame(oldvar = letters)`

title: Support cut for sql databases
description:
The ntile function is the primary way in dplyr to create an index of groups based on the values of some series. However, ntile does not support custom break points. 

Base R has a function called cut that provides similar functionality as ntile, but it can have custom break points be passed to it. Within dplyr, this works for local data frames, but it does not work for SQL databases.

I suggest adding support for cut so that you can create indices with custom break points and SQL databases in dplyr.

title: A better summary function
description:
I think that dplyr would benefit from having a function summarizing the data frame variables. It is surprising that the R base package has nothing better than the `summary` function to provide an overview of a data frame. In dplyr one can look at the data with for example `glimpse` or  `head`, but a concise display of key summary statistics would make data management easier. Summary statistics can provide more information than the raw data. For example one way to see that a join does not work is to look at the number of NA values. 

I have small function `describe()` [available here](https://github.com/bjornerstedt/assist/blob/master/R/describe.R) that shows what I mean. It takes the same arguments as `dplyr::select()`, and produces summary statistics as a data frame. 

```
describe(iris)

##                  mean min max   n   factor
## Sepal.Length 5.843333 4.3 7.9 150         
## Sepal.Width  3.057333 2.0 4.4 150         
## Petal.Length 3.758000 1.0 6.9 150         
## Petal.Width  1.199333 0.1 2.5 150         
## Species      2.000000 1.0 3.0 150 3 levels

describe(iris, matches("Sep"))

##                  mean min max   n
## Sepal.Length 5.843333 4.3 7.9 150
## Sepal.Width  3.057333 2.0 4.4 150
```

The output is not only useful for looking at the data in R. It is also close to what is often shown as Table 1 in journal articles (at least in applied econometrics).

title: Joining data frames with different internal character encodings (UTF-8 vs. latin1) fails
description:
When the join column(s) of two data frames has the same name but different internal encodings, the `dplyr` join functions fail. Example:

```
library(dplyr)
load(file("http://huftis.org/nedlasting/r/dplyr-encoding-join-problem.Rdata"))
```

The two data frames can be joined by the ‘løpenummer’ column:

```
> str(d1)
Classes ‘tbl_df’ and 'data.frame':  6 obs. of  2 variables:
 $ løpenummer: int  1 2 3 4 5 6
 $ foo       : int  176 114 148 154 181 120
> str(d2)
Classes ‘tbl_df’ and 'data.frame':  6 obs. of  2 variables:
 $ løpenummer: int  4 5 6 7 8 9
 $ baz       : int  24 46 45 10 35 16
```

But actually trying to join them fails with an error message:

```
> d1 %>% left_join(d2, by="løpenummer")
Error: cannot join on columns 'løpenummer' x 'løpenummer': index out of bounds 
```

The `left_join()` function does recognise that the data frames can be joined by ‘løpenummer’, but still fails:

```
> d1 %>% left_join(d2)
Joining by: "løpenummer"   
Error: cannot join on columns 'l�penummer' x 'l�penummer': index out of bounds 
```

Note that the ‘ø’ character is different in this error message. (On my system it’s shown as the ‘unknown character’ glyph.)

The two ‘løpenummer’ variables _do_ have the exact same name, as confirmed by:

```
> names(d1)==names(d2)
[1]  TRUE FALSE
```

But the character encoding is different:

```
> Encoding(names(d1))
[1] "UTF-8"   "unknown"
> Encoding(names(d2))
[1] "latin1"  "unknown"
```

I observe this bug on R 3.2.2, with the latest Git version (2015-11-05) of dplyr, on a 64-bits Linux system (though the problem is also present in the released 0.4.3 version in R 3.2.1 on a Windows system).

library(dplyr)

df %>% select(测试)

title: mutate_tbl.sql doesn't support in-place renaming

title: rowwise_df fails when there is some element whose name is the same as some existing function
description:
In the code below, `mean` of `result$mean` seems to be evaluated as `base::mean()`, not the column of a data.frame passed via pipe. I guess this is a problem related to hybrid evaluation.

``` r
iris %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  do(result=list(mean = mean(.$Sepal.Length))) %>%
  summarise(Species, mean=result$mean)
#> Error: invalid subscript type 'closure'
```

Here is a simpler example; the element `n` is interpreted as `dplyr::n()`

``` r
data_frame(x = replicate(5, list(n= 1), simplify = FALSE)) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  summarise(s = x$n)
#> Error: invalid subscript type 'closure'
```

These are OK:

``` r
# Use quotes
data_frame(x = replicate(5, list(n= 1), simplify = FALSE)) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  summarise(s = x$"n")

# Use [[]]
data_frame(x = replicate(5, list(n= 1), simplify = FALSE)) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  summarise(s = x[["n"]])
```

title: filter filtered out my filter!
description:
The general problem is that dplyr's exported `filter` function tramples over `stats::filter`. This is all fine and good in the context of a workspace/interactive session, because we are at least told as much:

```
R> library(dplyr)
Attaching package: 'dplyr'

The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

    filter, lag
```

But this also tramples calls to `filter` that are invoked within other packages that were previously loaded.

For instance, the [limma bioconductor package](http://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/limma.html), calls `filter` in its `tricubeMovingAverage` function, but `dplyr` will hose it:

```
R> library(dplyr)
R> library(limma)
R> tricubeMovingAverage(rnorm(100))
Error in UseMethod("filter_") :
  no applicable method for 'filter_' applied to an object of class "c('double', 'numeric')"
```

One way to get around this issue is to ask the limma authors (and who knows what other packages call `filter` assuming they will get `stats::filter`) to explicitly call `stats::filter`, or import `stats` in their `NAMESPACE`, however I can also imagine that a package author might be surprised to have to explicitly import functions from `base`, `stats`, etc. that they would (should(?)) reasonably expect to be available to them without special consideration.

So I'm left wondering what other options are available here? Unfortunately there is no alternate British spelling of the word filter that I'm aware of, which would have made this a bit easier :-)

Would promoting `filter` to an S3 generic in dplyr's `NAMESPACE` be one way to get around this problem? I could then imagine having `dplyr::filter` dispatch down to `stats::filter` if it's not called on a `tbl_df` (or `data.frame`, or whatever).

Or, perhaps, define a `filter_.numeric` (or `filter_.default`(?)) function which sends all the right arguments over to `stats::filter`

title: logic behind sql_translate(1e-10) == sql("0.0")?
description:
Even though Postgres can handle arbitrary floating point numbers, sql_translate converts small but reasonable floating point numbers to zero.

If `is.wholenumber(x)` then `sql_translate` evaluates `x` as `sprintf("%.1f", x)`.

I found this logic surprising. Is there a reason for this behaviour? If so, perhaps it could be documented more prominently?

title: how to properly support db functions in backends
description:
I am trying to thoroughly support database builtin functions in a couple of [backends](http://github.com/piccolbo/dplyr.spark.hive) I am working on. It's not clear to me which functions should be listed as aggregates and which as window functions. Looking at base_agg and base_win I see max, min, n, sum and mean are listed in both. I also saw a test that a select contains a win function affects how queries are built (use OVER PARTITION BY or not), but I don't see any of that sort for aggregate functions. I can build this somewhat artificial example

```
> (flights  %>% transmute(SUM(arr_delay)))
Source: Spark at:localhost:10000
From: flights [1 x 1]

  sum(arr_delay)
           (dbl)
1        2257174
> (flights  %>% transmute(sum(arr_delay)))
Source: Spark at:localhost:10000
From: <derived table> [?? x 1]

   sum(arr_delay)
            (dbl)
1         2257174
2         2257174
3         2257174
4         2257174
```

Since the database is case insensitive, `sum` and `SUM` are the same thing. But dplyr builds an OVER query in the latter case, but not in the former and that to the best of my understanding is because `SUM` is not listed among win functions but `sum` is and R is case sensitive. Moreover, exactly how to build the related entries for sql_variant is not very clear to me, and I just copied and modified the dplyr own src. Can we have a dedicated piece of documentation on this issue for backend devs? Or can we just make every function a window function by default and make the whole problem go away? It's pretty tedious with hundreds of built ins. Thanks

title: copy_to for PostgreSQLConnections fails for copying large tables to databases
description:
SUMMARY:
Add a `fast` parameter to `copy_to` so that for PostgreSQLConnections, it uses `RPostgreSQL::postgresqlCopyInDataframe` rather than `INSERT INTO ...`.

EXAMPLE:

```
library(dplry)
library(RPostgreSQL)
data_repo <- src_postgres(...)
n <- 10000000
df <- data.frame(x=1:n, y=runif(n))
system.time({data_repo %>% copy_to(df, "test_tbl")})
```

returns this:

```
 Error in postgresqlExecStatement(conn, statement, ...) :
   RS-DBI driver: (could not Retrieve the result : server closed the connection unexpectedly
         This probably means the server terminated abnormally
         before or while processing the request.
 )
 Error: C stack usage  308954544 is too close to the limit
 Error in postgresqlExecStatement(conn, statement, ...) :
   RS-DBI driver: (could not run statement: no connection to the server
 )
 Timing stopped at: 350.127 37.36 551.529
```

DIAGNOSING THE PROBLEM:
`db_insert_into`, called by `copy_to`, attempts to create a string of the values to insert,

```
values <- paste0("(", rows, ")", collapse = "\n, ")
```

This can be slow and consume lots of memory, causing `copy_to` to fail for copying tables of millions of rows to a database.

PROPOSED SOLUTION:
Its recognized that the fastest way to insert data into a Postgres database is to use the `COPY` command (http://stackoverflow.com/questions/758945/whats-the-fastest-way-to-do-a-bulk-insert-into-postgres). Indeed, `RPostgreSQL` has a poorly documented command `postgresqlCopyInDataframe` that does just that.

Adding a `fast` argument to `copy_to` and replacing the `db_insert_into(con, name, df)` line in `copy_to.src_postgres` with with this:

```
if(fast){
  #http://james.hiebert.name/blog/work/2011/10/24/RPostgreSQL-and-COPY-IN/
  #warning this doesn't report any errors on failure!
  field_names <- escape(ident(names(types)), collapse = NULL, con = con)
  fields <- dplyr:::sql_vector(field_names, parens = TRUE, collapse = ", ", con = con)
  sql <- build_sql(
    "COPY ", ident(name), " ", fields, " FROM STDIN;",
    con=con)
  dbSendQuery(con, sql)
  postgresqlCopyInDataframe(con, df)
} else {
  db_insert_into(con, name, df)
}
```

Then calling

```
system.time({data_repo %>% copy_to(df, "test_tbl", fast=T)})
```

return the impressively fast time of

```
    user  system elapsed
   9.906   0.368  13.788
```

Since `postgresqlCopyInDataframe` currently doesn't do very good error reporting (http://james.hiebert.name/blog/work/2011/10/24/RPostgreSQL-and-COPY-IN/), it's probably best to make it optional rather than the default.

title: False positive table already exists error with Postgres schemas
description:
SUMMARY:
    `db_has_table.PostgresSQLConnection` returns true when a table exists a schema that that is not on the search path, making `dplry::copy_to()` fail when it doesn't need to.

EXAMPLE:

```
library(dplyr)
library(DBI)
data_repo <- src_postgres(...)
con <- data_repo$con

# create decoy table in schema1
dbGetQuery(con, "CREATE SCHEMA schema1;")
dbGetQuery(con, "SET search_path TO \"$user\",schema1,public;")
dbGetQuery(con, "CREATE TABLE my_table (key INTEGER);")

# try to use dplyr::copy_to to create my_table in schema2
dbGetQuery(con, "CREATE SCHEMA schema2;")
dbGetQuery(con, "SET search_path TO \"$user\",schema1,public;")
my_table <- data.frame(key=c(1,2,3))
data_repo %>% copy_to(my_table, temporary=F)
## fails saying that my_table already exists.
```

DIAGNOSING THE ISSUE:
Before copying, `copy_to.sql_src` first checks if the table exists,

```
if (isTRUE(db_has_table(dest$con, name))) {
  stop("Table ", name, " already exists.", call. = FALSE)
}
```

Here, `db_has_table(con, name)` checks if `name` is in `db_list_tables(con)`. But `db_list_tables(con)` calls `DBI::dbListTable`, which returns tables in all schemas, not just the visible ones.

PROPOSED SOLUTION:
Make a `db_list_tables.PostgreSQLConnection` that instead calls

```
dbGetQuery(
    con,
    "SELECT relname FROM pg_class WHERE relkind IN ('r', 'v') AND pg_table_is_visible(oid);")[,1]
```

Using `pg_table_is_visible` is idiomatic for PostgreSQL (http://stackoverflow.com/questions/5062533/postgres-select-all-tables-in-the-current-search-path), and also returns temporary tables.

title: Type error when all values in group are NA when using group_by + mutate + ifelse
description:
This is probably related a bunch of issues (#958, #1432, #1381, for example) that produce "incompatible types" errors. When making a logical test in a `mutate(x = ifelse(...))` statement after defining a group, _if_ every value of `x` in that group is NA, dplyr will complain about variable types. This does not happen outside of groups:

```
example.df <- data_frame(group_id = rep(1:5, each=10),
                         year = rep(2001:2010, times=5),
                         x1 = rep(c(rnorm(9), NA), times=5)) %>%
  bind_rows(data_frame(group_id = 6, year = 2001:2010, x1 = NA))

# This works:
example.df %>%
  mutate(x2 = ifelse(x1 > 1, 1, 0))

# This doesn't;
example.df %>%
  group_by(group_id) %>%
  mutate(x2 = ifelse(x1 > 1, 1, 0))
# Yields: "Error: incompatible types, expecting a numeric vector"
```

The best workaround for now is to either avoid `mutate(ifelse())` calls inside groups, or to explicitly wrap `ifelse` statements with `as.numeric`, like so:

```
# This works:
example.df %>%
  group_by(group_id) %>%
  mutate(x2 = as.numeric(ifelse(x1 > 1, 1, 0)))
```

title: Repeated joining can cause duplicated column names
description:
Join operations add suffixes to avoid duplicated column names for (non-joining) columns. However, for repeated joining of similar data frames, duplicated column names can still occur. Example:

```
d1 = data.frame(id=1:5, foo=rnorm(5))
d2 = data.frame(id=1:5, foo=rnorm(5))
d3 = data.frame(id=1:5, foo=rnorm(5))

d = d1 %>% left_join(d1, by="id") %>%
  left_join(d2, by="id") %>% 
  left_join(d3, by="id")
```

This results in duplicated column names

```

description:

toy data

``` r
library(dplyr)

foo <- 
  data.frame(id = c(1,1,2,2,3,3), 
             date_of_x = as.Date(c("2015-01-01", "2015-01-02", NA, "2015-02-02",
                           NA,NA)),
             type = c("A","B","A","B","A","B")) %>% tbl_df

foo

     id  date_of_x   type
  (dbl)     (date) (fctr)
1     1 2015-01-01      A
2     1 2015-01-02      B
3     2       <NA>      A
4     2 2015-02-02      B
5     3       <NA>      A
6     3       <NA>      B
```

0.4.2

``` r
foo %>% group_by(id) %>% 
  summarise(most_recent = max(date_of_x, na.rm=TRUE),
            confirmed = !is.na(most_recent))

Source: local data frame [3 x 3]

  id most_recent confirmed
1  1  2015-01-02      TRUE
2  2  2015-02-02      TRUE
3  3        <NA>     FALSE

```

in 0.4.3: 

``` r
foo %>% group_by(id) %>% 
  summarise(most_recent = max(date_of_x, na.rm=TRUE),
            confirmed = !is.na(most_recent))

Source: local data frame [3 x 3]

    id most_recent confirmed
(dbl)      (date)     (lgl)
1     1  2015-01-02      TRUE
2     2  2015-02-02      TRUE
3     3        <NA>      TRUE
Warning message:
In max.default(c(NA_real_, NA_real_), na.rm = TRUE) :
 no non-missing arguments to max; returning -Inf

in 0.4.3, it returns a value of class Inf and in 0.4.2 one of class NA

Change is consistent with the behavior of max I guess but it broke some workflows (maybe just mine but I am unsure if i could just replace is.na with is.infinite and fix everything).  

May be working as it should, although im confused why it changed at all (i.e. why the previous one worked).

title: Unclear limitations on the calculations that can be performed in mutate.
description:
I’d like to use `mutate` to create a new column but the calculations are not entirely trivial.  Here is one example illustrating the kind of things I would like to do:

``` R
d %>%
  group_by(tid) %>%
  mutate(before.event = {
    idx <- which(diff(chars) < 0)[1]
     c(rep(T, idx), rep(F, n()-idx))
  })
```

This code produces an error message saying that assignments are forbidden.  So I tried the following work-around:

``` R

f <- function(x) {
  idx <- which(diff(x) < 0)[1]
  c(rep(T, idx), rep(F, n()-idx))
}

d %>%
  group_by(tid) %>%
  mutate(before.event = f(chars))
```

but this also produces an error message:

```
Error: This function should not be called directly
```

This is fairly surprising because I can of course use other functions in mutate, e.g:

``` R
d %>%
  group_by(tid) %>%
  mutate(test = min(chars))
```

I looked in various places for an explanation but couldn’t find one (man pages, GitHub page, introduction to dplyr, …).  There clearly seem to be limitations as to which things can be done and which functions can be used but it is not clear what these limitations are.  This can be of course be a little discouraging for new users.  So I’d say there is at least a documentation issue here.

While this issue could be addressed by improving the documentation, it would of course be much better if there weren’t any limitations in the first place.  I can think of many situations where it would be extremely useful if assignments and user-defined functions were allowed.  I really like dplyr's interface but the ability to use arbitrary code-blocks to carry out calculations in conjunction with `mutate` but also `summarise` would clearly set dplyr apart from alternative solutions like reshape and data.table.

title: rowwise() giving incorrect result in some situations
description:
Hi guys.  Granted that this is not generally a row-wise operation, I still think it would be good to bring to your attention.  The issue came about on Stack Overflow, where an error was discovered in the resulting data frame.

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/33090745/dplyrrowwise-mutate-and-na-error

A minimal example is as follows

```
data.frame(k = c(-1, 1, 1)) %>% 
    rowwise() %>% 
    mutate(l = ifelse(k > 0, 1, NA))
Source: local data frame [3 x 2]
Groups: <by row>

      k     l
  (dbl) (dbl)
1    -1    NA
2     1     1
3     1    NA
```

We believe that  row 3, column `l` should be 1, not NA as shown.

If you run the following code a few separate times, you will find that the incident above only occurs intermittently.

```
data.frame(k = rnorm(10)) %>% 
    rowwise() %>% 
    mutate(l = ifelse(k > 0, 1L, NA_integer_))
```

title: purrr's lambda function doesn't work correctly in dplyr::mutate()
description:
(I originally reported this issue in https://github.com/hadley/purrr/issues/103)

When I tried [this example of purrr](http://blog.rstudio.org/2015/09/29/purrr-0-1-0/), I found the code sometimes fails with the following error:

``` r
#> Error: invalid term in model formula
```

The error above seems to occur when ggplot2 is loaded. A minimal code to reproduce the issue is bellow.

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
d <- data_frame(training = list(mtcars, mtcars * 2))

# before ggplot2 is loaded, no error occurs
d %>%
  mutate(lm_result = map(training, ~ lm(mpg ~ wt, data = .)))
#> Source: local data frame [2 x 2]
#> 
#>               training lm_result
#>                 (list)    (list)
#> 1 <data.frame [32,11]>   <S3:lm>
#> 2 <data.frame [32,11]>   <S3:lm>

# after ggplot2, the very same code results in the error of `lm()`
library(ggplot2)
d %>%
  mutate(lm_result = map(training, ~ lm(mpg ~ wt, data = .)))
#> Error: invalid term in model formula
```

After some investigation, I found the `.f` is translated differently. But, I couldn't specify the cause...

``` r
debug_map <- function(.x, .f, ...) {print(.f); return(TRUE)}

library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
d <- data_frame(training = list(mtcars, mtcars * 2))

d %>%
  mutate(lm_result = debug_map(training, ~ lm(mpg ~ wt, data = .)))
#> ~lm(mpg ~ wt, data = .)
#> ...snip...

library(ggplot2)
d %>%
  mutate(lm_result = debug_map(training, ~ lm(mpg ~ wt, data = .)))
#> ~lm(list(manufacturer = c("audi", "audi", ...), model = c("a4", "a4", ...), displ = c(1.8, 1.8, ...), ...) ~ wt, data = .)
#> ...snip...

# If I use function(), it works fine
d %>%
  mutate(lm_result = debug_map(training, function(x) lm(mpg ~ wt, data = x)))
#> function(x) lm(mpg ~ wt, data = x)
#> ...snip...
```

title: slice(df,n) for n > nrow(df) inconsistency when using data.tables
description:
In [this SO post](http://stackoverflow.com/a/33045588/1191259), I noticed this difference:

```
df<-data.frame(Initials=c("a","a","b"),data=c(2,3,4))
my_rows = 1:2

df %>% group_by(Initials) %>% slice(my_rows)
#   Initials  data
#     (fctr) (dbl)
#1        a     2
#2        a     3
#3        b     4

library(data.table)
setDT(df) %>% group_by(Initials) %>% slice(my_rows)
#   Initials  data
#     (fctr) (dbl)
#1        a     2
#2        a     3
#3        b     4
#4        b    NA
```

Personally, I'd prefer to see the latter behavior and think it's more in keeping with standard R behavior, e.g., in `(3:1)[c(5,6)]`. However, based on https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/issues/1269 , I think it clashes with your design goals.

In any case, the two cases should give the same result if dplyr is to play nice with data.table objects.

title: filter() with an interior lag() operation fails on a factor column
description:
In this example, filter() logic using lag() appears to work fine on a factor **outside** of the dplyr filter() environment, but when used inside filter(), it is not providing the expected result:

``` r
# R 3.2.2 on Windows 7
# dplyr 0.4.2

library(dplyr)

#a data frame with Who as a character and Event as a factor
df_broken <- data.frame(Observation=c(1,2,3),Who=c("A","A","B"),Event=as.factor(c("R","S","R")),stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
#check structure
str(df_broken)

#the same data frame with both Who and Event as character
df_works <- data.frame(Observation=c(1,2,3),Who=c("A","A","B"),Event=c("R","S","R"),stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
#check structure
str(df_works)

#on the all-character representation, we successfully filter out the middle row with the logic as shown
answer_works <- df_works %>% filter(!(Event=="S" & lag(Event)=="R" & Who==lag(Who)))
#only two rows
answer_works

#when the lag(Event)=="R" check is now on a factor, all rows are returned
answer_broken <- df_broken %>% filter(!(Event=="S" & lag(Event)=="R" & Who==lag(Who)))
#Hmmm...still have all three rows?
answer_broken

#However, the same logic on the factor variable *outside of the filter() command* seems to be fine
flag <- !(df_broken$Event=="S" & lag(df_broken$Event)=="R" & df_broken$Who==lag(df_broken$Who))
#the middle entry of flag is FALSE
flag
```

title: Poor performance on dates compared to base R
description:
I've been using dplyr with lubridate-parsed date values. Everything is functional, but performance pales in comparison to base R when I've run the two side-by-side. If I'm doing a summarise or mutate to get the #of days between transactions, I could run:

``` r
df <- df %>% 
  group_by(PERSON_ID) %>% 
  mutate(DAYS_TO_LAST_TX = (TX_DATE - lag(TX_DATE) / edays(1)))
```

This code takes a while to run, whereas I could write equivalent base-R code and get it done much quicker, but with more lines of code.

title: An option to retain non-duplicated rows for function distinct
description:
Here is an enhancement.

From the manual of **distinct**: If there are multiple rows for a given combination of inputs, only the first row will be preserved.

It's useful only to get the non-duplicated rows (based a column) for function **distinct**. Here the non-duplicated rows is not as same as _unique_ because _unique_ keeps non-duplicated rows and representatives for duplicated rows. the problem for unique is the data is not true or paradoxical for the duplicated rows. 

For example:

a 1
b 1
c 2
s 4

distinct (only for 2nd column) will get 

a 1
c 2
s 4

distinct with the proposed option (only for 2nd column) will get 

c 2
s 4

Thank you.

title: Is select_impl() overly conservative regarding duplicate colnames?
description:
At https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/blob/master/src/select.cpp#L74 select_impl() checks whether there are duplicate column names and stops, if there are. Is this too conservative?

Suppose I've read in data in some way that results in duplicated column names (readxl or forced names, as below). There are colnames that are duplicates. I want to select some subset of columns that (at least potentially) doesn't include any of the duplicated columns.

``` r
df <- read.csv(text = "a,a,b
1,2,3")

colnames(df) <- c("a", "a", "b")

dplyr::select(df, b)
```

> Error: found duplicated column name: a

What bad things would happen were select_impl() less restrictive? Suppose a new rule that only the colnames you're selecting had to be unique within the data.frame. E.g., given colnames == "a", "a", "b", you would only be able to select column "b" without an error.

One could go further and say that select_impl() would select all columns with matching names... but that's probably too unintuitive and likely to result in unexpected results for casual users.

title: Support for Bioconductor DataFrame class?
description:
The Bioconductor project has their own implementation of data.frame in S4 called DataFrame, which basically works like a regular data.frame except that it can hold Bioconductor's S4 vector types such as Rle, List, and GRanges that cannot be stored as columns an ordinary data frame. What would be required to add support for the DataFrame class to dplyr operations? I would be willing to try my hand at it if it's not too complicated.

The following works as a quick an dirty implementation of mutate for DataFrame objects, but it only works if the conversion from DataFrame to data.frame succeeds. This would prevents it from working on any DataFrame containing S4 vector columns, which kind of defeats the point. 

``` R
mutate_.DataFrame <- function(.data, ..., .dots) {
    .data %>% as.data.frame %>% mutate_(.data=., ..., .dots=.dots) %>% as("DataFrame")
}
```

(Technically, this will succeed for some S4 vector columns that define coercions to primitive vectors/lists on conversion to a data.frame, but this is suboptimal because those columns would not be converted back to their original class by `as("DataFrame")`.)

description:
When I pipe a `data.table` into `mutate`, it returns nothing and breaks the rest of the chain.

I just observed this morning for the first time and I'm afraid I'm at a loss to pinpoint the specific change that caused it. I'm inclined to believe it was the `data.table` update to 1.9.6 that happened Sept 19, but I can't be sure.

 library(data.table)

title: dplyr verbs removing additional classes
description:
I'm building a package to work with objects that are a special case of a `tbl_df` in which there is 'interval' information in the columns (i.e. one column for `start` of interval and one column for `end` of interval). 

I have a constructor that adds a class to an existing `data.frame` or `tbl_df` (and some attributes too). But it seems that `dplyr` verbs like to remove any classes that I add. 

For example:

``` r
add_class <- function(x,name) {class(x) <- c(class(x),name); x}
```

``` r
df <- mtcars %>% add_class('something_new')
df %>% class()
[1] "data.frame"    "something_new"
```

But dplyr verbs strip the new class...

``` r
df %>% arrange(mpg) %>% class()
[1] "data.frame"
> df %>% filter(mpg > 30) %>% class()
[1] "data.frame"
> df %>% tbl_df() %>% class()
[1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
```

I notice that dplyr 0.4.3 now preserves attributes, but it looks like classes are still getting eaten. 

Is this something that's on anyone's radar? I haven't been able to find an issue for it.

title: Columns shouldn't be visible after `select` in SQL backends
description:
(apologies if this is a dupe, but I couldn't find the original)

Currently, for some SQL backends (at least `sqlite`), columns are still visible for `filter`ing after a `select`, eg

```
src_sqlite(path='Databases.db') %>% tbl("Databases") %>% select(id, name) %>% filter(description != 'temp')
```

will still filter on the `description` column, even though it should no longer be visible. This works as expected for dataframes:

```
> df <- data_frame(x = runif(10), y = x*2)
> df %>% select(a = x) %>% filter(y > 1)
Error: object 'y' not found
```

One option here is to just `collapse` inside `select`, though it's not clear whether that would put too much pressure on the query optimizer.

title: lead/lag inside mutate: doesn't accept single-element vector as default value
description:
When using `lead` or `lag` inside `mutate`, setting `default` as a length-one vector results in an error:

``` r
mutate(data_frame(x = 1:3), lead(x, default = x[1]))
#> Error: expecting a single value
```

This happens even when the vector isn't a slice of the data frame column:

``` r
mutate(data_frame(x = 1:3), lead(x, default = 1))
#> Source: local data frame [3 x 2]
#> 
#>       x lead(x, default = 1)
#>   (int)                (int)
#> 1     1                    2
#> 2     2                    3
#> 3     3                    1
mutate(data_frame(x = 1:3), lead(x, default = c(1)))
#> Error: expecting a single value
```

And it doesn't happen outside `mutate`:

``` r
x <- 1:3
lead(x, default = x[1])
#> [1] 2 3 1
lead(x, default = c(1))
#> [1] 2 3 1
```

Also fine when you assign the first element of the vector to a variable first:

``` r
d <- data_frame(x = 1:3)
dx1 <- d$x[1]
mutate(d, lead(x, default = dx1))
#> Source: local data frame [3 x 2]
#> 
#>       x lead(x, default = dx1)
#>   (int)                  (int)
#> 1     1                      2
#> 2     2                      3
#> 3     3                      1
```

If I'm not mistaken, this started happening after upgrading to 0.4.3. (I had code that relied on this behavior that started erroring after upgrading).  For what it's worth, the reason I want to do this at all is to do a wrapped lead/lag separately for different subsets of rows in a data frame.  So the desired behavior (which was working before the upgrade) is:

``` r
data_frame(x = rep(1:2, each = 3), y = 1:6) %>% 
    group_by(x) %>% 
    mutate(y_wrapped = lead(y, default = first(y)))

title: group_by fails when column names contains swedish characters
description:
Short summary: If columns of a data frame is selected with dplyr::subset(), group_by() can't handle column names with swedish characters (å,ä,ö,Å,Ä,Ö)

Example code here what's working and what's not.

```

# Script to show how dplyr::select() breakes dplyr::group_by() with swedish names
library(dplyr)

# Create data frame, column 1's name contains ä (specific swedish letters are åäöÅÄÖ)
my_df <- data.frame(användarnamn = letters[1:4], my_numvalues = 1:4, 
                    my_text = c("stop","break","my","code"),
                    extra_col = LETTERS[1:4])

# use dplyr::select() to subset columns, then dplyr::group_by
# group_by fails on swedish column names if the df is subsetted with filter.
# If not subsetted or subsetted with [,1:3], everything works

my_df %>% select(1:3) %>% group_by(my_numvalues)   # This works
my_df %>% select(1:3) %>% group_by(användarnamn)   # This fails
my_df[,1:3] %>% group_by(användarnamn)             # This works
my_df %>% group_by(användarnamn)                   # This works

# Same thing, but step by step
my_df_selected <- select(my_df, 1:3)
group_by(my_df_selected, användarnamn)             # This fails
group_by(my_df_selected, my_numvalues)             # This works

# and by %>% 
my_df_selected %>% group_by(användarnamn)          # This fails
my_df_selected %>% group_by(my_numvalues)          # This works

# The names of the orignal df and the filtered is identical
identical(names(my_df)[1:3],names(my_df_selected))
# The function base::make.names() doesn't change the name, it's already valid
identical(names(my_df_selected), make.names(names(my_df_selected)))

# copy to a new df to rename
my_df_selected_renamed <- my_df_selected
# rename the df with it's own old names passing make.names()
names(my_df_selected_renamed) <- make.names(names(my_df_selected_renamed))

# The orignal subsetted and the renamed df is identical
# according to base::identical()
identical(my_df_selected, my_df_selected_renamed)

# Here's the strange thing, it works now! Why??? I REALLY don't understand!
