title: Left Join Not Recognizing Type Errors in 0.2
description:
There seems to be an issue with the left_join command not recognizing numeric/integer typing differences. The weirdest part about it is that inner_join works fine, and that even the left_join problem goes away when the variables are sorted slightly differently. I've tested this on my Toshiba laptop as well as two RHEL research grids that I use.

``` R
library(dplyr)

# R Version 3.0.2
# dplyr version 0.2

mergeVars = c('id1', 'yr', 'id2')

# Should throw an error
left_join(data.frame(id = as.integer(1)), data.frame(id = as.numeric(1)))

f1 = data.frame(id1 = as.integer(85814), 
                yr = as.integer(2003:2005), 
                id2 = as.integer(10612))
f2 = data.frame(id1 = as.numeric(85814), 
                yr = as.numeric(c(2004, 2006, 2005, 2003)), 
                id2 = as.integer(10612), 
                val = as.numeric(5961))


f2Prime = data.frame(id1 = as.numeric(85814), 
                     yr = as.numeric(c(2003:2006)),
                     id2 = as.integer(10612), 
                     val = as.numeric(5961))

print(str(f1))
# 'data.frame':  3 obs. of  3 variables:
#   $ id1: int  85814 85814 85814
# $ yr : int  2003 2004 2005
# $ id2: int  10612 10612 10612
# NULL

print(str(f2))
# 'data.frame':  4 obs. of  4 variables:
#   $ id1     : num  85814 85814 85814 85814
# $ yr      : num  2004 2006 2005 2003
# $ id2     : int  10612 10612 10612 10612
# $ pri_dnum: num  5961 5961 5961 5961

print(str(f2Prime))
# 'data.frame':  4 obs. of  4 variables:
#   $ id1     : num  85814 85814 85814 85814
# $ yr      : num  2003 2004 2005 2006
# $ id2     : int  10612 10612 10612 10612
# $ pri_dnum: num  5961 5961 5961 5961
# NULL

print('Left Join')
print(left_join(f1, f2, by = mergeVars))
# [1] "Left Join"
# id1   yr   id2 val
#1 85814 2003 10612       NA
#2 85814 2004 10612       NA
#3 85814 2005 10612     5961

print('Left Join with Sorted Year')
print(left_join(f1, f2Prime, by = mergeVars))
# [1] "Left Join with Sorted Year"
# id1   yr   id2 val
#1 85814 2003 10612     5961
#2 85814 2004 10612     5961
#3 85814 2005 10612     5961

print('Inner Join')
print(inner_join(f1, f2, by = mergeVars))
# [1] "Inner Join"
# id1   yr   id2 val
#1 85814 2004 10612     5961
#2 85814 2005 10612     5961
#3 85814 2003 10612     5961

print('Merge')
print(merge(f1, f2, by = mergeVars, all.x = T, all.y = F))
# [1] "Merge"
# id1   yr   id2 val
#1 85814 2003 10612     5961
#2 85814 2004 10612     5961
#3 85814 2005 10612     5961
```

title: Mutate fails with incompatible type error
description:
Hello, (? related to [#390](https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/issues/390) )

Not sure if this is in fact a dplyr problem or a potential problem with "ifelse" inside mutate (or just me). I have a dataset with an "id" field (id_patients = numeric), operation date (opdate = posix date), and an interval which is numeric (pdfs_value). When the data is grouped by id, an attempt to mutate a new variable that is the sum of the opdate + pdfs_value fails with a type error.

Test data:

| id_patients | opdate | pdfs_value |
| --: | :-- | --: |
| 3 | 2007-01-10 | 761 |
| 3 | 2009-03-03 | 1345 |
| 4 | 2006-12-28 | 956 |
| 4 | 2007-04-05 | 858 |
| 4 | 2009-10-01 | 263 |
| 4 | 2010-07-12 | 214 |

``` r
Classes ‘grouped_df’, ‘tbl_df’, ‘tbl’ and 'data.frame': 6 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ id_patients: int  3 3 4 4 4 4
 $ opdate     : Date, format: "2007-01-10" "2009-03-03" "2006-12-28" ...

 - attr(*, "vars")=List of 1
  ..$ : symbol id_patients

```

``` r
test <-  data %>% group_by(id_patients) %>% mutate(pdfs_new = ifelse(opdate+pdfs_value>lead(opdate,1), lead(opdate, 1), opdate+pdfs_value))
Error: incompatible types, expecting a numeric vector
```

Removing the grouping lets the mutate work (although the date object is not preserved, but this is not a big deal) - but of course without the grouping, I do not get the desired effect.

``` r
test <- ungroup(new) %>% mutate(pdfs_new = ifelse(opdate+pdfs_value>lead(opdate,1), lead(opdate, 1), opdate+pdfs_value))
test$pdfs_new <- as.Date(test$pdfs_new, origin=origin)
```

| 4 | 2007-04-05 | 858 | 2009-08-10 |
| 4 | 2009-10-01 | 263 | 2010-06-21 |
| 4 | 2010-07-12 | 214 | 2006-10-12 |

From memory, this was not happening just a few weeks ago (sorry I haven't got a tighter time frame).

I know there are issues with the return from ifelse such as this on [SO](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/6668963/how-to-prevent-ifelse-from-turning-date-objects-into-numeric-objects) but this looks to be a different problem?

title: Granular class
description:
``` s
#' A granular variable.
#'
#' This function is chiefly used to provide extra knowledge about your data
#' to visualisation packages.
#'
#' @section Methods:
#' The granular class only provides methods for \code{\link{as.data.frame}}
#' and \code{\link{"["}}. These ensure that the resolution is not lost in
#' common situations, but no effort has been made to compute the correct
#' resolution of arithmetic or Math operations.
#'
#' @param x A numeric vector.
#' @param res The resolution of the vector. If not specified, will be
#'   estimated from the data. This is generally unsafe, in the same way
#'   guessing factor levels from data is unsafe.
#' @export
#' @examples
#' x <- granular(c(1, 3, 5))
#' x
#' y <- granular(c(1, 3, 5), 1)
#' y
granular <- function(x, res = resolution(x)) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(x))

  attr(x, "resolution") <- res
  class(x) <- c("granular", class(x))

  x
}

#' @export
print.granular <- function(x, ...) {
  print(as.vector(x))
  cat("Resolution: ", attr(x, "resolution"), "\n", sep = "")
}

#' @export
as.data.frame.granular <- function(x, ...) {
  df <- list(x)
  attr(df, "row.names") <- .set_row_names(length(x))
  class(df) <- c("data.frame")

  df
}

#' @export
"[.granular" <- function(x, ...) {
  granular(NextMethod(), attr(x, "resolution"))
}

#' @export
resolution <- function(x) UseMethod("resolution")
#' @export
resolution.granular <- function(x) attr(x, "resolution")
#' @export
resolution.integer <- function(x) 1L
#' @export
resolution.numeric <- function(x) min(diff(sort(x)), na.rm = TRUE)

x <- granular(1:10)
```

title: [FR] data.table::tables() equivalent
description:
It would be vey useful to have a `tables()` equivalent/extension in `dplyr` leveraging all the different classes `dplyr` employs. This would become very useful for multi `tbl` projects where memory is/may be limiting. 

```
library(data.table)
library(dplyr)

dt1 <- data.table(x=sample(c(T,F),1e6,T),y= rnorm(1e6))
dt2 <- CJ(letters,letters,1:10000)
df_tbl1 <- tbl_df(copy(dt1))
grp_tbl_dt <- tbl_dt(copy(dt2)) %>% group_by(V1,V2)

tables()    # NOTE:  df_tbl1 is missing!

# NAME            NROW  MB COLS     KEY     
# [1,] dt1        1,000,000  12 x,y              
# [2,] dt2        6,760,000 129 V1,V2,V3 V1,V2,V3
# [3,] grp_tbl_dt 6,760,000 129 V1,V2,V3 V1,V2   
# Total: 270MB
```

In  projects where one may have reference `tbl`s with `rle` encoding information for relevant (grouping) columns, index `tbl`s with bootstrap indices and the data `tbl`s with only measured values using tables() is useful to know which joins I need to make when I perform a summary.

title: Infix operator as a shortcut for subsetting
description:
I often want to subset a column of a data.frame after operating on it. Now that dplyr does not use %.%, I think it would be great to have it as a shortcut for subsetting a column and possibly simplify it to a vector.

If we have for example,

```
"%.%" <- function(x, col) x[[col]]
```

we could do:

```
data %.% "colname"
```

This would be useful because we cannot use $ or [ to subset the end result of a series of piping.

I like the dot metaphor because it conveys the idea of reduction.

Note that I'm still not sure what would be the most useful, a simplifying operator (returns a vector instead of a data.frame), or a preserving one (subsets through "select" and returns a data.frame). Maybe we should have both, implemented in two infix operators.

title: top_n parameter 'wt' does not work
description:
Something is broken in the substitution of the wt parameter in the top_n helper function.

```
> iris %.%
+  group_by(Species) %.%
+  summarise(w=mean(Petal.Width)) %.%
+  top_n(1, w)
Error in top_n(`__prev`, 1, w) : object 'w' not found
```

The equivalent spelled out with `filter(rank(...))` works fine

```
> iris %.%
+  group_by(Species) %.%
+  summarise(w=mean(Petal.Width)) %.%
+  filter(rank(w) <= 1)
Source: local data frame [1 x 2]

  Species     w
1  setosa 0.246
```

My experience with R at this level is limited, but I'm pretty sure the problem is that we're evaluating `is.null(wt)` at the beginning of the function; and adding `wt <- substitute(wt)` at the beginning will defer the evaluation sufficiently for this to work.  EDIT: or using `missing(wt)` instead of `is.null(wt)`

title: Function to replace values for specific rows
description:
I wonder if there is a possibility to add a general function to change values only for specific rows that satisfy a filter condition? Here is a simple example of such a function, I have in mind:

```
replace.if = function(.data,...,.if=NULL) {

  .if = substitute(.if)
  if (!is.null(.if)) {
    rows = eval(.if,.data)
    d = .data[rows,]
    d = mutate(d,...)
    .data[rows,] = d
  } else {
    .data = mutate(.data,...)
  }
  .data
}
# Examples
library(dplyr)
dat = cars[1:10,]
replace.if(dat, dist=dist*100, .if= speed==4)
replace.if(dat, dist=dist*100)
```

I think a quick implementation of such partial replacements would be really useful in many situations and this functionality is a very convenient feature of data.table. On the other hand, I don't know how hard it is to generally implement such a function in dplyr given that there are so many possible data sources. I also don't know a good verb as function name, perhaps 'modify'?

title: do and tbl_sql
description:
If dplyr creates some columns on the fly it works just fine in some cases but not at all in others (in particular do).

E.g.

``` R
Test<-Device %>%
  filter(DATE(dtm) >= min.date & 
         DATE(dtm) <= max.date &
           box %in% ids &
           energy > 0) %>%
  group_by(box,DATE(dtm))
```

The result appears to work just fine:

```
head(Test)
summarise(Test, min=min(TIME(dtm)))
as.data.frame(Test,n=-1)
```

But even a simple do fails:

```

Error in mysqlExecStatement(conn, statement, ...) :
```


title: do() gives error if returned values are not data frames
description:
The docs say:

> You can use do to perform arbitrary computation, returning either a data frame or arbitrary objects which will be stored in a list.

But it doesn't work this way. For example:

```
mtcars %>% group_by(cyl) %>% do(nrow(.))
# Error: Results are not data frames at positions: 1, 2, 3
```

The result I would expect is something like this (which presently works):

```
x <- mtcars %>% group_by(cyl) %>% do(data.frame(nrow = nrow(.)))
as.list(x$nrow)
# [[1]]
# [1] 11
#
# [[2]]
# [1] 7
#
# [[3]]
# [1] 14
```

Note that I'm just using `nrow` to illustrate; I know you can use `group_size` to get this result. The thing I'm actually doing returns a vector for each group, so there's not a simple drop-in replacement for it.

title: Using dplyr functions on grouped data frame with variable of class difftime generates error
description:
Using `dplyr` data manipulation functions on a grouped data frame which contains a variable of class `difftime` generates the error:

```
Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : 
  column 'the-name-of-the-difftime column' has unsupported type
```

I illustrate this using some toy data with a grouping variable (grp), a column with some values (val), two date columns (date1, date2), and a variable of class `difftime` (the difference between date1 and date2):  

```
df <- data.frame(
  grp =   c(1, 1,  2, 2),
  val =   c(1, 3,  4, 6),
  date1 = c(rep(Sys.Date() - 10, 2), rep(Sys.Date() - 20, 2)),
  date2 = Sys.Date() + 1:2)

df$diffdate <- difftime(df$date2, df$date1, unit = "days")
df
```

I tried to add the mean of vals within each group to the original data set. The **desired output** can be created using `ddply` :

```
library(plyr)
df_dd <- ddply(.data = df, .variables = .(grp), mutate,
               mean_val = mean(val))

df_dd
#   grp val      date1      date2 diffdate mean_val
#1   1   1 2014-04-04 2014-04-15  11 days        2
#2   1   3 2014-04-04 2014-04-16  12 days        2
#3   2   4 2014-03-25 2014-04-15  21 days        5
#4   2   6 2014-03-25 2014-04-16  22 days        5

str(df_dd)
# ...
# $ diffdate:Class 'difftime'
```

When I try to create the same output with `dplyr`, an error is generated

```
detach("package:plyr", unload = TRUE)
library(dplyr)

df %.%
  group_by(grp) %.%
  mutate(
    mean_val = mean(val)
  )
# Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : 
#   column 'diffdate' has unsupported type
```

Just to check, the same error is generated when the `difftime` variable is itself subject to the calculation, e.g.

```
df %.%
  group_by(grp) %.%
  mutate(
    mean_diff = mean(diffdate)
    )
```

...or when using (toy examples of) `summarise`, `filter`, `select` or `arrange`:

```
df %.%
  group_by(grp) %.%
  summarise(
    mean_val = mean(val)
  )

df %.%
  group_by(grp) %.%
  filter(
    sum(val) > 5
  )

df %.%
  group_by(grp) %.%
  select(-val)

df %.%
  group_by(grp) %.%
  arrange(-val)
```

The `difftime` variable does not cause any problem when `mutate` is used on an _ungrouped_ data frame:

```
df2 <- mutate(df, diffdate = difftime(date2, date1, unit = "days"))
df2
str(df2)

mutate(df2, mean_val = mean(val), mean_diff = mean(diffdate))
```

...or on an ungrouped 'tbl_df':

```
tbl <- tbl_df(df)
mutate(tbl, mean_val = mean(val), mean_diff = mean(diffdate))
```

Neither does the `difftime` variable cause any problem when various `dplyr` data manipulation functions are applied on a _grouped_ `data.table` version of df:

```
library(data.table)
dt <- data.table(df)
dt2 <- dt %.%
  group_by(grp) %.%
  mutate(
    mean_val = mean(val)
  )
dt2
# Source: local data table [4 x 6]
# Groups: grp

#   grp val      date1      date2 diffdate mean_val
#1   1   1 2014-04-05 2014-04-16  11 days        2
#2   1   3 2014-04-05 2014-04-17  12 days        2
#3   2   4 2014-03-26 2014-04-16  21 days        5
#4   2   6 2014-03-26 2014-04-17  22 days        5

str(dt2)

dt %.%
  group_by(grp) %.%
  summarise(
    mean_val = mean(val)
  )

dt %.%
  group_by(grp) %.%
  filter(
    sum(val) > 5
  )

dt %.%
  group_by(grp) %.%
  select(-val)

dt %.%
  group_by(grp) %.%
  arrange(-val)
```

My current quick and dirty workaround is to convert the `difftime` variable to `numeric`:

```
df$diffdate <- as.numeric(difftime(df$date2, df$date1, unit = "days"))
df %.%
  group_by(grp) %.%
  mutate(
    mean_val = mean(val)
  )
```

However, there are quite a few methods for the `difftime` class (see Detail in `?difftime`). Thus, it would be nice if `dplyr` could handle grouped data frames containing a variable of class `difftime`.

Search on SO and google for 'dplyr difftime "Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos)" :    column has unsupported type' gave no hits.

Thanks a lot for your great work with a fantastic package.

Best regards,

Henrik 

```
R version 3.1.0 (2014-04-10)
Platform: x86_64-w64-mingw32/x64 (64-bit)
data.table_1.9.2, dplyr_0.1.3, plyr_1.8.1
```

title: do() duplicates grouping column
do() should remove grouped_df class
description:
For example:

```
ToothGrowth %>%
  group_by(supp) %>%
  do(print(class(.)))
# [1] "grouped_df" "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
# [1] "grouped_df" "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
#  Error: Results are not data frames at positions: 1, 2
```

Because it currently keeps the class, you can't cleanly do this:

```
foo.grouped_df <- function(data) {
  do(data, foo(.))
}

foo.data.frame <- function(data) {
  # computation here
}
```

title: group_by should replace existing grouping
description:
I would love to regroup my data using a chained dplyr command:

``` R
group_by(diamonds, color) %.% filter(mean(carat)>0.24) %.% group_by(cut) %.% filter(mean(depth)>60)
```

The result is:

```
Source: local data frame [53,940 x 10]
Groups: color, cut

   carat       cut color clarity depth table price    x    y    z
1   0.23     Ideal     E     SI2  61.5    55   326 3.95 3.98 2.43
2   0.21   Premium     E     SI1  59.8    61   326 3.89 3.84 2.31
...
```

The second group_by is not replacing the first grouping, but it iw just added to it. It took me a while to realize that it needs to be `group_by(cut, add=F).`

For sure this is a more a usability preference, but especially when it comes to grouped operations, it's easy to miss an incorrect grouping, so it would be imho more clear (especially for new users) to change the default of add to FALSE. Then above code could would behave as written.

In a chained operation users might think about adding add=F. However, when using unchained  (line by line) scripting, many will tend to forget that they work with a group table and will get unexpected results when applying another group_by to it.

This seems related to #121 which was tagged as fixed, but I can't see how the fix works.

description:
Hi -

I'm writing a src for ImpalaDB and have struck a problem with the example:

```
player_info <- select(tbl(lahman_impaladb(), "Master"), playerid, hofid, birthyear)
hof <- select(filter(tbl(lahman_impaladb(), "HallOfFame"), inducted == "Y"),hofid, votedby, category)
inner_join(player_info, hof)
```

The resultant SQL is:

```
select `hofid`, `playerid`, `birthyear`, `votedby`, `category` FROM (SELECT `playerid` AS `playerid`, `hofid` AS `hofid`, `birthyear` AS `birthyear` FROM `Master`) AS `nwsrxxxpxw` INNER JOIN (SELECT `hofid` AS `hofid`, `votedby` AS `votedby`, `category` AS `category` FROM `HallOfFame` WHERE `inducted` = 'Y') AS `slijllmyxg` USING (`hofid`) LIMIT 10;
Query: select `hofid`, `playerid`, `birthyear`, `votedby`, `category` FROM (SELECT `playerid` AS `playerid`, `hofid` AS `hofid`, `birthyear` AS `birthyear` FROM `Master`) AS `nwsrxxxpxw` INNER JOIN (SELECT `hofid` AS `hofid`, `votedby` AS `votedby`, `category` AS `category` FROM `HallOfFame` WHERE `inducted` = 'Y') AS `slijllmyxg` USING (`hofid`) LIMIT 10
ERROR: AnalysisException: Unqualified column reference 'hofid' is ambiguous
```

If the hofid is fully qualified as ``nwsrxxxpxw`.`hofid``, then the problem is resolved, so I was wondering if you had any suggestions for doing this in a sensible way from within build_sql() as only the `con` object is passed at the time ident values are rendered?

Thanks,
Piers Harding.

Rolling join
description:
Would it be possible to add the rolling join feature to dplyr?

**Rolling join**, known also as last observation carried forward (LOCF), is an inequality join of two tables.

The example below contains two data frames:
-   **Ds (sales log)**, with _date of transaction_, _item id_, _customer id_, and _quantity sold_
-   **Dp (price list)**, with _date of publicaton_, _item id_, and _price published_

``` .r
library(data.table)

Ds <- read.csv(text = "
date, cust, item, sold
2010-01-19, 101, 2, 11
2010-01-22, 102, 1, 7
2010-01-24, 102, 2, 9
2010-01-25, 101, 2, 9
2010-01-26, 101, 1, 10
")
Ds <- data.table(Ds)
Ds <- Ds[, date := as.Date(date, format = ("%Y-%m-%d"))]
setkey(Ds, item, date)

Dp <- read.csv(text = "
date, item, price
2010-01-20, 1, 18.3
2010-01-20, 2, 38.3
2010-01-23, 1, 18.9
2010-01-23, 2, 48.9
2010-01-26, 1, 19.1
2010-01-26, 2, 59.1
")
Dp <- data.table(Dp)
Dp <- Dp[, date := as.Date(date, format = ("%Y-%m-%d"))]
setkey(Dp, item, date)
```

What we need is match the most recent price to every record of sales log _Ds_. This is where data.table comes to rescue with a neat one-liner.

``` .r
(Dt <- Dp[Ds, roll = TRUE])
```

title: Enhanced pipeline operator that allows more flexible parameter passing
description:
When I code in F#, it is quite enjoyable to use the pipeline operator `|>` in F#. It is glad to see the pipeline operator `%.%` defined in `dplyr` and it is quite powerful. 

I just create another pipeline operator `%|%` with the following code:

``` r
`%|%` <- function(x,f) {
  call <- match.call()
  if(is.name(call$f)) {
    f(x)
  } else if(is.call(call$f)) {
    env <- new.env()
    env$`.` <- x
    eval(call$f,envir = env)
  } else {
    stop("Error: unsupported type of function call")
  }
}
```

It not only allows me to call functions like: 

``` r
rnorm(100,10,1) %|% plot
```

but also is convenient to pass parameter in a more flexible way:

``` r
rnorm(100,10,1) %|% log %|% diff %|% plot(., col="red", type="l")
```

Note that `.` represents the result evaluated from the previous segment in the chain.

It also allows this:

``` r
rnorm(100,10,1) %|% log %|% diff %|% plot(x=., main=sprintf("Length: %d", length(.)), col="red", type="l")
```

Would this idea make the existing pipeline operator `%.%` more flexible and powerful?
The current one seems to be a special case of `%|%` in the way that
`dataframe %.% select(col1,col2)` equals `dataframe %|% select(.,col1,col2)`.

To make it back-compatible, if the call of `f` does not include `.` then the first argument should be replaced be the result (same as `%.%`); otherwise, when `.` appears, it should represent the previous result.

title: summarise or mutate with functions returning multiple values/columns
description:
With plyr, you can do something like

```
# VERY silly example...
ddply(data, .(col1, col2), function(df) {
  df$x <- 1:5
  df$y <- 6:10
  df
})
```

And get something with columns `col1, col2, x, y`, where there were 5 rows for each unique combination of `col1, col2`. I haven't figured out how to do this (in general) with dplyr. It seems like either you use summarise, and can only return one value for each new col; or you use mutate, and must add columns with the same dimension as the chunks.

Is there a way to do this in the general case? If not, could something be modified/added to allow this?

Thanks

Chris

title: Default for top_n
description:
Currently the default behavior of `top_n` is to use the last variable when none is specified. Just wondering if it would perhaps make more sense to use the indices. 

For example: 

```
iris %.% group_by(Species) %.% top_n(2)
```

will use the last variable `Species`. Of course, within each group, all values for Species are equal, so this will give us the entire data. 

So I'm wondering if `iris %.% group_by(Species) %.% top_n(2)` should express "the two first rows in each group"

title: group_by(.) %.% arrange()
description:
Wondering if it could be interesting to let this syntax: 

```
mtcars %.% group_by(cyl, disp) %.% arrange()
```

do this implicitly: 

```
mtcars %.% group_by(cyl, disp) %.% arrange(cyl, disp)
```

So an empty `arrange()` of a grouped data set would arrange it according to its grouping variables. 

This would be very cheap because the information is already in there, we would only have to sort the `labels` and reorganize the variables, we would not need to sort again. Furthermore we could keep the information that in the resulting data, groups are adjacent.

title: More comprehensive message for misusing '&&' and '||'
description:
Within expression of filter(), misuse of '&&' and '||' could not be warned.

For example, if this code

> data.frame(A = 1:3, B = c(1,2,2)) %.% filter(A == 2 & B == 2)

is wrongly written as:

> data.frame(A = 1:3, B = c(1,2,2)) %.% filter(A == 2 && B == 2)

It answers a 0-length data.frame without any warning.

I guess the difference could be presented like this:

> a <- data.frame(A = 1:3, B = c(1,2,2))
> with(a, A == 2 & B == 2)
> [1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE
> with(a, A == 2 && B == 2)
> [1] FALSE

Because the logical vectors behavior the same as above:

> data.frame(A = 1:3, B = c(1,2,2)) %.% filter(c(FALSE, TRUE, FALSE))
>   A B
> 1 2 2
> data.frame(A = 1:3, B = c(1,2,2)) %.% filter(FALSE)
> [1] A B

However, vectors with more than one elements behavior differently:

> data.frame(A = 1:3, B = c(1,2,2)) %.% filter(c(FALSE, TRUE))
> Error: incorrect length (2), expecting: 3
> data.frame(A = 1:4, B = c(1,2,2,3)) %.% filter(c(FALSE, TRUE))  # no expanding here, either
> Error: incorrect length (2), expecting: 4

I suggest dplyr provide warnings for one element vector, to make the misuse of '&&' and '||' easy to discover.

title: [chaining] - select must come before group_by
description:
In a chained dplyr (version 0.1.2) statement, the select() must come before group_by() when using multiple group by variables. Otherwise, only the last of multiple group_by() variables are used.

Reproducible example is available here:
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/22298223/dplyr-aggregation-incorrect

I can confirm that putting select() before group_by() solves the issue.

title: Use case for mutate(clean = TRUE)
description:
Per Hadley's suggestion, this was moved from the manipulatr google group. [link](https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/manipulatr/jGikqic2JOs)

Let's say I get a csv file with a bunch of variables named "XPF102", "FGR24D", and so on. There may be twenty of these.

From my data-dictionary, I see that "XPF102" is pressure in psi, "FGR24D" is a part-per-million of contaminant, and so on.

I have used plyr::summarise() to do two things at once (this could be what you are trying to get _away_ from in dplyr):

```
data_new <- plyr::summarise(
  data_old,
  pressure = XPF102 * 6894.75729,  # convert to Pa from psi (I know a function is more appropriate here)
  concentration_contaminant = FGR24D / 1.e6, # convert to proportion from parts-per-million
  ...
)
```

Using dplyr, I might have to do this:

```
data_new <- 
  data_old %.%
  mutate(
    pressure = XPF102 * 6894.75729,
    concentration_contaminant = FGR24D / 1.e6, 
    ...
  ) %.%
  select(
    pressure,
    concentration_contaminant,
    ...
  )
```

Doing this, I seem to have the opportunity to mistype a variable name by violating DRY.

Hadley suggested:

> Maybe an option to mutate like `clean = TRUE`?

I like the idea. My only (relatively uneducated) concern is if the user wants to name a variable `clean`, but I'm sure there is a clever way to avoid that.

Thanks,

Ian

title: Filtering on Dates converts the class of the date column
description:
Filtering on a date column converts the class of the date column to integer when the date column satisfies is.integer.  Here is a test suite of the expected versus actual behavior:

```
library(dplyr)

test_that("date class remains on filter",{
  x1 <- x2 <- data.frame(
    date = seq.Date(as.Date('2013-01-01'), by = "1 days", length.out = 2),
    var = c(5, 8)
  )

  is.integer(x1$date)
  x1.filter <- x1 %.% filter(as.Date(date) > as.Date('2013-01-01'))

  x2$date <- x2$date + 1
  is.integer(x2$date)
  x2.filter <- x2 %.% filter(as.Date(date) > as.Date('2013-01-01'))

  expect_that(class(x1.filter$date), equals("Date"))
  expect_that(class(x2.filter$date), equals("Date"))
})
```

title: Think about binned grouping
description:
``` R

bin <- function(df, var, binwidth, origin = NULL) {
  n <- nrow(df)

  var <- as.character(substitute(var))
  x <- df[[var]]

  if (is.null(origin)) {
    origin <- min(x)
  }

  bin <- (x - origin) %/% binwidth
  indices <- unname(split(seq_len(n) - 1, bin))

  attr(df, "indices") <- indices
  attr(df, "drop") <- FALSE
  attr(df, "group_sizes") <- sapply(indices, length)
  attr(df, "biggest_group_size") <- max(attr(df, "group_sizes"))
  attr(df, "labels") <- data.frame(bin = seq_along(indices))
  attr(df, "vars") <- list(quote(bin))
  class(df) <- c("grouped_df", "tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")

  df
}

binned <- bin(mtcars, disp, 30)
binned %.% summarise(n(), mean(disp))
```

title: src_mysql won't read password from my.cnf files
description:
Rather than saving passwords in code, the `MySQL` function of `RMySQL` recommends you send passwords and usernames through a .my.cnf file: 

> The preferred method to pass authentication parameters to the server (e.g., user, password, host) is through the MySQL personal configuration file ‘\$HOME/.my.cnf’ (or ‘c:/my.cnf’ under Windows).

In dplyr, the code for src_mysql() gives a default user of "root" and password of ""; those override any settings in the default.file for username or password, so there's no long any way to connect without storing the database password in the code.

The easiest solution is to simply not to pass any default parameters to dbConnect, and just include dbname and username through `...`; I posted a pull request along those lines [here](https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/pull/267)

title: group_by %.% mutate does not preserve tzone for POSIXct
description:
This was fixed for summarise (#252), but still occurs with `mutate` (only on a grouped df).  This is with the current development version of dplyr:

```
require(lubridate)
require(dplyr)

test.df <- structure(
  list(ID = c(rep(1,20),rep(2,20)),
       Date = structure(c(-247320000, -246196800, -245073600, -243864000,
                            -242654400, -241444800, -126273600, -123595200,
                            -121176000, -118497600, 1359385200, 1359388800,
                            1359392400, 1359396000, 1359399600, 1359403200,
                            1359406800, 1359410400, 1359414000, 1359417600,
                            55598400, 56116800, 58881600, 62078400, 64756800,
                            67348800, 69854400, 72964800, 76161600, 79012800,
                            1358589600, 1358676000, 1358762400, 1358848800,
                            1358935200, 1359021600, 1359108000, 1359194400,
                            1359280800, 1359367200), tzone = "GMT",
                          class = c("POSIXct", "POSIXt")),
       Val=rnorm(40)),
  .Names = c("ID", "Date", "Val"), row.names = c(NA, 40L),
  class = "data.frame")

out.df <- group_by(test.df, ID, fl_date=floor_date(Date, unit="month")) %.%
  mutate(length_x=n(), summary_date = 
           if (n() < 5) round_date(Date, "month") else floor_date(Date, "day"))

attr(out.df$summary_date, "tzone") # This is null
```

This works:

```
out2.df <-test.df %.% mutate(summary_date = round_date(Date, "month"))
attr(out2.df$summary_date, "tzone") # "GMT"
```

I left this as a comment in #252 after it was closed, so I thought it may have been lost - my apologies if it's already been captured.

title: dplyr::filter should not be preferred over stats::filter for numerical vectors
description:
This example is copied from R help (filter {stats}):

> x <- 1:100
> filter(x, rep(1, 3))

It's just calculating an moving average.

However after loading dplyr package (latest version from todays github), dplyr::filter seems to also apply to numerical vectors as well:

> library(dplyr)
> filter(x, rep(1, 3))
> 
> > Error in UseMethod("filter") :
> > no applicable method for 'filter' applied to an object of class "c('integer', 'numeric')"

Imho stats::filter should be still applied by default for numerical vectors.

title: summarise problems when using just-created summary columns
description:

I get slightly different values each time I run summarise, as shown below. It does work properly when I avoid reusing the just-created columns. So far I've only seen this when I have more than one summary column reusing a previously created summary column, which is why in all the examples below I've got columns `diff1` and `diff2`.

title: Mutate ignores certain arguments with data.tables
description:
Hi folks-

First, let me say thank you for creating a fantastic package! For me, the combination of dplyr and data.table is really excellent.

I think I may have found a small bug in how mutate() interacts with data.table:

```
library(dplyr)
library(data.table)

dt <- data.table(a=c('one', 'two', 'three'))
# This works:
str(mutate(dt, a=as.factor(toupper(a))))
# This appears to ignore the second assignment in the mutate function:
str(mutate(dt, a=ifelse(a == 'one', 'four', a), a=as.factor(toupper(a))))

# Tried the same with data.frames, and it worked:
df <- data.frame(a=c('one', 'two', 'three'))
str(mutate(df, a=as.factor(toupper(a))))
str(mutate(df, a=ifelse(a == 'one', 'four', a), a=as.factor(toupper(a))))
```

Please let me know what you think.

Thanks!

title: Allow summarise to work with list columns.
description:
The next version of `do()` will create columns that are lists of more complicated objects. This considerably expands the set of possible things you might want to do in `summarise()`. Fortunately most of these actions are going to be relatively expensive, and done on a relatively small set of objects (probably thousands, not million), but currently hybrid evaluation fails for a common case.

``` R
# Make data structure like do() will return in future
by_cyl <- split(mtcars, mtcars$cyl)
models <- lapply(by_cyl, function(df) lm(mpg ~ disp, data = df))
labelled <- data.frame(cyl = c(4, 6, 8), mod = I(models))

labelled %.% 
  group_by(cyl) %.%
  summarise(rsq = summary(mod)$r.squared)
# Error: binding not found: 'r.squared' 

lapply(models, function(x) summary(x)$r.squared)
```

Hopefully this is just a minor problem with the current implementation of hybrid `$`.

title: Grouping sets, Rollup and Cube for dplyr
description:
Hi,

I think it could be great to have the following verbs/operators in `dplyr`
- rollup
- cube
- grouping sets

In this page there's some information with example for each operator using postgres : http://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Grouping_Sets

For grouping sets I tried to work on the same example as in the above link :

``` s
 dput(cars)
structure(list(name = c("skoda", "skoda", "bmw", "bmw", "opel", 
"opel"), place = c("czech rep.", "germany", "czech rep.", "germany", 
"czech rep.", "germany"), count = c(10000L, 5000L, 100L, 1000L, 
7000L, 7000L)), .Names = c("name", "place", "count"), row.names = c(NA, 
6L), class = "data.frame")
```

``` s
library(dplyr)
## <postgres=# select name, place, sum(count) from cars group by grouping sets(name, place, ());
##  name  |   place    |  sum
## -------+------------+-------
##  bmw   |            |  1100
##  skoda |            | 15000
##  opel  |            | 14000
##        | germany    | 13000
##        | czech rep. | 17100
##        |            | 30100
## (6 rows)
cars %.%
    group_by(name) %.%
    summarise(sum = sum(count)) %.%
    rbind_list(
        cars %.%
        group_by(place) %.%
        summarise(sum = sum(count))) %.%
    rbind_list(
        cars %.%
        group_by() %.%
        summarise(sum = sum(count))
        )
##    name   sum      place
## 1  opel 14000       <NA>
## 2   bmw  1100       <NA>
## 3 skoda 15000       <NA>
## 4  <NA> 13000    germany
## 5  <NA> 17100 czech rep.
## 6  <NA> 30100       <NA>
```

The type of aggregation can be more complex :

``` s
## select name, place, sum(count) from cars group by grouping sets((name, place),name, place,());
##  name  |   place    |  sum
## -------+------------+-------
##  skoda | czech rep. | 10000
##  opel  | germany    |  7000
##  bmw   | germany    |  1000
##  bmw   | czech rep. |   100
##  opel  | czech rep. |  7000
##  skoda | germany    |  5000
##  bmw   |            |  1100
##  skoda |            | 15000
##  opel  |            | 14000
##        | germany    | 13000
##        | czech rep. | 17100
##        |            | 30100
## (12 rows)

rbind_list(
### select name, place, sum(count) from cars group by name, place
    cars %.%
    regroup(list(quote(name), quote(place))) %.%
    summarise(sum = sum(count)),

### select name, null, sum(count) from cars group by name, null
    cars %.%
    group_by(name) %.%
    summarise(sum = sum(count)),

### select null, place, sum(count) from cars group by null, place
    cars %.%
    group_by(place) %.%
    summarise(sum = sum(count)),

### select null, null, sum(count) from cars
    cars %.%
    group_by() %.%
    summarise(sum = sum(count))
)
##     name      place   sum
## 1   opel    germany  7000
## 2   opel czech rep.  7000
## 3    bmw    germany  1000
## 4    bmw czech rep.   100
## 5  skoda    germany  5000
## 6  skoda czech rep. 10000
## 7   opel       <NA> 14000
## 8    bmw       <NA>  1100
## 9  skoda       <NA> 15000
## 10  <NA>    germany 13000
## 11  <NA> czech rep. 17100
## 12  <NA>       <NA> 30100
```

I propose a the following syntax

``` s
cars %.%
    group_by() %.%
    grouping_sets(.(name, place), .()) %.%
    summarise(sum = sum(count))
```

or 

``` s
cars %.%
    group_by() %.%
    grouping_sets(list(name, place), list())
    summarise(sum = sum(count))
```

I think that it will be perfect on the `dplyr` ecosystem and we can have similar operators for `rollup` and `cube` as already implemented in [Hive](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/Hive/Enhanced+Aggregation,+Cube,+Grouping+and+Rollup) and some others ETL engines.

Here's an example of related question in SO : http://stackoverflow.com/questions/21366138/multi-level-aggregations-like-grouping-sets-via-ddply-or-other-r-function

Thanks

title: rbind_all problems with empty data.frames
description:
I'm having some problems with rbind_all() when reading data.frames from CSV files.

If a CSV file is empty (except for the header row) the data.frame it creates cause problems with dplyr/rbind_all()  and rbind_list().

The two errors I get are:
(1) Error: upper value must be greater than lower value
(2) Error: incompatible type (data index: 2, column: 'name', was collecting: character (dplyr::Collecter_Impl<16>), incompatible with data of type: LGLSXP

The code to replicate this is pasted here and in the gist: https://gist.github.com/coolbutuseless/8779729

``` R
library(dplyr) # dplyr 0.1.1.  R3.0.2

# Hi Hadley,
# I'm having some problems with rbind_all() when reading a lot of 
# data.frames from CSV files.
# If a CSV file is empty (except for the header row) the 
# data.frame it creates cause problems with dplyr/rbind_all() 
# and rbind_list()
# 
# Mike

#------------------------------------------------------------
# Create the data.frames and save to CSV files.
# The second CSV file only contains a header row and no data
#------------------------------------------------------------
csv_base <- data.frame(name=c('mike'), age=c(1))
write.csv(csv_base     , "csv1.csv", row.names=FALSE, quote=FALSE)
write.csv(csv_base[-1,], "csv2.csv", row.names=FALSE, quote=FALSE)


#------------------------------------------------------------
# Case 1: Don't specify colClasses in read.csv
# In this case the class of the empty columns in csv2 are unknown
# and are probably defaulting to numerics.
# So when rbind_list() tries to merge the different types it chokes, 
# even though there is no actual data to merge
#------------------------------------------------------------
csv1 <- read.csv("csv1.csv", as.is=TRUE)
csv2 <- read.csv("csv2.csv", as.is=TRUE)


rbind_list(csv1, csv2)
# Error: incompatible type (data index: 2, column: 'name', was collecting: character (dplyr::Collecter_Impl<16>), incompatible with data of type: LGLSXP

rbind_list(csv2, csv1)
# Error: upper value must be greater than lower value


#------------------------------------------------------------
# Case 2: If we do specify the classes, we still get the weird error
# "upper value must be greater than lower value"
#------------------------------------------------------------
csv1 <- read.csv("csv1.csv", as.is=TRUE, colClasses=c('character', 'numeric'))
csv2 <- read.csv("csv2.csv", as.is=TRUE, colClasses=c('character', 'numeric'))


rbind_list(csv1, csv2)
# Error: upper value must be greater than lower value

rbind_list(csv2, csv1)
# Error: upper value must be greater than lower value

#------------------------------------------------------------
# do.call() works OK
#------------------------------------------------------------
do.call(rbind, list(csv1, csv2))
```

title: Intro Vignette include chaining
description:
When I initially read the Intro vignette to dplyr I was impressed by speed but it didn't convince me to stop using the tried and true base functions I love (`split` `lapply`, `[[]]`, `transform`, `do.call`, `order` etc.).  However when I realized you can do chaining like ggplot2 as in:

```
library(dplyr); library(Lahman)

Batting %.%
  group_by(playerID) %.%
  summarise(total = sum(R)) %.%
  arrange(desc(total)) %.%
  head(5)
```

I saw a huge advantage in semantics.  You're not assigning and reassigning or wrapping everything in one convoluted call.

I would consider adding this type of example to the intro vignette as this is likely the first one people pick up.  This may be my own bias (or it was in the Intro and in my haste I missed it) and if so close this and file it appropriately.  

PS I love the combination of speed, easy of use ( a limited number of functions that have and few arguments), semantics (meaningfully named functions with chaining).

title: Write more about dplyr memory usage
description:
Starting from following email. Need to update to use changes. Should be a vignette.

---

We'll start by making a local copy of the internal dplyr function `dfloc()`. This function is very useful for helping us understanding how the memory in a data frame works.

``` r
library(dplyr)
dfloc <- dplyr:::dfloc
```

(dfloc will eventually be exported from dplyr once we've thought it through a bit more.)

`dfloc()` tells us the address of each vector in the data frame. 

``` r
dfloc(iris)
```

If these addresses change between operations then we know R has made a copy. It's important to think about data frames as collections as columns rather than monolithic objects because for many operations we can reuse existing columns and not use any extra memory

In base R, a surprising number of operations make copies of the individual vectors. For example, when you extract two columns from a data frame, their contents are actually copied. There's no reason to do this!

``` r
# Copies the first two columns
dfloc(iris[1:2])

dfloc(iris)
# Copies all the columns!
iris$blah <- 1
dfloc(iris)
```

(This is something that may improve in R 3.1.0 due to some work by Michael Lawrence)

The goal of dplyr is to avoid making copies when not needed:

``` r
dfloc(iris)
dfloc(group_by(iris, Species))
dfloc(mutate(iris, area = Sepal.Length * Sepal.Width))
dfloc(select(iris, 1:3))
```

Currently, `group_by()` doesn't make a copy, but `mutate()` and `select()` do, so we'll fix that for the next version. Once we've done that, any sequence of `mutate()`, `select()` and `group_by()` will only need to occupy a little extra memory (i.e. for the indices and new variables). Saving interim results will not have any effect on memory usage.

Obviously there's no way around `summarise()` making a copy, but it's usually not a big deal since you're reducing the size of the data so much. `arrange()` also has to make a copy, but generally you can avoid using it since it won't affect any statistical operation. If ordering is important (e.g. for computing a cumulative mean), dplyr provides ways to avoid copying the whole data frame and instead only reorder just the columns you need (see the windowing vignette for more details).

Altogether, this means that dplyr lets you work with data frames with very little extra overhead. Eventually, dplyr will never create a complete copy of the data frame unless you're sorting it, and will provide tools so that you never need to sort it. This should mean that you can keep using data frames, and don't need to switch to a more complex object with reference semantics (like a data table).

title: join by error in postgres when subsetting 'by' vector
description:
I'm getting the following error when straying from a natural join in postgres.  I haven't seen it documented yet.  

> Error in postgresqlExecStatement(conn, statement, ...) : 
>   RS-DBI driver: (could not Retrieve the result : ERROR:  column "stint" does not exist
> LINE 16: ..."playerID" AS "playerID", "yearID" AS "yearID.y", "stint" AS...

It can be avoided by not selecting the yearID variable in one of the tables to be joined.  A renaming may also avoid the issue.  I just tested with lahman_dt()
and I got the yearID.x/yearID.y behavior I expected.

```
library(dplyr)
my_db <- src_postgres(dbname='lahman')
Master <- tbl(my_db,'Master')
HallOfFame <- chain(tbl(my_db,'HallOfFame'),
                    filter(inducted=='Y' & yearID==2012))
```

title: More accurate handling of ...
description:
This was initially reported here: https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/issues/159

We need to respect (possibly nested) passing `...` to dplyr functions, e.g. this has to work: 

```
f <- function(...) {
  x_1 <- 1
  g(..., x_1 = x_1)
}
g <- function(...) {
  x_2 <- 2
  mutate(mtcars, ..., x_2 = x_2)
}

x_0 = 0
f(x_0 = 0)
```

Each contribution to `mutate`'s `...` is associated with an environment; This environment is where to look for data and where to evaluate calls. 

The current implementation uses the parent frame of the environment of `mutate` which is not generally correct.

title: .data.frame versions not using the correct environment
description:
Consider: 

```
f <- function(){
  df <- data.frame(a=1:4)
  today <- Sys.Date()
  now <- Sys.time()
  summarise(df, int = 1L, num = 1.0, 
    str = "foo", bool = TRUE, date = today, time = now)
}
f()
```

Because we have: 

```
summarise.data.frame <- function(.data, ...) {
  as.data.frame(summarise(tbl_df(.data), ...))  
}
```

and summarise uses this : 

```
.data_dots <- function(fun, DOTS = dots){
  f <- function(.data, ...){}
  body(f) <- substitute({
    parent_frame <- parent.frame()
    env <- as.environment(.data)
    parent.env(env) <- parent_frame
    FUN(.data, DOTS(...) , env )   
  }, list( FUN = substitute(fun), DOTS = substitute(DOTS)))
  attr(f, "srcref") <- NULL
  f
}
summarise.tbl_df <- .data_dots(summarise_impl, named_dots)
```

The `parent_frame` is not right, so summarise above does not find `today`. It works fine however if I do : 

```
summarise(tbl_df(df), int = 1L, num = 1.0, 
    str = "foo", bool = TRUE, date = today, time = now)
```

I guess the issue is the same for all functions using `.data_dots`. 

I'm not sure how to handle this. This seems to work:

```
summarise.data.frame <- .data_dots(summarise_impl, named_dots) 
```

But then this means that we can't pass `...` to `summarise`. So not good.

title: Optional parameter to control length of summarise
description:
It would be useful to have a parameter that states the number of values the function should return. It's sometimes useful to have a summary function that returns multiple values, like if you're computing a fixed set of quantiles. The values should run down the column, and the grouping variables should be repeated.

For example:

``` R
summarise(group_by(mtcars, cyl), mpg = quantile(mpg), .n = 5)
```

We don't need to label the values, since the user could always do that themselves:

``` R
qs <- c(0, 0.5, 1)
summarise(group_by(mtcars, cyl), mpg = quantile(mpg, qs), q = qs, .n = 3)
```

When `n > 1`, `summarise()` shouldn't drop the last group from the grouping, since you might want to summarise the values you just computed.

title: More informative output from equal_data_frame
description:
To be as useful as possible, `equal_data_frame` needs to return more detail than it is currently. Currently, it's fast (terminating as soon as the first difference is found), but for we need, informative messages are more important. That said, you don't want to print out pages of differences if you accidentally pass in two completely different data frames, so I think for each comparison we should display at most 10 differences, adding an ellipsis if that's only a subset of the total.
- Different number of columns: remove this check and fall through to 
  non-matching names
- Non-matching columns (order unimportant):
  
  Columns in x, but not in y: a, b, c
  Columns in y, but not in x: d, e, f
- Non-matching column names (order important)
  
  Check if columns match ignoring order. 
  - If so: "Same column names, but different order"
  - If not: fall back to order unimportant display
- Different column types.
  
  Incompatible column types: x (numeric/character), y (different levels) ...
  
  Looking at the code more, we may actually need to do some dispatch here.
  i.e. perhaps we need a compatable generic which could dispatch on the
  class.  This would make it possible to do better tests for factors (i.e.
  the levels match) and times (i.e. the timezones match).  If convert was 
  TRUE, they could be more flexible (but not sure how we'd communicate the
  promoted type back to the equality comparison code.)
- Different numbers of rows: remove this check and fall through to 
  non-matching row values
- Non-matching rows (order unimportant)
  
  Rows in x, but not in y: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, ...
  Rows in y, but not in x: 18, 20, 25
- Non-matching rows (order important)
  
  Check if rows match ignoring order. 
  - If so: "Same row values, but different order"
  - If not: fall back to order unimportant display

title: Efficient implementation of common ranking functions
description:
From [postgres](http://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.3/static/functions-window.html) and [bigquery](https://developers.google.com/bigquery/query-reference#windowfunctions)
- row_number: just counts from 1 to n
- rank: like rank(ties = "min") in R 
- dense_rank: no R equivalent, like rank with all gaps removed
- percent_rank: (rank - 1) / n
- cume_dist: number of rows preceding or tied with the current row / total rows
- ntile: cume_dist multiplied by n and rounded

Not sure about the exact differences of the various percentile type rank - probably need to read carefully and implement in single function (they may correspond to some of the different options in `quantile`)


At the moment, we don't recognize the call, because we look for a full match of `mean( {symbol} )`. 

The idea of hybrid evaluation is to iteratively peel off things we can rewrite internally, and eventually if we don't know how to handle the remaining expression, we call the R evaluator, but on a simpler expression. 

So for example with this expression: 

```
mean(Y) + sum(X) 
```

The first iteration of simplification would produce: 

```
mean_y + sum(X)
```

Replacing the sub expression `mean(Y)` by its value. Then also recognize sum, the expression would become: 

```
mean_y + sum_x
```

where sum_x is just a scalar value. 

Then we can imagine that we know how to handle internally adding two scalar values, so in that case we would not need the R interpreter at all.

title: Develop flexible SQL backend
description:
Packages reviewed: RPostgreSQL, RMySQL, MonetDB.R, RODBC, RJDBC

Differences:
- RPostgreSQL: has `dbApply` which could be used to implement `do`, multiple open connections, prepared queries use [special syntax](http://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.3/static/sql-prepare.html), windowing, explain output is json, subqueries need to be named, ANALYZE called automatically (but not on temporary tables)
- MonetDB.R: looks like prepared statements might be supported through dbSendQuery, no semi_joins?
- RMySQL: also has `dbApply`, no prepared queries
- RODBC: non-DBI, manual transactions

Other things that I may need to make generic:
- variable name escaping
- translation of R variable types to db types (for creation)

Steps to make dplyr adapt to different sql variants:
- Make query a base class and add subclasses for other databases
- Turn tbl_sqlite object into a tbl_sql object - method would dispatch on src/con

Changes needed:
- Query needs to become base class
- Existing tbl_sqlite methods should become tbl_sql methods
- When implementing first non-sqlite sql adaptor, gradually change

Postgresql and MonetDB clearly the most important and should be tackled first. MonetDB might be simpler to start with since it implements a more limited subset of sql.


```
e = summarize(d,
  cut2 = as.character(cut),
  cut3 = ifelse(cut2 == 'Fair', '*Fairest*', cut2))
count(e, ~cut2+cut3)


#########################
# MUTATE with REVALUE
# this works
e = mutate(d,
 cut2 = revalue(cut, c(Fair = '*Fairest*')) )
e = mutate(e,
 cut2 = revalue(cut2, c('*Fairest*' = '*Fairest of All*')) )
count(e, ~cut+cut2)

# this fails
e = mutate(d,
 cut2 = revalue(cut, c(Good = '*Fairest*')),
 cut2 = revalue(cut2, c('*Fairest*' = '*Fairest of All*')) )
count(e, ~cut+cut2)

# but this works!
e = mutate(d,
 cut2 = revalue(cut, c(Good = '*Fairest*')),
 cut3 = revalue(cut2, c('*Fairest*' = '*Fairest of All*')) )
count(e, ~cut+cut2+cut3)
```

title: Feature request: make unmatched = "error" the default for mutating joins
description:
Or an even better solution suggested below, but see my reasoning first. Feature request in title is because I suspect it would be easier to implement.

I think that the current default of unmatched = "drop" is leading to people unwittingly dropping data that they intended to keep, especially in the context of the current behaviour around column names, whereby joins without a specified join key are joined by all matching columns, and joins _with_ a specified join key create .x and .y suffixed columns for any non-join columns with the same name. 

Given this, prior to reading the detailed documentation of it, I had _thought_ that the default behaviour of mutating joins when not provided a join key was to treat all matching columns as join keys, and suffix all non-matching columns with the same name. I suggest that this should, in fact, be the default, since I can't be the only one with this misconception. **At the very least, it would be helpful to add a warning when data are dropped during a join**, since it is alarmingly easy to accidentally (and silently!) lose data when merging large dataframes with lots of shared columns. I think it would also be ideal to flag when data are dropped even when that is a specified behaviour. 

However, in my opinion  it would be better to make 'error' the default for unmatched (ideally naming the column as well as the row), and better still to have three options for unmatched data: 'drop', 'error', and 'suffix', where 'suffix' treats any same-named column as a non-joining column if there are any unmatched rows between x and y, and disambiguates them accordingly. Currently, as far as I understand there is no way to do this kind of merging easily and cleanly; instead it is necessary to learn in advance which columns do or do not match, and then create a join key based on that -- which can be a laborious process for large dfs. Using a full_join() will duplicate rows rather than columns, which is useful for not losing data, but inappropriate for many types of analysis. 

So, currently:
```
library(tidyverse)
x <- tibble(a = 1, b = 2)
y <- tibble(a = 1, b = 3)

# join with key
left_join(x, y, by = "a")
# A tibble: 1 × 3
#      a   b.x   b.y
#  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#1     1     2     3

# join with no key
left_join(x, y)
# A tibble: 1 × 2
#      a     b
#  <dbl> <dbl>
#1     1     2

# join with no key, unmatched option specified
left_join(x, y, unmatched = "error")
# Error in `left_join()`:
# ! Each row of `y` must be matched by `x`.
# ℹ Row 1 of `y` was not matched.

```

Suggested change (BEST):
```
# join with no key, default 
left_join(x, y)
# A tibble: 1 × 3
#      a   b.x   b.y
#  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#1     1     2     3


# join with no key, unmatched = "drop"
left_join(x, y, unmatched = "drop")
# A tibble: 1 × 2
#      a     b
#  <dbl> <dbl>
#1     1     2  
# 1 rows dropped from `y` that did not match `x`.

# join with no key, unmatched = "error"
left_join(x, y, unmatched = "error")
# Error in `left_join()`:
# ! Each row of `y` must be matched by `x`.
# ℹ Row 1 of `y` was not matched at Column `b`.

# join with no key, unmatched = "suffix" (suggested default) 
left_join(x, y, unmatched = "suffix")
# A tibble: 1 × 3
#      a   b.x   b.y
#  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#1     1     2     3
```

Alternative suggestion (second best, in my opinion):
```
# join with no key, default 
left_join(x, y)
# Error in `left_join()`:
# ! Each row of `y` must be matched by `x`.
# ℹ Row 1 of `y` was not matched at Column `b`.

# join with no key, unmatched = "drop"
left_join(x, y, unmatched = "drop")
# A tibble: 1 × 2
#      a     b
#  <dbl> <dbl>
#1     1     2
# 1 rows dropped from `y` that did not match `x`.
```

Absolute minimum request:
```
# join with no key, default 
left_join(x, y)
# A tibble: 1 × 2
#      a     b
#  <dbl> <dbl>
#1     1     2
# Warning: 
# ℹ Row 1 of `y` was not matched at Column `b`.
# 1 rows dropped from `y` that did not match `x`.
```
